tropes.html:
After Simba is visited by his father's spirit, a large gust of wind blows over the plain, signaling Simba's newfound resolve to return home and take his rightful place as king.
Rafiki: What was that?! (laughs) The weather, hah! Very peculiar, don't you think?
Simba: Yeah... Looks like the winds are changing.
Rafiki: Ah, change is good.
Simba: Yeah, but it's not easy.

tropes.name: Witch Doctor
tropes.html: Rafiki the mandrill acknowledges Simba (and later Simba's daughter) as the rightful heir, acts as Simba's wise mentor, and otherwise fills this role for the Pride Lands. However, the only actual magic he's seen to perform is a sort of scrying, when he discovers that Simba is still alive.

tropes.name: Woken Up at an Ungodly Hour
tropes.html:
The film has Mufasa being mildly exasperated with his energetic son Simba waking him up early in the morning.
Sarabi: Your son is awake.
Mufasa: Before sunrise, he's your son.

tropes.name: A World Half Full
tropes.html: An excellent example given how dark some of the film can be. Simba loses his father and is convinced by his uncle that it was his fault. He goes into exile for a long time but eventually overcomes his guilt after his father's ghost chides him and goes back to tell his uncle to step down and take his place. He ends up triumphing, of course.

tropes.name: Would Hit a Girl
tropes.html:
• Simba is willing to tackle his best friend Nala and start play fights with her, and later gets into a much more serious fight with her to protect Timon and Pumbaa from her. Downplayed somewhat because even though he is willing to pick fights with her, he's never actually beaten her in a fight, except for one time when they rolled down a hill together romantically and he finally managed to pin her, but that doesn't really count as a "fight".
  • Scar also hits Sarabi when she compares him to Mufasa.

tropes.name: Would You Like to Hear How They Died?
tropes.html: Scar does this during the final battle to Simba, who was blaming himself all movie for the death of his father. Which is all the provocation Simba needs to turn the battle around and kick Scar's ass.

tropes.name: Xanatos Speed Chess
tropes.html: A talent of Scar's although he ultimately does it a little too much much to his ultimate detriment. When his initial plan to have Simba be tricked into the Elephant Graveyard to have the hyenas eat him fails due to Mufasa’s intervention, Scar decides to alter the plan to have Simba a victim of wildebeest stampede so Mufasa will get involved, so he can personally kill him and have his hyenas finish the job with no protector this time around- allowing him to be king unquestionably. When Simba returns years later when the hyenas fail to follow through, Scar quickly goes from being panicked about losing the very loose grip he has due to his negligence leading to everyone hating him for causing the Pridelands to be a barren wasteland, to almost literally/mentally cornering Simba into allowing himself to be killed for his perceived guilt in killing Mufasa till Scar himself decides to play with his food and tell him the truth, causing Simba to turn the tables to expose him as the kin-regicide murderer he truly is. Scar desperate to avoid his nephew killing him for his crimes, verbally blames the hyenas in the hopes he’d spare him. Not only does this not work as Simba doesn’t buy a word of it, having already resolved himself to have Scar permanently exiled for his actions just so he doesn’t stoop to his level, but the hyenas that had arrived to aid him, overheard him betraying them, which angers them to the point that when he is defeated, they remind him of how they overheard his treachery when he attempts to manipulate them again, prompting them to eat him rather than indulge in his two-faced nature- something they were going to do even if he did defeat Simba, seeing how little he truly cared for them.

tropes.name: Xylophones for Walking Bones
tropes.html: A xylophone can be heard throughout "Be Prepared", but while bones are seen throughout, there aren't any living skeletons. One quick scene does come close, though: two hyenas are playing with some skeletons, pretending to make them dance. There's also a hyena playing the xylophone part on a ribcage.

tropes.name: You Are Better Than You Think You Are
tropes.html: The reason why Simba goes into exile is that Scar tells him he is to blame for Mufasa's death. Rafiki shows him that Mufasa is alive — inside of Simba — and his memory makes it clear to Simba that he doesn't blame his son for what happened, but tells him the right thing to do is return to Pride Rock and retake his place. As Simba is still hesitating, Rafiki whacks him with a stick to demonstrate how the past can hurt, but he can learn from it and then confront his demons. Simba decides to toss away Rafiki's stick and return.

tropes.name: You Have GOT to Be Kidding Me!
tropes.html:
This is Zazu's response to Mufasa making him take part in Simba's pouncing lesson.
Zazu: Oh no, Sire, you can't be serious! (groan) This is so humiliating.

tropes.name: You Killed My Father
tropes.html:
Scar kills Simba's father and convinces him that it was an accident, only to later tell him the truth in a moment of Evil Gloating, giving Simba a Heroic Second Wind.
Scar: I. Killed. Mufasa.
Simba: MURDERER!!!!!!

tropes.name: Your Worst Memory
tropes.html: Simba watched his father apparently fall from the cliff (only learning later that he was pushed) when he was a cub. He has a flashback to this memory when Scar reveals to Simba that he in fact killed Mufasa, giving him a Heroic Second Wind.

tropes.name: You Talkin' to Me?
tropes.html: Pumbaa launches into the first half of the speech after a hyena calls him a pig, then ends it with the line, "They call me ''MISTER Pig!''"

tropes.name: Youth Is Wasted on the Dumb
tropes.html: Simba and Nala go to the Elephant Graveyard despite being explicitly warned not to go there due to both curiosity and Simba’s desire to prove himself as brave with Nala tagging along because it’s fun. They nearly eaten by the hyenas, but are saved by Mufasa in the nick of time, who scolds Simba later that night for deliberately disobeying him and almost getting Nala also killed. Simba realizing his naive foolishness apologizes. This lesson doesn’t stick as he goes into the gorge where he roars, leading to a wildebeest stampede that kills his father, which leads to Simba becoming traumatized enough to run away and live a carefree life without responsibility till he finally wises up to take responsibility. Both critical events in his childhood were spurred on by his uncle Scar, who was manipulating events to have him killed with the second time, it was Scar himself that killed Mufasa- framing Simba for it. Retroactively, it was less youthful brashness that egged him and more of a misguided trust in his obviously evil uncle, which his wiser father, Mufasa, was also guilty of.

tropes.name: "You Used to Be Better" Speech
tropes.html:
Nala says this when Simba refuses to return to Pride Rock, overthrow Scar and take his rightful place as king.
Nala: What's happened to you? You're not the Simba I remember.
Simba: You're right, I'm not. Now, are you satisfied?
Nala: No, just disappointed.
Simba: You know, you're starting to sound like my father.
Nala: Good! At least one of us does!

tropes.name: You Won't Like How I Taste
tropes.html: When the hyenas complain to Scar about the lack of food, Scar just tells them to eat Zazu. Zazu gets terrified and tells the hyenas that he'd be too gamey and tough for them to chew. Scar snidely says he'll taste fine with some lemon.

tropes.name: Zen Slap
tropes.html: Shortly after the dialogue between Simba and his father's spirit, Rafiki smacks the former's head with his stick to teach him how to cope with the past. After dodging a second hit, Simba makes up his mind and decides to return to the Pride Lands (but not before snatching Rafiki's stick and throwing it away as a precaution).

tropes.name: Zerg Rush
tropes.html:
• At the climax of the movie, dozens of hyenas pounce on Scar and eat him alive. He barely gets time to struggle.
  • In the original script and some picture book adaptations, Scar doesn't make Simba "confess" to killing Mufasa. He sets the hyenas on him, nearly forcing Simba off the cliff. The reason why the lionesses don't help is because the ambush is too sudden, and they have a barricade of hyenas standing between them.

tropes.name: Accidental Murder
tropes.html: Chung-sook kicks Moon-gwang down the basement stairs, causing Moon-gwang's head to hit the concrete wall at the bottom. This doesn't kill her immediately, but with no treatment, she succumbs to the head injury some hours later.

tropes.name: Achievements in Ignorance
tropes.html: Ki-jeong, despite only pretending to be an art therapist and admitting later on to making up all of the psychology Technobabble she was spouting on the spot based on a single Google search, still somehow manages to correctly guess that Da-song had a traumatic incident happen to him when he was in first grade seemingly by just pure chance alone.

tropes.name: Alternate Monochrome Version
tropes.html: The film has a version alternatively labelled the Black-and-White Edition or the Director's Cut, released in a limited theatrical capacity and later on home media.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Ending
tropes.html: The final scene leaves viewers wondering if Ki-woo really will work hard enough to buy the house and one day free his father; we see a vision of this unfolding before it's revealed to be a fantasy, and the film instead ends on the note of Ki-woo telling his father to "take care until then". However, given the plot events and themes established up to that point, the film is mainly pointing towards one outcome — that this won't come to fruition.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html:
• References to "knowing your place" recur throughout, referring to both the Parks' house and social/moral standing.
  • "Sister". It's an affectionate name that Mrs. Park bandies around, using it specifically for Chung-sook. Ki-woo and Ki-jeong are brother and sister, and the story ends with him mourning her death. Moon-gwang also calls Chung-sook "sister" when trying to convince her to keep her secret in the basement.note The Korean term for sister depends on the relative age and gender of the speaker. Mrs. Park and Moon-gwang use "unni," a term used by women to address older sisters, while Ki-jeong is Ki-woo's "dongsaeng," a term for younger siblings.
  • Talk of having "a plan" and variations thereof is exchanged between the Kims during key moments of the film. Given their lot in life, the only ups they have are to stick together and ultimately just keep moving and thinking about how to get ahead. This theme receives a bleak variant near the start of the third act after the Kims' home is near-submerged by the torrential rain. Ki-woo asks his father what his plan from earlier was, and Ki-taek glumly replies that the best plan is no plan—nothing they do really matters, so at least they'll experience less disappointment if they don't plan ahead. The film ends with a slightly more hopeful (if only in theory) twist on this: Ki-woo writes out his plan to honestly earn his way to buying the Parks' old home, so that what's left of their family could be together again.

tropes.name: Ascetic Aesthetic
tropes.html: The Parks' wide-open, mostly glass, minimalist house — and Dong-ik's architecture firm — contrasted with the crowded, tiny underground flat the Kims live in.

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html: Deconstructed. Ki-jeong and Dong-ik are the most overtly dickish members of the two families, but this serves to drive home the horror of the massacre that kills them instead of detract from it.

tropes.name: Awful Wedded Life
tropes.html: It's implied that the Parks are in a loveless marriage, or maybe one that got boring from domestic life. Mrs. Park is introduced passed out on an outdoor table (possibly daytime drinking), while Mr. Park can be inattentive to his wife and kids, and derisively scoffs when Ki-taek asks him if he loves his wife. It is downplayed as the Kims have to admit they are still a very nice family, if only because "they can afford to be." Even still, it's later shown they are not lacking in their sex life.

tropes.name: Aw, Look! They Really Do Love Each Other
tropes.html: The Kims. There are multiple instances of this throughout the whole film, but most notably is how they band together to enter the Parks' home, their friendly scenes when left alone in the house, and the ending.

tropes.name: Bad "Bad Acting"
tropes.html: At home, in order to get Moon-gwang fired as a housekeeper, Ki-taek and his son Ki-woo rehearse the car interaction between him and Mrs. Park to convince the latter that her trusted employee has tuberculosis. Ki-taek over-acts while his son gives him proper direction.note It's even funnier from a meta-perspective. Ki-woo is played by Choi Woo-shik, who at the time of the film's release was an up-and-coming actor, and he is coaching Ki-taek's actor Song Kang-ho, a well-respected big-name actor in South Korea. Bong says it's the same as if "Ansel Elgort is teaching acting to Al Pacino."

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html:
• As the Kims drunkenly feast in the Parks' home, Ki-taek becomes angered by a comment from Chung-sook, sweeping the contents of the table onto the floor and grabbing her by the shirt collar. But she just smiles at him, and after a tense beat, they both burst out laughing. She puts him in a playful wrist-lock, causing him to cry in mock pain. For whatever their flaws, the Kims are not an abusive household.
  • It also seems that Ki-woo will be the one to die, as he's unconscious and being carried by a panicked-looking Da-hye, during the party. However, he surprisingly survives, having undergone surgery, while Ki-jeong, having initially seemed in a much better and conscious state after being stabbed, actually dies.

tropes.name: Batman Gambit
tropes.html: The Kims quickly realize that Mrs. Park is Super Gullible and Mr. Park, while astute, is blind to his privilege and prejudices, so they plan a whole series of these to infiltrate the Park household, and succeed beyond their best expectations, manipulating the Parks perfectly.

tropes.name: Beauty Inversion
tropes.html: An interview confirms that Choi Woo-shik, as Ki-woo, was deliberately styled to look worse next to a character like Min, who is reasonably wealthy. Among other things, he's given an unflattering haircut and conspicuously lower-quality clothing.

tropes.name: Becoming the Mask
tropes.html: Ki-woo appears to develop real feelings for Da-hye. The fact that he echoes Min's words about her verbatim implies that at least some of this is because he's latching on to the idea of what Min would do to justify his own behavior, however, because Min has feelings for the girl.

tropes.name: Beneath Suspicion
tropes.html: Ki-woo, for Min. This is explicitly why Min gets Ki-woo into the Parks, saying Ki-woo won't interfere in his relationship with Da-hye. Da-hye falls for him more or less instantly, and even Mrs. Park is attracted to him.

tropes.name: Big Fancy House
tropes.html: The Parks' home is lavish, spacious, and modern, specifically designed by a famous architect. It serves as a contrast to the Kims' cramped semi-basement.

tropes.name: A Birthday, Not a Break
tropes.html: Da-song was deeply shaken during a previous birthday. In the present day, his birthday party ends with the deaths of Ki-jeong, Mr. Park, Moon-gwang's husband, and potentially himself, and deeply traumatizes both families. Not to mention that shortly before this present-day birthday party of his, his mother was celebrating his newfound recovery, and then he has to witness the lady who helped him heal from his trauma get stabbed by the man he had mistaken for a ghost and bleed to death in front of him.

tropes.name: Black Comedy
tropes.html: The first half of the movie is rich with this, ranging from Ki-jeong deliberately putting her own panties in the Park family's car to make it seem that their driver likes having car sex in his own employer's car, to Ki-jeong fooling Mrs. Park with faux artistic lessons. Even after the Cerebus Syndrome kicks in, there's black comedy in the second half, too, like a dog licking some sausages on a skewer which is sticking out of a dead guy.

tropes.name: Blackmail
tropes.html: Moon-gwang and her husband threaten to send the Parks a video showing that the Kims are actually a family. This plan doesn't work out well for anyone involved.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: The movie opens and closes with a shot of socks hanging out to dry that moves down to reveal Ki-woo.

tropes.name: Bond Villain Stupidity
tropes.html: While Moon-gwang's Evil Gloating is understandable (and hilarious), her and Geun-sae's lording it over the Kim family ultimately gives the Kims the opportunity to re-gain the upper hand.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html: While on the way home during a torrential downpour, there is a lot of focus on Ki-woo trying not to slip on a particular set of steps. Towards the epilogue, one of the detectives tailing him falls down the stairs.

tropes.name: Capitalism Is Bad
tropes.html:
A central theme in the movie, which focuses on how social stratification takes a toll on the characters.
Bong Joon-ho (director): Rather than water being important in itself, water flows from top to bottom. I think that's the tragic and sad element in this film. Water always flows from the rich to the poor, it never flows the other way.

tropes.name: Central Theme
tropes.html: As with most of Bong Joon-ho's filmography, the film inspects aspects of the negatives of capitalism, and specifically examines how regardless of class, age, or situation, capitalism makes parasites of us all.

tropes.name: Cerebus Syndrome
tropes.html:
• The return of Moon-gwang to Mr. Park's house after she got fired is a huge one, marking the apparent shift from the film's comedic undertone to a more dramatic turn.
  • The Running Gag of Ki-taek smelling bad comes back in a big, completely serious way during the climax.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gag
tropes.html: Ki-taek's smell, and the Parks' insistence on commenting on it without knowing where it's coming from. It's introduced early on in a comedic light, then returns in a recurring manner, every time getting more serious and insulting Ki-taek's pride more until Mr. Park accidentally insults both a dying Geun-sae and Ki-taek by reflexively reeling in disgust from their "lower-class" smell, leading to Ki-taek fatally stabbing him in a fit of anger.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• The Kims' open window. Ki-taek tells his family to leave it open as the streets are fumigated so they can fumigate their house, which is portrayed as grim enough. However, when a heavy rain hits later on, having left the window open causes the flooding of their home.
  • The stone. Ki-woo considers using it as a weapon against a drunk man, then carries it everywhere. Later on, Moon-gwang's husband uses the same stone to hit Ki-woo on the head twice to a great effect, although he survives.
  • When Moon-gwang shows up to the house, she mentions that she cut the cord on the CCTV across the street so no one would see her enter the house. While that sets up that she has a secret reason to want to be there, the camera also lingers on it later on to explain why no one saw Ki-taek sneak back into the house to hide in the basement.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Skill
tropes.html:
• Morse code also plays important roles during the movie; Moon-gwang's husband uses the code to communicate to the outside world, and in the epilogue, Ki-taek uses the same code to tell his condition to his family after escaping from the authorities.
  • That Ki-woo was a Boy Scout also means that he, like Da-song, can understand Morse code when Ki-taek uses it to communicate with him at the end of the film.
  • Although it isn't as important, Chung-sook is a former athlete, so it makes sense that she'd be able to get the upper hand while in physical altercations with several people throughout the film.

tropes.name: Closet Shuffle
tropes.html: After the Parks come back early, the entire family (except for Chung-sook, the only one who's supposed to be there) has to frantically hide. Ki-woo initially hides under Da-hye's bed, while his sister hides under the coffee table in the living room. As members of the Park family move around, the various members of the Kim family all join each other under the coffee table until they're all under there. Unfortunately, the Parks decide to sleep on the couch to watch their son (who's in the yard), mere feet from where the Kim family is hiding. They don't notice them, but awkwardly start having sex on the couch.

tropes.name: Creepy Basement
tropes.html: There is a hidden underground bunker in the Parks' house designed by the architect that built it. It is an all-round unappealing room, being a drab, cramped space, and used for the unnerving purpose of hiding under the noses the house's real owners; Moon-gwang has been using it for four years to hide her husband from loan sharks and Ki-taek ends up in the same position at the end of the film, hiding in the bunker after he killed Dong-ik. In both cases, cabin fever can set in, making the squatters both desperate and unbalanced.

tropes.name: Cultural Translation
tropes.html:
Darcy Paquet worked on the English language subtitles with director Bong, and he used a few examples of this trope to simplify the connections in viewers' minds.
  • The film's "ram-don" dish is actually jjapaguri, a mix of Chapagetti (spicy black bean sauce) and Neoguri (seafood broth) brand instant noodles. The move to call it "ram-don" came from English-speaking audiences' stronger familiarity with ramen and udon noodles from Japan. The shot of the packaging was edited for the English-speaking markets to more prominently feature the words "ramyeon" and "udon" on them, to aide the audience in making the connection.
  • A reference to Seoul National University was replaced with Oxford University (as Bong loves England); and the mention of Korea's KakaoTalk app was replaced with WhatsApp.

tropes.name: Daydream Surprise
tropes.html: The film ends with Ki-woo narrating a letter to Ki-taek, detailing how he plans to earn enough money through honest work to buy the Park house he's hiding in to free him. We then see a sequence of them at some point in the future reuniting, at which point the film fades out and seemingly ends... only to fade back in to Ki-woo's despondent reality, where this is but a dream.

tropes.name: Deliberate Values Dissonance
tropes.html: Park Da-song is obsessed with Native Americans, specifically the highly Theme Park Version of them based on stereotypes that ignore differences between Native groups, and is blissfully unaware of the hardships they endured and still endure in the modern era. While his get-up would be considered highly questionable in modern North America, it's just a costume he can put on in South Korea, highlighting how upper-class people yet again are ignorant to the plights of the oppressed (it wasn't that long ago when his obsession was normal in North America).

tropes.name: Deconstructive Parody
tropes.html: Of a Korean drama staple where the underage daughter of a rich family falls in love with her tutor, especially when he's of a lower social class, and they must undergo a wait until she's in university to reveal their relationship to her parents. Min wants to do this with Da-hye, but Da-hye seems to have had no interest in him whatsoever, although she instantly becomes infatuated, bordering on obsessed, with "Kevin" (Ki-woo). While Da-hye does save Ki-woo's life in a desperate act of romantic anguish, the murder of Da-hye's father by Ki-woo's ends their relationship, and Da-hye moves with her mother out of Korea, so Ki-woo never sees her again.

tropes.name: Delivery Not Desired
tropes.html: Ki-woo, upon discovering his father's whereabouts, returns home to write a letter explaining to him a plan to get him out. The last scene of the movie however is him holding the letter with a downcast expression, with it sinking in he can't get it to Ki-taek, because he's hiding in someone else's house.

tropes.name: Despair Event Horizon
tropes.html:
Several very accurate and disturbing examples litter the film.
  • Geun-sae crosses it after Moon-gwang dies from her head injury in front of him. This causes him to go on a murderous rampage.
  • Ki-taek crosses it after escaping from the Park family mansion and finding his semi-basement home flooded, with all his family possessions ruined. He becomes incredibly nihilistic after this, and it doesn't take long for him to snap and murder Mr. Park. At the very least, he snaps out of it after taking refuge in the bunker under the mansion.
  • Ki-woo and Chung-sook cross it after Ki-jeong dies and Ki-taek hides under the house, separating them forever.

tropes.name: Dirty Commies
tropes.html: North Korea is brought up a few times for the sake of jokes. Which foreshadows the presence of the Parks' unknown bunker - the original owners of the house had it built because they feared a communist missile attack. During the initial standoff, Moon-gwang mimics one of North Korea's more infamous propagandists in mockery of the new bounty they have - namely, the fact they may be getting their jobs back. Part of the overarching theme asks if unrestrained capitalism and the suffering it causes is really any different from totalitarian communism's own ills.

tropes.name: Dissonant Serenity
tropes.html: Ki-taek, Mrs. Park, and Da-song are all blank-faced at various points during the film's climax. Justified as they're in shock. Ki-taek even says he was hoping the chaos would turn out to be All Just a Dream. In Mrs. Park and Da-song's cases, however, they pass out shortly after they've reached the point of blank-faced disbelief. For Ki-taek, there really is no waking up and escaping from the aftermath.

tropes.name: Doing In the Wizard
tropes.html:
Two examples in the movie exist, and when done they actually enhance the creepiness of the moments they are a part of:
  • Moon-gwang trying to push the cover to the secret bunker, which takes so much exertion she had to brace herself with both feet on the wall to do so. It's an incredibly jarring image, and the reaction of first-time viewers may be of the consideration she's non-human because of how unnatural it initially looks before they realize the logistics. The sheer desperation and intensity of Moon-gwang's actions then become more flooring.
  • Years ago, Da-song saw something the Parks refer to as a ghost, which peered over the edge of the stairs at him and sent him into a panicked seizure. It was in fact Geun-sae, Moon-gwang's husband, who'd been hiding in the secret basement and came up looking for food. When the flashback actually occurs, the audience already know of the couple's secret, and realize how close the Parks came to realizing they had squatters in the privacy of their home.

tropes.name: Double-Meaning Title
tropes.html:
The Kim family acts as a parasite to the Parks, leeching off jobs and money from them. Meanwhile, the housekeeper's husband acts as a more literal example, eating the family's food for years completely undetected. The Parks themselves are also parasites, happily (and obliviously) sustaining themselves on the labor (and by proxy, the misery) of people in the lower classes.
Bong Joon-ho: They can't even wash dishes, they can't drive themselves, so they leech off the poor family's labor. So both are parasites.

tropes.name: Downer Ending
tropes.html: Despite being eventually released from the authorities when they were caught in their crime, and regretting it enough to commit only to honest work from then on, the Kim family lost Ki-jeong along with their newfound wealth, Ki-taek is stuck living in the bunker below the Parks' home forever to avoid being imprisoned, the Parks lost their father and patriarch, and both Moon-gwang and her husband died tragically, without ever being able to tell their misgivings to the world. Ki-woo comes up with a plan of working hard and becoming rich to rescue Ki-taek from the house, but it is clearly a plan doomed to fail.

tropes.name: Dramatic Irony
tropes.html:
• Min callously tells Ki-woo that he wants him to take over the job as Da-hye's tutor for a year because Min wants Da-hye for himself and doesn't want a university student stealing her. When Ki-woo gets to the Park house, Da-hye shows absolutely no interest in Min and almost instantly becomes besotted with Ki-woo.
  • Mrs. Park is delighted to hire so many new employees based on recommendation because she assumes they'll be good workers, even referring to it as a "belt of faith". Too bad the audience has been watching the Kims essentially scam her this whole time.
  • Likewise, Mrs. Park obliviously commenting about what a blessing the rain had been because it will mean nice weather for her son's birthday party. The rain caused severe flooding in the poor part of town, and we just saw the devastating scenes of what this did to the Kims and many other people. This is a stark example of the Parks being either unaware of or indifferent to the basic realities of how poor people live.
  • At one point, Mrs. Park recounts to Mrs. Kim how her son got a seizure after encountering a ghost on his birthday. While Mrs. Park believes there is a ghost in her house, the viewers and Mrs. Kim already know that said ghost was actually Geun-sae looking for a meal.

tropes.name: Driver Faces Passenger
tropes.html: Ki-taek starts doing this as he gets comfortable in his role as driver until Mr. Park reprimands him to keep his eyes on the road.

tropes.name: Due to the Dead
tropes.html: In one of the closing scenes, Ki-taek digs a proper grave in the garden for Moon-gwang so she can rest in peace.

tropes.name: Eat the Rich
tropes.html: Present as a theme. The Kims are undoubtedly swindlers who take advantage of the Parks, but they also suffered poverty their entire lives. While the Parks are presented fairly sympathetically, their wealth and comfort at the expense of the people in their service contrasts very sharply to the living conditions and lifestyles of the Kims, and they're often unaware of the kind of damage their lifestyles do and make them blind to, such as falling to the Kims defrauding their other servants. This is ramped up by the end when Ki-taek, fed up with the Parks' Conspicuous Consumption and denigration of the lower classes, fatally stabs Mr. Park, who unwittingly insults him for the last time.

tropes.name: Elemental Motifs
tropes.html: Water, in the form of rain. Everything goes belly-up for the Kim family on a raining night, they come home to see their house flooded on account of the rain, tensions begin to boil over due to the Parks actually being thankful for the rain giving them a clear day, and Ki-woo leaves his scholar stone in a river. On a metaphorical level, water never goes up, only down; the lower class have next-to-nope hope of rubbing shoulders with the upper class, and the Kims' attempts to leave them worse off than they were before.

tropes.name: Environmental Symbolism
tropes.html: The Kims live in a semi-basement apartment looking into a slum alleyway. The Parks' home is a very modern, spacious oasis with glass walls and a yard guarded by hedges on three sides. Everything related to the Parks' home gives the sense of rising into the clouds, while going back to the Kims' home is like digging deeper into the Earth. Geun-sae, who's even poorer than the Kims, and has negative assets due to being in debt, lives in a basement below a basement—a damp, dark, trash-filled and windowless bunker.

tropes.name: Epilogue Letter
tropes.html: The movie ends with two letters from Ki-taek and Ki-woo being read out by them for the audience.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html:
• In their opening scene, the Kims try to piggyback on a neighbor's wifi because they have no cell service or wifi of their own, establishing them as both deeply impoverished and prone to mooching off others.
  • Ki-woo gets his own when he smooths out relations with a pizza shop owner and angles for an interview, establishing him as the scheming charmer of the family who will eventually spearhead all of their ploys with the Parks. Much like during later interactions with the Parks, they appear to cold-read the owner and play off her concerns with a part-timer to further their own interests.

tropes.name: Everyone Has Standards
tropes.html: Despite their extremely brutal physical fight, Chung-sook and Ki-taek agree not to kill Moon-gwang and her husband, and choose instead to go back to them. Unfortunately, it's too late.

tropes.name: Everyone Is Christian at Christmas
tropes.html: You can see a Christmas tree and some decorations stored in the Park basement, but otherwise they don't seem to be religious.

tropes.name: Everyone Knows Morse
tropes.html: Downplayed; Da-song and Ki-woo can recognize a Morse code message as they're current or former Scouts, but still require time to translate it. Nobody else catches on to the source of the code, which is the entryway lights — Geun-sae, and later Ki-taek, use a code taped to the wall next to the switch in the bunker.

tropes.name: Exploiting Another's Wealth
tropes.html: The plot revolves around how the destitute Kim family con their way into the lives of the privileged Park family by replacing their existing house staff, all in the hopes of getting their patronage and maybe marrying into them. The Kims, and especially Chung-sook, make it clear that they don't really feel guilt over their fraud since the Parks are rich enough to take it, and are painfully oblivious as to real world problems.

tropes.name: Faint in Shock
tropes.html: Mrs. Park collapses into the arms of the people around her after seeing Ki-taek kill her husband.

tropes.name: Fake-Out Fade-Out
tropes.html: The movie seems like it's about to end as Ki-woo reunites with Ki-taek. The screen fades to black only to fade back in on Ki-woo in the semi-basement, having imagined the previous scene.

tropes.name: "Fawlty Towers" Plot
tropes.html: Discussed by the Kim family during the night of the camping trip when Ki-woo mentions that if he and Da-hye were to actually start dating, he would likely need to keep up the whole "Kevin" charade for the rest of his life, going as far as to spend all the money he made from tutoring on hiring an actor and actress to pretend to be his mum and dad to avoid any suspicion at the inevitable Meet the In-Laws. Had Moon-gwang and her husband not existed, it's highly likely this is the direction the plot would've taken instead.

tropes.name: Fatal Flaw
tropes.html:
• Mr. Park exhibits classism towards poor people, saying in private that they have a smell he doesn't like and aren't supposed to cross a "line". This comes to a head at Da-song's birthday party, when him being put off by the smell of a man who's dying right in front of him causes Ki-taek to snap and kill him.
  • In general, the Kim's resentment of the rich. A lot of their actions are done out of resentment towards the rich, such as eating and drinking in the Park's house and Ki-taek stabbing Mr. Park because Mr. Park was disgusted by Ki-taek's and Geun-sae's smell leads to their downfall. Their resentment of the rich causes them to bite off more than they can chew with the former and causes them to act impulsively with the latter.

tropes.name: Fauxshadow
tropes.html:
• Ki-jeong asks Mrs. Park for the titles for the house over the phone, as if to suggest some larger scheme to eventually steal the Parks' identities. Mrs. Park is gullible enough to provide; however, the discovery in the Parks' basement happens before this can become relevant to the plot.
  • Da-song is the first to discover the stairs lights being used as Morse code. He translates the message, and although the Morse code becomes a plot point after that, Da-song's translation doesn't.

tropes.name: Finding a Bra in Your Car
tropes.html: Invoked. Ki-jeong leaves her underwear in the car to make it seem like the driver likes having sex there. This makes the Parks uncomfortable enough that they fire him, which was the plan all along.

tropes.name: First Law of Tragicomedies
tropes.html: The first two-thirds of the movie are a comedic farce about the poor Kim family ingratiating themselves with the rich but ignorant Park family. However, when the previous maid that the Kims got fired comes back and their apartment gets flooded, the story starts to take a much more serious turn and resolves in what's largely a Downer Ending.

tropes.name: First-World Problems
tropes.html: The living conditions between the Parks and the Kims are frequently contrasted, which reaches a tipping point with the rainstorm. While it completely floods the Kims' home and forces them to stay the night in a gym with a couple hundred other people also washed out, it just makes for a pretty vista for the Parks. The next day, the Parks are only concerned with an impromptu birthday party for Da-song and invite the Kims to attend, completely ignorant of what they'd just gone through. This only stokes the massive resentment that had been building, with ultimately fatal results.

tropes.name: Foil
tropes.html:
• The Parks and the Kims. Both are Nuclear Families consisting of a mother, father, daughter, and son, but the Parks are wealthy, distant, and live uphill; the Kims are poor, tight-knit, and live in a basement.
  • The Kims to Moon-gwang and her husband. They were all poor people from the same street, driven to the same disparity by unemployment, and had the same idea to live off of salary and pickings from the Park family, only Moon-gwang came first and her plans were even less morally grey than the Kim family. Their competition for the place as the Park family's secret parasite quickly drawn ugly sides out of all members of both families.

tropes.name: Food as Characterization
tropes.html:
Food is used throughout the film for both characterization and symbolism.
  • The Kims are a lower class family who starts off eating only packaged foods, but gains access to better foodnote Blue collar buffets, fast food pizzas, a family BBQ as their status improves. Perhaps symbolizing their "lower-class smell", they are also heavy drinkers, and they never stop drinking even at the peak of their prosperity.
  • The Parks are Sheltered Aristocrats who keep expensive, premium-quality*(Which can rival premium Wagyu beef in quality and cost) Hanwoo beef sirloin in the fridge but thoughtlessly mix it in with instant noodles. Their dogs also get custom dog food.
  • Geun-sae, who lives at the bottom of the lower class, survives by wolfing down tiny portions of food (a banana and milk in a baby bottle) delivered by Moon-gwang.
  • Food is also present in almost all of the key scenes of class conflict in the film, especially in the conflict of poor vs poorer between the Kims and Geun-sae/Moon-gwang.
    • The Parks drive Moon-gwang out of the house by triggering her peach allergy.
    • The door to the bunker in the Parks' house is hidden behind a shelf full of pickles.
    • The climax of the film takes place at lunchtime, and sees Geun-sae stabbing Ki-jung with a kitchen knife, Ki-jung throwing Da-song's cake onto Geun-sae's face, Chung-sook stabbing Geun-sae with a kabob skewer, and Ki-taek stabbing Dong-ik with the same kitchen knife. In the aftermath of the massacre, a scene shows a dog eating the kebab skewered onto Geun-sae's corpse.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
Several, in fact.
  • In the beginning, the Kim family leaves the window open as a gust of fumigation smoke enters their apartment. They leave it open again before a massive storm floods their whole home.
  • A joke or two about North Korea happens early on. These foreshadow the bunker under the Kim household, built in case of a North Korean invasion, which is central to the second half of the film.
  • Da-song is revealed early on to be afraid of ghosts, and that something happened in his house. We later learn that the ghost was really Geun-sae emerging from his hiding spot.
  • When Chung-sook allows Moon-gwang in, Moon-gwang does briefly clock in that Chung-sook left a mess of a meal but comments on it blithely as if she relates to Chung-sook's transgression. This hints that Moon-gwang had done other transgressions as a housekeeper.
  • Whenever Mr. Park enters the house, watch the lights.
  • Ki-taek lightheartedly attributes his family's newfound employment to Mr. Park, toasting to him during their celebratory meal. When Geun-sae is revealed, we find out that he's obsessed with Mr. Park. Following the climax, Geun-sae's obsession with Mr. Park lives on in Ki-taek, with the latter spending his days raving and bowing to the poster of Mr. Park in a manner highly reminiscent of how Geun-sae worshipped the man — except where Geun-sae was filled with deranged gratitude, Ki-taek is filled with remorse and guilt to haunt him forever.
  • Ki-woo tries to use Min's gift, the rock sculpture, to scare away the man who keeps on pissing by their household, even though it's meant to be decorative and metaphorical rather than a weapon. Later, Geun-sae actually bludgeons him with the sculpture, causing Ki-woo to bleed profusely — likely to death, if Da-hye hadn't found him.
  • As Ki-woo tries to get rid of a drunk man with a bottle of water, and another neighbor throws a bucket of water at them, Ki-jeong records the commotion and comments, "What a deluge." Later, their semi-basement house gets completely flooded by heavy rain.
  • Mr. Park complains that Moon-gwang eats enough for two people, though we never actually see her eat. Later, we learn that she's been feeding her husband in the Parks' bunker with the extra serving of food.
  • When enjoying their newfound employment, Ki-taek wonders about his not-so-lucky neighbor who got trapped in debts after his Taiwan cake shop went bankrupt. The neighbor is, in fact, Moon-gwang's husband, who ran away from debt collectors after his shop closed down.
  • Despite faking her way into the job and continuing to lie about her credentials, Ki-jeong turns out to be right that Da-song has been through trauma and that his drawings are reflective of said trauma. Specifically, Da-song saw Geun-sae appear from the basement on his last birthday, thinking he was a ghost, and his drawings are of Geun-sae's face.
  • While talking about Ki-taek disappearing after murdering Dong-ik, the news reporter stands in front of the brightly colored garage door, which he used to escape into the bunker.

tropes.name: Foreign Culture Fetish
tropes.html:
• Park Da-song got obsessed with Native Americans after spending time as a Cub Scout, which led him to build a teepee in his bedroom and his home's backyard. Of course, it's a rather superficial version of a singular Native American culture as opposed to an actual one and is divorced from any sentimental feelings regarding the hardships of Natives.
  • Mrs. Park is obsessed with American stuff and is completely won over because "Jessica" went to college in the United States.note Truth in Television — this is not an uncommon view in East Asia.

tropes.name: Genre Mashup
tropes.html: The closest definition to the film's genre, which mixes black comedy, tragedy, family drama and thriller concepts.

tropes.name: Gilded Cage
tropes.html: Downplayed. The basement is a regular basement, but it is in a beautiful house, which is stocked with delicious food and is preferable to prison or death/maiming by debt collectors. However, you can't leave, your movements are severely limited even around the house, and Geun-sae's state demonstrates how it can quickly go south.

tropes.name: Gone Horribly Right
tropes.html: The Kims' plan to trick the Parks into hiring all of them succeeds. However, the sudden return of Moon-gwang, who was fired by the Parks via the Kims' methods, and the subsequent discovery of her husband Geun-sae living in the house's bunker ultimately result in tragic consequences for both the Kims and the Parks.

tropes.name: Gory Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Initially played straight when Geun-sae crushes Ki-woo's head with the stone. However, it's very much subverted when Geun-sae does it the second time round.

tropes.name: Gratuitous English
tropes.html: Usually from the well-educated English tutor "Kevin" (actually a dropout named Ki-woo, though he is genuinely fluent) and Americanized art therapist "Jessica" (actually a born-and-raised Korean girl named Ki-jeong). Mrs. Park happily slips into this when they're around, too.

tropes.name: Greater-Scope Villain
tropes.html: The loan sharks searching for Geun-sae after they pulled usury on him.

tropes.name: Greed
tropes.html: The Kims' driving motivation. They scheme to get increasingly more wealth out of the Parks. The film contrasts this with the more passive and pervasive greed of the Parks, who lives of abundance and luxury without ever thinking of people beyond themselves.

tropes.name: Greed Makes You Dumb
tropes.html:
• The Fatal Flaw of the Kim family. After Kim Ki-woo manages to get the poor family some money by being an English tutor for the Park Family, he enacts a scheme where he has the Parks unknowingly hire the Kim family for various jobs. The family had already achieved their goals after all four of them are hired by the Parks in well-paying jobs, but they just can't help but want even more. Their pursuit of money and laxness end up becoming their undoing however, where they're caught red-handed partying together in the Park mansion by Moon-gwang and Geun-sae, leading to the tragic birthday party. This includes the death of Kim Ki-jeong, with Kim Ki-taek fleeing from the authorities after murdering Park Dong-ik in a fit of rage, the latter forced to live in the secret bunker of the basement of the Park mansion, like Geun-sae before him. By the end of the film, the Kim family lost Ki-jeong along with their newfound wealth, Ki-taek is stuck living in the bunker below the Parks' home forever to avoid being imprisoned, with the remaining Kim Ki-woo having the Tragic Dream of trying to buy the mansion back in order to save his father.
  • The film contrasts the Kim family's active greed with the more passive and pervasive greed of the Parks, who lives of abundance and luxury without ever thinking of people beyond themselves. Their desire to keep enjoying their comfortable lives without needing to deal with any of the dirty work makes them gullible when the Kims appear offering to solve their problems. They also don’t realize how the flaunting of their affluence breeds envy and resentment in the lower classes. Because of their failure to detect a powder keg situation building up right under their noses, they end up losing their family patriarch Park Dong-ik to a fatal stabbing—and possibly their son, Park Da-song, who has a seizure—so that the remaining Parks are forced to move out of the mansion.

tropes.name: Grey-and-Gray Morality
tropes.html: The Kims and Moon-gwang do very unethical and outright criminal acts to get their wealth quickly, but they come from very poor backgrounds that give them little or no opportunity to survive by honest means. On the other side of the spectrum, the Park family are spoiled upper-class individuals who are either oblivious to the hardships of the lower class or disparaging of their looks and conditions, but they aren't actively malicious. They have their own family problems which make it harder to notice the struggling of others, and while they benefit from the unfair system they aren't personally responsible for every bad thing that's happened to the Kims.

tropes.name: Halfway Plot Switch
tropes.html: Almost literally at the halfway point in the film, when Moon-gwang returns and we learn that her husband is living in the house's hidden bunker, what had been a Black Comedy about the Kims scamming the Parks becomes a cross between a thriller and a caper about the Kims going to extremes to avoid getting exposed — and that's not including the eventual horror as Geun-sae goes on an unhinged rampage.

tropes.name: Heel Realization
tropes.html: Ki-woo has this reaction before the birthday party incident, upon realizing the immense fraudulent actions his family had done so far.

tropes.name: The Help Helping Themselves
tropes.html: After they all get hired in the Parks' household, the Kims wait for the Parks to leave on a camping trip and then use their mansion for an unapproved party.

tropes.name: Home-Early Surprise
tropes.html: The Kims throw a party together at the Parks' place, assuming that the owners won't be back from their camping trip until the next day or so (despite the strong storm). Then Ms. Park phones in saying they will be back in 8 minutes. Cue a Mass "Oh, Crap!" reaction.

tropes.name: Horrible Camping Trip
tropes.html: We don't see the trip itself, but this is the cause for the Home-Early Surprise. The thunderstorm caused the river to overflow but the Parks tried their best for Da-song before giving up altogether and turning back.

tropes.name: Horrible Housing
tropes.html: The poor Kim family lives in a cramped, smelly semi-basement in a street that easily floods. This is contrasted with the rich Park family's lovely, spacious home that stands high above such problems.

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html:
• Chung-sook and Ki-taek having time to think things over and consider making amends with Moon-gwang and her husband. It's too late though.
  • Per director Bong, the scene accompanying Ki-woo's reply letter implies he eventually made enough money by honest means to buy the house and let Ki-taek have another breath of fresh air and a touching reunion, only to snap back at the very last scene to Ki-woo finishing the letter… in his still rundown semi-basement house. The entire scene of Ki-woo earning money and buying the house is a fantasy, made of wishful thinking.

tropes.name: Hypocritical Humor
tropes.html:
The film deals heavily in this.
  • There is a Running Gag where the Parks regale the Kims with stories of terrible misdeeds done against them while the Kims, who are themselves con artists, feign horror.
  • Mrs. Park repeatedly tells the Kims that she is a good judge of character and that trust is all-important to her, immediately before being tricked by them.
  • Ki-jeong chides Ki-woo for reading Da-hye's diary, then immediately starts reading it herself.

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html:
The Kims start to get cocky after a long string of successes, and make three foolish missteps in the same night:
  • The Parks go on a camping trip, and the Kims decide now's a perfect time to sponge off their house for its luxuries such as the food, drinks, Wi-Fi and bubble bath. Then rain strikes, which will surely make the Parks cancel their trip and turn back home the same night. But this doesn't occur to the Kims, who continue on with their little party and almost get caught when the Parks come home early. This first mistake leads to the second and third, since they wouldn't have happened if Ki-woo, Ki-jeong, and Ki-taek hadn't been in the house when they weren't supposed to be.
  • Then, when Moon-gwang appears at the door and begs to be let in to retrieve something important to her, Chung-sook lets her into the house. This would be a very bad time to have an attack of conscience because of the possibility that Moon-gwang might notice the other three Kims in the house. Even if the Parks or someone else found out afterwards that Moon-gwang had requested entry and been denied, Chung-sook would be able to justify her refusal: The person in question was fired for supposedly having a contagious disease (which Mrs. Park didn't want her husband to know, but the Kims might just have to spill it), and one could infer that her reason for returning was something shady she had hidden from the Parks.
  • The last and ultimately worst mistake is the other three Kims following Chung-sook and Moon-gwang down into the secret bunker instead of hiding upstairs, just because they want to eavesdrop. Unless they were also going to back up Chung-sook because they didn't trust Moon-gwang or in case there was something dangerous down there, which goes back to the fact that they shouldn't have let this person in the house to begin with. Upon hearing Moon-gwang's secret they accidentally fall down the stairs and blow their cover in front of Moon-gwang, who takes video evidence for blackmail.

tropes.name: I Ate WHAT?!
tropes.html: Ki-jeong is stunned when she realizes that the beef jerky she was eating was actually a dog treat.

tropes.name: Ignored Epiphany
tropes.html: In the shelter, Ki-taek tells his son that the only way for a plan not to fail is not to plan at all. This is what makes the final Fantasy Sequence so tragic. Ki-woo writes to his father that he has "a plan" to earn money legitimately to free Ki-taek from the bunker. With the pessimistic atmosphere of the entire ending, the audience can only extrapolate that Ki-woo's plan will indeed fail.

tropes.name: Incredibly Obvious Tail
tropes.html: The family gets tailed after the birthday incident and we see one clumsy detective stumbling while following Ki-woo.

tropes.name: Indulgent Fantasy Segue
tropes.html:
• Geun-sae and Moon-gwang have one of being able to have the Parks' house to themselves. They get lost in their own dream while holding the blackmail video message against the Kims, allowing the Kims to pounce on them and quickly regain the upper hand in the battle.
  • At the end of the film, as Ki-woo is writing his letter to Ki-taek, he has one of these where he envisions himself buying the Parks' former home so he can free Ki-taek from the bunker. One of the signs that it's just his imagination is that he, Ki-taek, and Chung-sook don't appear to have aged at all. Maybe it's not impossible that it could happen, but it seems unlikely.

tropes.name: Incurable Cough of Death
tropes.html: The Kims' scheme to get Moon-gwang fired involves making it seem like she has tuberculosis. It culminates in them getting her to cough into a napkin by taking advantage of a peach allergy and then secretly spraying it with hot sauce that looks like blood. Mrs. Park even says she didn't know people still got TB in high-income countries like Korea, but Mr. Kim convinces her it's the rich country with the highest infection rate.

tropes.name: Innocently Insensitive
tropes.html:
• Mrs. Park talks constantly on her phone, making Ki-taek carry her bags around for her, and fires Moon-gwang, who has worked for her family for years (and the one before her), on the word of someone who has barely worked for her. However, she is unaware of just about everything that the Kims know.
  • The Parks plans a lovely garden party last-minute and invite the Kims, not knowing that they had lost all their possessions in a flood and had to sleep in a gym along with other evacuees just the night before. Mrs. Park is even happy about the rain because of the good weather it will bring afterwards. Ki-taek seethes at this; later, Ki-woo muses on how relaxed, happy, and picture-perfect the upper-class is.
  • However, the idea is deconstructed in general. While the upper class are innocent and insensitive, their innocence is willful at best; being innocent is portrayed as a luxury and, as called out by several characters, not a defence of their insensitivity.

tropes.name: Instant Death Stab
tropes.html: Park Dong-ik drops dead almost immediately after getting stabbed in the heart by Kim Ki-taek.

tropes.name: Inter-Class Romance
tropes.html: Ki-woo from the penniless Kim family has a secret relationship with Da-hye, a rich man’s daughter. Also a Teacher/Student Romance mired in Questionable Consent.

tropes.name: Introspective Art
tropes.html: On the wall of the Park family room is a drawing by their youngest son of a scribbled figure with black eyes. Unbeknownst to them, as well as to the Kim until halfway through the film, this is actually Park Da-song's attempt at capturing the face of Geun-sae, a man who has been living beneath their house for years and scavenging food and supplies from the upstairs levels. One night, Da-song happened to see him in the midst of one of these thefts, but he noticed only the eyes that quickly noticed him and left.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html:
• Although they've lied and tricked their way into their jobs, the Kims actually appear to be quite proficient at their respective roles, especially Chung-sook, who is given eight minutes to cook a dish she's never heard of, and pulls it off. The implication is that the Kims had talent all along, but society was so cutthroat and exclusionary that they were never given the opportunity to prove themselves until they learned to bluff their way in.
  • Ki-taek, who regarded Geun-sae with both fear and contempt as a lunatic squatter threatening his "ownership" of the Park house, becomes trapped in the same exact situation Geun-sae was in: spending his days going insane and isolated in the basement, apologizing to the picture of Mr. Park, and flashing Morse code to the outside world in the vain hope that someone might help him. It's implied he may be stuck there for the rest of his life.
    • The reason Ki-taek stays in the basement is because if he goes above ground, he'll be arrested and sent to prison. However, he's essentially locked himself into solitary confinement in the basement, having to scrounge for food and living in a windowless room; prison would likely be a better option.
  • On a thematic level, the Kims, in their "heroic" efforts to Eat the Rich, ended up committing acts of Kill the Poor, and utterly destroy the lives of Moon-gwang and Geun-sae who are in an even worse situation than them.

tropes.name: Ivy League for Everyone
tropes.html:
• A downplayed version is that when Ki-jeong is trying to make herself sound qualified by lying about her background, she doesn't claim to have an Ivy League degree but instead mentions having attended Illinois State University. It's an above-average university from a prestigious country (American universities having a good reputation in East Asia), and thus decently impressive already, but obscure and specific enough to not seem like a fabricated detail.
  • Invoked. Ki-woo's fake transcript says he goes to Yonsei University, one of the three SKY schoolsnote Seoul National University, Korea University, and Yonsei University. and thus a candidate for the most prestigious university in Korea. The Parks presumably value his educational chops more highly than they otherwise would because of this name recognition.

tropes.name: Jerk Justifications
tropes.html: At one point, the Kims discuss that their targets are nice people, with just a twinge of guilt - but quickly brush it off, saying they're nice because they can afford to be. Ki-taek and Chung-sook also take a moment to wonder if the previous Park employees they got fired are now struggling with finding work like the Kims were before, but Ki-jeong convinces them to quit worrying about it because they didn't create the class system.

tropes.name: Karmic Death
tropes.html:
Of two very dark sorts, as both sides aren't monsters or traditionally good:
  • Ki-jeong is sharp-tongued, the most disdainful towards the Parks, the greediest of the Kim family, and personally executes the more heinous crimes to get the previous employees fired (such as getting the Parks' driver fired under suspicion of being a pervert and triggering Moon-gwang's deathly allergies). She outright mocks the Parks, and openly wonders why a family of idiots get everything, when the Kims deserve everything. She's the only one to actually die from Geun-sae's rampage.
  • Mr. Park is neglectful of his wife (and even derisive towards her) and the family (to the point where he's easily conned into firing his existing staff on flimsy evidence), is ignorant of his privilege, and is both consciously and unconsciously classist, lambasting Ki-taek for smelling "like the lower class" behind his back. When he reflexively shows disgust at Ki-taek and Geun-sae from the "lower class" smell, Ki-taek has enough and stabs him in a fit of rage.
  • In a Fate Worse than Death version, Ki-taek, who was one of the driving forces behind the scam, happily leeches off the Park family's good fortune, is indirectly responsible for killing Moon-gwang and sending Geun-sae into a fury, and kills Mr. Park in a spur-of-the-moment impulse, becomes trapped in Geun-sae's exact situation - rotting away inside a basement, diligently sending messages in the hopes his family might find him, and going insane. The ending implies he'll die there.

tropes.name: Karma Houdini
tropes.html: While Ki-taek becomes a fugitive after murdering Mr. Park, Ki-woo and Chung-sook are given little more than a slap on the wrist despite deceiving and exploiting the Parks, holding Geun-sae hostage in the basement, and accidentally killing his wife. Moreover, Ki-woo, who had planned to murder Geun-sae to keep him quiet, survives with no permanent damage despite being bludgeoned by Geun-sae. However, this is downplayed as they have still lost their sister/daughter and father/husband for their efforts, and are back to being poor.

tropes.name: Keep It Foreign
tropes.html: In the German dub, the new family at the end is not German but American and Ki-taek's comment about their food consisting of more than sausages and beer is changed to hamburgers and coke.

tropes.name: Kick the Dog
tropes.html: Literally. Chung-sook is not very gentle with one of the dogs. Ironically this is shown as she is claiming that she would be a very kind person if she were as wealthy as Mrs. Park.

tropes.name: Knows a Guy Who Knows a Guy
tropes.html: The Kims incrementally maneuver themselves into the Park household in this way, with each new addition telling Mrs. Park about this great new person to hire that they know from [x]'s [y]'s [z]. Deconstructed, since the Parks take the Kims at their word and never realize that they're being scammed.

tropes.name: Kubrick Stare
tropes.html: A masterful one when Geun-sae's pop over the top of the stairs into the kitchen.

tropes.name: Layered Metropolis
tropes.html: While only partially filmed in Seoul, the place where the Parks and Kims live is implied to be this - the Kims have to climb a bridge, a tunnel, and a hill to get to the Parks' mansion, while the Kims live in an underground apartment. Played for Drama when it floods due to this very thing.

tropes.name: Loan Shark
tropes.html: Evading them after falling into debt is the reason Geun-sae is hiding out in the underground bunker.

tropes.name: Malignant Plot Tumor
tropes.html: Early in the movie, the fact that the Kim family all shares the same smell due to their living conditions is treated as a footnote. Overhearing a conversation between the Parks about his smell causes Ki-taek to become increasingly conscious of their reactions to his smell, largely forgetting other issues like the couple in the bunker. It eventually reaches the point that Ki-taek murders Mr. Park over a Stink Snub in the middle of the climactic scene with Geun-sae.

tropes.name: Match Cut
tropes.html: Used a few times to contrast the flooded Kim apartment and the Park house. At one point, the film depicts Moon-gwang vomiting in the Park toilet followed by sewage shooting out of the Kim toilet, then very pointedly goes from Mrs. Park in her huge walk-in closet full of clothes to a gym where dry clothes are getting handed out to the Kims and the other displaced families.

tropes.name: Meaningful Echo
tropes.html: Ki-woo repeating "What would Min do?", Min's previous statement about Da-hye, word-for-word to his family who do not know that Min said it first. It indicates that much of Ki-woo's social climbing is rooted in his desire to be stylish, cool, and financially comfortable like Min. Indeed, "What would Min do?" becomes his mantra as the film progresses, only for Ki-jeong to eventually snap at him that Min wouldn't have gotten entangled in any of their trouble.

tropes.name: Mexican Standoff
tropes.html: The Kims end up in a variety with Moon-gwang and Geun-sae. After the Kims learn that Geun-sae is hiding in the basement, Moon-gwang and Geun-sae learns that they're a family and takes a video of them admitting to this, ending up in a version where instead of guns, they threaten each other with cell phones that demonstrate each other's secrets.

tropes.name: Mister Muffykins
tropes.html: While not an actively malicious person, Mrs. Park is an Idle Rich lady who keeps three pampered dogs — cared for by the servants, of course.

tropes.name: Mood Whiplash
tropes.html: A Bong Joon-ho specialty. The movie rapidly and seamlessly switches back and forth between farcical comedy, high-suspense thriller and genuine tragedy. The most defining example of this trope is perhaps Chung-sook kicking Moon-gwang down the basement stairs before the latter can reveal herself to the Parks, which is funny in a slapstick sense until she brutally hits her head on a wall at the bottom of the stairs.

tropes.name: More Deadly Than the Male
tropes.html: Chung-sook is hands down the most fearsome member of the Kim family in a fight, with her daughter Ki-jeong fairly ruthless as well. Moon-gwang is also no slouch, although she is more closely matched by her husband.

tropes.name: Motifs
tropes.html: Stairs. They are used many times and match the themes of social ascension and class difference between those at the top and those at the bottom.

tropes.name: Mutually Assured Destruction
tropes.html: Between the Kims and Moon-gwang. Moon-gwang has her husband in the basement, but also knows that the Kims are a scammer family. By coincidence, this happens in a fallout shelter meant for war with North Korea, which consistently promises to annihilate its southern neighbor if anything happens to it. As a minor gag, Moon-gwang mockingly mimics a North Korean propagandist when she and her husband are able to restrain the Kims.

tropes.name: National Stereotypes
tropes.html: After retreating into the underground bunker at the end of the film, Ki-taek finds out to his relief that the new German owners of the house live off of more than just beer and sausages.

tropes.name: Naturalized Name
tropes.html:
• A variation; the educated (and in Ki-jeong's case, Westernized) personas of Ki-woo and Ki-jeong are named "Kevin" (at the behest of Mrs. Park) and "Jessica". This is common Truth in Television with many East Asian families who become Westernized.
  • Mr. Park's given name is Dong-ik, but the English-language newspaper and magazine articles on display throughout the Park house call him "Nathan Park."

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html: Had Ki-woo not carried their stone with him down to the basement, Geun-sae wouldn't have broken out and hit Ki-woo in the head with it.

tropes.name: Nice Job Fixing It, Villain!
tropes.html: Moon-gwang cutting off the security camera. When she says it, the Kims have an Oh, Crap!-style reaction, and she was only thinking about herself, but it actually works out extremely well for them: it's how Ki-taek manages to escape the police and jail, sneaking back into the Park house.

tropes.name: No Good Deed Goes Unpunished
tropes.html: Played With. About the only thing that the Kim family does that could be considered altruistic in the movie is show some sympathy for Moon-gwang and risk exposure by allowing her inside and letting her get something from the basement. This indirectly leads to the events exposing their charade, getting one of them killed, another on the lam, and destroying the Park household as well. However, the deed that directly ignites the conflict between the Kims and Moon-gwang and her husband is Chung-sook threatening to call the police on them.

tropes.name: Nuclear Family
tropes.html: Both the Kim and Park families consist of a husband, a wife, a daughter, and a son.

tropes.name: Oblivious to Her Own Description
tropes.html: Ki-jung narrating how the housekeeper Moon-gwang is a total Bitch in Sheep's Clothing who walks around the Parks' house as if she owns it feels pretty rich (no pun intended) coming from her seeing as she literally takes a luxurious bubble bath in said house her first night in it.

tropes.name: Offhand Backhand
tropes.html: A variant; Chung-sook pulls off a rather impressive example when she knocks the rampaging Moon-gwang down the stairs with a backfoot so swift that Mrs. Park, who is standing close by, doesn't even notice.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html:
• Da-song bonds deeply with "Jessica" and becomes very fond of Chung-sook, with the former being strongly implied as to what helps him to recover from the trauma of seeing "the ghost in the house". This is, until that fateful birthday party comes around.
  • Ki-taek bonds with Mr. Park over the long hours and hardships they've both faced, which makes Mr. Park's admission that he hates Ki-taek's "low-class smell" hit all the harder.

tropes.name: Poor Communication Kills
tropes.html: Exploited by the Kims, who correctly predict that Mrs. Park will avoid sharing key information with her husband if it could reflect poorly on her.

tropes.name: The Power of Family
tropes.html: The Kims are a subdued example, as a family of con artists who work as an indivisible team, whether packing pizza boxes or covering up an accidental murder. They possess intense Undying Loyalty for each other, and the minute Ki-woo gets lucky in getting a cushy tutoring job at the Parks, his immediate instinct is to put his sister up as an art therapist, and they work on helping his parents also get jobs there. Even though it ultimately ends tragically, leaving Ki-jeong, his sister, dead, Ki-woo's first instinct is still to promise in a letter to his father in hiding that he will find a way for them to be back together.

tropes.name: "Psycho" Strings
tropes.html: In the second half of the movie, a quiet set of these plays whenever Ki-taek is feeling aggrieved by the Parks.

tropes.name: Questionable Consent
tropes.html: Ki-woo, who is in his mid-20s, begins a relationship with Da-hye, an underage high schooler whom he is tutoring.

tropes.name: Race to Clean Up
tropes.html: With the Parks away on a camping trip for the weekend, the Kims take the opportunity to throw a party in the large, well-stocked house, living the high life for a change. That is until Chung-Sook gets a call from Park Yeon-kyo to tell her that they have had to call off the trip because lf rain and are heading back. Cut to the family frantically cleaning up the mess of their party before the Parks arrive and their ruse is up.

tropes.name: Rage Breaking Point
tropes.html:
• After Moon-gwang dies from her head injury, her husband absolutely can't take it well, and goes on a final rampage to kill all members of the Kim family. He'd also undergone an even slower version while being locked in a basement to avoid debt collectors.
  • The silent denigration Ki-taek feels when he repeatedly overhears Mr. Park mention "the queer scent he couldn't describe, but can detect from Ki-taek and from the metro", combined with helping the Parks throw a lavish birthday party right after the night they evacuated from their completely flooded house (after a brawl and a miserable escape in the rain) does a hefty number on Ki-taek's dignity and sanity. When he sees Mr. Park reeling once more from the smell of him and Geun-sae, he finally snaps and fatally stabs him in the chest.

tropes.name: Reading Your Rights
tropes.html: It's the first thing Ki-woo hears as he awakens in the hospital from the climactic rampage that left him with a brain injury courtesy of Geun-sae, his sister slain by Geun-sae's hand, and his father on the run after killing Mr. Park. Ki-woo cannot stop laughing.

tropes.name: Red Herring
tropes.html: Originally, viewers are led to believe that Da-song's skill for being able to read Morse code would somehow reveal the truth behind the Kim family and Moon-gwang and her husband's true conditions since her husband used the codes to reveal Moon-gwang's death to Mr. Park's family. But at the time, Da-song's crash birthday party is on its way, and he apparently forgot to tell his findings to everyone. However, the Morse code does come back into play at the very end of the film, when Ki-taek uses the same method to send a message to Ki-woo.

tropes.name: Red Herring Twist
tropes.html: When the Parks come home early, the Kims have to clean up their mess very fast and the camera lingers suspiciously on the dirt under the sofa. Ki-jeong also cuts herself on some glass, leaving a smear. Later, their trash seems to have disappeared and the Parks don't detect the smell of alcohol even though they can smell Ki-taek, who is hidden under the table.

tropes.name: Relative Error
tropes.html: Da-hye initially mistakes siblings Ki-woo and Ki-jeong — or rather "Kevin" and "Jessica" — for boyfriend and girlfriend.

tropes.name: Rewatch Bonus
tropes.html:
• Da-song's creepy drawings of a wide-eyed man with white pupils. Upon first glance, Ki-woo calls it a chimpanzee, to which Mrs. Park says that it's a self-portrait. Neither are correct; they're of Moon-gwang's husband Geun-sae, the "ghost" he saw on the night of his birthday.
  • Watch the lights each time Mr. Park enters the house. Geun-sae is manually activating them with his head from the basement.
  • When Moon-gwang goes down to get some plum extract from the basement, she seems rather astonished by Mrs. Park following her and calling her name. Note how she's right in front of the cabinet which hides the bunker.

tropes.name: Roaring Rampage of Revenge
tropes.html: Following his wife's death, Geun-sae walks into Da-song's birthday party with the intention to do this. However, the results are mixed. Geun-sae himself dies, but he manages to slash some innocent guest and kill Ki-jeong. Dong-ik dies, but it's not a direct result of Geun-sae's rampage. Da-song may also have died from the climax, but it's very uncertain. Geun-sae also tried to kill Ki-woo, but the younger man miraculously survives his near-fatal injuries.

tropes.name: Rule of Symbolism
tropes.html:
• The scholar stone Min gifts the Kims;
    • According to him, the stone is supposed to bring them wealth. Fittingly, Ki-woo says it keeps clinging to him throughout the film, and he eventually almost dies after being hit on the head with it. Following this, Ki-woo leaves it in the river, symbolizing his desire to rise through society by honest means.
    • As is seen at one point, the stone floats. That's because it isn't a real rock. It's meant to bring wealth, and therefore hope, to Ki-woo, but both the rock and its promise turn out to be hollow after all. However, this probably saves Ki-woo's life when being struck over the head with it by Geun-sae.note Director Bong Joon-ho actually didn't expect the stone to float, yet what a felicitous, thematically powerful accident its floating became.
    • At the film's end, Ki-woo places it in a river among several other rocks, and it instantly becomes indistinguishable. It's easy to see this as reflective of the fact that the Kims are just one part of a great collective with hollow hopes and schemes, the lower class, and that they blew their chance to stand out from that collective due to their greed and overreaching.
  • The film's visual storytelling is thoroughly vertical;
    • The Kims are poor and live underground, while the Parks live uphill and never even use the metro, above them both economically and literally. Geun-sae is also below even the Kims, trapped in a windowless bunker and buried in debt.
    • The Kims' household is a "semi-basement." Bong Joon-ho has described this sort of household as something that is firmly below ground, but doesn't want to believe it is, just like the people living in it.
  • Also, the smell of poverty, although only Mr. Park mentions it. It eventually becomes the final trigger for the tragic conclusion of the film.
  • The Cowboys and Indians motif reflects the arrival of a group of newcomers to push out the house's previous inhabitants.
  • The metaphorical line between the rich and the poor, which is a recurring theme in the movie, can actually be "seen" through other lines (the lines on the windows, the lights above dividing the Parks and their employees, etc).

tropes.name: Scenery Dissonance
tropes.html: The events that unfold at Da-song's birthday party, perhaps the most climactic and shocking in the whole film, take place in broad daylight, beginning with Geun-sae stabbing Ki-jeong and ending with Ki-taek stabbing Mr. Park.

tropes.name: Secret Diary
tropes.html: When the Kims are lounging in the Parks' house while they're away, Ki-woo and Ki-jeong's first act of debauchery is to steal Da-hye's secret diary and read it. When the Parks come home early, Ki-jeong tosses it back to her brother and he has to scramble to return it to Da-hye's room.

tropes.name: Secret Room
tropes.html: The secret bunker below the actual basement, designed by the architect of the house in case the North Koreans invade. The entrance is hidden behind a set of cupboards and was never disclosed to the Park family when they bought the house.

tropes.name: Sheltered Aristocrat
tropes.html: The Park family. Driven home ironically as Mrs. Park calls Ki-jeong "too innocent" to explain the incident she staged herself.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• Mr. Park's company is named "Another Brick."
  • The architect of the Parks' house is named Namgoong, who shares the name with Song Kang-ho's character in Bong's previous film Snowpiercer.
  • Alfred Hitchcock's picture can be seen on the spine of a book on a shelf at the Park house. Bong Joon-ho has said that Hitchcock was a major inspiration for the film, and you can spot some allusions to his work as well.note The Halfway Plot Switch and the theme of opportunistic criminals who unwittingly meet up with genuinely disturbed people are clearly modeled on Psycho, while Hitchcock's final film Family Plot also seems to get a few nods, with working class con artists who are good at roleplaying, a secret bunker, and a scene set in the garage of a fancy house.

tropes.name: Slobs Versus Snobs
tropes.html: Viewed through the lens of social stratification. The lower class Kims are the Slobs, while the upper-class Parks are the Snobs; the Parks are polite but privately look down on poor people, while the Kims scam the Parks.

tropes.name: Snooty Haute Cuisine
tropes.html: The Park family are Sheltered Aristocrats who keep expensive, premium-quality Hanwoo beef sirloin in the fridge but thoughtlessly mix it with instant noodles.

tropes.name: So Much for Stealth
tropes.html: The Closet Shuffle in which the Kims, except Chung-sook, hide around the Park house from Moon-gwang as Chung-sook leads her into the basement. The remaining three's enthusiasm to see what she's hiding in there leads to them all going down to the basement, and ultimately falling down the steps, revealing that they are all con artists and giving Moon-gwang a reason to blackmail them.

tropes.name: Spiritual Antithesis
tropes.html: To the previous Palme d'Or winner Shoplifters. Both share the same premise of an eccentric family in poverty trying to make their living by committing petty crime, and came from neighboring countries in East Asia (South Korea and Japan).
