The major difference is that Shoplifters explores the theme of familial bonding with a Lighter and Softer tone, whereas Parasite is a more Darker and Edgier take on that premise with pitch-black comedy. Film critic Justin Chang summed it up on Twitter after seeing it at the Cannes Film Festival: "PARASITE is like SHOPLIFTERS on pricey Korean bath salts".

tropes.name: Spotting the Thread
tropes.html:
Done numerous times throughout, especially by the Park kids.
  • Da-hye immediately notices that "Kevin" seems much more familiar with "Jessica" than he pretends to be. She believes them to be in a relationship and tries to get rid of "Jessica" — but in this case, he can tell her he doesn't have any feelings for her without letting on that they're brother and sister.
  • Da-song notes that the Kims smell the same. Both the older Parks assume that Da-song is referring to the "smell of poor people", and laugh it off embarrassedly.

tropes.name: Stink Snub
tropes.html: The Kim family all shares a similar smell due to their living conditions. In the first part of the movie, it's treated as a minor footnote to address as part of their masquerade. However, after overhearing the Parks discuss his smell in-depth, Ki-taek becomes very aware of their subtle responses to him.

tropes.name: Sure, Let's Go with That
tropes.html: When Ki-taek asks Dong-ik if he loves his wife, he laughs derisively, then does a Beat, before going with this trope as a response.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html: Moon-gwang's Tap on the Head doesn't just knock her out for a while; the untreated head injury kills her some hours later.

tropes.name: Symbolic Censored Eyes
tropes.html: The posters for the film, designed by Kim Sang-man, feature members of the Kim and Park families outside the Parks' residence. The eyes of the poor Kim family are obscured by black censor boxes, while the rich Park family's eyes are hidden by white ones. One interpretation of this is that parasites like worms don't have eyes, but they can sense light — similarly, the Kims have black bars, which symbolize darkness and living underground (poverty) just like they do in the movie, whereas the Parks have white bars suggesting light and living above ground (wealth). Another interpretation is their overall blindness to their own personal evil. Additionally, in East Asia, "black censors over eyes" are used for censoring mugshots of criminals...which they are.

tropes.name: Tagline
tropes.html: An early one (used in Australia, New Zealand and Singapore) was "Misplaced familyhood"; the more prominent one, used for the film's American release, was the more symbolically descriptive "Act like you own the place."

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html: Combined with hypocrisy. In the middle of the film, right before it shifts to tragedy, Mrs. Kim claims that the Parks are only nice because they're rich, and that if she had it all, she'd be kinder. At this point, the Kims have already wormed their way into the Parks' good graces and effectively have free access to their property. Then the conflict for the rest of the film is kickstarted by Mrs. Kim trying to sell out Moon-gwang and Geun-sae, who are in a similar rough position to the Kims.

tropes.name: Tragedy
tropes.html: What the film is ultimately about. While Ki-woo's original goal is to earn some honest money for his unemployed family, he and the rest of his family eventually get blinded with greed, and it becomes the reason for their downfall.

tropes.name: Thousand-Yard Stare
tropes.html:
• Come the end of Da-song's birthday party, Ki-taek has one of these, first from the shock of seeing his children mortally wounded, then from seeing Mr. Park disgusted by Geun-sae's smell, at which point he finally snaps and kills him with the same distant, glassy look, as if his brain is on autopilot.
  • Mrs. Park and Da-song also grow blank-faced at various points from shock during the film's climax. However, they pass out shortly after they've reached this point of disbelief.

tropes.name: Toilet Humor
tropes.html: Played for truly bleak humor with the Kims' toilet overflowing during the flood, as Ki-jeong is sprayed with shit repeatedly as she tries to retrieve her prized possessions.

tropes.name: Tragic Mistake
tropes.html: The Kims had a decent little racket going, while deceitful in how they acquired their jobs they still provided the services they were paid for. They take things too far by using the house for their own amusement while the Parks are gone on a camping trip. When Moon-gwang arrives, it sets them on edge as almost exposing their deception. They also overcrowd the panic room, which does expose them and turns the situation into a Mexican Standoff with who will tell the Parks first. It gets worse from there.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Lie
tropes.html: The trailers give the impression that the film will be about the Kim family having to contend with the Parks' Creepy Child, Da-song. In actuality, Da-song is an eccentric but harmless kid, and the true antagonists are former housekeeper Moon-gwang and her husband, the latter of whom is completely absent from the previews.

tropes.name: Two-Act Structure
tropes.html: The first half of the movie is a series of comic adventures as the Kim family, all four of them, scam their way into the household and lives of the super-rich Park family. Almost exactly halfway through the film, the old housekeeper, Moon-gwang, returns to the Park home and reveals the big secret it contains, which starts the gorier, bloodier, darker, and much more violent second part of the movie.

tropes.name: Unknown Rival
tropes.html:
• Arguably one of the most ingenious things about the film's plotting is that the Kim family and the Park family are somehow simultaneously this to each other, the Kims having disdain for the rich for their lack of problems or perspective in life while the Parks look down on poor people who don't "know their place" and "cross a line". It's only when Mr. Park visibly recoils at a dying Geun-sae's smell does Kim Ki-taek finally put two and two together and realise the other man is the exact kind of rich person his family was talking about earlier and stabs him in a fit of rage.
  • Inverted with Geun-sae, who spends most of his time in the basement fanatically bowing to pamphlets of Mr. Park and praising him for working so hard to afford such a big house for him and Moon-gwang to squat in, who is completely bewildered when a utterly psychotic homeless-looking man suddenly charges into his son's birthday party with a knife and stabs a random partygoer while screaming about respect – a man he'd never even seen before in his life, let alone met.

tropes.name: Useless Security Camera
tropes.html: When Moon-gwang makes her fateful return to the house, she mentions that she disabled the security camera pointing at the house so no one would know she returned. This proves crucial to the ending of the film.

tropes.name: Weaponized Allergy
tropes.html: The housekeeper Moon-gwang is deathly allergic to peaches. The Kim family exploit this to get her fired by inducing an allergic reaction and framing it as tuberculosis. Later, when Moon-gwang and her husband Geun-sae are threatening to expose the Kims as scam artists, Ki-jeong gets the upper hand by running to get some peaches from the fridge and rubbing them in Moon-gwang's face.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html: The existence of the stairs to the underground bunker makes for a Wham Shot in itself, but when Moon-gwang calls out "HONEY!" as she frantically descends, we realize that somebody is down there, too.

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html: One that shifts the course of the entire film: when Moon-gwang gets Chung-sook's help pushing a cabinet aside to reveal an underground bunker.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html:
• When Moon-gwang returns to the Park residence, she seems to have some lacerations on her face. Her husband asks what happened, and she says she'll tell him later, but she never gets the chance, and we never find out either. Maybe she got them while trying to access that security camera she disabled?
  • At the end of the film, it's never revealed what becomes of Mrs. Park or Da-hye, or even whether Da-song survives his seizure.
  • Lampshaded example: While celebrating their new lifestyle, Ki-taek and Chung-sook take a moment to wonder what happened to the previous Park employees they got fired and if they're now struggling with getting work like the Kims were before. Ki-jeong tells them to dismiss the notion because it's not their problem to worry over since they didn't create the class system. They do find out about Moon-gwang soon enough though...

tropes.name: You Are Too Late
tropes.html: Ki-taek and Chung-sook both decide that they were too harsh on Moon-gwang and resolve to help her. Unfortunately for them, she has already died from the head injury Chung-sook unwittingly gave her.

tropes.name: Based on a True Story
tropes.html: On Count Philippe Pozzo di Borgo and Abdel Sellou's.

tropes.name: Bavarian Fire Drill
tropes.html: In the opening scene when Driss gets caught by the police over his speeding he bluffs the officers that they will have blood on their hands if their don't let them pass. It works - to the point he makes them escort him and Philippe to the nearby hospital.

tropes.name: Beard of Sorrow
tropes.html: Philippe grows one after sending Driss away.

tropes.name: Blue Blood
tropes.html: Philippe. Other than the pedigree and implication of coming from Old Money, it doesn't amount to much, given the story is set in modern France.

tropes.name: Bratty Teenage Daughter
tropes.html: Philippe's daughter, who is using to her advantage both Philippe's condition and the fact that there is a grand staff in the mansion. First Driss, and then Philippe talk some sense into her.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html: After a lot of talk about ears being erogenous we see the interviewer of the delivery company reaching for hers when Driss' comments amuse her.

tropes.name: Brutal Honesty
tropes.html: Driss' shtick is being very upfront, without any ill intentions - he just never, ever beat around the bush.

tropes.name: The Caretaker
tropes.html: Driss' new job is being a caretaker for Philippe.

tropes.name: Costume-Test Montage
tropes.html: Philippe, before going to his date, checks various configurations of jackets, scarves and hats.

tropes.name: Cultured Badass
tropes.html:
• Driss has become something of one towards the end, having at least some of Philippe's refinement brush on him, while still keeping his Simple-Minded Wisdom of a Lovable Rogue.
  • Philippe too. He's an art commissioner attending classical music concerts (and having live performances in his mansion), but he ended up in a wheelchair due to a paragliding accident and still glides, even if as a passenger.

tropes.name: Dark and Troubled Past
tropes.html: Both Driss and Philippe. Philippe developped a lot of self loathing after his accident and the loss of his wife while Driss is an ex-convict from the suburb with a really difficult relationship with his cousins and aunt.

tropes.name: Did Not Get the Girl
tropes.html: Played straight with Driss, due to Incompatible Orientation. Subverted with Philippe, as he first refuses, then finally accepts to meet Eleonore at the end.

tropes.name: Distracted by the Sexy
tropes.html: Driss points the fork at Philippe's cheek instead of his mouth when being distracted by Magalie (Audrey Fleurot) walking by.

tropes.name: Don't You Dare Pity Me!
tropes.html: What makes Philippe want to hire Driss is him being completely unphased by his condition and being very upfront.

tropes.name: Driven to Suicide
tropes.html:
• Driss bluntly says that he'd be if he were in Philippe's place. Philippe instantly points out that he's in no condition to even end his life.
  • Amusingly, this trope is later Played for Laughs with Philippe's daughter.

tropes.name: Eating the Eye Candy
tropes.html: Philippe's daughter does it when she passes next to a shirtless Driss.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html:
• You know what kind of person Driss is just by his rather rude behaviour in the recruitment scene.
  • Even earlier, in the first scene of the movie. Upon being pulled over for speeding, Driss deftly outwits the policemen by claiming that Philippe needs to get to the hospital, and Philippe even starts to convulse and foam at the mouth to prove it. Driss had earlier bet to Philippe that he could get a police escort to the hospital and he does, and they drive victoriously along, all set to Earth, Wind & Fire's "September."

tropes.name: Ethical Slut
tropes.html: Driss. He's a small-time crook that was just released after serving six months, perfectly capable of playing up Scary Black Man archetype, openly smokes weed and hires hookers for erotic massage... but he's at the same time the heart of the film, who, despite his blunt demeanour, is the most caring and compassionate person around and someone Philippe can rely on no matter what.

tropes.name: Fee Fi Faux Pas
tropes.html: Driss, when leaving the interview, mentions that Philippe doesn't have to get up. He notices his faux pas immediately.

tropes.name: Feet-First Introduction
tropes.html: When the camera pans over the men waiting for the job interview, it goes for their shoes. All neatly polished, combined with ironed trousers... and then it reaches a pair of worn trainers, after which Driss is shown in establishing shot. With this simple trick audience knows how much he doesn't fit there.

tropes.name: Get Out!
tropes.html: Early on, Driss' aunt tells him to leave the apartment immediately, being done with him and fed up with his antics.

tropes.name: Gilligan Cut
tropes.html: More than once, Driss says there's no way he's doing something, only to end up doing it a few moments later.

tropes.name: Godwin's Law of Facial Hair
tropes.html:
Towards the end of the movie, Driss shaves Phillipe's face in preparation for his date. He has some fun with it, cutting it "José Bové" style, then handlebar, before changing it to the infamous toothbrush 'stache. Driss proceeds to come up with Hitler-related banter.
Phillipe: No. Please. No. No, no, no. No!
Driss: You mean nein! Don't you feel like invading countries right now?

tropes.name: How We Got Here
tropes.html: The movie opens with a scene towards the end of the movie after Driss and Philippe reunited. Then we skip back to how it all started.

tropes.name: I Have Many Names
tropes.html: Driss is short for Idriss, but his birth name is Bacari.

tropes.name: Incompatible Orientation
tropes.html: Driss spends a lot of time in the film hitting on Magalie, who turns out to be a lesbian.

tropes.name: Innocent Bigot
tropes.html: Driss is both obnoxious and very blunt when handling the issue of Philippe's condition. Which is in no small part why Philippe hires him.

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: The nurse that replaces Driss qualifies, as well as Philippe's neighbors, who use Philippe's entry as their particular parking place despite parking being forbidden there.

tropes.name: Jerk with a Heart of Gold
tropes.html: Played with. Driss can put Gregory House to shame with his rude behaviour. On the other hand, he is a genuinely caring and charming person, whose sense of humour carries the whole film, and who takes a great deal of time and effort making people around him feel better. By any means necessary.

tropes.name: Lipstick Lesbian
tropes.html: Magalie is a very feminine secretary and personal assistant to Philippe. She's always elegant, well-groomed and highly sophisticated in general - but much to Driss' shock, turns out to be a lesbian. Something that everyone knew, but deliberately kept him in the dark as a joke on his constant advances toward Magalie.

tropes.name: Male Gaze
tropes.html: The camera lingers on Magalie's behind when she walks by Driss feeding Philippe.

tropes.name: Manic Pixie Dream Girl
tropes.html: Driss to Philippe, as he will stop at nothing to make sure his employer-and-then-friend is happy, despite his condition.

tropes.name: "Nighthawks" Shot
tropes.html: There is a shot of Philippe and Driss sitting in a restaurant at night that is framed like the painting.

tropes.name: Odd Couple
tropes.html: Driss, a Working-Class Hero employed as a caretaker by Philippe, a tetraplegic Blue Blood. Eventually leading into Odd Friendship.

tropes.name: Pair the Spares
tropes.html: Yvonne and Albert, the gardener. It's even lampshaded by Driss.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html: When Driss has to take Philippe for a ride he refuses to put him in the handicapped-friendly car and instead make the extra effort to put him in the Jaguar. It's one of the first nice thing Driss do for Philippe who mostly wanted a merciless caretaker.

tropes.name: Plot-Mandated Friendship Failure
tropes.html: Downplayed. Two-thirds in, Philippe tells Driss to leave, with no ill intentions, simply seeing how badly Driss needs to handle family affairs. He soon regrets his decision, but is too proud and stubborn to call Driss back. When the rest of the staff approach Driss, he instantly goes to see Philippe and get him back on track.

tropes.name: The Power of Friendship
tropes.html: While Philippe (obviously) remains a tetraplegic, his friendship with Driss gives him the will to have a less reclusive and more uplifting life.

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html: One scene makes prominent use of M&M's.

tropes.name: Purple Prose
tropes.html: Philippe shows hints of this when dictating a poem to the woman he corresponds with. He is obviously a cultured man, but a great poet he is not - the poem is made of a lot of boring comparisons and little else.

tropes.name: Race Lift
tropes.html: Driss, and by extension his family. The character is Senegalese in the film but the man that inspired him is an Algerian, Abdel Sellou.

tropes.name: Real-Person Epilogue
tropes.html: Before the end credits, a short clip of the real tetraplegic Philippe Pozzo di Borgo and his assistant Abdel Sellou is shown as both are Watching the Sunset.

tropes.name: Scary Black Man
tropes.html: Taking into consideration his posture, strength and being a former criminal, who still likes to carry a telescopic baton in his bag, Driss does fit this trope nicely.

tropes.name: Sexy Secretary
tropes.html: Magalie, of the elegant variety. Driss is ogling her right from the start, but the camera itself often follows her in a lingering way, too.

tropes.name: Simple-Minded Wisdom
tropes.html: Driss is a low-brow street crook who might be Book Dumb, but that doesn't make him stupid. His simplemindedness is also part of what makes Philippe take a liking to him.

tropes.name: Snobby Hobbies
tropes.html: Philippe is a connoisseur of modern art and even drags Driss along to show him some. As a paraplegic, he can't engage much in sports he used to enjoy, but even so, their relationship lets him get back in the figurative saddle. Driss is all fine with luxury cars, but paragliding's not his thing.

tropes.name: Strong Family Resemblance
tropes.html: Subverted. Philippe tells Driss that he can see that him and Adama are brothers. They are actually cousins.

tropes.name: Terrible Interviewees Montage
tropes.html: From the viewpoint of Philippe. All the applicants we see in the beginning are not edgy enough, until Driss shows up.

tropes.name: True Art Is Incomprehensible
tropes.html: Discussed. Driss doesn't really understand modern art, to the point where he heavily mocks it; then he tries his hand at abstract painting. He starts with the intent of making a mockery out of it, but the painting itself turns out quite profitable when Philippe sells it as the work of an "up-and-coming artist" - to mess with the snobby, snooty people he buys art from.

tropes.name: Worst Aid
tropes.html: When Driss learns that Phillipe's daughter has attempted to commit suicide via Immodium, he jokes that next, she'll overdose on Tylenol. In actuality, Tylenol is very easy to overdose on. Twice the prescribed dosage can easily create irreversible liver damage in many people. Downing a larger amount can doom you to a slow and painful death, even if you seek medical aid immediately.

tropes.name: The '80s
tropes.html: The movie takes place from 1980 to 1983.

tropes.name: '80s Hair
tropes.html: Tony's sister Gina sports a massive hairdo even by the era's standards.

tropes.name: Actually Pretty Funny
tropes.html: When Tony is trying to charm Elvira after she rebuffs his advances, he asks if she'll kiss him if he wears her hat. Despite trying to keep her Ice Queen demeanor, the sight of him in her hat breaks her into laughter.

tropes.name: Adaptation Expansion
tropes.html: The film takes some basic plot elements and characters from the original and expands on them greatly. The prequel comic Devil in Disguise, meanwhile, further explores Tony's past in Cuba. Among other things, it highlights not only why he has such a hatred for communists like Rebenga which go beyond self-interest, and why Tony's mother doesn't buy into his lies in the movie.

tropes.name: Adaptational Attractiveness
tropes.html: Tony Montana is certainly easier on the eyes than Tony Camonte.

tropes.name: Adaptational Heroism
tropes.html: Tony Montana has far more moral standards and likable characteristics than his original counterpart Tony Camonte. For one thing, it's pretty hard to imagine Camonte even having any second thoughts about killing children or putting any sense of morality before self-interest in the same that way Montana does. Even their last stands are quite a bit different from each other. In the original film, Camonte fights and goes down fighting against the police, whereas Montana fights off but ultimately loses to a rival druglord's death squad. Furthermore, Montana's incestuous feelings toward his sister are far more ambiguous here, while Camonte leaves little to nothing to the viewers' imaginations.

tropes.name: Adaptational Name Change
tropes.html:
• Tony and Francesca Camonte -> Tony and Gina Montana
  • Guido Rinaldo -> Manny Ribera
  • Poppy -> Elvira Hancock
  • Johnny Lovo -> Frank Lopez
  • Ben Guarino -> Mel Bernstein
  • Tom Gaffney -> Omar Suarez
  • Louis Costillo -> Hector the Toad

tropes.name: Adaptational Villainy
tropes.html: Mel Bernstein is an openly-corrupt cop who solicits bribes from Tony and is happily on Lopez' payroll, nothing like the incorruptible Inspector Ben Guarino of the original film.

tropes.name: Addiction-Powered
tropes.html: Just before the climactic confrontation with Sosa's goons, Tony takes a huge dose of cocaine. Combined with the adrenaline of the ensuing firefight, he's able to withstand being shot multiple times and takes out several of his attackers, even taunting them as they pepper him with bullets. It takes The Skull shooting Tony in the back with a shotgun to finally kill him.

tropes.name: Anadiplosis
tropes.html:
Tony Montana sums it up:
Tony: In this country, you gotta make the money first. Then when you get the money, you get the power. Then when you get the power, then you get the women.

tropes.name: Anger Born of Worry
tropes.html: Happens when Tony's mother tells him to go to Gina's house to find out what is going on, since she knows Gina is being secretive and she believes that Tony is responsible for this behavior. After getting so angry at Tony that she forgets how to speak English and starts yelling at him in Spanish, Tony's mother is seen crying in the doorway.

tropes.name: Animal Metaphor
tropes.html: Tony has a pet tiger and calls Elvira a tiger.

tropes.name: Anyone Can Die
tropes.html: The film goes out of its way to show that those working in the drug trade often end up meeting sudden, gruesome deaths because of the impulsive violence of the gangsters involved in it. The entire sequence with Tony's friend Angel getting brutally killed by Hector the Toad happens very quickly with little buildup, and Omar's death is obliquely hinted at moments before it happens, with Sosa offering a justification after the fact. After Tony kills Alberto, people Tony cares about start dropping like flies, and ultimately Tony himself dies at the end.

tropes.name: Ain't Too Proud to Beg
tropes.html: Frank Lopez desperately pleads for forgiveness from Tony after failing to assassinate him, even offering him $10 million and Elvira to spare his life. It sort of works.

tropes.name: Alliterative Name
tropes.html: Mama Montana.

tropes.name: Alas, Poor Villain
tropes.html:
• Tony gets shot in the back after losing everything and descending to madness trying to stay in power. Shortly before that, he picks up the phone on his office desk for a moment, then sets it back down. There's nobody left to call: Manny and Gina are dead, Frank is dead, Sosa wants him killed, his mother has disowned him, and Elvira has left him for good. Tony has absolutely nobody left.
  • Poor, poor Angel. It's horrifying the way Hector saws him off-screen.

tropes.name: All Your Base Are Belong to Us
tropes.html: The film climaxes with a massive assault on the Montana compound.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Ending
tropes.html: The ending of Scarred for Life is this. After finally gunning down Alejandro Sosa in cold blood, coked-up and power-hungry Tony finds himself in a Mexican Standoff with Elvira and a DEA strike team. A shot rings out, but it's anyone's guess on who pulls the trigger first.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Situation
tropes.html:
• Are Tony's feelings for his sister Gina really incestuous (subconsciously or otherwise)? Or, on the other hand, is it simply obsessive, overzealous (and ultimately dangerous) protectiveness] because he views Gina as the one true source of light within his life? Gina even accuses him of being an incestuous freak after Tony blows away her fiancé, his best friend.
  • Twice over. Tony has some suspicions that Omar was responsible in some manner for the deal with the Colombian dealers going sour, which resulted in his friend Angel's death. However, he never acts on this suspicion and Omar is later on killed for an unrelated accusation: being a police informant. This too is never given any definitive proof beyond Sosa's own words and a brief phone call Sosa's henchman takes, and Frank at least is not convinced.
  • Sosa claims that Omar Suarez was a police informant who had put other gangsters in prison after he kills Omar by hanging him from a helicopter. But other than his own statements and the brief phone call we see him take from his henchman Alberto, the audience is never given any definitive proof of this otherwise. Though it's not as if Tony cares, since he never liked Omar, who might have been responsible for Tony’s friend Angel’s death. If Omar wasn't a rat, then one has to wonder: what other motivation could Sosa have had to want to kill him? For what it's worth, Sosa did actually name the names of those that Omar had presumably put behind bars.
  • Did Sosa really know that the journalist would have his wife and kids with him? If he did, then it seems like he would have bothered to mention this little fact to Tony and Alberto beforehand, and possibly find a different, more subtle way to kill him.
  • Will Sosa go to prison for his crimes? Or will he continue to carry out his criminal activities unscathed? When he calls Tony just before the climax, the tone of his voice shows that he is clearly not happy with the turn of events. Regardless, he still takes down Tony's empire in revenge.
  • Did Alberto know English? He ignored Tony until Tony spoke to him in Spanish, but told Tony to shut his mouth when Tony was insulting him in English. If he did know English, why did he ignore Tony until Tony spoke to him in Spanish? If he didn't know English, why did he tell Tony to shut up when Tony was insulting him in English?

tropes.name: Ambiguously Jewish
tropes.html: People not familiar with the fact that Miami has a significant Cuban Jewish community (or that there are Cuban Jews)note In fact, Manny's actor Steven Bauer is himself Cuban Jewish. might miss that Frank Lopez references a Yiddish word ("chazzer") for "pig" and wears a Chai necklace.

tropes.name: Ambition Is Evil
tropes.html: Ambition is what drives Tony's criminal impulse during his rise.

tropes.name: And This Is for...
tropes.html:
Frank Lopez to Rebenga via Tony and his knife.
Tony: Rebenga! From a friend you fucked!

tropes.name: Animal Lover
tropes.html:
Tony seems to like tigers. He has tiger-print seats and even has one as a pet. He also seems to like flamingos.
Tony: [changing the channel to a nature documentary about flamingos] Manny, look at the pelican fly. Come on, pelican!

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: "The world is yours". Tony sees it on a Goodyear blimp note (advertising PanAm Airlines), and he adopts it as his own motto.

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html:
• Elvira asks Tony "What makes you so much better than me?". Tony has no response.
  • When Tony observes that a cable van has been parked near his house for three days, Manny asks him, "You've been watching it for three days?", to which Tony has no response.

tropes.name: Artifact Title
tropes.html: The movie is the Setting Update of an older film based on a novel that fictionalizes the life of Al Capone, whose nickname was "Scarface". However, the new version is set in early 1980s Miami instead of 1920s Chicago and doesn't feature Capone or a Capone Expy (and Tony's scar isn't as prominent as Capone's).

tropes.name: Artistic License – Explosives
tropes.html: The 40-millimeter grenade rounds that Tony fires from his M16/M203 combo are designed to arm themselves only after they've flown at least 30 yards downrange, so that the shooter doesn't get caught in the blast. Tony fires at much closer distances, so the rounds should just put big holes/dents in whatever they hit.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Pharmacology
tropes.html: This movie seems to take place in an alternate reality where no one overdoses on cocaine... On the other hand, it is pretty realistic in regard to the long-term effects of cocaine use, namely paranoia.

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html:
• All of Tony's victims (with the exception of Manny) fall into this, especially the backstabbing snake Frank Lopez. There's a reason Tony calls him a "piece of shit" when he orders Manny to kill him. And then there's Hector, whom no one feels sorry for.
  • Frank's right-hand man Omar Suarez, who gets exposed as a police informant and killed when he angrily decides not to go with Sosa and Tony's business dealings. He shows signs that he'd look down on others regardless of the profession. Suarez tried to get Tony killed when Hector was planning to turn on him, so nobody feels any sorrow at the moment Suarez meets his demise.
  • Marta. Considering she helped Hector kidnap Tony and Angel, and even pointed a gun at them while the latter was carved up with a chainsaw by Hector, you're not likely to feel bad for her when Manny kills her to save Tony.

tropes.name: At Least I Admit It
tropes.html: As noted under Evil Versus Evil, Tony throws this in the face of Sosa and his men. Given what Sosa does, Tony's not totally wrong.

tropes.name: Ax-Crazy
tropes.html:
• Tony is the embodiment of this trope in the second half of the movie. In general, he's more than ready to use lethal weapons, mostly guns.
  • Hector the Toad as well, who kills Tony's associate with a chainsaw.

tropes.name: Bad Reason to Do Good
tropes.html:
Tony is very protective of his sister Gina, to the point where he beats up Fernando (a drug dealer) when he catches the two making out in the restroom. According to Manny, this stems from possessiveness.
Manny: Come on, Gina. Put yourself in his place, okay? Right now, you happen to be the best thing in his life. The only thing that's any good, that's pure.

tropes.name: Badass Boast
tropes.html:
Some of the most famous lines from the movie.
Tony: D'you wanna fuck with me? Okay. You little cockroaches... D'you wanna play rough? OK, SAY HELLO TO MY LITTLE FRIEND!

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html: After Tony and Manny kill Frank and Mel, Manny asks Tony "What about Ernie?". Ernie starts sweating bullets and fidgeting in terror… until Tony asks him if he wants a job.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch Comment
tropes.html:
Tony delivers one to an immigration officer.
Immigration Officer: Ever been in a mental hospital, Tony?
Tony: Yeah, on the boat coming over.

tropes.name: Bald of Evil
tropes.html:
• Alberto is balding and is one of Sosa's more ruthless thugs.
  • Frank is balding and tries to have Tony assassinated.

tropes.name: Be Careful What You Wish For
tropes.html: Tony gets everything he ever wanted; wealth and power. The sheer volume of both ends up consuming him and causes his catastrophic downfall.

tropes.name: Being Evil Sucks
tropes.html: Throughout the movie, Tony's ascension to the top of Miami's criminal underworld leaves him a miserable, unhinged husk of a man. He loses all of his friends, relatives and associates, his empire, and finally his life.

tropes.name: Beware the Quiet Ones
tropes.html: The Skull and Alberto don't speak much, if at all, and are merciless assassins.

tropes.name: BFG
tropes.html: Tony's "little friend", an M16 with an M203 grenade launcher.

tropes.name: Big Brother Instinct
tropes.html:
A creepy and malicious example with Tony Montana:
  • He beats up Fernando after seeing him groping Gina's ass, then scolds Gina and slaps her.
  • He shoots Manny when he finds out he has been sleeping with Gina.

tropes.name: Big Fancy House
tropes.html: Most notably, Tony buys a huge mansion with a famously gaudy interior and decor.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html:
• Hector referred to Tony as "Car'e Cicatriz" which is Spanish for "Scar Face."
  • Tony says in the bathtub "por nada" (for nothing), showing how he is starting to realize how meaningless it is to live in luxury.
  • Tony hostilely calls Frank "amigo" (friend) when talking to him at the club.
  • At the beach, Tony calls a bikini-clad woman "sabrosura" (tasty).
  • In the bathroom scene, Manny tells Tony "Cuidado, cuidado que te pasa a ti, se te cae", which translates to "Be careful, be careful, it's happening to you, you'll fall". This foreshadows Tony's death.

tropes.name: Blatant Lies
tropes.html: Tony hands his mom a thousand dollars. His mom, knowing him all too well, asks him who he killed for it. He insists that he didn’t kill anyone and is working for an anti-Castro group where he gets a lot of political contributions.

tropes.name: Blood Is Squicker in Water
tropes.html: Tony Montana's death.

tropes.name: Bloodier and Gorier
tropes.html: Massively so compared to the 1932 original. Even with the laxer censorship standards over the 50 years that had passed between the two, this was considered an exceptionally violent film that shocked audiences when it was first released.

tropes.name: Boom, Headshot!
tropes.html:
Happens several times.
  • Alberto gets shot in the head by Tony, splattering his brians all over the passenger car window.
  • Hector is shot in the head by Tony.
  • Nick the Pig gets killed by The Skull this way in the climax.
  • Frank gets shot in the face by Manny Ribera with a suppressed pistol on the orders of Tony Montana after the latter promised that he would not kill him.

tropes.name: Boring Insult
tropes.html: After Tony Montana makes it big, his wife Elvira tells him he's become boring because all he talks about is money. It's true— they have nothing in common besides snorting coke.

tropes.name: "Both Sides Have a Point" Remark
tropes.html:
Unusually, Sosa and Frank unwittingly prove their strengths and weaknesses by talking to Tony separately, who takes it all into account:
  • Sosa's words aren't without truth regarding Frank's poor judgment; the idea that Frank could have a police informant within his own ranks shows that he's an idiot who, for all his talk of flying low, has no idea how to keep his men in order and effectively run a business.
  • Frank's warning to Tony about not going to Sosa holds more water; he says that Sosa will send a hit squad after him if he fails to hold up his end of the deal, and that anyone who doesn't show complete obedience to Sosa will end up dead.
  • In the end, Tony goes with Sosa, but Frank's warnings about Sosa's vengeful nature come back to bite Tony in the ass when Tony refuses one of Sosa's orders and kills his underling— resulting in Tony and his empire being completely wiped out.

tropes.name: Bottomless Magazines
tropes.html: Uzi submachine guns are shot as though they had a several-foot-long belt in their magazines. Gun barrels would go red hot after so many bullets in one go note Al Pacino actually burned his hand pretty badly on the M16; you can see it in the film when he grabs the barrel after a burst of fire and then quickly lets go.; the Uzis don't. Tony's own M16 seems to have the equivalents of Phalanx CIWS ammunition domes for magazines, too. However, it should be noted that in the final shootout, Tony is shown reloading his rifle multiple times.

tropes.name: Bowdlerise
tropes.html:
The TV version, to wonderful extents.
  • Where'd you get that beauty scar, tough guy? Eating pineapple?
  • This town's like a great big chicken just waiting to get plucked.
  • Why don't you try... sticking your head in the toilet.
  • On some channels, the chainsaw scene was cut completely, skipping to him running outside.

tropes.name: Break the Haughty
tropes.html: Elvira has a breakdown in the restaurant.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html: Manny tells Elvira that Tony has been dragging him to the zoo to look at tigers and saying he's been thinking of buying one. In the "Push it to the Limit" montage, a tiger is shown tethered to a tree like a dog in Tony's yard.

tropes.name: Briefcase Full of Money
tropes.html: Or duffel bags, in this case— several of them. This is how Tony and his crew deliver cash to the bank for laundering.

tropes.name: Broken Bird
tropes.html:
• Gina. After Tony kills Manny, she completely loses it and tries to kill him.
  • Elvira as well. She gives off a vibe of deeply regretting many of her choices in life, as she bitterly refutes Tony's claim that America is the "land of opportunity". And, of course, there's her devastating and on-point "The Reason You Suck" Speech to Tony in her final scene in the restaurant.

tropes.name: Broken Pedestal
tropes.html:
• Gina was fully willing to look the other way at Tony's criminal activity (and as Tony found out, she wasn't exactly an angel herself). But as time went on, she realized what a terrible person he really was becoming.
  • Sosa to Tony. He considered Sosa as his equal partner and enjoyed their working relationship. But when Sosa offers to make Tony's legal problems go away if he carries out a hit on his cartel's behalf, Tony takes it as a personal insult and that Sosa always regarded him as a thug. Seeing no other options, though (and refusing to even consider jail time), he complies under duress.

tropes.name: Brooklyn Rage
tropes.html: Borderline with Frank Lopez. While Frank has the typical Cuban English accent, he can sometimes berate Tony with a New York accent, as well, with phrases like "coño my ass."

tropes.name: Brother–Sister Incest
tropes.html: Tony's violent protectiveness toward Gina has serious elements of this. She throws it in his face towards the climax after he killed Manny and had her brought to his house: she pretends to force herself onto Tony so she can kill him. It's more ambiguous than in the original film, though.

tropes.name: Bullying a Dragon
tropes.html: Although it's for a good reason, Tony defying Sosa's orders, killing one of his henchmen, and even screaming at him over the phone, despite knowing Sosa has many political connections and a much larger drug empire, and well after seeing him torture and kill Omar, is Tony walking headfirst into this trope.

tropes.name: But Not Too Foreign
tropes.html: Tony says that his father was American.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Richard Belzer as The Babylon Club emcee.

tropes.name: Canon Foreigner
tropes.html: Alejandro Sosa doesn't have an equivalent character in the original film, though he bears some resemblance to Inspector Guarino insofar as he becomes Tony's ultimate antagonist and the cause of death. In the original, Tony successfully killed off all potential rivals, and his death was at the hands of the police instead of other criminals.

tropes.name: The Cartel
tropes.html: Led by Sosa from Bolivia, and it is from there that Tony gets most of the drugs that he distributes. Tony is given a last chance mission to avoid jail time, and after he fails it, it is Sosa's cartel who send their men to kill Tony at the climax of the film.

tropes.name: Celebrity Paradox
tropes.html: One of Tony's men brags about once working with Marlon Brando on a movie. This is an obvious allusion to The Godfather, in which Pacino played Brando's son, Michael Corleone.

tropes.name: Chainsaw Good
tropes.html: Tony's friend Angel is killed with a chainsaw during his first drug deal in the States.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html:
• According to an interview by De Palma, Gina appears for the first time as the woman in the pink bikini in the beach scene, who Manny spots as she's walking away and points out to Tony (who hasn't seen Gina since she was a child and didn't recognize her at first), long before she appears more conservatively-dressed at the family house. According to De Palma, the scene was supposed to be a subtle indicator of Gina's promiscuity.
  • Two of Sosa's top killers, Alberto and "The Skull," appear briefly during Omar and Tony's visit to Sosa in Bolivia. They're the ones who beat Omar bloody and hang him from a helicopter. Alberto is later sent to do the New York assassination with help from Tony, and the Skull is the one who finally kills Tony.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Hobby
tropes.html: Tony's history as a soldier is mentioned twice at the beginning of the movie and becomes relevant in the finale when Tony is able to kill nearly twenty of Sosa's men.

tropes.name: The Chessmaster
tropes.html: Sosa, pretty much from his first scene. It's very heavily implied (e.g., by killing Omar on a questionable pretext) that his entire plan was to use Tony as his Miami distributor and to squeeze out existing rivals. He appeared to already have a massive hit squad practically ready and waiting in Miami to attack Tony's mansion at a moment's notice.

tropes.name: Cluster F-Bomb
tropes.html:
The entire movie. This video sums it all nicely.
  • Lampshaded by Elvira when she complains about Tony's swearing; at that point, it's the 107th f-bomb in the movie.
  • Notable for being the first movie ever to have over 200 uses of the word.

tropes.name: Conditioned to Accept Horror
tropes.html: Tony barely reacts to seeing Angel get dismembered with a chainsaw.

tropes.name: Conservation of Ninjutsu
tropes.html: Hector the Toad, as well as Thug army < Tony < The Skull.

tropes.name: Conspicuous Consumption
tropes.html: Tony goes all in for this after he takes over Lopez's operation. A huge mansion, tigers, and gaudy statuary on the grounds, a beauty salon for Gina, the works.

tropes.name: Contrast Montage
tropes.html: The movie cuts between scenes of the fun and raucous party in the nightclub and the boring conversation between Manny and Gina in the car.

tropes.name: Contrived Coincidence
tropes.html: The day Tony and Alberto are supposed to assassinate the journalist just happens to be the same day the journalist decides to take his wife and kids with him. Chi Chi, who has been spying on him for a while, tells Tony that the wife and children usually take the other car and has no idea why they're taking his car today. An ambiguous example since it's not clear if Sosa knew the target's wife and kids would be in the car with him.

tropes.name: Corrupt the Cutie
tropes.html: Tony's mother accuses Tony of "destroying" Gina.

tropes.name: Cutting Corners
tropes.html: One of the biggest mistakes in Tony's "Rise and Fall" Gangster Arc is his deciding to ditch Jerry, the banker who he was using to launder his money, when he needs to take a bigger commission to cover the laundering. Tony decides Jerry is just being greedy and finds a cheaper one, who happens to be an undercover DEA operative.

tropes.name: Crowd Panic
tropes.html: Happens at the nightclub when Frank tries to have Tony assassinated. Several people start freaking out and fleeing the area.

tropes.name: Dark Reprise
tropes.html: The music that plays when Gina is trying to kill Tony is her main theme of the movie, but in a darker and more eerie tone.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: Devil in Disguise, which covers Tony's Start of Darkness, is more serious and grim in tone than the movie. There's little in the way of levity in how it portrays both Castro's Cuba and the Mafiosos seeking to take him down through Tony.

tropes.name: Dead Guy on Display
tropes.html: Alejandro Sosa tells Tony Montana that his colleague Omar Suarez is a police informant. Sosa hands Montana binoculars so he can watch Suarez being thrown from a helicopter with a rope around his neck.

tropes.name: Deadly Euphemism
tropes.html: Tony tells Bernstein he's getting him a first class ticket to the resurrection.

tropes.name: Death by Irony
tropes.html: Tony falling from a relatively high ground over people around him into the swimming pool, next to a statue carrying a globe with his "The World Is Yours" motto.

tropes.name: Death Glare
tropes.html:
Tony does this twice.
  • First, when he sees Fernando groping Gina.
  • Second, when he finds out Manny has been sleeping with Gina.

tropes.name: Defensive "What?"
tropes.html:
Tony does this in response to the other restaurant patrons staring at him after Elvira throws a fit and leaves him.
Tony Montana: What you lookin' at?

tropes.name: Defiant to the End
tropes.html:
• Hector the Toad is unable to escape, being full of bullet holes and struggling to walk when Tony finds him. Hector yells at Tony, "I'll kill you!" before being shot to death in the head and body by Tony.
  • Even after dropping his M16 and being shot several times, Tony keeps yelling taunts and insults at Sosa's hitmen — right up to the moment the Skull unloads a double-barrel shotgun into his back.

tropes.name: Defrosting Ice Queen
tropes.html: Played with. It's made clear that Elvira doesn't love Tony so much as she tolerates him. He ends up taking her along after Frank's death, and the "Push It To The Limit" montage shows that she's more interested in indulging in her drug/alcohol habits instead. She later looks at their marriage and life as them being "losers" and leaves, despite Tony's efforts to make her stay. But there were times when they started to get along— a key scene in support of this trope is when Tony succeeds in making Elvira laugh in spite of herself when he puts on her hat.

tropes.name: Dehumanizing Insult
tropes.html: Sosa calls Tony a monkey over the phone after the latter screws him over.

tropes.name: Descent into Addiction
tropes.html: Tony and Elvira become addicted to cocaine as he rises up the ranks of the dealers/distributors.

tropes.name: Despair Event Horizon
tropes.html: When Tony finds Manny and Gina together, he kills Manny in a fit of anger. The reason why it fits here instead of Moral Event Horizon is that, during his Villainous Breakdown, he regrets acting on impulse like that. He truly passes it when one of Sosa's men kills Gina, culminating in an Unstoppable Rage.

tropes.name: Deuteragonist
tropes.html: Manny Ribera, Tony's best friend and right-hand man.

tropes.name: Didn't Think This Through
tropes.html: Tony shows up at his mother's house in a fancy suit, not thinking this will raise suspicion as to how he got the money to buy that as an illegal immigrant.

tropes.name: Dies Differently in Adaptation
tropes.html: In the original 1932 version, Tony Camonte meets his end when the police gun him down. However, in the remake, Tony Montana's demise comes at the hands of Sosa's minions who shoot him to death.

tropes.name: Disproportionate Retribution
tropes.html: Tony shoots Manny when he finds out the latter has been sleeping with Gina.

tropes.name: Dirty Cop
tropes.html:
• Mel Bernstein, a narcotics cop who's in league with Lopez.
  • In Scarred for Life, Harley Wabash and Deacon Tooms are two corrupt DEA agents who aren't above Police Brutality or sniffing "evidence" if it means using Tony as a pawn to get at Sosa. Tony eventually tries to kill them when he proves to be beyond their ability to control though Tooms survives to track him down in Bolivia with a full strike team.

tropes.name: Doomed Moral Victor
tropes.html: Played with: Tony does not kill the Bolivian anti-drug activist, with the circumstances leading to Tony's death.

tropes.name: Downer Ending
tropes.html: Where to begin? Tony was disowned by his mother, his sister and his best friend are dead (with the latter by Tony's hands), his empire is in ruins, and he finally dies after a massive shootout with Sosa's men.

tropes.name: The Dragon
tropes.html:
• The Skull, for Sosa.
  • Manny Ribera becomes Tony's right-hand man in his emerging drug empire. He's relatively tame for a villain.

tropes.name: Dramatic Gun Cock
tropes.html: Tony, holding Frank at gunpoint, does this after Frank admits to setting up the hit on him.

tropes.name: Dramatic Irony
tropes.html: In Devil in Disguise, a young Tony is offered a deal by the Mob to have Castro killed in exchange for safe passage to the US. While he ultimately rejects the deal upon learning of the CIA's involvement in favor of another solution (and comes out of it in one piece), he's nowhere near as lucky when he's roped into a similar predicament by Alejandro Sosa, especially when he's in no position to refuse.

tropes.name: Dramatically Missing the Point
tropes.html:
When Manny turns Gina down because he wants her to find a decent guy and stay away from the gangster life, she asks him if he's afraid of Tony and then asks him if he's afraid of her.
Manny: Hey! I'm not afraid of anybody, okay? That's not the point here!

tropes.name: Drone of Dread
tropes.html: The score uses this, particularly whenever Tony sees his sister Gina cavorting with another man.

tropes.name: Drugs Are Bad
tropes.html: Everything starts going downhill for Tony when he starts getting high on his own supply.

tropes.name: Dude, Where's My Respect?
tropes.html:
Manny's reaction to being told by Tony to stay out of the Seidelbaum negotiation.
Manny: What the fuck are you talking about, okay? I'm your partner, okay? You're not gonna trust me with that kind of thing, who the fuck you're gonna trust?

tropes.name: Dying Alone
tropes.html: Tony gets shot in the back after losing everything and descending to madness trying to stay in power. Shortly before that, he picks up the phone on his office desk for a moment, then sets it back down. There's nobody left to call: Manny and Gina are dead, Frank is dead, Sosa wants him killed, his mother has disowned him, and Elvira has left him for good. Tony has absolutely nobody left.

tropes.name: Dying Moment of Awesome
tropes.html:
• A coked-up Tony, armed with an M16 with a grenade launcher, singlehandedly battles a small army of hitmen while shouting obscenities before a shotgun blast to the back kills him. It's easily the most iconic scene in the movie.
  • When given the opportunity to escape from Sosa’s assassins, Nick instead opts to stay behind and briefly attempts to hold some of them off with just a pistol before being murdered by The Skull.

tropes.name: Emotional Language Shift
tropes.html:
Tony and other Cuban characters lapse into Spanish when surprised or annoyed.
Tony: ¿Qué te pasa? TranslationWhat's wrong with you?

tropes.name: Ending by Ascending
tropes.html: Inverted. The movie ends with The Skull descending Tony's staircase.

tropes.name: Epic Launch Sequence
tropes.html: The eponymous boats leaving Mariel harbor.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html:
• Tony seems like a harmless petty crook at the beginning of the movie… until he stabs Rebenga.
  • Tony sees that Sosa is not to be messed with when the latter has a man hung from a helicopter.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Loved Ones
tropes.html: Tony tries to take care of those he loves even as he becomes a bigger criminal and acts like a general jerk. His affection for Gina, in particular, is very strong, although laced with incestuous implications. Subverted and deconstructed later in the film, as he eventually becomes a malignant presence in their lives when he drives Elvira away, kills Manny because he proposed to Gina, and locks Gina up in his own mansion out of an obsession with "protecting" her.

tropes.name: Even Bad Men Love Their Mamas
tropes.html: Tony tries to provide for his mother, but the relationship is strained due to her being aware of Tony's criminal activities. She refuses any money and demands he leave.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html:
• Tony does not kill women or kids, which gets him in serious trouble with Sosa. Carries over to The World Is Yours. Men too, so long as they're "not stupid enough to fuck with [Tony]."
  • Ernie is clearly horrified and even a little bit choked-up when he sees that Tony has just impulsively murdered Manny.

tropes.name: Evil Has a Bad Sense of Humor
tropes.html:
Tony has a dark sense of humor.
Tony: I kill a communist for fun, but for a green card... I'm gonna carve him up real nice.

tropes.name: Evil Versus Evil
tropes.html:
Tony is no saint, but Sosa and the other gangsters are worse.
Tony Montana: What you lookin' at? You all a bunch of fuckin' assholes. D'you know why? You don't have the guts to be what you wanna be. You need people like me. You need people like me so you can point your fuckin' fingers and say, "That's the bad guy." So... what that make you? Good? You're not good. You just know how to hide, how to lie. Me, I don't have that problem. Me, I always tell the truth. Even when I lie. So say good night to the bad guy! Come on. The last time you gonna see a bad guy like this again, let me tell you. Come on. Make way for the bad guy. There's a bad guy comin' through! Better get outta his way!

tropes.name: Exact Words
tropes.html:
Frank begs Tony not to kill him right before the latter takes control of his entire operation, and Tony tells Frank that he won't kill him. Manny will.
Tony: Manolo, shoot that piece of shit!

tropes.name: The Exile
tropes.html: Tony and Manny. The movie begins with them and a bunch of other criminals being exiled from Cuba.

tropes.name: Face Death with Dignity
tropes.html:
• Before Manny and Chi Chi arrive and save the day, Tony seems to have gotten comfortable with the idea of being dismembered with a chainsaw.
  • While clearly sweating buckets and fidgeting with terror after Tony and Manny have killed Frank and then Mel, Ernie never sobs or begs for his life like they both did (although the latter of whom recanted and angrily cussed at Tony before being killed), instead just keeping quiet and bracing himself for the inevitable. His courage in the face of death could have even been a possible reason for why Tony decided to spare his life and offer him a job instead of killing him.

tropes.name: Face Palm
tropes.html: Shortly after Tony kills Manny, Tony buries his face in his hands and says "Oh Manny. Why'd the fuck I do that?"

tropes.name: Fade to Black
tropes.html: Happens after Tony sees the "The World is Yours" blimp.

tropes.name: Fan Disservice
tropes.html: As a large group of heavily armed men sent by Sosa slowly surround Tony's villa, Gina shows up in front of Tony, drugged-up on pills and nearly naked (wearing only panties and a bathrobe), confronting Tony with extreme hate, no longer willing to live and wanting him dead, too.

tropes.name: Faux Affably Evil
tropes.html: Alejandro Sosa is a superficially affable drug lord who always keeps a polite tone even as he hangs Omar Suarez from a helicopter.

tropes.name: First-Name Ultimatum
tropes.html:
• Tony's mom only ever calls him "Antonio".
  • Manny is referred to as "Manolo" whenever things get serious.

tropes.name: Flippant Forgiveness
tropes.html:
After Tony kills Manny, a distraught Gina walks into his office partially nude with a pistol in her hand, pretends to forgive him and acts as if she's inviting him to fuck her.
Gina: Is this what you want, Tony? You can't stand for another man to be touching me. So you want me, Tony?
Tony: What you talking?
Gina: Oh, is that it? I'm all yours now, Tony. I’m all yours now!

tropes.name: Food Slap
tropes.html: Elvira throws a glass of water in Tony's face during their argument in the restaurant.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
• When Frank tells Tony that Sosa will send a squad of hitmen after him if he doesn't make good on the new deal that Tony negotiated with Sosa on his behalf. Guess what happens to Tony at the end?
  • While Frank and Tony hit it off famously at first, Tony privately tells Manny later that while he likes Frank, he thinks that Frank's too soft to be a major player for long. Tony is proven to be correct.
  • An immigration officer points out Tony's pitchfork tattoo and says it means "an assassin or something". Tony is soon revealed to be a ruthless killer.

tropes.name: Forced from Their Home
tropes.html: Shortly after letting him inside and seeing that he hasn't given up his criminal ways, Tony's mom kicks him out and tells him she doesn't want him in her house.

tropes.name: Forced to Watch
tropes.html: Tony is cuffed to a shower pole and forced to watch Angel get dismembered with a chainsaw.

tropes.name: Foreign Cuss Word
tropes.html:
Used several times throughout the movie:
  • "'Cause you've got your head up your culo [Spanish for buttocks], that's why."
  • "Coño" (Spanish for cunt/damn) is said 15 times.
  • "Last chance, pendejo [motherfucker in Spanish]!"
  • "Maricón" (Spanish for faggot) is said twice.
  • "I'm no fucking criminal. I'm no puto [Spanish for male prostitute] or thief."
  • "¡Quieto! ¡No te muevas, cabroncito!" (Spanish for "Stop! Don't move, you little motherfucker!")

tropes.name: Foreign-Language Tirade
tropes.html: After berating Tony for corrupting Gina, Tony's mom starts yelling at him in Spanish.

tropes.name: Foreign Remake
tropes.html: Bollywood's Agneepath (1990), albeit somewhat loosely.

tropes.name: Friendless Background
tropes.html: Subverted with Elvira. Tony assumes she has no friends and offers to be hers, but she tells him she has enough friends.

tropes.name: From Camouflage to Criminal
tropes.html: Before coming to America, Tony was in the Cuban Army and was a veteran of the Cuban intervention in the Angolan Civil War.

tropes.name: George Lucas Altered Version
tropes.html: The soundtrack was revamped for the movie's 20th anniversary, with some music removed and all gunshot sounds being replaced. Up until the release of the Blu-ray, this mix was utilized in all future releases of the film (and to its credit, the Blu-ray release presents the original mix as a 2.0 stereo track).

tropes.name: Get Out!
tropes.html:
• Tony's mother throws him out after he tries to offer her and Gina some of the money he's been making.
  • When Tony catches Gina in the restroom with Fernando, he grabs Fernando and tells him to get out.

tropes.name: Getting High on Their Own Supply
tropes.html:
The Trope Namer. Tony Montana is the most well-known victim of this trope in fiction.
Frank: Lesson number one: Don't underestimate the OTHER guy's greed!
Elvira: Lesson number two: Don't get high on your own supply.

tropes.name: Gilligan Cut
tropes.html: When Tony gets busted in a sting, complete with laundering on camera, he boasts to the agents that his lawyer will easily get him off the hook and that the feds will soon be working in Alaska, so "dress warm". The next scene has Tony's lawyer admitting that the case against Tony would be so airtight that the best he could do for Tony would be 3-5 years in prison.

tropes.name: Gold Digger
tropes.html: Elvira only seems to be interested in men who are rich. Starting out as Frank's mistress, she then later becomes Tony's wife after his newfound wealth.

tropes.name: Good Colors, Evil Colors
tropes.html: The poster is half black and half white to symbolize Tony's ambiguous morality.

tropes.name: Good Scars, Evil Scars
tropes.html: Subverted. Tony has a huge scar on one side of his face; at the very beginning of the film, he says he got it in an accident when he was a child.

tropes.name: Good-Times Montage
tropes.html: Push it to the limit! The LIMIT!

tropes.name: Gory Discretion Shot
tropes.html:
• The chainsaw scene is a shining example; not even DePalma would include such a violent act in his movie. It's easy to forget that we don't actually see what the chainsaw does to Angel.
  • When Nick the Pig begins to fire on Sosa's men invading the compound, The Skull sneaks up on him, levels his shotgun mere inches from Nick's head, and the camera moves Nick out of frame before The Skull kills him.

tropes.name: Gratuitous Spanish
tropes.html: Plenty of Spanish words are casually inserted among otherwise English dialogue and phrases.

tropes.name: Grenade Launcher
tropes.html:
Tony's M203 in the final battle.
Tony Montana: Say 'ello to my little friend!

tropes.name: Guns Do Not Work That Way
tropes.html: The "unshattered glass" version of the trope shows up when Tony shoots Alberto to keep him from blowing up a car containing their target's wife and kids; blood and brain matter appears on the window behind the assassin, but the glass stays perfectly intact.

tropes.name: Gut Feeling
tropes.html: During the drug deal, Hector initially acts overly friendly, but his body language shows he is quite nervous. Tony picks up on this, as well as Marta's stoic gaze, that something is not right here.

tropes.name: Heh Heh, You Said "X"
tropes.html: Tony is rather amused by a news anchor’s use of the phrase "finger in the dike".

tropes.name: Hair-Trigger Temper
tropes.html:
• Tony is aggressive and is almost always on the brink of a cocaine-fueled rage. Nearly everything sets him off, especially people who go near his sister. Not even his best friend Manny is safe from this, as Tony kills him on the spot as soon as he sees them together.
  • Omar tries to pull a gun on Tony after their first altercation.

tropes.name: Heel Realization
tropes.html:
On top of his drug-addled Villainous Breakdown at the end of the film, the two "what if" sequels explore Tony coming to terms with his inner demons after surviving his canonical death, but in very different directions.
  • The World is Yours has Tony undergo Character Development, realizing that his actions brought about the deaths of (and alienation from) those he loved or cared about. This leads him to become more of a Noble Demon, particularly by not Getting High on Their Own Supply again and making an effort to learn from his mistakes.
  • Scarred for Life has Tony instead pinning the blame entirely on Sosa and everyone but himself. This leads him to become even more unhinged (including doubling-down on his drug addiction), though not entirely, as he still feels genuine remorse for treating Elvira poorly upon seeing her again and tries not to piss off too many people until the end.

tropes.name: The Hero Dies
tropes.html: Tony does indeed die at the end.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html: Chi Chi dies fighting off Sosa's assassins.

tropes.name: Heterosexual Life-Partners
tropes.html: Tony and Manny.

tropes.name: Hiding Behind the Language Barrier
tropes.html:
• It's evident that most people at the refugee camp don't understand English since nobody reacts to Tony and Manny's conversation about getting green cards.
  • At the beach, Tony calls a bikini-clad woman "sabrosura" (tasty).
  • After Elvira tells Tony that Frank never talked about money, Manny says something to Tony in Spanish.

tropes.name: Hoist by His Own Petard
tropes.html: Mel arrogantly plays both sides in the growing Lopez/Montana feud, trying to shake down both men simultaneously and then doing nothing to protect Lopez when Tony gets the upper hand. Even after Tony has Lopez killed in cold blood, Mel continues to assume his job title makes him untouchable. Wrong.

tropes.name: Hookers and Blow
tropes.html: The film pretty much runs on this trope, given the nature of Tony Montana's work and... leisure activities.

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: The end of the film. Tony looks like he might be able to hold out against the gangsters besieging his mansion, even standing up to a hail of gunfire. Then the Skull empties a shotgun into his back.

tropes.name: Hotter and Sexier
tropes.html: Being set in 1980's Florida instead of 1930's Chicago helps.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html:
• Tony. He rages at his sister Gina for partying at the same nightclub he does and at Elvira for abusing drugs despite snorting mountains of cocaine himself and previously not doing anything to stop her.
    • He cuts ties with Jerry and his bank because he doesn't want to pay extra, and yet when Tony gets busted in a sting operation, not only does he pay a five million dollar bail he offers to double his lawyer's initial fees because he's that desperate to avoid any jailtime (which his lawyer bluntly informs him is impossible).
  • Elvira, to a lesser extent. She tells Tony that becoming a millionaire has made him unable to stop talking about money, but the only reason she married him in the first place was because of his newfound wealth.

tropes.name: Hypocrite Has a Point
tropes.html:
• While Tony rages at Gina for going to the same nightclub he goes to, he did do her a favor as she was about to have unprotected sex with a drug dealer.
  • It's not like Elvira would be together with Frank or marry Tony if they weren't rich and powerful like a drug lord, but she's not wrong when she points out what an asshole Tony has become as time has gone on.

tropes.name: I Have No Son!
tropes.html:
• When Tony meets his mother in America, she disowns him because of his criminal lifestyle.
    Tony's Mother: Son? I wish I had one! He's a bum! He was a bum then and he's a bum now!
  • Also Tony inverts this with his opinion of his Disappeared Dad.
    Tony: Forget Papa. We never had one.

tropes.name: I Just Want My Beloved to Be Happy
tropes.html: Manny's reason for initially rejecting Gina is that he thinks she's too good for him.

tropes.name: I Just Want to Be Free
tropes.html: Before he gets involved in the Miami drug trade and becomes greedy and power-hungry, all Tony wants is freedom.

tropes.name: I Need a Freaking Drink
tropes.html: After witnessing the deaths of Frank and Bernstein, Ernie (one of Frank's men) is sure he'll be next. When Tony offers him a job instead, he picks up a bottle of whiskey and takes a long pull from it.

tropes.name: Ice Queen
tropes.html: Elvira. She's aloof and sarcastic, making plenty of jabs at Tony and Lopez. Given that both men are powerful drug dealers, one can understand her disdain (hypocritical though it may be).

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html:
• Deliberately ignoring Tony's warnings about getting it on with his sister was never going to end well for Manny. And by this point, he was well aware that his friend had a hair-trigger temper that could go from zero to murder in the span of moments.
  • Tony, having already seen what happens to anyone even suspected of disloyalty to Sosa, decides to go against him in New York and kills his henchman in order to save a journalist's life. The consequences are disastrous.

tropes.name: An Immigrant's Tale
tropes.html: Tony Montana is an illegal immigrant who was exiled from Cuba and arrives in Miami, Florida.

tropes.name: Implacable Man
tropes.html: Tony in the end, from the huge amounts of cocaine he took.

tropes.name: Improbable Infant Survival
tropes.html: Thanks to Tony's firm, if twisted, moral code.

tropes.name: Innocently Insensitive
tropes.html: When Tony is already in a bad mood, he hears the nightclub stand-up comedian say "But my favorite Cuban of all time has to be Ricky Ricardo", which only makes him feel worse.

tropes.name: Instant Death Bullet
tropes.html:
• In the chainsaw scene, two of the mooks are killed instantly by single bullets when Tony's friends come to save him.
  • Tony has Manny kill Frank after the failed hit on Tony at the nightclub. He is killed with a single shot from a silenced pistol.
  • Tony kills Sosa's hitman "Shadow" before he can remotely detonate the bomb in the car of an activist threatening to expose Sosa. Tony shoots him through the head, killing him instantly.
  • The final scene where Sosa's army of hired killers storm Tony's mansion, killing Tony's men, several on both sides are felled by single instant death bullets.
  • Tony kills many of Sosa's men directly in his retaliatory rampage after Gina is killed by one of Sosa's assassins coming through Tony's office window. Tony, despite wildly firing from the hip on full auto from an M-16, manages to kill several of Sosa's men instantly with a single shot each.
  • There are several aversions throughout the film where certain characters are killed with multiple gunshots. The most notable example is Tony's own death at the very end.

tropes.name: Insulting from Behind the Language Barrier
tropes.html:
• After Alberto refuses to go with Tony's suggestion to wait until the journalist is alone so they can kill him without killing his wife and children, Tony tells Ernie and Chi Chi "This fucking guy" since he knows Alberto doesn't understand English.
  • Zigzagged at the climax. Tony switches between insulting the assassins (who only understand Spanish) in Spanish and English.

tropes.name: In the Back
tropes.html:
• After taking numerous machine gun bullets during the climax, Tony is finally put down by a shotgun blast to the back from the enigmatic henchman the Skull.
  • Chi Chi gets shot in this fashion when he tries desperately to pound on the door to Tony's office as Sosa's henchmen attack the compound.

tropes.name: Intimidating Revenue Service
tropes.html: Tony can survive rival cartels, threats from within and even the legal service. What he can't fight is a tax evasion charge.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html:
In introducing him to the world of crime, Frank tells Tony that Nacho Contreras is a "chazzer", a Yiddish word for "pig" which describes someone who doesn't fly straight. Tony repeats the description to Frank after surviving the latter's attempt to have him killed.
Tony: You know what a chazzer is, Frank? That's a pig that don't fly straight.

tropes.name: It's All About Me
tropes.html:
• Tony's motivation for marrying Elvira is to show everyone he can conquer her, and his overprotectiveness of Gina stems from her being the only pure thing in his life.
  • Elvira almost entirely motivated by self-interest and material wealth, caring neither about Frank nor Tony for who they are as people, and only about the status she gets from them.

tropes.name: It's Cuban
tropes.html: Tony becomes such a powerful and wealthy drug lord that he can afford Cuban cigars.

tropes.name: It's Snowing Cocaine
tropes.html: Near the climax of the film, Tony is seen surrounded by piles and piles of cocaine (which makes sense since he's a dealer), and uses it to take and inflict a lot of punishment before he goes down.

tropes.name: Just in Time
tropes.html: Manny and Chi Chi arrive and shoot Hector and Marta just when the former is about to kill Tony with a chainsaw.

tropes.name: Karma Houdini
tropes.html:
• Sosa... until the games and Scarred For Life. However, it can be inferred that Sosa would have been arrested since he failed to assassinate the journalist who would have implicated him.
  • Jerry the banker is no longer employed by Tony because of the increased fees he wanted to charge Tony due to his claiming that bank regulators are getting suspicious, but there is no comeuppance shown in Jerry being a money launderer for a drug lord.
  • Manny, briefly. He talks Tony into switching bankers to Seidelbaum, who turns out to be an undercover cop who gets Tony into the legal trouble that indirectly leads to his downfall. Manny could legitimately have been killed for that alone. Of course, none of this matters once Tony sees him and Gina together.
  • Inverted with Mel, who thinks he's getting off easy after Tony and Manny kill Frank in retaliation for an assassination plot. Then Tony decides to pop a sudden bullet in his stomach, then gives him a second shot in the heart to finish him off for good.

tropes.name: Karmic Death
tropes.html: Frank Lopez dies in almost the exact same scenario he had tried to kill Tony in: he has someone else do the job for him.

tropes.name: Kick the Dog
tropes.html: Sosa's henchmen Alberto and the wife and children that would have been in the exploding car.

tropes.name: Lady Looks Like a Dude
tropes.html: Tony tells Gina that the last time he saw her, she looked like a little boy.

tropes.name: Language Fluency Denial
tropes.html: Discussed. Tony tells Manny he should have kept his mouth shut during the immigration interview.

tropes.name: The Last Dance
tropes.html: Tony's last stand.

tropes.name: Lonely at the Top
tropes.html: In spades. Even Tony lampshades this when he's sitting miserably in a restaurant with his wife and the closest he had to a proper friend who can barely stand him at this point.

tropes.name: Love at First Sight
tropes.html: After laying eyes on Gina for the first time, Manny tells Tony she's beautiful and wonders why Tony never mentioned her.

tropes.name: Made of Iron
tropes.html:
• Tony at the end, due to being seriously coked-up.
  • Hector the Toad absorbs roughly half of a magazine from Manny's submachine gun, and then falls three stories out of a window. He still just barely has enough left in him to walk a short distance before Tony finds him and finishes him off in the street.

tropes.name: Major Injury Underreaction
tropes.html: Tony Montana is shot a number of times through the torso. As he is currently high on cocaine, it just makes him angry.

tropes.name: Malaproper
tropes.html: During his first meeting and initial negotiations with Sosa, Tony describes how smuggling coke over the waters of Panama is so much riskier because of Naval surveillance. He states that "it's no duckwalk anymore" (as opposed to "cakewalk").

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: The surname "Montana" is Spanish for "mountain".

tropes.name: Mo' Money, Mo' Problems
tropes.html: Played for Drama, where money is shown to corrupt people inside and out. In the second half of the film after the Good-Times Montage of Tony becoming more rich and powerful, the next scene shows Tony desperate to keep his money, eventually turning to a DEA sting operation that leads to a string of undoing events, culminating in Tony alienating everyone and getting everyone he loves killed.

tropes.name: Mood Whiplash
tropes.html:
• Tony's reunion with his family goes downhill when his mom asks him “Who did you kill for this, Antonio?” after he hands her a wad of cash, which she rejects and then starts yelling at him before kicking him out of the house.
  • Tony is almost assassinated at the nightclub.

tropes.name: Montage
tropes.html: The song appears in the film in the montage sequence that demonstrates Tony Montana's rise in wealth and position after he kills Frank Lopez (Robert Loggia) and takes over as the head cocaine trafficker in Miami.

tropes.name: Morton's Fork
tropes.html: Even if Alberto wanted to spare Gutierrez' family, it's not like he had a whole lot of choice in the matter— missing their shot would've probably just put him in Sosa's crosshairs along with Tony.

tropes.name: Motor Mouth
tropes.html: Tony. He likes to talk for whoever is in earshot. Lampshaded by Alberto, who tells him to shut his mouth when he's talking about how sick it is to kill a mother and her children. At this point he's speaking in English, a language that Alberto doesn't understand, but Ernie and Chi Chi do.

tropes.name: Ms. Fanservice
tropes.html: Manny's girlfriend/hookup doesn't do much for the story but gives male viewers a nice ass and boobs to look at.

tropes.name: Multiple Gunshot Death
tropes.html: Tony takes several magazine's worth of bullets in the raid on his mansion before The Skull shoots him In the Back with a shotgun. The mound of cocaine he snorted beforehand probably helped.

tropes.name: My God, What Have I Done?
tropes.html: When Tony fully realizes that he killed Manny in a rage, he immediately wishes he could take it back.

tropes.name: My Sister Is Off-Limits
tropes.html: Gina, according to Tony.

tropes.name: Nebulous Criminal Conspiracy
tropes.html:
• When Sosa meets with Tony in Bolivia to plan the assassination of the journalist, others present are several high-ranking political, military, and business figures in Bolivia and their "friend from Washington," and it's stated that other "friends" they have in Washington can make sure Tony doesn't have to do any jail time on the charges he's facing.
  • Devil in Disguise has the Mafia (and the US government indirectly) plotting to have Fidel Castro killed, settling on having a Cuban like Tony do the job. When he learns of the CIA being involved, however, he refuses, as that wasn't part of the original deal.

tropes.name: Never Going Back to Prison
tropes.html: What motivates Tony into a new deal with Sosa, as Tony can't stomach jail anymore, not even a short three-year stint.

tropes.name: Never Hurt an Innocent
tropes.html:
Never Hurt an Innocent: Tony follows this rule.
Tony: I never fucked anybody over in my life that didn't have it coming to 'em.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Title
tropes.html: There's a very brief exchange of two lines of dialogue in the opening scene calling attention to Tony's facial scar. It's never mentioned again and the fact that he has a scar has no bearing on anything else that happens in the movie. It's just there to justify the title of the film, which is, of course, a loose remake of the 1932 film that was much more obviously about an Al Capone stand-in.

tropes.name: Nice Job Fixing It, Villain!
tropes.html: Sosa asks Tony to assist Alberto with the assassination of a journalist since the latter doesn't understand English. What Sosa didn't count on was that the target's wife and kids would be with him. Tony calls off the assassination, telling Alberto they should wait until the journalist is alone so they can kill him without killing his wife and children. Alberto refuses to go with Tony's suggestion, saying that if Sosa says they do it now, they should do it now. Tony obeys Alberto, but kills him just before the latter can blow up the car. While Tony's intent was only to save the guy's wife and children, Sosa mentions that the journalist found the bomb under his car and has hired security and will expose his drug operation on national television.

tropes.name: No Antagonist
tropes.html: All of the conflicts in the movie come from Tony's ambition and self-destructive tendencies. All of his enemies (with the exception of Rebenga and Hector the Toad) are former friends whom he betrays on his own accord. Frank was a Benevolent Boss who took Tony in when he had nothing and only turned on him when Tony undermined his authority too many times. Sosa was his closest ally and protected him from the law enforcement, only for Tony's Honor Before Reason tendency to blow it and land his friend in hot water.
