Even Tony's legal troubles come solely from his greed and ego preventing him from just paying the money launderer his cut.

tropes.name: No Full Name Given
tropes.html:
Several examples.
  • Hector the Toad.
  • Alberto the Shadow.
  • Subverted with Tony's mom. Her first name is given as Georgina in the Closing Credits.

tropes.name: No Good Deed Goes Unpunished
tropes.html:
• Tony commits exactly two semi-decent acts over the course of the entire film, both of which kick back on him. He tries to give some money to his mother, only for her to disown him. Later, he refuses to help kill the journalist's wife and kids, leading Sosa to declare war on him.
  • Frank takes Tony in when he was a two-bit dishwasher and gives him his start in the crime business. In return, Tony makes a dangerous deal behind his back, possibly colludes with a rival to kill his right-hand man (Tony didn't, but Frank has no way of knowing that), tries stealing his girlfriend and then openly disrespects him in front of said girlfriend. It's no wonder that Frank feels the need to have Tony killed to protect his authority and his business.

tropes.name: No, You
tropes.html:
Elvira does when Tony tells her she is stoned. He is, but so is she.
Tony: Go home. You're stoned.
Elvira: I'm not stoned. You're stoned.

tropes.name: Noodle Incident
tropes.html: We never do learn how Tony got that scar... though given his nature, there are many plausible scenarios. In the novelization of the film script, however, we learn that Tony got it from the husband of a woman he was having an affair with back in Cuba.

tropes.name: Not Helping Your Case
tropes.html: Sosa calls Tony a monkey. Tony's reaction? To start chimping out.

tropes.name: Not What I Signed Up For
tropes.html: In Devil in Disguise, Tony is shown to have made a deal with a Mafioso to have Castro killed in exchange for easy passage into America. When he finds out the CIA's involved, however, Tony is quick to bail, though not before killing the Mob contact.

tropes.name: Not What It Looks Like
tropes.html: After killing Angel, Hector tries to kill Tony and is shot several times by Manny but survives and manages to escape the building. Tony runs outside, catches him up to him, and shoots him in the head, much to the shock of several bystanders. To them, it looks like a Conspicuously Public Assassination, but it is actually a revenge shooting that just happened to be in public.

tropes.name: Novelization
tropes.html: By Paul Monette.

tropes.name: Number Two
tropes.html: Manny to Tony.

tropes.name: Offscreen Moment of Awesome
tropes.html: Gina tells Tony that she and Manny are married— only after Tony has killed Manny.

tropes.name: Offscreen Villainy
tropes.html: Rebenga's background as a military torturer in communist Cuba is only ever mentioned and is never shown onscreen.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
• Not said, but Ernie and Chi Chi definitely looked at each other to convey this when Tony blew Alberto's head off to effectively call off the hit they were supposed to perform.
  • Tony's banker displays a more subdued type of this expression during the Good-Times Montage. At first, when Tony and the crew bring huge duffle bags full of cash into the bank, he's eager to meet with them and start up a business relationship. As they keep making visit after visit, though, he stares out the window at them with a completely stunned look on his face, since the bank is a legitimate business and the effort to launder Tony's obscene wealth would draw the wrong kind of attention.

tropes.name: One-Man Army
tropes.html: Tony becomes this in the final scene.

tropes.name: Only Known by Their Nickname
tropes.html: Sosa's top henchman is only known as The Skull.

tropes.name: Only Sane Woman
tropes.html: Tony's mother. She's the most level-headed character in the movie.

tropes.name: Oppressive Immigration Enforcement
tropes.html: The movie begins during the "Mariel Boatlift" in 1980, a mass exodus of Cuban refugees caused by several factors, including an economic downturn in Cuba, former immigrants trying to bring their families to the U.S, and the Castro regime seeing an opportunity to get rid of their "undesirable" citizens. Regardless of origin, the refugees end up herded into poorly funded camps like "Liberty City" in Miami and are generally treated as subhuman, especially by immigration officials, who see them as Fidel Castro "dumping his garbage" on the United States. However, while most of the refugees are portrayed as innocent victims of xenophobia and racism, others, such as Villain Protagonist Tony "Scarface" Montana, Manny Ray, Angel, and Chi-Chi, are all genuine criminals with no legitimate claim for citizenship.

tropes.name: Orange/Blue Contrast
tropes.html: In the scene of Frank Lopez's death, Tony's sky-blue suit strongly pops out against the meeting room's tropical sunset wallpaper.

tropes.name: Out-of-Context Eavesdropping
tropes.html: It isn't really clear if the assassin who killed Gina understood English; even if he did, he didn't know Gina was Tony's sister or that Tony had just killed her husband, and she never really says anything that makes it clear that she's trying to kill Tony.

tropes.name: Outliving One's Offspring
tropes.html: Mama Montana is last seen crying at her doorstep, so it's very likely she lives to the end.

tropes.name: Parental Abandonment
tropes.html: Tony's father has left the family.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html: Tony giving Ernie a job after blowing away Frank and Mel Bernstein right in front of him. Also Tony killing Alberto rather than letting him blow up a car with two children in it.

tropes.name: Plausible Deniability
tropes.html: Tony is roped into a ploy by the Mafia (and indirectly, the US government) to have Fidel Castro killed in the prequel Devil in Disguise, believing that it would be easier (and more convenient to deny in the event of failure) if a Cuban assassin were to do it. Upon finding out the CIA's involved, however, Tony abandons the deal and kills his Mob contact, deciding to take his chances by crossing over with his friends instead.

tropes.name: Police Are Useless
tropes.html: Despite Tony executing Hector the Toad in broad daylight in front of over a hundred witnesses, he's never connected to the murder. Additionally, none of them seem to notice how in the climax his estate becomes a massive warzone. The only police officer to play any role in the story is Mel Bernstein, and he's on Frank's payroll and Tony has him killed with no blowback.

tropes.name: Politically Incorrect Villain
tropes.html: According to Tony, he does not like working with Colombians. He also derisively refers to Italians as "Guineas" (which is funny considering Pacino himself is an Italian American). In everyday life, he is a foulmouthed drug-dealing guy with increasing amounts of prick characteristics and was this close to officially being a wife beater in an argument at a restaurant.

tropes.name: Pre-Mortem One-Liner
tropes.html: The famous quote under ''Memetic Mutation.”

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html:
• One of the assassins at the Babylon Club is seen drinking Bavarian Löwenbräu beer. In the scene where Tony demands the money to be recounted, the box which houses the money is a Löwenbräu.
  • Tony Montana's mansion is equipped with a Sanyo video surveillance system.
  • There's a Pan Am blimp that seduces Tony with the promise that “The World Is Yours.” In a later scene, Pan Am appears again, but this time it’s a mere helicopter, and it’s coming in for a landing.

tropes.name: Profane Last Words
tropes.html: From Bernstein, Gina, and Tony himself.

tropes.name: Properly Paranoid
tropes.html: Subverted in Scarred for Life. He makes a more conscious effort to not only be more careful in his choice of allies but invests extensively in security to avoid being caught off-guard. These all fail in deterring Sosa, however, though Tony's brash efforts to claw back up inadvertently drawing his attention don't help either.

tropes.name: Psycho Serum
tropes.html: The partial-Implacability through cocaine.

tropes.name: "Psycho" Strings
tropes.html: The creepy tune that picks up every time Tony notices a guy hanging around Gina a little too closely.

tropes.name: Race Traitor
tropes.html:
• A reoccurring element throughout the film is Tony being treated like crap for being a poor migrant on account of being fresh off the boat— it's what motivates him to move into crime. Later, he meets drug kingpin Sosa, an upper-class, white Bolivian snob who speaks English perfectly and hobnobs with other elites and treats Tony like a guard dog: a useful, loyal tool. Upper-class non-mestizo in Latin America are stereotyped to be backstabbing elitist asshats, and sure enough, when Tony is facing prison, Sosa forces Tony into an unwinnable situation that either forces him to commit a heinous deed against his morals for a crime he'll likely go to jail for anyway, or betray him.
  • Tony's mother accuses him of giving Cubans everywhere a bad name, and one of the cops who arrest him for money laundering tells him, "You call yourself a Cuban? You make a real Cuban throw up!"

tropes.name: Railing Kill
tropes.html:
• One of Sosa's Mooks topples over a railing after getting shot by Tony in the climax.
  • Tony himself crashes through a railing into a pool when The Skull shoots him.

tropes.name: Rasputinian Death
tropes.html: Tony takes an improbable number of bullets to the torso in the final shootout with Sosa's death squad and isn't even fazed, but this might be explained by the fact that he had his face buried in a mountain of coke just before. It takes a shotgun blast at close range from behind and a fall off a balcony to finally kill him.

tropes.name: Reassigned to Antarctica
tropes.html: Tony threatens Seidelbaum and the other federal agents with this when they arrest him in the money laundering sting, saying they'll all be working in Alaska once his lawyer gets through with them.

tropes.name: "The Reason You Suck" Speech
tropes.html:
• When Tony visits his family, he gets an earful from his mother about how people like him give Cubans a bad name and how throwing money around is not going to earn her respect.
    Georgina: You know, all we hear about in the papers is animals like you and the killings. It's Cubans like you who are giving a bad name to our people. People who come here, work hard and make a name for themselves. People who send their children to school—!
    Gina: Mamá, what are you saying? That's your son!
    Georgina: Son?! I wish I had one. He's a bum. He was a bum then, and he's a bum now. [to Tony] Who do you think you are, hmm? We haven't heard a word from you in five years. Cinco años. You suddenly show up here, throw some money around, and think you can get my respect. You think you can buy me with jewelry?
    Tony: Come on, Mamá...
    Georgina: You think you can come into my house with your hotshot clothes and your jail manners and make fun of us?
  • During dinner with her husband and Manny at some fancy restaurant, Elvie gets tired of Tony's continuous taunting and fires right back at him. And then she walks out on him and is not seen again. After that, Tony himself gives quite an epic one towards the crowd while he's drunk (see Evil Versus Evil above).
  • Tony's mom screams at him when Gina goes missing about how he's worthless and a bum and got Gina into this situation in the first place.

tropes.name: Remember the New Guy?
tropes.html: Mel Bernstein asks Tony if he remembers him, but this is the first time we see him.

tropes.name: Riddle for the Ages
tropes.html:
• We never do find out if Sosa's assassins know English.
  • Gina asks Tony if he wants her romantically, but we never find out if he does since all he does is give her a confused look and ask her what she's talking about.

tropes.name: Riddled and Rattled
tropes.html:
At the film's climax, Tony Montana gets into a shootout with Sosa's hit squad, with them at ground level and Tony at the top of the staircase leading to his office. He gets shot a couple of times and eventually ends up standing in plain sight screaming and cursing at the gang members as he takes at least a half dozen hits in rapid succession, although at this point he's running on adrenaline, fury, and the massive dose of cocaine he took shortly before the hit squad arrived, so he's able to shrug off the pain. He's then shot in the back with a double-barrel shotgun at point blank range by "the Skull", Sosa's chief enforcer, and falls dead into the fountain below the stairs.
Tony: Go ahead! I take your fucking bullets! You think you kill me with bullets? I take your fucking bullets! Go ahead!

tropes.name: "Rise and Fall" Gangster Arc
tropes.html: The film depicts Tony making a name for himself in the cocaine trade, eventually becoming a fabulously wealthy drug kingpin. However, his addiction to cocaine, fits of rage, and impulsive behavior ultimately leads to his undoing and death.

tropes.name: Roaring Rampage of Revenge
tropes.html: When Sosa's army is storming his mansion, Tony is too coked up and depressed from how badly his life has gone to do anything to stop them... until one of the hitmen shoots his little sister Gina.

tropes.name: Ruder and Cruder
tropes.html: The Trope Codifier— Scarface was one of, if not the, most profanity-laced films of its time, and its popularity and acclaim helped to normalize the use of frequent profanity in any film production up to that point.

tropes.name: Same Language Dub
tropes.html: The two immigration officers that interview Tony at the start of the film were dubbed by Charles Durning and Dennis Franz.

tropes.name: Sanity Slippage
tropes.html:
• Tony gets crazier every passing week or month due to his coke addiction. This is further exaggerated in Scarred for Life, where he not only lapses back into his old habits, but becomes even more unhinged as he tries clawing back up in his quest for revenge.
  • Gina loses it after Tony kills Manny without realizing that the two are now married.

tropes.name: Say My Name
tropes.html: When Tony reunites with his family, his mom says "Antonio?" and Tony says Gina's name upon seeing her.

tropes.name: Scare Chord
tropes.html: The soundtrack suddenly gets eerie when Tony snaps at Manny for calling Gina beautiful.

tropes.name: Scars Are Forever
tropes.html: Tony Montana has a scar across his right eye from a knife fight as a kid.

tropes.name: Screw the Money, I Have Rules!
tropes.html: Tony's mother when he briefly reunites with her and offers her and his sister some money he had gotten... from less than honest ways.

tropes.name: Screw the Rules, I Have Money!
tropes.html: After Tony gets busted for money laundering, he offers to pay his lawyer $800,000 to get him off the hook, figuring that it should be enough to buy off the Supreme Court if necessary. The lawyer tells him that it won't do any good due to the overwhelming evidence against him.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html: In Elvira's last appearance, she decides that she's had enough and tells Tony, "I'm not going home with anybody! I'm going home alone. I'm leaving you. I'm leaving you. I don't need this shit anymore."

tropes.name: Serendipitous Survival
tropes.html: Manny leaves the nightclub to take Gina home right before the assassination attempt on Tony.

tropes.name: Setting Update
tropes.html: Keeping in line with how the 1932 version was set contemporary to its release, the remake takes place in its own "today," the early 80s.

tropes.name: Seven Deadly Sins
tropes.html: Tony is ravaged by all of them, save maybe Sloth. Among these, his most fatal flaws are Wrath and Pride.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• Tony Montana was named after football star Joe Montana.
  • The Mafioso Tony encounters (and soon has blown up) as a kid in Devil in Disguise resembles Fredo Corleone as he looked while in Havana during the events of The Godfather Part II, right down to his white suit.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html:
Brian De Palma made it clear that he had done his research on the Mariel boatlift and the Miami drug trade through various elements in the movie and his interactions with real-life individuals involved in these events. Here are some ways in which De Palma demonstrated his research:
  • De Palma and screenwriter Oliver Stone visited the Mutiny Club, a real-life drug hangout in Miami, during their research for the film. Stone mentioned in an interview that he took De Palma to the Mutiny Club, which was a popular spot frequented by drug dealers and celebrities during the cocaine heyday of the 1970s-80s.
  • During the filming of the movie, De Palma, Stone, and actor Al Pacino stayed at the Mutiny Hotel, further immersing themselves in the environment and culture associated with the Miami drug trade.
  • De Palma and the filmmakers drew inspiration from real-life figures involved in the Miami drug trade. For example, the character of Tony Montana, played by Al Pacino, bore a resemblance to Mario Tabraue, a Cuban exile and chairman of a smuggling operation. Tabraue's extravagant lifestyle, including owning a zoo with big cats, mirrored aspects of Tony Montana's character in the film.
  • While much of movie was shot in Southern California, the filmmakers saved one of the most violent scenes for South Florida's iconic Ocean Drive on South Beach. This choice of location added authenticity to the portrayal of the Miami drug trade.

tropes.name: The Siege
tropes.html: The final siege of the mansion at the end of the movie.

tropes.name: Smite Me, O Mighty Smiter
tropes.html: Invoked by Tony himself, where his restriction of jobs to kitchen duty leads him to continue down the path to a life of crime. And again during the finale when he yells at his attackers as he gets shot many times in the mansion, just before The Skull kills him.

tropes.name: So Long, Sentry
tropes.html: There are always a lot of armed cronies keeping Tony's mansion secure. Only a couple last long enough to even fight back when an army of hitmen creep into the estate in the climax.

tropes.name: The Sociopath
tropes.html: Alejandro Sosa, a cartel boss who thinks nothing of having a man hanged from a helicopter, ordering a lawyer's wife and children killed to make sure he's eliminated, or sending an army of goons to kill the man who stops it.

tropes.name: So What Do We Do Now?
tropes.html: Ernie and Chi Chi ask Tony this after he screws Sosa over and kills Manny.

tropes.name: Spiteful Spit
tropes.html: Tony spits at Hector the Toad while he's captured and verbally attacked by him and his henchmen.

tropes.name: Start of Darkness
tropes.html: Devil in Disguise shows Tony's slide from petty crimes as a kid into underworld notoriety in Castro's Cuba before he and Manny flee to America.

tropes.name: Stealth Pun
tropes.html: Tony says “Say hello to my little friend!” while high on cocaine. One possible side effect of cocaine is erectile dysfunction.

tropes.name: Stock Footage
tropes.html: The opening sequence is accompanied with shots from the actual Mariel boatlift.

tropes.name: Stock Shout-Outs
tropes.html: "Say hello to my little friend!", when pulling out a BFG.

tropes.name: The Stool Pigeon
tropes.html: Sosa believed Omar to have been this and dealt with him thusly.

tropes.name: Stunned Silence
tropes.html: Tony goes silent after killing Manny, immediately regretting what he did.

tropes.name: Sudden Principled Stand
tropes.html: Throughout the film Tony has been a drug dealer and a murderer, generally getting worse and worse. But seeing Sosa's hitman about to kill the target while the man's wife and kid are in the same car makes him draw the line.

tropes.name: Suddenly Bilingual
tropes.html: In the climax, Ernie speaks to Chi Chi in Spanish.

tropes.name: Suddenly Speaking
tropes.html: Alberto has no dialogue until he is paired with Tony for an assassination mission.

tropes.name: Sunglasses at Night
tropes.html: The Skull, adding to his creepiness.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Bad Native Language
tropes.html: Tony, who is supposed to be a Cuban immigrant, tells Alberto "¡Olvida! Matamos este tipo solo. Sin mujer, sin hijos." which is subtitled as "Forget it! We kill this guy alone. No wife, no kids." A native Spanish speaker would have said "¡Olvídalo! Matamos solo a este tipo. No a la mujer ni a los niños".

tropes.name: Tagline
tropes.html:
Several.
  • He was Tony Montana. The world will know him by another name... SCARFACE.
  • The world is yours.
  • He wanted to live the American Dream until the end.
  • He loved the American Dream. With a vengeance.

tropes.name: Talking to the Dead
tropes.html:
Happens twice.
  • Tony rants angrily at Alberto's corpse after killing him.
    Tony: What do you think I am, huh?! What do you think I am, a fucking worm like you?! I told you, man, I told you! Don't fuck with me! I told you, no fucking kids! No, but you wouldn't listen, why, you stupid fuck, look at you now!
  • After Gina is gunned down, Tony goes into denial and starts talking to her corpse.
    Tony: Look at your face. It's all dirty. Please, talk to me! Don't be mad at me. Come on, Gina. I love Manny, you know? I love him. And I love you too, you know? Give me a smile.

tropes.name: Tattooed Crook
tropes.html: While it wasn't as obvious as the other examples, Tony Montana has a tattoo on his hand showing that he was in prison.

tropes.name: Teeth-Clenched Teamwork
tropes.html: Omar and Tony hate each other's guts pretty much from the moment they meet. But they work as associates to get the deal with Sosa on the table (despite bickering amongst themselves a lot more than actually negotiating with Sosa). Of course, Sosa kills Omar, thinking him an informer, and to send a message to Tony not to screw with him. Tony really couldn't care less that Omar is gone.

tropes.name: Terms of Endangerment
tropes.html:
• Tony hostilely calls Frank "amigo", which is Spanish for "friend".
  • Sosa calls the journalist "our friend" when talking about killing him. Downplayed as Sosa recognizes that killing said journalists cannot be done.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html:
• Greeting Tony at the door while wearing nothing more than a bathrobe was a really bad way for Manny to tell Tony that he and Gina were seeing each other, especially given Tony's Hair-Trigger Temper temper and his earlier warnings to stay away from her.
  • Frank. For a gangster, he doesn't take security very seriously. Anyone can walk up to his unlocked office, which has a single henchman as its solitary line of defense, and whack him on the spot. This is precisely what Tony does after Frank sends a failed hit after him.
  • Alberto tries to go ahead with blowing up Gutierrez and his family, even when it's become very clear to him that Tony won't do it.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Jerkass
tropes.html: Tony starts out the film as a crook, but it's not until he gains power that he allows himself to become a cocaine-addicted wreck. He constantly curses and acts like a cantankerous prick towards even his possible friends, and gets called out on it by almost everyone close to him.

tropes.name: Tragedy
tropes.html: A classical crime tragedy. Tony is shown to be a ruthless criminal who nonetheless has redeeming qualities, is loyal to his friends, and cares for his family. However, his many flaws and an increasingly severe cocaine addiction bring a swift end to his criminal empire and in the end, Tony loses everything he built and everyone who ever cared about him is either dead or hates his guts. Even at the end, it's generally hard not to feel bad for Tony.

tropes.name: A Tragedy of Impulsiveness
tropes.html:
• Tony Montana's aggressiveness certainly didn't win him any allies, but you know he's doomed when he calls off the hit on the journalist by killing Alejandro Sosa's henchman, Alberto the Shadow. It was for a good reason, but if he'd thought out his actions, he could have avoided the situation without antagonizing the only person who could have fixed the mess he was in. Then later he kills Manny Ribera (his best friend), in a fit of rage, driving Gina (his sister), to try to kill him.
  • This happens again in Scarred for Life. Tony's obsession with taking vengeance on Sosa is matched only by his erratic impulsiveness. That winds up leading him down to an ever more self-destructive path, despite being given a chance by Elvira to start over as a free man. Ultimately leading to Tony's inner demons winning out, as he not only kills Sosa but greedily tries grabbing the latter's Bolivian empire even as the DEA closes in on him.

tropes.name: Tragic Mistake
tropes.html:
• Tony killing Sosa's hitman resulted in antagonizing the one person who could have helped him out of his mess.
  • Getting high on his own supply brought its own set of problems, among them an impaired sense of judgment. This, combined with his increasingly violent protectiveness about his sister, resulted in him gunning down his right-hand man Manny.
  • Frank was absolutely correct: the guys that survive in this business are the ones who manage to stay underneath the radar. Those who want it all make powerful enemies and are noticed by the police— which is exactly what happens.

tropes.name: Tranquil Fury
tropes.html: Tony does this when he kills Manny out of rage for sleeping with his sister, Gina, before she revealed that they're married. In fact, instead of yelling, he looks at him in furious silence and shoots him without saying a word.

tropes.name: Trophy Wife
tropes.html: Elvira is this to Tony.

tropes.name: Two-Act Structure
tropes.html: The movie is split into two distinct acts. The first act is about Tony rising to the top of the Miami underworld. The second act is how everything goes to hell for Tony and everyone around him.

tropes.name: Unstoppable Rage
tropes.html: Played straight then subverted at the mansion siege. It's also one of Tony's easily-seen traits.

tropes.name: Unwitting Instigator of Doom
tropes.html: Riding high as a kingpin, Tony gets fed up with his money launderer's high fees (on what by that point is only score-keeping the money) and goes shopping for cheaper. Unsurprisingly, the cheap one is also a federal sting. Everything else bad in the second half more or less flows from this.

tropes.name: Uptown Girl
tropes.html: Subverted. Tony is attracted to Elvira because of her wealth, but it soon becomes clear that they don't love each other.

tropes.name: Uriah Gambit
tropes.html: It is very heavily implied that Omar Suarez knew Hector and crew were likely to turn on Tony and sent him on the "job" so he'd be killed.

tropes.name: Used to Be a Sweet Kid
tropes.html: Subverted in Devil in Disguise. Even before the Cuban Revolution, Tony was already something of a troublemaking kid (even being involved in having a Mafioso killed), and would only get worse from there.

tropes.name: Villain with Good Publicity
tropes.html: Frank Lopez. He's a friendly-acting, gregarious philanthropist who sponsors a little league baseball team. Too bad that he's also a murderous drug kingpin.

tropes.name: Villainous Breakdown
tropes.html: Tony in the last several minutes of the movie. He is left alone in his office, coked out of his mind, being hit with the Heel Realization of killing his best friend Manny. Seeing Sosa's men on the security monitors, he tries to recover. He tries to gather his thoughts, muttering to himself "We gotta get organized", but there's no one to listen. He picks up a phone but drops it without dialing as there's nobody to call. He needs someone he can trust to help him, but he's either driven away or killed everyone that fits that profile. He's all alone and about to die and almost only has himself to blame. The only thing that snaps him out of it is when Gina gets gunned down by said men, and even then it's only enough to make him decide to kill as many of them as he can in a coked-up blind fury.

tropes.name: Villainous Friendship
tropes.html: Tony and his eventual Dragon Manny Ribera start the film as apparent friends, which doesn't change as they start a criminal empire in Miami. Manny eventually gets fed up with Tony's more malicious behavior, like beating up his sister's touchy boyfriend. When Manny secretly elopes with Tony's sister, his friend goes nuts and kills Manny in a cocaine-fueled rage.

tropes.name: Villainous Incest
tropes.html: Tony can't have his sister and consequently doesn't want anyone else to have her. This is thrown back at him right before she's gunned down.

tropes.name: Villainous Valour
tropes.html: There's a variation of this trope for Tony Montana. In by far the most famous scene in the movie, he gets high on cocaine, grabs an M16, and takes on a veritable army of goons alone. Even when badly injured by gunfire, he stands and taunts his assailants. It takes a shotgun shell to the back at point blank range to finally put him down for good.

tropes.name: Villain Protagonist
tropes.html: Tony, a crass criminal drug dealer, and occasional hitman, murders his boss to get to the top, is a controlling misogynist who becomes a cocaine-addicted wreck, and burns all his bridges on his power trip.

tropes.name: Villains Never Lie
tropes.html: It's never proven outside of Sosa's claims that Omar Suarez was an informant for the police, but the only one who casts doubt on the claims is Sosa's rival, Frank Lopez.

tropes.name: When She Smiles
tropes.html: Elvira only smiles once in the entire movie.

tropes.name: White-Collar Crime
tropes.html: Tony enlists a bank manager to launder his drug money. When the manager later tries to charge a higher percentage, Tony drops him and turns to a different office, only to end up getting busted by the feds for tax evasion and violation of the RICO statute, specifically money laundering.

tropes.name: White Shirt of Death
tropes.html: Played straight when Tony stabs Rebenga and when Manny is shot by Tony. Inverted at the ending: Tony wears a black suit over his white shirt at the ending's shootout.

tropes.name: Would Hit a Girl
tropes.html: Tony smacks his sister after standing up to a man he sees groping her ass and taking her to the men's bathroom to do cocaine and make out.

tropes.name: Would Not Shoot a Civilian
tropes.html: Tony Montana refuses to carry out a hit that would also kill the target's wife and kids. Tony's moral code allows him to kill only in defense or retaliation (in his words "I ain't never fucked nobody that didn't try to fuck me first"). His willingness to take part in that hit in the first place (the target being an activist who'd done nothing to him) showed that his principles were on the decline. His fellow mobsters don't share the same moral views, which results in his downfall.

tropes.name: Would Hurt a Child
tropes.html: Tony tells Alberto in Spanish that they should wait until the journalist is alone so they can kill him without killing his wife and children. Alberto disagrees, saying that if Sosa wants them to carry out the assassination now, they should do it now.

tropes.name: Wouldn't Hurt a Child
tropes.html: How Tony proves he's not so bad. It's an interesting example because protecting children by killing Sosa's assassin leads directly to Tony's death— on the other hand, he's only in that situation because he was becoming worse and agreed to help kill an innocent man who'd done nothing to him. The moral of that particular story is left ambiguous.

tropes.name: You Bastard!
tropes.html: The movie itself spends the first half of its duration challenging our sympathies for the protagonist, then it hits the audience in the face that at least some people in the general public need people like him to point out who's the "bad guy".

tropes.name: You Have GOT to Be Kidding Me!
tropes.html: When asked by an immigration officer if he likes men or likes to dress up like a woman, Tony can only respond "What the fuck is wrong with this guy, mang?"

tropes.name: You No Take Candle
tropes.html:
Tony sometimes forgets how to speak English properly.
Tony: What you talking?

tropes.name: Younger Than They Look
tropes.html: Gina looks very mature for a 19-year-old. Mary Elizabeth Mastrantonio was actually 24 when she played her.

tropes.name: Abusive Parents
tropes.html: It's revealed that the murder victim was an abusive dad to the accused. It is also implied Juror #3 may have been this to his own son.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html: Juror #3 sarcastically refers to Juror #12 as "the boy in the grey flannel suit." Lee J. Cobb (Juror #3) appeared in the film The Man In The Grey Flannel Suit in the previous year.

tropes.name: Actually Pretty Funny
tropes.html: Downplayed as the character doesn't seem to consider it actually funny, but after the knife display (see Dude, Not Funny! below), Juror #8 doesn't even blink, and agrees that there was no harm done.

tropes.name: Adaptational Nice Guy
tropes.html:
Of all people, Juror #4. In the original 1954 TV movie, when Juror #10 goes on his prejudiced rant towards the end, Juror #4 basically intimidates him into shutting up by telling him that if he opens his mouth again, he (#4) will "split his skull". This makes it seem like #10 only relents because he's too terrified not to (not that #4's reaction is not understandable, given the nature of #10's rant). But in the 1957 movie, when Juror #10 asks why they aren't listening to him, #4 merely says quietly "I have. Now sit down and don't open your mouth again." This seems to make #10 realize at last just how much the others despise him, and he shuts up not because he's frightened but because he's ashamed to realize that he doesn't speak for anyone else.
  • An ambiguous example with #10 himself. In the original movie, after #3 changes his mind, #10 states he still believes the boy is guilty but will vote not guilty because he knows, after his rant, that they won't listen to him. In the 1957 movie, when he's asked if he still thinks the boy is guilty, he merely shakes his head while staring, leaving it unclear if, like the original, he just feels defeated or if he genuinely realizes there is doubt to the boy's guilt.

tropes.name: Affably Evil
tropes.html: For a flexible definition of "evil", since he is more of an antagonist than a villain (although his actions would lead to the death of a kid): Juror #4 is calm, polite, doesn't mock Juror #8 or his doubts, and only brings up factual arguments for his position. He doesn't act out of malice or prejudice, but because he sincerely believes the kid to be guilty.

tropes.name: Aggressive Categorism
tropes.html:
Juror #10 is one of the last holdouts for a guilty verdict. As time goes on, it becomes clearer and clearer that he doesn't care about the evidence; the defendant is a young man from the slums, and for #10, that is enough to think he's guilty. None of the other jurors, even #3 and #4, agree with him and instead ignore his last rant about the defendant until he runs out of steam.
Juror #10: Look, you know how these people lie! It's born in them! I mean, what the heck? I don't have to tell you! They don't know what the truth is! And lemme tell ya: they don't need any real big reason to kill someone, either! No sir!

tropes.name: Ambiguous Situation
tropes.html: The killing itself. The audience is never shown if the defendant did murder the victim or if he's innocent. But that's the entire point of the movie.

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html:
• Juror #8 catches #10 in a bit of a contradiction early on regarding his prejudiced views about not trusting the boy due to people like him being "born liars", which earns him a cold, sarcastic reply.
    Juror #8: I'd like to ask you something: you don't believe the boy's story, how come you believe the woman's? She's one of "them", too, isn't she?
    Juror #10: (smile fades; angrily) ...You're a pretty smart fellow, aren't you?
  • A very intense one happens after #8 baits #3 into lashing out at him.
    Juror #3: Lemme go! I'll kill him! I'll kill him!!
    Juror #8: You don't really mean you'll kill me, do you?

tropes.name: Artistic License – Law
tropes.html: Juror #8 performs outside research and enters a second knife into the proceeding, both of which are massive violations of the rules. US Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor stated that if this did happen and the judge found out, it would lead to a mistrial. Even worse, he leaves it behind in the table at the end of the 1957 film. Probably a good thing we cut to credits when we do.

tropes.name: Ask a Stupid Question...
tropes.html:
Juror #6: What kind of a bum is the defense attorney?
Juror #8: That's exactly what I've been asking.

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html: The murder victim was an abusive father.

tropes.name: Awesomeness by Analysis
tropes.html: Juror #9, who provides great insights on the eyewitnesses based on their appearances at court, and in turn gives fairly logical reasons for why their testimonies might not be truthful.

tropes.name: Believing Their Own Lies
tropes.html:
• At the start of the deliberations, Juror #3 opens by claiming to have no personal bias towards the case. It quickly becomes apparent that this is far from the truth, and #3 himself is the last one to realize it.
  • Juror #9 also suggests that this trope could explain why the old man testified that he saw the defendant fleeing the murder scene, when his ability to have done so was severely in doubt. He was so eager for the chance to be part of a murder investigation and trial that it overrode his good sense.
  • The same goes for the bespectacled woman who claims to have witnessed the murder itself. In fact, at no point does anyone allege that any witnesses deliberately lied, only that since none of them actually saw the victim being stabbed, they may have erroneously assumed that things they saw or heard on that night were directly connected to the murder when they actually weren't.

tropes.name: Beware the Quiet Ones
tropes.html: Juror #4 is soft-spoken, calm, and polite. He is also the one who sternly answers Juror #10 when he goes on his prejudiced tirade and shuts him up for good. In some versions, it's taken further as he threatens him with physical violence.

tropes.name: Blind Without 'Em
tropes.html: An important plot point: Juror #9 recalls that a key witness in the murder case had marks on her nose suggesting that she usually wears glasses, though opted not to in court. #8 points out that she was unlikely to be wearing them in bed late at night when she claims to have seen the murder from all the way across the street, thereby making her less than credible as a witness. This is one of the revelations that heavily swings Juror #4 to favor a not guilty verdict. As a glasses-wearer himself, he says noone wears eyeglasses to bed.

tropes.name: Bottle Episode
tropes.html: The film could be considered the Trope Codifier: with the exception of the first and last scenes, set in the other interiors and exterior of the NYC Country Courthouse, and a brief moment in a restroom, the entire movie takes place in a small room where the jurors perform their deliberation. In said room the only actions are heavy arguments and occasional attempts at throwing a punch at each other.

tropes.name: Break Them by Talking
tropes.html:
• Played straight initially when Juror #8 baits #3 into lashing out in a rage (thus proving his point about Ineffectual Death Threats).
  • Inverted when Juror #10 goes on a bigoted diatribe, is shunned by everybody in the room one by one, and spends the rest of the film in defeated silence.
  • Inverted again when Juror #3 breaks himself by going on a similar rant, only to find that the room has gone dead silent over the pitiable wreck he has made of himself.

tropes.name: Building of Adventure
tropes.html: Except for the opening and closing scenes in the courtroom itself, the story never leaves the jury room.

tropes.name: Career-Revealing Trait
tropes.html: Shown in some capacity by most of the characters, most notably Jurors #4 and #8. They argue early in the movie about whether it’s more important for evidence to be possible or probable. Juror #4, a stockbroker who works based on probabilities, argues that it is not probable for the defendant to have done certain things. Juror #8, an architect whose job it is to prevent any chance of danger, argues that it is possible and that possibility should be enough to halt the case against him.

tropes.name: Character Filibuster
tropes.html:
• Juror #10 has a particularly nasty, racism-filled rant against "the likes of him [the accused]" that causes the other jurors to turn away from him one by one, until #4 shuts him up:
    Juror #10: Listen to me!
    Juror #4: I have. Now sit down and don't open your mouth again.
  • Juror #3 has a smaller one, but in his case he breaks down all by himself afterwards.

tropes.name: The Charmer
tropes.html: Juror #12, a smartly-dressed Motor Mouth adman, presents this way early on. He is very friendly to the other jurors and tries to defuse the tension when they fight. He loses this trait and turns hesitant and unsure later on, flip-flopping his vote according to who cowed him last.

tropes.name: Chromosome Casting
tropes.html: All of the jurors are male, since only men served on juries when it was written. It's right in the title. However, theatrical adaptations now often avert this.

tropes.name: Clueless Mystery
tropes.html: An interesting twist on it: the details all appear on screen, but in the end, we never learn the truth about the murder that led to the trial in the first place, as the ending is ambiguous as to whether or not the defendant was truly guilty.note While he is found not guilty, the jurors themselves even note that they can't be 100% certain that the boy didn't murder his father. They have merely established reasonable doubt to believe that he didn't; this is the entire meaning behind the United States Judicial System's concept of "innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt"; the burden of responsibility lay with the prosecution, not the defense, to prove guilt to the jury, rather than the responsibility of the defense to prove innocence, and if the jury mistakenly decleres "not guilty" to someone who was in truth guilty, then the failure, again, rests with the prosecution for not providing sufficient evidence or a solid enough case beyond a reasonable doubt.

tropes.name: Common Nonsense Jury
tropes.html: Only barely averted and thoroughly explored. If not for the actions of Juror #8, the accused teen would have been voted "guilty" within a couple of minutes because of things as dumb as racing to get to a baseball game, racism, and misplaced rage from a family dispute. The jurors are forced to admit their skewed priorities as the play goes on.

tropes.name: Cool Old Guy
tropes.html: Juror #9, the oldest member of the cast and the first to support #8. He is also an excellent observer, even better than juror #8 himself, and the key to winning over some of the staunchest supporters of a guilty verdict.

tropes.name: Corner of Woe
tropes.html: Juror #10 retreats to one when, after one of his bigoted rants goes too far, Juror #4 shuts him up. From that point on, #10 rarely participates in any of the deliberations, only weakly showing an acknowledgement that his vote is "not guilty" when a poll is taken (ironically, after #4 changes his vote after the woman's testimony about clearly seeing the killing is discredited).

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html:
• Juror #4, who quips back at some of the less-than-reasonable theories.
  • #7 is a less subtle version, whose hostile wisecracks contribute little to the proceedings except added tension in the room.

tropes.name: Dingy Trainside Apartment
tropes.html: This is discussed as a plot point in the testimony of a witness, as she supposedly heard and saw a murder through a passing elevated train going by between her window and the accused's. This also raises questions about whether another witness could have heard what he claimed with the train going by.

tropes.name: Dissonant Serenity
tropes.html:
Juror #8 remains calm when Juror #3 is pretending to stab him (the other jurors are standing up, worried that #3 is actually going to stab him).
Juror #3: Now...nobody's hurt...right?
Juror #8: Right. Nobody hurt.

tropes.name: Dude, Not Funny!
tropes.html: The other jurors' reaction to #3 pretending to raise the knife to stab #8, considering the tensions between them. The only exceptions are Juror #4, who simply rolls his eyes at the theatrics, Juror #5, who seems like he's trying to inspect something (he moments later points out the improper handling of a switchblade, another sign the defendant might not be the assailant), and Juror #7, who simply leans forward in his chair, almost as if he hoped it would happen.

tropes.name: Empathic Environment
tropes.html: The rainstorm. And to a lesser extent, the fan, which finally starts up when the votes start to swing in favor of acquittal.

tropes.name: Environmental Symbolism
tropes.html: As tempers rise, the room seems to get more and more claustrophobic. That's not just an effect of the camera: the actual walls of the set were gradually moved closer in as the film goes on, making the room smaller and smaller.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html:
• Juror #8 is first seen pondering at the window of the jury room before being called over to begin deliberations. Notably, he isn't shown speaking and chattering excitedly like most of the jurors, hinting that the majority sentiment won't go through as easily as previously thought.
  • During the initial vote, some jurors raise their hands right away to vote guilty, while the rest except for #8 are more reluctant, showing who will be the hardest to win over.

tropes.name: Everyone Has Standards
tropes.html:
• Juror #3 may be vicious and want to see the defendant executed, but even he is unwilling to listen to #10's bigoted tirades. Even Juror #4, who comes off as a Jerkass at times, and is strongly convinced of the defendant's guilt, has had enough of #10's bigotry, and tells him as such in no uncertain terms.
    • Juror #3 is also the first to jump on Juror #7 for changing sides for no reason, and makes it clear that he respects the jury system throughout. He simply doesn't realize that his subconscious bias is the reason he's pushing for conviction. Once he figures it out, he changes his vote to Not Guilty.
  • Juror #8 (and #10) doesn't look too impressed when the jurors (note #1, #3 and #12) are playing a game rather than listening to the evidence.
  • Interestingly, juror #11 provides a heroic example when juror #7 switches sides to what seems to be the new winning one. Realizing that he is only interested in cutting it short, juror #11 is utterly appalled by his attitude and refuses to accept it.

tropes.name: Explain, Explain... Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: Juror #3 is at first adamant that the old man's testimony is a vital part of the trial, but when it becomes clear that the old man may have been exaggerating what he saw, he says "Half the time he was confused. How can he be positive about anything?" and immediately realizes that he just discredited his own argument.

tropes.name: Extremely Short Timespan
tropes.html: It's not established exactly at what time deliberations started, but it's implied they started no later than noon, through a rainstorm that started late in the afternoon, and finally winding down sometime after 6 pm, of the same day. The editing makes it feel like it's happening in Real Time, but the outside lighting and weather reminds us that it's actually taking a bit longer.

tropes.name: Fire-Forged Friends
tropes.html: Jurors #8 and #9, who were the first to vote "not guilty" and swayed most of the others with their arguments, exchange names at the end, implying they've formed a bond through the rigorous deliberation.

tropes.name: Forcing a Mistrial
tropes.html: Discussed repeatedly. Initially, eleven of the jurors vote in favor of convicting the defendant, but the verdict must be unanimous or there will be a mistrial. The lone dissenter manages to bring over to his side all but one juror, who, despite having seen evidence that the young man is likely innocent, threatens to force a hung jury anyway and let the defendant be retried. He finally realizes that he is projecting his feelings about his own son onto the defendant and agrees to vote not guilty.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: #3's breakdown is set up very early in the movie, when he first goes to the cooler and stares at the photo of his son.

tropes.name: Freudian Excuse
tropes.html: Juror #3 spends the movie continuously trying to convict a young man where there is more and more reasonable doubt for his guilt because his relationship with his son appeared to have gone very sour. It's a classic case of Psychological Projection. He realizes this at the end, though, and changes his stance.

tropes.name: Fulton Street Folly
tropes.html: The film is set in a New York City courtroom, and the opening and closing scenes were shot on location at the New York State Supreme Court Building in Lower Manhattan.

tropes.name: The Generic Guy
tropes.html: The jurors don't all get the same amount of focus, but most of them get at least one moment or trait to really set them apart from the others. Juror #1 doesn't really get this so much. He's one of the jurors with the fewest lines and mostly just serves as the one who will officially read out the verdict once it's reached but plays very little role in actually reaching it. Juror #6 also gets very little characterization; the only thing that's ever really revealed about him is the fact that he works as a interior painter.

tropes.name: The Ghost
tropes.html: The witnesses mentioned are never shown, only described by the jurors—specifically Juror #9, who does so to make observations and hypotheses about them.

tropes.name: Gone Horribly Right
tropes.html: Juror #3 set out to toughen his son up after seeing him run away from a fight. He succeeded; his son got into a fight with him, punched him out, left, and they haven't spoken to one another for years.

tropes.name: Graceful Loser
tropes.html: When his argument is refuted, Juror #4 simply says "I'm convinced. Not guilty."

tropes.name: Grey-and-Gray Morality
tropes.html: Though the pro-acquittal side is painted A Lighter Shade of Grey.

tropes.name: Grin of Audacity
tropes.html: Juror #3 insists that anyone who shouts "I'm gonna kill you" has to mean it, Juror #8 baits #3 until the latter is so angry that he charges #8 shouting "I'll kill him! I'll KILL him!" as #1, #5 and #7 hold him back. This prompts #8 to say "You don't really mean you'll kill me, do you?" with a slight but disarming grin, and #3 promptly backs down.

tropes.name: Guile Hero
tropes.html: Juror #8. His smarts kick-start the plot.

tropes.name: Heat Wave
tropes.html: One of the jurors remarks that it's supposed to be the hottest day of the year, and most of them are sweaty and agitated in the poorly-ventilated deliberation room. Things get a little better once they manage to get the wall fan running.

tropes.name: Heel Realization
tropes.html:
• When, in the middle of his furious insistence that the defendant is guilty, Juror #3 sees the picture of his estranged son and rips it to pieces, you can see in his face that he has just figured out what he was really doing.
  • Vaguely implied for Juror #10. When he rants at length about how "they" (the unspecified social/ethnic group the defendant belongs to) are by nature nothing but a bunch of hotheaded liars and killers, the way all eleven of the other jurors respond with silent open contempt for his views, followed by #4's command to sit down and not say another word causes him to go practically catatonic. He spends the remainder of the deliberation silently staring at nothing, and after #4 changes his vote to not guilty, #10 soon follows. It is left ambiguous, if this means he was actually rethinking his views, or if he just felt defeated. The original teleplay and the Showtime version aren't as ambiguous; when the final vote is taken, #10 flat out says he believes the defendant is guilty, he's just voting "not guilty" cause he's done butting heads with the others.

tropes.name: Hollywood Law
tropes.html:
• Juror #8 states that he went walking in the defendant's neighborhood, and found a copy of the supposedly unique switchblade knife in a local store. He presents it to the jury to prove his point. In a real jury proceeding, the term for this is "juror misconduct." Jurors are not permitted to perform their own investigations, or admit their own evidence (the second knife), and they're really not supposed to consider evidence not presented in court. If it were to come out that #8 did all this, it's possible (though unlikely, given the double jeopardy prohibition) the verdict could be set aside, and #8 could be charged for his actions. There is at least an acknowledgement that #8 broke the law by buying the knife, but nobody brings up that searching for a knife is misconduct. Of course, none of the jurors are lawyers, so it's possible that they didn't recognize the acts as such.
  • In addition to considering evidence not introduced in court, the jurors outright disregard many of the witness testimonies that were introduced in court, for reasons that the prosecutor and defense attorney never actually brought up as possible issues (like the fact that one of the witnesses may or may not have been nearsighted). In Real Life, only a judge has the final say on whether or not statements in court can be considered credible, and jurors aren't supposed to disregard witness testimonies unless a judge instructs them to disregard them. That said, this doesn't always stop it from happening, since once someone has witnessed something, it can't just be erased from their mind. This is why both prosecution and defense have to be careful not to cause situations or statements that could influence the minds of the jury to give their side a disadvantage.
  • The jury seems to be operating under a "slightest possible doubt" basis instead of beyond a reasonable doubt.

tropes.name: Hypocritical Humor
tropes.html:
This exchange, which is even funnier when considering that Juror #11 is an immigrant to the US from Europe.
Juror #10: He's a common, ignorant slob. He don't even speak good English.
Juror #11: He doesn't even speak good English.

tropes.name: I'll Kill You!
tropes.html: The jurors talk about how the accused shouted, "I'll kill you!" at the victim shortly before the murder. Juror #3 insists that no one would say such a thing unless he means it, but is ultimately forced to back down when he shouts the same thing at Juror #8.

tropes.name: Immigrant Patriotism
tropes.html: Juror #11 takes a moment to gush about the jury trial system, and how it could only happen in a democracy like the United States. They never say where he came from, but the implication is that the country he was from is not a democracy. He also berates #7 for refusing to take the process seriously, and makes a point to make sure he is speaking English more properly than the bigoted natural-born #10.

tropes.name: Indy Ploy
tropes.html: After initial discussions are seemingly going nowhere, and some of jurors become more openly hostile towards him, Juror #8 asks for another vote to be taken, and states that if all 11 vote guilty again, he'll give up his argument and change his vote to guilty so they can go in with a unanimous verdict. Luckly for him, Juror #9, while still not entirely convinced the defendant is innocent, nevertheless says #8 is making good arguments, and changes his own vote to not guilty to allow #8 to continue the deliberations because he wants to hear more.

tropes.name: Ineffectual Death Threats
tropes.html:
Invoked. Juror #3 fixates on the evidence that a neighbor heard the defendant yell "I'll kill you!" during a fight, and when it's pointed out that people say that sort of thing all the time and don't mean it, Juror #3 says, "Oh no... if you say that, you mean it." Juror #8 baits him with insults until Juror #3 attacks him and must be held back by the others.
Juror #3: I'll kill him! I'll kill him!
Juror #8: You don't really mean you'll kill me, do you?

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html:
• Juror #3 is argumentative, dismissive of others, and voraciously adamant in seeing the defendant get executed. Subverted in the end when he realizes he's been projecting his animosity towards his estranged son on the defendant, who also had a combative relationship with his father, the murder victim. Once the Heel Realization kicks in, he immediately votes not guilty. Also, after butting heads with Juror #8 the whole film, #8 stays behind and helps #3 back into his suit jacket, the animosity between them gone.
  • Juror #10 doesn't have any logical reason for his guilty vote; he's just extremely prejudiced, to the point where he eventually drops all pretenses and goes on a lengthy bigoted tirade to which the other jurors refuse to listen.
  • Juror #7. Aside from constantly insulting the other jurors with his constant pithy remarks, he doesn't care what the decision of the jury is. He's only concerned with catching a New York Yankees baseball game. At least the most vicious jurors voted guilty because they believed in it, regardless of the lunacy of their reasoning. That said, when called out on this, he does say that he doesn't believe the accused is guilty. Fortunately, the game is rained out during the deliberation, so he can relax and pay attention for once.

tropes.name: Jerk with a Heart of Gold
tropes.html: Juror #4 initially comes off like a bit of an aloof jerk, but by the end he proves to be one of the more reasonable jurors, calling out #10 for his bigoted rant, changing his verdict when given sensible reason to do so, and clearly regretful at the end when he realizes where he went wrong with his prior reasoning.

tropes.name: Jury Duty
tropes.html: Well, yeah. The characters run the whole gamut of taking the duty very seriously (Juror #8's stance on this drives the whole plot, and Juror #11 later claims the responsibility to be one of the greatest things about American democracy) to being almost entirely dismissive of it (Juror #12 is more concerned with doodling and talking about his work than he is with the deliberations, and Juror #7 is mostly upset that he's potentially missing attending a baseball game; both get called out for this). Notably, Jurors #3 and #10 are taking it seriously, but are too hung up on their own emotional baggage to approach it objectively.

tropes.name: Karma Houdini
tropes.html: All the Jurors in the end give the same verdict: "not guilty". If the kid is actually guilty, he gets away with murdering his father. If he is genuinely innocent, the real killer is still at large and unsuspected. Of course, within the realm of the movie, the investigation would be considered ongoing, so it's more of a matter of them not covering the part where someone actually gets caught and convicted as guilty, since that's not the focus.

tropes.name: The Lancer
tropes.html:
• Juror #9 acts as this, to some extent, to Juror #8. #9 is the first person to side with #8, and helps him out when he's arguing with the others.
  • As does #4 to #3. #4 provides logical reasoning for all of #3's passionate arguments, and is the last person other than #3 himself to change his mind.

tropes.name: Lampshade Hanging
tropes.html: "You know, it's interesting he'd find a knife exactly like the one the boy bought!" Double lampshaded by #3's response asking what's so interesting about it.

tropes.name: Let Me at Him!
tropes.html: Juror #3, after being provoked by Juror #8, lunges at him out of rage, only to be held back by Jurors #5, #6 and #7.

tropes.name: Locked in a Room
tropes.html:
A deliberation room. Lampshaded by #5 and #10.
Juror #5: I never knew they locked the door.
Juror #10: Sure, they lock the door. What'd you think?
Juror #5: I don't know. It just never occurred to me.

tropes.name: Meaningful Echo
tropes.html: During Juror #10's racist rant, each of the other jurors turns away from him in disgust and eventually tell him to shut up. When Juror #3 starts shouting at the end, the other jurors listen in silence, as they realize that #3 is in the middle of an emotional breakdown and needs time to let it out and process it.

tropes.name: Minimalism
tropes.html: Apart from a very short prologue and epilogue, the entire play/film takes place in the jury room (and an adjacent bathroom).

tropes.name: Minimalist Cast
tropes.html: At the beginning of the film, other people (such as the defendant and the judge) are briefly shown, but for the rest of the film, we only see the twelve jurors (and the bailiff, briefly). The play doesn't show anyone but the jurors and the bailiff, with the judge's voice only being heard from off-stage.

tropes.name: Monochrome Casting
tropes.html: Perhaps unsurprisingly for a film made in The '50s, the jury is all-white (although one is an immigrant with a noticeable accent). Later productions often avert it.

tropes.name: Motive = Conclusive Evidence
tropes.html: This is used as one of the main thrusts behind the drive to convict the defendant. The defendant had yelled "I'LL KILL YOU!" at the victim shortly before the victim had died, and this was taken as "evidence". Juror #3, the one most adamant for a conviction, argued that no one says something like that unless they truly mean it, and during the course of the film, Juror #8 gets #3 so angry that he lunges at #8, screaming "I'll kill him! I'LL KILL HIM!" before #8, remaining calm and cool, throws this line of reasoning right back in his face: "You don't really mean you'll kill me, do you?"

tropes.name: Named by the Adaptation
tropes.html: None of the jurors were named in the play. In the film, two of them are given names in the epilogue.

tropes.name: Nameless Narrative
tropes.html: No names are used for any of the jurors, and not even for the victim or defendant. The film added an epilogue not in the play that gives last names for Juror #8 (Davis) and Juror #9 (McCardle).

tropes.name: Non-Specifically Foreign
tropes.html:
Several characters are noted for their ethnicity or nationality, but what ethnicity or nationality they are is never stated. Most notably, the defendant is either of some sort of ethnic minority or lower social class and lives in a slum, which has several of the jurors, particularly #10, predisposed into mistrusting him. Juror #5 is noted several times to have a similar background to the defendant, while #11 is from an unspecified foreign country and is proud to be participating in an American democratic process. While the vagueness allows for staging of the play to get creative, the examples from both films being:
  • The film's interpretation has the defendant appearing to be Italian or possibly Latino; #5 is played by Jack Klugman, who is Jewish; and #11 is played by George Voskovec, who is Czech (born in what was then part of the Austro-Hungarian empire).
  • In the 1997 version, the defendant is explicitly Latino, #5 is Black (as are #1, #2, and interestingly enough, #10, whose racism stems from being a card-carrying member of the Nation of Islam movement), and #11 is Latino instead of European — and not the only immigrant this time, as #4 sports a thick German accent.

tropes.name: Notably Quick Deliberation
tropes.html: If not for Juror #8, the jurors would have declared the kid guilty in five minutes, tops.

tropes.name: "Number of Objects" Title
tropes.html: 12 Angry Men.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: Juror #3's face when he realizes that he's just contradicted his own argument subtly, but wonderfully, evokes this sentiment.

tropes.name: The Oner
tropes.html: A few, such as one towards the beginning, in which each of the jurors establishes himself as the camera pans around the room and focuses briefly on several different conversations; and one when Juror #8 goes to wash his hands and other characters duck into the bathroom to chat with him.

tropes.name: Paper Destruction of Anger
tropes.html: Juror #3 rips up a photo of his son during his breakdown and then he finally votes not guilty. He was voting "guilty" simply because of the bad relationship he has with his estranged son, not because of the facts.

tropes.name: Perfect Health
tropes.html: Averted. Juror #10 has a head cold. It's not a plot point or anything. He just has a head cold. It's one of many distractions that cause some jurors to want to rush through the deliberation and go back to their lives.

tropes.name: Precious Photo
tropes.html: Juror #3 tears up his photo of himself with a young man (presumably his son, who he has not spoken to in years) in a fit of rage, and quickly regrets it.

tropes.name: Profiling
tropes.html: The defendant's background is the main reason Juror #10 wants a guilty verdict. It is not made clear what the background of the defendant is, however, presenting a generalised prejudicial outlook from Juror #10. It is possible that the defendant is of an ethic minority, or belongs to a lower class in the eyes of #10.

tropes.name: Psychological Projection
tropes.html: It becomes clear by the end that the real reason Juror #3 is so insistent on a guilty conviction is because he's projecting his own problems with his son onto the case.

tropes.name: Realistic Diction Is Unrealistic
tropes.html: While there are plenty of impassioned speeches, the trope is less severe than most examples since the characters often stutter or pause at key points.

tropes.name: Reality Has No Soundtrack
tropes.html: The music plays four times.

tropes.name: Real Time
tropes.html: Fully in the play, the film takes it even further, with not only almost all of the movie taking place in real time, but almost all of that period is set in one room. Even more remarkably, it had to be shot four times, each from a different angle with one of the walls removed to accommodate the camera, with the jurors getting progressively more sweaty and dishevelled. When all four angles were cut together, it worked perfectly in continuity.

tropes.name: "The Reason You Suck" Speech
tropes.html:
Juror #11 to Juror #7, after the latter changes his vote just to break the deadlock:
Juror #11: What kind of a man are you? You have sat here and voted guilty with everyone else, because there are some baseball tickets burning a hole in your pocket? And now you've changed your vote because you say you're sick of all the talking here?
Juror #7: Now listen, buddy!
Juror #11: Who tells you that you have the right to play like this with a man's life? Don't you care?
Juror #7: Now, wait a minute! You can't talk like that to me!
Juror #11: I can talk like that to you! If you want to vote not guilty, then do it because you are convinced the man is not guilty, not because you've had enough. And if you think he is guilty, then vote that way. Or don't you have the guts to do what you think is right?

tropes.name: Remake Cameo
tropes.html: More like Remake Reappearance. Joseph Sweeney (Juror #9) and George Voskovec (Juror #11) reprise their roles from the 1954 TV version.

tropes.name: Reverse Grip
tropes.html: Used as a point of contention between the jury. Allegedly the accused stabbed downwards into the victim using the reverse grip. However, Juror #5, who is from the slums, points out that nobody who has experience in knife fights would ever use this with a switchblade, as it would be suicide to pause for a second to change to it in a fight.

tropes.name: Rhetorical Request Blunder
tropes.html: A plot point: The defendant was overheard yelling "I'll Kill You!!" to the victim, who later ended up stabbed to death. Rogue Juror #8 points out that this doesn't necessarily prove the defendant was the murderer, as anyone might say something like that in a fit of anger. To prove the point, Juror #3 later becomes so angry at #8 that he yells "I'll kill you!", to which #8 retorts, "You don't really mean you'll kill me, do you?"

tropes.name: Riddle for the Ages
tropes.html:
• Who killed the man if the defendant was not guilty? For that matter, is the defendant not guilty in the first place? We never get an answer. Even Juror #8 acknowledges the kid probably is guilty, it's just that "probably" is not "beyond a reasonable doubt."
  • What are the names of the 12 angry men in particular? The movie adaptations add the names Davis and McCardle to Jurors #8 and #9 respectively, but the names of the remaining 10 jurors are left unrevealed.

tropes.name: Rogue Juror
tropes.html:
If not the Trope Maker, definitely the Trope Codifier. Juror #8 is the sole holdout on a case which appears to indicate that the accused is definitely a murderer. However, as the jury is forced to analyze the evidence in detail, they slowly discover that almost all of it is flawed in some way. Worth noting that, unlike some other examples, the rogue juror isn't convinced of the suspect's innocence either; he just wants to make sure they've done their job properly, as the accused is facing a mandatory death sentence. It leaves the question of the suspect's guilt or innocence ambiguous in the end. However, because there was reasonable doubt, a verdict of "not guilty" is appropriate.note Interestingly, while #8 is trying to get everyone else to do their job properly, he is not. Conducting your own investigation and bringing a weapon into the jury room are both serious juror misconduct. This leads to a bit of Values Dissonance between laypeople and legal professionals watching the same film/play.
  • Towards the end of the film, Juror #3 becomes this for the other side, after all the other jurors have decided there's enough doubt that they can't justify a guilty verdict.

tropes.name: Sadist
tropes.html: Juror #8 deliberately calls Juror #3 one to rile him up to make a point, that people don't always mean what they say.

tropes.name: Scary Minority Suspect
tropes.html: Very little is known about the defendant except that he's some kind of ethnic minority. Despite this, most of the jurors are eager to say he's guilty and get the trial over with, although only the most vindictive juror admits to outright racism.

tropes.name: Screw the Rules, I'm Doing What's Right!
tropes.html: The jurors are expressly forbidden from going and getting their own switchblade knives, in part because they're illegal to purchase. Juror #8 does so anyway, to demonstrate that the supposedly rare handle of the murder weapon is not uncommon, as he manages to find another knife with the same intricate design on the handle and purchase it cheaply. It's among the first few flaws that begin to tear a hole in the supposedly airtight case by the prosecution, as they argued the defendant had to be guilty due to the "rarity" of the knife.

tropes.name: Second-Hand Storytelling
tropes.html: Since the film is about a jury deliberating a crime, we only ever see the jurors talking. All information about the crime is related to us by them discussing it amongst themselves.

tropes.name: Self-Defeating Argument
tropes.html: As the debate becomes more heated, Juror #3 leans heavily on the testimony of the old man downstairs in order to confirm that the defendant is guilty; however, Juror #8 argues that the old man might not have actually seen the defendant running downstairs after the murder, since he might not have been fast enough to make it to the door in the time between murder and escape. Juror #9 points out that the old man was very positive when he said that this time was fifteen seconds, and in a rage, Juror #3 shouts ""He was a old man! Half the time he was confused! How can he be positive about anything?" In the moment of silence that follows, #3 winces and closes his eyes in frustration, realizing he's just scuppered his own argument.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: When Juror #7 briefly whistles while the experiment to determine if the old man could have gotten to the door on time is being set up (before Juror #2 tells him to stop), he's whistling the theme of Laurel and Hardy.

tropes.name: Shut Up, Hannibal!
tropes.html:
Juror #10 digs his own grave when he starts shooting his mouth off about how inferior the lower classes are. By the time he's finished, when everyone has clearly stopped listening, this trope — delivered by #4 — is all it takes to shut him up for the rest of the movie.
Juror #10: Listen to me! Listen!
Juror #4: I have. Now sit down and don't open your mouth again.

tropes.name: Silence, You Fool!
tropes.html:
In the 1957 film, Juror #3 impolitely orders Juror #2 to be quiet, when he interrupts him:
Juror #3: Okay, let-let's get to the point. What about the switch knife, they found in the old man's chest?
Juror #2: Uh, wai-wait a minute, there's some people who haven't talked yet. Shouldn't we go in order?
Juror #3: They'll get their chance to talk — BE quiet a second, will ya?
Juror #2: (sags his head a bit)

tropes.name: Silent Treatment
tropes.html: How everyone reacts when Juror #10 flies off the handle about the inferiority of the lower classes. Even the ones who were still in favor of conviction. It shames 10 enough that he stares off in space quietly in the corner for the rest of the film. And after he's told by Juror #4 to sit down and not open his mouth again, he's silent for the rest of the film, only shaking his head "no" when Juror #8 asks him if he still believes the defendant is guilty.

tropes.name: Sinister Switchblade
tropes.html:
The murder weapon is a switchblade, but the blade's reputation even extends to its non-usage; Juror #4 is appalled when Juror #8 pulls out an identical blade to prove that there are more copies of the supposedly rare knife than previously thought.
Juror #4: It's against the law to buy or sell switchblade knives.

tropes.name: Skewed Priorities
tropes.html: Juror #7 is more concerned about attending a baseball game he has tickets for, so he just wants them all to agree on a verdict as quickly as possible. He switches sides as soon as it is apparent that a majority now favor acquittal, without offering any reasons. Juror #11 calls him out on it.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Gender Inequality
tropes.html: The only characters are the members of an all-male jury. Some modern versions (including the 1997 remake) try to correct this by making the judge a woman. Others simply opt to re-title the play "Twelve Angry Jurors" just so that some of the jury can be women.

tropes.name: Speech-Centric Work
tropes.html: The film consists of the twelve jurors debating whether or not the defendant is guilty.

tropes.name: Spotting the Thread
tropes.html: A variant where the party isn't lying at all: at one point, #4 rubs his nose due to his glasses and #9 notices he has marks from where the nose pads are. #9 points out the witness who claims she saw the murder from her bed had the same marks, but didn't wear her glasses to court. #8 establishes that the witness is not reliable because it's incredibly unlikely she'd be wearing glasses to bed, especially when she said she was trying to sleep when the murder happened.

tropes.name: The Spock
tropes.html: Juror #4 is certainly the most rational of the group, concerning himself purely with the facts. Despite being one of the last holdouts in favor of conviction, he listens to all of his opponents' arguments with an open mind. Once all of his objections have been rebutted, he changes his vote without complaint.

tropes.name: The Stoic
tropes.html: Similar to the above, Juror #4 is also the most calm and collected of the jurors, never raising his voice or showing strong emotions of any kind. He's not completely stoic, though, as a few scenes evidence. He becomes visibly unnerved while being interrogated by Juror #8, and towards the end, expresses annoyance towards Juror #3 (for his obnoxiousness), Juror #9 (for badgering him with seemingly-inane questions instead of getting to the point), and Juror #10 (for being obviously prejudiced against the defendant, instead of arriving at a guilty verdict because of the facts).

tropes.name: Stoic Spectacles
tropes.html: Juror #4 is a "rational stockbroker, unflappable, self-assured, and analytical".

tropes.name: Thunder Equals Downpour
tropes.html: One thunderclap, cue rainstorm.

tropes.name: The Un-Reveal
tropes.html: Did the boy really kill his father? If he didn't, who did? Since the play and film only see the case from the jurors' perspective (not the police's), it is never discovered. All that is known is that there is reasonable doubt as to the boy's guilt — which, under the laws of the United States, is enough to keep him from being convicted. Truth in Television, of course — jurors not working on an obvious Open-and-Shut Case rarely get "closure" as to whether or not they were right.

tropes.name: Unwanted Assistance
tropes.html: Near the conclusion, when Jurors #3 and #4 are the last ones still arguing for conviction, #4 is clearly annoyed at having his rational arguments undermined by #3's not-so-rational cheering from over his shoulder.

tropes.name: Verbal Tic
tropes.html: Juror #10 seems to have one of these, you know what I mean? *sniff*

tropes.name: Video Credits
tropes.html: Although the jurors each have a number, and they sit in order, these are used to help distinguish the names of actors with their faces.

tropes.name: Villainous Breakdown
tropes.html:
• When Juror #10 delivers his famous rant. "Listen... listen to me...."
  • And Juror #3 shortly afterward. Made somewhat more poignant by the reactions of the other jurors; where they reacted to #10's breakdown with silent anger, they watch #3's meltdown with something closer to pity, as most of them realize why he is really pushing for a guilty verdict even as he denies the true reason, not just to the other jurors but to himself.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
Each time a piece of evidence is found to be wanting, a Wham Line usually reveals the flaw, i.e. "No one who had used one of these knives would hold it like that." "What movie did you see that night?" etc. One especially notable one (for how thoroughly it demolishes a key piece of evidence):
Juror #8: The old man according to his own testimony — "I'm gonna kill you", body hitting the floor a split second later — would have had to hear the boy make this statement with the el [elevated train] roaring past his nose! It's not possible he could have heard it!

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html: Juror #8 pulls out a switchblade and sticks it into the table right next to the "unique" murder weapon, showing that they are identical.

tropes.name: Worthy Opponent
tropes.html: Both Juror #8 and #4 debate their points without getting too personal, each seems to be just as factual as the other, and #4 certainly seems to view #8 this way.

tropes.name: You Are Number Six
tropes.html: The jurors are only ever referred to by their numbers, though Jurors #8 and #9 introduce themselves to each other at the end of the film adaptations.

tropes.name: You Wouldn't Shoot Me
tropes.html:
• Juror #3 is asked to re-enact the stabbing process on Juror #8. Given the tension between the two men, and #3's almost maniacal bloodthirstiness, there's a definite tension as to how "real" #3 will make the re-enactment. Lampshaded by the alarmed reactions of most of the other ten jurors as he draws back the knife.
  • Referring back to the I'll Kill You! example above, Juror #8 afterwards remarks, "You don't really mean you'll kill me, do you?"

tropes.name: Always Identical Twins
