tropes.html: A pair of elderly women twins are seen buying food at the local fruit stand. They also Finish Each Other's Sentences.

tropes.name: Animate Inanimate Object
tropes.html:
• When Amélie falls asleep, the animals in the pictures on the wall above her bed come to life and talk about her. Her pig-shaped bedside light then pulls a cord to switch itself off.
  • A set of photos from a photo booth comes alive and talks to Nino. At first, they speak in unison, but then they talk individually.

tropes.name: Anonymous Public Phone Call
tropes.html: Amélie, in a nearby cafe, calls a payphone next to a passer-by to make him walk into the phone booth and find a present she's left there for him. She plays a similar trick on Nino later.

tropes.name: Anywhere but Their Lips
tropes.html: Played with during the final kissing scene.

tropes.name: Artistic License
tropes.html:
According to the narrator in the epilogue, "Félix Lerbier learns there are more links in his brain than atoms in the universe." If you think about it for a second, that's physically impossible. It should have been "than stars in the universe".
  • This is sometimes quoted as more possible links in the brain than atoms in the universe, which is mathematically possible.

tropes.name: Aside Glance
tropes.html:
Plenty from Amélie.
  • She does one after her coup to return the photo album to Nino succeeds.
  • The last shot of the movie has Nino and Amélie on their motorbike both turn and make faces at the camera.

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html: Amélie takes revenge on the grocer on behalf of Lucien. He almost suffers a nervous breakdown, but he's such a Hate Sink that the audience enjoys it.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html:
• The narrator announces that the following event will change Amélie's life forever. We see Amélie reacting to TV footage about the death of Princess Diana, and it looks like this will be the driving force behind her change. But then, the scene goes on to show that it's her Dramatic Drop that triggers the Inciting Incident when it causes her to find an old metal box, which contains childhood memorabilia hidden by a boy who lived in her apartment decades earlier.
  • Nino gets one. While he is waiting for Amélie at the cafe, a beautiful girl walks in, smiling in his general direction. But then she is revealed to be somebody else's date.

tropes.name: Birds of a Feather
tropes.html: Amélie and Nino are quiet little oddballs who are very kind but aren't all that good at making friends.

tropes.name: Blind Driving
tropes.html: During their Romantic Ride Sharing in the finale scene, Amélie playfully covers Nino's eyes with her hands while he's driving his moped through the streets of Paris, both of them riding without helmets.

tropes.name: Blithe Spirit
tropes.html: Amélie's mission after finding the box of trinkets is to affect the lives of those around her in a positive way.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html: Collignon's father comments that his wife was still squeezing her son's toothpaste when he was aged fifteen. Later, Collignon uses toothpaste, only to find that it is foot cream, in an almost identical tube.

tropes.name: Bully Magnet
tropes.html: Apparently, Nino was this at school, which is shown by him being forced into a wastepaper basket by his classmates, and placed on the teacher's desk.

tropes.name: Cacophony Cover-Up
tropes.html: Amélie tries to cover up Georgette's Immodest Orgasm with the steamer of the coffee machine.

tropes.name: Cannot Spit It Out
tropes.html: Amélie's games with Nino, ostensibly designed to whet his interest in her, are in fact because she's painfully shy and terrified of approaching him. The two times she does actually set up an honest meeting to approach him, she freezes up and lets the moment slip past.

tropes.name: Career-Ending Injury
tropes.html: Madame Suzanne's backstory. She fell from a horse which ended her circus career.

tropes.name: Cassette Craze
tropes.html: Gina's obsessive stalker Joseph is at the café where she works every day, using a dictating machine to take notes on her every movement. When he then moves on to Georgette, he demonstrates his stalking by playing back all the references to "camel hair" (belonging to a particular male) in quick succession.

tropes.name: Cat Scare
tropes.html: Inverted. When Amélie daydreams about Nino coming in through her beaded doorway and the beads rustle, she turns around and rather than being relieved to see a cat, is understandably disappointed to find her cat.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html:
• Amélie's air stewardess friend Philomène, who is introduced just as one of the other regulars of Café des Deux Moulins. She's the one who's been taking the pictures of the gnome in different parts of the world. She jokingly tells Amélie she got the nickname "Snow White" for it.
  • Philomène's cat applies as a minor example, too. See above for Cat Scare.

tropes.name: The Chessmaster
tropes.html: An unexpected example. Amélie is the less-common benevolent version of this trope, manipulating people and events in such a way as to bring them happiness without ever revealing her intentions (or sometimes even her involvement).

tropes.name: Choosy Beggar
tropes.html: Amélie offers some change to a beggar hanging around at a Paris train station, but he declines since he doesn't work on Sundays.

tropes.name: Chore Character Exploration
tropes.html: In the sex shop where they work, Nino and Eva casually discuss Amélie, while busily putting prices on sex toys. Madeline Wells is seen dusting banisters while Lucien talks to her.

tropes.name: Clock Tampering
tropes.html: A variant, in that Amélie changes the alarm on Collignon's clock to four o' clock in the morning. He gets up and starts opening his shop, realises that his surroundings are unusually quiet, and looks at his watch. Later, Lucien is running the shop on his own, saying that his boss "is sleeping among the cauliflowers".

tropes.name: Cloudcuckoolander
tropes.html: Amélie is very shy, so she mostly lives in a world of her own imagination. Much of the supporting cast are also a bit quirky.

tropes.name: Collector of the Strange
tropes.html: Nino. Before he started gathering ID photos, he collected footprints in wet cement and recorded funny laughs.

tropes.name: Coming and Going
tropes.html: In the opening scene, a man crosses the name of his recently deceased friend out of his little black book at the exact same moment as the title character's conception (only the sperm entering the egg is shown).

tropes.name: Commonality Connection
tropes.html: The Narrator emphasises the similarities between Amélie and Nino's childhoods, with one desiring a brother and the other a sister. Downplayed as they never find out about each other's childhoods, but it's clear these shared experiences helped develop their similar (eccentric) personalities, which are what make them such a good match.

tropes.name: Companion Cube
tropes.html: Possibly Amélie's father's garden gnome, which is the only thing he cares about in his retirement. To persuade her father to travel, Amélie steals the gnome, and gets her friend Philomène to send photos of the gnome in front of famous world landmarks to her father. This is emphasised more in the stage play, with the song "I'm better off in my back yard" dedicated to the gnome.

tropes.name: Compartment Shot
tropes.html: We see Amélie reaching for that treasure box from inside the wall.

tropes.name: Cool and Unusual Punishment
tropes.html: Amélie pays back cruelty with cruelty throughout her life. When she is a child, a neighbor fools her into thinking that her camera causes accidents, so as punishment she sits on his roof, listening to the football game on the radio and unplugging his TV connection at vital moments. As an adult, she plays pranks on the grocer to torment him for his mean-spirited treatment of his assistant.

tropes.name: Cool Old Guy
tropes.html: Raymond Dufayel, the shut-in in Amélie's building. He serves as a mentor to Amélie and delivers the monologue begging her not to follow his example that finally breaks her out of her shell.

tropes.name: Crazy Jealous Guy
tropes.html: Joseph, who possessively smothers any woman he is interested in. This causes him to stalk Gina, and sabotage his potential relationship with Georgette.

tropes.name: Creative Closing Credits
tropes.html:
The main characters are seen as photos in Nino's album, including the face of the unseen narrator. The opening credits are also very subtly creative: the young Amélie is seen doing quirky things related to the credits, including:
  • For "costume", she wears cherries on her ears.
  • For "set design", she knocks over a line of dominoes.
  • For "music", she plays her hair like a stringed instrument.
  • For "sound", she drinks noisily through a straw.

tropes.name: Creator's Culture Carryover
tropes.html: One French quirk is the convention of door handles being a knob on the side that you pull to open, and a lever on the side that you push to open. When Amélie is gaslighting Collignon, she swaps the handles on his bathroom door. He automatically tries to push down the lever handle which is not there, and does a Double Take when he notices.

tropes.name: Cult Soundtrack
tropes.html: The soundtrack, composed by Yann Tiersen, received rave reviews and even went platinum in Canada. Its songs are still used as atmospheric music in a wide range of media.

tropes.name: Death by Looking Up
tropes.html: Amélie's mother meets this fate, courtesy of a suicidal Canadian tourist jumping off a church roof and landing on her.

tropes.name: Digital Bikini
tropes.html: When the movie was shown on the satellite TV channel Ovation TV, a bikini was photoshopped on the topless dancer Nino asks to cover for him at work.

tropes.name: Dope Slap
tropes.html: In one of his Kick the Dog moments, Collignon slaps Lucien on the back of his head.

tropes.name: Dramatic Drop
tropes.html: The movie uses this to get the plot started, as Amélie reacts in shock to hearing news of Lady Diana Spencer's death and drops the lid of her perfume flask.

tropes.name: Dramatic TV Shut-Off
tropes.html: Played with, with the young Amélie taking her revenge on a neighbour, by disconnecting his television aerial while he is watching football; she has a radio with her, so she knows when the best moments are.

tropes.name: Driver Faces Passenger
tropes.html: One of the things Amélie does not like is drivers in American films who don't watch the road. Cut to a scene from the American film Father's Little Dividend where the actor drives a desk and looks at his passenger 99% of the time. In the DVD director's commentary, Jean-Pierre Jeunet comments on how difficult it is to find a clip exhibiting this trope when you're specifically looking for one.note If he only had TV Tropes available at the time...

tropes.name: Ear Ache
tropes.html: When he finds his box of treasures, Bretodeau has a flashback to his childhood. He wins all the marbles at school in one go, and is busily gathering them up while the other children line up for lessons. The teacher seizes his ear to bring him into line, just as the seams on his pocket burst, and the marbles go everywhere.

tropes.name: Empathic Environment
tropes.html: It starts raining when young Amélie's goldfish gets dumped into the creek.

tropes.name: Eye-Covering Surprise
tropes.html: In the last few moments of the film, Amélie flirtatiously covers Nino's eyes while she is riding with him on his moped.

tropes.name: The Fantastic Trope of Wonderous Titles
tropes.html: The French title, at least.

tropes.name: Fast-Forward Gag
tropes.html: This happens when Amélie prepares her forged letter to Madeline Welles. The action is sped up while she uses scissors to cut a letter into small pieces, before gluing them together in a different order.

tropes.name: Feedback Rule
tropes.html: The intercom at Nino's sex shop is giving off a feedback sound whenever it's being operated.

tropes.name: Feet-First Introduction
tropes.html: The mystery man is at first seen only by his feet, with distinctive red shoes. Later it is revealed that this is the bald man who keeps mysteriously reappearing in Nino's album of discarded passport photos, and for a simple reason: he is the photo booth repair man, discarding his test photos.

tropes.name: Forged Message
tropes.html: One of Amélie's neighbors is bitter that her husband left her for another woman, then died in a plane crash. So Amélie creates a fake letter to convince the neighbor that the husband wanted to reconcile with her, had left his mistress, and was on his way home when the plane crashed.

tropes.name: For Happiness
tropes.html: Amélie's acts of kindness to make those around her happy.

tropes.name: The Freelance Shame Squad
tropes.html: The laughing crowd in front of Collignon's shop after Amélie delivers her imagined joke about him not having a heart.

tropes.name: French Accordion
tropes.html: Though actually a French film, Amélie features a lot of musette in the soundtrack to evoke a timeless mood, befitting a story set in a Magical Realism Sugar Bowl version of Paris.

tropes.name: Friendless Background
tropes.html: Both Amélie and Nino. Amélie was homeschooled, while Nino was bullied by the other children.

tropes.name: Fun with Bubble Wrap
tropes.html: As the film tends to list the likes and dislikes of many of the characters, the narration notes that while Gina's ex-boyfriend Joseph is stalking her to see who she goes out with next, the only thing he likes doing is popping bubble wrap, and he is shown doing this beneath the cafe table.

tropes.name: Gaslighting
tropes.html: Amélie sneaks into her grocer's apartment and subtly messes with his stuff, changing the size of his slippers, the numbers on his speed dial, etc., to punish him for mocking his ambiguously handicapped and one-armed employee.

tropes.name: Gay Paree
tropes.html: Paris comes across as a sumptuous and beautiful wonderland, though the real Paris is significantly dirtier. On his English-language DVD commentary, Jeunet jokes that in real life Paris is totally horrible, except for his native Montmartre.

tropes.name: Gender-Blender Name
tropes.html: Amélie meets a female Dominique Bretodeau who seems to take quite a liking in her.

tropes.name: Glass Slipper
tropes.html: Amélie has a Love at First Sight moment when bumping into Nino at a Parisian subway station. He doesn't notice her at all and quickly rides off with his scooter. However, a photo album falls off when he takes a sharp corner and Amélie picks it up. It helps her to get in contact with Nino, who, after noticing his loss, leaves stickers around the station with his phone number.

tropes.name: Good Feels Good
tropes.html: The catalyzing moment in the film is when Amélie realizes that improving people's lives makes her feel good, so she sets about secretly meddling in others' affairs.

tropes.name: Guilt Complex
tropes.html: Young Amélie temporarily believes she caused all misery in the world after her neighbor planted that idea in her head.

tropes.name: Helping Granny Cross the Street
tropes.html: In one scene, Amélie is helping a blind man across the street and even further.

tropes.name: Her Code Name Was "Mary Sue"
tropes.html: Amélie has multiple Imagine Spot moments where she watches documentaries about Lady Diana and puts herself into them. While one such spot obviously leads to Amélie getting a Downer Ending, she is nonetheless pristine in those spots as the documentary narration makes her into a selfless martyr that the world can't go on without.

tropes.name: A Hero Is Born
tropes.html: The movie begins with the conception of the heroine.

tropes.name: Hypochondria
tropes.html: Georgette is a straight example in combination with Sickly Neurotic Geek, given all the medicine she's witnessed taking, while Amélie herself ends up an accidental example because her excitement over paternal contact is mistaken for a heart condition.

tropes.name: I Have This Friend
tropes.html: Oddly, done by the advice-giver. Raymond notes that Amélie is too shy to talk about herself. He gently coaxes her into it by pretending to ask for motives behind a figure in his painting, and deliberately suggesting ones similar to what he's seen of her.

tropes.name: Imagine Spot
tropes.html: Used a lot, like when Amélie pictures herself as Zorro, or when Nino is late and her extended train of thought leads her to believe that he'd been captured and taken hostage by the Afghan Mujahideen, whom he joins and is now living in Afghanistan raising goats.

tropes.name: Immodest Orgasm
tropes.html:
• When Amélie wonders how many couples are having orgasms at that moment, we get a montage of the couples doing so.
  • Joseph gives Georgette one of the immodest kind. See Right Through the Wall.

tropes.name: I Need a Freaking Drink
tropes.html: Collignon needs one after the shenanigans Amélie puts him through. Unfortunately, the liquor is spiked with a handful of salt resulting in him performing a Spit Take.

tropes.name: Informed Attractiveness
tropes.html: In Nino's dream, the headshots in one of his pictures come alive and argue over whether Amélie is all that attractive. Some will only say that she's rather pretty, but another insists that she's beautiful. Interestingly, the character was written for Emily Watson and was probably going to be somewhat Hollywood Homely before Audrey Tautou was cast.

tropes.name: Interactive Narrator
tropes.html:
The narrator's comments are sometimes directly addressed by Amélie to the audience. There is also one time when the woman in a coma wakes up and speaks to the audience.
Narrator: Sometimes, on Friday nights, Amélie goes to the cinema.
Amélie (whispering directly at the camera): What I like is turning around in the dark to look at other people's faces...

tropes.name: I Want My Mommy!
tropes.html: After Collignon gets sufficiently gaslighted, he decides to call his mother; only to find that the speed dial for his mother has been changed to a psychiatric helpline.

tropes.name: Karmic Trickster
tropes.html: The role Amélie takes in dealing with the grocer's treatment of Lucien.

tropes.name: Knuckle Cracking
tropes.html: Gina, Amélie's co-worker, takes a liking to this activity.

tropes.name: Lady Drunk
tropes.html: Madeleine Wallace.

tropes.name: Leave the Two Lovebirds Alone
tropes.html: When Amélie and Nino finally get together, Lucien keeps filming them making out from across the street, only for Dufayel to tell him off.

tropes.name: Lies to Children
tropes.html: Amélie's neighbor makes the gullible young girl believe that by operating her camera she was responsible for a car crash. He gets his comeuppance soon enough.

tropes.name: Linked List Clue Methodology
tropes.html: Amélie leaves lists of clues for Nino to find to help him find her, so she does not have to approach him directly: she leaves blue arrows for him to follow, which lead him to a telescope, which he can look through to see where she is. She later leaves a torn-up photo of herself for him to find, telling him to meet her in the café.

tropes.name: Living Photo
tropes.html: Nino keeps a photo booth photograph by his bedside which suddenly starts talking to him, reminding him that there is a girl in love with him.

tropes.name: Like You Were Dying
tropes.html: Inverted; it's Dufayel, old and sick, who prods young and vibrant Amélie into living her life.

tropes.name: Love at First Sight
tropes.html: Implied with Amélie who fell in love with Nino when she saw him by the photo machine at the metro station.

tropes.name: Lustful Melt
tropes.html: Amélie dissolved into tears because of heartbreak after she Cannot Spit It Out and Nino leaves the cafe.

tropes.name: Magic Realism
tropes.html: Everywhere, from the talking photographs to Amélie watching an old-style newsreel on her own life (arguably a Shout-Out to Citizen Kane and of course Mother Teresa and Florence Nightingale)...

tropes.name: Metaphorgotten
tropes.html: The metaphorical comparison of the unfinished girl in the painting to Amélie quickly disintegrates when she gets fed up with Raymond's prying.

tropes.name: A Minor Kidroduction
tropes.html: A large portion of the first act is relating to Amélie's childhood, in which she begins showing her defining characteristics.

tropes.name: Missing Mom
tropes.html: Amélie loses her mother to an accident early in her life. Her death leaves Amélie behind with an absent-minded father.

tropes.name: Missing the Good Stuff
tropes.html: A young Amélie gets her revenge on an unpleasant neighbor by sneaking onto his roof with a portable radio during an important soccer match and pulling the plug on his TV antenna whenever a goal is about to be scored. It drives him crazy.

tropes.name: Mistaken for Cheating
tropes.html: Joseph sees Gina dropping a note into Nino's pocket and assumes that she was giving Nino her number while it actually was a note from Amélie.

tropes.name: Modest Orgasm
tropes.html: During the sequence when Amélie is imagining how many people are in the midst of orgasm ("fifteen!"), the last woman's O sound is somewhere between a gasp and a squeak.

tropes.name: Modesty Bedsheet
tropes.html: It was more like a Modesty Human Shield. In both scenes Amélie was naked and had a person over her.

tropes.name: Monochrome Casting
tropes.html: The film is set in Montmartre, an area of Paris with a large immigrant population, but the cast, with the exception of Jamel Debouze, is exclusively white.

tropes.name: Monochrome Past
tropes.html: The flashbacks to Nino's childhood are in black and white.

tropes.name: Mountaintop Healthcare
tropes.html: In one Imagine Spot, Amélie sees herself as a Red Cross nurse in the Alps pushing Dufayel around in a wheelchair.

tropes.name: Ms. Imagination
tropes.html: Amélie has created an imaginary world to make up for the lack of friends.

tropes.name: Multiple Head Case
tropes.html: A variant with Living Photos. Amélie leaves a note for Nino, written on the back of a set of four identical passport photos of a man. Later, when these photos are by Nino’s bed, they talk to him, at first in unison, then individually.

tropes.name: Narrative Filigree
tropes.html: The Movie. Amélie frequently delves into irrelevant events, such as marking Amélie's conception occurring at the exact time that a fly is crushed, that wine glasses "dance" on a moving tablecloth unseen, and that an elderly gentleman erases his deceased friend from his notebook of phone numbers. Additionally, almost every named character (or animal in the case of Philomène's cat) is noted as liking or disliking something in order to give detail to the world. The minor subplot about the death of Princess Diana also qualifies.

tropes.name: Narrator
tropes.html: The narrator will tell you about the plot, the characters, and even the characters' likes and dislikes. These are given nods and shout outs almost every time the character in question appears on-screen. A good example of this is Bretodeau, whom the narrator tells us likes snitching the chicken oysters while fixing dinner, and is later shown at his daughter's house fixing dinner for them and her son, giving the boy the oysters.

tropes.name: Neat Freak
tropes.html: Amélie's parents. Her father likes polishing his shoes, emptying his toolbox, cleaning it thoroughly, and putting everything back. Her mother likes dusting with the slippers on her feet, as well as emptying her handbag, cleaning it thoroughly, and putting everything back.

tropes.name: Not Listening to Me, Are You?
tropes.html:
Amélie's father is distracted because his favorite gnome went missing and sent him pictures from various cities around the world. So he fails Amélie's test of attention:
Amélie: I had two heart attacks and had to have an abortion because I did crack while I was pregnant. Other than that, I'm fine.
Raphaël (absent-mindedly): Good.

tropes.name: Not the Intended Use
tropes.html: Raymond Dufayel keeps a video camera focused on the clock on a shop outside his window, so that the time is always on his television screen, and saves him having to wind up his clocks. However, he does use it as a video camera later in the film.

tropes.name: An Odd Place to Sleep
tropes.html: After Amélie has stolen her father's garden gnome, she misses the last train home, and sleeps in a photo booth.

tropes.name: One-Track-Minded Artist
tropes.html: Dufayel embodies this trope as a symptom of his profound isolation. For two decades, he has compulsively reproduced Renoir's Luncheon of the Boating Party, yet his artistic quest always stalls on one detail: capturing the gaze of the girl with the glass, who he feels is on the outside looking in. This artistic stagnation is a direct mirror of his own life. The painting becomes his primary tool for mentoring Amélie, as he challenges her not to become like the girl in the painting—a perpetual spectator. Inspired by her, he finally shatters his own decades-long creative loop, and is last seen joyfully painting a vibrant, abstract version of the painting, signifying his personal and artistic liberation.

tropes.name: One-Word Title
tropes.html: The film's English title in contrast to the original French name.

tropes.name: Overly Long Gag
tropes.html: Amélie's imagined second reason as to why Nino is late: just before he was able to reassemble the photo clue, a long saga involving Nino being captured by terrorists and travelling to a foreign country.

tropes.name: Overly Long Scream
tropes.html: The child Amélie lets out a very long and high-pitched continuous scream when her only friend, her pet goldfish jumps out of its bowl. The scream stops abruptly when the fish is returned to the bowl.

tropes.name: Painting the Medium
tropes.html: The mother's Twitchy Eye is pointed out with on-screen text.

tropes.name: Paper Destruction of Anger
tropes.html: When she thinks Nino has got together with Gina, Amélie tears down some of Nino's "Où & quand?" posters that she'd put up on her walls.

tropes.name: Parental Neglect
tropes.html: A non-malicious variation. Amélie's father was so distant that, when he gave her occasional check-ups, the rare contact with her father would make her heart race; since he believed this was a result of a heart condition, he had her home-schooled by her neurotic mother, forcing Amélie to hide in her imagination.

tropes.name: Pet Fish in Distress
tropes.html: To highlight Amélie's somewhat chaotic and isolated childhood, her only friend is a goldfish in a small bowl, and the hostile home life makes the fish jump out of the bowl. Amélie does an Overly Long Scream while the fish thrashes around on the floor, and is eventually scooped up and returned to the bowl. Amélie's mother then howls "ENOUGH!", and she and Amélie sadly tip the fish out of the bowl into a river, dropping the bowl in as well.

tropes.name: Photo-Booth Montage
tropes.html: Played with. The film has a montage of Amélie looking through other people's discarded photos from such a booth, which her love interest has collected into an album.

tropes.name: Photo Montage
tropes.html: The Creative Closing Credits feature Nino's carefully compiled photo album, now with pictures of all the film's characters added.

tropes.name: Politically Incorrect Villain
tropes.html: The grocer Collignon, constantly picking on the mentally disabled Lucien and calling him names.

tropes.name: Poor Man's Porn
tropes.html: The grocer reveals that he found a lingerie catalog from Lucien where he'd pasted Lady Di's face over the model's.

tropes.name: Protagonist Title
tropes.html: Both the French and English titles of the movie are named after Amélie herself.

tropes.name: Public Secret Message
tropes.html: When Amélie and Nino are described as the childhood friends that never were, the young Amélie and Nino are seen flashing lights out of their windows at each other.

tropes.name: Race for Your Love
tropes.html: Aborted. In the final act when Amélie can't spot Nino outside her house, she rushes for the door to chase after him but he is already standing in front of her door.

tropes.name: Raven Hair, Ivory Skin
tropes.html: Amélie, especially on the poster.

tropes.name: Reconstruct the Remains
tropes.html: Nino has an album of people's rejected passport photographs, which he has obtained by searching for the pieces under photo booths around Paris, and sticking them together. When Amélie tries to make Nino notice her, she disguises herself with a hat and mask, takes passport photos of herself, and leaves the pieces for him to find, with instructions of where and when to meet her. He does find them, and is seen using tweezers to put the pieces together.

tropes.name: Recycled Soundtrack
tropes.html: A good deal of the soundtrack is taken from Yann Tiersen's other albums.

tropes.name: Red/Green Contrast
tropes.html: The film uses red and green predominantly in its color palette, with the color blue used to make objects stand out.

tropes.name: Returning The Mac Guffin
tropes.html: Amélie finds a small metal box of somebody's childhood treasures from the 1950s, hidden behind a loose tile in her bathroom. She goes to great lengths to track down the owner of the box, and return it to him.

tropes.name: Rhythm Typewriter
tropes.html: The track "Pas si simple" starts with a typewriter as the lead-in to the rest of the music, and keeps the rhythm pattern in the background.

tropes.name: Right Through the Wall
tropes.html: Georgette and Joseph in the café bathroom, making all the cups and crockery rattle. Amélie covers up the sound of The Immodest Orgasm by running the espresso machine.

tropes.name: Romantic Ride Sharing
tropes.html: This happens in the end sequence of the movie, when Nino and Amélie are shown riding down the streets of Montmartre on a motorcycle, teasing one another playfully and generally being so deeply in love that they are completely oblivious to the world around them.

tropes.name: Rule of Funny
tropes.html: It's very unlikely to find the toothpaste and foot cream tubes in someone's bathroom look alike. But it makes for a great prank.

tropes.name: Scenery Porn
tropes.html: The film is gorgeously shot and uses beautiful locations throughout Gay Paree. In fact, Parisians complained that the locations used in filming were cleaned so thoroughly that they didn't match the surrounding ambiance once the film crews left.

tropes.name: The Scream
tropes.html: Collignon lets out the first of a few when he realises he's brushing his teeth with foot cream.

tropes.name: Screams Like a Little Girl
tropes.html: When Collignon causes a dramatic short circuit thanks to Amélie's prank.

tropes.name: Seasonal Baggage
tropes.html: To symbolise the years between Amélie's childhood and adulthood, a Time-Passes Montage of her teddy bear in the garden is shown, through the four seasons.

tropes.name: Separated by the Wall
tropes.html: Amélie and Nino being separated by the apartment door towards the end of the movie.

tropes.name: Sex Montage
tropes.html: In one scene, Amélie amuses herself by wondering "how many couples are having orgasms right now?" She correctly guesses "Fifteen!" after a montage of every single one.

tropes.name: "Shaggy Dog" Story
tropes.html: Through his hobby of collecting discarded ID photos, Nino becomes fascinated with a sinister-looking individual, who took photos of himself in every single booth in Paris before immediately throwing them away, and spends a good deal of time wondering what his secret could be. It takes almost the entire movie and a good deal of suspense-building until it's revealed that he's just the repairman.

tropes.name: Shamed Before the Whole School
tropes.html: When Dominique Bretodeau comes across a marble in his box of childhood treasures, there is a flashback to a tragic day at school, in which he wins all the marbles from the other children. As he shovels them into his pockets, the teacher blows the whistle for the end of recess. When Bretodeau continues shovelling up the marbles, his teacher drags him over by the ear, just as his pocket bursts, and the marbles go everywhere.

tropes.name: Shipper on Deck
tropes.html: Amélie for Georgette and Joseph. It goes poorly.

tropes.name: Shrine to the Fallen
tropes.html: The father builds an elaborate shrine for the deceased mother.

tropes.name: Shrinking Violet
tropes.html: Amélie and Nino. They are both shy, quiet, and friendly but have a hard time making friends.

tropes.name: Significant Reference Date
tropes.html: The film begins on the morning of August 31, 1997 - the date that Diana, Princess of Wales, died. Amélie learning this news is what sets off the plot.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Fourth Wall Hardness
tropes.html: Semipermeable Fourth Wall. The narrator is one that is sometimes an Interactive Narrator, though these scenes are never key to the plot and are just done for comedic purposes. Amélie also occasionally makes an Aside Glance at the camera, and the ending sequence also has both Amélie and Nino doing one together at the camera.

tropes.name: Smash to Black
tropes.html: After Amélie's mother is hit by the suicidal tourist, the scene cuts to black.

tropes.name: Stage Whisper
tropes.html: Parodied. A prompter from a cellar window provides Amélie with a punchy comeback to Collignon insulting Lucien.

tropes.name: Stuffed into a Trashcan
tropes.html: When Nino is introduced, the flashback shows him having been bullied this way in school.

tropes.name: Suddenly Shouting
tropes.html: Raymond Dufayel suddenly shouts at Lucien, while Lucien is chatting about Lady Di, and disturbing his concentration.

tropes.name: Surprising Domestic Discovery
tropes.html: The main plot of the film begins when Amélie accidentally discovers a loose tile in her bathroom, behind which is hidden a small box of relics from somebody's childhood in the 1950s. She makes it her mission to find out whose box this was, and to give it back to him.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Mundane Reason
tropes.html: There is a sinister-looking bald man who keeps taking photos of himself in photo booths all over Paris, and the reason he is doing it is that he is the booth repair man, who takes test photos of himself, then discards them.

tropes.name: Talking with Signs
tropes.html: When Samantha is dancing in the peep-show booth to loud music, Nino tries to ask her if she can replace him on the till at four o'clock. First he tries bellowing above the music, then pointing to himself and holding up four fingers. Finally he resorts to writing a note and holding it up.

tropes.name: That Cloud Looks Like...
tropes.html: Exaggerated for the sake of magic realism.

tropes.name: Toilet Throne
tropes.html: Reflecting her quirky character, Amélie is briefly seen sitting on the toilet while studying the letters from her neighbour's late husband. She is clothed, implying she is not actually using the toilet, and is surrounded by candles and the letters on the floor, implying she has been there for some time.

tropes.name: Time Capsule
tropes.html: Dominique Bretodeau's treasure box which he left behind by accident in the 1950s.

tropes.name: Time-Passes Montage
tropes.html: A brief one just before Amélie grows up, showing a teddy bear in the garden through the four seasons.

tropes.name: Tossing Rocks at Your Window
tropes.html: Amélie visits her father's house late at night, but cannot enter because the door is locked. She picks up a pebble, and is about to throw it at the window, then she sees the garden gnome, and decides to take it with her, as part of a special plan to persuade her father to travel.

tropes.name: Trickster Girlfriend
tropes.html: Amélie begins as this for Nino, since she plays cat-and-mouse with him without even revealing her face; it's mostly due to shyness, though.

tropes.name: Tunnel of Love
tropes.html: Played with. Amélie's first meeting with her future love interest Nino is on a ghost train, where Nino is dressed as a ghost, and strokes her face while saying "Whooooooo!"

tropes.name: Twice Shy
tropes.html: Amélie and Nino: both very shy and introverted people (and also more than a little quirky) which makes them perfect for each other, but alas, they Cannot Spit It Out (until the very end of the movie, that is.)

tropes.name: Twitchy Eye
tropes.html: Amélie's mother, cited as the sign of a nervous person.

tropes.name: Undignified Death
tropes.html: Amélie's mother is leaving Notre-Dame de Paris, having just prayed for the conception of a second child, when a Quebecois tourist committing suicide lands on her, killing them both.

tropes.name: Unflattering ID Photo
tropes.html: Nino collects ugly passport photos that people have torn up and discarded, and puts them in an album.

tropes.name: Vehicle Vanish
tropes.html: Amélie finally gathers her courage to face Nino at the train station, but then a luggage car blocks her way. After it passes, Nino has disappeared from the phone booth.

tropes.name: Weather Report Opening
tropes.html: Inverted. The weather report is the final line of the film: "...Meanwhile, at the Sacré-Cœur, the nuns are practicing their backhand. The temperature is 24 degrees, humidity 70%, atmospheric pressure 990 millibars."

tropes.name: Weird Homeschooled Kid
tropes.html: Amélie has been homeschooled until her mother dies, and then after that, presumably does not receive education at all, only seeing her father. As a young woman, she is a Cloud Cuckoolander who lives alone, and wants the world to be a nicer place, and sets about trying to improve everybody's lives, in highly inventive and unusual ways.

tropes.name: Woken Up at an Ungodly Hour
tropes.html: The movie sets the grocer Collignon's alarm clock for four in the morning, as revenge for him being cruel to his employee Lucien. Collignon gets up, gets dressed, but does not notice that something is wrong until he starts opening his shop, and realises that the street around him is deserted, except for a few rats.

tropes.name: World-Weary Waitress
tropes.html: The café owner Suzanne. After thirty years behind a bar, she has seen it all, is an expert on love at first sight, and can even give you the recipe: take two regulars, tell each of them the other fancies them, and leave them to stew: it works every time. Amélie tries this out with Joseph and Georgette.

tropes.name: Zorro Mark
tropes.html: In an Imagine Spot, Amélie sees herself as Zorro leaving a Z mark on Collignon's apartment door.

tropes.name: Adaptational Location Change
tropes.html: The original manga was set in Japan. The film moves the setting to South Korea.

tropes.name: After-Action Patch-Up
tropes.html: After collapsing from fighting many mooks in a hallway, Oh Dae-Su awakens to find himself back in Mi-Do's apartment with his wounds bandaged and a sleeping Mi-Do by his side.

tropes.name: Age-Gap Romance
tropes.html: Oh Dae-su is old enough to be Mi-do's father. And he is.

tropes.name: Ain't Too Proud to Beg
tropes.html: Perhaps one of the darkest versions in cinema. After learning that he was tricked into having sex with his own daughter, Dae-su breaks down, begging Woo-jin not to reveal this to her. He licks Woo-jin's shoes, promises to be his dog, and even cuts out his own tongue.

tropes.name: Alas, Poor Villain
tropes.html: Right before Woo-jin commits suicide, we have a sad flashback to when his sister committed suicide. Quentin Tarantino was at a screening of the film, and was shocked to find himself crying for a character who had been completely despicable for the entire prior duration of the movie.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Ending
tropes.html: Dae-su is re-hypnotized to erase the truth of Mi-do being his daughter from his memory so that they can live a happy life together. The two embrace, with Dae-su breaking into a smile that slowly turns into a look of pain. The film ends there, leaving whether or not the hypnosis worked, whether or not he was ever hypnotized, whether or not any of it will be enough to heal Dae-su's mental scars, and even whether or not any of the above actually happened all unknown.

tropes.name: And Then What?
tropes.html:
A central theme of the film: what will Oh Dae-su and Woo-jin do when their goals are achieved? This is something Woo-jin realizes too when Oh Dae-su cuts out his tongue and he orders the box to not be opened.
Woo-jin: Now...what joy will I live for now?

tropes.name: And Your Little Dog, Too!
tropes.html: Lee Woo-jin threatens to kill Mi-Do if Oh Dae-Su doesn't complete his mission by July 5th.

tropes.name: An Insert
tropes.html: One of the most epic examples in all of cinema. After trying and failing to save his falling sister, Woo-jin - in flashback - extends his hand out over the bridge, and slowly curls the fingers as if holding a gun, his present reality and his memory merging. We hear the click back in reality as he mimes cocking it, then pulls the - BANG. Cut back to the elevator, and we see he's blown his head open.

tropes.name: Answer Cut
tropes.html: In the film's opening prologue as Oh Dae-Su keeps a suicidal man from falling by holding him by his tie, the man asks him who is he. As present day Oh Dae-Su speaks "My name is...", it cuts back to 15 years prior as a younger and intoxicated Oh Dae-Su as he is being held in jail for his behavior.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Biology
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su states that lack of sunlight has left him depleted of Vitamins A and E, which are dietary vitamins—sunlight is only responsible for the production of Vitamin D.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html:
• "Laugh, and the world laughs with you. Weep and you weep alone."
  • ''Even though I am no better than a beast, don't I have the right to live?'"

tropes.name: Ass Shove
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su finds some suppositories and asks Mi-Do what they are for. Mi-Do tells him that is the medicine she gave to him rectally. She defends herself, asking him how else could she give him medicine while he is unconscious.

tropes.name: Attempted Rape
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su barges into the bathroom Mi-Do is occupying and attempts to rape her. She manages to fight him off and he leaves.

tropes.name: Attempted Homewrecker
tropes.html: In the flashback to 15 years prior, Oh Dae-Su is told by the police at the station and one half of a couple to stop hitting on another man's girlfriend. The drunk Oh Dae-Su denies this.

tropes.name: Awful Truth
tropes.html: The reveal that he fell in love and had sex with his own daughter utterly breaks Dae-su, who resorts to desperate begging and eventually cutting out his own tongue just so that Woo-jin won't tell her the truth. In the aftermath, he has the hypnotist wipe his memories of the truth just so he can keep living.

tropes.name: The Bad Guy Wins
tropes.html: Woo-jin gets his revenge, though he has an emotional breakdown and shoots himself in the head almost immediately afterwards. Nobody wins, really.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html: Never call Soo-ah a "slut" in front of Woo-jin, as Joo-hwan learns the very hard way.

tropes.name: Bewildering Punishment
tropes.html: Dae-su has forgotten about the incest rumor he spread in high school and hence fails to link that incident to his cruel imprisonment.

tropes.name: Big "NO!"
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su screams this when Mi-Do tells him she is about to open a large purple box in front of her. He begs her not to open it, as the box contains information that reveals they're father and daughter.

tropes.name: Black Comedy
tropes.html: While the film is an incredibly dark and disturbing action thriller about revenge, it surprisingly has a lot more humor in it than you might expect.

tropes.name: Bloodless Carnage
tropes.html: Not bloodless by any stretch of the imagination, but not nearly as gory as you might expect either. There's no blood at all in the Hallway Fight except for a trickle on Oh Dae-su — the guy who won. A guy getting stabbed in the eyeball is surprisingly clean as well.

tropes.name: Boom, Headshot!
tropes.html: Woo-jin commits suicide with a gun to his temple. Earlier, he stops Mr. Han from denying his revenge on Dae-su by using the gun to cap him in the head.

tropes.name: Bound and Gagged
tropes.html: This happens on multiple occasions, including to an innocent dentist, Mr. Park, the man who ran Dae-su's prison, and Dae-su himself.

tropes.name: Brother–Sister Incest
tropes.html: Woo-jin and his sister.

tropes.name: Brutal Brawl
tropes.html: The fights in this movie are very realistic, and brutal for it.

tropes.name: Brutish Character, Brutish Weapon
tropes.html: Dae-su's only weapon in the hallway fight is a claw hammer. Earlier, he also uses it to torture Mr. Park, the keeper of the prison.

tropes.name: But for Me, It Was Tuesday
tropes.html:
An exceedingly rare "heroic" example: Oh Dae-su accuses Woo-jin of hypnotizing him to forget that he was the initial cause of the events that led to Woo-jin's sister's suicide. However:
Lee Woo-jin: You weren't drugged. You just forgot. It wasn't important to you.

tropes.name: Car Cushion
tropes.html: The suicidal man lands on a car behind Dae-su, killing himself and his pet.

tropes.name: Cartwright Curse
tropes.html: Lee Woo-jin promises to kill every woman Oh Dae-Su loves until the day he dies.

tropes.name: Central Theme
tropes.html: Vengeance Feels Empty.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Boomerang
tropes.html: Mi-Do promises Oh Dae-Su that when she's ready to make love with him, the sign she gives him is the song "The Face I Miss" (which Oh Dae-Su used as a masturbatory aid while he was imprisoned). When Oh Dae-Su rescues Mi-Do from her attackers and tells her he loves her, Mi-Do gives him the sign by singing "The Face I Miss" and they make love in a motel.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• The angel wings for Dae-su's daughter are mentioned at the beginning of the film by Dae-su himself, and later on, they appear at the film's climax when Mi-do wears them.
  • The television in the hotel room. It's how Woo-jin managed to plant the attraction to Mi-Do in Dae-su's mind.
  • The scissors in Woo-jin's apartment. Dae-su later uses them to cut off his own tongue to appease Woo-jin.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html: Dae-su's daughter, who is discussed in the prologue and given a few mentions afterwards. It turns out she's actually Mi-do.

tropes.name: The Chessmaster
tropes.html: Lee Woo-jin. And as the film picks up speed, he gets faster.

tropes.name: Combat Breakdown
tropes.html: The famous Hallway Fight starts with numerous henchmen launching themselves at Dae-su with great energy as he demolishes them with seemingly superhuman strength, and ends with all parties involved throwing weak punches and aimless swings from exhaustion while struggling to get their breath back.

tropes.name: Confession Triggers Consummation
tropes.html: After Oh Dae-Su decides to trust Mi-Do and tells her everything, even confessing his love for her, Mi-Do affirms her love for him and lets him know she's ready to make love with him by singing "The Face I Miss".

tropes.name: Color Motif
tropes.html:
• Woo-jin and his machinations are associated with purple throughout the film, which is found on his umbrella, his handkerchiefs, his gift boxes, the Purple Blue Dragon restaurant, and more.
  • There are constant parallels between Mi-do and Soo-ah, Woo-Jin's sister, throughout the film. One of them is that both Soo-ah and Mi-do dress in predominantly red clothing and are associated with a red color (Soo-ah's red bike and umbrella, the red wallpaper in Mi-do's apartment and prison room).

tropes.name: Crazy-Prepared
tropes.html: Everything Dae-su does was predicted by Woo-jin, and to a lesser extent, everyone Dae-su interacts with has their exact reactions plotted out, all the way down to it being heavily implied that Mr. Han knows he'll have to be shot by Woo-jin to stop him from killing Dae-su and fulfilling Woo-jin's vengeance. About the only things Woo-jin didn't account for was Joo-hwan slandering his sister and causing him to kill Joo-hwan in a rage, and if the hypnosis on Dae-su and Mi-do to begin their incestuous relationship would (initially) work.

tropes.name: Cruel Twist Ending
tropes.html: The trope itself isn't a spoiler, as it's par for the course as a Park Chan-wook film and part of the Vengeance Trilogy. For this film, it's that Mi-do is Dae-su's daughter.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html:
• Dae-su vs. an elevator full of mooks. It's so incredibly one-sided that we don't even get to see it happen — Dae-su just smiles, and we cut immediately to him stepping out of the elevator over the unconscious or dead bodies of the goons he's just demolished. And this is after he just got through an entirely different, equally bruising brawl with a hallway full of guys, and still has a knife sticking out of his back that he barely seems to notice.
  • Conversely, the fight with Mr. Han has Dae-su get absolutely destroyed, and he would have even gotten killed had Woo-jin not suddenly shot Mr. Han in the head.

tropes.name: Cutlery Escape Aid
tropes.html: Dae-su uses a spare chopstick to carve a hole into the prison wall. This escape attempt is eventually rendered vain when he gets officially released.

tropes.name: Cycle of Revenge
tropes.html: One the villain fully set up as part of his Batman Gambit.

tropes.name: Day Hurts Dark-Adjusted Eyes
tropes.html: When Dae-su exits the suitcase on the rooftop, he has problems adjusting to the daylight because his eyes have been used to dim indoor light for 15 years.

tropes.name: Dead Man's Switch
tropes.html: Woo-jin has a remote control to stop his pacemaker at will which he uses as leverage against Dae-su when the latter threatens him with torture. Woo-jin explains that he would kill himself instantly and Dae-su would never learn why he was imprisoned for 15 years. Subverted at the end when Woo-jin reveals that the remote was actually a laser pointer; not only that, when Dae-su vengefully grabs the control thinking he can stop Woo-jin's heart, it actually starts a reel-to-reel player with an audio recording of Dae-Su and Mi-Do having sex. One last piece of humiliation..

tropes.name: Death by Transceiver
tropes.html: No Joo-hwan gets killed by Woo-jin while he and Dae-su are communicating via headset.

tropes.name: Determinator
tropes.html: Even after getting mobbed by a dozen guys and stabbed in the back during the famous Hallway Fight, Dae-su simply will not stay down.

tropes.name: Disproportionate Retribution
tropes.html: Subverted. Woo-jin appears to present his plan as this, as he says that his reason for locking up Dae-su for fifteen years is that "Oh Dae-su talks too much." This ends up not being the case at all, however, because what Oh Dae-su talked too much about happened to result in Woo-jin's reputation being destroyed and his sister killing herself. It's still extremely disproportionate, but not as much.

tropes.name: Dramatic Irony
tropes.html: After making love, Oh Dae-Su narrates that he feels like he should be thanking his prisoners for all those years in captivity. If he hadn't been in there, would Mi-Do have liked him still.

tropes.name: Downer Ending
tropes.html: Director Park Chan-wook called the final scene "a sad ending that's happy, or a happy ending that's sad." Dae-su and Woo-jin have been left utterly destroyed by the pursuit of revenge, with the latter killing himself as soon as he leaves Dae-su to his misery. Horrified at the knowledge that he had been tricked into sex with his own daughter, Dae-su begs a hypnotist to free him from his memories, but it's ambiguous if it worked. If it did, then Dae-su and Mi-do will live together with neither knowing of their true relationship; if it didn't, then Dae-su will be haunted by the Awful Truth for all his days.

tropes.name: The Dragon
tropes.html: Mr. Han, Woo-jin's silent and imposing bodyguard. He shadows his employer throughout the film, assisting him in his plots and protecting him from Dae-su. When Dae-su enters the climax of the film, Mr. Han is his last physical challenge, beating him quite severely.

tropes.name: Dressing to Die
tropes.html: Woo-jin takes a hot shower and puts on his best suit before later going into the lift to commit suicide, which is heavily implied to have been his plan all along.

tropes.name: Driven to Suicide
tropes.html:
• As it turns out, the entire film's plot is kicked off by the suicide of Woo-jin's lover after a young Dae-su lets it loose that she was sleeping with Woo-jin, her brother. The rumor morphs to claim that she was having sex with all the male students and got pregnant, causing her to experiences a phantom pregnancy that drove her over the edge.
  • Woo-jin later kills himself out of shame and emptiness as his revenge on Dae-su is complete, but has brought him nothing.
  • There's also the man with the dog that Dae-su meets after his release who goes through with it anyway.
  • Dae-su also tries to kill himself at least twice during his imprisonment, but his captors stop him.
  • If Oh Dae-Su does complete his mission, Lee Woo-jin will kill himself instead of Mi-Do as promised.

tropes.name: Driving Question
tropes.html: Who imprisoned Dae-su, and why? Woo-jin reveals that the question Dae-su should've been asking was, why did Woo-jin release him specifically after 15 years?

tropes.name: Ear Ache
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su manages to stab Mr. Han in the ear with a pair of scissors.

tropes.name: Elevator Action Sequence
tropes.html: Subverted. After the ridiculously intense hallway fight, Dae-su makes it to the elevator at the end of the hallway and finds it packed full of reinforcements for the guys he just beat up, who stare at him — and the fallen bodies of their comrades littering the hallway — in disbelief, before Dae-su smiles, and we immediately cut to him exiting the elevator packed with their unconscious or dead bodies.

tropes.name: The Ending Changes Everything
tropes.html: After The Reveal regarding Woo-jin's motives and the true nature of Dae-su and Mi-do's relationship, at least half the film starts to look very different for viewers on subsequent watches. The actual ending also plays a part, as Dae-su's painful smile can lead to different interpretations of what exactly happened in the previous scene.

tropes.name: Ends with a Smile
tropes.html: Subverted. Oh Dae-su embraces Mi-do after his meeting with the hypnotist and smiles... but it's unclear if his memories of the horrifying revenge Lee Woo-jin manipulated him into have truly been erased, and Dae-su's grin becomes a pained grimace.

tropes.name: Enemy Mine
tropes.html: Subverted. Mr. Park says he is siding with Dae-su after Woo-jin cuts off his hand, but it is later revealed that Woo-jin handsomely compensated Mr. Park for his hand and that he has been working for him the entire time.

tropes.name: Enigmatic Minion
tropes.html: Mr. Han, Woo-jin's silent bodyguard. He gets one line in the whole movie, and almost kills Dae-su before getting shot in the head by his employer.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html: After much begging from Dae-su, Woo-jin tells the prison warden not to reveal the Awful Truth to Mi-do.

tropes.name: Eye Scream
tropes.html: Oh Dae-su stabs one of Woo-jin's henchmen in the eye with a broken toothbrush. We don't see anything gory, though.

tropes.name: Face Death with Dignity
tropes.html:
• Subverted. Woo-jin takes a hot shower and puts on his best suit before going into the lift to calmly commit suicide. But then he cries during his memory of Soo-ah, his deceased sister, before shooting himself.
  • It's implied that Mr. Han knows he'll have to be shot by Woo-jin to be stopped from killing Dae-su. When he hands Woo-jin the murder instrument, it's with his usual stoicism.

tropes.name: Face Framed in Shadow
tropes.html: An example worthy of Brando during Woo-jin's suicide.

tropes.name: Fan Disservice
tropes.html:
• The first time audiences see the sex scene between Oh Dae-su and Mi-do, it's probably tantalizing. Once they're hit with the revelation of Mi-do being his daughter, the scene is much less appealing in retrospect or upon repeated viewings. Even then, Mi-do cries out that she's in pain during the scene.
  • Mi-Do's bare breasts are exposed as she's molested and held captive by the antagonist's men.
  • Lee Woo-jin and his sister Lee Soo-ah getting caught sex in an empty classroom by Oh Dae-Su. It starts out innocently with a playful chase around the room and Lee Woo-jin taking pictures of her. Then Lee Woo-jin tries to pry her legs open and Soo-ah protests many times, even telling him "No" and "Stop" before she gives up.

tropes.name: Faint in Shock
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su passes out while in the middle of eating a live octopus due to a fever. Mi-Do lampshades this, asking Oh Dae-Su why does he faint if he trained so much. The fainting was all part of Lee Woo-jin's hypnosis working. Mi-Do faints after finding Mr. Park's severed hand in a box delivered to her and Oh Dae-Su.

tropes.name: Faux Affably Evil
tropes.html: Woo-jin might be pretty charming, but that demeanor actually hides a twisted, vengeful self. The prison warden cries that Woo-jin was just so polite the entire time he was forced to give up his hand as penance for Dae-su. What's more, Woo-jin never stops being polite even as he breaks down Dae-su during the climax and reveals that his revenge is complete.

tropes.name: Feel No Pain
tropes.html: Due to his fist training, Dae-su doesn't mind Mi-do biting his hand during her interrogation.

tropes.name: Finding the Bug
tropes.html: Oh Dae Su mentions wanting to chop off Mr. Park's hand. Later, the villain sends him Mr. Park's severed hand in a box. This causes Oh Dae Su to realize he is bugged and go to a professional to find it. It was located in the heel of his shoe.

tropes.name: Finger in the Mail
tropes.html: Dae-su and Mi-do receive a box with a severed hand in it. Turns out it belongs to Mr. Park.

tropes.name: Fingore
tropes.html: Mr. Park defects to Dae-su's side after Woo-jin amputates his hand. That's the cover story: in reality, Park gave his hand up willingly to gain Dae-su's trust, and the entire reason Park has a new prison in the final act is that it was payment for his hand.

tropes.name: Florence Nightingale Effect
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su falls for Mi-Do after she nurses him back to health in her apartment twice. This was deliberately invoked on Woo-jin's part to get them together.

tropes.name: Forceful Kiss
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su rushes into the bathroom and plants a kiss on Mi-Do as he attempts to force himself on her. She defends herself by hitting him in the head.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
So, so much.
  • Mr Park notes that imagination can have ruinous effects on a person. It definitely did for Soo-ah.
  • When Mr. Han gives Park a box full of cash, Park smiles fondly at his hand and adjusts his pinky ring. A subtle hint that he willingly gave up his hand as part of Woo-Jin's plan.
  • When Dae-su and Mi-do meet for the first time, they note that the other looks somewhat familiar. They should — they are father and daughter.
  • Dae-su and Mi-do share similar hallucinations. Evidently, In the Blood.
  • In the flashback scene where Dae-su Oh first speaks to Lee Soo-ah, Lee Soo-ah is shown reading a book by Sylvia Plath, an American poet who committed suicide.
  • One of Mi-Do's attackers jokes about having his tongue chopped off by Oh Dae-Su for touching Mi-Do with it. By the end of the film Oh Dae-Su is the one chopping his own tongue out because of the guilt that he had unknowingly had sex with his own daughter who is also his girlfriend Mi-Do.
  • Lee Woo-jin acts so calm during his revenge quest against Oh Dae-Su. The one time he loses composure is when he overhears Joo-hwan slut-shaming his dead sister and he stabs him to death with a broken CD as a weapon. He cries not long afterwards. That's because she wasn't just his sister. She was his incestuous lover.
  • Oh Dae-Su holding up a suicidal man to prevent him from falling to his death in the opening foreshadows the exact way Lee Woo-jin tried and failed to prevent his sister Lee Soo-ah from jumping to her death.
  • When the Mysterious Stranger contacts Oh Dae-Su over the phone at the restaurant, Oh Dae-Su accuses him of hypnotizing him. Oh Dae-Su was right on the money about the hypnosis.

tropes.name: Genre Mashup
tropes.html: While Oldboy is first and foremost a revenge film with hints of neo-noir, it also has elements of dark tragicomedy, drama, action-thriller, and mystery.

tropes.name: Glad-to-Be-Alive Sex
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su and Mi-Do make love not long after their harrowing ordeal with some of the attackers sent by the antagonist.

tropes.name: Gluttony Montage
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su travels from restaurant to restaurant with Mi-Do trying to pinpoint the same dumplings made for his prison meals. After a while, he vomits from trying too many dumplings.

tropes.name: Got Over Rape Instantly
tropes.html: Mi-Do is in tears after the ordeal of being sexually assaulted by Park and his henchmen. Despite her trauma, she gets over it in a matter of minutes and even offers herself to Oh Dae-Su after he rescues her.

tropes.name: Gory Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Two merciful occurrences: when Dae-su rips out Mr. Park's teeth with the fork of a hammer, and when he cuts his own tongue out.

tropes.name: Grey-and-Gray Morality
tropes.html: Every character has their fair share of regret, tragedy, suffering, and vices that cause everything they end up going through. The one exception may be Mi-do, who ends up in the center of everything whether she wants to be or not.

tropes.name: Hallway Fight
tropes.html: In what is arguably the film's most well-known scene, Oh Dae-su fights his way through a long hallway of mooks, armed only with a hammer, for around three uninterrupted minutes.

tropes.name: Hereditary Suicide
tropes.html: An unusual variation by way of Together in Death due to the role of Brother–Sister Incest. Soo-ah commits suicide by jumping off a bridge due to either being or believing that she's pregnant with (her brother) Woo-jin's baby. After Woo-jin exacts his revenge on Dae-su decades later, he shoots himself.

tropes.name: Hidden in Plain Sight
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su striking up a romance with a much younger woman while trying to locate his missing daughter? Turns out the younger woman was actually his long-lost daughter all along.

tropes.name: Holding Hands
tropes.html: Mi-Do holds hands with Oh Dae-Su as he devours a live octopus and passes out from a fever.

tropes.name: Hourglass Plot
tropes.html: The story begins with Dae-su looking to take revenge on the person responsible for locking him up for fifteen years. He eventually finds his target Woo-jin, who later informs Dae-su that he hypnotized Dae-su into falling in love with his own daughter as revenge for Soo-ah's death. It is at this point that Dae-su loses interest in killing Woo-jin and begs for mercy instead.

tropes.name: How We Got Here
tropes.html: The movie begins with a tense High-Altitude Interrogation scene on a rooftop. Then we cut back 15 years to show how Dae-su ended up on that rooftop.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su wanted to rip the heads off of Mr. Park and the rest of the men who sexually harassed Mi-do. This coming from the same man who had also attempted to rape her Mi-do while she was using the bathroom days earlier.

tropes.name: Immodest Orgasm
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su and Mi-Do achieve this during their first time lovemaking in his hotel room.

tropes.name: Implied Rape
tropes.html: When Oh Dae-Su finds a group of men in his hotel room holding Mi-Do captive, her breasts are exposed, one of the men are holding her panties, and the others tauntingly ask Oh Dae-Su if he is going to cut off his tongue too because it wasn't just his hands that touched Mi-Do's breasts.

tropes.name: Imperiled in Pregnancy
tropes.html: Lee Soo-ah was pregnant with her brother's baby when she committed suicide.

tropes.name: Improvised Weapon
tropes.html: A claw hammer, a CD, and a toothbrush are all used as deadly weapons at different points of the film.

tropes.name: Innocently Insensitive
tropes.html: Upon learning that Oh Dae-Su's daughter was adopted out to a family in Sweden and the only phone number needed to contact her is a dead one, Mi-Do asks Oh Dae-Su if they should visit her grave, causing him to tear up.

tropes.name: Instant Illness
tropes.html: After collapsing from a fever, Oh Dae-Su figures out that a lack of needed sunlight depletes the human body of vitamins A and E so he is not immune to influenza.

tropes.name: Intentionally Self-Inflicted Disability
tropes.html: Type 5 and Type 6. After learning the Awful Truth from his opponent Woo-jin, Oh Dae-Su grabs a pair of scissors and cuts his tongue out on purpose, not only to atone for his spreading malicious rumors about Woo-jin and his sister back in high school but to protect his girlfriend Mi-Do from the truth that they're long-lost father and daughter.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html:
Played for Laughs:
Oh Dae-su: Can the imaginary training of fifteen years be put to use? [successfully defeats several thugs] Apparently, it can.
[later] during the Near-Rape Experience
Oh Dae-su: Can the imaginary training of fifteen years be put to use? [is fought off by a helpless young woman] No. It can't.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html: The dramatic variant - before Dae-su goes to confront Woo-jin, he has Mi-do temporary locked up for her own safety. Mi-do understands, and prays that Woo-jin will kneel in front of Dae-su and apologize for everything he's done. Dae-su jokingly tells her to pray for a better man. However, after The Reveal, it is Dae-su who is on his knees begging for Woo-jin's mercy.

tropes.name: Isolation-Induced Infatuation
tropes.html: Type 3. The villain's main plan starts with kidnapping and separating the male protagonist away from his family and isolating him inside a small prison cell from any physical and social contact with other humans for 15 years with only the use of a television for his entertainment. Once the protagonist is released, he immediately falls in love with the first human he befriended, a young sous chef named Mi-Do. The pair falling in love despite only having just met wasn't a coincidence. The villain anticipated this happening as both he and his hypnotist were the ones responsible for breaking down Oh Dae-Su and Mi-Do psychologically so they could end up together.

tropes.name: Jabba Table Manners
tropes.html: Upon being given a live octopus by sous chef Mi-Do as he requested, Oh Dae-Su forgoes all manners and stuffs the live octopus into his mouth and messily devours it, much to Mi-Do's amazement.

tropes.name: Jar Potty
tropes.html: In the flashback to 15 years prior, Oh Dae-Su is drunk and has to use the bathroom. Unable to find a proper bathroom, he uses the wastebasket in the police station to relieve himself.

tropes.name: Jumpscare
tropes.html: A loud sharp noise is heard as the bright sunlight from the outside hits Oh Dae-Su's eyes.

tropes.name: Knockout Gas
tropes.html: To prevent any of the goons getting ID'd, the 'prison' Dae-su finds himself in uses gas to sedate him whenever they need anything from him - be it health checkups, blood to frame him for a murder, or stopping his suicide attempts.

tropes.name: Laughing Mad
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su unnerves Park by laughing in his face, which stops Park from removing any more of his teeth with a hammer.

tropes.name: Lampshade Hanging
tropes.html: Woo-jin directly points out that Vengeance Feels Empty. Fitting for such a terrifying villain to know what kind of film he's in.

tropes.name: Laser-Guided Karma
tropes.html: Because Oh Dae-Su exposed Lee Woo-jin's incestuous relationship with his sister Lee Soo-ah, Lee Woo-jin tricked Oh Dae-Su into entering an incestuous relationship with his long-lost daughter Mi-Do as payback.

tropes.name: Loners Are Freaks
tropes.html:
• Dae-su is understandably a traumatized, barely-social mess from 15 years of isolation. The prison warden casually mentions anyone imprisoned for over a year gets schizophrenia that's only staved off by medication. Some of his first actions are to rob a woman in broad daylight, ignore a suicidal man, and act like a real creep to a sushi chef he's just met - and that's before he demands a live octopus to scarf down. He later tries to rape Mi-do, then runs away apologizing like a sorry little child.
  • Mi-do "happily" admits she regularly hallucinates insects, is heavily implied to be friendless outside of a mysterious internet stranger who is Woo-jin, easily forgives Dae-su for trying to rape her, and near-immediately proposes noncon play to cheer him up. In fact, Mi-do sympathises with Dae-su's constant hallucination of bugs because loners hallucinate insects, especially ants, and guess what she's been hallucinating?
  • It turns out it's deliberately cultivated by Woo-jin as both punishment and to make the chances of making them fall into an incestuous relationship easier, as they bond over their isolation and weirdness. Furthermore, it's implied Woo-jin and his sister were also weird loners, despite being apparently perfect, and their incest also sprung from it.

tropes.name: Lost in Translation
tropes.html: When Oh Dae-su is released from his prison, he talks to a gang of kids who act like they don't understand him. The Korean language had drastically changed over those fifteen years, and Dae-su is speaking a very different dialect than the modern one. Unfortunately, this was lost in the English subtitles. While he does ponder over an insult he's never heard before from the kids and how much time has changed, it's translated as "fucktard".

tropes.name: Love at First Sight
tropes.html: Invoked. Oh Dae-su and Mi-do fall in love with each other almost instantly - the film at first implies it's beacuse they're both emotionally-scarred and desperately lonely, but it turns out because they've been hypnotized to do so as part of the villain's plan.

tropes.name: Man Bites Man
tropes.html: Mi-Do bites Oh Dae-Su's hand when he's interrogating her on the mysterious person known as "Evergreen".

tropes.name: Meaningful Echo
tropes.html:
Suicidal Man/Dae-su: Even though I'm no better than a beast, don't I have the right to live?
Cell Poster/Photo Album: Laugh and the world laughs with you. Weep and you weep alone.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: Park Chan-wook claims that the leading character's name, Oh Dae-su, is derived from Oedipus. The tragic hero in Greek mythology who ended up loving his own mother.

tropes.name: Meaningless Villain Victory
tropes.html: Woo-jin spends decades plotting his revenge on Oh Dae-su for accidentally revealing Woo-jin's incestous relationship with his sister and her resulting suicide: locking Oh Dae-su away for 15 years, killing multiple people, and tricking Oh Dae-su into having sex with his own daughter. Woo-jin gets the revenge he sought for so long, before realizing that revenge did not bring him any closure for his sister's death, and after centering his entire life around his revenge quest, his life lacks a purpose now that his quest is over. As the elevator descends, all he can do is morosely relive his sister's suicide and her plea to let go before he puts his gun to his temple and kills himself.

tropes.name: Missing Floor
tropes.html: The illegal prison that Oh Dae-su was held in for 15 years is located on an unlisted floor in a high-rise, which is accessed by pressing the elevator buttons for floors 7 and 8 at the same time. The "warden" of the prison refers to the location as "floor 7.5".

tropes.name: Mook Chivalry
tropes.html: Double Subverted. Cheol-woong's gang initially fights Oh Dae-su together as a group. The problem they face is that he just won't stay down. The more they throw themselves at him, the more he bashes their heads in with his hammer. Eventually, they become so tired and beaten down, they become reluctant to actually continue fighting him, leading to them trying to fight him one at a time.

tropes.name: Mook Horror Show
tropes.html: Also Double Subverted. While Dae-su demolishes the guys in the hallway at first, eventually they overpower him with sheer force of numbers, and he's pushed to exhaustion, beaten down, and eventually knocked down and stabbed. This makes it all the more terrifying for the guys in the hallway when he stands back up and starts kicking ass again. When he gets to the elevator at the end of the hallway and finds it full of mooks, all we see is him giving a sly grin before there's a Smash Cut to him stepping out of the elevator...and over the unconscious or dead bodies of the guys he's just slaughtered.

tropes.name: Mutilation Interrogation
tropes.html: Oh Dae-su tracks down the illegal holding facility where he was kept for 15 years after being kidnapped off the streets. Dae-su asks the warden who it was that paid him to keep him imprisoned, and when the warden doesn't answer, he duct-tapes him to his chair. He then uses his claw hammer to pry out the man's teeth one at a time, telling him that he owes him one tooth for each year of his life that was stolen from him. After about 7 or so, he gives the warden a chance to talk, with the implication that he'll continue through with all 15 if he doesn't.

tropes.name: My Fist Forgives You
tropes.html: Mr. Park and the goons that Oh Dae-su beat up hunt him down for revenge. Just as they're about to torture him, Woo-jin calls them to tell them to back off and Mr. Han shows up to give them a lot of money. Mr. Park is content with the payoff and leaves, though he does whack Oh Dae-su on the head with a bat once for good measure.

tropes.name: My Girl Is Not a Slut
tropes.html: Joo-hwan marks himself as an Asshole Victim by callously gossiping about Soo-ah's death, calling her a slut and wondering if he should have gotten in on that in high school. It's not a pleasant thing to say about any dead girl, but it really hits an overhearing Woo-jin hard on a personal level, and is one of the very few times that someone cracks through the controlled scenario he's spent so many long years constructing.

tropes.name: My Secret Pregnancy
tropes.html: After Oh Dae-Su spread the rumors of him catching Lee Woo-jin and Lee Soo-ah in the act together, Lee Soo-ah commits suicide to protect her brother's reputation. She knew that the public would react negatively if the truth came to light about her consensual incestuous relationship with Lee Woo-jin and her carrying his baby.

tropes.name: Near-Rape Experience
tropes.html: Interestingly, Dae-su barging into the bathroom and attempting to rape Mi-do shortly after he wakes from a fever is Played for Laughs, and she plays it off with a smile shortly afterwards.

tropes.name: Nemesis Magnet
tropes.html: Apparently Dae-su made a lot of enemies in his time because of his unpleasant nature. He wonders which of them was responsible for the punishment he received.

tropes.name: Note to Self
tropes.html: To keep track of time while he plots his escape, Oh Dae-Su documents his captivity in prison by marking his hand in ink for the next 15 years. One line for each year.

tropes.name: Offscreen Villain Dark Matter
tropes.html: One big mystery is how the Hell is one man with a grudge six steps ahead of Dae-su, splashing cash to give to him as a "gift", renting out an apartment in infamously expensive Korea just to spy on Dae-su, and locking a man in a Korean mafia's prison for 15 years, well over the amount most criminals can afford? As it turns out, Woo-jin managed to become the president of an unspecified but enormous MegaCorp, and the film further implies he had deep ties with the Korean mafia that helped him kickstart his business and allow armies of goons to do his bidding.

tropes.name: One-Man Army
tropes.html: Dae-su beats down over a dozen men, and then immediately deals with another six or seven without being much worse for wear aside from being beaten and having some blood on his head...oh, and, you know, a knife wound in the back.

tropes.name: The Oner
tropes.html: A number of them throughout the film, the most well-known of them being a lengthy scene in which Oh Dae-su takes on over a dozen men in a hallway armed with just a hammer.

tropes.name: Parental Incest
tropes.html: Dae-su unknowingly has sex with his daughter.

tropes.name: Pay Evil unto Evil
tropes.html: Dae-su's torture of Mr. Park, though he tortures him only for information on why he was imprisoned.

tropes.name: The Penance
tropes.html: Dae-su cuts out his tongue to atone for unwittingly causing Woo-jin's sister to commit suicide.

tropes.name: Pensieve Flashback
tropes.html: The flashback at the highschool has adult Dae-su in place of the teenage Dae-su peeking through the window to watch Woo-jin and his sister fooling around.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html: Right before the famous Hallway Fight, Dae-su takes one of the bad guys hostage with a knife across his throat, but tells the others his blood type and deliberately lets him go so two of them can take their wounded comrade away before the others rush him.

tropes.name: Picture-Perfect Presentation
tropes.html: The scene transition from the internet cafe to the Sangnok highschool happens seamlessly from a photograph on the high school's webpage to live-action footage of Dae-su and Mi-do arriving at the place.

tropes.name: Please Wake Up
tropes.html: Mi-Do pleas for Oh Dae-Su to wake up after he passes out from a combination of eating a live octopus, a high fever, and hypnosis.

tropes.name: Poor Man's Porn
tropes.html: While imprisoned, Dae-su wanks off to female pop artists on TV since this is all he has for titillation.

tropes.name: Potty Emergency
tropes.html: In the prologue, a intoxicated Oh Dae-Su complains to the police about having to pee really bad so he relieves himself in a wastebasket.

tropes.name: Pretty Little Headshots
tropes.html: The close-up shot on Woo-jin's temple after he blows his brains out reveals a tiny headwound.

tropes.name: Prematurely Grey-Haired
tropes.html: By the end of the film, Oh Dae-Su is sporting premature grey hair on his head as a result of the trauma he has endured.

tropes.name: Primal Scene
tropes.html: The flashbacks show Oh Dae-Su catching Lee Woo-jin and his sister Lee Soo-ah in the middle of having sex, kick-starting the rumors that ended her life and started Woo-jin's quest for revenge.

tropes.name: Pregnancy Scare
tropes.html: Lee Soo-ah was pregnant with her brother's baby when she died. Lee Woo-jin insisted that Oh Dae-Su spreading the false rumors about Lee Soo-ah's pregnancy caused her body to falsely believe it was expecting.

tropes.name: Post-Rape Taunt
tropes.html: When Oh Dae-Su threatens to cut off Mi-Do's attacker's hands because they touched her breasts, one of them asks if he's going to cut off his tongue too. "I'm going to chop off your hand because you touched Mi-Do's breasts! "And what about my tongue?"

tropes.name: Psychological Horror
tropes.html: The story begins with Dae-su being kidnapped and imprisoned in a motel room for fifteen years, with a montage showing his gradual Sanity Slippage as a result of the isolation. When Dae-su is eventually released, the film becomes more of a mystery-thriller as Dae-su roots out the truth behind his lockup. It plunges back into horror when Dae-su finds out that his daughter, whom he presumed had been adopted by a family overseas, was in truth Mi-do—and that Woo-jin had manipulated the both of them into committing incest.

tropes.name: Psychosexual Horror
