tropes.html: Has elements of this, especially later on. Dae-su and Mi-do are in truth father and daughter, and Woo-jin hypnotizes the both of them into falling in love and having sex. When Dae-su finds out the truth, he maims and humiliates himself, desperate for Mi-do to stay ignorant.

tropes.name: Psychopathic Man Child
tropes.html: After acting cool and collected for the entirety of the movie prior, Woo-jin shows hints of this as he reveals the truth to Dae-su.

tropes.name: Punch a Wall
tropes.html: A large part of Oh Dae-su's self-training. He has a human silhouette drawn on the wall of his jail cell as a target.

tropes.name: Rape Is a Special Kind of Evil
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su wanted to beat up the men who sexually harassed Mi-do.

tropes.name: Really Gets Around
tropes.html: From No Joo-hwan, we learn that Dae-su had 260 women in his life before getting imprisoned, and Dae-su has to go through every one to make sure they weren't the ones who put the hit out on him.

tropes.name: Rescue Romance
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su and Mi-Do's relationship progresses not long after he rescues her from some attackers. This was orchestrated by the antagonist all along to get them together.

tropes.name: The Reveal
tropes.html: Mi-do is Oh Dae-su's daughter.

tropes.name: Ripped from the Phone Book
tropes.html: Before heading out of Mi-do's apartment, Dae-su rips a page from the phone book with the address of the dumpling place.

tropes.name: Roaring Rampage of Revenge
tropes.html: Deconstructed, as both Dae-su and Woo-jin are out for revenge, which ultimately proves self-destructive.

tropes.name: Sacrificial Lion
tropes.html: Joo-hwan, Dae-su's best friend, is murdered by Woo-jin after revealing the source of Woo-jin's motivations due to calling his sister a whore. Dae-su takes his death quite badly.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su leaves Mi-Do's apartment after finding her chatting online with a mysterious person known as "The lonely prince in the high tower".

tropes.name: Sex for Solace
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su and Mi-Do have sex in a love motel to make the other feel better not long after being attacked by Park and his men.

tropes.name: Self-Inflicted Amnesia
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su is so psychologically broken over the events of the climax that he seeks out the aid of a hypnotist to hypnotize him into forgetting the whole traumatizing ordeal. Despite Oh Dae-Su's efforts, the film's ending implies that the hypnosis wasn't successful, as his smile turns into a painful grimace as he embraces Mi-do.

tropes.name: "Shaggy Dog" Story
tropes.html:
• Dae-su never gets his revenge, and Lee Woo-jin, out of shame, penance, and realizing it accomplished nothing, kills himself after getting his revenge.
  • Park Chan-wook points out in the commentary how many of Dae-su's efforts ultimately turn out to be pointless; for example, just before Dae-su manages to escape via the hole he has carved in his wall, he is released by his captors.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• To Bride of Frankenstein, which is briefly shown on the TV in Dae-su's prison.
  • To Titus Andronicus, including the scene with the tongue, the abuse of a sibling., and the unorthodox revenge plan involving a familial trick.
  • The prison Dae-su was locked in is located on the seventh-and-a-half floor of a building.
  • On the wall of Mi-do's bedroom, there's a picture of King Kong (1933).
  • Mi-do's mysterious friend who turns out to be Woo-jin taunts Dae-su as being the The Count of Monte Cristo, also focusing on a man locked up for years before escaping to enact revenge.
  • The line on the painting of Dae-su's cell reads "Laugh and the world laughs with you. Weep and you weep alone." These are the first lines of Ella Wheeler Wilcox's famous poem, "Solitude".
  • The recurring painting on the wall of Oh Dae-su's confinement complex is "The Man of Sorrow" by Belgian painter James Ensor.
  • Princess Diana's funeral is shown on TV as Oh Dae-Su attempts his prison escape.

tropes.name: Silence Is Golden
tropes.html: Dae-su's violent reaction to learning Mi-do is his daughter has all of the scene audio replaced with a somber, ambient music cue.

tropes.name: Sins of Our Fathers
tropes.html: Mi-Do gets orphaned, her mother is murdered, and she's unknowingly hypnotized into an incestuous relationship with her presumed-dead father...all for a gossipy comment her father made when he was a teenager.

tropes.name: Skyward Scream
tropes.html: Mi-Do's screams are loud enough to be heard outside of the building as Oh Dae-Su races back to rescue her.

tropes.name: Snow Means Love
tropes.html: By the film's ending, Mi-Do and Oh Dae-Su share a loving embrace as a couple, with Mi-Do telling him she loves him. Unfortunately, she is blissfully unaware that the man she loves is her father and it's left ambiguous whether or not Oh Dae-Su's re-hypnosis to wipe his memory worked.

tropes.name: Soundtrack Dissonance
tropes.html: Vivaldi's Winter plays while Oh Dae-su rips Mr. Park's teeth out.

tropes.name: Stalker Without a Crush
tropes.html: Woo-jin has obessively tracked Dae-su and Mi-do's every movement from the very moment Dae-su was released.

tropes.name: Suicide, Not Murder
tropes.html: Double subverted. It looks like Soo-ah committed suicide after the rumors started circulating, but when Dae-su is at Woo-jin's penthouse, he finds a picture of her taken at the dam where she died, and it seems that Woo-jin killed her to cover up their incestuous relationship during her phantom pregnancy, making it look like a suicide. In the end, it's revealed that Woo-jin was trying to stop Soo-ah from committing suicide, but she convinced him to let go of her.

tropes.name: Surprise Incest
tropes.html: Mi-do is Dae-su's daughter, and he only finds out after they've had sex. Setting this up was Woo-jin's revenge and why he locked him up all those years.

tropes.name: Symbolic Mutilation
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su forcibly extracts 15 of Park's teeth as payback (1 for each year of Oh Dae-Su's imprisonment) and to get information on his captor's whereabouts. Later, Oh Dae-Su cuts his own tongue off as it was the very same thing that spread the malicious rumors and ruined two people's lives. He also cuts his tongue out to keep the truth hidden from Mi-Do.

tropes.name: Teen Pregnancy
tropes.html: Lee Woo-jin and Lee Soo-ah were teenagers in high school when she became pregnant and Oh Dae-Su spread the rumor about the two having sex.

tropes.name: Taught by Television
tropes.html: Dae-su has learned his fighting moves from watching kickboxing on TV.

tropes.name: Tears of Fear
tropes.html: A frightened Mi-Do has tears running down her face as she is sexually assaulted by Park and his henchmen and Oh Dae-Su is attacked.

tropes.name: Tick Tock Tune
tropes.html: The opening credit sequence has ticking and gonging sounds alongside images of clocks.

tropes.name: Title Drop
tropes.html: The key to solving the Driving Question of the film lies in Dae-su's high school—Evergreen Old Boys.

tropes.name: Token Romance
tropes.html: Subverted in the case of Oh Dae-su and Mi-do, since it happening is part of the villain's revenge scheme.

tropes.name: Tongue Trauma
tropes.html: Dae-su ends up cutting out his own tongue as a symbol of penance. One of Mi-Do's attackers jokes about her boyfriend Oh Dae-Su doing this to the man after he molested Mi-Do.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Badass
tropes.html: Deconstructed. Fifteen years in a private prison have turned Dae-su into a fearless killing machine, but all of this fits right into the villain's plan.

tropes.name: The Tooth Hurts
tropes.html: The tooth-pulling scene. Oh Dae-Su gets information out of Park by pulling 15 of his teeth. Park exacts revenge by attacking Oh Dae-Su in Mi-Do's apartment and faking removing one of his teeth.

tropes.name: Tragedy
tropes.html: One of the most harrowing ones in film history. Fittingly, the story is patterned on that of Oedipus, one of the best known Greek tragedies.

tropes.name: Tragic Villain
tropes.html: Woo-jin is one of the best examples in cinema. Through the course of the movie, he murders people, imprisons a man for 15 years, tortures him, and tricks him into sleeping with his daughter, all for revealing a nasty secret. But when the film flashes back to Woo-jin on the bridge, desperately holding on to his sister as she hangs over the water, you realize that he is ultimately a broken man who needed an excuse, no matter how flimsy, to continue living, as once he gets his revenge, he promptly commits suicide.

tropes.name: Trauma Conga Line
tropes.html: The ending is this in spades: Dae-su learns that, by gossiping about their incestuous relationship, he indirectly caused Woo-jin's sister to commit suicide; Woo-jin reveals Mi-do is Dae-su's daughter, and they had sex because he orchestrated it; Dae-su is pummelled by Mr. Han for trying to kill Woo-jin; Dae-su cuts his tongue out in a desperate attempt to stop Woo-jin from telling Mi-do; Woo-jin commits suicide, denying Dae-su his revenge; and finally, Dae-su gets re-hypnotized to forget everything, although it's unclear if it works, and he's last seen still with Mi-do. Considering that this all happens after he was imprisoned for fifteen years and his wife was murdered...

tropes.name: Übermensch
tropes.html: Oh Dae-su takes on many aspects of an Ubermensch during his imprisonment. Ultimately, his character is a massive subversion. Everything he does has been accounted for. He has no control of his own fate, and everything he does plays into Lee Woo-jin's hands. By the end of the movie, he is a very, very broken man.

tropes.name: Ugly Guy, Hot Wife
tropes.html: Oh Dae-su and Mi-do. They are both this and The Ugly Guy's Hot Daughter due to Parental Incest. Justified, since Woo-jin hypnotized them into falling in love with each other.

tropes.name: Ugly Hero, Good-Looking Villain
tropes.html: The anti-hero protagonist Oh Dae-Su is unkempt in his appearance with an out-of-shape body and lacking good fashion choices in comparison to his opponent Lee Woo-Jin who dresses sharp and maintains his physical appearance through diet and exercise.

tropes.name: Underestimating Badassery
tropes.html: The gang of kids underestimate Dae-su's fitness and get their asses kicked hard.

tropes.name: Undressing the Unconscious
tropes.html: Dae-su is unsettled when he learns that Mi-do administered a suppository to him while he was unconscious. On two occasions, Oh Dae-Su finds himself changed out of his clothes and into his boxers. Justified, since the first one is due to him recovering from a fever and the second one is due to needing bandages and disinfectant for his knife wound.

tropes.name: Unreliable Narrator
tropes.html: This is downplayed in the case of Dae-su, as his narration of events is trustworthy until the ending in which he meets the hypnotist. As the film points out, there is only one set of footprints in the snow, meaning that the meeting between the hypnotist and him, along with the later Laser-Guided Amnesia he underwent, may not have happened.

tropes.name: Unwitting Pawn
tropes.html: Mi-do, and to a lesser extent Oh Dae-su, in Woo-jin's plans of revenge.

tropes.name: Vengeance Feels Empty
tropes.html: This is, rather explicitly, the entire point of the film. After destroying Dae-su, Woo-jin states he has nothing to live for now that he's had his vengeance. He briefly feels joy over exacting his revenge, but moments later he returns to being an empty shell mourning the loss of his sister. So after successfully completing his massive, 15-year Batman Gambit, cue Woo-jin blowing his brains out in an elevator.

tropes.name: Victory Is Boring
tropes.html: His revenge plot against Dae-Su was all Woo-jin had to live for, and he commits suicide when it's done.

tropes.name: Villain of Another Story
tropes.html: Mr. Park. Though he plays a big role in Oh Dae-su's story on account of imprisoning him, it's established that Mr. Park runs a decades-long criminal enterprise of locking people away in a private residence as torture. Even without Woo-jin setting the plot in motion, this is something that would have always been going on.

tropes.name: Villainous Breakdown
tropes.html: Woo-jin, immediately preceding his suicide.

tropes.name: Vomit Indiscretion Shot
tropes.html: Oh Dae-Su vomits outside of a restaurant after eating so many dumplings.

tropes.name: Wardens Are Evil
tropes.html: Mr. Park is in essence a warden to a criminal enterprise that imprisons people.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
Several.
  • After being kidnapped and locked in the hotel room, Dae-su hears the television broadcast saying that his wife has been brutally murdered...and his DNA was found at the crime scene. And that's within the first fifth of the movie.
    News Reporter: Kim Ja-Hyun's body was found with a deep stab wound in the neck. Being a cold-blooded murder with nothing valuable stolen, police suspect that the motive was out of hatred. Her husband, Oh Dae-Su, disappeared a year ago and is being searched for. According to the witnesses, Oh Dae-Su drank often, causing trouble with his wife, and the neighbors said they fought frequently. Blood samples found at the scene matched Oh Dae-Su's. Fingertips found on a cup also matched Oh Dae-Su's. Sources said that Oh Dae-Su undoubtedly visited his wife recently. The stolen family photo album, the only missing item, also backs their theories.
  • Then nearer the end:
    Oh Dae-Su: You slept with your sister. You slept with your sister. And I started the rumor. That's why your sister died.
    Lee Woo-jin: Looking through the mirror reminds me of that day. Doesn't it?
    Oh Dae-Su: Erasing my memory and telling me to find the truth was unfair. I won. So die like you promised.
    Lee Woo-jin: Think you forgot that day because you were hypnotized? Are you sure? Know the real reason why you can't remember? Let me tell you. You just forgot. Is that too bland? But it's true that you just forgot. Why? Since it's not your business. Your rumor got so out of hand that Soo-ah being pregnant became a rumor. My sister got sucked into that rumor, and began believing it. So her period stopped, and her belly began to swell. Funny, isn't it? Ever thought how a girl would feel bearing both her child and her nephew? Understand now? Your tongue got my sister pregnant. It wasn't Lee Woo-jin's dick. It was Oh Dae-Su's tongue.
  • Also near the end, and both are an Armor-Piercing Question.
    Lee Woo-jin: Ever heard of post-hypnotic suggestion? You suggest something during hypnosis, and then acted it out in your weakened state. Still haven't figured it out? "You lead a stranger to your place. Who the hell are you?". We hypnotized both of you. One very fortunate thing was that compared to others both of you were highly receptive to hypnosis. Isn't this fun? One word gets you pregnant. One word gets you in love. But no matter how receptive the two of you were to hypnosis, and no matter how good of a hypnotist Ms. Yoo is, getting people to fall in love isn't easy. So, know how we did it? Your first suggestion, of course, was to go to that restaurant, right after your release. Next, to react to the mobile phone's melody. When you heard this, you were supposed to say something. And Mi-Do was to react to the man who said this. When she grabs your hand, your reaction would be, of course, (Oh Dae-Su passes out due to hypnosis). Your gravest mistake wasn't failing to find the answer. If you keep asking the wrong questions, you'll never find the right answer. It's not "Why did Woo-jin imprison me?" It's "why did he release me" One again...why did Woo-jin release Oh Dae-Su after...15 years??
    Lee Woo-jin:My sister and I loved each other despite knowing everything. Can you two do the same?

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html:
At the climax of the film, Dae-su finds a picture book of some old photos which contains pictures of his missing infant daughter. As the pictures progress and she ages up, she turns out to be none other than his lover Mi-do, much to his horror.
  • After exacting his revenge on Dae-Su, Woo-jin goes into the elevator, smiling. However, his face then slowly falls into an anguished frown and his head tilts down to cast his features in darkness, extending his hand downwards as he remembers his sister's suicide.

tropes.name: White Hair, Black Heart
tropes.html: Mr. Han has bleached white hair.

tropes.name: Whole-Plot Reference
tropes.html: The story is basically The Count of Monte Cristo crossed with a reversed form of Oedipus.

tropes.name: The Worf Effect
tropes.html: After training nonstop for over a decade during his imprisonment, Dae-su is good at fighting, but he's a One-Man Army only because the people he fights are hired thugs. When he goes up against Mr Han, a trained bodyguard, he does much worse, and only wins by sheer luck.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html: Nick reaches for the last drink on a tray too late and it's snatched by someone else. That exact thing happened to Peter Parker in Spider-Man 2.

tropes.name: Adaptation Distillation
tropes.html: The film cuts out Nick and Jordan's relationship as well as Gatsby's father and the owl-eyed man showing up to Gatsby's funeral, and the scene where Nick meets Tom after Gatsby's death.

tropes.name: Adaptation Dye-Job
tropes.html:
• Jordan has dark yellow "hair like an autumn leaf" in the book and is also described as being tanned due to being a golfer in the book, but she's a pale-skinned brunette here.
  • Daisy's hair color is somewhat ambiguous, she's described as both fair-haired and dark-haired in the book; here she's cast as a blonde. Interestingly, Daisy and Jordan have been depicted as blonde and brunette, respectively, in every film version since the '40s.
  • Tom in the book is described as "straw-haired", but is depicted with dark hair in the film.

tropes.name: Adapted Out
tropes.html: Gatsby's father, Henry C. Gatz, doesn't show up to his funeral as he does in the book. A deleted scene would have included him, though.

tropes.name: Aloof Dark-Haired Girl
tropes.html: Jordan, thanks to Adaptation Dye-Job.

tropes.name: Anachronism Stew
tropes.html:
• The soundtrack, filled with contemporary Pop Star Composers and a highly lauded dubstep duo. A deliberate artistic choice very much like what Luhrmann did for Romeo+Juliet and Moulin Rouge.
  • Gatsby's car is a Duesenberg. The model A would have fit the era of the movie (the first Duesenbergs were made in 1921), but the model used in the movie was an SJ model, which didn't start production until 1929.note The car was actually a Duesenberg II, an homage model that started production in the late 70s.
  • New York City didn't have that many skyscrapers in the 1920s.
  • In 1922, Art Deco was still in its early stages in France and wouldn't be nearly as flamboyant as it is in the film until the 1930s.

tropes.name: Anti-Hero
tropes.html: Leonardo DiCaprio plays up Jay Gatsby's dark side, with him nearly punching Tom (in the novel, he merely argues with him), and ordering a rogue gangster beat up outside his gates by his gang.

tropes.name: Art Deco
tropes.html: The movie's titles in the opening and in most of the promotional material.

tropes.name: Author Avatar
tropes.html: Nick is intended as this for F. Scott Fitzgerald. Tobey Maguire was likely cast because of his resemblance to Fitzgerald.

tropes.name: Award-Bait Song
tropes.html: "Young and Beautiful" by Lana Del Rey, and "Over The Love" by Florence + the Machine.

tropes.name: Beard of Sorrow
tropes.html: Nick grows a beard following Gatsby's death.

tropes.name: Big Fancy House
tropes.html: The Buchanan mansion is very large, fitting their wealth. Gatsby's mansion is verging on Big Fancy Castle or Bright Castle, considering his Nouveau Riche status.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html: 'Ad Finem Fidelis', the Latin motto on Gatsby's front gate, translates into 'Faithful to the End'.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: For Nick and only Nick. The experience causes him to go through a nervous breakdown and commit himself to an asylum, but while he's in there, his doctor encourages him to write about what he witnessed while in West Egg. This, along with getting to talk to his doctor in the first place, grants him some catharsis and he ends the movie on the path to recovery.

tropes.name: Blonde, Brunette, Redhead
tropes.html: Myrtle Wilson and her sister Catherine are redheads, to go with blonde Daisy and brunette Jordan.

tropes.name: Blood Is Squicker in Water
tropes.html: Not only Gatsby getting shot in the pool but also the brief shot of Gatsby tossing out the water he used to get Myrtle's blood off his car.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html:
• The first and last shot of the movie is of the green light.
  • The short guitar riff in the overture that goes from 1:00 to 1:30 comes back full circle in the end credits theme "Together" by The xx.
  • The movie opens with Gatsby's ring emblem being presented alongside the logos in the midst of CGI Art Deco scenery, then pulling out of view as the camera follows it into the film proper. The same scene plays in reverse at the very end, with the camera pulling back into the Art Deco space and the emblem reappearing.

tropes.name: Catchphrase
tropes.html: Gatsby calls everyone "old sport".

tropes.name: Cigarette of Anxiety
tropes.html: Daisy tries to light one after Gatsby pressures her to tell Tom that she never really loved him, and fails. Gatsby lights it for her.

tropes.name: Conspicuous Consumption
tropes.html: Gatsby's whole persona seems based on this; Tom is a slightly lesser example.

tropes.name: Cool Cars
tropes.html: As it is in the book, both Tom and Gatsby possess one. Tom's car is an absolutely anachronistic Auburn Boattail Speedster 851 (first produced in 1935), while Gatsby has a rakish and garish Duesenberg Model SJ dual-cowl Phaeton. Both, in reality, are replica cars made to allow the actors to drive comfortably without hurting a genuine antique.

tropes.name: Costume Porn
tropes.html: Everyone looks very sharp in their sparkling twenties outfits.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: Baz Luhrmann is the waiter that brings Nick to Jordan's table to meet for tea after his lunch with Gatsby.

tropes.name: Deliberate Values Dissonance
tropes.html: Tom Buchanan's racist speech, already present in the source material to make him an unsympathetic person, is made even worse here by having him deliver his bigoted perspective while standing in front of an African American man working for him.

tropes.name: Diegetic Switch
tropes.html: Several times in the movie, it's made clear that the people onscreen are dancing to the modern hip-hop soundtrack. But in some cases, the soundtrack is actually sung in a style consistent with 1920's jazz (with the original song overlaying it as well). This is most noticeable in the Speakeasy ("$100 Bill") and one of the party scenes ("Young and Beautiful").

tropes.name: Double Standard: Rape, Female on Male
tropes.html: Catherine borderline raped Nick during the apartment party. While sitting on his lap, she offers him one of her “nerve pills” which he declines. She then pops one in her mouth and kisses him, and makes him drink to swallow it. Nick is then shown very inebriated and Catherine continuously smooches him, while never explicitly shown drinking herself, and later drags him off for sex. Were the genders reversed it likely wouldn’t have been portrayed as romantic.

tropes.name: Downer Ending
tropes.html: Tom Buchanan's mistress (Myrtle) is run down by Daisy in Gatsby's car, for which he takes the blame. As this goes on, Buchanan tells Myrtle's husband where Gatsby lives. Gatsby goes swimming as Nick goes to work, but, while he's gone, Gatsby is murdered by the husband, who then commits suicide. Daisy and Tom pack up and go, leaving Gatsby to take the blame for Myrtle's death. Nobody attends his funeral but Nick, and his reputation is completely destroyed. Nick then loses faith in the world and commits himself to an asylum, though he ends the movie starting to recover.

tropes.name: Drives Like Crazy
tropes.html: Every main character who gets behind the steering wheel, from Gatsby to Tom to Daisy, who ends up killing Myrtle by hitting her with Gatsby's car.

tropes.name: The Flapper
tropes.html: Jordan and Catherine, full stop. Daisy merely plays at it.

tropes.name: Forceful Kiss
tropes.html: Nick receives several of these from Catherine shortly after meeting her.

tropes.name: Foregone Conclusion
tropes.html: The beginning of the film makes it very clear Jay Gatsby is dead.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: The dead leaves blowing around Gatsby's room during Daisy's first visit in about mid-to-late July and the touch of fall leaves as the group leaves the Buchanans on "the last, certainly the hottest day of summer" might show how Gatsby's dream is already dying; Gatsby's yellow car (driven by Tom) running over a watermelon on the way to Wilson's gas station.

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: Swimming in his pool, Gatsby awaits the call of Daisy, anticipating that she will agree to run away with him. It is clearly shown that Daisy does indeed reach for her phone. Back at his mansion, Gatsby hears the ring and regains hope. But after Gatsby is shot, the audience sees that Daisy had backed away and that it was really Nick, at work, who was trying to reach Gatsby.

tropes.name: How We Got Here
tropes.html: The framing device is Nick explaining the source of his depression and disillusionment to his doctor at a sanitarium he's checked into following the events of the summer.

tropes.name: Kissing Cousins
tropes.html: Brought up humorously by Daisy when she visits Nick and discovers how his house is full of flowers courtesy of Gatsby, and murmurs that he must be in love with her.

tropes.name: Large Ham
tropes.html: Joel Edgerton has his moments as Tom Buchanan, particularly in the scene where he confronts Gatsby about his affair with Daisy and proceeds to mock him about his upbringing, complete with an almost cartoonishly Evil Laugh.

tropes.name: Leitmotif
tropes.html: Every time the green light at the end of Daisy's dock is visible onscreen, even when it's out of focus, the background music has the same note swelling in time with the light's pulse.

tropes.name: Logo Joke
tropes.html: The opening logos are shown as flat on a grayscale film full of scratches and hairs, ending on Gatsby's glyph, which slowly moves away as the picture moves from 2D to 3D and given color as the glyph turns into the green light. The same thing happens in reverse during the credits.

tropes.name: Lonely Funeral
tropes.html: Unlike in the book where Owl Eyes and Gatsby's father come to visit, it is only Nick who attends Gatsby's funeral. Not the case in one of the deleted scenes, however.

tropes.name: Loud Gulp
tropes.html: Gatsby does one during the tea time with Daisy and Nick, probably due to nervousness.

tropes.name: Moody Trailer Cover Song
tropes.html: One trailer had Filter's cover of '60s pop classic "Happy Together" by The Turtles.

tropes.name: Mouth-to-Mouth Force-Feeding
tropes.html: At Tom and Myrtle's party, Catherine forces Nick to take one of her "nerve pills" by planting it in his mouth via a kiss.

tropes.name: My Friends... and Zoidberg
tropes.html: At Gatsby's party he introduces Nick and Daisy enthusiastically to his guests. He introduces Tom with considerably less enthusiasm and refers to him dismissively as "the Polo player".

tropes.name: Ooh, Me Accent's Slipping
tropes.html: DiCaprio's is not entirely consistent. Considering Gatsby's Nouveau Riche status, this may be less bad acting than good acting.

tropes.name: Poirot Speak
tropes.html: The Buchanan family's majordomo speaks with a stereotypically thick French accent.

tropes.name: Politically Incorrect Villain
tropes.html: Tom rants about race-mixing and keeping the lesser races down and calls Meyer Wolfshiem a 'kike', making him more overtly racist than he is in the book.

tropes.name: Pop-Star Composer
tropes.html: Jay-Z contributes to the score, and is also one of the film's executive producers.

tropes.name: Promoted to Love Interest
tropes.html:
• In the novel, Nick and Catherine at Myrtle's apartment just talk. In the 2013 film, she immediately flirts with him and they share passionate kisses, before eventually having a one-night stand.
  • Inverted with Nick's affair with Jordan Baker. He does try to pursue her and finds himself implicitly rejecting the chance of a relationship at the end, whereas in the book, they mutually break up. As revealed by deleted scenes, the relationship between Nick and Jordan was initially in the film.

tropes.name: Rage Breaking Point
tropes.html: Gatsby finally snaps at Tom, violently shoving a tray of glasses to the ground before pinning him to a table and threatening to punch him while screaming in his face. This was most likely at least partly because at that point, Daisy had just admitted that she'd be lying if she said she never loved Tom, and couldn't bring herself to break up with him as Gatsby had hoped. Before this, Gatsby had been convinced that she never realy loved him and that breaking up with him wouldn't be so hard, so this really put a dent in his goal to recreate the past and be with her. This, combined with Tom continuing to condescendingly taunt him and his upbringing, finally proved too much for him to take, leading to his outburst. Of course, only moments later, he snaps out of it, and his horrified expression just screams "my gosh, what have I done?".

tropes.name: Real Men Wear Pink
tropes.html: Gatsby wears a pink suit at the climax.

tropes.name: Reconstruct the Remains
tropes.html: Daisy receives a very expensive pearl necklace from Tom Buchanan as an engagement gift. She gets drunk the day of her wedding and dramatically rips the necklace off, trying to cancel the ceremony (after receiving a letter from her former fling Jay Gatsby). Daisy's mother and her best friend Jordan quickly re-string the pearls and fix the necklace while Daisy sobers up in the bath; the wedding continues as planned with Daisy wearing Tom's necklace.

tropes.name: Recursive Canon
tropes.html: The film reveals Nick as having written the novel while undergoing psychiatric treatment.

tropes.name: Retraux
tropes.html:
• The film opens and ends with a grainy footage of the credits while jazz music plays, making it look like a film from the 1920s.
  • The scenes of Gatsby's wartime experience look like treated footage of old period-era World War One newsreels.
  • There are times when the film looks colorized to match the colorized Stock Footage.

tropes.name: Right Through the Wall
tropes.html: Nick has an uncomfortable moment when Tom drags him along for his rendezvous with Myrtle, as he can hear them right through the walls.

tropes.name: Ripping Off the String of Pearls
tropes.html: Compared to the book, the film takes a few liberties with the scene right before Daisy's wedding to make it more dramatic and visually appealing. In both versions, Jordan informs Nick that Tom gifted Daisy a pearl necklace "valued at three hundred and fifty thousand dollars" as an engagement/ wedding present. In the book, a languidly drunk Daisy deposits her pearls into a waste basket next to her bed and tells Jordan to return them. In the film version, a violently drunken Daisy rips the pearls off her throat, screaming and crying as she casts them down a long hallway. The magnitude of her action is emphasized by a low angle shot that shows the pearls rolling away from her.

tropes.name: Sigil Spam
tropes.html: Gatsby's JG logo. It even extends to the credits, which are separated by versions with the director and producers' initials (may be confused with JZ).

tropes.name: Spiritual Successor
tropes.html: Has a lot in common with Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge, with acidic party scenes, the Framing Device of a depressed writer glorifying an object of (platonic or romantic) affections after the latter’s death, complicated relations, and even a scene where the main male tells his rival that the main woman doesn't love him. Could be considered either a retread or a more realistic deconstruction of Moulin Rouge.

tropes.name: Standard Snippet
tropes.html:
• Johann Sebastian Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor, during the intro to Gatsby's party. Played on screaming jazz trumpet before transitioning into standard organ, as played by Ewing Klipspringer ("dubious descendent of Beethoven").
  • George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue standing in for "The Jazz History of the World," doubling as Diegetic Music for The Reveal of Gatsby's identity.

tropes.name: Statuesque Stunner
tropes.html: Jordan Baker (Elizabeth Debicki) is at least 6ft.

tropes.name: Stepford Smiler
tropes.html: Daisy is definitely one. While she tends to act like a typical woman from the 20's, it's revealed early on that she's really dealing with a lot of emotional baggage, a lot of which is a result of her marriage with Tom, which is really a lot more unhappy than it appears. And later on, we also discover that she was really planning on marrying Gatsby all those years ago, but when he went off to war and didn't return for several years, she ended up marrying Tom, only to discover right before the wedding that Gatsby was still alive, which sent her into a major Heroic BSoD, since by that point, she couldn't get out of the wedding. When we see her at the altar, the smile she's wearing could barely look more fake.

tropes.name: Stocking Filler
tropes.html: Myrtle and her sister Catherine wear some very fancy stockings and socks, in a variation of real 1920s trends.

tropes.name: There Are No Therapists
tropes.html: Pleasantly averted. Nick starts to get his life back together after committing himself to an asylum thanks to a caring doctor who encourages him to talk about what happened to him when he was part of Gatsby's circle.

tropes.name: Third Wheel
tropes.html: Nick finds himself as the third wheel in Gatsby and Daisy's affair and Tom's affair with Myrtle.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Spoil
tropes.html: Gatsby's in bed with Daisy in the very first trailer; if you read the book they also include Daisy saying "You (Gatsby) always look so cool", which is practically a love confession in front of Tom; there's also a scene that might be George Wilson going for his gun. There's also a bit in the second trailer where Myrtle is struck by the car.

tropes.name: Truer to the Text
tropes.html: The film is much more faithful to the original novel than prior adaptations, to the point of frequently quoting Fitzgerald's text as it was published in 1925. The only major liberties are the modernized soundtrack and the framing device of Nick recounting the story to a therapist in an asylum (and even that serves to give an in-universe reason for the extensive narration).

tropes.name: '20s Bob Haircut
tropes.html: Obviously a fashion statement/trend worn by women in the film, considering it's set in The Roaring '20s. Although Daisy's and Jordan's hairstyles look anachronistic, with them sporting shingles, which only came out in 1923.

tropes.name: Unlimited Wardrobe
tropes.html: Gatsby tosses his shirts to Daisy like confetti.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html:
• Joseph Gordon Levitt previously hit it off with a girl called Autumn on 3rd Rock from the Sun. Both times his character is named Tom (or Tommy).
  • Tom's line about how pretty girls get away with treating people badly mirrors Joseph Gordon Levitt's famous speech in 10 Things I Hate About You - where Cameron chews out Bianca for doing so.

tropes.name: Affectionate Parody
tropes.html: Played with in the "Expectation versus Reality" sequences. The Expectation parts follow this by showing what it would be like if it was part of a legitimate Romantic Comedy (what Tom thinks he's in): occasionally emotional, at times cheesy, almost always in his favor. The Reality parts subvert or deconstruct those, usually by Tom messing up a line, not looking as suave as he thinks he is, or even failing to act at all because he's so flustered.

tropes.name: Aloof Dark-Haired Girl
tropes.html:
Tom and his co-worker friend initially assumed Summer to be this.
Tom: That sucks. Why is it pretty girls think they can treat people like crap and get away with it?
McKenzie: Centuries of reinforcement!

tropes.name: Ambiguous Ending
tropes.html: Will Tom find real lasting love with Autumn, or will it be another failed relationship? Since we only see them on the first day of their meeting, guessing in either direction is pure speculation.

tropes.name: AM/FM Characterization
tropes.html:
• Tom is a fan of British alt-rock bands such as The Smiths, Joy Division, The Pixies and The Clash. The love for this music he developed at a young age is described by the narrator as a major influence on his beliefs on love.
  • Deconstructed in the case of Summer. She is a fan of similar kinds of music, which is a large reason for why Tom is drawn to her. This contributes to his idea that she is his destined girl and that built the fantasy of her which caused so much dysfunction in their relationship.

tropes.name: Anachronic Order
tropes.html: The film begins on Day 488 and then jumps around among the 500 days as Tom (through the narrator) recalls them.

tropes.name: The Artifact
tropes.html: The flashback to Summer cutting her hair off in her teen years is a remnant from when she was conceived as having short blonde hair (you know, a pixie haircut) — as it would have been an Important Haircut for her.

tropes.name: Aside Glance
tropes.html: Tom, at the very end of the film, after finding out that the girl he's just met is named Autumn. It's practically a non-verbal Here We Go Again!.

tropes.name: Benevolent Boss
tropes.html: Vance, Tom's boss, notices the latter's invokedCreator Breakdown and makes him use his misery to be more work-productive instead of firing him. Still didn't work, sadly.

tropes.name: Better than a Bare Bulb
tropes.html: The movie repeatedly calls out its usage of conventional romantic comedy tropes.

tropes.name: Big Brother Instinct
tropes.html: Tom starts to act protective over Rachel when she starts listing boy's names in her class.

tropes.name: Bigger Is Better in Bed
tropes.html: In the case of one of Summer's ex-boyfriends, who was subsequently nicknamed Puma.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html: When Tom and Summer are riding in a car and Tom asks Summer what they are doing there is a song in French playing on the radio. It is "Quelqu'un m'a dit" by Carla Bruni. The chorus of this song is "Quelqu'un m'a dit que tu m'aimait encore, somebody told me that you still loved me." During a lull in the conversation what is heard of the song translates to "somebody told me that destiny doesn't care about us. That it gives nothing and promises everything. It's said that happiness is within reach so we reach out our hand and found ourselves crazy."

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: Tom and Summer don't get back together, but he's on the path to achieving his dreams, she's in a happy relationship, and he might have a good relationship starting.

tropes.name: Blind Date
tropes.html: Tom goes on one with a girl named Alison after Summer dumps him; as he's still too distraught to do anything but talk about his breakup with Summer, the date with Alison doesn't go well.

tropes.name: Bluebird of Happiness
tropes.html:
During Tom's Happy Dance with half of Los Angeles, a Disneyesque cartoon bluebird flies in, lands on his finger, and then winks at the camera as it flies off.
  • In a deleted scene depicting a more depressing version of this moment, a much less adorable bird flits around Tom's head, much to his annoyance. The bird then takes a crap on his shoulder.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: The movie begins and ends on Day 488.

tropes.name: Boy Meets Girl
tropes.html: Deconstructed. The narrator even introduces the film as "a story of boy meets girl", but is quick to note that this is not a love story.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html: The Graduate gets referenced in the opening narration, and Tom and Summer are seen watching it in one of the final scenes.

tropes.name: But Not Too Bi
tropes.html: One of Summer's previous serious relationships was with a woman named Charlie, but in the proper story, Summer only shows romantic interest in men.

tropes.name: Cassandra Truth
tropes.html:
Rachel absolutely nails the flaw in Tom's thinking before he and Summer have even kissed:
"Just because she likes the same bizarro crap you do doesn't mean she's your soul mate."

tropes.name: Cerebus Call-Back
tropes.html: Done the other way round. Tom finds a card saying "I love us" and looks at it sadly. It then flashes back to inform us that he wrote the card inspired by his relationship with Summer.

tropes.name: Character Development
tropes.html: As the film progresses, Tom matures greatly. He stops seeing women as objects that he can project his ideals onto, and drops his It's All About Me attitude towards his relationship with Summer. He is also able to turn his life around, quitting his job in the greeting card company and pursuing a job as an architect, which is what he wants to do. His growth in the film is best illustrated in his final conversation with Summer, where he genuinely wishes her to be happy, and when he asks out Autumn without hesitation and doesn't get angry when she initially rejects him.

tropes.name: Color Failure
tropes.html: Late in the movie when Tom is depressed over his breakup with Summer, he's depicted in monochrome in one scene.

tropes.name: Color Motif
tropes.html: Blue is associated with Summer, which according to Word of God was done to bring out her actress' blue eyes. Throughout the film, Tom sees and ignores many objects with this color, which serves as Foreshadowing (see below).

tropes.name: Comedic Work, Serious Scene
tropes.html: The climax sees Tom's expectations of getting back together with Summer shattered as he realizes he's at her engagement party.

tropes.name: Comically Missing the Point
tropes.html:
• Tom completely misinterpreted the ending of The Graduate as a child, contributing to his tendency to romanticize relationships as an adult. Summer, however, seems to get it, as she leaves the cinema crying and Tom just can't understand why.
  • It's shown fairly evidently in the script, where it is shown that after his college girlfriend (briefly mentioned in the film) broke up with him in a flashback by using a song he showed her as a metaphor (skipping the song that she used to like), Tom misinterprets it and tells her it's a "great fucking song."

tropes.name: Coming of Age Story
tropes.html: The movie is in many ways a story of Tom growing from being a young adult who is in many ways an adolescent (working a job he has no passion for, being naive about how love and relationships work, and even his style of dress) to a (hopefully) more functioning and happier adult.

tropes.name: Commitment Issues
tropes.html: Summer appears remarkably calm about her previous failed relationships, chalking up their failures to "Life." So it comes as quite a surprise when she marries her post-Tom boyfriend within less than a year. You wonder how her lifelong fear of emotional intimacy will affect her marriage down the road....

tropes.name: Creator Breakdown
tropes.html:
In-universe example; Tom writes increasingly caustic and inappropriately cynical greeting card messages as his relationship with Summer deteriorates.
"Roses are red, violets are blue, fuck you, whore."

tropes.name: Crowd Song
tropes.html: A Crowd Dance, to be more accurate, since the characters onscreen are not the ones singing: the morning after Tom and Summer spend their first night together, Tom giddily struts down the streets of L.A., where he is joined by a crowd of dancers, a marching band, and animated birds, all set to Hall and Oates' "You Make My Dreams".

tropes.name: Did Not Get the Girl
tropes.html: The audience knows this from the start.

tropes.name: Did You Just Have Sex?
tropes.html: One of Tom's friends asks him this, not realizing that Summer is in the other room, listening.

tropes.name: Dogged Nice Guy
tropes.html: Deconstructed. To further his relationship with Summer, Tom goes out of his way to protect her from another suitor asking her out, which ends with him getting knocked out by said suitor. In the aftermath, Summer isn't impressed by Tom's violence, leading to him dropping the "nice guy" act and angrily asking her if they were going to be more than friends. Even after their breakup, Tom hasn't really let go of Summer. Notably, when Summer invites him to a party at her apartment, he only sees the invitation as another opportunity to impress her and win back her love. Tom's plan doesn't pan out as well as he thought it would, and he just ends up in a worse spiral after realizing that Summer was engaged to someone else.

tropes.name: Drowning My Sorrows
tropes.html: After Tom discovers that Summer's marrying someone else.

tropes.name: Drunken Song
tropes.html: McKenzie is absolutely plastered at karaoke and completely fails to stay on rhythm during "God Bless the USA."

tropes.name: Empathic Environment
tropes.html: Through the changing seasons within the animation that ties the timeline together. Summer: Tom and Summer's relationship begins. Autumn: It begins to fracture. Winter: They've broken up and he's depressed. Spring: He meets Autumn and realizes life goes on.

tropes.name: Entitled to Have You
tropes.html: Because Tom believes in the concept of One True Love, he thinks that he and Summer are destined to be together. Even after they break up, Tom still believes that Summer is his fated soulmate. After Summer invites him to a party, he tries to rekindle his relationship with Summer, not realizing that Summer moved on to another man.

tropes.name: Epunymous Title
tropes.html: On Summer being both a name and a time.

tropes.name: Expository Hairstyle Change
tropes.html: When Tom at least tries to get over his break-up with Summer, he now wears his hair slicked back. Summer's hair is worn up when she sees Tom after their break-up. After she's been married she appears with her hair slightly longer and curled, and the fringe swept to the side.

tropes.name: The Faceless
tropes.html: Summer's husband never has his face shown.

tropes.name: False Soulmate
tropes.html: Summer, for Tom. She basically has to tell him to his face that she wasn't actually the one for him, despite his conviction.

tropes.name: Le Film Artistique
tropes.html: During his post-break up depression, Tom sits through a collection of European monochrome movies that strangely resemble events from his own life.

tropes.name: Flat Character
tropes.html: Appropriately enough, since we're only really seeing her through Tom's eyes, we don't know all that much about Summer beyond her taste in books and music. We know Tom's career aspirations and meet his family members and close friends, but Summer doesn't get any of these. Even in her professional life, Summer is defined by her proximity to another man, being Vance's assistant.

tropes.name: Foregone Conclusion
tropes.html: The narrator tells us right near the start, "This is a story of Boy Meets Girl. But you should know up front, this is not a love story. "

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: Summer has an art installation of paper cranes in her apartment. All but one are blue (a colour strongly associated with her throughout the movie), and the odd one out is red (the color that Autumn is wearing when Tom meets her). Guess which crane Tom picks to fidget with? Also an example of Colour-Coded for Your Convenience.

tropes.name: Fourth-Date Marriage
tropes.html: The entire story, including Tom's post-break-up depression, takes place over a little less than a year and a half. Consider how Summer spends less than half that time (days 288-500). Most couples spend more time between the engagement and the wedding than Summer took meeting a total stranger and getting married to him... which suggests that her big Love Epiphany might be just another whim.

tropes.name: Freeze-Frame Bonus
tropes.html: Summer's engagement ring is visible from the moment she greets Tom in both the "Expectations" and "Reality" scenes.

tropes.name: Freudian Excuse
tropes.html: According to the narrator, Summer doesn't believe in love because as a young girl, she witnessed her parents go through a divorce.

tropes.name: Freudian Slip
tropes.html: Summer fakes one in order to gently tease Tom and to let him know that she overheard the Did You Just Have Sex? conversation between him and his friend.

tropes.name: Friends with Benefits
tropes.html: Summer resists Tom's efforts to put a label on their relationship; she prefers to enjoy things the as they are without an implied commitment she isn't sure she can give.

tropes.name: Happy Dance
tropes.html: Tom after his first night with Summer... along with everyone else in the street he's walking down.

tropes.name: Hard Truth Aesop
tropes.html: No matter how much a love interest may be attractive to you, loves the same things you do, feels perfectly compatible to your own personality, is in a sexual relationship with you, adding up to how much you love them, they may simply not love you in that way in return, that it's their right to feel that way, and it's up to the jilted person to learn how to live with it.

tropes.name: Here We Go Again!
tropes.html: The film ends with Tom meeting a new girl at a job interview. Her name? Autumn. Day 1.

tropes.name: Heroic BSoD
tropes.html: Tom's response upon learning that Summer has gotten engaged to someone else.

tropes.name: Heroic Resolve
tropes.html: Days 456-476 shows Tom somehow starting to get his act together again.

tropes.name: Hollywood California
tropes.html: Set in Los Angeles; Tom, having trained as an architect, takes Summer on a tour of his favorite buildings around the city. This doesn't include any instantly recognizable Hollywood landmarks.

tropes.name: Homage
tropes.html: Specific scenes from Children of Paradise, Persona (1966), The Seventh Seal, and The Graduate. More generally, the films of Woody Allen, especially Annie Hall.

tropes.name: How We Got Here
tropes.html: The first day of Tom and Summer's relationship we see is Day 488, near the end of it — in fact, exactly two hundred days after she dumped him, and several days after she married someone else. The rest of the movie jumps back and forth through the five hundred days to explain How We Got Here.

tropes.name: Hypocritical Humor
tropes.html:
Incessant.
Summer: All we do is argue.
Tom: That's bullshit!

tropes.name: In Medias Res
tropes.html: Related to the Anachronic Order, we see the effects of their breakup in the first scene, before we even meet the couple.

tropes.name: Introspective Art
tropes.html: After Summer breaks up with Tom, Tom's greeting cards take an unpleasant turn, to the point that he ends up leaving the company altogether and making another go at being an architect.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html: Because of the film's Anachronic Order, we often hear the echoed version first. One of the reasons the movie is in some ways Better on DVD. One in particular has them at a hardware store and Tom makes a joke about the uselessness of showfloor appliances, which Summer is apathetic over. It then jumps to earlier in their relationship when they sort of became a couple after an afternoon of goofing around in the same place making the exact same kind of jokes. One was cute and charming, the other incessant.

tropes.name: "It" Is Dehumanizing
tropes.html:
A variant. A Jerkass at a bar who failed to pick up Summer saw her with Tom and lashes on him/them with this trope.
Jerkass guy: I can't believe this is your boyfriend!

tropes.name: I Want My Beloved to Be Happy
tropes.html:
In his final meeting with his ex Summer, the more mature Tom wishes her well in her marriage.
Tom: Summer, I really do hope that you are happy.

tropes.name: Just Friends
tropes.html: Despite being Friends with Benefits, the core of the tension between Tom and Summer is his desire to be more than Just Friends, and her desire not to.

tropes.name: Karaoke Bonding Scene
tropes.html: At an office party, Tom sings the Pixies's "Here Comes Your Man" for the benefit of his crush on co-worker Summer.

tropes.name: Lampshade Hanging
tropes.html: Of Romantic Comedy conventions. Usually (but not always) by the narrator. Usually (but not always) subverted or deconstructed.

tropes.name: Lemony Narrator
tropes.html: The narrator gets sarcastic when talking about Tom's more childish beliefs, noting that they stem from Tom's misreading of The Graduate.

tropes.name: Love at First Sight
tropes.html: Tom's taken with Summer the moment he sees her. Summer seems to evoke this response from most men she meets.

tropes.name: Love Hurts
tropes.html: The primary theme of the movie.

tropes.name: Lucky Charms Title
tropes.html: The brackets for the number (500).

tropes.name: Manic Pixie Dream Girl
tropes.html: The titular Summer is a deconstruction. She has traits of a Manic Pixie Dream Girl such as a bubbly personality, a love of indie music and her quick chemistry and romance with Tom. However the film opens with Summer having dumped Tom. We see throughout the film that she repeatedly tells Tom she only means this as a fling, not something long-term. Tom sees her as his Manic Pixie Dream Girl but she does not exist for him, instead ending the relationship and later getting engaged to someone else.

tropes.name: Master of the Mixed Message
tropes.html:
From Tom's point of view, Summer. It seems like every time she tells Tom she's not interested in something serious (and despite it being obvious that he is), she immediately throws a curve ball in the form of hand-holding, kisses or sex. Just before she breaks up with him, she impulsively kisses Tom in the street. The worst example is when they have a huge fight, Summer tries to tell him they are Just Friends, he storms out, and Summer goes over to his place in the morning, in the rain, and has sex with him, which he interprets to mean she wants to stay in the relationship. However, from her perspective she is very clear with what she wants, not putting labels on their relationship and holding the understanding that things might change overnight.
  • A lot of the misunderstanding can be attributed to different (or selective) communication styles. Summer believes she is very clear in her repeated vocal statements that she does not want a relationship, yet she seems oblivious of how her actions could be interpreted by Tom. Tom, for his part, focuses on her actions and ignores what she says.

tropes.name: Match Cut
tropes.html: In one transition, a happy, just-got-laid Tom enters an elevator...and on a later day, a depressed Tom walks out.

tropes.name: Maybe Ever After
tropes.html: Tom and Autumn. They agree to go on a date later, but what becomes of it is up in the air.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: Summer and her possible successor, Autumn. Also, the names Tom Hansen and Summer Finn are a Shout-Out to Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.

tropes.name: Meet Cute
tropes.html:
There are two examples in the film, and they have something in common: one party was already interested beforehand while the other was oblivious to that person's existence. The first time, it's Tom who's already interested and Summer who's been oblivious; the second time, it's Tom who's been oblivious (too caught up angsting over Summer) and Autumn who's already interested.
  • On Day 4, Tom and Summer break the ice when Summer notices that he is listening to her favorite band The Smiths.
  • On Day 500 of Summer/Day 1 of Autumn, another more standard example occurs between Tom and Autumn as they wait to interview for the same job.

tropes.name: Mood Whiplash
tropes.html:
• Between romantic elation and romantic disappointment. Repeatedly.
  • Tom's reactions to breaking up with Summer is both funny and heartbreaking.

tropes.name: Narrator
tropes.html: The movie's narrator frequently comments on both the events and themes of the movie.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html: The title and trailer imply that the movie is about the 500 days in the relationship between Summer and Tom. In fact, Summer breaks up with Tom on Day 288, and the remaining days document his attempts to get over her. Furthermore, most viewers of the trailer expected the movie to be a straight Romantic Comedy rather than a deconstruction.

tropes.name: Nice Jewish Boy
tropes.html: Tom was originally written to be explicitly Jewish, speaking fluent Yiddish and attending Rachel's bat mitzvah.

tropes.name: Obliviously Beautiful
tropes.html: Summer attracts many male admirers while simply going about her day, and she never seems to notice any of them.

tropes.name: Oblivious to Love
tropes.html: Summer is pretty obtuse about Tom's feelings for her.

tropes.name: Only Sane Man
tropes.html: Rachel, who points out that "just because some cute girl likes all the same bizarro crap you do... that doesn't make her your soulmate." To Tom's surprise but not the audience's, she's right.

tropes.name: OOC Is Serious Business
tropes.html: Tom can tell something's up with Summer in the days leading up to their breakup. She's much quieter than usual, she ignores his attempts at joking around, she avoids physical contact, and she even bursts into tears out of nowhere (possibly lamenting the conversation she knows she must have with him).

tropes.name: Perspective Reversal
tropes.html: In the beginning, Tom is hopelessly romantic, while Summer does not believe in love. By the end of the movie, their dispositions toward love are inverted.

tropes.name: Postmodernism
tropes.html: Plenty, including the nonlinear narrative, the spontaneous dance sequence, the onscreen count of the actual 500 days, and one scene which contrasts "Expectations" vs. "Reality" via Split Screen.

tropes.name: Precocious Crush
tropes.html: Tom's little sister Rachael says all her friends have crushes on him, and we see them all looking and smiling at him.

tropes.name: Pursue the Dream Job
tropes.html: Tom eventually makes something good of his heartbreak, refreshing his architecture portfolio and applying for jobs at local firms. We don't know if he ever gets one, but he does seem to get a few interviews, so we know it's not totally hopeless.

tropes.name: Raven Hair, Ivory Skin
tropes.html: Summer's beauty and very dark hair have been noted several times.

tropes.name: Reasonable Authority Figure
tropes.html: Tom's and Summer's boss.

tropes.name: Red Herring
tropes.html: In a sense. One of the opening shots shows Summer with a ring on her finger. It turns out not to belong to Tom but another man.

tropes.name: The Reveal
tropes.html: At a party Tom already finds just about unbearable, he suddenly notices Summer's engagement ring.

tropes.name: Rivalry as Courtship
tropes.html: Downplayed; Tom meets Autumn as they are both waiting to interview for the same job, and they jokingly wish each other bad luck.

tropes.name: Romantic Comedy
tropes.html: A Deconstruction of the genre in the general vein of Annie Hall and Manhattan.

tropes.name: Romantic Runner-Up
tropes.html: The main character is one of these. While he was completely in love with her, she wasn't at all in love with him. The key theme is the difference between his expectations and the reality of the situation.

tropes.name: Roses Are Red, Violets Are Blue...
tropes.html: "Roses are red, violets are blue, / Fuck you, whore." Arguably qualifies as a Precision F-Strike, too.

tropes.name: Seasonal Motif
tropes.html: The love interest Summer is fun but flighty and unpredictable. The bereavement card project Tom works on when he's depressed after their breakup is called The Winter Collection. The girl Tom meets at the end is called Autumn.

tropes.name: Secondary Character Title
tropes.html: While Tom and Summer are equally billed as co-leads, the film focuses more on Tom than Summer.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Beauty
tropes.html: Summer is considered World Class beauty.<!--* {{Shorttank}}: Tom's younger sister, Rachel.-->

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• The Meaningful Names Tom Hansen and Summer Finn are a Shout-Out to Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.
  • See also Suspiciously Specific Denial for an incredibly obscure Shout-Out in the guise of a fake Take That!.
  • Summer calls Tom "young Werther". Notice the potential parallel?

tropes.name: Shower of Love
tropes.html: Tom and Summer did this to emulate a porn movie. It doesn't go too smoothly.

tropes.name: Single-Target Sexuality
tropes.html:
• Despite their breakup,Tom still pines for Summer even while he tries to convince himself that he didn't actually like her. Even on his blind date, he can't stop talking about Summer (albeit not exactly the nicest things, but still). When Summer meets him again, Tom formulates a plan to get back with her.
  • Tom's obliviousness towards Autumn, who had seen him before, but he never noticed her until they meet.

tropes.name: Slow Clap
tropes.html: Subverted; after Tom gives an impassioned speech and quits his job at the greeting card company, his friend and coworker McKenzie begins to clap, but quickly stops when nobody joins him.

tropes.name: Soul-Crushing Desk Job
tropes.html: Tom wants to be an architect, but he ends up at a greeting card company. Although there is no hostility in the office, Tom feels that his job is monotonous and boring. Moreover, he has no passion for it. The upside is meeting Summer. By the time Tom and Summer break up, Tom undergoes a downward spiral, and the final straw for him that drives him to quit this job is a boardroom meeting with ranting about inspirational quotes on love.

tropes.name: Spit Take
tropes.html:
Summer: They used to call me Anal Girl.
(Tom spit-takes)
Summer: ...I was very neat and organized.

tropes.name: Stalker with a Crush
tropes.html: Very early in Tom's relationship with Summer, one of his friends teases him that he's one of these toward Summer. Of course she overhears.

tropes.name: Stupidest Thing I've Ever Heard
tropes.html: Tom's thoughts about Summer's "PENIS!" game.

tropes.name: Suspiciously Specific Denial
tropes.html: The film's opening disclaimer: "AUTHOR'S NOTE: The following is a work of fiction. Any resemblance to persons living or dead is purely coincidental. Especially you Jenny Beckman. Bitch."

tropes.name: Take That!
tropes.html:
• The film opens with the message "Especially you Jenny Beckman. Bitch." According to an interview by screenwriter Scott Neustadter, Jenny Beckman was an ex-girlfriend who broke his heart and thus became the inspiration for Summer's character.
  • Tom complains how modern fashion is about wearing big sunglasses, getting tattoos, and carrying little dogs in handbags.

tropes.name: Take This Job and Shove It
tropes.html: One integral moment for Tom is a disgruntled speech he gives in a meeting about how greeting card companies offer nothing but superficial statements that, by commodifying them, devalue the genuine emotions they're supposed to evoke, creating falsehoods no dissimilar from hyper-romantic films and pop songs. He tops off the rant by quitting and walking out, saying that "there's enough bullshit in the world without my help."

tropes.name: They Wasted a Perfectly Good Sandwich
tropes.html: After Summer dumps him, Tom leaves the diner in a fury without so much as a bite of the pancakes the waitress just delivered.

tropes.name: Thinks Like a Romance Novel
tropes.html: Tom was raised on "sad British pop music and a total mis-reading of the movie The Graduate", and it shows.

tropes.name: This Is for Emphasis, Bitch!
tropes.html:
• "Especially you Jenny Beckman. Bitch."
  • "Better luck next time... bitch."

tropes.name: Time Title
tropes.html: The film takes a look at Tom and Summer's quasi-relationship from Tom's perspective, numbering the days and events that lead to its buildup and eventual downfall.

tropes.name: Token White
tropes.html: Tom and Summer attended a wedding of a co-worker (former in Summer's case) near the end of the film. The wedded couple and their guests are almost all African-Americans. Since Tom and Summer already broke-up at this point, they no longer count as a Token Minority Couple.

tropes.name: Tragic Hero
tropes.html: Both Tom and Summer. By the end of the movie, they decide to make their lives less tragic by going their own way, with Tom himself becoming a great architect.

tropes.name: Tranquil Fury
tropes.html: Tom, going through post-breakup depression, smashing plate after plate with a blank expression.

tropes.name: Troubling Unchildlike Behaviour
tropes.html: Tom is notably creeped out that Rachel, who is a preteen, has knowledge of how relationships work (not to mention PMS).<!--* TrueBlueFemininity: Summer most of the time.--><!--* TruthInTelevision: Applies to most of the movie, but the Expectations vs. Reality scene is so excruciatingly truthful that it's heartbreaking.-->

tropes.name: Viewers Are Geniuses
tropes.html: The Anachronic Order, of course. In addition, the film includes throw-away allusions (including running gags) to Shakespeare, Magritte, Hopper, Serrano, Bergman, Wilde, and Goethe. Plus, you know, obscure stuff.

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html: Tom seeing Summer's engagement ring.

tropes.name: What Is This Thing You Call "Love"?
tropes.html: Summer is first defined through her seeing no long-term meaning in love, a sentiment that Tom disagrees with, seeing it as something very real but only knowable when you feel it. Through finding and marrying another man, Summer grows into and acknowledges Tom's original stance, although Tom has since moved on from it.

tropes.name: Wise Beyond Their Years
tropes.html: Tom's pre-teen sister Rachel is the youngest main character but understands romantic relationships better than Tom and his friends do.

tropes.name: Wrong Genre Savvy
tropes.html: Many of the characters think they're in a conventional romantic comedy, but they're actually in a deconstruction of one.

tropes.name: Action Girl
tropes.html: Jane Smith knows how to kick ass just as much as (and by her kill count, even more than) her husband.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html: Adam Brody is wearing a Fight Club T-shirt while being interrogated by John (Brad Pitt). Presumably, Tyler Durden was played by somebody else in this universe. John's yellow/orange sunglasses later in the movie are also suspiciously similar to a pair seen on Tyler Durden.

tropes.name: Air-Vent Passageway
tropes.html: Played with; the building where Jane works has security lasers everywhere to keep intruders out — including the vents. Justified as Jane is an assassin and has used such tactics in the past.

tropes.name: Amazon Brigade
tropes.html: Jane's agency seems only to hire women, although their boss and at least some of their operatives (not seen) are male.

tropes.name: Anti-Hero
tropes.html: Although they are sympathetic and romantic characters, Jane and John are still professional murderers. And while their targets shown in the movie aren't exactly nuns feeding the homeless, it is never firmly established if either of the two organizations they work for are actually on the side of good. The most the film provides on the subject is a comment from Jane to her target about "selling big guns to bad people" before she kills him, but there's nothing to indicate whether or not the specific job is typical of her hits. There is also the matter of a line of dialogue (cut from some versions of the film) in which, while discussing how many people they've killed, John asks if Jane's claimed number of 312 includes innocent bystanders.

tropes.name: Armor Is Useless
tropes.html:
• Averted in one scene when Jane, unaware, shoots John, he's wearing a vest.
  • In the climactic scene, this is a downplayed trope. Our anti-heroes are shown to be wearing bulletproof vests, but the impacts still clearly hurt.

tropes.name: Arson, Murder, and Jaywalking
tropes.html:
• Out of all the various things they've done to each other in the course of their cover... all the lies, fakery, and trying to kill each other... the thing that seems to upset John the most is that Jane hired actors to play her parents for events like their wedding and holidays, though that as he notes, it's because he brought his real parents.
    John Smith: I can't believe I brought my real parents to our wedding!
  • The reverse, Jane seems overly upset at John for being married once before (briefly, in Vegas, then annulled)
    Jane: What's her name and social security number?
    John: No, you're not going to kill her.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Geography
tropes.html: Bogotá, Colombia, in real life, is a major city of nearly 7 million (at the time of filming) with a mild-to-cool climate thanks to its high-altitude location. Here it's portrayed as a small river-side town where the sun always shines, people listen to flamenco music and there's no need for clothes. To make things worse, a soldier speaks with a heavy Mexican accent. Even the actors said that they've never been to Bogotá, or Colombia, for that matter.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Gun Safety
tropes.html:
John runs across the yard with his gun drawn and finger on the trigger, accidentally shooting Jane's windshield when he collides with a fence.
  • He also muzzle sweeps Jane with a shotgun a few times during the big shootout at the end. Along with "keep your finger off the trigger until you're ready to shoot" (see above), this is the first thing anyone learns about safely handling a weapon.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html: After making the hit at the hotel, Jane jumps from the balcony and rapidly descends on a cable. It brakes to a stop with no apparent control on her part, and allows her to land effortlessly on the sidewalk without jarring.

tropes.name: Aside Glance
tropes.html: Subverted. John asks Jane to dance a tango with him as a subtle way to disarm her in public without anyone noticing. Jane follows suit and at one point drops out of frame, seemingly to her knees. John looks at the camera and winks suggestively, implying Jane is on her knees for a much more "adult" reason. The Reveal Shot shows he's winked at an elderly couple, who are gaping because Jane is removing a pistol from John's ankle holster.

tropes.name: Audible Sharpness
tropes.html: Cutting bread should not be that loud.

tropes.name: Aw, Look! They Really Do Love Each Other
tropes.html:
Quite possibly the most non-standard use of this trope, as the Smiths both have this moment as they're pointing guns at each other.
John: I can't do it.
Jane: RRGH. COME ON.
Both: [sex]

tropes.name: Back-to-Back Badasses
tropes.html: The penultimate scene is the Smiths taking this posture when they confront a much larger group of assassins.

tropes.name: Basement Dweller
tropes.html: Eddie, having been divorced, is living with his mother despite his arsenal of weaponry. He insists this is a valid lifestyle choice.

tropes.name: Battle Couple
tropes.html: The Smiths reignite their marriage one scene before they form an alliance against their former employers.

tropes.name: Beauty Is Never Tarnished
tropes.html: Despite a knock-down dragout fight that destroys their home and includes multiple blows to the face and kicks to the torso, neither Smith sports a bruise when the neighbors and neighborhood security show up to inquire about the noise.

tropes.name: Black Boss Lady
tropes.html: She doesn't appear onscreen, but Mr. Smith's boss is voiced by Angela Bassett. Inversely, Mrs. Smith's Boss is voiced by Keith David.

tropes.name: Bluffing the Authorities
tropes.html: John and Jane's all out brawl attracts the attention of their neighbors, who call neighborhood security (who is entirely unconcerned); however, by the time the officers arrive their interaction has evolved into a different kind of physical encounter, and security aren't interested in looking too closely at the obviously happy couple. The destruction visible through their open door is explained away as renovations to the house.

tropes.name: Boyfriend Bluff
tropes.html: The Meet Cute they have in Colombia when the military is on edge looking to detain any foreigners traveling alone because someone was just assassinated. They're both using the other as protection but don't know (and don't seem to ask) why the other is going along with it.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: John and Jane meet a marriage counselor in the first and last scene, who asks them about their sex life.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html: The "Scale of 1-10, how is the sex?" question. It shows up in the opening to show how disconnected John and Jane are (they don't even understand the question) and at the end to show they're fully back on board ("Ask the sex question!").

tropes.name: Brutal Brawl
tropes.html: The midpoint features a home destroying one between Jane and John where they find out it's an even fight.

tropes.name: Bullet Dodge
tropes.html: In the final shootout, John and Jane twice duck an anti-tank missile being fired at them.

tropes.name: Camera Spoofing
tropes.html: When Jane's team think they have John cornered in an elevator at a construction site and have the one he's in quickly fall to the ground level, it turns out anticipated this and had the camera footage swapped around so Jane's team actually dropped a vacant elevator car.

tropes.name: Car Fu
tropes.html: Well, ATV-fu to be specific. John takes out a few agents in his zeal to rescue Jane during the final fight.

tropes.name: Casual Danger Dialogue
tropes.html: The Smiths bicker over newly revealed marital secrets while in the middle of a car chase/gun fight with pursuing assassins.

tropes.name: Celebrity Paradox
tropes.html: The Tank wears a Fight Club t-shirt. No one even thinks that John looks remarkably similar to Tyler Durden.

tropes.name: Combat Pragmatist
tropes.html: During the fight through the house, both of them, especially Jane, use various household implements, including curtains. Doubles as a Brick joke, as John had mentioned earlier in the movie that he objected to them.

tropes.name: Contract on the Hitman
tropes.html: When both the agencies that the Smiths worked for found out who their spouse worked for, they compromised and decided to put them on a collision course to take each other out.

tropes.name: Covert Group with Mundane Front
tropes.html: Baked in throughout the movie, as both the titular characters work in deep cover. Both of them work out of supposedly legitimate business fronts, complete with armed support staff. Their house itself qualifies, with secrets and weapon caches buried so deep (particularly beneath the shed) that they’re able to keep them hidden from each other.

tropes.name: Cut the Juice
tropes.html: John tells Jane to cut the power while infiltrating the prison, then frantically shouts at her to turn the lights back on because he's found himself in a Darkened Building Shootout. Unfortunately it takes a lot longer to get the power back up again.

tropes.name: Dance Battler
tropes.html: A variation - in the last battle John and Jane fight their enemies together in a gun-fight to the tune of the Assassin's Tango (or "Mondo Bongo," in the Director's Cut).

tropes.name: Dead Sparks
tropes.html: The Smiths' problem at the start of the film is that their marriage has floundered. After five (or six) years, they've lost their connection.

tropes.name: Destructo-Nookie
tropes.html: With the destructo- part coming before when they're trying to kill each other. They literally take their beautiful home apart in their efforts to kill each other to the point where they're forced to step over bits and pieces of trash and debris from the fight after they've made up.

tropes.name: Developing Nations Lack Cities
tropes.html: The film begins in Bogotá, Colombia, which is portrayed as a river town rather than the cosmopolitan city it is.

tropes.name: Destroy the Evidence
tropes.html: When John manages to invade the HQ of Jane's firm, they immediately wipe the hard drives and torch a bunch of documents in an incinerator.

tropes.name: Discreet Drink Disposal
tropes.html: John dumps out the martini Jane gave him after he notices an out-of-place bottle of drain cleaner.

tropes.name: Dish Dash
tropes.html: When Jane catches the wine bottle, it signals the Internal Reveal.

tropes.name: Does This Remind You of Anything?
tropes.html:
Does This Remind You of Anything?
  • John returning home from a hit is reminiscent of a cheating husband returning home after an affair. He drives home quietly, puts his wedding band back on, and picks at the red stain on his collar (blood instead of lipstick).
  • While interrogating their target, the couple argue as if they're disagreeing on how to raise a child. At one point, John even says, "Can we not argue in front of the target? It sends mixed signals."
  • When John and Jane are comparing their body counts, it sounds like a couple comparing numbers of past partners, including John feeling pointedly emasculated when his wife has a higher count than his. Bonus: "Some were two at a time."

tropes.name: Dominatrix
tropes.html: Jane dresses as one to get close to a target in one scene. It turns out that tying up a client under the guise of seduction puts one in a great position to kill him.

tropes.name: Double Entendre
tropes.html:
• Because the violent nature of the couple's interactions are a metaphor for their rocky relationship, it's only natural that we get a few of these, including:
    Mr. Smith: I don't exactly keep count, but I would say... high fifties, low sixties. Been around the block, but you know, the important thing is—
    Mrs. Smith: Three hundred and twelve.
    Mr. Smith: Three hundred and twelve? How?
    Mrs. Smith: Some were two at a time.
  • Certain cuts of the film have John's line, "Are you counting innocent bystanders?" (followed by Jane smacking the mesh barrier between them), partly because people thought they really were talking about sexual partners.

tropes.name: The Easy Way or the Hard Way
tropes.html:
After kidnapping "The Tank", Mr. Smith offers him a choice between three possibilities: A) The Tank tells the Smiths what they want to know, B) Mr. Smith inflicts Fingore on The Tank to get him to spill the beans, or C) The Tank suffers an unspecified Cruel and Unusual Death. As The Tank has no stake in the plot against the Smiths, he chooses option "A".
John Smith: [to Benjamin Danz] Option A: You talk, we listen, no pain. Option B: You don't talk, I remove your thumbs with my pliers, it will hurt. Option C: I like to vary the details a bit but the punchline is... you die.

tropes.name: The Elevator from Ipanema
tropes.html: Twice during the climactic shootout. First they escape an army of assassins by jumping in an elevator and heading to the second floor. They are greeted by the other half of the army of assassins and retreat back to the first floor. Both times we get a cheerful instrumental of "Girl from Ipanema".

tropes.name: Empathic Environment
tropes.html: Thunder sounds when things start heating up between John and Jane during their Mating Dance in Bogota.

tropes.name: Extended Disarming
tropes.html: While doing the tango, John and Jane remove guns and knives from each other's body.

tropes.name: Fanservice
