tropes.html: When you have two people who are consistently voted the two most attractive people in the world, it's inevitable. In the third quarter of the film. Jane is wearing a man's oxford that just barely functions as a miniskirt. John is in nothing but a tight V-neck and boxers.

tropes.name: Fun T-Shirt
tropes.html: "The Tank" is seen wearing a Fight Club T-Shirt, as Actor Allusion.

tropes.name: Fun with Subtitles
tropes.html: "Five or six years ago..."

tropes.name: Good Cop/Bad Cop
tropes.html: During the interrogation scene with the Tank, but they both try to play the bad cop. It works, but only because they're obviously enjoying one another's violence (despite the ongoing negotiations of their evolving relationship) and the Tank was just a plant and has no reason to lie once he's stalled long enough.

tropes.name: Hand Signals
tropes.html: Spoofed when John and Jane start using them to squabble with each other.

tropes.name: Happily Married
tropes.html: Happily Married. It's zigzagged, as back when they first get married, they are in newlywed bliss, and then their double-lives cause them to have marriage trouble, to the point where they are trying to kill each other while they are dancing (the tango, incidentally). After they deal with their double lives, they become this once more.

tropes.name: Hidden Supplies
tropes.html: Both of the Smiths have their own weaponry cache in their shared home. Fitting with their cover as the stereotypical Manly Man and Girly Girl, John's is under the shed and Jane's is in the oven ("I've never cooked a day in my life, sweetie.").

tropes.name: Hitman with a Heart
tropes.html: Though they don't have problems killing their targets or other professionals (guards and soforth), they do seem to try and avoid innocent casualties. John even takes the time to shout warnings and get civilians to run away when he's just ditched a bomb. During the fair scene, John casually hands one of the stuffed toys they won to a little kid.

tropes.name: Hoist by Their Own Petard
tropes.html: The agents sent to eliminate the Smiths used a drone to drop a bomb on them in the basement, which rolled onto the fuel tanks, causing the entire house to blow up. This ends up costing the agents their lives and allowing the couple to get away.

tropes.name: I Need a Freaking Drink
tropes.html: After the Internal Reveal, John and Jane both go to have a drink with their co-worker confidantes.

tropes.name: Imperial Stormtrooper Marksmanship Academy
tropes.html: In the final scene, a large group of "highly trained assassins" are unable to take down the protagonist duo despite having them outnumbered. There's bullet dodging involved but there's a lot of bullets where they don't need to.

tropes.name: In Love with the Mark
tropes.html: An odd variant, as they don't rekindle their romance until after they learn they're each other's targets. And have a massive fight about it.

tropes.name: Indy Ploy
tropes.html: John, in general, is much more prone to improvisation, contrasting with Jane who prefers to plan assignments down to the last detail. Both are extremely capable.

tropes.name: Informed Judaism
tropes.html: John and Jane are trading details about their real backgrounds. After a fight scene with mooks hired to take them out, Jane informs him she's Jewish.

tropes.name: Internal Reveal
tropes.html: Both of them find out the other's identity when they are assigned to take out the same target, but neither knows that the other knows. John deliberately drops a wine bottle as a test, which Jane passes (or fails depending on your perspective) when she catches it.

tropes.name: Interrupted Intimacy
tropes.html: Their bout of Destructo-Nookie is interrupted by their neighbours... who bring the police.

tropes.name: Ironic Nickname
tropes.html: The Smiths both pursue a mark known as "The Tank"; when they find him, he turns out to be a slender, slightly nerdy-looking individual played by Adam Brody.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html: To live with their covers, John plays the role of a Manly Man who loves poker and spends his time puttering around in the shed, while Jane plays the Girly Girl housewife who is obsessed with curtains and furniture. In reality, he's the sensitive boy and an art history major while she's the aggressive go-getter with a much higher body count. To play with this even further, in their careers, they play the roles straight. John is a go-it-alone type whose cover is construction work and where he hangs out with his loser womanizing best friend, while Jane works with a team (all women) who provide her intelligence and keep her sharp in the field (white collar women tend to form tight-knit bands, where men stereotypically work alone, shout, and throw things).

tropes.name: Kiss-Kiss-Slap
tropes.html: The beginning portion of the film shows Jane and John sharing a steamy kiss when they first meet and cuts it to the present where they're in a dead marriage. When they are assigned to killing each other, the kisses officially stop and the slapping commences. Then they rekindle the passion and it turns into Slap-Slap-Kiss.

tropes.name: Latin Land
tropes.html: The Smiths first met in Bogota (In Name Only).

tropes.name: Let's Dance
tropes.html:
The film plays this three times.
  • In the first act, when they meet in Bogota, they get a little dancing in to Mondo Bongo before hooking up and falling in love.
  • In the second act, they do a sexy tango to disarm one another in full view of the public so neither can turn on the other.
  • In the third act, they reprise their Mondo Bongo dance, only this time they're Back-to-Back Badasses (and sometimes Front to Front) while they take down an army of assassins.

tropes.name: Leaning on the Fourth Wall
tropes.html:
• During their tango/mutual patdown in the hotel, when Jane drops to her knees in front of John, he winks broadly, seemingly at the camera. The camera then reverses to show he's actually winking at an older couple who are dancing nearby, shocked at their aggressive sexuality (and the gun Jane takes out of John's ankle holster and throws across the room).
  • When Jane's second-in-command tells her "this is as far as we go," she ain't kidding. That is the last time we see her or any of her subordinates in the movie. Unintentional, to be sure, but still.

tropes.name: Lipstick Mark
tropes.html: Not exactly. In one scene, John comes home, slips on his wedding ring, and looks at a red stain on his collar. Suffice it to say, he wasn't having an affair, and the red stain was bit more organic in nature than lipstick.

tropes.name: Living with the Villain
tropes.html: Both characters put up a front of normal life for each other while they go about their real jobs as assassins working for rival firms — until they're both given assignments that lead to their paths crossing.

tropes.name: Lodged Blade Removal
tropes.html: Played for laughs. During the climactic battle, Jane accidentally (or possibly accidentally on purpose) hits John in the leg with a thrown kitchen knife. He barely reacts, except to be clearly frustrated with her, and pulls it out saying "We'll talk about this later!"

tropes.name: Made of Iron
tropes.html: Both the Smiths - both walk off bullet impacts (through bulletproof vests) without much trouble, plus all the damage they do to each other, and neither seems to mind walking across shattered glass barefoot the next morning.

tropes.name: Masculine Girl, Feminine Boy
tropes.html: The film zigzags this. In their professional lives, John follows the masculine business stereotype of being a lone wolf while Jane follows the feminine business stereotype of organizing a competent team to support her in the field. Initially, during the masquerade, they also play stereotypical roles at home, with Jane as the wife who cooks dinner every night (she never cooked a night in her life) and cares about window treatments and John as the bored husband who spends his time on game nights and puttering around in the shed (she keeps her weapons in the stove that never gets used and he keeps his under the shed). When the masks come off, it turns out that he was an art history major who loves sappy romantic ballads and recognized her father (her fake father) from Fantasy Island, and she's the aggressive, Violently Protective Girlfriend Green-Eyed Monster who has a much higher body count than him and has to be talked down from killing his ex-wife (it was a drunken Vegas thing).

tropes.name: The Masochism Tango
tropes.html: They spend the entire middle section of the film trying to kill each other once they realize that they are rival assassins with missions to kill one another. This leads to a Brutal Brawl in their home with them finding they are equally matched. And it ends because they both realize that they can't pull the trigger on each other. This is even lampshaded because the pair falls in love dancing a tango at the start of the film, they disarm each other in public mixing in some light jabs at on another at the halfway point, and the song that played during their first tango plays again when they get to the kissing part of Slap-Slap-Kiss.

tropes.name: The Masquerade Will Kill Your Dating Life
tropes.html: Or rather, smother your marriage. Learning the other's identity starts the process for their relationship renewal.

tropes.name: Matching Bad Guy Vehicles
tropes.html: While driving on the freeway, John notices a black car following them. After a moment, four more cars appear from behind the first one, now forming a V.

tropes.name: Mating Dance
tropes.html: The tango scene after the two use each other as cover to avoid suspicion from the Colombian military. Considering the Romance on the Set that ensued between the respective actors, this one probably carries a lot of Reality Subtext.

tropes.name: Men Are Tough
tropes.html: Implied along with Women Are Wiser in the differences between Jane and John's offices. Jane's office is high tech, sleek, equipped with body scanners and an underground secret base located in downtown Manhattan. John's on the other hand, is on the waterfront in a run down building and his main hub are two elderly people and a computer. This may only be part of the camouflage, however.

tropes.name: Metaphorically True
tropes.html: When Jane asks how John's poker game went, he responds "I got lucky." Not that he was lucky in the card game, but that he assassinated his target "Lucky".

tropes.name: The Mountains of Illinois
tropes.html: Inverted with the depiction of Bogotá (see "Artistic License — Geography" above). More to the point, Bogotá is shoehorned into a valley in the middle of the Andes, with downtown at 8660 ft/2640 m elevation. This◊ is what Bogotá really looks like.

tropes.name: Mr. Smith
tropes.html: Once, and only once, is "John Smith" lampshaded; when Jane orders her agency to search the databases. Her second-in-command points out that it's the one of, if not THE, most common male names in English.

tropes.name: Mundane Utility
tropes.html:
One of the early hints at Jane's secret life comes when she fixes the way a curtain is hanging by balancing perfectly on a chair that is standing on only one of its legs. In stilettos.
  • At the same time, in the yard, John offhandedly sinks a no-look basket at long range, implying he has some skills, too.

tropes.name: Murder, Inc.
tropes.html: Both the Smiths secretly work for seperate assassination firms.

tropes.name: Mutual Masquerade
tropes.html: Neither John nor Jane know that the other is secretly an assassin.

tropes.name: Mysterious Employer
tropes.html: Both Smiths work for agencies, but those agencies and their goals are completely unspecified.

tropes.name: Naked People Are Funny
tropes.html: Though Jane is wearing a Modesty Bedsheet after the neighbors show up to complain about the noise, it's implied that John proudly answers the door with his junk on full display, if partly to confound said neighbors and get them to go away with no more questions asked.

tropes.name: Neck Snap
tropes.html: Jane's first onscreen kill is to break a man's neck while pretending to be a prostitute.

tropes.name: Noodle Incident
tropes.html:
• Whatever it was that happened in Canada.
    Jane: That was you?
  • This is used for most every instance of them talking about a past job. What job did Jane take that saw the use of percussion grenades? Where was John that made taking a chopper the only, or the fastest, way of getting to their anniversary dinner on time? Who was Jean-Luc Gaspard that Jane was so jealous of John's elimination of him? We are never told.

tropes.name: Not Staying for Breakfast
tropes.html: Subverted. In Colombia after they first meet, Jane wakes up to find John gone. He then walks into the room carrying breakfast. Then they get back to the passionate sex and drop their breakfast on the floor.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
John chases a lead on the mystery hitwoman who left a laptop in the desert, managing to get a billing address for it. He freaks out when discovering that it's the IT company Jane's the CEO of.
John: Holy Mary Mother of God.

tropes.name: Orgasmic Combat
tropes.html: The Destructo-Nookie scene above does start with them in a knock down drag out fight with each other, destroying most of their home, but ends with them making out in the wreckage.

tropes.name: Outside Ride
tropes.html: After she tries to run him over, John gets an extended one on Jane's car.

tropes.name: Paid-for Family
tropes.html:
Jane's parents are not her real parents. She hires actors for occasions like the wedding and vacations.
Jane Smith: [driving a stolen minivan] My parents died when I was five. I'm an orphan.
John Smith: Who was that kind fellow who gave you away at our wedding?
Jane Smith: Paid actor.
John Smith: I said— I said I saw your dad on "Fantasy Island"!

tropes.name: Playing Drunk
tropes.html: In the scene where we see John "at work," he pretends to be drunk and wanders into a room full of targets, asking for a round of poker. He sits down and plays cards with them, tricking them into letting their guards down and eventually shooting them all dead.

tropes.name: Police Are Useless
tropes.html: Subverted. John and Jane's Destructo-Nookie, which started as a genuine full-blown shootout, causes the police to be called. But when they answer the door naked and obviously satisfied, the situation is defused.

tropes.name: Poor Communication Kills
tropes.html: Justified in that they are both trying to hide their double lives as assassins from what they believe to be their normie spouse. That said, doing so almost ends up with both of them killing each other.

tropes.name: Powerful People Are Subs
tropes.html: Jane disguises herself as a dominatrix to get close to a mob boss. He likes it when she ties him up and whips him, not so much when she breaks his neck and escapes out the window.

tropes.name: Pre-Mortem One-Liner
tropes.html:
Both of John and Jane's first onscreen kills included giving a parting word to their targets.
  • When Lucky comes back to the poker game John joined, he asks if John's looking for a job. John responds, "You are the job," before shooting him with a hidden pistol then opening fire on the other gangsters.
  • While playing the part of a Dominatrix and asking if her client's been bad, she leans in close and asks in a whisper, "Have you been selling big guns to bad men?" The target can only grunt in confusion before Jane snaps his neck.

tropes.name: Professional Killer
tropes.html: The true occupation of the Smiths is to take out hits on other people.

tropes.name: Properly Paranoid
tropes.html: Both the Smiths have taken extreme precautions for just about any scenario... except realizing their spouse is a rival agent. Even then, many of the precautions come in handy. John can't even be voice-traced from the answering machine message because he's made sure to include electronic distortion as if it were malfunctioning.

tropes.name: Punch-Clock Villain
tropes.html: Both of them are professional killers, but it's only their job. Their civilian covers are perfectly sociable.

tropes.name: Race Against the Clock
tropes.html: They get 48 hours to kill their spouse. Eventually they chose not to.

tropes.name: Red Oni, Blue Oni
tropes.html: Not immediately obvious, because both John and Jane are action protagonists; however when you look at their approaches, both to their job and their life, John is the 'Red' - he tends to make things up as he goes along, knows roughly how many people he has killed, where as Jane plans things, and knows EXACTLY how many people she has killed. See also the entry below for Uptight Loves Wild.

tropes.name: Relationship Reboot
tropes.html: Invoked by John once they decide not to kill each other and start telling the truth to one another: "We're going to have to redo every conversation we've ever had." (Note, again, Masculine Girl, Feminine Boy. John is the one who wants to dig in on the emotional stuff while Jane has to have it dragged out of her.)

tropes.name: Resignations Not Accepted
tropes.html: Neither of them are allowed to quit their assassin job.

tropes.name: Revealing Skill
tropes.html: Jane confirms John's suspicions that she's an assassin by catching an open wine bottle with far better reflexes and coordination than an average house-wife.

tropes.name: Scar Survey
tropes.html: Discussed rather than seen. The morning after their Destructo-Nookie, John and Jane are talking about past hits, and the permanent injuries they have as a result.

tropes.name: Shady Lady of the Night
tropes.html: Early in the film, Jane Smith disguises herself as a hired dominatrix in order to get close enough to a mob boss she's been hired to assassinate.

tropes.name: Shaking Her Hair Loose
tropes.html: Jane goes to see a mark pretending to be a prostitute with her hair pinned up. The first part of the seduction is shaking her hair out.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: Jane works with a team of Action Girls, including Stephanie March, Jennifer Morrison, and Kerry Washington, and her boss is a disembodied voice from a speaker.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html: When they fight, Jane is much more prone to using improvised weapons to bridge the physical gap between her and John. Female aggressors with male victims are much more likely to use weapons in domestic violence incidents for exactly that reason. It's also exactly what someone with Jane's build should do in a real fight against someone bigger.

tropes.name: Single Tear
tropes.html: After Jane thinks she's killed her husband with an Elevator Failure.

tropes.name: Slap-Slap-Kiss
tropes.html: Or more truthfully Bang Bang "Bang" as they abruptly end their Brutal Brawl to have sex once they realize they really do love each other.

tropes.name: Smithical Marriage
tropes.html: When they first meet, John and Jane hook up with each other, pretending to be a couple to escape the Colombian authorities. However, they don't register under Smith, which is a pity.

tropes.name: So Much for Stealth
tropes.html:
• John and Jane managed to silently take down several mooks, only for John to knock over a stack of cans. Cue autofire.
  • John is sneaking through the house, knocks over a china vase which he catches in mid-air... only for the lid to fall off and smash on the floor. Jane opens up on the noise.

tropes.name: Stealth Pun
tropes.html:
After failing to take the other out.
John: I missed you.
Jane: I missed you too.

tropes.name: Soundtrack Dissonance
tropes.html: Mondo Bongo (the song playing during the Dance of Romance in Bogota) plays during the final shootout. Still though, they're falling in love all over again and while they might be dodging bullets instead of exchanging glances, they are dancing.

tropes.name: Spanner in the Works
tropes.html: Jane and John having the same target, "the Tank", lead to them ruining each other's attempt to eliminate "the Tank" before he can be safely be transferred in his new prison, with Jane shooting and injuring John, to which he retaliates by shooting her hideout with his rocket launcher, which also ruins her explosive trap as the car n which "the Tank" is held is spared by the detonation. This fiasco is what leads to them discovering each other's secret and targeting each other.

tropes.name: Stocking Filler
tropes.html: Jane wears garters for one of her jobs. With knives.

tropes.name: Stripping the Scarecrow
tropes.html: John and Jane Smith, cornered in a home decorating store in their casual clothes, with mercenaries outside surrounding them, decides to strip two mannequins for better clothing. Without knocking them over, in the next shot we see John and Jane Smith smartly-dressed and two naked mannequins in the background.

tropes.name: Super Multi-Purpose Room
tropes.html: John and Jane both have a Wall of Weapons - his under the shed, hers inside the oven.

tropes.name: Table Space
tropes.html: Not quite super long but otherwise there. John has to get up and walk across the dining room to drop the bottle, forcing Jane to catch it and reveal the charade.

tropes.name: Tampering with Food and Drink
tropes.html: Suspecting John to being a spy, Jane is home early and prepares a dinner for "a special occasion". John picks up on this when he sees the Drano cleanser where the martini shaker was and dumps his drink into a potted plant to avoid poisoning. He then notices a poison label in the kitchen mirror's reflections as he takes a nervous bite of his pot roast.

tropes.name: Technician vs. Performer
tropes.html: Jane is a no-nonsense perfectionist with a whole team of operatives to coordinate her hits, John relies more on Indy Ploy and works alone outside of getting his materials from his "coworkers". Jane is stealthy in her job and kills no more than necessary, John makes a bit of a show and will readily take out three more guys who happen to be guarding his target.

tropes.name: That Poor Cat
tropes.html: Heard when John is rushing through the bushes to the house.

tropes.name: That Poor Plant
tropes.html: On the receiving end of a suspected drain cleaner-laced martini.

tropes.name: This Is Gonna Suck
tropes.html: When sneaking through the house, John accidentally bumps a ceramic jar with his elbow. He manages to catch it just before it falls... and then the lid falls off the jar and shatters on the floor. His face a split second before the crash just screams this, as he knows that the noise is going to tip off his whereabouts to Jane.

tropes.name: Tuxedo and Martini
tropes.html: Jane's agency is full of flashy technology and attractive women. John is more of the "Stale Beer and T-Shirt" variety of spy. This is reflected in everything they do. Jane's away-from-home workspace is in an upscale office building, while John's is a little back-room upstairs office. Her weaponry is behind an elaborate slide-away oven; John's is in a cellar under the toolshed. She sets up with a top-of-the-line sniping rifle and sighting equipment, while he pretends to be a scruffy nobody taking a piss and tries to take out the target with a rocket launcher. On the other hand, John identifies Jane by recovering her laptop and tracing one of the chips, like a proper hi-tech spy, while Jane does it by seeing John's walk and identifying him by instinct, just using her gut.

tropes.name: Uptight Loves Wild
tropes.html: Mrs. Smith meticulously plans everything out and Mr. Smith prefers just to wing it. He complains that "There's no air around you! Everything has to be controlled!" while she hates his improvisation... until they come to the final fight and go into a perfect flow state where they, apparently, kill everyone they ever worked with.

tropes.name: Use Your Head
tropes.html: During the fight with her husband, Jane responds to John's taunting by hitting him with a teapot and headbutting him.

tropes.name: Villain Protagonist
tropes.html: A double-dose, as both John and Jane are assassins for hire. The entire conflict comes about because their employers are competitors, rather than either of them being anything like traditional good guys.

tropes.name: Violently Protective Girlfriend
tropes.html:
Violently Protective Girlfriend : By the end of the movie, Jane has become this.
Jane: What's her name and Social Security Number?!

tropes.name: The Voice
tropes.html: We never see the faces of either Jane's or John's boss, just a digitized distorted face, making both of them this.

tropes.name: Was It All a Lie?
tropes.html:
Both John and Jane suspect the other of lying about their love for each other, but neither is willing to admit their own in case the other uses this to try and kill them.
Mr. Smith: Web of lies!

tropes.name: Why Am I Ticking?
tropes.html:
John gets a bomb placed in his jacket.
Bystander: Do you know you're ticking?

tropes.name: Win Her a Prize
tropes.html: Invoked: John and Jane, two of the world's best assassins, visit a fair for a date, where they each try their hand at a shooting gallery. All of Jane's shots are off-target, and John can't resist the urge to show off a little, hitting every target but one (presumably remembering not to blow his cover just in time). He attributes his success to beginner's luck. Then Jane gets her back up and buys another go-round, hitting every target with ease, also claiming "beginner's luck."

tropes.name: With Catlike Tread
tropes.html:
While sneaking around during the final battle, John takes out several opponents without making a sound... until he turns around and knocks over a stand of cans with the barrel of his shotgun.
  • During the fight in the house, he manages to sneak around without getting seen, until he knocks over a vase. Even then, he manages to catch it... only for the lid to fall off and shatter on the floor, giving away his location.

tropes.name: Women Are Wiser
tropes.html: Implied, with Jane's organization seeming bigger, better-funded and more professional than John's, and Jane having a much higher bodycount than her husband. In terms of their methods, this overlaps with Uptight Loves Wild, with Jane carefully planning her assassinations and John preferring the Indy Ploy.

tropes.name: Would Hit a Girl
tropes.html: John is more than willing to punch his wife (among other things) when he finds out she's a rival assassin. This is a rare instance in which the male character is not called out, likely because his wife gives as good as she gets.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html:
• One of the more prominently featured artifacts that Jack collects is a set of aviator shades - perhaps previously owned by a certain naval aviator?
  • He enters an underground base suspended on a cable.
  • Another of his treasured artifacts is a faded New York Yankees ballcap, like the one Tom Cruise wore in the first half of War of the Worlds (2005).
  • Jack is at one point covered in ash, after witnessing an alien device vaporize someone in front of him.

tropes.name: Aerial Canyon Chase
tropes.html: A high-speed canyon chase ensues between Harper and three drones after he stops being loyal to Sally.

tropes.name: After the End
tropes.html: The primary setting is Earth after it was devastated by an interstellar war.

tropes.name: Alien Abduction
tropes.html: What happened to the real Jack and Victoria. It was Harper's decision to uncouple the piloting section from the crew section as it was being swallowed by the Tet that prevented the rest of the Odyssey's crew from becoming clones.

tropes.name: Alien Invasion
tropes.html: By a race referred to as "Scavengers," or "Scavs" for short. The setting is in the aftermath, about 60 years afterwards, and The Remnant haunt the Earth's underground. Or so Jack believes. Turns out, the Alien Invasion was actually by the Tet, a gigantic autonomous AI, and the Scavengers are the human resistance.

tropes.name: Alien Sky
tropes.html: The wreckage of the destroyed Moon.

tropes.name: And Starring
tropes.html: "And Melissa Leo." note as Sally

tropes.name: Apocalyptic Log
tropes.html: The flight recorder playback of the Odyssey.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html:
• The poem that Jack reads in the library ("Horatius at the Bridge" by Thomas Babington Macaulay) is quoted several times and is directly relevant to the plot:
    And how can man die better than facing fearful odds,
    For the ashes of his fathers, and the temples of his Gods?
  • Also, "effective team." If they stop being an effective team, Jack and Victoria are killed and replaced.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: "Are you an effective team?" Sally's cheerful sign-off to Jack and Vika at the start of each day, meant as an affirmation of their loyalty to the mission. It resurfaces throughout the film in increasingly pointed ways, culminating in a Meaningful Echo when Jack flies the payload into the Tet at the climax, coolly announcing "We are a more effective team".

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html:
• The Moon is still in several large pieces that haven't orbited each other nor fallen back together after 60 years.
  • The buildings of Manhattan are buried under an improbable amount of dirt, and probably couldn't take the weight of that much dirt on top of, around and on their sides without being in much worse shape. Tsunamis and earthquakes are mentioned, but they would probably have destroyed the buildings rather than just buried them all. However this all makes for some stunning, beautiful visuals.
  • The Tet appears to be in an orbit around Earth that is at most a couple of hundred kilometers high, yet it appears to lose line of sight (and communication) with Tower 49 for around 12 hours each night. Such a low orbit would normally mean that the Tet would orbit Earth within a much shorter time, meaning it might be offline for less than an hour before rising above the horizon again note  The International Space Station orbits Earth in about 90 minutes and is 400 kilometers high . The 12-hour orbital period shown in the movie would correspond to a much higher orbit of several tens of thousands of kilometers.
  • Put a Cool Bike on its twin stands, pull a winch cable out of the front, rappel down into a building. How does that work? It seems unlikely that the bike would be heavy enough or anchored well enough by the two stands to hold Jack up, especially with the acrobatics he goes through on the end of that line.

tropes.name: Ascetic Aesthetic
tropes.html: How the Tet and anything related to it (the Towers, the suits, the drones, the firearms) is represented. Borders Everything Is an iPod in the Future in some places (like the Towers' communication consoles).

tropes.name: Award-Bait Song
tropes.html: Oblivion

tropes.name: Babies Ever After
tropes.html: The movie's epilogue which shows Julia tending the garden at Jack-49's secret cottage with a three year-old girl which is most definitely his.

tropes.name: "Back to Camera" Pose
tropes.html: The film shows the protagonist atop a rocky mound in a post-apocalyptic New York, looking up at a waterfall cascading off the Empire State Building.

tropes.name: Belly-Scraping Flight
tropes.html: Happens a few times to Jack's aircraft, sometimes with its belly scraping the side of a canyon because it's capable of flying in several different orientations.

tropes.name: Big Applesauce
tropes.html: The movie happens in a virtually unrecognizable New York State. What remains of the Empire State Building is a plot-important location.

tropes.name: Big Damn Heroes
tropes.html:
• The drone coming to Jack's rescue during the Scavs' ambush on the remains of the New York Public Library, and the drones sent to intimidate the Scavengers when they capture Jack and Julia. Although considering The Reveal that follows, they could be considered more of a Villainous Rescue in action.
  • When the unarmored drone being repaired in Tower 49 is reactivated it immediately kills Victoria and is getting ready to shoot Jack, but in the nick of time Julia saves him by blowing away the drone with the Bubble Ship's guns.
  • During the final shootout between the drones and the Scavengers on the bunker, one of the drones is about to shoot Julia and some human civilians. Julia picks up a gun and shoots the drone ineffectively... but is enough of a diversion for Sykes to be able to shoot it in the back with no problem. Beech also mans a turret and shoots it out with one of the drones, destroying it although he ends up injured because of it.
  • A swarm of drones swoop down to finish off La Résistance. Sykes and Kara order everyone inside while they make a clearly suicidal attempt to hold them off. Fortunately they're a Keystone Army and fall out of the sky the moment the Tet is destroyed.

tropes.name: Billed Above the Title
tropes.html: Downplayed. The movie poster has Tom Cruise's name appear in small letters right above the title.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: The Earth is finally saved from the Tet after 60 years of a war that humanity pretty much lost, and that which remains of humanity finally will have a chance to rebuild. All that it cost were the lives of the Drone Tech 49 clone of Jack Harper and Malcolm Beech. Julia has a daughter and the 52nd Drone Tech clone of Harper has finally found her after looking for her for three years.

tropes.name: Blind Alley
tropes.html: During the Aerial Canyon Chase, with three drones closing in, Jack veers sideways and ducks his Bubbleship behind a waterfall, cutting his engine signature and visual profile completely. The drones blast past without registering him, buying him the moment he needs to regroup and get behind them.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: Jack finishes his Opening Monologue with "I can't shake the feeling that Earth is still my home". The last scene of the movie has Jack closing with "And I am home".

tropes.name: Bulletproof Vest
tropes.html: The suit Jack wears for most of the movie is a pretty effective Space Clothes kind of armor. We see how effective it is when Sergeant Sykes shoots him in the chest during the interrogation scene. At the least, it can take 9mm rounds with nothing to show for it but one hell of a scare.

tropes.name: The Cake Is a Lie
tropes.html: "There is no Titan".

tropes.name: Catapult Nightmare
tropes.html: Jack awakes this way from another dream of Julia at the lake, at the moment when she calls out for him.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Boomerang
tropes.html: The fact that drone fuel cells are pretty devastating when they go off comes to bite both sides of the conflict in the ass a few times.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
Lots of them:
  • The Logo Joke shows the Tet and the Odyssey, the latter being easy to miss. Repeated reminders about the Tet's blind spot make this especially relevant later in the film.
  • Jack's Recurring Dreams about a viewfinder on the Empire State Building. It's where the original Jack Harper proposed marriage to Julia.
  • The picture of Jack and Vika in the apartment. It's the picture Victoria took in the Odyssey just before arriving at the Tet.
  • The fact that the Scavs aka La Résistance have been stealing drone fuel cells.
  • The fact that lightning strikes force electronics (such as the Bubble Ship's and the drones') to reboot if struck while flying.
  • The constant reminding to Mission Control to please send parts and armor to repair the drone on Tower 49, which Sally keeps disregarding. Julia's Big Damn Heroes moment later on is also a good example of Worf Had the Flu because of it.
  • The missing drone mentioned at the beginning. It was captured by La Résistance, but it's intended use to carry a nuke to the Tet ends up sadly subverted.
  • The Bubble Ship and the drones using voice recognition to identify Jack. The latter comes in use when Jack first rescues Julia from the crashed Odyssey (since they're programmed to not shoot him). As for the former... as Jack discovers, all that it's necessary to use another clone's ship is to change the Tech operator number you say for ID, which comes in handy because he needs to use it to save Julia's life after she's accidentally shot.
  • The Odyssey's flight recorder. And its nuclear reactor core.
  • The Scav communications equipment that Jack deactivates on the ruins of the Empire State Building. And the building itself.
  • The fact that the drones can track Jack's DNA comes back to bite the ass of the Scavs during the final act.
  • When Jack first reports about finding Julia to Mission Control, Sally says there is a great deal of interest up there in bringing her up to the Tet. During the Trojan Prisoner gambit, Jack mentions this back to Sally to be allowed into the ship.
  • When Jack first starts checking the wreckage of the crashed Odyssey, he opens a Human Popsicle capsule which is empty, and when the Scavs arrive, you can see them taking that capsule. It becomes pretty important later on as it is the capsule Julia goes into thinking that she and Jack will do the Trojan Prisoner gambit and Jack then transports to his cabin, where she will be safe. The capsule is labeled "J. Harper"—it belonged to her (real) husband.
  • A minor one: when Jack first disables the communications equipment in the Empire State, he takes a gorilla plushie that was on the room and puts it among his collection of scavenged stuff. He remembers seeing the child who dropped it later. Also, Julia's child is seen playing with it in the movie's epilogue.
  • When Jack first checks up on the downed Drone 166 in the opening scenes, he affixes the loose fuel cell to the frame with chewing gum because he doesn't have the proper tools with him to do a better job. When Drone 166 comes back online after his fight with Jack 52, he reaches into the open hatch and is able to yank the fuel cell out quickly and easily because it was just chewing gum holding it in.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html:
• The deactivated drone that is being repaired on Tower 49.
  • Jack Harper. Clone Number 52, to be specific. Shaken after encountering Jack 49 and Julia, he seeks her out after encountering the survivors.
  • Drone 166, which Jack goes out to fix in a routine job during the expository opening scenes. It comes back to "save" him from the Scav ambush at the buried NY City Library, it arrives at the Odyssey crash site to dispose of survivors, and then it becomes the lead drone and most persistent foe chasing after Jack when he escapes with Julia.

tropes.name: *Click* Hello
tropes.html: When Jack and Julia return to Malcolm Beech's underground base, they are welcomed not with words but with the sound of Sykes racking his weapon behind them.

tropes.name: Clone Army
tropes.html:
The Tet cloned an army of astronaut Jack Harper to conquer earth, then switched to drones and had the Jacks maintain them.
  • It's left unexplained why Tet would send out Harper clones instead of the superior Attack Drones to fight the human forces, though given how often the coversations between Vika and Sally concern a lack of spare parts for the drones and the unacceptability of losing one, it can be inferred the drones are either non-replaceable or at least much more resource-intensive than clones are.

tropes.name: Companion Cube
tropes.html: Harper's Bubble Ship has a bobble-head figurine glued to the instrument panel that Jack calls "Bob" and occasionally talks to. He makes a point of gluing it to his fellow clone's replacement Bubble Ship's dashboard after his first one gets wrecked.

tropes.name: Conveniently Timed Attack from Behind
tropes.html: When a drone has the surviving humans cornered at the underground base and is seconds away from wiping them all out, Sykes shoots it from behind at the last possible moment.

tropes.name: Cool Bike
tropes.html: Harper's motorcycle-which is collapsible so it can be carried on the Bubble Ship's storage space, has integral winch and sensors, and is pretty rugged. Pity that it gets stolen early in the movie, and then soon after Harper gets it back it runs out of gas.

tropes.name: Cool Mask
tropes.html: The Predator-style masks that the Scavs wear. Made of Stealth Bomber material (as well as the rest of their armor), with voice distortion, and very intimidating. It's no wonder they look like rampaging aliens during the first act.

tropes.name: Cool Plane
tropes.html: The "Bubble Ship" (see Future Copter below). Visually speaking, the drones, as well.

tropes.name: Cool Starship
tropes.html: The "Tet" space station, and the Odyssey (for how little time it appears on-screen, anycase)

tropes.name: Covers Always Lie
tropes.html: The page image poster shows a waterfall cascading down by the Empire State Building, but in the film it is buried up to the observation deck all around. Another poster shows the George Washington Bridge free and at an angle, while in the movie it is half-buried and standing straight.

tropes.name: Cryo Sickness
tropes.html: When Julia is woken from her cryogenic escape pod, the first thing she does is vomit. It also turns out she is dehydrated. She makes a full recovery from this state though.

tropes.name: Dark Is Not Evil
tropes.html:
• The evil-looking Scavengers all wear dark colors and live in dark underground areas, but are eventually revealed to be a human resistance force led by Malcolm Beech with noble goals.
  • The Tet is a pretty ominous-looking black obelisk in space, but Jack describes it as being something like a human Mission Control HQ. Jack's wrong. The Tet is monstrous.
  • At first, our hero Jack, Victoria, their home and all their equipment is pure white, establishing them as the good guys. As Jack continues his trip away from the evil side and towards the good, his white uniform becomes darker and closer to black. Notably, the Odyssey crew wear very dark gray uniforms which are nearly black. Also, the real Sally wears black, but when the Tet is impersonating her, it crops close to her face and doesn't show her black jacket.

tropes.name: Detonation Moon
tropes.html: A torn-apart moon is a constant sight during night sequences. Malcolm Beech reminisces when it was blown apart to cripple the human race pre-invasion.

tropes.name: Die Laughing
tropes.html: Combining the savoring of the imminent doom the Tet is facing and Jack's one last comment to Sally, Beech does this as the bomb lights off.

tropes.name: Doppelgänger Gets Same Sentiment
tropes.html: The epilogue reveals that Julia is settling into a life with another Jack clone, Jack 52, who tracked her down after three years. She recognizes him as the same man she loved — and he clearly feels the same pull toward her, having searched for the house Jack 49 had described building for her. For Julia, the soul is the same even if the body is a copy.

tropes.name: Double Meaning
tropes.html: When Vika is killed by the drone-in-maintenance, Mission Control absolves Jack from blame by telling him that drones are unreliable. She wasn't only referring to the robots.

tropes.name: Drone of Dread
tropes.html: The soundtrack makes use of the drone sounds.

tropes.name: Dying Moment of Awesome
tropes.html: Jack 49 and Malcolm Beech.

tropes.name: Earth-That-Was
tropes.html: Earth was nearly destroyed during a war against a race of alien invaders known as Scavengers. They were only defeated by the use of nuclear weapons, which left most of the planet irradiated and uninhabitable.

tropes.name: Everybody's Dead, Dave
tropes.html: The fate of the entire Odyssey crew except for Julia. Bonus whammy points for this information being given to her by a clone of her own husband.

tropes.name: Everything Is an iPod in the Future
tropes.html: The Bubble Ship in particular is a prime example, all sleek curves and shiny white surfaces.

tropes.name: Evil Cannot Comprehend Good
tropes.html: Inability to understand the human psyche is where the Tet's plan falls apart. It thought it could just stick a male and female together and have them be content. It thought just killing one that was being inconvenient (Viki 49) would be brushed off. It thought all humans would have an aversion to death. It thought that invoking godhood would deter defiance.

tropes.name: Exact Words
tropes.html: During his trip to Tet's core, Jack is stopped by a pair of drones, Sally having deduced that he has misled her about the nature of his return. Jack then replies quite honestly that he's returned because it's the only way humanity would survive. He just doesn't give her the specifics.

tropes.name: Expendable Clones
tropes.html: Jack and Victoria, given Victoria 49's fate.

tropes.name: Eye Lights Out
tropes.html: At the tower, the "death" of the drone that Julia is able to shoot down is signaled by its red light going out.

tropes.name: Fade to White
tropes.html: The abduction of Jack and Vika by the Tet sixty years earlier is shown as a brief flashback, ending on a blinding flash of white as the Tet takes them, leaving what actually happened to them — and how their identities were stripped away and replicated — entirely to the audience's imagination.

tropes.name: Failed Future Forecast
tropes.html: When Jack discovers the ruins of a stadium while repairing a drone, he recounts the story of the last Super Bowl ever played there, describing the winning team's comeback in vivid, almost reverent detail. The game is dated to 2017, by which point the film expected the New York Giants to be the champions. In reality, the 2017 Super Bowl was won by the New England Patriots.

tropes.name: The Film of the Book
tropes.html: Of a Graphic Novel, actually. It was begun by the film's director, as it happens. However, as of 2021 it still hasn't been finished or printed yet and most likely due to the movie's lukewarm reception (and that he intended it to be a movie rather than graphic novel in the first place), never will.

tropes.name: First Contact
tropes.html: The Odyssey mission was originally meant to be a manned mission to Titan, but was repurposed into this instead when they discovered an alien craft entering the solar system. To say that it Went Horribly Wrong is a massive understatement.

tropes.name: Flashback Cut
tropes.html: When Jack tracks a beacon signal to the ruins of the Empire State Building, the moment he steps onto the platform triggers a flash of his forbidden pre-wipe memories breaks through.

tropes.name: Flashback Effects
tropes.html: Jack's memories of Julia at New York City are depicted in black and white.

tropes.name: Forbidden Zone
tropes.html: The radiation areas.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
• Beech expresses the desire to see the look on the Tet's face when they detonate the bomb. He got his wish.
  • Jack's conversation with Victoria at the beginning about the last Super Bowl before the Alien Invasion (especially, that the last play on it was a "Hail Mary" pass) becomes pretty important later on in context (the plan regarding the Trojan Prisoner is a "Hail Mary" play).
  • The phrase about sacrifice Jack finds in a book sets up his final sacrifice.
  • Even the Logo Joke contains an example; while your attention might be captured more by the large pyramidal object orbiting the Earth and the obviously ruined and drained nature of the continents, if you look closely a tiny blip of light can be seen hovering around the word UNIVERSAL. It's the Odyssey, locked in orbit around Earth out of sight of the Tet.

tropes.name: Framed for Heroism
tropes.html: While investigating the library cave, Jack fires his handgun at an approaching enemy — and the target explodes in spectacular fashion completely disproportionate to a single pistol shot. Jack stares at his gun in genuine bewilderment before realizing the drone hovering behind him actually took the shot.

tropes.name: Future Copter
tropes.html: The VTOL craft that Jack flies around, the Bubble Ship. With guns (which can fire in any direction, even straight backwards), autopilot (and remote piloting), ejecting cockpit, voice-recognition lock, remotely-accessible surveillance cameras, storage space for a Cool Bike, and the capacity to fly up to space.

tropes.name: Genetic Memory
tropes.html: Within both Jack Harper 49 and 52, which causes the original to be, in a sense, "reincarnated" in both.

tropes.name: Genre Throwback
tropes.html: Joseph Kosinski's word is that it's meant to evoke sci fi movies of The '70s. What we see wouldn't be (that much) out of place in a Heavy Metal or Mœbius comic.

tropes.name: A God Am I
tropes.html: Though done more as a Badass Boast. When Jack quotes the line about "the temples of his Gods", the Tet replies: "I created you, Jack. I am your God."

tropes.name: Go for the Eye
tropes.html: Along with the engines, this is one of the few unshielded points on the drones.

tropes.name: Happy Flashback
tropes.html: Jack and Julia, before the war.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html: Jack 49 and Malcolm Beech.

tropes.name: Hero Stole My Bike
tropes.html: Harper got both ends of the trope. La Résistance steals his motorcycle after an attempted ambush on the beginning of the movie, and he steals the Bubble Ship of one of his fellow clones when his own gets wrecked near the end.

tropes.name: Homeworld Evacuation
tropes.html: The film has humanity attempting to escape a ruined Earth that has been wrecked during an Alien Invasion war, settling a new colony on Titan. Of course, this is a big damn lie, but saying any further details is a massive spoiler.

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: Jack and Julia return to the resistance base so Jack can reprogram the drone for an attack on the Tet. The drone is loaded on a vehicle and the doors are opened...just as three drones arrive outside and catch everyone not wearing their stealth gear. The reprogrammed drone is then destroyed in the subsequent shoot-out.

tropes.name: Hope Sprouts Eternal
tropes.html: At least one small valley within the area of the state of New York remained forested. Harper found it, and it's where he keeps his collection of scavenged memorabilia and a small cottage he built. Him trying to give Victoria a small plant (presumably from this place) and her casually throwing it away, justifying it as the plant possibly being contaminated with radiation, is another sign of Victoria's Stepford Smiler behavior.

tropes.name: Human Popsicle
tropes.html: Julia and the rest of the Odyssey crew.

tropes.name: Human Shield
tropes.html: The only reason Julia isn't killed on landing is that Jack physically stands between the drone and her pod. Without the ability to get orders from the Tet, the drone withdraws. It's this act that convinces Beech that Jack is more than just a clone.

tropes.name: I Just Shot Marvin in the Face
tropes.html: Dramatic example. During the fight between Jack-49 and Jack-52, they are struggling for a gun. The gun goes off, hitting Julia on the stomach. This prompts Jack to knock out his opponent who is understandably shocked to have shot the woman he's seen in his dreams and steal his ship to get to the Tower and retrieve medical equipment to save her.

tropes.name: "I Know You're in There Somewhere" Fight
tropes.html:
Basically what Beech tries on Jack after he sees him display curiosity (studying a book) and protectiveness/disobedience (protecting Julia's pod against the drone). We can assume from Sergeant Sykes' skepticism that this tactic has been tried before and failed — presumably without Julia's presence to awaken their memories and feelings other captured 'Jack' soldiers refused to accept the evidence, like Victoria when confronted with Jack's wife.
  • Of special note pointing out Beech's tactic. When he reveals the captured drone to Jack for the first time, Jack refuses to help. He has Jack shot (his spacesuit protects him from damage), to put him under stress and then has Julia brought out on her knees execution style with a gun put to her head. This incites a reaction from Jack. While at first this ruthlessness seems out of character, it's just Beech bluffing to intentionally stoke Jacks feelings and memories and set him on a path that will "bring him back"

tropes.name: Incendiary Exponent
tropes.html: The drone on Tower 49 right after it gets reactivated by the Tet and vaporizes Victoria 49 is briefly on fire for no reason other than looking pretty scary (and floating into the room through recently-shot curtains).

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html:
Between Mission Control and Victoria, Jack's partner.
Mission Control: Are you an effective team?
Victoria: We are an effective team.
(When Victoria betrays Jack)
Mission Control: Are you still an effective team?
Victoria: We are not an effective team.

tropes.name: I Want My Jetpack
tropes.html: By 2017 (a mere 4 years after the movie's release), we were supposed to have self-contained "delta sleep" capsules that allow humans to survive for up to 60 years in hibernation and all of the space hardware we need to send a manned mission to Titan. This did not happen.

tropes.name: Kill and Replace
tropes.html: Jack and Victoria were astronauts on a mission to Titan when Mission Control picked up the Tet and sent them to investigate. They were captured, cloned and probably killed. Then their clones were sent back to Earth to maintain equipment while the Tet drains the world of water to power itself.

tropes.name: Laser-Guided Amnesia
tropes.html: Jack and Vika have had their pre-war memories wiped, officially so they cannot be exploited by enemies if captured. The real reason is more straightforward — keeping them ignorant of the fact that they are clones prevents them from rebelling against the mission entirely.

tropes.name: Last Fertile Region
tropes.html: Jack has discovered a secluded valley with a lake where things can still be grown, a rare pocket of life in an otherwise devastated Earth. He keeps it secret, visiting on his own time and slowly furnishing it as a retreat from his assigned duties.

tropes.name: Last Kiss
tropes.html: Before placing Julia in the pod that will carry her up to the Tet, she and Jack share a quiet kiss goodbye.

tropes.name: Light Is Not Good
tropes.html: The white-suited humans in their clean, sterile towers. Sure, they're more-or-less good people, but they're unwittingly maintaining the Tet's ongoing obliteration of humanity. Similarly, the shiny, white, disturbingly Trigger-Happy Attack Drones.

tropes.name: Logo Joke
tropes.html: The Universal logo features Earth with coastlines consistent with much of the oceans being drained. It also shows the "Tet" space station floating over it, as well as the Odyssey, which is easier to miss. This becomes a plot point. Why doesn't the Tet already have Julia, if it wants her so badly? The Odyssey is in its blind spot!

tropes.name: Mars Needs Water
tropes.html: Humanity has rigs draining all of Earth's oceans to produce fusion energy in order to send the rest of humanity to Titan. Actually, the Tet itself is gathering it to finish off humanity and power its trip to another planet and begin again.

tropes.name: Meaningful Echo
tropes.html:
• Stanza XXVII of Horatius (The Lay). Gets used three times. First time is just a random passage of a book Jack scavenged that he reads aloud. The second time it's said by Malcolm Beech to tell Harper that he's different from the army of Harper clone soldiers that assisted in devastating the planet, since he has curiosity and they were 'soulless'. The third time is said by Harper right before his Heroic Sacrifice by setting off the nuke inside of the Tet.
"And how can man die better
than facing fearful odds
for the ashes of his fathers
and the temples of his gods."
  • When Jack flies the nuclear payload into the Tet at the climax, he coolly announces "We are a more effective team" — a direct callback to Sally's constant check-ins asking whether Jack and Vika are an "effective team", turned back on her in what are her final moments.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: The Odyssey is the name of an ancient greek poem which describes Odysseus' journey home from the Trojan war, during which he gets lost for 10 years. Similarly, the spaceship Odyssey returns to Earth after being lost in space for a long time.

tropes.name: Meaningful Rename
tropes.html: Julia Rusakova makes a point of presenting herself as Julia Harper when she and Jack go back to the bunker. When the Trojan Prisoner gambit is being worked on, she enters a capsule with a Meaningful Name on it. See Chekhov's Gun for details.

tropes.name: Mirror Match
tropes.html: A rare live-action version. Jack Harper-49 vs Jack Harper-52.

tropes.name: Monumental Damage
tropes.html: One of the first things we see during Jack's Opening Monologue is the Pentagon smashed almost beyond recognition by a huge crater. The New York Public Library is completely underground. The Empire State Building is buried up to its observation deck, leaving only the gift shop and the spire above ground. The Statue of Liberty is broken up and scattered, with the torch-holding hand visible during a high-speed canyon chase. The One World Trade Center building, taller than the ESB and prominent in the flashbacks, is nowhere to be seen in the present time, implying that whatever wasn't buried was demolished. Meanwhile, the majority of Washington has completely disappeared, replaced by a massive floodplain and a significantly wider Potomac River.

tropes.name: Monumental Damage Resistance
tropes.html: The Capitol Building and the Washington Monument are free and still standing, everything else is gone.

tropes.name: Morning Routine
tropes.html: Before the film's title card, we see Jack with Vika eating breakfast, exercising, and leaving for work in his bubble ship while his voice-over narrates the fall of humanity.

tropes.name: Mortal Wound Reveal
tropes.html: Non-lethal example. During the fight between Jack-49 and Jack-52, they are struggling for a gun and it goes off. Julia (and the audience) only notices that she is hit by discovering the blood on her hand several moments later.

tropes.name: Multinational Team
tropes.html: The NASA mission.

tropes.name: Murphy's Bullet
tropes.html: During the brutal hand-to-hand fight between Jack 49 and his clone Jack 52, a single shot is fired at close range — and finds Julia, who is standing well clear of the fight, hitting her in the gut.

tropes.name: Nipple and Dimed
tropes.html: The nude swimming scene, showing off pretty much everything they could of Andrea Riseborough and still have a PG-13 rating - including light shining through her thigh gap.

tropes.name: No Endor Holocaust
tropes.html:
The Tet is in low orbit and explodes in a giant explosion. No one is hurt.
  • Hell, the freaking Moon was destroyed before that! Whatever happened later, couldn't be much worse.

tropes.name: Nuke 'Em
tropes.html: The resistance sabotage a fusion reactor, and later the Tet.

tropes.name: Offhand Backhand
tropes.html: The Drones' weapons can turn independently of each other and the general facing of the drone. Several of these ensue whenever the drones fight.

tropes.name: Offscreen Airplane Pull-up
tropes.html: In an early mission, Jack's Bubbleship struggles and dives into a canyon and drops below the rim, vanishing from sight entirely. It looks for all the world like he just flew himself into the rock face, until the craft comes roaring back up out of the canyon in triumph.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
• When Jack is dropping down into the pit to get one of the drones, he finds out that the drone signal was fake and it was all a trap, he starts to escape successfully - and then the line snaps and he falls back into the pit.
  • Beech gives a small one when Julia Rusakova reintroduces herself as Julia Harper, revealing that she and the original Jack were secretly married, so Beech realizes that single factor might have been the only thing that made "bringing back" Commander Jack Harper at all possible.

tropes.name: One-Word Title
tropes.html: "Oblivion", meaning to be forgotten - as stated by Jack at the beginning, Jack and Victoria have chosen to forget the war so as not to interfere with his job. ...Or so he thinks.

tropes.name: Opening Monologue
tropes.html: Provided by Harper while we get brought up to speed on the characters and situation and see a montage of Scenery Porn (The skies and some parts of the planet that look less wasteland-y), Scenery Gorn (the shot of the bombed-out Pentagon - with implications of it having been ground zero for a nuclear strike during The War - and the remains of New York and Washington, DC), Technology Porn (Tower 49, the Bubble Ship, the collector vessels, the guns and the Tet), Fanservice (Shirtless Scene and Toplessness from the Back) and some Irony in that most of the info is unwitting bullcrap on Jack's part.

tropes.name: Our Weapons Will Be Boxy in the Future
tropes.html: Jack's rifle, and the guns on the drones and bubble ship too. Though not the human's weapons.

tropes.name: Outrun the Fireball
tropes.html: Happens to Jack during the final shootout with the drones inside of La Résistance's bunker - complete with visible Oh, Crap! moment as he starts to run away just before the explosion.

tropes.name: People Jars
tropes.html: Inside the Tet, Jack discovers row upon row of stasis pods, each one containing a floating clone of himself and Vika, suspended in fluid and kept in reserve for future deployment. It is the moment the full scale of what the Tet has done with them finally becomes undeniable.

tropes.name: Percussive Maintenance
tropes.html: Jack does this to make the Bubble Ship restart when it gets struck by lightning the first time.

tropes.name: Plummet Perspective
tropes.html: When Harper descents into the abandoned library, there is a huge chasm at the bottom which several objects fall into for effect.

tropes.name: Post-Apocalyptic Dog
tropes.html: Jack discovers a shaggy dog early on and almost shoots it by accident.

tropes.name: Posthumous Narration
tropes.html: Subverted. In the epilogue, we're initially made to think Jack's narration is this, but it turns out to be Jack 52 looking for Julia.

tropes.name: Precision F-Strike
tropes.html: Jack: Fuck you, Sally. *detonates fuel cells*

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html: A really bizarre example: in the final scene when the human survivors arrives to Jack's hidden valley, one of said survivors has a sweater with the Coca Cola logo printed on it and he spends a significant amount of time front and center amongst the crowd.

tropes.name: The Promised Land
tropes.html: Jack and Vika have been told that humanity has relocated to Titan and that they will join the colony there once their tour of duty ends. It is entirely fabricated — there is no colony, and the Tet has no intention of letting them go, and there are no survivors to join.

tropes.name: Pyrrhic Victory
tropes.html: It initially appears that the humans have defeated the aliens, but at the cost of the Earth. It's actually the opposite. The aliens have conquered the Earth, but they haven't yet managed to successfully wipe out the humans.

tropes.name: Ramming Always Works
tropes.html: While set on a much smaller scale, drone 166 does this to Jack 49's bubbleship a couple of times. The final time knocks him to go into the radiation zone.

tropes.name: Recurring Camera Shot
tropes.html: The scene where Jack finds Julia's sleeper pod, with her visible through the viewport while he looks down at her from the right with a hand on the pod, is mirrored later when he puts her back into it right before he flies up to the Tet.

tropes.name: Retirony
tropes.html: Throughout the movie, both Jack and Victoria mention that they had two weeks remaining on their mission before being sent to the Tet, where they would go with the rest of the human survivors to their new home in the moon of Titan. It's all a lie anyway. It's unclear what the Tet would actually do to them when that time comes, but considering the movie doesn't hold back in showing its monstrosity...

tropes.name: The Reveal
tropes.html: The war with the Scavs never happened the way it's told. Rather, the Tet kidnapped the real Jack and Victoria, cloned them a thousand times and used them to Kill All Humans and Take Over the World to be able to use the ocean water as a fuel source for itself.

tropes.name: Rewatch Bonus
tropes.html: A lot of the earlier scenes, especially the ones between Jack and Victoria, take on added meaning when you learn The Reveal.

tropes.name: Saharan Shipwreck
tropes.html: At one point we see Harper riding his Cool Bike across a plane with lots of shipwrecks sticking out of the ground.

tropes.name: Scavenger World
tropes.html: The underground world beneath the surface of the Earth, where the remaining humans live.

tropes.name: Scenery Gorn
tropes.html: Most of the Earth has been wrecked and we get lots of shots of crumbled, bombed, and/or partially buried landmarks (among them the Empire State Building, the New York Public Library, Brooklyn Bridge, the Pentagon (implied to have been ground zero for a nuclear strike during the Alien Invasion war) and Washington, DC).

tropes.name: Scenery Porn
tropes.html: But the few bits of untouched scenery we do see such as Jack's hideaway are beautiful. The film was also filmed on location in Iceland and the wasteland is pretty damn beautiful as a result.

tropes.name: Sci-Fi Writers Have No Sense of Scale
tropes.html:
• The film's backstory includes a manned mission to Saturn's moon Titan in 2017- merely four years after the movie's release date. NASA doesn't even have concrete plans for a mission to Mars. Such a mission isn't likely to materialize until the 2030s. Also, it seems FTL communication is already possible by 2017, which did not come to pass in reality.
  • Also, even if cracking the Moon caused massive tidal waves and earthquakes, there wouldn't be enough sedimentation to completely bury New York up to the Empire State's observation deck.
  • The fracturing of the Moon would result in the destruction of life on Earth, except maybe a few extremophile bacteria extremely deep in the crust. It would continue to break into smaller parts and send debris to Earth in increasing amounts until the atmosphere was heated to thousands of degrees and the sky would be solid white with falling stars.
  • As is often the case in such films, the final explosion just was as big as it needed to be; in this case, the "nuke" had the explosive yield of several hundred hydrogen bombs.

tropes.name: Scream Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Jack has to remove a bullet from Julia's stomach himself, out in the open, with no anesthetic, using a futuristic medical device. He warns her it's going to hurt, the film cuts to a wide shot of the surrounding landscape, and her scream carries across the empty wilderness.

tropes.name: Second-Person Attack
tropes.html: When Scavs ambush Jack at the pod landing site, one of them buttstrokes him across the head in a blow shown entirely from his point of view.

tropes.name: Sensor Suspense
tropes.html: The first time the Bubble Ship is struck by lightning, we get a glimpse of the Ship disapearing from the Tower's sensor display, much to the distress of Victoria.

tropes.name: Sergeant Rock
tropes.html: Sykes is the no-nonsense, battle-hardened member of Beech's survivor group, the kind of soldier who has kept fighting long after any reasonable person would have given up. Complete with one-liners, Jack Bauer Interrogation Technique, and Big Damn Heroes moment.

tropes.name: Shiny-Looking Spaceships
tropes.html: The winners of the war deploy clean, shiny and very advanced weapons and crafts. An early hint about something strange going on, as a Used Future befits a post-apocalyptic civilization.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• Several to 2001: A Space Odyssey, such as the shape of the drone pods, Jack being suddenly denied access to the base, the red glaring eye of the eerie antagonist or the name of the space mission to the unknown, The Odyssey. Jack Harper's situation at the beginning of Oblivion is essentially a deconstruction of what happens to Dave Bowman at the end of 2001: aliens have abducted the first human astronaut to make contact with them, put him up in a luxurious all-white set of rooms, and made him into their servant.
    • Not to mention, The Tet very likely references how the Monolith originally had a tetrahedral shape in Arthur C. Clarke's original The Sentinel short story.
  • The number of shout outs to the Mass Effect series in this movie is rather astounding:
    • Jack's rifle looks almost exactly like the Viper Sniper Rifle from Mass Effect 2. It also sounds the same with similar-looking glowing blue projectiles.
    • Jack Harper has the same name as (Mass Effect spoiler) The Illusive Man.
    • (spoiler for Mass Effect 3) Fridge Brilliance: The Illusive Man was Indoctrinated!
    • "Welcome back, Commander." although this is a massive case of Irony consodering where and when this is said.
    • The soundtrack is at times reminiscent of the Mass Effect soundtrack.
    • The Big Bad is a giant sentient spaceship with a god complex.
    • However, Sally's voice, her Deadpan Snarker attitude, and the turrets, along with the cloning of two people, using them as test subjects, setting up individual areas, the remarkably mechanized voice when approaching the core, and the glaring red eye when confronted are much closer to GlaDOS. All we need now is a literal Companion Cube and we have a post-apocalypic Portal!
    • The drones resemble the Oculus fighters. The scene where the drones attack the human base is very similar to the scene near the end of Mass Effect 2 where an oculus breaks into the Normandy's cargo hold.
    • Mass Effect 3's final downloadable content Citadel has the plot revolves around the clone of Commander Shepard, and its climax is the clone and the original Commander getting into a Mirror Match battle. Guess what happens in this film?
  • There's also a nice shoutout to the Fallout series, with the present year being 2077, the same as the Great War. Considering the vital part nukes take place in the back story, it's hardly a coincidence. Also, in the making-of features, we learn that the Scavs' base is called Raven Rock - the same as The Enclave's base in Fallout 3. Raven Rock is a real place too, in any case.
  • The name Sally might be a shoutout to Sally Calypso from the Doctor Who episode "Gridlock". The character was a newscaster who communicated with everyone solely via video transmissions, and also turned out to be a recording of a person long dead.
  • The chase scenes through the city are more than a bit reminiscent of Star Wars: A New Hope.
  • Several to Planet of the Apes: There's a shot of the Statue of Liberty during the chase (and buried ruins of the Empire State Building and other New York City landmarks evoking the 1968 film's sequel), and astronauts in cryosleep who crash back to an Earth long after apocalyptic cataclysms, and then does an inversion from Apes; there, three male astronauts survive to return to Earth but the sole woman astronaut did not due to a cryosleep failure, while here Julia and three male astronauts survive the long cryosleep and the crash of the "Odyssey", but a drone kills the other three still asleep in their pods.
  • There are nods to Zardoz, as the protagonists both stumble upon a library in the ruins which catches their interest, and one particular book they find becomes important. And like the "Tabernacle" A.I., the Tet boasts that it's a "God".

tropes.name: Shut Up, Hannibal!
tropes.html:
At the end, you get this doozy:
Sally: I created you, Jack. I am your God.
(a beat as Jack and Beech share a glance)
Jack: Fuck you, Sally.
(Jack detonates the fuel cells as Beech laughs at Jack's flippancy)

tropes.name: Slow-Motion Fall
tropes.html: Happens when the rope snaps and Harper falls back into the cave.

tropes.name: Smash to Black
tropes.html: When Jack gets apprehended by the scavengers. The screen goes black after the Darth Vader-like figure knocks Jack out with his gun.

tropes.name: Someone to Remember Him By
tropes.html: At the end, Julia tends a garden while her two-year-old daughter plays nearby. Subverted, sorta, when it's revealed that Jack-52 note the other Jack that was in the Mirror Match who was shaken from seeing Julia himself had joined up with Sykes and company and searched for the hidden cottage he knew was out there.

tropes.name: Space Elevator
tropes.html: Jack and Vika's home, Tower 49, is a sleek modernist platform suspended high in the atmosphere and tethered to the ground far below by a cable. It serves as their living quarters, operations hub, and communications relay, literally elevating them above the ruined world they're meant to be cleaning up.

tropes.name: Star Scraper
tropes.html: Jack works from a Sky Tower located on a 3000 foot spindle. Another such tower is simply placed on a high mountain.

tropes.name: Suicide Mission
tropes.html: Jack volunteering to personally fly the bomb into the Tet. When Malcolm mentions he would love to be there to see "that thing's face" when it detonates, Jack points out flatly that it would be a one-way trip. Malcolm shrugs it off with "Yeah, but it would be Worth It" — and it turns out he meant that literally, having stowed away in Julia's pod to ride along to the end.

tropes.name: Taking You with Me
tropes.html: How Jack and Malcolm save the world from Tet.

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html: Jack laughs gleefully while being fast-winched out of the Scav ambush — only for his rope to snap.

tropes.name: Together in Death
tropes.html: What Julia thinks (and accepts) will happen during the Trojan Prisoner gambit. Jack has other ideas.

tropes.name: Tomato in the Mirror
tropes.html: He's not the real Jack Harper, but a clone. He works for the Tet, which is stealing the planet's water for fuel. And he's just one of many; we follow the 49th, which fights the 52nd later on, and Beech mentions that the Tet used an army of Harper clones as foot soldiers during the war.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Spoil
tropes.html: The fact that humanity isn't completely dead and there's a resistance led by Morgan Freeman would have been a great plot twist if it hadn't been included in the very first trailer. Fortunately, there are other twists that the trailer managed to omit.

tropes.name: Trust Password
tropes.html: Standing at the viewfinder on the observation deck of the Empire State Building, Julia begins recounting the memory of Jack's proposal: "Look through here..." and Jack quietly finishes it with her, "...and I'll show you the future." A detail that could only come from the real thing, and the final confirmation of everything she has been telling him.

tropes.name: Try and Follow
tropes.html:
Employed twice by Jack when chased by the three drones.
  • First Jack steers his Bubbleship directly into a thunderstorm and threads through the turbulence at speed, pulling clear just as a lightning bolt strikes his pursuers and temporarily disables them. He already knew he could make it through, having survived an earlier unplanned flight through a storm with his engines knocked out — the drones, apparently, did not have that data.
  • During the Aerial Canyon Chase, with one drone still on his tail, Jack spots a narrow vertical gap in a canyon wall and threads his Bubbleship straight through it. The drone cannot follow and smashes into the rock face.

tropes.name: Two-Person Pool Party
tropes.html: Begins with Jack being made "Rule of Pool-compliant". For extra male Fanservice, Victoria's the one character we see naked (her shadow from behind), with Jack ending up shirtless afterwards.

tropes.name: Underwater Kiss
tropes.html: From the Two-Person Pool Party trope above.

tropes.name: Unreliable Narrator
tropes.html: Jack has no memory from before he began his current job - his Opening Monologue is entirely based on what Sally tells him (and Sally herself is an Unreliable Expositor).

tropes.name: The Un-Reveal
tropes.html: The origin, motives and nature of the Tet — is it an Artificial Intelligence stealing the energy it needs, or is it acting on behalf of an unseen alien race?

tropes.name: Vehicular Assault
tropes.html: During the Aerial Canyon Chase, one of the drones tries to ram Jack's bubble ship against the canyon wall but fails. The last one however succeeds in doing a Taking You with Me, crashing into the bubble ship and forcing them to eject.

tropes.name: Vomit Indiscretion Shot
tropes.html: When Julia wakes up from her cryosleep, she repeatedly pukes cryo-liquid on camera.

tropes.name: Wait Here
tropes.html: After crash-landing in the off-limits radiation zone, Jack tells Julia to stay with the downed ship while he scouts a way out. Naturally, she follows him anyway — and immediately catches a stray bullet in the stomach for her trouble during the firefight that follows.

tropes.name: Waking Up Elsewhere
tropes.html: Julia wakes up at the cottage after passing out from her gutshot.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
• "I'm your wife."
  • "No. We are not an effective team."
  • "The drones were designed to kill humans."

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html: Jack demanding to know who Julia is — and her answer is simply, "I'm your wife." Two words that reframe everything he thought he knew about himself.

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html: After Jack goes into the forbidden territory of the Radiation Zone and crash-lands with Julia, he finds another person who had landed in a Bubble Ship, and as a quick zoom-in shows when they're face-to-face... it's another Jack.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html:
• Jack 52 gets to grow old with Julia. What happened to the Victoria 52 that we saw?
  • And to the other 50+ Jacks and Victorias that presumably must be out there somewhere.

tropes.name: Why Don't Ya Just Shoot Him?
tropes.html: Averted. Sgt Sykes actually does that when Jack 49 initially refuses to cooperate. Fortunately he was wearing a Bulletproof Vest, and Sykes was using a low-caliber handgun, so while it knocked Jack down, it did stop the bullet.

tropes.name: Worf Had the Flu
tropes.html: The drone on Tower 49. See Big Damn Heroes and Chekhov's Gun.

title: Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb
original_title: Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb

tropes.html: Burpleson 3-9180 is the number of the booth phone from which Group Captain Mandrake is calling the President to try and stop the bombers from attacking Russia.

tropes.name: Accidental Pervert
tropes.html: Col. "Bat" Guano, heading an Army division that fought its way into an Air Force base, takes British military attaché Group Captain Mandrake to be "some kind of deviated prevert" who killed the commanding general for "finding out about his preversion and organizing a mutiny of preverts" — most likely on the evidence of his odd accent and uniform.

tropes.name: Action Bomb
tropes.html: Major T.J. "King" Kong rides the nuke down to its destination below, thereby causing the Soviets' doomsday device to detonate and end the world.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html: Mandrake tells Guano, played by the son of the Mad Hatter, that Ripper had gone "as mad as a March Hare."

tropes.name: Adaptational Explanation
tropes.html: The stage play has Strangelove testing robotic limbs on himself to explain why his Evil Hand does Nazi salutes and how he can walk at the end.

tropes.name: Adaptation Expansion
tropes.html: The stage play adds a bit more to the ending to make it less abrupt. After discussing the plan to hide away in the mineshafts to survive the fallout, the President is escorted against his will to his own private sealed mineshaft.
