[T]his thing turns out to be half as important as I figure it just might be, I'd say that you're all in line for some important promotions an' personal citations when this thing's over with. That goes for every last one of ya, regardless of your race, color, or your creed. Now, let's get this thing on the hump. We got some flyin' to do."

tropes.name: Rule of Symbolism
tropes.html:
An odd example, the table in the War Room has a green top, like a poker table, implying the leaders are gambling and bluffing with the human race. It doesn't show on screen, as the movie is black and white, but Kubrick insisted on it anyway.
  • The film's rated PG and pretty inoffensive compared to what's in movies today, but still Strangelove has been seen as an allegory of sex "from foreplay to explosion." The film is loaded with sexual imagery and innuendo, mostly phallic symbols and sexually-charged character names. The opening sequence of B-52s being fueled in midair looks a lot like planes having sex, and the background song is "Try a Little Tenderness." Then, of course, there's the famous image of Kong riding the bomb. It's probably no coincidence that the bomb looks an awful lot like a giant penis sticking between Kong's legs. (The airmen have written "Dear John" and "Hi there" on those bombs.) And let's not forget the series of massive explosions that destroy the earth, which, in a certain light, seem about as orgasmic as a thing can be. Maybe the film is trying to show all the Cold War posturing and build up of nuclear arms as a massive case of a penis-measuring contest. The whole thing is about males not feeling sexually potent or virile, and generally trying to prove how tough they are. The scene where Gen. Ripper explains to Mandrake the first time he ever became aware of the "Commies" draining his precious bodily fluids seems to support that idea. It's also probably no coincidence that Ripper is named after Jack the Ripper, the infamous murderer of prostitutes who had some weird sexual proclivities, like, oh, murdering prostitutes for example.
  • Strangelove has a black-gloved arm that he can't control. The black glove belonged to Kubrick, who wore them on the set to protect his hand from the hot lights he was handling. Sellers thought it would be a great prop for Strangelove, and it also reminded him of the black-gloved mad scientist in Fritz Lang's 1927 film Metropolis.

tropes.name: Sanity Slippage
tropes.html:
Kubrick's thumbprint:
  • General Ripper might have had a better grip on reality at some point in his backstory, as he was able to pass the safeguard tests, and neither Turgidson nor Mandrake ever suspected he would do something so crazy with his bomber force. Major Kong mentions that he knows General Ripper personally, and he believes Ripper would only have ordered the attack if there was a damn good reason.
  • Dr. Strangelove's repressed Nazi sympathies come out enthusiastically at the end, where he becomes an unambiguous Mad Doctor.

tropes.name: Scientist vs. Soldier
tropes.html: Admittedly, everyone is equally unsuited for addressing the threat, but the titular doctor actually acknowledges the Cobalt-Thorium G bomb as a horrific risk to all life everywhere, while General Buck Turgidson wistfully wishes that the US had one of their own.

tropes.name: Sealed Orders
tropes.html: The bomber crews only unseal their targeting orders after the attack command is given.

tropes.name: Secondary Character Title
tropes.html: The good doctor is a memorable character, to be sure, but definitely not the main one.

tropes.name: Secret Test
tropes.html: Mandrake remarks that the Pentagon is going too far in testing their readiness, not yet realizing that the nuclear war alert at Burpleson Air Base is a conspiracy by General Ripper. Meanwhile, onboard the Leper Colony, Lieutenant Zogg speculates that it's a test: "give the go code, and see who would actually go." Major Kong rejects that idea, saying that General Ripper would only give these orders in a real emergency.

tropes.name: Sensor Suspense
tropes.html: When the Soviet air defense missiles are approaching the Leper Colony, the plane’s onboard radar display shows the missile blips rapidly gaining on them.

tropes.name: Serious Business
tropes.html: Inverted. It's the audience who gags at the enormity of the implications. The majority of the characters — either by circumstance or by training — are so tunnel-visioned that they comically miss the bigger picture.

tropes.name: Sex Is Evil
tropes.html:
General Ripper's insane conspiracy theories came about after experiencing confusion over sexual intercourse. He didn't know what a refractory period was, and thus interpreted his post-coital exhaustion as the woman stealing his "vital essence..."
  • Sex Is Evil, and I Am Horny: But he still finds it important to mention to Mandrake that he still sleeps with women, he just doesn't "let them have his essence." Sounds like prostate cancer waiting to happen.

tropes.name: Sex Is Violence
tropes.html: The film's central theme is men fulfilling sexual urges through war. General Ripper unleashes Armageddon in an act of insane paranoia brought about by sexual frustration. On the other hand, General Turgidson is saner than Ripper, but he's still a horndog whose trip to the War Room prevents him from having a sexual dalliance (presumably an affair) with his secretary. He's soon roused to lusting for war once it becomes clear that the nation has few other options.

tropes.name: Sexy Secretary
tropes.html: Turgidson's bikini-clad playmate, Miss Scott.

tropes.name: Shoot the Shaggy Dog
tropes.html: A film about the dangers of nuclear Armageddon that ends with, of course, nuclear Armageddon.

tropes.name: Short Title: Long, Elaborate Subtitle
tropes.html: Dr. Strangelove: Or, How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• Strangelove is an expy of Rotwang from Metropolis, and the black and white chiaroscuros are also a nod to German Expressionism.
  • The bomber being called Leper Colony may be a Shout-Out to Twelve O'Clock High (probably the movie).
  • The “our precious bodily fluids” line was one to Madison Grant's concept of "germ-plasm", which was what made Nordic people (the people Grant put the highest in his work) supposedly superior.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html:
The movie is filled with references to military life and quite obscure research. Also subverted. What the cockpit of a B-52 looked like was classified, so Kubrick and crew just made what a B-29 would look if the plane was shaped like a B-52, based on only one photo of a B-52's cockpit. They were so close to being exactly correct that they were briefly investigated to make sure there was no spying going on! Also, all the procedures inside the aircraft (e.g. going through the checklists) are absolutely believable.
  • Also, the combat scenes could easily pass as actual war footage, with the exception of Gen. Ripper hip-firing a M1919 machine gun (but then again, he is crazy).

tropes.name: Silly Reason for War
tropes.html: One of the darkest examples ever: Ripper is willing to drop nukes on the Soviet Union and start World War III (not realizing that this will trigger the Doomsday Machine) simply because he's blaming the Russians for his sexual impotence.

tropes.name: Simple, yet Awesome
tropes.html: Dr. Strangelove explains that the concept of the Doomsday Machine is this as a weapon of nuclear deterrence: when you are burying nukes instead of building machines to deliver them anywhere in the world there is just no limit to how much yield you can pack, a computer programmed to make everything go "boom" if certain conditions are fulfilled removes certain aspects of Realpolitik from the table, and this can all be achieved with technology available to even the most basic of nuclear powers. However, he also explains that the machine is Awesome, but Impractical "for the reasons that are now being shown".

tropes.name: Skewed Priorities
tropes.html:
• When President Muffley phones Premier Kissov to warn him of the rogue nuclear attack that’s about to hit the Soviet Union, Kissov temporarily derails the very important conversation because he’s wounded at the thought that Muffley doesn’t consider him enough of a friend to call him up just to chat. Might have something to do with him being drunk when Muffley calls him.
  • Soon after Dr. Strangelove explains his plan for the top U.S. officials and a selected part of the population to descend into mineshafts so they can spend 100 years waiting for the surface to become inhabitable again, General Turgidson starts ranting about the possibility of the Russians stashing away nuclear weapons or expanding to additional mineshafts so they will have outbred the Americans by the time everyone returns to the surface: he demands that the president not allow a "mineshaft gap." He doesn’t see the irony in trying to perpetuate the kinds of paranoid war preparations that caused this nuclear apocalypse in the first place, or that he’s putting the cart before the horse when they haven’t even properly started their survival preparations yet.
  • "As You Know, the Premier loves surprises." And thus the fact that Russia has an ultimate weapon, which itself would be one heck of a surprise to unveil, was kept a secret until it was too late.

tropes.name: Slave to PR
tropes.html:
Turgidson suggests to capitalize on the mistake and do a full scale attack. Muffley shuts this down with an aversion of Would Be Rude to Say "Genocide". Turgidson slaps back.
Muffley: You are talking about mass murder, not war [...] I'm not going down in history as the greatest mass murderer since Adolf Hitler.
Turgidson: Perhaps it might be better, Mr. President, if you were more concerned with the American people than with your image in the history books.
Muffley: General Turgidson, I've heard quite sufficient from you. Thank you very much.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Gender Inequality
tropes.html: The film has precisely one female in the movie, a secretary who is also a Playboy centerfold model.

tropes.name: The Smurfette Principle
tropes.html: Miss Scott is General Turgidson's mistress and the only female character in the entire movie. Too bad she doesn't get enough screen time to develop a personality.

tropes.name: Soundtrack Dissonance
tropes.html:
• The ending montage, of course.
  • In-universe, the playing of pleasant civilian music over the radio during a supposed nuclear attack is what clues Mandrake into Ripper's lie.

tropes.name: Soviet Superscience
tropes.html: Discussed and Subverted with the Russian Doomsday Machine. Initially, the U.S. officials react as if it’s an impressive technological feat, and the ominous name alone reinforces this perception. However, Strangelove is quick to explain that such a world-ending device is actually within the reach of even the smallest nuclear power; it merely requires the will to build it. This backs up Ambassador De Sadeski's statement that the Soviet Union was all but bankrupting itself through the high-tech arms race before they embraced the Doomsday Machine as a cost-saving measure, and that they built it for a fraction of the money they normally spend on defense in a year.

tropes.name: Spared by the Adaptation
tropes.html: In the novelization, General Ripper escapes from the chaos at Burpleson on his private plane rather than commit suicide.

tropes.name: Space Whale Aesop
tropes.html: Don't launch an unprovoked nuclear attack, because you might trigger a doomsday machine. Downplayed because a doomsday device is not so improbable and disconnected from the attack.

tropes.name: Spy Cam
tropes.html: The Russian ambassador is accused of trying to take pictures of the War Room using a camera disguised as a pack of cigarettes. The ambassador claims that the spy camera was planted. It turns out that the ambassador may have been telling the truth — his spy camera was disguised as his pocket watch (unless you believe that the ambassador brought two hidden cameras with him).

tropes.name: Stealth Pun
tropes.html: Dr. Strangelove is strangled by his glove.

tropes.name: Stiff Upper Lip
tropes.html: Mandrake for a while, until "Bat" Guano's obstructionism makes him lose it.

tropes.name: Stock Footage
tropes.html: The film opens using stock footage of a KC-135 tanker plane refueling a B-52 bomber and closes using archival footage of atomic bombs exploding.

tropes.name: Straight Man
tropes.html: Peter Sellers plays two of these, oddly enough. His third role more than makes up for it.

tropes.name: Straw Character
tropes.html: President Muffley is a well-meaning but ineffectual liberal (look-up the meaning of "merkin," or, for that matter, "muff"), and General Ripper and Turgidson are insane "John Bircher" conservatives.

tropes.name: Stupidest Thing I've Ever Heard
tropes.html: Pronounced by Major Kong during his initial incredulous reaction when the crew receives the go ahead codes for "Plan R."

tropes.name: Suddenly Shouting
tropes.html: "If you keep it a secret! WHY DIDN'T YOU TELL THE WORLD, EH?!" And later, "MEIN FUHRER! I CAN WALK!"

tropes.name: Suicide Mission
tropes.html: The crew of the damaged Leper Colony can either turn back, with a slim chance of reaching safety, or press on to almost certain death. Eventually, the plane's damage increases to the point they have to abandon their original primary target and hit a target of opportunity if they want even a slim chance of making it to a possible target of safety with their remaining fuel. And then Major Kong rides the bomb to oblivion, making it a literal suicide mission for him in particular!

tropes.name: Superweapon Surprise
tropes.html: The Doomsday Machine, "as you know, the Premier loves surprises." It was meant to be announced the following Monday.

tropes.name: Survivor Guilt
tropes.html: President Muffley discusses it paraphrasing Khrushchev; won't "the living envy the dead?" Strangelove quickly dismisses this worry, noting that the designated survivors will say their goodbyes and go underground before they witness any of the horrors that will ensue, which he suggests will allow the survivors to think of those they left behind with fond nostalgia rather than anguish.

tropes.name: Sword of Damocles
tropes.html: The Doomsday Machine was meant to act as a deterrent by way of mutually assured destruction...or at least this was the plan. General Ripper's machinations set it off less than a week before Russia was going to announce its existence.

tropes.name: Taking You with Me
tropes.html: The Soviets build a network of cobalt bombs capable of annihilating all life on Earth. They will be set off automatically if anyone makes a nuclear attack on the USSR. Unfortunately, they failed to tell anyone. They were planning on announcing it on the following Monday, because "the Premier loves surprises."

tropes.name: Techno Babble
tropes.html: In the lead-up to the bombing, Zogg runs through a series of increasingly absurd-sounding procedures, including "arming alignment factor zero mode" and "auto CDC into manual Teleflex link". The technical jargon underscores the absurdity and grim humor of the fact the plane's crew are about to start World War III for literally no reason.

tropes.name: Theme Naming
tropes.html:
Almost all of the major characters' names have sexual connotations:
  • The title character is self-explanatory.
  • General Jack Ripper is named after a serial killer who targeted prostitutes.
  • Colonel Mandrake is named after a plant which, in many mythologies, is said to encourage fertility or childbirth.
  • President Merkin Muffley: his first name "merkin" is the term for a pubic wig. "Muff" is a slang term for female genitalia.
  • Ambassador DeSadesky is named after the Marquis de Sade, a French nobleman infamous for his violent and blasphemous sexual fantasies.
  • Soviet Premier Kissoff, whose name evokes "kissing."
  • Major "King" Kong is named after a monster known for its uncontrollable, destructive fascination with a human woman.
  • General Buck Turgidson's first name evokes the thrusting/bucking of intercourse. "Turgid" is a term meaning "swollen" or "firm," usually in reference to an erection.
  • One of the bases the American bomber is targeting is "Laputa." In Spanish, "la puta" means "the whore" or "the bitch."
  • Dr. Strangleglove has a—wait a minute….

tropes.name: This Is a Work of Fiction
tropes.html: The US version has this kind of disclaimer: "It is the stated position of the U.S. Air Force that their safeguards would prevent the occurrence of such events as are depicted in this film. Furthermore, it should be noted that none of the characters portrayed in this film are meant to represent any real persons living or dead." Actually a subversion or a false reassurance since it conveys the stated position of the Air Force about the subject but not the acknowledgement of the filmmakers, and most of the main characters are definitely caricatures of real life figures.

tropes.name: This Is Not a Drill
tropes.html: Ripper: Group Captain, I'm afraid this is not an exercise.

tropes.name: Those Wacky Nazis
tropes.html: Dr. Strangelove is portrayed as a comically bizarre weirdo who is revealed to be completely insane at the very end of the film. He's gleeful that the Soviet and American world order is going to end in nuclear hellfire, completing what the Nazis couldn't do, and his plans for a post-apocalyptic humanity are ideal for Might Makes Right fascism to reign supreme.

tropes.name: Throwing Off the Disability
tropes.html:
"Mein Führer! ...I can walk!"
  • It would have been subverted in the original ending, where he collapses immediately afterwards.

tropes.name: Truth in Television
tropes.html:
• A 2014 article in The New Yorker by Eric Schlosser confirmed what many had long suspected: that despite the disclaimer placed in front of the movie and the scorn heaped upon its plot by the military establishment at the time, for many decades it was entirely possible for someone other than the US President to launch a nuclear first strike without authorization.
  • The 24-hour B-52 squadrons within 2 hours of their targets inside the USSR? They were part of Operation Chrome Dome.
  • Fears that the Russians are trying to corrupt American institutions through other means, on the other hand, are alive and well on both sides of the aisle (though they'll often disagree on which institutions they're gunning for.)
  • A nuclear bomb salted with cobalt would indeed produce more fallout than a a standard device. And yes, it can render affected regions uninhabitable for 100 years.
  • The Russians did in fact invent an automated nuclear response system, known as "Dead Hand", but it wasn't completed until the 1980s.
  • Ripper's paranoia about water fluoridation was based on real conspiracy theories about the effects of fluoridation, some of which persist to this day on both extremes of the political spectrum, minus the "vodka-drinking Russians did it" part.
  • The babbling about a "doomsday gap" and a "mineshaft gap" was a nod to alleged "bomber gap" of the mid-1950s and rhetoric from the 1960 presidential campaign when John F. Kennedy had attacked Nixon and the Eisenhower Administration for allowing the Soviets to open up a "missile gap" between themselves and the United States (in fact, the USA actually had more missiles). This kind of discourse would continue in the seventies with the so-called "Cruiser gap."
  • The fact that Strangelove is obviously a former Nazi isn't far-fetched. The US imported/impressed many German scientists after World War II (as did the Soviets, for that matter), the most famous being Wernher von Braun, who designed the V2 rocket for the Nazis and later turned his talents to designing missiles for the Army and NASA. It was his design team's Saturn rockets that ultimately took humanity to the moon in 1969, and von Braun himself became a minor media celebrity in his own right.

tropes.name: Try Everything
tropes.html: Gen. Turgidson explains that they're trying every possible permutation for the CRM-114's prefix code to issue the recall order, but with over 17,000 possible prefixes (17,576 precisely), it'd take three days to transmit all of them. They've got less than two hours to issue the order.

tropes.name: Two-Keyed Lock
tropes.html: The pilot, bombardier, and electronic warfare officer each have to operate the first and second safety switches to arm the bombs.

tropes.name: Unaccustomed as I Am to Public Speaking...
tropes.html: Major Kong reckons he ain't much of a hand at makin' speeches, but ends up delivering a pretty solid one anyway.

tropes.name: Unbuilt Trope
tropes.html: The movie created General Ripper. However, the Trope Namer isn't a bombastic military man and acts calm, collected, and suave. The keyword being "acts." Ripper's ability to hide his nervous breakdown from the psychological evaluations, Mandrake, and everybody else is what allowed him to be in the position of power he needed to be in to set his demented plot into motion. The news of his insanity is a shock to everyone involved. Buck Turgidson could be seen as the more standard version of this trope, with his loud threats against Communism, but was (wisely) ignored by the diplomatic President Muffley. Ultimately, Turgidson comes to realize the disaster that will unfold.

tropes.name: Understatement
tropes.html:
• General Turgidson gets several of these in quick succession when he informs the President of the United States that General Ripper, a lower-echelon American military commander, has ordered a nuclear attack on the Soviet Union without the approval or knowledge of the White House or the Pentagon.
    • When the President asks how General Ripper could possibly order such an attack, Buck says:
      Gen. Turgidson: Although I hate to judge before all the facts are in, it's beginning to look like General Ripper exceeded his authority.
    • The President questions how the Human Reliability Tests didn't catch General Ripper's burgeoning psychosis:
      Gen. Turgidson: Well, I don't think it's quite fair to condemn the whole program because of a single slip-up, sir.
    • Buck advocates following General Ripper's lead and to launch an all-out nuclear attack on Russia:
      Gen. Turgidson: Mr. President, I'm not saying we wouldn't get our hair mussed. But I do say no more than 10 to 20 million killed, tops... depending on the breaks.
    • When the President is talking with the Soviet Premier, he attempts to describe what Ripper did in a similar fashion.
      Pres. Muffley: ...One of our base commanders, he had a sort of...well, he went a little funny in the head. You know. Just a little funny. And uh, he went and did a silly thing...

tropes.name: Unusually Uninteresting Sight
tropes.html: As Strangelove's right arm throws Nazi salutes and tries to strangle him, no one else reacts to this, as if they see it all the time and are completely used to it. Or perhaps they're just so perplexed by it that they don't even know how to react.

tropes.name: Unwitting Pawn
tropes.html: The crew of The Leper Colony. Poor guys are just following orders. They don't know that the guy who gave them has lost it.

tropes.name: Vengeful Vending Machine
tropes.html: Col. Guano has to shoot a Coca-Cola vending machine to get change for a crucial phone call to the President. He gets Coke squirted in his face.

tropes.name: Viewers Are Geniuses
tropes.html: The "survival kit" includes, among others, nylon stockings. While this can be lost to today's audience, in the '60s soldiers were issued nylons — to wear under their uniforms for warmth.

tropes.name: Villainous Breakdown
tropes.html: General Ripper is calm and in control for much of the film, but toward the end, he starts to seem visibly unhinged and disheveled. It begins when he starts explaining his motivations and sexual impotence to Mandrake and only grows worse as his base is seized. When his men surrender and he realizes he's going to be tortured for the recall code, he reaches his wits' end and kills himself.

tropes.name: Visual Innuendo
tropes.html:
There are a number of phallic and sexual images throughout the film to highlight its theme of sexuality.
  • The famous opening credits sequence of planes refueling in a way that looks like sexual congress, especially that between dragonflies.
  • General Ripper is particularly fond of compensating for his impotency with enormous cigars (and a machine gun).
  • Major Kong straddles the strikingly tubular bomb just before it explodes.

tropes.name: Vodka Drunkenski
tropes.html:
• Even though we hear only President Muffley's side of the conversation, it's quite obvious that Premier Kissov is sloshed out of his gourd. It's explained earlier when DeSadesky warns Muffley beforehand of an intoxicated Kissov.
  • General Ripper asks Mandrake if he has ever seen a Russian drinking water and then "concludes" that they only drink vodka.

tropes.name: The War Room
tropes.html:
The Trope Codifier (just see the Trope page). A huge, elaborate set designed by Ken Adam. Also sparked the most famous quote from the movie.
President Muffley: Gentlemen, you can't fight in here! This is the War Room!

tropes.name: Water Source Tampering
tropes.html: General Ripper has a paranoid belief that there is a Communist conspiracy involving water fluoridation which will lead to contamination of everyone's "precious bodily fluids" (i.e., sexual fluids).

tropes.name: We Have Reserves
tropes.html:
General Turgidson's attitude towards America's civilian population, arguing that losing 10-20 million people to Soviet nuclear retaliation is "regrettable, but nonetheless distinguishable" from losing 150 million if the U.S. fails to launch an all-out attack.
General Turgidson: Mr. President, I'm not saying we wouldn't get our hair mussed...

tropes.name: We Will Meet Again
tropes.html: The memorable final montage plays the song of the same name over images of atomic explosions, implying the two superpowers are destined to trade blows ever after.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
Setting aside the evident parodic elements at this point in the film, it can still be argued that General Ripper has a logical reason for his behavior, as he spends every moment utterly calm and polite. Mandrake (and the audience) only start to realize he's insane with this line:
"Mandrake, have you ever seen a commie drink a glass of water?"

tropes.name: Whatever Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: A table full of pastries is visible in the War Room in some scenes. It was meant for the original Food Fight ending, and thus would have been a Chekhov's Gun instead.

tropes.name: What Were You Thinking?
tropes.html: Dr. Strangelove angrily asks the ambassador why the Soviets didn't tell the world about their Doomsday Device before activating it. He meekly replies it was supposed to be a surprise for the Premier.

tropes.name: Windmill Crusader
tropes.html: Ripper, for his belief that the Russians are using water fluoridation to "sap and impurify our precious bodily fluids."

tropes.name: World Gone Mad
tropes.html:
Every single group of people are various sorts of insane, incompetent, and/or incapable of focusing on the important subject at hand...except for the bomber crew, who are all well-trained and manage to adapt to the various obstacles in their path. Too bad they're the one group that desperately needs to fail to avoid global annihilation.
  • Mandrake isn't too bad, either. He manages to figure out the recall code and get the attack canceled...except for one plane...

tropes.name: Xanatos Speed Chess
tropes.html: Despite Kissov bungling the announcement of the Doomsday Machine and General Ripper going off half-cocked, Strangelove essentially takes over the US government shortly after the climax of the film, with none the wiser.

tropes.name: You Are Too Late
tropes.html: Instead of stopping the attack that would set off the doomsday weapon, the characters fail, and a small amount of the population has to flee to underground bunkers in order to survive, while the majority dies from radiation poisoning.

tropes.name: 20 Minutes into the Future
tropes.html: Possible case. Jim sees a copy of the Evening Standard with the headline “EVACUATION”. While there is no date on this, an unused prop (with slightly different stories) is dated October 2006. The film itself was shot in 2001-2002 and there are several indicators of the actual year the film was made, including the tax discs on vehicles, suggesting it had been planned to be set in 2006 before they decided on a Present Day setting. The sequel 28 Years Later is explicitly being set in 2030, confirming that the Rage outbreak began in 2002.

tropes.name: Abandoned Hospital Awakening
tropes.html: Jim wakes up in an Abandoned Hospital the eponymous twenty-eight days after the Zombie Apocalypse begins. He winds up in an abandoned hospital again after being shot during the climax.

tropes.name: Action Film, Quiet Drama Scene
tropes.html:
We get a few, largely thanks to Jim, the idealist.
  • He reminisces over family photos after discovering his parents committed suicide rather than try to survive the plague.
  • Frank invites the group to observe the beauty of surviving horses, running, playing.
  • Jim holds his hand out the window of the cab on the way to Manchester, enjoying the air playing over him.

tropes.name: Action Survivor
tropes.html: Jim and the other survivors. He in particular survived early on through sheer dumb luck.

tropes.name: Adrenaline Makeover
tropes.html:
• Even if this trope is related with female characters, it goes for Jim. He started as The Load, ended up as badass.
  • Arguably applies to Hannah as well. Her father initially joins forces with Jim and Selena so that they can take care of her if something happens to him. But she ends up saving them at the end when she kills Major West.

tropes.name: Affably Evil
tropes.html: Major West. From the start, there's something ominously odd about how imperturbable the character seems to be.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Situation
tropes.html: Selena mentions radio reports of infected in New York and Paris just before transmissions cut out, but it's revealed the virus was successfully contained in Britain. It's not clarified whether these were simply false reports, suppressed outbreaks, or a deliberate attempt to mislead survivors from escaping by implying there was nowhere to go.

tropes.name: Animal Wrongs Group
tropes.html: Activists releasing infected chimps are the cause of Britain going to zombie hell.

tropes.name: Anonymous Benefactor
tropes.html: Right at the start of the main story, once Jim wakes up, someone - maybe a doctor or a nurse - covered the blinds, locked his hospital room door, and shoved the key under the door, so that he could get out if he woke from his coma.

tropes.name: Anti-Villain
tropes.html: Major West is perhaps the most visible example of a villain in the entire movie. And the movie itself heavily implies that he's just gone completely insane. Of course, with the total exception of Sergeant Farrell and Private Jones, the rest of the soldiers really are just complete scumbags, with Corporal Mitchell being the most outright villainous.

tropes.name: Apocalypse Anarchy
tropes.html: Apparently, suicide was more common than not, as was an increase in church attendance. And then there's the military...

tropes.name: Apocalypse How
tropes.html: Regional/Societal Disruption. Despite radio reports that the virus has reached Paris and New York, it turns out to be confined to Britain, as they realise on seeing an aeroplane flying over at high altitude, so either the reports were wrong or the virus was successfully contained. At least until the sequel happens.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: "Hello" is probably the most frequently uttered word throughout the movie, particularly by Jim. It's also the word that Selena made out of curtains to get the plane's attention.

tropes.name: Art Shift
tropes.html: While the majority of the movie was famously shot on low-grade digital cameras, the epilogue switches to lush 35mm film, signalling that the nightmare is over.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Biology
tropes.html:
• The rate at which the Infected vomit blood should kill them from dehydration and/or blood loss within a matter of hours. There's also the speed at which the virus infects its victims. A virus that induces intense rage is theoretically feasible, but infected victims are shown to take less than a minute to go from normal to mindlessly enraged. In reality, even an exceptionally aggressive virus would take several days to infect a victim to a point where their behaviour would start to change.
  • The eggs being off to the point of being inedible and with the taste to match it, some four weeks after delivery to the store. Even without any extra care for the duration, they should be still fine. However, this might be deliberate, simply to point out what an awful cook Jones is. Same goes with the rotten apples and citruses in the supermarket, which at worst would get dried up and wrinkled (including the irradiated ones), rather than outright rotten into a pulp - that would take them another four-five weeks.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Geography
tropes.html:
• Jim’s walk around London takes him the long way around.
  • The radio message says that the blockade is to the northeast of Manchester. When Jim breaks back into it, there are signs for the M6 and M55. These motorways meet outside Prestonnote where the M55 starts before heading west, which is north west of Manchester.
  • In addition, the blockade is said to be on the M602 motorway, which is an urban motorway to the west of Greater Manchester in real life.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Military
tropes.html: During a radio message, a solider says "I repeat". "Repeat" is reserved for artillery fire. The proper phrase to repeat a message is "I say again".

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html:
• The animal rights activists who got the whole apocalypse going in the first place may count as well, considering that they weren't above roughing up a mild-mannered scientist who was only a Punch-Clock Villain at best. They also ignored his countless pleas against unleashing the virus, and didn't think it was odd that nearly all the chimps were in completely sealed cages. For their troubles, they end up getting ripped apart by the infected chimps, and either died or became the first infected humans.
  • Corporal Mitchell and most of the soldiers start off as amiable to the surviving trio, but they're actually a group of violent psychopaths who murder one of their own for a disagreement, attempt to kill Jim for the same reason, and plan to rape Selena and Hannah. Jim goes on a Roaring Rampage of Revenge on them at the end, and despite how fearful they may have been in their final moments, they deserve it.
  • Major Henry West as well since he's the one who made the plan to have any female survivors as sex slaves, had Farrell murdered because he did not want to go along with the plan and shot Jim for killing his men even though it was self-defense.

tropes.name: Badass Adorable
tropes.html: Hannah certainly by the end. She's still a very cute teenage girl, but she takes it on herself to man the getaway car and get rid of West herself.

tropes.name: Badass Longcoat
tropes.html: As long as Selena is in Crazy Survivalist mode, she wears one. Made of leather, no less!

tropes.name: Bathe Her and Bring Her to Me
tropes.html: A variation. The soldiers dress Selena and Hannah up in fancy gowns before they intend to rape them.

tropes.name: Batter Up!
tropes.html: Jim's weapon of choice is a wooden baseball bat. Selena jokingly calls him "Babe Ruth."

tropes.name: Battle in the Rain
tropes.html: Jim's Roaring Rampage of Revenge in the final act takes place during a thunderstorm; any outside scene has him and the others drenched within seconds.

tropes.name: Beware the Nice Ones
tropes.html: After being subject to a few too many rounds of cruelty and knowing Selena and Hannah are going to get raped by West's men, Jim proves why the cute ones are the ones to watch out for. The same applies to Hannah, who backs the cab containing West straight into the entryway of the house, knowing that his infected soldiers will get him.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html: In the end of the film, the pilot of the plane is speaking Finnish on the radio. The very last words he says are, "Lähetätkö helikopterin?" which means "Will you send a helicopter?"

tropes.name: Body Horror
tropes.html: The Infected fall immediately into violent rage and vomiting blood. The end of the movie shows that they're succumbing to starvation and dehydration, wasted and suffering.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html:
• The movie begins and ends with a 28-day time skip, and both time-skips open with Jim waking up in a bed in recovery after suffering a near-fatal injury which he was treated for inside a hospital building.
  • In the unused alternate ending, the final scene of the movie would have been Jim dying in a hospital, just like how he woke up in recovery in one.
  • The one word that Jim was emphatically bellowing over and over without response in the movie's beginning, "HELLO", is the same word that the surviving characters splay across a field with huge cloths in the movie's final scene, successfully catching the attention of a Finnish patrol jet who seemingly calls for a helicopter.

tropes.name: Bottomless Magazines
tropes.html: Played Straight when West's men defend their outpost from a sudden Zerg Rush of infectees.

tropes.name: Broken Bird
tropes.html: Selena has this attitude. According to Naomie Harris, she and Danny Boyle came up with a backstory to explain it: Selena apparently had to kill her entire family in one afternoon due to the infection — including a baby brother.

tropes.name: Broken Record
tropes.html: Jim's first seven spoken words are all, "Hello?" Understandable, seeing as the city seems devoid of human life.

tropes.name: Cerebus Call-Back
tropes.html: Inverted. At the end, Jim says to Selena "you looked alright in this, you know" as she's sewing the Help sign. She's using the dress the soldiers made her wear to get raped in.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Skill
tropes.html:
A few:
  • Selena is a chemist or pharmacist. It helps to sleep, it helps to get stoned and more or less saved Jim in the end.
  • Hannah's ability to drive and doing it recklessly. Doesn't sound that important or strange, but she's about 14.

tropes.name: Convenient Coma
tropes.html: Played with. Jim went into a coma somewhere around the outbreak; he was a bike messenger and got hit by a car. When he wakes up, he is very weak, malnourished, and dehydrated. Most likely a week or two more and he would simply expire. Subverted in the case of his parents. They were almost sure he was dead, so they committed suicide. However, whatever his injuries were that landed him in the coma in the first place, they don't impede him on his journey to becoming a badass.

tropes.name: Conveniently Empty Roads
tropes.html: In the famous post-apocalyptic sequence where Jim wanders through the deserted London after having Slept Through the Apocalypse due to a coma, the roads (including the capital city's major roads such as Westminster Bridge) aren't just devoid of people, the number of vehicles that are crashed or otherwise aren't neatly parked somewhere can be counted on one hand. This is in contrast to the sequel's shots of a deserted London.

tropes.name: Crazy Survivalist
tropes.html: Although Selena isn't exactly crazy (yet), she's incredibly ruthless and will leave anyone behind if they can't catch up, distrusts others, and openly mocks any plans for salvation. "Staying alive is as good as it gets." She warms up once she's spent some time with the others, though. Naomi Harris explained that she and Danny Boyle came up with a back story that Selena had to kill her whole family in one afternoon, including her younger siblings, to explain her harsh outlook on life.

tropes.name: Creepy Child
tropes.html:
• The infected boy from the roadside bar. While being extremely dangerous, he's not even 10. After easily subduing him, Jim openly struggles with himself if he should kill the kid, especially when he speaks — the only infected to do so in the entire film.
  • Hannah, due to being given Valium by Selena right before the soldiers plan to rape her. She's this for the soldiers in universe — asking who will be the replacement if Henry is killed, right in the middle of the night. She sobers up a little before Jim finally gets into the mansion.

tropes.name: Creepy Crows
tropes.html: A distressed Frank sees a crow pecking at the corpse of someone at the station they were all meant to find refuge in. Angrily, Frank tries to wave it off...only for the movement to cause infected blood to drop into his eye and infect him.

tropes.name: Deadly Scratch
tropes.html:
The Infected are so aggressive and infectious that when Selena sees her companion Mark nursing a small wound after a fight, she kills him on the spot without hesitation.
Selena: I didn't know he was infected, okay? He knew. I could see it in his face.

tropes.name: Deconstructed Trope
tropes.html:
Of some popular zombie tropes.
  • The very same traits which make the Rage virus so apocalyptically dangerous and enable it to reduce the entire country to a depopulated wasteland within a month also completely stop it short of ending the world; the violent, visible insanity of the infected renders it impossible to conceal a bite victim, and the fact that infectees succumb to rapid, shrieking, mindless madness within seconds of infection means it's impossible for the virus to spread over any distance a human body can't travel on foot (across seas or oceans, say). Sergeant Farrell reckons that while Great Britain has indeed collapsed, the virus has actually remained contained to the island while the rest of the world is still functioning normally with Britain in quarantine; he's later proven right when Jim sees the contrail of a jet in the sky, proving that there are other survivors.
  • Furthermore, the Infected never think to eat or generally preserve their own lives, and so they starve to death en masse within a couple weeks.
  • Especially amusing given that this is pretty much the film that started and codified the Technically Living Zombie trope. The first movie to showcase this kind of apocalypse outright proves why it's impossible!

tropes.name: Destroy the Security Camera
tropes.html: The Animal Wrongs Group activists who infiltrate the research lab at the beginning of the movie are shown spraying the security cameras on their way in.

tropes.name: Dissonant Serenity
tropes.html:
• The soldiers are a bit too gleeful about killing the infected, and then "flirting" with Serina afterward.
  • Throughout his third-act rampage, Jim is calm and often has a faint smile on his lips.

tropes.name: Distant Prologue
tropes.html: The movie's opening is of when it all began, with an Animal Wrongs Group breaking into a Cambridge laboratory that's conducting inhumane experimentation, and ignoring the local scientist's desperate warnings that the captive chimpanzees are infected with an apocalyptically-virulent Hate Plague. The activists' actions enable the virus in the chimps to officially cross to humans, and then the movie skips ahead to the main time frame, starting 28 days later.

tropes.name: Distant Finale
tropes.html: The movie's ending skips ahead another 28 days, when the Infected are dying off from starvation, the surviving main characters have taken refuge at a rural cottage in Cumbria, and they manage to signal a Finnish patrol jet to rescue them.

tropes.name: Does This Remind You of Anything?
tropes.html: Danny Boyle notes on the DVD commentary that Bedford's death at the hands of the infected Mailer and Clifton was deliberately shot in such away as to almost look as though they were sodomising him.

tropes.name: The Dog Bites Back
tropes.html: After losing her dad in a staged situation and almost getting raped, Hannah drives a cab containing West right into the hands of Mailer, giving him a painful, agonising death.

tropes.name: Door-Closes Ending
tropes.html: The original ending ended with the door closing as Selena and Hannah left Jim's body behind, going into an uncertain future.

tropes.name: Downer Ending
tropes.html: Danny Boyle has stated that the "true ending" — as opposed to of the Focus Group Ending of the final cut — has Jim dying in the abandoned hospital after being shot by the soldiers. You can imagine why this was reduced to a mere alternate ending. Downplayed — it's much more of a Bittersweet Ending in that Selena and Hannah survive and are presumably rescued.

tropes.name: Dressed to Cook
tropes.html: Private Jones is portrayed as being the youngest of West's soldiers that take over the country house. He's also "the resident tin-opener" (cook, but not a good cook). He wears a pink frilly apron to cook in, demonstrating the association between women and cooking, along the lines of Feminine Women Can Cook.

tropes.name: Driven to Suicide
tropes.html: Jim's parents, seeing the outbreak and thinking that their son had died, kill themselves. So, apparently, did many other people.

tropes.name: Driver of a Black Cab
tropes.html: Frank avoids this stereotype, but a deleted scene shows Selena and Jim taking turns driving his black cab and doing their best London cabby impersonation, much to his annoyance. The DVD Commentary mentions that you can't drive a black cab without experiencing an irresistible urge to do this.

tropes.name: Earn Your Happy Ending
tropes.html: The ending as released. Jim survives, all the main characters survive the mansion assault at the end, the infected begin to die off from starvation, and a passing jet sees their distress message laid out in the grass and radios in a rescue. Although it does get a Happy Ending Override in 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple.

tropes.name: The End Is Nigh
tropes.html: A bit of graffiti◊ written on the wall, when Jim walks through London. "The end is EXTREMELY FUCKING nigh."

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html: Frank has an absolutely fantastic one, in the very same scene explaining how he managed to survive for so long, what motivates him, and what kind of person he really is. All within the span of about 90 seconds.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html: Jones is fully on board with the plan to rape the women and is fine with killing Farrell for refusing to participate. However, he balks when Mitchell wants to kill Farrell slowly with a bayonet, and shoots him to spare him that fate.

tropes.name: Evil Overlooker
tropes.html: The most common variety of the above poster adds a pair of Infected eyes◊ to the background.

tropes.name: Exact Words
tropes.html: The radio message being broadcast by the military says "the answer to infection is here." West's 'answer' is nothing to do with curing the virus, but rather a plan to rebuild civilisation the hard way, starting with the capture of sex slaves to placate his despairing soldiers.

tropes.name: Extreme Melee Revenge
tropes.html: After the soldiers imprison and almost rape a woman and teenage girl, Jim beats the crap out of every soldier in the complex (aided by an unwitting zombie) and gouges out Mitchell's eyes with his thumbs.

tropes.name: Eye Scream
tropes.html: Jim himself does this to Corporal Mitchell, shoving his thumbs into his eye sockets.

tropes.name: Failed a Spot Check
tropes.html: The unnamed animal rights group intruders were so busy documenting "animal abuse" that they completely failed to register how agitated the chimpanzees were, so the woman apparently leading the group opens one of the cages against the advice of the researcher. So naturally, she gets attacked by the chimp she unleashed, which she then tells the rest of her group to beat to death.

tropes.name: Fan Disservice
tropes.html:
• Jim spends about a third of the film shirtless or outright naked. Let's just say that he was in a coma and didn't eat for about a month. In the third act, the disservice is even stronger — Jim is not only shirtless, but also covered in blood and going around killing everyone.
  • When you get to see Selena in her underwear, it's because the soldiers stripped her and are planning to rape her as well as Hannah.
  • Numerous infected are naked, including a topless woman.

tropes.name: A Father to His Men
tropes.html: Major West is friendly and sociable with his troops, even comforting one of them as they die. There are indications that he is starting to take this role literally, that rather than just a commanding officer he now sees himself as the head of a family that he has plans to begin expanding.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
• The attack of the Infected in the tunnel before the characters go shopping repeats when Jim looses Mailer and kills the soldiers.
  • The soldiers neglecting to make their presence known until Frank gets infected and they have to put him down seems to run counter to them trying to save uninfected people...then it turns out they're trying to capture women as Sex Slaves, and while Jim's small and (seemingly) pacifistic enough to not pose a threat to that, Frank the Papa Wolf very much would.
    • Jim also watches the soldiers driving Frank's cab around in circles, careless and carefree after having just shot the cabbie dead.
  • When Farrell hits Mitchell to protect Jim and Selena from him, West calls him out but instead of questioning why he did it, he just stares at him and orders him very coldly to move the bodies from the infected attack off the lawn. He has probably intuited that the troops were starting to get too openly aggressive with Selena and that Farrell had stepped in, telling Clifton to "slow down" so he can reveal the plan in due course.
  • "Mitchell, I swear to god this is going to end badly for you..."
  • Shortly after Selena meets Jim, she mockingly asks him if one of his plans for the future involves both of them eventually falling in love and having sex. While they're not shown having sex, they do end up falling in love and are a couple by the end of the movie. 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple shows Jim having a daughter named Sam, with it being implied that she's his and Selena's child.

tropes.name: Four Is Death
tropes.html: A subtle case. 28 days is exactly four weeks.

tropes.name: Furniture Blockade
tropes.html: Shopping trolleys have been dumped in the stairwells of the tower block where Frank lives, not only to slow down the Infected but also because the noise of anyone trying to climb over them serves as an alarm.

tropes.name: Gallows Humour
tropes.html:
When Jim walks around the deserted London, we see a bit of graffiti in a church;
The End Is Extremely Fucking Nigh

tropes.name: Ghost City
tropes.html: The first two-thirds of the film take place in a mostly-abandoned London.

tropes.name: Go Mad from the Apocalypse
tropes.html: Deconstructed and reconstructed with Major West. He tells Jim that both before and after the Zombie Apocalypse, all he ever saw was "people killing people" (i.e. nothing has changed). However, he then reveals that he's been forced to take in Hannah and Selena for his men to rape them. The soldiers had lost all and any faith in humanity, so West "had to" give them the hope of repopulating the UK.

tropes.name: The Guards Must Be Crazy
tropes.html: The Animal Wrongs Group spraypaints over a bunch of security cameras (making a neat trial pointing out where they're going), and then once they've reached the lab they slam the phone down when the scientist in there calls security. This does not trigger any apparent response from the lab's security.

tropes.name: Happy Ending Override
tropes.html: Each sequel (both the movie and comics continuities) employ various degrees of this against the seemingly-happy ending where the main characters are happy together and now look set to be rescued. In the comic series, they're all separated after being rescued, with Jim in particular getting put in prison and scheduled to be executed for his (completely justified) murders of British army personnel, and Selena closing herself off once more while stuffed into a Norwegian refugee camp. The movie canon employs a comparatively tamer override in 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple, with the revelation that the rescue apparently never came for the main characters after all, and Jim is still stranded in infected Britain (though he's still happy and relatively well-off), with Selena and Hannah's statuses unknown.

tropes.name: Hate Plague
tropes.html: A rather literal example, as it's a virus that drives anyone infected by it into a berserk fury that results in them mindlessly attacking anyone they see.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html: Intentional or not, Sergeant Farrell does buy Jim enough time to escape while Jones and Mitchell bicker over how they'll kill the sergeant; Jones thinks to just shoot him while Mitchell wants to do it slow with a bayonet. Then they bicker when Jones shoots Farrell as a twisted form of mercy.

tropes.name: Hidden Depths
tropes.html: Sergeant Farrell, who muses on Earth's 'return to normalcy' once humanity is gone, and later shows himself to be a fan of The Simpsons. When Major West asks him what he used to do/be before he joined the army, Farrell just stares at him and doesn't answer.

tropes.name: High-Pressure Blood
tropes.html: The film incarnates the trope as Mailer. Is he vomiting? Is he bleeding from the mouth? He's literally gushing blood onto people. And he never runs out. Unluckily for them, The Virus spreads on contact with the eyes or mouth. It looks like they are trying to hold their breath while someone aims a firehose at their face.

tropes.name: Homage
tropes.html: Frank, Jim, Hannah, and Selena go shopping in an allusion to Dawn of the Dead (1978).

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: For a minute, it seems that Private Jones may actually escape the mansion, only to be ambushed and killed by Jim with a bayonet.

tropes.name: Horrifying Intro, Calm First Chapter
tropes.html: Downplayed. The film opens with an Animal Wrongs Group breaking into a lab running experiments on chimps, only for carnage to ensue when they release one of the subjects, resulting in the activists being infected with the Rage Virus, slaughtering each other, and triggering an outbreak. Cut to the title. Cut to Jim waking up from a coma in an Abandoned Hospital, only to find that he's Slept Through the Apocalypse; an eerie but peaceful montage follows in which Jim wanders the empty streets of London, trying to figure out what happened.

tropes.name: Humans Are the Real Monsters
tropes.html:
Major West has come to this conclusion.
Major West: This is what I've seen in the four weeks since infection. People killing people. Which is much what I saw in the four weeks before infection, and the four weeks before that, and before that, and as far back as I care to remember. People killing people... Which to my mind, puts us in a state of normality right now.

tropes.name: I Warned You
tropes.html: Jim was absolutely right that driving into a tunnel is obviously a shit idea.

tropes.name: Important Haircut
tropes.html: When Jim shaves without water or soap and crops his hair, he stops being The Load.

tropes.name: Improbable Infant Survival
tropes.html: Oh no, not here. Both the church and roadside bar are probably the most disturbing places in the whole film thanks to the aversion of this trope. But at the same time, Hannah survives.

tropes.name: Impromptu Fortress
tropes.html:
• Frank and Hannah are holed up at the top of a block of flats, barricading the stairs with shopping carts, and Frank has procured a set of police riot gear to fight the infected off.
  • The soldiers took over a nearby manor house and turned both the gated park surrounding it and the vicinity of the building into military fortifications using sandbags, razor wire and landmines. It's nowhere near an actual fortress, but it still works effectively and has an air of formal, military sophistication to it despite the improvised state.

tropes.name: In-Camera Effects
tropes.html: All of the scenes of the infected were shot with the shutter speed of the Canon XL-1 camera set very high, resulting in an unsettling and "jumpy" look.

tropes.name: Indy Ploy
tropes.html: Jim's improvised plan for freeing Selena and Hannah in the finale is massively risky and relies a great deal on luck. He has no idea how many of the soldiers will be drawn to the blockade when he sounds the siren. Returning to the manor house, he frees the infected Mailer and gambles on making it to Selena and Hannah before Mailer or any new infectees do, facing new obstacles head-on, constantly improvising. His luck only runs out when they get as far as the escape vehicle, only to be shot by West, who managed to returned from the blockade on foot in the meanwhile.

tropes.name: Inexplicable Cornered Escape
tropes.html: Inverted, since it's the person closing to the corner that's in danger, not the one hiding. During the finale, when Major West and Private Davis are searching through the barricade, Jim is sneaking at the back of the truck. While Davis is closing in on his position, half-expecting a trap, he moves parallel to the side of the truck. But by the time he reaches the back of the vehicle - Jim is no longer there, with merely five seconds passing.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html: Frank notes how painfully ironic it is that he's unable to get water for himself and his daughter because there's been no rain in England.

tropes.name: It Gets Easier
tropes.html:
• Selena is a pharmacist and used to be a regular gal. But when you meet her for the first time, she casually murders infected as if nothing and then doesn't hesitate for a second when having to kill Mark before he succumbs to the virus. That's about ten days since she killed a human for the first time. Her backstory has her having to kill her own family in self-defense, and then just going from there.
  • At first, Jim barely even tries to defend himself and is in deep shock due to all the violence he's experiencing. Later on, he gets his first kill by reluctantly bashing a kid's head open with his bat, having no other choice and still struggling with it a few days later. But by the final act, he runs around the blockade and manor and kills the soldiers one-by-one in cold blood, without so much as blinking.

tropes.name: Karmic Death
tropes.html: Corporal Mitchell. And also, Major West at the end.

tropes.name: The Last Man Heard a Knock...
tropes.html: The audience and Jim begin the movie unsure if anyone is alive except Jim. Inevitably, he runs into other survivors.

tropes.name: Late to the Tragedy
tropes.html: Jim after waking up in the hospital from his coma.

tropes.name: Lethal Chef
tropes.html:
Jones, resident tin opener.
Major West: Jones, did you notice while cooking that these eggs are off?
Jones: I thought the salt might cover the taste, sir.

tropes.name: Let Me Get This Straight...
tropes.html: Jim: No, no. See, this is a really shit idea... And you know why? Because it's really obviously a shit idea. So we drive into a tunnel full of crashed cars and broken glass... It's really fucking obviously a shit idea!

tropes.name: Living Is More than Surviving
tropes.html:
Invoked, discussed, mocked, reconstructed, subverted, double subverted... Let's just say the whole film is one huge ride of this trope. The entire Character Development of Selena is built around it. When Jim meets her for the first time, she's already a jaded survivalist utterly loathing the sole concept; by that time she lost everyone she ever cared for and had to personally kill more of them just to stay alive. She then has a series of misadventures along with Jim, Frank and Hannah, going back and forth from warming up and remaining on the edge. By the end of the story, she gleefully embraces there are still things to live for, even if the journey to that realisation was extremely painful.
Selena: Staying alive is as good as it gets.

tropes.name: The Load
tropes.html: Jim is for the first act of the film a complete airhead. In his defense he's come out of a coma to find the whole world flipped upside down, but his bumbling still gets Mark killed and nearly Selena as well. He quickly starts getting more competent as the plot unfolds.

tropes.name: Luckily, My Shield Will Protect Me
tropes.html: One of the things Frank looted somewhere around the city was a riot shield, along with other bits of riot gear. He makes a great use of the shield, easily stopping charging infected in a tight staircase.

tropes.name: The Ludovico Technique
tropes.html: One of the chimpanzees in the lab at the beginning is being forced to watch scenes of human violence on multiple screens.

tropes.name: Madden Into Misanthropy
tropes.html: Major West and the soldiers.

tropes.name: Male Frontal Nudity
tropes.html: Cillian Murphy's penis is on full display in his first scene. One of the infected running towards Major West during the barricade ambush is also completely naked.

tropes.name: Meaningful Echo
tropes.html:
• Perhaps a bit of a stretch, but Jim's story begins with him alone, frightened, and confused, desperately wandering abandoned London, screaming "HELLO!" over and over and receiving no answer. It ends with him and his loved ones in a secure countryside home, creating a "HELLO" message together that is most assuredly answered.
  • Another example is Selena's promise to kill anyone who endangers her "in a heartbeat", just like she did with Mark.
    Jim: [with a sly smile on his face] That was longer than a heartbeat.

tropes.name: Men Are the Expendable Gender
tropes.html: Subverted. Of the two female characters in the movie neither dies, while Jim is the sole male survivor of 28 Days Later. The fact that in the 'real ending' Jim dies and the girls still survive only rubs more salt in the wound. However Jim's mother commits suicide to avoid infection before the film starts, the first infected human was a woman, there are many corpses of women among the piles of dead, and a few female infected pop up.

tropes.name: Mercy Kill
tropes.html:
• Sergeant Farrell gets shot by Jones before Mitchell can bayonet him. Funny enough, Jim later kills Jones by bayonetting him.
  • Invoked when Selena hands Hannah a handful of Valium pills before they are both to be raped. And subverted - Selena is making sure Hannah, a teenage girl, will be simply too stoned to care.

tropes.name: Mildly Military
tropes.html: Invoked, though not addressed directly. There are signs that proper discipline is starting to break down among West's men, and that he is willfully starting to treat them as a family rather than his subordinates. The soldiers are boorish and almost childlike even when on duty, and are willfully and openly insubordinate towards Sergeant Farrell, the only one who does not buy into West's plan for survival. Other subtler signs can also be seen, such as Clifton sitting down to dinner wearing a hat (and West only indirectly rebuking him like a frustrated father) and Davis' unruly hair.

tropes.name: Mirror Character
tropes.html: Jim's brutality during the climax was designed to draw parallels between the infected and Jim's own intense rage towards the soldiers. It shows. So much that Selena and Hannah mistake him for an Infected.

tropes.name: Missing Mom
tropes.html: It's never explained what happened to Hannah's mother and it's actually left quite ambiguous.

tropes.name: Money Is Not Power
tropes.html:
Mark talks about the early days, when people were trying to escape the country.
Mark: I remember my dad had all this cash. He thought maybe we could buy our way onto a plane, even though cash was completely useless. Ten thousand other people had the same idea.

tropes.name: Mood Whiplash
tropes.html: The introduction scene for Frank and Hannah goes from frantic escape and brutal fight to an awkward toast with crème de menthe and father-daughter bickering. It's so extreme, even in-universe Jim and Selena are completely puzzled, since they just barely got away with their lives and are clearly in adrenaline-induced shock.

tropes.name: Mook Horror Show
tropes.html: Once Jim finally snaps, he proceeds to methodically hunt down each and every one of the soldiers at the mansion. The result plays very much like this trope — up to him doing Offscreen Teleportation.

tropes.name: Moral Myopia
tropes.html: West's "You killed all of my boys.". Several of whom were preparing to rape Selena and Hannah, a 14-year-old girl, which was disturbing even by West's standards.

tropes.name: Muscles Are Meaningless
tropes.html: Jim is toned but pretty damn scrawny, he's still capable of taking out Mitchell in the finale and killing him via bashing his skull against the wall and gouging his eyes out.

tropes.name: Naïve Animal Lover
tropes.html: The events were kicked off by a bunch of animal-rights activists liberating a bunch of infected chimps from a lab.

tropes.name: Naked on Arrival
tropes.html: The first time we see Jim, he's naked.

tropes.name: Nice Day, Deadly Night
tropes.html: Mark and Selena caution Jim early on that they should only travel during daylight unless they have no choice. Indeed, both in London and at the Manchester mansion's area, the infected appear to spend the daytime hiding and sleeping in derelict buildings so long as they aren't disturbed by a survivor intruding nor drawn out by the sounds of gunfire, whereas at night, they're on the prowl looking for victims.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html:
• Nice job breaking out those lab monkeys, activists in the intro!
  • Also to Jim, for lighting a candle and thus alerting the Infected where he and the others were hiding.

tropes.name: Nightmare Sequence
tropes.html: Jim wakes up and finds out that he's alone in a desolated area with a herd of horses fleeing (a telltale sign of the presence of Infected people). His reaction is just a terrified "Hello!" shouted repeatedly. Then we learn that it's just his nightmare. The same scene, with the same Scare Chord is used right after, as a Schmuck Bait for adiency.

tropes.name: Noble Demon
tropes.html: One interpretation of Major West. Most likely that's how he excuses his own actions.

tropes.name: Noble Shoplifter
tropes.html: After gamboling through a deserted supermarket, the heroes leave behind a credit card.

tropes.name: Nobody Here but Us Statues
tropes.html: Jim hides from his executioners in the third act by diving into a field of corpses and playing dead.

tropes.name: No FEMA Response
tropes.html: While society has entirely collapsed in Great Britain's mainland, the outbreak hasn't spread beyond the island due to natural barriers (the sea enclosing Britain), coupled with the very short incubation time between exposure and full-on Rage rendering it impossible for any zombie infectees to slip through airport terminals. Granted, it has been less than a month, and other governments may have still been trying to figure out how to help, assuming that their first aid missions weren't overrun or driven out by the spreading outbreak.

tropes.name: Not a Zombie
tropes.html: Jim's first encounter with an infectee is a former priest, and he is naturally reluctant to attack him despite his inhuman snarls and flailing arms.

tropes.name: Nothing Is Scarier
tropes.html: One of the freakiest moments in the film is actually towards the beginning, when Jim wanders through a desolate and silent London. The quiet but gradually climaxing song that plays in that scene is there because after about five minutes of abject silence, the car alarm almost killed the test audiences. Yes, they had to tone down the Nothing Is Scarier because of how well it worked.

tropes.name: Nothing Left to Do but Die
tropes.html: Major West explains to Jim this is what his soldiers were starting to think after no contact from HQ and no relief ever came to them - even if they were to somehow make it, there is just nothing for them to do after the Infected starve to death, nothing to achieve and no reason to continue living at all. So West "promised them women".

tropes.name: Officer and a Gentleman
tropes.html: Played with in Major West, who uses it to sucker in the women as sex slaves for his men. He justifies his actions with the more noble goal of trying to ensure a future for all of humanity, though he admits that the plan started with the more immediate aim of saving his men from suicidal despair.

tropes.name: Offscreen Moment of Awesome
tropes.html: Major West manages to escape a horde of infected at the barricade by himself after Jim starts setting off his ambush, making it back to the manor on foot.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
• Frank's scene with the crow dripping blood into his eye, and immediately after. Heartwrenching as he realises he has literally seconds to apologise and tell his daughter how much he loves her, and then has to push her away before the infection takes hold, for her own safety.
  • The dawning realisation the characters have when Major West explains what exactly he meant by "the answer to the infection".

tropes.name: Only One Name
tropes.html: Most of the survivors, as well as the soldiers. Major Henry West is the only character to have his full name revealed - we never find out the surnames of the civilians or the first names of the soldiers.

tropes.name: Only Sane Man
tropes.html: Among the soldiers, Sgt. Farrell. He's the only one of the soldiers who refuses to take part in West's plan to 'repopulate' the world, the only one who's figured out that the rest of the world quarantining Britain (which is, after all, a relatively small island) is a lot more likely than these people being the last human beings on Earth, and the only one among the soldiers to begin to realise (or care) that Major West has gone completely batshit insane.

tropes.name: Our Zombies Are Different
tropes.html:
Though the filmmakers tried to avoid making a "zombie movie", many consider the Infected to simply be another archetype of "zombie". Unlike typical zombies up to that point, the Infected were aggressive, extremely fast, and while they did bite and tear people apart, they didn't actually eat them (and the fact that they aren't technically dead since the virus in this movie only makes them crazy and out of control and not reanimate them as mindless cannibalistic corpses).
  • Despite trying not to be a zombie film, the Infected of 28 Days Later started the modern idea of "sprinting zombies". Dawn of the Dead (2004), as well as the video game Left 4 Dead, cited 28 Days Later as direct inspiration for their own mindless killing machines.

tropes.name: Parental Substitute
tropes.html:
• The desire for a father figure, and finding the strength to overcome it, is a key aspect of Jim's character arc. He spends the first act listless and helpless following the loss of his own family. Unlike Selena, he jumps at the chance to join Frank and Hannah's family unit in the second act - he begins to act like a goofy big brother to Hannah, and even accidentally calls Frank "dad" after waking from a nightmare. In the third act, he again gladly accepts the apparent safety offered by the soldiers and looks to West as another replacement paternal figure, before finally "growing up" and realising that he has to take charge of his own fate if he wants to survive.
  • Selena and Jim become this for Hannah by the end of the movie, her father having died during the action.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html:
• Major West comforts one of his dying men.
  • Said dying man refusing to let Mitchell bayonet Farrell, opting to shoot him first.

tropes.name: Post–Wake-Up Realization
tropes.html: Jim has been in a coma since the apocalypse started. He wakes up, leaves the mysteriously abandoned hospital...and slowly realises what has actually happened.

tropes.name: Precision F-Strike
tropes.html:
• It's a really fucking obviously shit idea!
  • In written form, THE END IS EXTREMELY FUCKING NIGH.
  • Frank, upbeat and hopeful, loses it when they reach the Manchester blockade and realize there's nothing and no-one.
    Frank: We have to go.
    Selina: Yeah.
    Frank: GO FUCKING WHERE?!

tropes.name: Rage Breaking Point
tropes.html: Frank loses all hope when they reach the Manchester blockade and find it deserted. He calms down a few moments later, but then he gets infected with Rage.

tropes.name: Researching the Monster
tropes.html: Major West ordered his men to chain Pvt. Mailer right before he turned under the Rage virus. He keeps Mailer chained and locked inside a walled courtyard, with the goal to see how long it will take for an infected to die out of either dehydration or at least starvation. This backfires horribly in the finale, as Jim releases Mailer and he attacks the unsuspecting soldiers inside the mansion. And ultimately, Mailer beats West to death.

tropes.name: Ripped from the Headlines
tropes.html: Of a sorts. The Infected were inspired both by real life epidemics - foot-and-mouth disease and mad cow disease - and recent anthrax and bio-terrorism scares in London. The reasoning was that George Romero's zombies were inspired by the fear of nuclear attack, while a more modern cultural fear was disease outbreaks. They were also influenced by many hot social issues such as road rage, hospital rage, air rage, etc. There was a lot of research done on the things that had happened in Rwanda and Sierra Leone.

tropes.name: Roaring Rampage of Revenge
tropes.html: Jim himself at the film's climax.

tropes.name: Scenery Gorn
tropes.html: The directors in their commentary were amazed at how they achieved a sense of ruin by blocking traffic for a few seconds. The film also has some really beautifully framed and executed shots that they shot with DV cameras to give it a really gritty feel.

tropes.name: Scenery Porn
tropes.html: On the flipside, there are some downright beautiful shots of the British landscape as Jim, Hannah, Selena, and Frank make their way north to Manchester.

tropes.name: Scream Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Frequently applied so that what the Infected actually do to their victims is left to the imagination. Particularly notable at the very end of the film when Mailer drags West away to his doom, and Christopher Eccleston really screams like someone who knows that he's about to die.

tropes.name: She Cleans Up Nicely
tropes.html: In-universe for Selena and Hannah from the soldiers' perspective. Not to the viewers though as the soldiers plan to rape them, and Hannah is a child.

tropes.name: Shirtless Scene
tropes.html: Stupid Sexy Murphy.

tropes.name: Shoot Out the Lock
tropes.html: Selena does this in the alternative ending to get to the medical cabinet. Unlike the typical example, she doesn't target the lock directly, but instead uses the impact force of a bullet to simply tear a hole on the cabinet's door right next to it, rendering the otherwise intact lock useless.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• The entire premise of the film (an escaped experimental virus causes mental degeneration, inducing dangerous, erratic behavior among those infected) appears to recall George Romero's The Crazies (1973).
  • (Literally) The manner in which Jim calls out for any survivors while leaving the hospital perfectly mirrors the way that Anthony Delio does with a microphone in Romero's Day of the Dead (1985).
  • Also, Jim waking up in the hospital to find London abandoned mirrors the beginning of The Day of the Triffids.
  • The crimson eyes sported by the "zombies" appear to take direct inspiration from those appearing on the eponymous living dead in The Living Dead at Manchester Morgue.
  • One of the soldiers talks about his favourite joke from The Simpsons, from Treehouse of Horror III. This was mentioned in the DVD commentary for that episode by Al Jean. Though Jean calls the movie "28 Days" and thinks it was about vampires.

tropes.name: Slept Through the Apocalypse
tropes.html:
The protagonist Jim was comatose in a hospital through the initial outbreak and evacuation. He wakes up naked in an abandoned hospital and spends a while wandering around an eerily empty London, trying to figure out what happened. Then he goes into a church full of dead bodies and meets his first zombies. The trope is almost referenced by name in the Suicide Note left for Jim by his parents:
With endless love, we left you sleeping. Now we're sleeping with you. Don't wake up.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Idealism Versus Cynicism
tropes.html:
This is more than complicated. Selena is on the cynical end, to the point where she kills her companion without a single second of hesitation just to be sure he will die before infection takes hold. Frank is on the idealism and optimism side (at least when compared with any other character) and Jim is in the middle and going back and forth from one side to another. Frank is eventually killed by the soldiers he was trying to find, while Selena's cynicism is wearing out, as she is getting closer with Jim. Then there is Major West, who is as cynical as Selena. In the original ending Jim died just after embracing the idealism side, so the cynicism actually won, but test audiences found it way too depressing. Which leads to Selena embracing the optimistic side of the scale and the upbeat ending.
  • And even if you consider Frank as a person on the idealism side, without a direct comparison with more cynical characters, he's a Knight in Sour Armour.

tropes.name: Sole Surviving Scientist
tropes.html: There is a tie-in comic covering events between both films with a scientist who played a role in the creation of the Rage Virus. He admits this to a girl that he had escaped a holding facility with, and plans to atone by becoming one of these, being that he's one of the few people alive (maybe the only one) who knows anything about the virus and has the best chance of curing it. Unfortunately, she had lost her parents earlier during the initial outbreak, and lost her brother during the escape. Apparently learning that the guy she'd been helping was the root cause of those things is too much for her, so first she kisses him, then grabs his gun and shoots him. Then lets herself be killed by the soldiers pursuing them. So much for that.

tropes.name: Stylistic Suck
tropes.html: The film was shot with cheap and disposable cameras to achieve its realistic look. Even in post-production, Boyle himself went out of his way to make the footage look even worse.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html: The film not only completely averts Convenient Coma, but, more importantly, makes malnourishment a factor, even if some high-calorie food is being provided. Initially, Jim is weak, dizzy and quickly gets winded, both from his coma, but also because his body is given nothing but sugar (via chocolate bars and soft drinks) while it has already "eaten" all the body fat reserve.

tropes.name: Swarm of Rats
tropes.html: While Jim, Selena, Frank and Hannah change a flat tyre inside a darkened tunnel, one of these suddenly appears... and turns out to be fleeing ahead of a Swarm of Infected.

tropes.name: Team Dad
tropes.html: Frank. To the point where Jim actually calls him dad while half-asleep.

tropes.name: Time-Passage Card
tropes.html: The movie combimes this trope with a Title Drop.
