  • At the end of "The Confrontation", Valjean escapes Javert by jumping off a window into a body of water. At that point in the original novel, Valjean was recaptured and brought back to the galleys, but escaped by pretending to drown.
  • As Young Cosette sweeps and sings "Castle on a Cloud", if you freeze at the right moment, there's a momentary live-action reproduction of the famous engraving of Cosette sweeping◊ that became the musical's emblem.
  • The elephant statue from the Brick makes a cameo in the film.
  • The presence of Santa Claus during the "Master Of The House" sequence is not just because the movie was released in December 2012, it's because the corresponding sequence in the book does in fact take place on Christmas Eve.
  • Valjean and Cosette being chased through the streets of Paris by Javert before climbing over a wall to escape and take refuge in a convent is straight out of the book.
  • Valjean being greeted by the Bishop as he walks into heaven. In the book, when he tells Cosette that he already has a priest and points upward, the narration implies that the Bishop is indeed bearing witness to his impending death.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html: The international trailer seems to show Valjean is an active member of Les Amis, and the movie's climax is a final showdown between him and Javert.

tropes.name: Nice Job Fixing It, Villain!
tropes.html: The Thénardiers' appearance at Marius and Cosette's wedding results in them being able to find Valjean so they can thank him for changing their lives and allowing him to be at peace moments before he dies.

tropes.name: No Help is Coming
tropes.html: The student revolutionaries know they can't prevail by themselves, but are counting on their actions inspiring others to join the fight. As the siege on their barricade drags on, it becomes increasingly apparent that they're on their own. They refuse to surrender, and are eventually overwhelmed. They bang on the doors of the civilians begging to be let in but the doors stay closed.

tropes.name: Object-Tracking Shot
tropes.html: After Valjean tears up his parole record and tosses it away, the camera follows a piece that floats up to the sky then swiftly falls as the film does the first Time Skip to "At The End of the Day". May be a possible Call-Back to an older adaptation that used a similar shot.

tropes.name: Offscreen Teleportation
tropes.html: Javert. Constantly. To the point of being somewhat memetic.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: When told by Enjolras that they are the last barricade standing and that the people have not arisen like they thought, the remaining students stare blankly at each other, thinking "What am I dying for?"

tropes.name: The Oner
tropes.html: The film sometimes pushes its (primarily film rather than stage) actors really hard in this regard. The most magnificent example of this is probably Anne Hathaway's spectacular rendition of "I Dreamed a Dream", which is done in one take and goes through Dull Eyes of Unhappiness, nostalgia, regret, sobbing, rage, and panicked gasping all while keeping the camera focused firmly on her face.

tropes.name: Ooh, Me Accent's Slipping
tropes.html:
• The accent that Sacha Baron Cohen uses as Monsieur Thénardier varies from kind of lower-class British to slightly over-the-top French when he's trying to impress someone. May be appear odd and somewhat jarring due to the fact that he's the only one to use a French accent and play with the Translation Convention.
  • Valjean in early scenes (especially What Have I Done?) sounds suspiciously Irish.
  • Despite the fact that the lead roles went mostly to Americans and Australians, it's surprising that so many people's solos have various shades of English accents throughout the movie.
  • Northern Irish. Fra Fee (Courfeyrac) can't seem to keep his Northern Irish accent from making frequent appearances. For example, the slip that occurs at around 0:35 of this scene.

tropes.name: Opening Scroll
tropes.html:
Opens with one, clarifying that this film is not about THE French Revolution, but a later rebellion, the Paris Uprising of 1832.
1815. TWENTY SIX YEARS AFTER THE START OF THE FRENCH REVOLUTION. A KING IS ONCE AGAIN ON THE THRONE OF FRANCE.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html:
See Worthy Opponent.
  • Also, once the fighting begins between the Army soldiers and the French citizens, a disguised Javert helps a fallen Courfeyrac to his feet amidst the chaos.

tropes.name: Piano Drop
tropes.html: During the barricade construction scene, someone throws a piano out of a top floor window to add to the structure.

tropes.name: The Plague
tropes.html: "Plague" was substituted for "The winter's coming on fast, ready to kill" on "At The End Of The Day". Considering the squalid conditions, an outbreak isn't so farfetched.

tropes.name: Punctuated!  For!  Emphasis!
tropes.html:
"The Confrontation"
Valjean: "All I did was STEAL! SOME! BREAD!"

tropes.name: Pyrrhic Victory
tropes.html: Javert is horrified by the army's victory against the students.

tropes.name: The Queen's Latin
tropes.html: The cast is primarily composed of American and Australian actors. Not only do most of them speak The Queen's French, but many of the lower-class characters speak Cockney French.

tropes.name: "Ray of Hope" Ending
tropes.html: The revolutionaries lose the fight against the corrupt government, but Marius survives and gets married to his beloved Cosette, Valjean dies in peace, and the epilogue suggests the revolution will fight another day in liberating France.

tropes.name: Real After All
tropes.html: The majority of characters in the stage musical are pessimistic about the existence of the afterlife and God. The movie's ending refutes this.

tropes.name: Reckless Gun Usage
tropes.html: Enjolras took away a musket from the hands of a reckless student in "ABC Cafe".

tropes.name: Remake Cameo
tropes.html:
• Colm Wilkinson, the original Jean Valjean, as the Bishop of Digne.
  • Frances Ruffelle, the original Eponine, has a cameo as one of the whores in "Lovely Ladies". Apparently, her character was dubbed "Most Fabulous Whore".
  • Hadley Fraser, who has played Marius, Javert and (most famously) Grantaire, is the officer leading the attack against Les Amis ABC.
  • Katie Hall and Gina Beck are some of the women on "Turning".
  • Katy Secombe, who played Mme. Thénardier in the 2011 London production, appears as a woman aiding the Friends of the ABC (she's the lady whose red flag was taken by Marius during "One Day More").

tropes.name: Ridiculously Difficult Route
tropes.html: Unlike in the source materials where they are Absurdly Spacious Sewers, the sewers in this adaption are this. Valjean has to force himself and Marius through a tiny tunnel, and the parts where the ceiling is high enough to stand are so filled with gunk that it's easier to drown.

tropes.name: The Rival
tropes.html: Inspector Javert makes it his life mission to capture Valjean after he breaks his parole. Averted by Eponine and Cosette, as Eponine as a child isn't shown (at least onscreen) to be as nasty to Cosette as her parents are, and as adults, despite the love triangle between them and Marius, the two never actually meet.

tropes.name: Rule of Symbolism
tropes.html:
• Javert's habit, if you can call it that, of walking on high ledges. Weird? Yes. Dangerous? Yes. Demonstrative of his belief that he is morally superior (and therefore higher), that God will not let him fall as he literally walks the straight and narrow path, and Foreshadowing for his eventual death? Oh hell yes.
  • The eagle and night sky behind Javert forming an angelic wing and void.
  • The barricade erected by the doomed revolutionaries has coffins mounted on the front of it. It has a big red coffin and a small blue one. What were Enjolras and Gavroche wearing?
  • As Valjean prays to God in "Bring Him Home", a giant eye "Looks Down" on him from a billboard in the background.
  • In "A Little Fall of Rain", Eponine and Marius lean on a French flag, with the words "La Mort" clearly visible. And what does it mean? Death. Makes one wonder what's going to happen to her and the barricade boys.
  • Colm Wilkinson, who played the original Jean Valjean in the stage version, appears as the Bishop of Digne. When he gives Hugh Jackman's Valjean the silver candlesticks in the movie, he is Passing the Torch of Jean Valjean. Plus a number of actors that make up the barricade boys also played Marius or Enjolras in the stage versions.
  • "Don't they know they're making love to one already dead?" sings Fantine at the end of "Lovely Ladies", and for "I Dreamed A Dream," she spends the next few minutes in a box resembling a coffin, complete with pillowsnote Anne Hathaway even said in an interview with Jon Stewart that, among the many, many takes of "I Dreamed A Dream" that were shot, one of them was entirely inside a coffin.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html: As the revolt starts going badly for the students, many try to escape the barricade into the near-by houses. The occupants lock them out instead.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• When Marius asks Eponine to tail Cosette for him, they spar lines set to the melody of "I Was Made For Loving You" by Kiss.
  • The hymn sung on the barricade has chords and a melody that suspiciously sound at times like the "Chant des Partisans", the hymn of the French Resistance during World War II.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html:
• During Javert's roof walking sequence in "Stars", there is a shot of Notre-Dame without her spire. It's accurate, since the original one was demolished during the 18th century prior to this time period, and the building of the one that lasted until the 2019 fire did not begin before 1845. Also accurate? The depiction of the area of Saint-Michel as one huge dirty hovel.
  • The uniforms Javert and the constables wear also count: the 1823 version sports the fleur-de-lis, the traditional symbol of the French monarchy. On the 1832 version, it has disappeared, since the July Monarchy had dropped its use in 1831.
  • Avoided entirely in the opening scene however, which uses the wrong version of the French flag (the tricolor was the Revolutionary flag, replaced by the crown and three fleurs-de-lis of the Bourbon royal family after Napoleon's defeat in 1815).

tropes.name: Sickening "Crunch!"
tropes.html: In "Javert's Suicide"

tropes.name: Signature Style
tropes.html: The film, like The King's Speech, is filled with distinctive walls with distressed layers of paint, eye-catching bricks, or battle damage, along with an unsteady and claustrophobic camera.

tropes.name: Slasher Smile
tropes.html: The john who tries to rape Fantine.

tropes.name: Small Start, Big Finish
tropes.html: The film's version of "I Dreamed A Dream", moreso compared to the stage version as it begins with Fantine laying in a bed almost murmuring as she laments the state of her life. The accompaniment swells in the last verse and her singing incorporates more belts.

tropes.name: Stealth Pun
tropes.html: After the final battle at the barricade, when Valjean flees with Marius into the sewers to avoid capture, there is a shot of Javert searching for him with that Determinator face he has. Cut to Valjean in the sewers, and the background music is now the melody of the Work Song from the beginning, when it was accompanied by the lyrics "look down, look down".

tropes.name: Sung-Through Musical
tropes.html: Much like the original musical, the movie's dialogue is almost entirely sung-through. However, it does have dialogue that's regularly spoken, albeit it only happens occasionally.

tropes.name: Take a Third Option
tropes.html: Javert's solution of whether To Be Lawful or Good — morally, he can't continue to harass a man who saved his life, but legally he can't let a convict go free — is to kill himself.

tropes.name: A Taste of the Lash
tropes.html: Valjean is not shown being flogged during his time as a convict, but in the "Work Song", he's got injuries suggesting that it's happened to him.

tropes.name: That Poor Cat
tropes.html: In "Master of the House," we see Thenardier chopping off a cat's tail and placing it in a mincer to pretend it's beef.

tropes.name: Thousand-Yard Stare
tropes.html:
• Marius sports this briefly after the events at the barricade. It takes a love song from Cosette to pull him out.
  • And another one, though brief, is at the end where the dead people start singing "Do You Hear the People Sing? (Reprise)". As Marius is hugging Cosette, his gaze briefly, but perceptibly, shifts into this - Word of God has stated this is because Marius can actually hear them singing. Cosette's gaze also shifts in much the same way, implying that she can hear them too.

tropes.name: Truer to the Text
tropes.html:
Though the film primarily adapts the stage musical, it also changes or adds in a few details to be closer to the original novel.
  • Several additional scenes from the book that were cut for the play are added back in; see Adaptation Expansion.
  • The scene where Javert informs the Mayor about "Valjean's" arrest is rewritten to portray him as ashamed about his seeming false accusation, to the point of asking him to dismiss him for it.
  • Quite a few circumstances around Éponine's death are far closer to the novel than the musical:
    • In the original book, Cosette leaves a note in the garden for Marius after Valjean tells her they're leaving; Éponine finds, takes, and conceals it from Marius in an attempt to sabotage the relationship, but later gives it to him after being fatally wounded. Marius then sends Gavroche to deliver a letter of reply to Cosette at her new address. This is also how it plays out in the movie (with the possible exception that Éponine doesn't seem to be actively trying to break up Marius and Cosette by taking the note, and just does so in a Moment of Weakness), which is a change from the stage production, in which Marius sees Éponine at the barricade and sends her (rather than Gavroche) to deliver his reply in an attempt to keep her safe and out of danger, while Cosette never writes him a letter at all.
    • How Éponine gets shot also changes; in the novel, where she is a Yandere, she tricks Marius into going to the barricade so they can die together, but ends up Taking the Bullet for him so she can die before he does. The stage play changes this to her simply being shot when she returns to the barricade after delivering Marius's letter for him. Since, as mentioned above, Éponine does not deliver this letter in the film, this is changed back to her Taking the Bullet to save Marius when he's about to be shot by the enemy (though, thanks to her Adaptational Heroism in the play and movie alike, she did not lure him to the barricade here).
    • This also causes a small detail of the ending to change. In the theater version, right as Valjean is dying, the deceased Éponine appears as an angel to guide him to the afterlife together with Fantine, presumably due to his kindness to her when she delivered Marius's note. Because she did not do so in the film, Valjean doesn't know her, and thus, when he dies at the end of the film, it's only Fantine's and the Bishop’s spirits who appear to him, which was also the case in the original book.

tropes.name: We Have Reserves
tropes.html: The soldiers who crushed the revolt. There's so many of them that their dead weren't even properly gathered, in contrast with the students who laid side by side.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
You just know the ABCs are definitely doomed.
"We're the only barricade left."
"CANNONS"!

tropes.name: What the Hell, Hero?
tropes.html:
• How Fantine responds to Valjean's intervention in her arrest - he might not recognize her, but she clearly recognizes him as the factory owner whose refusal to intervene months ago led to her being fired and eventually forced into prostitution in the first place.
    Fantine: You let your foreman send me away - yes, you were there and turned aside!
  • Not all of the students are happy about Marius' gunpowder stunt. Combeferre (the blond in the blue vest and red tie), in particular, practically shouts at Marius' face, "What were you thinking, Marius?! You could have gotten us all killed! My life is not yours to risk, Marius!"

tropes.name: Where It All Began
tropes.html: Valjean dies in the convent where his life began anew. He even brought back the candlesticks the Bishop gave him.

tropes.name: Worthy Opponent
tropes.html: Between Javert and Gavroche. When Valjean asks to kill Javert, Gavroche lets him have a pistol but looks upset, and also looks grim when he hears the gunshot a moment later. Javert is also aghast when he discovers Gavroche's body, and pins a medal on him in respect of his bravery.

tropes.name: Would Hurt a Child
tropes.html: Gavroche, even more so than in the stage adaptation, with a long, extended scene of him defying a soldier's orders and getting shot at while singing "Little People", until the soldier eventually hits him square for the kill, with no Gory Discretion Shots to hide the fact that a soldier just killed a child.

tropes.name: You Are Number Six
tropes.html: Javert insisting on calling Jean "24601" even after Jean has been paroled.

tropes.name: You Have No Chance
tropes.html: Said word for word by the Loudhailer to Les Amis.

tropes.name: Action Prologue
tropes.html: The film's prologue mostly consists of a terrifying action sequence in which infected storm a farmhouse, and Don escapes by the skin of his teeth.

tropes.name: Actionized Sequel
tropes.html: While the first film depicted the aftermath of the rage virus, the sequel shows the carnage of a new outbreak and the military's attempts to fight it back. The second half of the film is essentially one long fight between both the infected and the army.

tropes.name: After the End
tropes.html: The premise of the sequel involved attempts by the U.S. military to recolonize Britain after all the Infected have apparently died off.

tropes.name: Airstrip One
tropes.html: As mentioned in the page quote above, the military-operated safe zone on the Isle of Dogs is designated District One.

tropes.name: Air-Vent Passageway
tropes.html: Andy uses one to escape a locked room after the infection spreads amongst the crowded civilians in District 1. Justified in that Andy is small enough to fit inside an air duct.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Ending
tropes.html: While things certainly aren't looking good during the epilogue, with at least one group of infected rampaging through Paris, the credits roll before the audience finds out how widespread the new outbreak actually is. It's also left to the imagination whether Andy's infection eventually changed from asymptomatic to symptomatic, if he spread it by some other means, or indeed if the outbreak came from a different source altogether. This also leaves the fates of the three survivors up in the air.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Situation
tropes.html: After becoming infected, Don crosses paths with his children on more than one occasion and it even seems that he may have recognised them and started hunting for them specifically. He also manages to take shelter during the firebombing that wipes out scores of other infected in the final stage of the Code Red order. Whether he actually has retained the intelligence to perform these actions intentionally, or if it is a series of coincidences, is left up to the viewer.

tropes.name: America Saves the Day
tropes.html: Inverted. While initially having things under control, by the end of the film the infection has broken out and the U.S. military fails to contain it. The catastrophe could've been averted if they just had more guards posted on watch.

tropes.name: Apathetic Citizens
tropes.html: They've all just survived a viral outbreak. One assumes that even the ones who were outside of the UK and returned had been shown videos and been told how virulent the Infected were before they even returned. Yet when they are herded to a secure location for their own safety — no matter how unsafe that actually turned out to be in the end — they bicker and complain to the troops about it.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Gun Safety
tropes.html: Snipers are shown passing time by using the scopes attached to their rifles, rather than binoculars, to spy on residents of the district.

tropes.name: Badass Normal
tropes.html: When the infected begin breaking into the house Don stays behind and holds them off at the breach for quite a while with only a crowbar, buying time for the rest and only retreating when he loses his weapon.

tropes.name: Bloodier and Gorier
tropes.html: Compared to 28 Days Later, Weeks ramps up the violence and gore. While Days mostly cuts away before a lot of the carnage comes about or only shows it briefly, Weeks makes no such creative choices and goes out of its way to show as much violence as possible. This can be seen in the opening scene with how graphic the killing is, the scene where Infected Don kills Alice, and one scene where a helicopter's blades chop up a horde of infected.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html:
• Like the first movie, this one begins and ends with a time skip directly themed around the number 28.
  • The movie begins and ends with one or two of the Harris family traveling over water to escape the infection, after having lost the rest of their survivor group plus one of their own family.

tropes.name: Censored Child Death
tropes.html: The boy is presumably brutally killed by the Infected in the opening minutes, but it's not shown. Alice, who was with him, survives, though she doesn't describe his death. Likewise, Tammy and Andy are heavily implied to have died in the chaos that broke out in France, but it is also not shown.

tropes.name: Comic-Book Time
tropes.html: The original film is set in 2002, the year of its release. This film is set seven months after the original outbreak, so in theory late 2002/early 2003, yet things such as car number plates, Andy’s football shirt and the new Wembley Stadium being featured suggest it is now 2007, the year of this film’s release.

tropes.name: "Could Have Avoided This!" Plot
tropes.html: If the kids didn't decide to sneak out from the apartment and outside the district, none of the film's events would have occurred.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: Weeks is a significantly darker film than Days. Not only is the film more violent, it shows a new outbreak happening, which means the audience actually sees a massive body count on screen, instead of arriving after it has already happened. Additionally, the film depicts the graphic deaths of the elderly, children, and mothers, something the original film also chose to mostly do offscreen. Finally, Weeks has a Downer Ending instead of Days's canon ending which is presented as triumphant.

tropes.name: Death by Pragmatism
tropes.html: Inverted. When the quarantined civilians inside Sector One initially break out, chased by/mixed with Infected, the U.S. soldiers are ordered to only fire on infected. This causes their lines to be swamped by panicking civilians and infected that weren't identified fast enough. Since the crowd of civilians and infected were coming out of one large set of doors, with multiple automatic weapons trained on it, if the soldiers had unloaded immediately on everyone coming through, they might have been able to stop the infection right there.

tropes.name: Decoy Protagonist
tropes.html: Robert Carlyle's character Don who we start the movie following is either this or a Sacrificial Lion.

tropes.name: Distant Prologue
tropes.html: The first roughly ten minutes of the movie take place in the midst of the original outbreak in Britain, before Jim in the first movie woke from his coma, chronicling how Don left his wife Alice behind during an Infected attack where she was overrun. The movie then skips ahead to the main time frame, twenty-eight weeks after Jim's awakening on Day 28.

tropes.name: Downer Ending
tropes.html: London has been decimated once again by the virus and the subsequent firebombing, all of the thousands of London settlers have been horribly killed, and the Infected have made it to France. The survivors' fates are left up in the air - it's possible they survived, but the plague spread to the mainland via Andy. 28 Years Later reveals the virus was stopped by nuking Paris.

tropes.name: Eiffel Tower Effect
tropes.html: We know that the final scene takes place in France by the fact that the Eiffel Tower appears in the background.

tropes.name: Elites Are More Glamorous
tropes.html: Doyle is a Sniper with Delta Force. It reflects in his pure Badassness.

tropes.name: "End Is Nigh" Ending
tropes.html: The film ends with Infected rampaging in Paris 28 days after the main time frame, meaning that after two movies of being confined to Britain, the Rage virus has broken containment and looks set to inflict Britain's fate upon all of continental Europe and possibly also continental Asia.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html: Doyle is introduced joking with Flynn. Later, when he spots a couple having sex, he laughs incredulously and moves on to watch Tammy and Andy jumping on their beds, which charms him. All of this establishes that Doyle is a pretty good dude.

tropes.name: Evil States of America
tropes.html: American soldiers are the antagonists as they slaughter all the civilians in the containment zone. Two soldiers defy their orders and try to get the two kids to safety so that their resistance can be studied to potentially create a cure or vaccination, but they get no cooperation from command, leading to the contagion breaking quarantine.

tropes.name: Eye Scream
tropes.html: After reuniting with his wife, Don gets infected by the virus and kills Alice by gouging her eyes out. This is a direct comparison to the first movie's hero, who does the same to a soldier without being infected.

tropes.name: False Reassurance
tropes.html: "Everything's fine, I'll be back in a moment." The soldier does return in a moment, but as an infected.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: Scarlett notes that Andy's heterochromia can run in the family, foreshadowing other genetic abnormalities that he might have inherited.

tropes.name: Friendly Sniper
tropes.html: Doyle, a Delta Force sniper, decides to abandon his post after the military decides to kill everyone to keep the virus contained. He spends the rest of his time in the movie protecting the main characters and other survivors.

tropes.name: Go Mad from the Apocalypse
tropes.html: In the distant prologue set in the midst of the original 28-day outbreak, Alice is a sane and stable survivor before she loses all her comrades in the countryside during an Infected attack. Twenty-eight weeks after Jim in the first film woke from his coma, when a solitary Alice is found by her son, she's near-catatonic and has been living in squalid conditions in a den that she's made in her family's old London house, barely able to string words or sentences together, and oblivious to the giant U.S. military presence that has swooped in and has been constructing a huge safe zone next door to her den for weeks.

tropes.name: Harbinger of Impending Doom
tropes.html:
When a frantic child is allowed into the barricaded home that Don, Alice, and a group of other survivors are holed up in just weeks after the infection began, his arrival portends the events to come.
Child: My mum, my dad... They're trying to kill me. There's others too.
Don: How many others?
Child: ... Loads.

tropes.name: Helicopter Blender
tropes.html: When Flynn's helicopter is spiraling out of control thanks to an unwanted passenger, he manages to make do with his situation and leans the helicopter towards an approaching horde of infected, blades first. It's as graphic and wonderful and horrifying as much of the film.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html:
• Doyle pushes off the others to safety before getting torched by one of the extermination squads. Possibly foreshadowed with this line:
    "Their [Tammy's and Andy's] lives are far more valuable than mine...or yours."
  • The people in the basement safe room when an infected Don bursts in. Even as everybody is screaming and panicking, they have enough clearheadedness to recognize Andy as a child, lift him up over their heads and crowd-surf him over the carnage, and then shove him into a ventilation shaft knowing only he would fit in.

tropes.name: Horrifying Intro, Calm First Chapter
tropes.html: The first fifteen minutes introduce a group of survivors amid the first Rage Virus outbreak, only for the Infected to find their safehouse and tear their way through its defences, resulting in the inhabitants being almost completely wiped out. Don, having run for his life, is the only survivor. The movie then cuts to twenty-eight weeks later, after all the Infected have succumbed to natural causes, and chipper American soldiers are repopulating London with wide-eyed kids who escaped the outbreak abroad.

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html:
• If either the Chief Medical Officer or Sgt. Doyle had bothered to explain why the children were so important, even to the children, someone might have been more careful and we might just have avoided the infection of France and the breach of the sea border which was holding back the infection.
  • The lack of the most basic security measures in District One. No effective barrier on bridges and few guards. It's about as easy as sneaking out of high school grounds during lunch break.
  • The lack of any Anti-Rage security measures. No panic rooms. Individual homes are not fortified. Furthermore, the soldier put all the civilians in one big room, which is perfect to spread the Rage.
  • If the military had placed even one guard on a woman they had every reason to believe was an asymptomatic infected, or ordered one placed on her immediately after they confirmed this, all would have been well.

tropes.name: It Can Think
tropes.html: The Infected in this movie seem to have a bit more going on upstairs than the ones in 28 Days Later, particularly Don, who not only manages to survive the firebombing of District 1, but tracks his children through London all the way to the Underground. He also uses a gun as a blunt weapon when he kills Major Scarlett. He's not the only Infected to survive District 1, either, which implies he's not the only one who's retained some measure of intelligent reasoning.

tropes.name: Jerk with a Heart of Gold
tropes.html: Jacob, in only ten minutes of total screentime in the opening of the movie, comes across as extremely cynical and rude, angrily putting down Karen's delusions that her boyfriend is going to come back alive in a harsh and brusque manner. Despite this, he still rushes to help her when the Infected attack her first, and he furthermore lingers to try and save the elderly couple amid the Infected attack until there's absolutely no hope of saving either of them.

tropes.name: Love Hurts
tropes.html: And how. An estranged couple, each thinking the other dead, reunites and is happy that they're both alive and well... and kiss, starting the plague anew (and directly leading to the Eye Scream mentioned above).

tropes.name: Man on Fire
tropes.html: Doyle is set on fire with a flamethrower by a clean-up crew after he sacrifices himself to give their car a push start.

tropes.name: Mercy Kill
tropes.html: Doyle shoots a soldier being attacked by the infected to spare him a much more painful death.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html: You singlehandedly thwarted the attempt to repopulate Britain and spread the infection to continental Europe! I hope you're happy!

tropes.name: Oddball in the Series
tropes.html: As of the release of 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple, 28 Weeks Later stands out for a few reasons among the other films in the series. It is the only film without close involvement of Alex Garland and Danny Boyle (mostly being handed off to an outside director, screenwriter, and DP), it was shot entirely on film (Days and The Bone Temple were shot on digital cameras, and Years was shot on the Iphone 15 Pro Max), it focuses entirely on action and suspense over a Central Theme, and has a Downer Ending, instead of a happy or Bittersweet Ending.

tropes.name: Outrun the Fireball
tropes.html: While the US Military is fire bombing the surface, the survivors manage to barely outrun the explosion after making their way underground. And impressively enough so does the Infected Don.

tropes.name: Pistol-Whipping
tropes.html: After the Infected Don catches up to the remaining survivors, he fights Scarlet and steals Doyle's gun from her before using it to bash her head in with the butt of the rifle.

tropes.name: Pre-Apocalyptic Conclusion
tropes.html: The movie ends with the closing shots revealing that the virus has broken out in France, meaning the whole of continental Europe — and potentially also continental Asia and Africa — are now more than likely doomed to share the same fate as Britain.

tropes.name: Quarantine Failure
tropes.html:
• The military maintains a fortified quarantine district within London for survivors to wait out the Rage virus that overran Britain in the first film. Despite its Quarantine with Extreme Prejudice policy, it falls apart:
  • One of the main characters is bitten and becomes a Typhoid Mary. Despite this, he lets a sympathetic pilot take him to France, spreading the virus into continental Europe.

tropes.name: Room Full of Zombies
tropes.html: One of the infected creates this by getting into a room of normal people during a lockdown.

tropes.name: Scylla and Charybdis
tropes.html: As Code Red was being executed, a survivor in a warehouse remarked, "We take one step out that door, if the infected don't get us, the snipers will."

tropes.name: Shoot Everything That Moves
tropes.html: When the American military is unable to stop the spread of the contagion, they move to the final stage of containment: killing every civilian in Britain.

tropes.name: Shoot the Shaggy Dog
tropes.html: The virus spreads to France.

tropes.name: Technically Living Zombie
tropes.html: The Infected, again.

tropes.name: Time Title
tropes.html: The story begins twenty-eight weeks after the events of the first film.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html:
• The Virus wiped out the entire population of Britain in under a month, but apparently despite the fact that the Virus was only contained due to Great Britain being an island, the U.S. military deemed a mere six months to be enough time to adequately classify it as safe. Realistically, Great Britain would have been kept under a UN Quarantine for decades if not centuries to eliminate any lingering trace of The Virus before any attempt at recolonisation began.
  • There are multiple instances throughout this movie where the second outbreak would have been easily prevented if only the US military had decided to post more guards or have additional security measures, leading to a situation where instead of being crazy, the guards don't appear to even exist!
  • The little kid from the prologue. Whilst he can be forgiven for not losing the infected pursuing him before knocking on the first door he saw in desperation (it's actually impressive that he got far enough ahead of the infected that they weren't anywhere in sight when he was on the doorstep), when the infected attack the house several minutes later, the boy decides to run away instead of staying with the others.
  • The adults in the prologue don't figure out that the infected following the children will probably have followed him to their house and thus could be hammering at their windows and doors at any moment.
  • The old woman at the start of the film. Instead of running away from the infected, she decides to stay behind and argue with her husband.

tropes.name: Typhoid Mary
tropes.html: Alice is an asymptomatic Rage carrier, and it's shown at the end that Andy has become one as well.

tropes.name: Unbuilt Trope
tropes.html: Of the Technically Living Zombie, continuing from the previous film. While the rage virus is devastating in the short term, the infected's mindlessness leaves them with no ability to care for themselves, and the film begins after Britain's hordes have died off from simple starvation and dehydration.

tropes.name: Villain Has a Point
tropes.html: Despite the moral grey area in what they do, the US military's ultimate goal is to prevent the virus from spreading to the rest of the world, which could bring about the end of humanity. And if the US government had succeeded in killing the survivors, Andy would never have brought the Rage virus across the English channel and presumably infected France.

tropes.name: Viewers Are Goldfish
tropes.html: About 15 minutes after the opening we're treated to a flashback to it.

tropes.name: Zombie Apocalypse
tropes.html: The Technically Living Zombie apocalypse from the first film is revealed to have been successfully contained in Britain, but it's not quite over yet.

tropes.name: Zombie Puke Attack
tropes.html: Some "infected" constantly hemorrhage high-pressure blood out of their mouths.

tropes.name: Freeze-Frame Ending
tropes.html: As the zombies rush at the survivor in "Welcome to London."

tropes.name: Interquel
tropes.html: "77 Days Later" is explicitly this. Jim can be heard calling for help early in the short, clarifying that the protagonist is up on the roof at the same time as Selena and Mark meet up with Jim, and then it ends as NATO forces fly into Britain for the beginning of 28 Weeks Later.

tropes.name: My God, What Have I Done?
tropes.html: One survivor in "Welcome to London" smashes an attacker's head in with a brick - only to realize, after he's dead, that he wasn't infected. This is enough to drive the survivor over the Despair Event Horizon and he gives up in the face of the (actual) infected.

tropes.name: Not Quite Saved Enough
tropes.html:
• "Jealous Rage" ends with the husband and wife being reunited, both still alive. However, when he realizes that she's been cheating on him and their baby is dead, he locks her in the bedroom with their Rage-infected baby.
  • The protagonist of "77 Days Later" dies by slashed wrists in the throes of suicidal despair....as he looks up and sees the helicopters from NATO arriving to clear the area.

tropes.name: Rouge Angles of Satin
tropes.html: In "77 Days Later", "martial law" is spelled as "Marshall law."

tropes.name: Shirtless Scene
tropes.html: The survivor in "77 Days Later" spends much of time on the rooftop shirtless.

tropes.name: Sexy Shirt Switch
tropes.html: Implied. The wife in "Jealous Rage" is wearing an oversized men's shirt and has presumably been meeting her now-dead boyfriend.

tropes.name: The Scourge of God
tropes.html: In "Jealous Rage", the cheating wife and her boyfriend are both killed (though the wife is Killed Offscreen), while the faithful husband is apparently spared.

tropes.name: While Rome Burns
tropes.html: In "The End is Extremely Fucking Nigh", a pair of friends get high and smoke as they watch the burning of a major city (likely a bombing).

tropes.name: Abusive Parents
tropes.html: Paula, particularly in Act Two. She gets better and expresses sincere regret for her actions in Act Three.

tropes.name: Abusive Personality Shift
tropes.html: ZigZagged with Chiron's mother who starts out as loving, but as she descends to addiction, and becomes frustrated with her child's visibly campy mannerisms, she begins yelling at him and, is implied ot yell a homophobic slur at him in a moment shown in silent slow motion, and in his teen years, is mostly absent and neglectful. In the third act, the adult Chiron visit his mother who is in an inpatient rehab facility, and she does apologize for her past behavior, though we can hardly see any reaction from him, as he has been hardened by prison and working in the drug trade.

tropes.name: Addiction Displacement
tropes.html: Paula has switched from drugs to regular cigarettes when apologizing to Chiron.

tropes.name: The Aggressive Drug Dealer
tropes.html: Averted with Juan. While his job is never glamorized or portrayed as being okay, exactly, it's never demonized, either. He's never seen pushing his product on anyone, and avoids discussing it with Chiron, until Chiron asks him point-blank if he's a dealer. Juan is portrayed as a likable, honest, genuinely nice guy who's a good father figure to Chiron — selling drugs is just his job.

tropes.name: All of the Other Reindeer
tropes.html: Chiron was viciously ostracized throughout his life.

tropes.name: Ambiguously Bi
tropes.html: Kevin's sexuality is never identified explicitly, though he seems to be attracted to women as well as Chiron, and mentions that he fathered a child with one of his ex-girlfriends. Chiron himself seems to spend a lot of his time in the "Black" segment figuring out whether Kevin is still attracted to men.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Criminal History
tropes.html: Adult Kevin has been to prison and is still on parole for 18 months at the time of meeting Chiron, for "some stupid shit, same stupid shit we always get sent up for."

tropes.name: Amicable Exes
tropes.html: Downplayed. Act 3 has Kevin reveal to be a father and admits that while he and his son's mother don't like each other, they do get along for their kid's sake.

tropes.name: Anguished Declaration of Love
tropes.html: The film ends with Chiron tearfully admitting his love for Kevin, who reciprocates.

tropes.name: Appropriated Appellation
tropes.html: After originally disliking the nickname, Chiron eventually starts answering to "Black" in Atlanta.

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html:
• When Juan confronts Paula about how her drug use hurts Chiron, Paula mockingly asks him why, if he cares so much, he doesn't just stop selling drugs to her. His answering silence says it all.
  • And when Chiron, after asking Juan if he sells drugs, asks if his Mom does drugs. Not only is Juan silent in response, but he seems near tears.

tropes.name: Babies Ever After
tropes.html: Downplayed. The woman with who Kevin had a son isn't seen in either of the first two Acts.

tropes.name: Bath of Poverty
tropes.html: Early on, Chiron is shown heating water over the stove and using dish detergent for his bath because his mother can't afford hot running water or bath soap.

tropes.name: Beware the Quiet Ones
tropes.html: Chiron spends most of his youth being viciously bullied by almost everyone around him for being socially withdrawn, but we see glimpses of his breaking point when Terrel repeatedly harasses him over his mom and Juan's girlfriend. Chiron eventually snaps to the point he breaks a wooden chair over Terrel's head, causing him enough pain that he starts curling up on the floor, showing that he had potential for violence all along.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: Chiron is forced to sell drugs to support himself thanks to having prior record with his physical response to homophobic bullying he went through in his youth, he's scarred enough to have never formed any intimate relationships since high school, and it's heavily implied that most of the damage done to him is permanent. However, despite all that, he ultimately reconciles with his mother and Kevin, starting a relationship with the latter and thus finally coming to terms with his sexuality, showing that at least some of his wounds will heal.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: In "Little", the film's first act, Chiron's surrogate father figure, Juan, makes ends meet by dealing crack at the height of the drug's epidemic. In "Black", the film's final act, Chiron is himself forced to sell drugs to make ends meet after being arrested for assaulting Terrel.

tropes.name: Break the Haughty
tropes.html: Implied with Terrel. After Chiron breaks a chair over his head, he curls up into a ball on his side as tightly as he can, implying that he's crying from the pain and doesn't want anyone to see.

tropes.name: The Bully
tropes.html: Terrel constantly harasses and belittles Chiron.

tropes.name: Bully Brutality
tropes.html: Terrel is a homoantagonistic asshole. He constantly harasses Chiron, culminating in pressuring Kevin, Chiron's Only Friend, to hit Chiron. After which Terrel and his posse kick the downed Chiron.

tropes.name: Bully Magnet
tropes.html: Poor Chiron had it worse ever since he was a little kid. Though he represses his feelings of homosexuality throughout his adolescence, he still becomes a target for the bullies because of his social awkwardness, frail physique and for not being traditionally masculine. It's only after Chiron stands up to one of his bullies and beats them senseless when he becomes noticeably manlier and masculine, though this is mostly just a front he uses to adapt into the harsher reality of adulthood.

tropes.name: Bury Your Gays
tropes.html: Averted. While the film is frequently tragic (some of which is due to Chiron being attacked by homophobic bullies), none of the gay or bi characters die.

tropes.name: But for Me, It Was Tuesday
tropes.html: Both a downplayed and non-malicious example. Chiron's sexual encounter with Kevin was a hugely life-shaping event. For Kevin, it wasn't forgotten, but it wasn't the life-changing event that it was for Chiron.

tropes.name: Calling the Old Man Out
tropes.html: Chiron only has a few words to say as an adult when Paula says she didn't become clean for him to end up as a drug dealer, but they are tinged with anger about her hypocrisy and that she only seems to care when it's too late. In fact, he threatens to leave and he can this time since he's independent and doesn't rely on his mother to feed or house him. It's only because Paula apologizes and says he doesn't owe her any love that he's willing to hear her out.

tropes.name: Camp Gay
tropes.html: As a child, Chiron loves dancing, and during a confrontation between Juan and Paula, Paula, Chiron's mother talks about "the way he walks" and how that makes him a Bully Magnet. After going to jail for taking revenge on his bully, Chiron grows up in the criminal underworld, and has to erase every trace of his mannerisms, growing up to become almost an Armored Closet Gay.

tropes.name: Cannot Spit It Out
tropes.html: The last sequence of the movie is a particularly well-done version. Both Chiron and Kevin keep dancing in circles before the declaration of love comes.

tropes.name: Capitalism Is Bad
tropes.html: Implied Trope. The characters never outright say this, but the poverty the characters experience is implied to be a significant contributing factor to their criminal activities, since they have to eat somehow, and they have few or no options to support themselves outside the criminal underworld.

tropes.name: Celebrity Paradox
tropes.html: A musical example; in the "Black" segment, Chiron listens to Jidenna's "Classic Man," the video for which features Janelle Monáe.

tropes.name: Character Development
tropes.html:
Rather than story, this is the central focus of the film. Nearly every major character who appears in more than one act has an arc towards self-acceptance or maturity.
  • Kevin shows this the most. He starts as a kid trying to fit in, and is coerced by a bully into beating up his best friend for the crime of being gay. Kevin knows it's his fault that Chiron snaps the next day by beating up Terrel with a chair, which leads to the former's life of crime. Even so, it takes ten years and fathering a child for him to muster the courage to find Chiron, who now goes by Black, and apologize to him. Chiron knows that Kevin is sincere in his apology because the latter has a stable life as a cook and presumably had relationships with women. Kevin also seems to implicitly promise he'll help Chiron escape the life of drug dealing.

tropes.name: Childhood Friend Romance
tropes.html: Chiron has one of these with Kevin. It ends when Chiron is sent to juvie, but possibly reinstated when they meet again as adults.

tropes.name: Coming of Age Story
tropes.html: The major theme of the work is Chiron growing and finding out who he is.

tropes.name: Coming-Out Story
tropes.html: A downplayed example as we never see Chiron truly "out" himself publicly, but the movie ends with Chiron accepting himself and his love for another man. The downplaying of this is a huge case of Truth in Television for LGBT+ individuals of color, for whom the "coming out" narrative is a rarity in part due to the difficulties involved with intersecting identities, which has historically led to them being misperceived by white LGBT+ individuals as self-hating or as suffering from internalized homophobia. Given this, the film acts as a vivid showcase of the additional tribulations black gay men face compared to their white counterparts and how many of their own experiences with coming to terms with their sexuality are forced into subtlety as a result of these hardships.

tropes.name: Cool Car
tropes.html: Juan drives a baby blue 1973 Chevrolet Impala on large chrome rims, and later, Chiron drives a black 1978 Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme with a souped up engine. Both have a crown shaped air freshener on their dashboard. Chiron's car also has a custom plate "BLACK305" referencing both his nickname, and the area code for Miami.

tropes.name: Cool Kid-and-Loser Friendship
tropes.html: Deconstructed. Part 2 shows that Chiron is still ostracized by his peers while Kevin has become somewhat popular. However, their relationship proves to be detrimental given how Terrel pressured Kevin into beating up Chiron.

tropes.name: Crossing the Burnt Bridge
tropes.html: It makes up a huge portion of the third act. Paula has been asking Chiron to visit her in rehab several times. Kevin calls, inviting Chiron to dinner in Miami. Both of them betrayed him in act two, in different ways. Understandably, Chiron goes to the visits expecting nothing, only more disappointment.

tropes.name: Death Glare
tropes.html: Chiron has turned this into an art form as an adult; he spends most of the time glaring stonily. Subverted by the fact that in his case it's a non-threatening gesture, but a trait he inherited from his childhood. He's rather taciturn and often prefers others to lead his conversations, meaning for the most part he's awkwardly staring at the other person as they navigate the discussion. The few exceptions where this trope is almost literally applicable is during his confrontations with the middle-school bullies in the second act, and towards his Mother (and Kevin towards the end of ii) where it's used to express dejection and/or defiance.

tropes.name: Delinquents
tropes.html: Chiron's retaliation towards Terrel lands him in juvie. As a result, the third act has a considerable amount of discussion on how that path shaped him.

tropes.name: Descent into Addiction
tropes.html: Paula's struggle with crack is documented over three acts, as she regresses from a relatively functional addict in Act One to an addled addict in Act Two. In Act Three, we learn she's a recovered addict.

tropes.name: Dirty Coward
tropes.html: Terrel spends a majority of his screen time getting his peers to help him beat up Chiron. When Chrion retaliates by breaking a chair over Terrel's head, Terrel crumples to the floor and doesn't get up. As Chiron is being forcibly led out of the room following his violent act, Terrel can be seen curling as hard as he can into a ball, presumably crying in pain. This heavily contrasts Chiron who, despite being physically weak and alone, never completely gives in to being bullied and defies his bullies even after being repeatedly beaten and harassed.

tropes.name: Disappeared Dad
tropes.html: Juan asks Little if he knows where his father is. He does not, which leads to Juan becoming a Parental Substitute.

tropes.name: Drugs Are Bad
tropes.html: Much more nuanced than this trope is normally handled. Drugs are more portrayed as tragic than outright bad. Paula's addiction is a terrible thing, of course, but she's still ultimately portrayed sympathetically and Juan and Black are both drug dealers whose personalities (but NOT their trade) are shown in a positive light, even though their profession is seen In-Universe as being unfortunate.

tropes.name: Earn Your Happy Ending
tropes.html: Chiron suffers horrifically throughout the film, but eventually comes to a point of self-acceptance and manages to renew his romance with Kevin.

tropes.name: Early Personality Signs
tropes.html: Chiron's awkwardness, quietness, and social distance is seen in the first act and carries all the way to the third.

tropes.name: Elemental Motifs
tropes.html: Water always surrounds Chiron. He was "baptized" in the river by Juan, has his first sexual experience with Kevin near the ocean, compares himself to a bundle of drops that just want to roll away, soaks his face in ice near the end of Act 2 and in the beginning of Act 3, and the film ends with a young Chiron facing a body of water.

tropes.name: Et Tu, Brute?
tropes.html: Kevin is Chiron's Only Friend in school and First Love so Terrel coercing Kevin into attacking Chiron is his breaking point, leading him to finally retaliate.

tropes.name: Erotic Dream
tropes.html: As a teen, Chiron dreams about Kevin having sex with a girl. As an adult, after the call from Kevin, he has a dream of him, and wakes up with a stain on his boxers.

tropes.name: Foil
tropes.html:
Paula and her unnamed companion serve largely to highlight their differences to Teresa and Juan.
  • Paula is Chiron's biological mother who frowns upon Juan's relationship with Little, yet Teresa is shown to be more a mother to Chiron than Paula ever could be. Paula sneers at how Chiron might be gay, while Teresa is open and accepting. In the second act, Paula even forces Chiron from home for the night and Teresa is there for him, ready and willing to help him with anything he needs.
  • Like Juan, Paula's companion refers to Chiron as "Little Man" and is tied to the underworld of drugs. Unlike Juan, he does not care about Little's well-being and instead is making his homelife even worse by enabling Paula's drug habit.

tropes.name: Forgiveness
tropes.html:
Forgiveness
  • For all the reasons he has to be angry at her, including the emotional and physical abuse, Black eventually works up the courage to visit his mother in rehab and forgive her. She tells him he doesn't have to, considering all that she's done, and he only needs to know that she loves him.
  • Kevin beat up Chiron in high school, and allowed the local bully to beat him up further, as a result of peer pressure. It takes years for Kevin to look up Chiron, who has now become a drug dealer and essentially trapped in that world thanks to the bullying, and to apologize to him. They end up rekindling their relationship.

tropes.name: Friendly Neighborhood Gangster
tropes.html: Juan is a fairly prominent drug-dealer in his neighborhood, but he's friendly to his employees, his clients, and he winds up taking a neighborhood youth under his wing just because.

tropes.name: Gayngst
tropes.html: By age 11 this is already factoring into Chiron's life. It contributes to his "otherness" and even his own mother screams homophobic slurs at him. In both childhood acts it's the bullies' favorite reason for picking on Chiron.

tropes.name: Gayngster
tropes.html: Chiron grows up to be a heavily muscled drug dealer, who's in love with another man.

tropes.name: Generation Xerox
tropes.html: Black is a drug dealer who clearly styles himself after his Parental Substitute Juan. Aside from the career "choice," he drives a car similar to Juan's (with an identical dashboard ornament and warning lights in similar places) and his personal appearance and mannerisms echo Juan's.

tropes.name: Gold Tooth of Wealth
tropes.html: grown up Chiron wears gold fronts, something Kevin is shocked seeing on him. Paired with a long gold chain, a gold watch and a bracelet, and his Cool Car show that he's been doing well as a drug dealer.

tropes.name: Grey-and-Gray Morality
tropes.html: Everybody, including the drug dealers, are just trying to deal with the hand life gave them. The closest thing to a villain is Chiron's bully. Even Paula, shown in the second act in a particularly harsh light, is proven to ultimately be a decent person that's been dealt a rough hand but is striving to redeem herself and keep herself clean. Borders on White-and-Grey Morality, but none of its characters (apart from possibly Teresa) is depicted without any significant flaws.

tropes.name: Had to Come to Prison to Be a Crook
tropes.html: Chiron was a good kid, pushed past his breaking point and retaliated against a borderline psychopathic bully. But it set him down a path that he couldn't break free from, ultimately becoming a drug dealer.

tropes.name: Hate Sink
tropes.html: In a movie full of complex characters who operate on White-and-Grey Morality, Terrel is probably the only outright evil or sadistic one.

tropes.name: Have I Mentioned I Am Heterosexual Today?
tropes.html: In the second act, Kevin is introduced talking about having sex with a girl, despite the fact that it soon becomes clear that he's more than likely bisexual.

tropes.name: Have I Mentioned I Am Sexually Active Today?
tropes.html: Combined with Have I Mentioned I Am Heterosexual Today?, Kevin was introduced in the second act stealth-bragging about getting caught by a teacher having sex with a girl. The veracity of the statement is... indeterminate, given teenagers' tendency to inflate the truth.

tropes.name: Homage
tropes.html: The cinematography and the visual style of this film homages Wong Kar-wai many times. Similarly, during a scene you can hear a version of Cucurrucucu Paloma, sung by Caetano Veloso, which was previously used in Wong Kar Wai's Happy Together and Almodovar's Talk to Her, both films that touch the same topics of identity and masculinity that this movie does.

tropes.name: Horrible Housing
tropes.html: Paula and Chiron's living situation goes from modest to bad to worse from the beginning of the film, through Paula's Descent into Addiction, to the point that when Chiron is a teenager their home is an untidy hovel.

tropes.name: Humans Are Flawed
tropes.html: As mentioned under Rousseau Was Right, this film has elements of both tropes. Its Grey-and-Gray Morality certainly recalls this trope, as do the unpleasantness of the setting and the significant, destructive social challenges its characters face. However, ultimately most of its characters are shown, beneath their flaws, to be decent people overall, probably pushing it closer to Rousseau Was Right.

tropes.name: Humble Goal
tropes.html: Kevin says that a meager existence as a short order cook, barely scraping by monetarily, isn't much, but it's a life, which he never had before.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html:
• Paula initially doesn't want Little to consort with Juan, a drug dealer despite the fact that she herself is a junkie.
  • Paula also throws this back at Juan who is furious that she's a crack-addict despite the fact that she gets it from his organization.

tropes.name: I Got Bigger
tropes.html: Skinny, quiet "Little" grows up to be a strong, barrel-chested man, and Kevin wryly comments on the change a few times.

tropes.name: Idiosyncratic Episode Naming
tropes.html: Each of the film's three acts is named after the name Chiron goes by during it: "Little," "Chiron," and "Black."

tropes.name: The Immodest Orgasm
tropes.html: Chiron experiences this on the beach while Kevin gives the former a handjob while the two share a kiss.

tropes.name: In-Universe Catharsis
tropes.html: Subverted. Terrel is set up to be such a Hate Sink when Chiron finally reaching his Rage Breaking Point and smacking him over the head with a chair seems cathartic for him. However, the rest of the film examines how this negatively impacts Chiron's life going forward. Despite being a fundamentally decent person, he ends up becoming defined by this single act in his life, and he ultimately ends up in a life of crime because he has few or no other options.

tropes.name: Inherent in the System
tropes.html: Apart from Terrel, none of the characters are depicted as bad people, but the film also implies that few of them had much in the way of choices, and their actions are depicted as being largely the results of their circumstances. As a result, the film's portrayal of both addicts and drug dealers is more sympathetic than the usual one, but it does so without glamorising their circumstances at all.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html: By the time Paula gets clean, and to break from the cycle of drug abuse, her only child has become a dealer.

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: Terrel is definitely this. He's an intensely homophobic bigot to an almost homicidal degree who convinces his friends to beat up Chiron and pressures his Only Friend do the same. He's also pretty hostile to other students as well, with a small detail of him pushing one of them for simply bumping into him.

tropes.name: Jerkass Realization
tropes.html:
• It's implied that Kevin felt this after beating up Chiron, when Chiron fought back by beating the tar out of Terrel. Ten years of growing up and having a kid of his own make him realize that he needs to apologize to Chiron for ruining his life. It goes further when he learns that Chiron has become a drug dealer, probably due to the criminal record, and is upset about that.
  • Chrion's mother Paula has been staying long term at a rehab facility later in life, and apologizes to Chiron for his difficult childhood when he visits her.

tropes.name: Junkie Parent
tropes.html: Chiron's mother cares more about drugs than her own son. She's very neglectful and abusive.

tropes.name: Karma Houdini Warranty
tropes.html: Kevin beats up Chiron under the influence of peer pressure. He gets off scot-free, while Chiron is sent to juvie for attacking Terrel with a chair. We find out that Kevin later had various relationships with women and has a legitimate job as a short-order cook in a diner. Kevin is legitimately bowled-over and guilty when Chiron casually reveals that thanks to his criminal record, he decided to go into drug dealing because there weren't many options for him. Chiron also points out Kevin has no right to judge him, after what happened.

tropes.name: Kids Are Cruel
tropes.html: Chiron's first scene is him being chased by a Gang of Bullies, and his Only Friend is Kevin, who only talks to him when no one else is around. Later, even Kevin turns on him at Terrel's instigation, and when Terrel and his friends beat Chiron down, no other students come to his defense.

tropes.name: Killed Offscreen
tropes.html: Juan dies between Acts I and II. The funeral is given a casual mention in the second act, averting characters mentioning it awkwardly to tell the audience.

tropes.name: Latino Is Brown
tropes.html: Lampshaded by Juan. Being a black Cuban he is an aversion, but he acknowledges the prevalence of this perception when he says most Americans don't realize there are black people living all over the world.

tropes.name: Love Redeems
tropes.html: By the end of the film. Chiron has reconciled with Kevin and his mother. This redeems all of them.

tropes.name: Manly Gay
tropes.html: Grown up Chiron aka. "Black" is muscular, silent, dresses in dark clothes (save for the gold jewelry around his neck and wrists and teeth) and drives a muscle car, and works as a boss for a group of drug dealers with a gun on his side.

tropes.name: Manly Tears
tropes.html: Juan silently breaks down in the aftermath of Chiron's Armor-Piercing Question. Later, Kevin's apology for his actions as a teenager causes Chiron to shed a tear.

tropes.name: Maybe Ever After
tropes.html: Throughout the third section Chiron and Kevin skirt around discussing their teen romance, until Chiron finally admits that he's never touched another man since Kevin. The movie ends with them silently sitting on the bed together, Kevin with his arm around Chiron's shoulder, leaving it unclear whether Kevin has actually returned Chiron's affections or is simply comforting a troubled friend. The original screenplay, however, clears this up by including the beginning of their sexual encounter that night.

tropes.name: Meaningful Rename
tropes.html: Juan explains to Little that a man chooses what he's called. As such, as a teen Chiron refuses to be called "Little" anymore, and as an adult takes the name Black.

tropes.name: Mentor Occupational Hazard
tropes.html: Juan dies sometime between "Little" and "Chiron".

tropes.name: Must Make Amends
tropes.html: Kevin invited Chiron to Miami to apologize for what he did, and to try to offer a better life.

tropes.name: Nice Guy
tropes.html:
• Even though Juan sells drugs, he clearly acts as a caring and loving father figure for Chiron.
  • Teresa, who acts as a mother figure to Chiron when Chiron's actual mother falls short (And she falls short in many ways.)

tropes.name: Monochrome Casting
tropes.html: The film has an all-black cast. White extras aren't even seen until the third act.

tropes.name: My God, What Have I Done?
tropes.html: Paula is crying when admitting she knows Chiron's life is messed up because of her bad parenting. She says he doesn't owe her any love or forgiveness.

tropes.name: No Antagonist
tropes.html: Other than the harshness of the setting, there is no primary antagonist in the film; the closest being the kids who bully Chiron.

tropes.name: Nocturnal Emission
tropes.html: Chiron has one while dreaming about Kevin after he calls him unexpectedly one night.

tropes.name: Nurture over Nature
tropes.html: In the whole Nature Versus Nurture debate, Moonlight falls over to the "nurture" side. All the characters live in poverty and deal with drugs and violence throughout their neighborhood, however Chiron doesn't ( at least, not at first) and sticks out like a sore thumb due to his nature and how he dresses and acts. The other characters either deal or do drugs and/or partake in violent activity but it's clear that underneath it all, they're just trying to survive and navigate and they're ultimately decent people (barring Terrel from the second act).

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: Kevin as an adult has this as a dawning reaction when Chiron reveals, without changing his tone, that when he was in juvie, a drug dealer recruited him to run a block when he was released, and he has since become a lord in his own right.

tropes.name: Once Done, Never Forgotten
tropes.html:
• Played for Drama. Chiron becomes defined in the legal/educational systems by his single act of striking Terrel over the head with a chair, which is implied to be a direct cause of his occupation as a drug dealer in the third act: people with criminal records have extremely difficult times finding legitimate employment in much of the United States.
  • Chiron is initially cool with Kevin when they reunite about a few decades later, and a bit confused about why the latter wants the former in his life again. He obviously hasn't forgotten the bullying. Kevin has the decency to look guilty about beating up Chiron as a kid, while skirting around the issue. It's not until Kevin apologizes that Chiron starts to soften.

tropes.name: Parental Substitute
tropes.html: Juan and Teresa act as surrogate parents to Chiron in his youth, since his mother is a drug addict and his father is out of the picture. The irony of this is noted by Chiron's mother, however — because Juan sells drugs to the community, he's part of why she's a Junkie Parent in the first place.

tropes.name: Pay Evil unto Evil
tropes.html: Terrel goes to such major lengths to harass Chiron for his sexuality including beating him up, that Terrel gets no sympathy when Chiron smashes a chair over him.

tropes.name: Peer-Pressured Bully
tropes.html: Terrell coerces Kevin into punching out Chiron, despite the fact that they're long friends and have recently had a homoerotic experience together. In this case it's less "to be popular" and more "to keep a target off his back" because Kevin doesn't want to have that same sadistic bully turn his sights on him.

tropes.name: Peer Pressure Makes You Evil
tropes.html: Kevin beats Chiron per Terrel's demand, which costs him the former's friendship.

tropes.name: Period Shaming
tropes.html: The film has an interesting case where the stigma against menstruation is leveraged against a cis male character, Chiron. His bully, Terrel, mockingly says that Chiron "forgot to change his tampon" in the middle of class as a way to demean and emasculate him because he's gay.

tropes.name: Rage Breaking Point
tropes.html: After being bullied for years, Chiron finally loses it after Terrel convinces Kevin to beat him up, and then Terrel and his Gang of Bullies given him a further beatdown. After breaking down in the school counselor’s office, Chiron comes in the next day, heads straight for class, picks up a wooden chair, and bashes Terrel unconscious with it.

tropes.name: Rousseau Was Right
tropes.html: Overall, Moonlight falls somewhere between this and Humans Are Flawed, but it's probably closer to this. Most of its characters are shown to be fundamentally decent people who are sometimes simply forced to do unpleasant things as a result of their circumstances. Even Paula, who is outright abusive to Chiron in the second act, ultimately becomes a reformed, sincerely repentant person in the third, and it's implied that most of her actions in the second act were consequences of her not being in her right mind. The only completely malicious character with no redeeming qualities at all is Terrel.

tropes.name: Show, Don't Tell
tropes.html: The movie is relatively light on dialogue, instead often electing to inform viewers through actions and pictures rather than words. For example, Little's declining homelife isn't explicitly stated, but rather shown by the empty space where his TV used to be (indicating that his mother pawned it for drugs) and him taking a bath by heating water on the stove while his mother is nowhere in sight.

tropes.name: Single-Target Sexuality
tropes.html: Kevin is the only person Chiron's ever been intimate with, even as an adult. Though it's ambiguous as to whether it's because of this trope or because of Chiron's lingering Gayngst.

tropes.name: Slice of Life
tropes.html: The film is a series of vignettes depicting Chiron growing up, with no straightforward plot beyond Chiron's self-realization.

tropes.name: Small Role, Big Impact
tropes.html:
• Juan only appears in roughly a third of the film, but is a huge influence Chiron's maturation into an adult. The fact that Mahershala Ali won an Oscar for the role shows just how big an impact he had on the story.
  • Terrel only appears in the second act with no real characterization beyond "bully" and even less screen time than Juan. He still ends up playing a pivotal role in Chiron's life by forcing Kevin to beat Chiron up, which drives Chiron to bash his head in with a wooden chair. Chiron gets sent to juvie as a result and by the third act has not only become a drug dealer because his criminal record makes it impossible to find legal employment, but also hasn't spoken to Kevin in over a decade.

tropes.name: Society Is to Blame
tropes.html: While not explicitly stated, it's heavily implied that Chiron mostly became a drug dealer because he didn't have any other options available to him as a result of his record. In many American states, it's difficult bordering on very nearly impossible for people with criminal convictions to find legitimate employment, so this is Truth in Television. This is also a general theme throughout the film: many people in the criminal underworld are depicted as mostly decent people who simply have few (maybe no) other options to get by. See also Inherent in the System above.

tropes.name: Spiritual Antithesis
tropes.html: To Richard Linklater's Boyhood. Both films are about a coming-of-age of a boy from his childhood to adulthood, but the two's setting and the production were a polar opposite. Boyhood took 12 years to shoot while Moonlight took a less than a month. The former used the same actor to play a straight middle-class caucasian, while the latter used three actors to play a gay lower-class black man at three stages in his life. The former took place in suburban Austin, Texas while the latter took place in a housing project area of Miami, Florida.

tropes.name: Straight Gay
tropes.html: Chiron isn't particularly flamboyant to begin with, but he becomes progressively more straight-passing as he ages into adulthood. As a kid he was instantly pegged as being gay, as an adult, less so.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Happy Ending
tropes.html: Despite the film's bleak subject matter, Chiron comes to a state of self-acceptance and renews his romance with Kevin.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html:
• It's mentioned that Teresa is still alive, and keeps in contact with Chiron. In other movies, she would be enough of a Morality Chain to help him out. Chiron loses her positive influence when he goes to juvie, and she had her own problems after Juan died. He merely tells his mother that Teresa is "fine".
  • Paula has gotten into rehab and cleaned up her life. This also causes her to have a Heel Realization about how she treated her own son while under the influence. Thing is that she only sobered up after Chiron had a stint in the prison system and realized she was a terrible mother. They even laugh about this bitterly when Paula says he can talk to her about his nightmares. For this reason, he refuses to visit her in rehab for a long time, until Kevin invites him to Miami. At one point he threatens to leave when he calls out her Parental Hypocrisy for being a druggie and then judging him for selling the same products, because his suffering as a child wasn't enough to make her stop.
  • When Kevin looks up Chiron and invites him to Miami, he makes small talk, hoping that Chiron's life is okay. He's stunned to learn that Chiron, thanks to having a criminal record which leaves him unable to hold a legitimate job, is a drug dealer. This was after he commented that Chiron had the right idea to own a car because Miami commutes are killer. How else would a convicted felon have a Cool Car?

tropes.name: Symbolic Baptism
tropes.html: Juan taking Chiron into the ocean to teach him how to swim, marking the moment when Chiron learns how to become self-reliant. Director Barry Jenkins even described it as "a baptism".

tropes.name: Three-Act Structure
tropes.html: Each act of the film depicts Chiron at a different stage in his life — as a child in "I. Little", as a teenager in "II. Chiron", and as an adult in "III. Black."

tropes.name: Time-Shifted Actor
tropes.html: Chiron is played by Alex Hibbert (child), Ashton Sanders (teen), and Trevante Rhodes (adult), while Kevin is played by Jaden Pinter (child), Jharrel Jerome (teen), and André Holland (adult).

tropes.name: Title Drop
tropes.html:
Juan's story to little Chiron at the beach, which drops the title of both the film and the unpublished play it's based on. As with most title drops it highlights one of the main themes of the film, which is the power of being your own person vs letting other people say who you are for you:
Juan: This one time, I run by this old... this old lady. I was running, howling. Kinda of a fool, boy. This old lady, she stopped me. She said...[imitates old lady voice] "Running around, catching a lot of light". "In moonlight, black boys look blue". "You're blue". "That's what I'm gonna call you: 'Blue'."

tropes.name: Toxic Friend Influence
tropes.html: Kevin's friendship with Terrel doesn't amount to anything good, especially not for Chiron.

tropes.name: The Unseen
tropes.html: Teresa isn't seen in "Black," only mentioned in conversation.

tropes.name: Used to Be a Sweet Kid
tropes.html: Early vignettes we see of Chiron as a kid show him mostly as a quiet, unassuming boy, who comes alive at dance class. Years of bullying, then a cycle of jail and work as a drug dealer turn him into the muscle-bound, gun holding Black.

tropes.name: What the Hell, Hero?
tropes.html: Chiron gives Kevin a well-deserved Death Glare for telling him that dealing drugs isn't him. As he aptly points out, Kevin made it a point to not know him. Kevin tries to respond with an Armor-Piercing Question but customers interrupt him. When he comes back, Chiron bluntly asks if Kevin called him just to tell him off.

tropes.name: What You Are in the Dark
tropes.html: By the time they are adults, Kevin has a stable job, a child, and previous relationships with women. In short, he has everything he wants, or so it seems, and can fit in with heterosexual norms. Yet Kevin realizes that he still has some mistakes to fix, and invites Chiron to Miami. Chiron is even confused as to why someone who betrayed him wants to see him again and nearly doesn't go.

tropes.name: You Are Better Than You Think You Are
tropes.html: Kevin angrily tells Chiron that he deserves more than a life dealing drugs.

tropes.name: 20 Minutes into the Past
tropes.html: The film released in 2002 and is set in 1995, the year before Eminem released his debut album.

tropes.name: The '90s
tropes.html: The film is set in 1995. Moreover, rap artists such as Wu-Tang, Mobb Deep, Biggie Smalls, and several others are heard playing throughout the film.

tropes.name: Actually Pretty Funny
tropes.html: Even Wink cracks up when Jimmy drops the line "How can six dicks be pussies?" during his climactic freestyle. In turn, you can see Rabbit crack a smile at Lotto's Leave It to Beaver line. He even admits to Sol George that the line was so good it almost got him.

tropes.name: Ad Hominem
tropes.html: A powerful tactic among rappers. This is how Jimmy wins the rap duel at the end, preempting Papa Doc's Ad Hominem rap by acknowledging he's white trash before revealing that Papa Doc is actually Clarence, a well-off lad from the upscale suburbs with a good education at Cranbrook and happily-married parents — a total alien from such a neighborhood as downtown Detroit.

tropes.name: Alcoholic Parent
tropes.html: Stephanie, Jimmy's mother.

tropes.name: Amazingly Embarrassing Parents
tropes.html: Stephanie becomes this to Jimmy when Wink and Alex drop by at his trailer.

tropes.name: At Least I Admit It
tropes.html: This is what wins Rabbit the battle against Papa Doc in the film's climax. He basically owns up to all his flaws before Papa Doc even has a chance to use it against him, something the latter didn't have the guts to do himself.

tropes.name: Audience Participation
tropes.html:
• Lil' Tic battling Rabbit in the intro:
    "Rip the rabbit head off, toss it to Hugh Hefner, 'cause I don't play boy, now tell me who's fresher?"
    "YOU ARE!"
  • Rabbit pulls it off twice in the final battle, spurring the crowd to raise their hands, and getting a response with this line from the chorus of Shook Ones, Pt. II:
    "This guy don't wanna battle, he shook, 'cause ain't no such things as..."
    "HALFWAY CROOKS!"

tropes.name: Autobiographical Role
tropes.html: This movie basically tells Eminem's life story... if he never got a record deal.

tropes.name: Aw, Look! They Really Do Love Each Other
tropes.html: Jimmy and his mother may snark at one and other, but in the end they genuinely care for each other. This is proven twice, when Jimmy fights Greg for hitting his mom and when near the end when his mom won bingo, the first thing she does is offer to make him pancakes.
