    • Finally, him being quickly replaced with Jason Momoa refers to all of Kevin Spacey's scenes in All the Money in the World being hastily reshot with Christopher Plummer after it turned out that Spacey was a sexual predator and pedophile.
  • When we're reintroduced to Jody, she's fending off various production personnel in a way that's pretty pointed at all the usual headaches of running a set – among them are smartass scriptwriters who think meta-references to the fact the third act of the movie is rushed will make it better and angry set supervisors who don't realize their constant chewing out of the guys in charge of special effects makes them less likely to respect their authority.
  • Gail is an abominable amalgamation of every Hollywood producer who sabotages movies: she's a Girlboss Feminist who misuses "toxic masculinity" at anything a man does, even when it's trying to stop her from murder, maintains Tom's "down-to-Earth actor" facade at all costs down to covering up an Accidental Murder with glee, and tries to take over the film several times, both to make sure the movie is dumbed down for the Lowest Common Denominator and also to cover up the death. Furthermore, her attempt to take over the movie is a common IRL Horrible Hollywood tactic: studio executives and "producers" will Wag the Director and force plot changes for the worst in a bid for "wide appeal" or even for Self-Fanservice at the cost of an actual film, then pin the resulting mess on the director, who'll be blackballed by every studio for a failure that wasn't their fault.

tropes.name: Tattooed Crook
tropes.html: Doone the drug dealer has his scalp tattooed with leopard spots.

tropes.name: Television Geography
tropes.html: The chase scene seemingly teleports the characters across Sydney at one point, starting beneath the Harbour Bridge, driving south through the city, exiting the city on a freeway, then suddenly back at the Harbour Bridge, this time driving through it, and heading south through the city again.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html: In the post credits scene when trying to escape the police after the helicopter crash, Tom tries to get reception as he runs to the pyrotechnics area, but as soon as he gets three bars of signal, the pyrotechnics detonate, killing Ryder.

tropes.name: Troubled Production
tropes.html: In-Universe the shoot for Metalstorm has gone too long, is vastly over budget and being re-written on the fly, and when Colt is summoned by the producer Gail, the film's star Tom Ryder has been missing for days. except he's not actually missing and Gail knows this, as the star had accidentally killed his new stunt man, and they need a Fall Guy to take the heat

tropes.name: Vehicular Kidnapping
tropes.html: Midway through the film, Colt and Alma are tased by bad guys who drag Alma into a garbage truck, which Colt then pursues in one of the film's setpieces.

tropes.name: Villain Respect
tropes.html: When Gail orders Ryder to shoot Colt, Ryder hesitates because he says that Colt is one of the best stuntmen he’s ever had.

tropes.name: Villainous Breakdown
tropes.html:
• While he's running away and hiding in fear during the climax after Colt forced him to do the truck jump with him, Ryder hasn't truly lost it until he's surrounded by police and running while trying to call his agent and escape—and while it's debatable as to how much of it is attributed to how dumb he already is, this in turn leads to his Karmic Death too.
  • Gail even after threatening the camera guy with a gun to get the recording in which Ryder confessed is able to switch back to being calm while trying to convince Jody nothing is wrong and to go with her. It's only when Jody smacks her in the face that Gail realizes she can't gaslight her anymore and then just totally loses all the cool she has left, becoming hostile and crazed for the majority of the climax—though she attempts to get it back when cops have her and Ryder surrounded after that though.

tropes.name: Where Does He Get All Those Wonderful Toys?
tropes.html: While it is all but stated that they are his usual protection detail, with Tom the kind of person who'd hire amoral killers for the job, one has to wonder where does a Hollywood movie star and/or movie producer get a hold of half a dozen mercenaries willing to kill, kidnap and frame people at the drop of a hat to begin with?

tropes.name: Working with the Ex
tropes.html: Colt and Jody dated while working together on multiple films when she was still just a camerawoman. After breaking his back in a stunt gone wrong, Colt chooses to cut all ties with everyone including Jody. She doesn't take it well, to say the least; her first movie as director is essentially her working through the breakup with the main character and his love interest representing Colt and Jody respectively. She is initially furious when Colt is brought on to be Ryder's stuntman again.

tropes.name: Writing by the Seat of Your Pants
tropes.html: In-Universe, the plot of Metalstorm is constantly being re-written on the fly.

tropes.name: You Didn't See That
tropes.html: Jody gives Colt a finger gun gesture at one point, after having been embarrassed at Colt's repeated use of the gesture and is quickly embarrassed at her own, insisting Colt saw nothing.

tropes.name: Accentuate the Negative
tropes.html: After Murphy's first test against the EM-208, all anyone wants to talk about (with the possible exception of Dr. Norton) is how his reaction time was slower than the robot — ignoring the fact that his decisions were better choices than the robot's. Indeed, given that an ED-209 gunning down a child was a problem, Murphy's behavior should have been exactly what they wanted.

tropes.name: Action Film, Quiet Drama Scene
tropes.html: There's a fantastic and gut-wrenching scene about a third of the way in where Murphy sees what he's become and nearly has a mental breakdown in front of Dr. Norton as a result.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html:
• Sellars insists that they make RoboCop all black, which is funny considering that's what they did with Michael Keaton's Batman.
  • Mattox's Villainous Breakdown upon seeing RoboCop up and running after his vitals went offline. His growling "damn damn damn" sounds particularly familiar. Not to mention that his idea of "what's greater than a hero" is "Dead hero." Consider Rorschach's eventual fate.

tropes.name: Adaptation Name Change
tropes.html: OCP, the corporation that created RoboCop in the original film trilogy, is now called OmniCorp in the reboot. The ending reveals that OCP is actually the parent company of OmniCorp, making the latter analogous to the Security Concepts division from the original.

tropes.name: A.I. Is a Crapshoot
tropes.html: Averted. The discussion is not strictly on the quality of the programming, but other factors between a programmed response and intelligent decisions. The ED-209 series has a similar "all-or-nothing" attitude to the ones in the original series, as they make no distinction between suicide bombers with assault rifles and a kid with a butcher knife (versus the original not recognizing when an individual has gone from armed to unarmed). This either/or factor is used later in the film, as Lewis manages to save Murphy and disarm the OmniCorp security knowing they will not attack enemies unless they are armed.

tropes.name: All There in the Manual
tropes.html:
• According to supplementary materials, RoboCop's cyborg body is made from graphene as opposed to titanium laminated with Kevlar. It's also stated that the ED-209s and EM-208s are also made from graphene.
  • According to the toy-line, the silver body is called "RoboCop 1.0" and the black body is "RoboCop 3.0". The proposed version that could transform between a combat and safety mode is likely the missing 2.0. Doubles as a Mythology Gag as the RoboCop 2 from the first movies didn't last long either.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Law
tropes.html: Like in the original film, the part of the plot in which Murphy investigates his own attempted murder (which goes as far as machine-gunning Vallon dead, shooting a fellow (crooked) detective in the shoulder and threaten to blow away the (equally crooked) Chief of Police) would run into bigger legal consequences because of the conflict of interest (and unlike the original film, there is no mind wipe and everybody in Detroit knows Robocop is Alex Murphy). Not to mention the incriminating evidence is played to a precinct full of cops, which (combined with probable cause) would make it impossible to cover the matter up permanently. The people at OmniCorp do question the whole mess once it's over, but only as how much it became an accidental boost to their PR.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Linguistics
tropes.html: The OmniCorp plant in China has signs in Traditional Chinese characters. The People's Republic of China mainly uses Simplified Chinese.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Medicine
tropes.html: After his murder attempt it is stated that Murphy had 80% of his body covered in 4th degree burns. To those not familiar with the burn scales, 4th degree burns are burns that reach the muscles and bones. Having 80% of his body covered in 4th degree burns would mean there would be nothing but charred muscles and bones to recover and Murphy would have died on the spot long before the EMT could reach his body.

tropes.name: Beta Outfit
tropes.html: Several designs are shown for the suit before the company settles on the sleek, black design.

tropes.name: BFG
tropes.html: It's outright stated that nothing smaller than a .50 cal Beowulf round will harm RoboCop.

tropes.name: Big Brother Is Watching
tropes.html: Downplayed, but it's still there. There are CCTV cameras all over Detroit, and Murphy can wirelessly access the entire network at will. He also has the backlog for the cameras, allowing him to pin crimes on people months or years after the fact. He can trace cell phones whenever he wants. Finally, all of this is correlated in real time with the police database. When he's first linked up, Murphy racks up nearly 200 pending arrests on the spot. What keeps it from being a completely straight example is that only Murphy is capable of doing this. The police have neither the time nor manpower to correlate all this data, while Murphy has a computer linked to his brain that can.

tropes.name: Bloodless Carnage
tropes.html: RoboCop himself, naturally, has no blood. It's zigzagged when he shoots Vallon because you can see blood has definitely pooled around Vallon's body yet he has no visible entry wounds despite Murphy unloading an entire magazine into him. Averted when Murphy guns down Sellars at the end. A spray of blood is visible on the ground behind him.

tropes.name: Body Horror
tropes.html:
• Murphy's car bomb injuries are pretty damn horrific. Fourth degree burns to over 80% of his body. Double amputations. Permanent blindness in one eye. Tinnitus. Lower spine was severed from upper spine, leading to a lifetime of paralysis. Loads of internal bleeding. Seeing his mutilated body on life support wasn't pleasant in the slightest.
  • By the time Murphy becomes RoboCop, the only parts of his original body that he still has are his right hand, lungs, heart and his head with his brain exposed. In the original film, these were the areas of the body where Murphy was shot up by Clarence Boddicker. Murphy is so horrified by the sight he asks never to see himself like this again. However we do see him resting comfortably this way at the end of the movie, showing that he's become more comfortable with his nature.
  • The film also demonstrates that all of the fluids and fats inside what remains of Alex are "piped out" daily and replaced with fresh blood and proteins, suggesting that whatever remains inside him inevitably breaks down on a cellular level, and that he needs regular (daily) maintenance in order for the remainder of his organic components to not break down completely.

tropes.name: Bottomless Magazines
tropes.html: During his attack on the OmniCorp HQ, Murphy uses both his pistol and M2 Battle Rifle to deliver an incredible amount of lead on the ED-209s. This is telling, considering that Mattox tells Murphy early on that his M2 Battle Rifle holds 30 .50 Beowulf rounds.

tropes.name: Broad Strokes
tropes.html: The premise is virtually identical, with comparable characters and similar themes, but the overall story is much different, allowing the movie to address different themes than the original did. In particular, Murphy was not clinically dead and emerges aware of himself as RoboCop with free will slowly peeled away by manipulating his programming and body chemistry, the inverse of what happens in the original. The story itself is basically a complete inversion of the original. The original is basically a resurrection story, with Murphy really being dead (subsumed by RoboCop) for the bulk of the film, only really becoming himself at the end, though there are some plot points about how his behavior is controlled by his programming. In the remake, Murphy is Murphy throughout the film, but the programming controlling his actions becomes more and more strict, forcing him to fight to reclaim his own free will.

tropes.name: Car Bomb
tropes.html: Murphy is caught by one.

tropes.name: The Cavalry
tropes.html: Lewis leads a SWAT team into OmniCorp to help Alex.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html: In the intro, the overseas press crew is issued red bracelets which mark them as priority assets, to be defended at any cost. In the climax, it's revealed that this doubles as a Restraining Bolt, preventing Murphy from attacking anyone wearing one.

tropes.name: Contrasting Sequel Main Character
tropes.html: Alex Murphy in the 1987 film goes from being a cold unemotional robocop to getting his personality back. Alex Murphy in the 2014 film starts from being a human being and gets colder as the film goes along.

tropes.name: Convection, Schmonvection
tropes.html: The bomb in Alex's car doesn't seem to cause much damage to the house behind it.

tropes.name: Cowboy Cop
tropes.html: Alex Murphy isn't as blatant of an example like Dirty Harry, but his aggressive pursuit of corruption compels Vallon to attempt an assassination. Murphy's chief, Karen Dean is also unhappy with Murphy's methods, and this is actually because she's working along with John and Andre as connections to the underworld.

tropes.name: Crapsack World
tropes.html: The world is a little better than the original but is still bad. Certain fish are in danger of extinction due to overfishing by Sushi restaurants, Brazil has legalized all types of drugs, Greenpeace is now a terrorist group, and Tehran is now under occupation by a US droid army who are so effective in fighting that most citizens choose to accept it out of fear. Meanwhile, crime in Detroit has gotten so bad that the city set up video cameras everywhere and yet this still doesn't stop criminals from committing crimes in front of a camera. Also, gangs now have access to military hardware like assault rifles and grenades.

tropes.name: Create Your Own Villain
tropes.html: A two-way street here. The RoboCop project was nothing more than a publicity stunt done by Sellars to help OmniCorp win some political battles and get a domestic robotics drone contract. With Murphy going against their parameters, Sellars starts worrying he may be just as much a liability and once they get the popular vote he plans on having him quietly terminated, revealing his villainous core. Of course, he had created a super cop and Alex reacts to the termination order as an attempt to kill a cop.

tropes.name: Cybernetics Eat Your Soul
tropes.html: Discussed. Dr. Norton is introduced counseling a patient who is afraid his prosthetic arms would rob him of his ability to play music, assuring him that the music comes not from his arms, but from his mind. After Murphy is converted into a cyborg, he remains the same dedicated police officer and loving family man he was before. Unfortunately, what Sellars essentially wants out of Murphy is to be a machine through-and-through, and when his reaction times lag behind an ED-208 due to taking caution like any good officer would, he coaxes Norton into lowering his dopamine levels, repressing his humanity and turning him into a soulless machine. It isn't until he is confronted with how his newly robotic demeanor is affecting his wife and son that he begins the struggle to reclaim his humanity.

tropes.name: Deadly Dodging
tropes.html: Murphy defeats some ED-209s by making them shoot at each other.

tropes.name: Disastrous Demonstration
tropes.html: Inverted, though it looks like it'll be played straight at first. Minutes prior to his public unveiling, Murphy is given an upload of the entire police database and all CCTV footage for the past few years. Murphy suffers a Heroic BSoD when he sees the footage of his own near-death. Ordered to get him on his feet immediately, Dr. Norton tampers with Murphy's neurochemistry to almost completely repress his emotions. Basically running on autopilot, Murphy stomps past his family and ignores the Mayor's outstretched hand, scanning them and everyone else in the crowd for potential threats. Then he spots Thomas King — a man wanted for murder — and wastes no time jumping into the crowd and shooting the guy in the back, scaring the crowd half to death. Novak subsequently is shown spinning the story as an example of Murphy's new amazing robotic abilities and the incompetence of the human police, pointing out the uniform cops that are standing literally steps away from the wanted felon who fail to notice him.

tropes.name: Does This Remind You of Anything?
tropes.html:
• The claim that robots are incorruptible is a recurring theme in the movie. No matter whether this could be "true", their makers are still corruptible and can tamper with these robots in their favor. The theme becomes a metaphor of the law and lawmakers who are also lawbreakers; machine glitches are as analogous to loopholes in the law.
  • The subtle satire of how OmniCorp's droid armies in foreign countries are hailed by the media, yet the American public objects being under robotic law enforcers via the Dreyfus Act, with Sen. Dreyfus using children as a main point of argument. By the film's conclusion, the public remained against droid enforcers except the sole humane cyborg as their own crimefighter, all the while other countries' insurgents and their children who are against soulless droids remain gunned down.

tropes.name: Dramatic Irony
tropes.html: Early on, Murphy and Lewis accuse a gun runner they're investigating of being a cop, when they themselves are cops. Though it appears to be just a ploy to scare the gun runner into revealing who he's working for.

tropes.name: Eagleland
tropes.html: The Novak Element basically has this for the show itself. The last shot of the movie has Novak adamantly declaring that America is the greatest country in the world, whilst a holographic American flag waves in the background.

tropes.name: The Evils of Free Will
tropes.html: When paired off against an EM-208 in the simulator, Murphy turns out to be several seconds slower as his reflexes are affected by human decision-making processes. Under pressure from his boss to get results, Dr. Norton writes Murphy's software so that it takes over in combat situations, while signals are sent into Murphy's brain giving him the illusion of controlling events. Although Murphy's decisions are slower than the EM-208s, they're generally better decisions, including using cover and clearing corners instead of just charging in guns blazing and trying to talk down a hostage taker rather than immediately gun him down.

tropes.name: Evil, Inc.
tropes.html: OmniCorp is deep in this trope. The discussion early in the film that leads to the creation of the RoboCop project has Sellars and his subordinates angrily mentioning that every day that they are not allowed to sell their combat drones in America they are almost literally bleeding billions of dollars of unexploited market.

tropes.name: Evil Plan
tropes.html: OmniCorp stands to make a lot of money if they can sell their robots in America. They create RoboCop to sway public opinion so they can do this. The rest is keeping their creation under control.

tropes.name: Expy
tropes.html: OmniCorp Security is based on the Urban Rehabilitators from RoboCop 3, as both groups use grey camouflage.

tropes.name: Expanded Universe
tropes.html: The Boom! comics highlights how Sellars has tried to make RoboCops out of mortally wounded soldiers who fought overseas. They all resulted in failures.

tropes.name: Flyaway Shot
tropes.html: Near the end of the film, the camera "zooms out" of the rooftop of the final confrontation showing a wounded/damaged Alex (Robocop) Murphy and a dead Raymond Sellars after their final confrontation. The ascending shot seems to suggest that Alex may not have survived the battle, but Alex is fine and has been upgraded with new components to repair his damaged body, before the film ends.

tropes.name: Funny Background Event
tropes.html: Most of the news that scrolls along the bottom explains the general state of the world in 2029. Apparently, many Americans are now illegally entering Mexico, and we've made first contact via SETI. Oddly enough, the aliens had deemed us dumb. There's also the bit where Greenpeace, now a terrorist organization, have been hacked by a Wikileaks hacker.

tropes.name: Greek Chorus
tropes.html: Pat Novak hosts segments of "The Novak Element" at several points of the film to discuss the plot's advancements in a way that his pro-OmniCorp views get to shine.

tropes.name: Gone Horribly Right
tropes.html: OmniCorp wants to make Alex Murphy into a hero, someone that people can "rally behind". Murphy becomes such a successful hero that he starts investigating their shady dealings.

tropes.name: Gory Discretion Shot
tropes.html: Near the start, a bunch of suicide bombers choose to attack the OmniCorp robots in Tehran with the purpose of getting themselves killed on international television. After their attack is repelled, the son of one of them takes a knife and rushes down from his apartment to try to charge an ED-209. The camera cuts from the ED-209's Robo-Cam POV shot of the boy to outside, where we only see it blasting away (and the view is very quick since Mattox covers the camera and the camera is quickly rotated back to Novak's reporter).

tropes.name: Great Offscreen War
tropes.html: Some sort of armed conflict arose between the US and Iran in the past, leading to the superpower nation invading and occupying the latter country with the massive robot army now seen in the nation's capital of Tehran by the start of the film.

tropes.name: Gun Kata
tropes.html: During the warehouse training scene, a "not in control" Murphy takes on 54 robotic opponents in close quarter combat with firearms. While his movements are not as traditionally fluid, it is unmistakably his own brand of the style.

tropes.name: Guns Do Not Work That Way
tropes.html: The movie makes it seem as though a .50 caliber round is some sort of magical bullet that offers significantly more damage regardless of the medium, as it is specifically this caliber which can penetrate RoboCop's armor. In the big shootout, he gets into trouble when the bad guys pull out .50 AE Desert Eagles. Those actually deliver only slightly more kinetic energy than the standard 5.56 mm NATO rifle round, vs. a .50 BMG rifle round will punch with almost ten times as much energy. 7.62mm NATO rounds would likewise reach the threshold. In reality, if RoboCop can shrug off common rifle rounds, those Desert Eagles shouldn't do much to him.

tropes.name: Homage
tropes.html: Kinnaman's grey suit motif is very similar to Weller's 1987 suit down to every intricate detail.

tropes.name: Humans Are Morons
tropes.html: As noted under "Funny Background Event", aliens believe this and have asked SETI to stop trying to contact them. Given the actions of some people in this movie alone (not to mention even the whole franchise), no-one can really blame them.

tropes.name: I Cannot Self-Terminate
tropes.html: When he realizes his condition, Murphy initially wants to die, and is in no condition to do it himself. Dr. Norton talks him out of it.

tropes.name: I Have a Family
tropes.html: When Murphy tries to interrogate Jerry for Vallon's whereabouts, Jerry begs for mercy, stating he has a wife and kids. Unfortunately for Jerry, Murphy has access to the criminal database and a quick search reveals that not only has Jerry's wife left him for domestic abuse, he also has no children.

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html:
• The established-to-be image-conscious OmniCorp deciding to upload the police database into Murphy's head right before the unveiling press event. Murphy freaks out upon witnessing his own murder, forcing them to dial down his emotions to nothing (thus defeating the point) just so they can walk him out. Everything from then on is a result of this blunder, and it's only thanks to him identifying and arresting a wanted criminal in the crowd (and the press spinning this into an argument in favor of robots in law enforcement) that they're able to avoid a potential PR disaster. Had they simply waited to perform the upload when they weren't on the clock, they could have eased Murphy through the process, rather than taking such drastic action.
  • Soon after the police database was uploaded to Murphy, it is discovered that a wanted fugitive, Thomas King, felt it wise to attend the unveiling of Robocop and chance being identified, even by regular cops and people who may have studied King's mugshot and remembered the crimes he's wanted for. Murphy's software immediately detects King's bio-metrics as King's vicinity is scanned, and he's arrested and read his rights.
  • One of Vallon's men uses an unencrypted cell phone while at his boss's headquarters despite the fact they can be traced through such. Vallon even earlier insists a pair of Dirty Cops have their cell phones off when they visit. Naturally, Murphy finds Vallon through said phone.

tropes.name: Interrupted Intimacy
tropes.html: Murphy is smooching with his wife in their bedroom when the car alarm is set off to lure him outside, into the blast radius of the bomb planted in the wheel well.

tropes.name: It's Personal
tropes.html: Once Murphy overcomes his programming, he gets right back to investigating who blew him up.

tropes.name: Job-Stealing Robot
tropes.html: The central crux of the plot is OmniCorp's dastardly attempts to get America to accept the deployment of Attack Drones inside of the United States, which would endanger the jobs of law enforcement personnel as well as the "robot mistakes civilian for criminal and kills them" risk factor.

tropes.name: The Law of Diminishing Defensive Effort
tropes.html: Less prominent than in the original 1987 film, but it's still there. Murphy is much more agile and it's shown he does make an effort to dodge incoming fire and utilize cover at least some of the time, but one of his favored tactics is still to walk out into the middle of the room and shoot everything while being shot at from multiple angles.

tropes.name: Life-or-Limb Decision
tropes.html: During his fight with the squad of ED-209s, Murphy ends up getting his left, completely robotic, arm trapped underneath one he's disabled. With others bearing down on him, he takes his gun and shreds the arm at the elbow to free himself.

tropes.name: Lighter and Softer
tropes.html: The film is rated PG-13 compared to the very hard R rating of the original. Though the reveal of exactly how much of Alex Murphy is left makes you wonder how it squeaked by with a PG-13.

tropes.name: Lightning Bruiser
tropes.html: Murphy is faster and way more agile than the original 1987 version, being able to run at high speeds (doing about 30 mph), leap tall walls in a single bound, and even dodge gunfire and rockets. He's still a super-strong, heavily-armored robot, although perhaps slightly less nigh-invulnerable than the original version owing to his slimmer physique and more biological components. The original 1987 Mighty Glacier design is presented as a "combat mode" Beta Outfit concept design which is ultimately rejected by OmniCorp.

tropes.name: Logo Joke
tropes.html: Instead of Leo the Lion roaring in the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer symbol, we hear Novak going through his vocal warm-up exercises before his talk show goes to air.

tropes.name: Loophole Abuse
tropes.html: The Dreyfus Act prevents armed robots being deployed in the US so OmniCorp uses the cyborg RoboCop since he's technically an armed human.

tropes.name: MegaCorp
tropes.html: Downplayed with OmniCorp, which is primarily a defense contractor with a branch into cybernetic limbs for amputees. They're actually part of the original movie's OCP.

tropes.name: Movie Superheroes Wear Black
tropes.html: Amusingly done as part of an In-Universe marketing strategy to make RoboCop look cooler. Early set photos showed the black version of the suit, which upset fans until it's revealed the classic silvery blue is still in the movie. At the end he goes back to the blue.

tropes.name: Mythology Gag
tropes.html:
The entire movie has similar plot and characters to the 1987 original intermingled with elements from its two sequels.
  • RoboCop (1987)
    • The film even begins with a heavily-armed ED-209 opening fire on a knife-wielding child, mirroring Mr. Kinney's death in the boardroom at the start of the first film.
    • Murphy's only remaining biological components are the parts that, in the original movie, are where he gets shot by Clarence Boddicker's gang in a shotgun firing squad execution.
    • The fact that he still has a functional hand also recalls Bob Morton's decision to ditch the original Murphy's good arm even though it could have been saved, since he wanted him to be all robot save the brain.
    • Murphy tasting "peanut butter" in his mouth while Dr. Norton is working on his brain is a nod to how the organic paste that RoboCop had to rely on for sustenance tasted like "baby food".
    • During Murphy's VR training, Rick Mattox inverts the "I'd buy that for a dollar!" catchphrase that Bixby Snyder used in the first film in a banal sitcom. Here, it's an off-handed remark about Murphy's response times being several seconds slower than the EM-208 robot's.
    • The film references the original 1987 RoboCop grey suit as its prototype design. A version dubbed "combat mode" is an exact copy of that design, before it's rejected in favor of the "more tactical" black refit. After the black suit redesign and the plot reached its climax, they revert Murphy back to the first design in true Bookends form.
    • The term "Red Asset", identified by a electronic bracelet as VIPs, refers to the secret, classified Fourth Directive within RoboCop's programming which prevents him from harming OCP officers.
    • The RoboCop Catch Phrases "Thank you for your cooperation" and "Dead or alive, you're coming with me" are used in a more ironic context. He also threatens an arrested criminal with "You have two seconds to comply."
    • Murphy's assaults on John Biggs' drug laboratory and Vallon's warehouse are a reprise of the raid on Boddicker's cocaine factory. Likewise, his assault on the ED-209s at OmniCorp recalls his showdown with Dick Jones' ED-209 at OCP Headquarters.
    • Like before, Murphy's footsteps are loud. Joel Kinnaman went as far as to model his version of RoboCop movements off of Peter Weller, with a little bit more fluidity.
    • Murphy takes out an ED-209 by making it fall down from one floor to another, much like the original was defeated by falling down stairs.
    • Sellars mockingly offers his arms out for handcuffs, knowing that he is protected thanks to Murphy's Restraining Bolt, just as Dick Jones did in the first movie.
    • Nikko deleted Directive 4.
  • RoboCop 2
    • Twofold: Dr. Norton disassembling Murphy and showing him what remains of his body is a nod to 1) RoboCop being dismantled by Cain's Nuke Gang and 2) the scene where Cain's preserved brain, spine, and eyes watch Dr. Faxx's harvesting procedure.
    • Vallon's got snitches in the Detroit police force, just like Cain's Nuke team.
    • Hob destroys Murphy's gun hand. This time around, Murphy had to shoot his own (robot) arm to break free from an ED-209's wreckage.
    • Tom Pope suggests crippled cops with muscular builds for the RoboCop project. Dr. Norton objects because of the subjects' mental and emotional instability, making Dr. Norton the complete antithesis of Dr. Juliette Faxx.
    • RoboCop now rides his own motorcycle and his black armor glows bright blue under fluorescent lights.
    • Murphy is overwhelmed by the police crime database uploaded into his brain, similar to the hundreds of politically-correct directives given to him by OCP in the second film to satisfy the focus groups.
    • Once again, Lewis uses an armored troop transport to slow down and harm a larger robot, in this case, using a Oshkosh Sandcat to ram into an ED-209. In the original, Anne Lewis used an APC to pin RoboCain against the wall.
    • Pope's proposed design for RoboCop, being able to transform into a "Safety Mode" with police lights, is similar to the design of one of the failed RoboCop 2 prototypes that just commit suicide upon being released.
  • RoboCop 3
    • Murphy being able to handle various weapons rather than a single sidearm.
    • OmniCorp's robot army in other countries is very similar to the Rehab project that will pave the way for Delta City, prompting rebels to fight back much like the Iranians.
  • Leans into Unexpected Character with RoboCop's new bike, a pretty faithful recreation of the toy-only Robocycle released for RoboCop and the Ultra Police.
  • RoboCop: The Series gave Murphy a whole slew of less-lethal options, to make the show more family-friendly. This Murphy's pistol only fires less-lethal "taser" style rounds, with a lethal PDW/SMG if he needs a bigger iron.

tropes.name: No Such Thing as Bad Publicity
tropes.html:
In-Universe example.
  • When OmniCorp learns that Chief Karen Dean was working with crime boss Antoine Vallon thanks to Murphy, they at first fear a backlash from the public over the scandal. However, Sellars uses the news to their advantage with Pat Novak's help by praising RoboCop exposing police corruption, and using the whole affair as proof that robots are superior to corruptible human law enforcement.
  • Murphy's emotions have been so repressed he ignores his family and all the VIPs at his press conference because he's too busy scanning everyone for potential threats. Then he leaps into the crowd and tasers a man wanted for murder. The fact that a wanted killer was undetected in a crowd containing some of the city's top law enforcement officials is again used to showcase RoboCop's superior abilities.
  • Even the Iranian suicide bombers wait until they're on television before attacking. Likewise the attack is also given a positive spin on Novak's show, emphasizing the US troops who didn't die through the use of robots, as opposed to the Iranians who did, or whether the robot occupation is achieving anything.

tropes.name: Not Helping Your Case
tropes.html: The group that attacked the robots at the beginning of the film. In the end, all that happened was they got killed for their trouble and proved to the world that the robots did what they were programmed to do: defeat terrorists without the lost of a human life.

tropes.name: Offhand Backhand
tropes.html: Daniels tries to shoot Murphy the moment he turns his head away, but Murphy does a Quick Draw and shoots Daniels without even looking at him. Justified as Murphy's target software would have already plotted Daniel's position.

tropes.name: Post-Cyberpunk
tropes.html: In contrast to the original, this version gives OmniCorp and the government some redeeming features, society is pretty much the same but with better technology, and the good aspects of robotics are emphasized rather than the bad.

tropes.name: Quick Draw
tropes.html: Murphy walks into the police station and confronts a fellow officer with evidence of him being a Dirty Cop. Despite the evidence playing on the computer screens for the entire department to see (or perhaps because of this) he decides to draw his weapon to kill RoboCop, who is sitting right in front of him with his armored visor up, suffering visible gunshot damage from an earlier battle. Unfortunately for him, Murphy's enhanced cyborg reflexes are working just fine and his software accurately predicts that the soon-to-be victim is about to shoot him.

tropes.name: Relative Button
tropes.html: His wife and son leads to Alex overriding his protocols.

tropes.name: Restraining Bolt
tropes.html: Just like in the original, RoboCop is hit with one. The red bracelets prevent him from attacking anyone wearing one. When Raymond Sellars makes the mistake of pointing a gun at his wife and son, however, Alex overpowers the command and shoots him.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html: The OmniCorp guards have this attitude in plenty near the ending after seeing one of their own being tazed by Murphy.

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html: OmniCorp turns out to be part of OCP, which plans to review its droid program.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• The 1987 RoboCop's design has encumbered speed due to his heavy armor, but the 2014 RoboCop implements superhuman speed, jumping and reflexes akin to the obscure Japanese police-cyborg 8 Man After. The new Alex Murphy is also a detective rather than a police officer, much like Detective Yokoda before he became 8-Man.
  • RoboCop's NI-408 sidearm resembles the modified Lawgiver Mark II more than the 1987 Auto-9.
  • The ED-209s making animal noises not only reminds one of the original ED-209s, but calls to mind the Gekkos from Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots and Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance. Also, Murphy jumps onto a ED-209 to disable it at close range, like Raiden does with some of his aerial attacks. Mind you, he's not as successful as Raiden is.
  • The noises that Murphy's combat software and non-combat software makes when it's analyzing and running scenarios and all of that fun stuff, is the same sound effects used for the Terminators in Terminator Salvation.
  • In running through modular design variations, one is showed able to switch to a slimmer version with police lights on his shoulders. "It transforms. Kids love it."
  • The man with the prosthetic hand plays "Concerto de Aranjuez" which is the basis for "Follow Me", a song appearing prominently in Ghost in the Shell Innocence (the 2004 movie), a film that shares many similar themes with RoboCop.
  • When Robocop is interrogating two dirty cops at the police station, he concludes by coldly quipping "Thank you for your cooperation, you can cuff him now Jack." This is a call back to RoboCop (1987) when Robocop thanks the liquor store owners for their support when Murphy confronts the robber. However, some viewers did read this as Robocop thanking the now-unconscious robber so this may even be a shout-out to that idea.

tropes.name: Show Within a Show
tropes.html: Pat Novak's The Novak Element, a satire of right-wing talking head programmes.

tropes.name: Storming the Castle
tropes.html:
• Vallon is holed up in a warehouse with a massive amount of ordinance, and when he learns that Robo is directly headed for him, he throws up all the proximity mines, guns and support he has at his disposal. Robo is able to power through these defenses and take out the entire group of mobsters.
  • The final battle has Murphy storm the OmniCorp building to take down Sellars while fighting off an army of ED-209s and Mattox.

tropes.name: Suicide Attack
tropes.html: A group of suicide bombers go after OmniCorp's drones in the opening, managing to take out an ED-209 and one of the humanoid EM-208 drones. The intent was to get themselves caught on camera doing it as a statement against the drone use in their country. They specifically make it a point to avoid getting anyone other than themselves killed, as that would send the wrong message.

tropes.name: S.W.A.T. Team
tropes.html: Jack manages to round up a SWAT element to bust into OmniCorp. Unfortunately, they are cornered by the ED-209s (accompanied by armed guards) and are forced to be disarmed. However, they gives Murphy enough time to reach the helipad.

tropes.name: Take That!
tropes.html: A scrolling news ticker reads that Americans are becoming illegal immigrants in Mexico, a potshot against citizens who malign foreign immigrants coming the other way.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html: There's the son of the suicide bomber at the beginning, who rushes at a 12-foot-tall military mech with a knife. Those things are hard to destroy with explosives and high caliber ammo, a knife isn't going to do anything. On the other hand, the bombers' objective was solely to die live on international television, so if that was the son's goal as well, it did everything he needed it to. Alternatively, the ED-209 thought the boy was going to use the knife to harm other people.

tropes.name: Weapon Wields You
tropes.html: When paired off against an ED-208 in the simulator, Murphy turns out to be several seconds slower as his reflexes are affected by human decision-making processes. Under pressure from his boss to get results, Dr. Norton writes Murphy's software so that it takes over in combat situations, while signals are sent into Murphy's brain giving him the illusion of controlling events.

tropes.name: Zero-G Spot
tropes.html: The news ticker on The Novak Element at one point mentions that the President has approved astronauts bringing hookers into space.

tropes.name: Meet Cute
tropes.html: Averted. Jamie meets Maggie when he is pretending to be an intern (with a doctor's permission) and reacts unprofessionally when she takes off her top for a medical examination. Maggie clocks who he is immediately, but waits until the appointment is done to attack him in the parking lot and take his photo.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: Sure, Jamie and Maggie end up together, but they're both very much aware that she will eventually lose all physical and mental coordination.

tropes.name: Bowdlerise
tropes.html: The Spanish subtitles are hilarious because they have all the swear words censored... in a film with graphic sex scenes. It seems talking about sex is bad, but not showing sex.

tropes.name: The Charmer
tropes.html:
Jamie even lampshades it, delightfully enough.
Jamie: You're gonna like me eventually. Everyone does.

tropes.name: Defrosting Ice Queen
tropes.html: Subverted. Jamie eventually does convince Maggie to be his girlfriend, but she doesn't change her behavior until the very end.

tropes.name: Diagnosis from Dr. Badass
tropes.html: Trey, who has noticed that Jamie is throwing out his Prozac samples, approaches him at the dumpster and punches him in the stomach, causing the latter to keel over and writhe on the ground in agony. Trey helpfully tells Jamie EXACTLY what type of pain he's delivering.

tropes.name: Double Entendre
tropes.html:
Jamie's comment that "it's hard to believe" that Pfizer is making an erection drug starts Maggie off on a tangent.
Maggie: It's hard to believe. It's gonna be pretty huge though. When I think of the size of the problem, and that it's growing larger, really....I just can't even imagine, to have found a solution to the stiffest, hardest, wow, Pfizer must be swelling with pride— [Jamie starts tickling her] Stop tickling me because you have a limp sense of humor!

tropes.name: Dramatic Irony
tropes.html: Jamie works as a Drug Rep for Pfizer, the creator of Viagra, and he soon begins successfully selling the drug. Later on, he engages in a threesome at a party, taking Viagra to stimulate himself; he ends up having a negative reaction to the drug, which leaves him with a painfully erect and extremely sore penis, forcing him to go to the hospital. Yes, it turns out that the sex obsessed Viagra salesmen can't take Viagra himself.

tropes.name: Fanservice
tropes.html: Both leads spend a good portion of the film naked.

tropes.name: Friendly Tickle Torture
tropes.html: Jamie attacks Maggie with tickles during a scene on the couch. Like pretty much everything else they do in the movie, it ends with them having sex.

tropes.name: The Film of the Book
tropes.html: It's loosely based on the 2005 non-fiction book Hard Sell: The Evolution of a Viagra Salesman.

tropes.name: Find the Cure
tropes.html: What leads to Jamie and Maggie's breakup at the end of the second act. After hearing from another caretaker exactly how Maggie's illness is likely to progress, Jamie becomes determined to find some kind of helpful treatment for her, first trying with cutting-edge doctors and progressing to quacks giving presentations at cheap convention centers. Maggie becomes scared that Jamie will only love her if she is healthy, and breaks up with him to prevent him from growing to resent her as she sickens.

tropes.name: Home Porn Movie
tropes.html: Jamie and Maggie make one. Later, Jamie catches Josh watching it and masturbating, and is thoroughly disgusted.

tropes.name: Interchangeable Asian Cultures
tropes.html: One character makes a terrible, "sexy" pun about her friend's race as a lead-up to a threesome. "She's Thai, and I'm Thai-curious." Which is made worse by the fact that the girl is blatantly Filipino.

tropes.name: Jerk with a Heart of Gold
tropes.html:
• Jamie is this, though it takes a while for even him to realize it. He mostly cares about only himself, after having always been looked down-upon for his slacker tendencies. He starts showing his softer side when he and Maggie start actually dating.
  • Maggie comes off as abrasive to most people, but she helps organize regular trips to Canada for herself and her elderly friends, all to get much needed medication.

tropes.name: Morally Ambiguous Doctorate
tropes.html: Doctor Stan Knight, played by Hank Azaria. Jamie and Bruce see him as the key to expanding their sales of Zoloft, as other doctors will follow his lead if he agrees to proscribe it. Jamie therefore repeatedly approaches him, and is successfully able to bribe him to let Jamie shadow him for a few hours, pretending to be an intern. This is horribly unethical for a number of reasons, but really goes over the line when he lets Jamie watch him examine Maggie's bare breasts.

tropes.name: Ladykiller in Love
tropes.html: Part of the plot of the film. Jamie is initially a womanizer, and he's happy when Maggie wants a sex-only relationship. However, he still ends up developing feelings for her. When he first says "I love you" to her, he has a panic attack, because he never said this to anyone before.

tropes.name: The Loins Sleep Tonight
tropes.html: Jamie doesn't have this to begin with, but excels at profiting off it once Viagra hits the market and he can sell it. However, he does experience it at the end during a pajama party, and ends up taking Viagra.

tropes.name: Modesty Bedsheet
tropes.html: Averted. Jamie and Maggie have a ton of sex but don’t bother to cover up. When, in a moment of brief shyness, she pulls her sheet up to her collarbone, Jamie gets off the bed and it uncovers her boob and she doesn’t bother to cover it up again.<!--* OscarBait: A rare example of one that doubles as a SexComedy.-->

tropes.name: Present-Day Past
tropes.html: There's the introduction of Viagra and Prozac, and there's the bit with '90s ghetto blasters at the start, and the cellphones are more-or-less accurate. Nothing else sets this is '96. One character justifies being addicted to Internet porn by saying "Isn't everybody?" No, not in '96 they weren't. Not even in '97. Seriously, cast your mind back to how much porn there was on the Internet when the first Grand Theft Auto came out. There's even a scene Josh compares Jamie's penis to the Eye of Sauron, back before there was a common consensus on what that actually looked like, it being 5 years before The Lord Of The Rings was a movie. Not to mention in the beginning of the film, there's Flat-screen LCD TV's in the background.

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html:
For Pfizer and their products (mostly Viagra and Zoloft), but it's somewhat subverted in that the entire company comes off looking like a bunch of douchebags. Zoloft's top competitor, Prozac, is also shown to be quite effective. The downside of using Viagra as a party drug is also shown, with Jamie having to go to the emergency room when his erection refuses to go away.
  • And lots of Bud and Bud Light abound.

tropes.name: Race for Your Love
tropes.html: Jamie races Maggie's bus to Canada at the climax to proclaim his love for her and assure her he will always be there for her as her condition worsens.

tropes.name: Raging Stiffie
tropes.html: Jamie takes viagra to have a threesome at a pajama party, after he has trouble getting it up, but afterwards is forced to go to the emergency room because of a painful case of Priapism.

tropes.name: Sexy Coat Flashing
tropes.html: Maggie comes over to Jamie's apartment, and opens her coat, revealing that she's naked underneath. Then she notices that Josh is in the room. But - much to his disappointment - Josh didn't see her well because he did not have his glasses on.

tropes.name: Sleeping with the Boss
tropes.html: Sleeping with the Boss'sWife: Jamie sleeps with his manager's girlfriend, in the backroom of the electronics store they all work in. Naturally they accidentally activate one of the electronics and project the noise of their lovemaking to the entire store, alerting the boss. Jamie is promptly fired.

tropes.name: Starving Artist
tropes.html: Maggie works in a coffee shop, but lives in a classic artist's loft. She used to be a painter, but her illness has progressed to the point where she cannot hold a paintbrush steady, so she has switched to photography. She doesn't have health insurance though, so makes regular trips to Canada to purchase the numerous medications she needs to treat her condition.

tropes.name: Traveling Salesman
tropes.html: After Jamie is fired, Josh uses his connections to get him into the Pfizer sales training program, after which he becomes a pharmaceutical rep for the Pittsburg area. He's mentored by Bruce, a veteran pharmaceutical rep who dreams of making enough sales to break into the Chicago market.

tropes.name: Unsympathetic Comedy Protagonist
tropes.html: The men in this film are all misogynistic jerks. Jamie is eventually redeemed by The Power of Love.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: Jamie starts steeling Prozac samples from one of the doctors he is courting as a client, replacing it with Zoloft samples from his own company, and tosses the Prozac in a dumpster outside the doctor's office. An unhoused man notices this, and keeps showing up to take the discarded Prozac. The final time Jamie does this, the same man shows up again, this time wearing a worn out suit and having showered/shaved, and comments that he has a job interview later before scampering off with the drugs. Clearly he had taken the drugs repeatedly, but he's never seen again after this.

tropes.name: #1 Dime
tropes.html: Lilo's photograph of her parents who were killed in a car accident.

tropes.name: Accidental Misnaming
tropes.html: The Grand Councilwoman calls Jumba and Pleakley "Jumbo and Blinkey" after firing them for not recovering Stitch quickly enough for her. Gantu corrects her, and she reacts with "Whatever!"

tropes.name: Adorable Abomination
tropes.html:
• Stitch, who was originally designed as an indestructible prototype experiment, becomes one of these when he disguises himself as a dog in order to take refuge from Jumba on Earth. When Jumba is fired and decides to track Stitch on his own:
    Jumba: Come on, what's the big deal?
    Stitch: Inga tu smeeshta!
    Jumba: I'll put you back together again... I'll make you taller, and not so fluffy.
    Stitch: I like fluffy!
  • Later on, when Stitch is attempting to rescue Lilo from Gantu:
    Stitch: Aloha!
    Gantu: Grr! You're vile, you're foul, you're flawed!
    Stitch: Also cute and fluffy!
  • Even in his true form, he's still adorable. Also, several characters react with shock and horror to his dog disguise and consider him deformed or mutated. Lilo is the only human character whose initial reaction to him isn't negative.

tropes.name: Aerial Canyon Chase
tropes.html: The climax involves Jumba, Pleakley, Nani, and Stitch flying in a giant spaceship to save Lilo from Gantu, who accidentally captured her while attempting to capture Stitch (he escaped), by chasing him down a series of volcano-filled canyons located all over Hawaii. Originally, they were going to go after Gantu by chasing him down with a stolen passenger jet into the capital city of Honolulu, but due to 9/11, the scene had to be reanimated into what we see in the final version of the film.

tropes.name: Affably Evil
tropes.html: Jumba Jookiba may constantly boast over his status as an evil genius, and he may have created over 600 super-destructive aliens, but he's a pretty decent and sociable guy overall.

tropes.name: Affectionate Gesture to the Nose
tropes.html: Stitch breaks Lilo out of the capture capsule on Captain Gantu's now-pilotless starship. Lilo, surprised that Stitch made the effort, remarks, "You came back." This is met with Stitch's Meaningful Echo, "Nobody gets left behind." For this, Lilo gives him a kiss on his large nose. Stitch is at first surprised by this gesture, but smiles at the sincerity and gratitude it conveys.

tropes.name: Air-Vent Passageway
tropes.html: Part of Stitch's escape from the prison transport ship. Justified, because Stitch is small enough to fit into them and he can squeeze into impossibly tight places.

tropes.name: Alien Blood
tropes.html: Stitch has pink blood, seen when a blood sample is drawn by Gantu at the start of the film.

tropes.name: Alien Non-Interference Clause
tropes.html: Downplayed. The Grand Councilwoman is all for moving the council's forces to Earth to detain Experiment 626, down to gassing the planet being her first choice, all in a tone that implies this to be a standard procedure if not the Godzilla Threshold. It's not until Pleakley vouches for the endangered mosquito population and their "primary food source" of humanity not being ready to know of extraterrestrial life that she decides on a more covert means of capturing 626.

tropes.name: Aliens in Cardiff
tropes.html: Aliens land on a small island in Hawaii.

tropes.name: Aliens Speaking English
tropes.html: Justified in Stitch's case, he's super-intelligent and learns it over the course of the film. As for the other aliens, not even handwaved.

tropes.name: Aliens Steal Cable
tropes.html: The Federation seem to be mostly ignorant of Earth and its culture, but there are a few examples of this in the film. Pleakley has a View-Master which he uses to learn about Earth, Jumba has apparently heard "Hound Dog" before (he recognizes it and declares, "I love this song!" when it starts playing, which might be an Elvis Has Left the Planet joke), and Stitch knows the Punch Buggy game (though he, at least, has been on Earth a few days and could have picked it up during that time).

tropes.name: Alliance of the Alienated
tropes.html: The film is about two alienated souls (literally, one is an alien) finding belonging and purpose caring about each other. Lilo is a little girl whose bizarre interests mean she struggles to make friends with the other girls, and much of her unruly behavior is a way of coping with the loss of her parents. Stitch is a genetically engineered creature who was created for the sole purpose of destruction, and he is quickly deemed a menace in the eyes of the Galactic Federation. When Lilo meets Stitch (disguised as a dog) at an animal shelter, she sees Stitch as an orphan who was "left behind" like her, and chooses to adopt him. Her kindness causes Stitch to question what he is. This comes to the point that he starts to see that his being with Lilo can put her in danger and nearly decides to leave her and Nani for their safety. Things come around in the end, and true to the film's theme, Lilo's broken family not only mends itself but extends, with Stitch, Jumba, and Pleakley becoming part of it.

tropes.name: Alliterative Name
tropes.html: Jumba Jookiba.

tropes.name: All of the Other Reindeer
tropes.html:
• The movie shows that Lilo is rejected by her peers for being "weird", while Stitch is rejected by the Galactic Federation (this is at least marginally understandable, however, given Stitch's destructive powers and fondness for anarchy).
  • The trailers and print advertising played around with this, showing Stitch being rejected by various members of the Disney Animated Canon; the tagline was "There's one in every family."

tropes.name: All There in the Script
tropes.html: Lilo and Nani's last name (Pelekai) has never been verbally referred to by any character in this film. It appeared on the adoption paper where Lilo is written as Stitch's owner. It wouldn't be until Leroy & Stitch where Lilo was finally referred to with surname attached.note Then again, ʻohana has nothing to do with family names, which probably explains why it's been acknowledged very few times by Disney.

tropes.name: Alternative Foreign Theme Song
tropes.html:
• An odd case. "Baby You Belong" by American singer Faith Hill was used as the theme song in the Japanese version, while it was relegated to an obscure album track everywhere else.
  • The UK release replaced one of the Elvis tracks ("Suspicious Minds") with a cover version from Gareth Gates, who was popular at the time of this film's release.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Situation
tropes.html: It's not the focus of the movie but Pleakley saying that mosquitos are an endangered species unique to Earth suggests that every other species on Earth (from humans all the way on down to bacteria) can be found in abundance throughout the rest of the universe. Whether that means that Humanity Came from Space or that Human Aliens / Transplanted Humans are out there in the universe is unclear — though Cobra Bubbles' words at the end imply that the "mosquitos are an endangered species" thing was created as a partial-ploy to convince aliens to leave Earth alone by having it designated as a "wildlife reserve" to "rebuild" the mosquito population.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Syntax
tropes.html: During Cobra Bubbles' first meeting with Nani and Lilo, he asks if Nani often leaves Lilo home alone. He's looking at a drawing on the fridge that Lilo did of herself with an arrow pointing to her and the words "Me Alone." It could be interpreted as her being left home alone, or being lonely because she doesn't have any friends. Unfortunately for Nani, Cobra Bubbles seemingly interprets it as the former.

tropes.name: Amusing Alien
tropes.html:
• Pleakley for being a Know-Nothing Know-It-All with regards to Earth.
  • Stitch himself is also a good example.
  • Most of the aliens in the film are quirky and funny, even The Comically Serious Grand Councilwoman and Captain Gantu.

tropes.name: And Then What?
tropes.html:
Briefly played for drama in the scene where Stitch, after trashing Lilo's room, looks around impatiently, and Jumba observes:
Jumba: Now this is interesting.
Pleakley: What?
Jumba: 626 was designed to be a monster, but now he has nothing to destroy. You see, I never gave him a greater purpose. What must it be like to have... nothing... not even memories to visit... in the middle of the night?

tropes.name: Annoying Younger Sibling
tropes.html: Lilo is sometimes this to Nani, especially during the scenes before and during Bubbles's first visit, and the scene in the luau. Nani even says this to Lilo during their argument ("You're such a pain!").

tropes.name: Answer Cut
tropes.html: The prologue ends with Jumba asking Pleakley: "Tell me, my little one-eyed one. On what poor, pitiful, defenseless planet has my monstrosity been unleashed?" Cut to Earth — Hawaii, specifically.

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html: "ʻOhana means family. Family means nobody gets left behind — or forgotten."

tropes.name: Area 51
tropes.html:
• While finding Stitch's exit from hyperspace to be Earth, the aliens refer to our planet as being "Quadrant 17, Section 005, area 51. A planet called Eee-arth."
  • Cobra met the Grand Councilwoman in Roswell, they recognize each other.

tropes.name: Arson, Murder, and Jaywalking
tropes.html:
• A fairly lighthearted take on it, but Stitch is programmed to destroy buildings, back up sewers, reverse road signs, and steal everyone's left shoe.
  • Pleakley also adds, sarcastically, as they're riding on a motorbike to save Lilo, that he was "hoping to add theft, endangerment, and insanity to the list of things I did today!"
  • Gantu, when pursuing Stitch, remarks: "You're vile, you're foul, you're flawed!"
    Stitch: ALSO CUTE AND FLUFFY!!!

tropes.name: The Artifact
tropes.html: The spaceship chase scene at the end of the film originally had the good guys flying a passenger jet, but 9/11 made that one a no-go, so it was changed to being Jumba's personal ship instead. Since most of the animation and setpieces got reused, it results in Jumba having a very unusually 747-like ship.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Animal Care
tropes.html:
• For one thing, tropical saltwater fish should not be fed peanut butter sandwiches.
  • Dogs should never eat or drink anything with caffeine in it. If Stitch wasn't an alien and was an actual Earth dog (and this were Real Life), Lilo would have probably unintentionally killed him for letting him drink coffee.
  • Spray bottles should only be used to stop bad behavior, such as chewing or jumping. Trying to teach a dog to play fetch by squirting it with a spray bottle is a good way to get a dog that doesn't enjoy playing and becomes afraid of you.
  • The woman who works at the pound says she thought Stitch was a dead dog when he was first brought in. Leaving him in a pen with living dogs would be a big no-no in that case.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html:
• Stitch, who possesses super-strength, is able to pull a semi-truck to a stop. In truth, regardless of how strong he is, a creature of Stitch's size could never do these things because the ground would give way beneath him by transference of forcenote Pushing a car out of the snow is difficult for the same reason. Unless he had some kind of super-anchoring powers.
  • When Stitch plays ukulele at the beach, Lilo plugs in an amplifier, despite the ukulele itself—a wooden string instrument—not being connected to said amp.

tropes.name: Ash Face
tropes.html:
Nani: David! Did you light yourself on fire AGAIN?!
David: Nah, just the stage.

tropes.name: Author Vocabulary Calendar
tropes.html: "Abomination!" is used to draw early parallels between Lilo and Stitch; both have the word applied to them early on (Stitch by the Galactic Councilwoman, and Lilo hypothetically by herself). The two "Does this look infected to you?" lines serve a similar purpose.

tropes.name: Bad Liar
tropes.html: Nani goes frantically looking for Lilo, with Cobra Bubbles showing up to inspect her house a moment later. Nani tries to hide any and all signs of bad housekeeping that would make her look like a bad guardian, but Cobra can clearly see that the situation has taken a turn for the worse and gives Nani three days to improve it.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html: The first night Jumba and Pleakley were on Earth, Jumba takes issue with Pleakley trying on female wigs...and not sharing them.

tropes.name: Be Careful What You Wish For
tropes.html: Nani asks for something tough at the dog shelter, and gets a pet who is bulletproof, fireproof, and survived being hit by a truck.

tropes.name: Becoming the Mask
tropes.html: Stitch. He starts out masquerading as a dog for protection, but eventually Lilo's love causes him to do a Heel–Face Turn. The signifying moment is when, after having rescued Lilo only to be arrested by the United Galactic Federation, he corrects the Grand Councilwoman that his name is Stitch, not Experiment 626.

tropes.name: Behind the Black
tropes.html: At the start of the denouement, Stitch is blindsided and handcuffed by the Grand Councilwoman and twelve alien velociraptor cops, somehow already assembled on a wide-open, coverless beach without anyone noticing.

tropes.name: Belly-Scraping Flight
tropes.html: During the Aerial Canyon Chase, Jumba's spaceship comes close enough to the ground to knock the sunburned tourist's ice cream cone out of his hand with its wingtip. In the deleted version with a hijacked 747, at one point the plane scrapes its landing gear against the side of a skyscraper in Honolulu.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html:
• Calling Lilo crazy or bringing up her dead mom in disparaging conversation. In the second case she gets so mad not even Stitch bothers to stop her.
  • Don't touch the photograph of Lilo, Nani, and her parents:
    Lilo: Be careful of that! You don't touch this! Don't ever touch it!
  • Don't call Jumba an idiot scientist, especially if you don't want your newspaper reporting on his arrest to get ripped up and eaten.

tropes.name: Beware the Nice Ones
tropes.html: Lilo can turn very nasty when provoked. She bit Mertle and punched her in the face for calling her crazy. She also yells at Stitch for attempting to touch her family photo, and is disgusted when Stitch reveals his true form to her after the house is blown up, shoving him away and ordering him to leave.

tropes.name: Beyond Redemption
tropes.html: Deconstructed in regards to Stitch. The Grand Councilwoman, unlike Gantu, at first tries to reason with him, then when he responds to her effort by saying something in Tantalog that is apparently considered incredibly obscene, she writes him off as a hopeless abomination and a danger who has to be banished to a desert asteroid. Throughout the rest of the movie, as Stitch grows far beyond his programming on Earth, it's clear that the Grand Councilwoman judged him far too soon, which almost leads to the galactic council arresting and banishing a fully-rehabilitated person, until she sees for herself how far he's come and she manages to amend his fate via Loophole Abuse.

tropes.name: Big Bad Ensemble
tropes.html: An interesting take on this; the Grand Councilwoman serves this role in the story, but in a larger context, she's actually the galaxy's Big Good. So, she's the Big Antagonist. Gantu is a more traditional one, as despite his technically good intentions he's apathetic at best to the collateral damage his manhunt for Stitch may cause. In the first and second acts, Jumba serves as the main antagonist and is the main source of conflict, but by the end of the film, he ultimately gets redeemed and becomes a hero.

tropes.name: Big Good
tropes.html: The Grand Councilwoman, as described in the above example, is a Reasonable Authority Figure who only serves a Big Bad role because Stitch is a monster initially.

tropes.name: The Big Guy
tropes.html: Gantu, both in command, as he is the Captain of the Galactic Armada, and in size, as he is possibly the biggest character on the ship.

tropes.name: Big "NO!"
tropes.html:
• Pleakley lets out three, each louder than the last, outside the house as Jumba attacks Stitch inside, throwing things through the roof.
  • Gantu lets out an angry one after he fails to shoot Stitch after blasting him off his ship with the afterburners.

tropes.name: Big Sister Instinct
tropes.html:
• Nani has this for Lilo, as they have only each other until Stitch comes along and does her best to take care of her.
  • Lilo, despite technically being his owner, becomes more of a sibling to Stitch, using Elvis Presley as a role model, with Stitch ultimately redeeming himself by enlisting the help of Jumba, Pleakley, and Nani to rescue Lilo from Gantu.
  • David Kawena displays Big Brother Instinct with Lilo, and Stitch, as a spear counterpart to Nani, diving into the ocean to rescue Lilo and Stitch from drowning after Jumba unsuccessfully tries to capture Stitch, and making at least two trips to bring Lilo's ʻohana and the aliens to the mainland after Stitch defeats Gantu.

tropes.name: Big, Stupid Doodoo-Head
tropes.html:
• Nani is almost hit by a car as she rushes back home to meet with the social worker. She shouts at the driver, "Watch where you're going, stupidhead!" It comes back to bite her when said "stupidhead" turns out to be the social worker assigned to her.
  • "Stupidhead" returns later in the film as Stitch's insult to Gantu when they stare each other down during their fight.

tropes.name: Big "WHAT?!"
tropes.html:
From Jumba.
Stitch: (Saying something along the lines of "Let's help save Lilo.")
Jumba: WHAT?!
(See Blunt "Yes" below.)

tropes.name: Big "YES!"
tropes.html:
• David lets out a loud "YEAH!" onstage when we first see him at the luau.
  • Near the end of the second surfing session, Stitch stands up on the surfboard and shouts "Yeah!", right before Jumba swims up behind him and snatches him.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html:
• Lilo has a sign on her door that says "Kapu", which is Hawaiian for "keep out" (related to the word "taboo", which is Tongan).
  • The name 'Lilo' means "generous one" in Hawaiian. It can also be interpreted as "lost" and this would give the song title "He Mele No Lilo" a loose translation as "Lullaby of the Lost".
  • The name 'Nani' means "beautiful" in Hawaiian.
  • "Lilo, you lolo, do we have a lobster door? No! We have a dog door! We are getting a dog!"
  • David uses the Hawaiian greeting "Howzit", which is Hawaiian slang for "How's it going?"
  • The 3 truck drivers use Pidgin (a mix of Hawaiian, Japanese, English, and other languages, some of which has made it to the mainland) "What we wen hit?" (What we went and hit?) and "It stay unda da truck" (It is under the truck.)
    • The song "Hawaiian Roller Coaster Ride" also uses some: "No biggie brudda" which means what it sounds like.

tropes.name: Blatant Lies
tropes.html:
• During Jumba's trial when he denies creating new lifeforms.
    Jumba: I would never ever (Stitch is presented as evidence) ...make more than one!
  • We see in the sequel material that this is a lie, too, made obvious in the original by that fact that Stitch is designated Experiment 626. Sequel also shows that he was literally caught red handed when he was finishing creation of Stitch.

tropes.name: Blind Jump
tropes.html: The hyperspace jump that sends Stitch to Kaua'i was entirely blind because his stolen cruiser's navigation systems weren't working. He was fortunate to land on a habitable planet, and more so for landing on an island instead of the water.

tropes.name: Bluffing the Advance Scout
tropes.html:
The Space Police are prepared to destroy Earth to get rid of Stitch, but Pleakley insists against it because Earth is considered a nature reserve for mosquitoes. Turns out this was because of an enterprising CIA agent (better known as the social worker Cobra Bubbles) convinced visiting aliens that mosquitoes are a rare and endangered species..
Cobra: Saved the planet once: convinced an alien race that mosquitoes were an endangered species.

tropes.name: Blunt "Yes"
tropes.html:
Jumba: After all you put me through, you expect me to help you, just like that?! Just like that?!
Stitch: Ih. ["Yes."]
(Beat)
Jumba: Fine!
Pleakley: "Fine?" You're doing what he says?!
Jumba: He is very persuasive.

tropes.name: B-Movie
tropes.html: Stitch sees one showing in a TV store window display, emulating it by acting like a monster. The movie in question is Earth vs. the Spider.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: When Stitch is first presented to the Galactic Council, the Grand Councilwoman initially tries to reason with him, and only sentences him to exile after he rudely rebuffs her attempt. At the end of the film, she is preparing to exile Stitch once more, but when he asks to say goodbye to Lilo and Nani, she realises that he's grown beyond his programming and can now be reasoned with, and agrees to commute his sentence so he can stay on Earth with his Family of Choice.

tropes.name: Bowdlerise
tropes.html: The scene of Lilo hiding in a clothes dryer was redrawn specifically for the United Kingdom release, where Lilo is instead hiding in a commode with a pizza box for a door. The reason for the change is due to the UK's legally-enforced stance of displaying dangerous behaviour that younger, more impressionable viewers may attempt to replicate. As strange as this change seems on the surface, it's hard to blame the UK for making Disney do this, as an estimated 2,000 kids a year get into clothes dryer accidents, some of which turn fatal, so enforcing this trope isn't a bad idea. This edit was also either removed from TV broadcasts (side-stepping the problem with an ad break) or altered as above, and has since become the standardized version of the film in all regions, beginning with its Disney+ release. The 2022 Blu-ray release and future 2-Disc Big Wave Edition prints from the same year replaced the original theatrical version (found on the first two Blu-ray releases and all prior DVD releases) with the UK edit, and in 2025, nearly all digital releases of the film have now been edited to use the UK edit, and the Ultra HD Blu-ray release that year is also using the edit.

tropes.name: "Both Sides Have a Point" Remark
tropes.html: The crux of the conflict between Cobra Bubbles and Nani: Bubbles is completely right that Nani is clearly severely struggling to raise Lilo (especially with Stitch's arrival complicating things immensely) and that it might be better for both if Lilo was taken away, but Nani is also correct that she is doing everything she can to raise Lilo right and that taking her away from her family would be tragic and traumatic.

tropes.name: Break the Cutie
tropes.html: Lilo and Nani are currently dealing with the loss of their parents and other problems, such as social isolation, before Stitch comes along and his trouble destroys their house.

tropes.name: Breaking the Fourth Wall
tropes.html: Lilo and Stitch look directly towards the viewer twice during their dance at Mrs. Hasagawa's fruit stand. Just before that, when Lilo gets Stitch to move his hips to the side, he looks at the viewer and oohs in wonder before the duo immediately go into their dance. A more subtle fourth wall-break happens earlier in the film when Stitch is adopted (as detailed under Easter Egg below).

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html:
• In the beginning of the film, the Grand Councilwoman prepares to gas Earth to ensure 626's termination, which Agent Pleakley, the council's Earth expert, protests since, apparently, the planet is a wildlife reserve for the endangered species mosquito, with the "primitive humanoid lifeforms" being their food of choice. It gets a follow-up throwaway joke in the middle of the film when Pleakley gets his first close-up experience of mosquitos' feeding method. Then, it's apparently forgotten about until the end, when Cobra Bubbles is explaining how he knows about aliens and reveals that he's the one who persuaded them that mosquitoes were an endangered species so that Earth would be protected by the Federation.
  • The frog Stitch threatens soon after arriving on Earth reappears later when Gantu has captured Lilo. A truck also appears in both scenes.

tropes.name: Broken Dialect, Impactful Speech
tropes.html:
Stitch/Experiment 626 generally, when he speaks at all, speaks in childish, flawed English. Near the end of the film, when the Grand Councilwoman asks who Lilo and Nani are to Stitch, Stitch slowly explains to her, showing how much he's grown from his beginnings as a chaotic evil creature:
This is my family. I found it, all on my own. It's little, and broken. But still good. Yeah. Still good.

tropes.name: Brown Note
tropes.html: Whatever it is that Stitch says in the courtroom, it causes three members to faint on the spot, and a robotic one starts vomiting nuts and bolts.

tropes.name: Brutal Honesty
tropes.html:
Cobra Bubbles, after his first visit to Lilo's and Nani's house:
Cobra Bubbles: Let me illuminate to you the precarious situation in which you have found yourself: I am the one they call when things have gone wrong, and things have indeed gone wrong.
(to Lilo) Call me next time you're left here alone.
(to Nani) In case you're wondering, this did not go well. You have three days to change my mind.

tropes.name: Bullethole Door
tropes.html: In the fight scene, Jumba fires a bunch of plates around where Stitch is standing, causing the segment to collapse on top of him.

tropes.name: Call a Smeerp a "Rabbit"
tropes.html: "I got a new dog, his name is Stitch!"

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html:
• When he first emerges from his ship on Earth, Stitch encounters a frog and nearly shoots it because of his homicidal tendencies. During the climax, he saves a frog (possibly the same one) from being collateral when Gantu shoots at him.
  • When Stitch is first introduced, Jumba states he is fireproof, among other things. One of the things we see him doing in the montage at the end is working alongside David as a fire dancer, and because of his extra set of arms, he is able to hold four flaming poles, as opposed to David's two.
  • Stitch uses a red police cruiser to escape from Planet Turo at the beginning. At the end, Jumba, dressed as Santa Claus, presents Lilo and Stitch with two smaller but similar cruisers at Christmas, and Stitch's one looks like a smaller version of the one he used to escape earlier.

tropes.name: Came from the Sky
tropes.html: Lilo and Nani see something crash near their house. Nani doesn't seem to care but Lilo thinks it's a shooting star and makes a wish for a friend, "Maybe an angel, the nicest angel you have." Cut to a decidedly non-angelic Experiment 626 emerging from the wreckage.

tropes.name: Can-Crushing Cranium
tropes.html: Stitch crushes a can with his head as he wanders around the house, at a loss to what to do next.

tropes.name: Car Fu
tropes.html:
Stitch is easily strong enough to pick up Nani's Volkswagen Beetle and smack Jumba with it, even referencing the "punch buggy" Car Ride Game in the process.note When you see a Volkswagen Beetle, you say "[Beetle color] punch buggy!" and lightly punch the guy next to you.
Stitch: Blue punch buggy! [smacks Jumba with it] No punch back! [throws it at Jumba]

tropes.name: Carnivore Confusion
tropes.html: Lilo thinks it's horrendous to feed a tuna sandwich to Pudge, who is a fish just like tuna is. Though Pudge is not a tuna fish, he seems more in line with Hawaii's native tropical fauna.

tropes.name: Casual Danger Dialogue
tropes.html:
There's a moment during the fight between Stitch and Jumba. While the two of them are causing reckless destruction to the house, Lilo calls Cobra Bubbles, the social worker assigned to her wellbeing, and informs him that aliens are attacking her house and trying to steal her "dog", and hangs up in relief because her dog found the chainsaw. All said with the same tone of voice a kid would use to call a parent about a mild inconvenience that resolved itself.
Lilo: (on the phone) Hello, Cobra Bubbles? Aliens are attacking my house.

tropes.name: Catapult to Glory
tropes.html: A variation occurs when Stitch uses an exploding tanker truck to launch himself at Gantu's spaceship.

tropes.name: Catch and Return
