tropes.name: Promotion to Parent
tropes.html: Nani, who struggles to balance out her job, social workers, the loss of her parents, Lilo's strange coping methods, and Stitch. Lilo admits that she likes her more as a sister than a mom — done realistically; Nani is young, she has an Annoying Younger Sibling, and is trying to balance it all out.

tropes.name: Protected by a Child
tropes.html: Stitch initially uses Lilo as a human shield.

tropes.name: Punctuated Pounding
tropes.html:
When Stitch confronts Gantu, the latter tries to pound him into a pulp, with this exchange:
Gantu: You're vile! [punch] You're foul! [punch] You're flawed! [punch, he actually hits Stitch]
Stitch: [effortlessly lifts Gantu's fist] Also cute and fluffy! [lifts Gantu overhead and chucks him right out the cockpit's window]

tropes.name: Puni Plush
tropes.html: The character designers were explicitly told to avoid straight lines and harsh angles, and rectangular objects have dulled corners, probably as a deliberate contrast with the then-rampant abuse of straight lines in Western animation. This becomes somewhat more amusing when the creator's DeviantArt page is viewed, which continues the same style, but includes artistic nudes and 1950s style pinups with a Hawaiian theme.

tropes.name: Rain Means Death
tropes.html:
It's implied that Lilo and Nani's parents were killed in a car accident during a heavy rainfall, as Lilo notes to Stitch:
Lilo: That's us before... it was rainy, and they went for a drive.

tropes.name: Reality Has No Subtitles
tropes.html: Characters in the movie speak Hawaiian without subtitles.

tropes.name: Reasonable Authority Figure
tropes.html:
• The Grand Councilwoman is rather reasonable for being the head of the Galactic Federation, although like most aliens, she believes Pleakley when he tells her to spare Earth from destruction because mosquitoes are endangered. She's also willing to give Stitch a chance to speak for himself when he's initially introduced at Jumba's trial, rather than outright condemning him. Then at the end of the film, she expresses regret at having to take Stitch in after he's shown to have calmed down and matured somewhat, and seems rather satisfied when Lilo provides a loophole as to why the Grand Councilwoman can't take Stitch.
  • Cobra Bubbles serves as an antagonist, but he's by no means a bad person. He clearly doesn't want to take Lilo away from Nani in spite of a mountain of (inaccurate) evidence that she can't really handle Lilo, and gives her every chance in his power for her to prove she can turn things around which makes it all the more heartbreaking when he gives up and decides he's got no choice but to take Lilo away. Later on, after Stitch rescues Lilo, he tells the Grand Councilwoman that his newfound family may be a bit dysfunctional, but they still have a number of redeeming qualities. At the end, Cobra reminds Lilo that she purchased Stitch from the shelter, and Lilo produces the ownership papers, which clarifies that Lilo is Stitch's adopter and guardian.

tropes.name: Recruiting the Criminal
tropes.html: To catch the dangerous genetic experiment, the Intergalactic Alliance sends the Mad Scientist who created him, since he's the only one who knows how to defeat him.

tropes.name: Red Is Heroic
tropes.html:
• Inverted with the red police cruiser Stitch steals to escape from the Galactic Federation, as he is a Villain Protagonist at this point. The same applies for the red jumpsuit he wears until he gets hit by three trucks.
  • Played straight with the mostly red mu'umu'u Lilo wears throughout the film.

tropes.name: Red Ones Go Faster
tropes.html: Stitch escapes custody by stealing a specifically-colored space police cruiser. It gets destroyed when he crash lands on Earth, though.

tropes.name: Rejected Apology
tropes.html:
Lilo tries to apologize to Mertle for attacking her, but she rejects it.
Lilo: I'm sorry I bit you... and pulled your hair... and punched you in the face.
Mertle: Apology NOT accepted. Now get out of my way before I run you over!
(Stitch then pushes Mertle off of her trike)

tropes.name: Remaster
tropes.html: The 2025 Ultra HD Blu-ray marked the first time a hand-drawn Disney movie received a physical Dolby Vision release. (Before 2025, Walt Disney Animation Studios only applied Dolby Vision to 4K theatrical prints and digital/streaming copies.)

tropes.name: Reminder of Duty
tropes.html: Captain Gantu is taunting Experiment 626 while in confinement when 626 bites him on the finger. Gantu is about to shoot him with his blaster at point-blank range when another officer, who's barely as big as his foot, reminds the Captain that he's still on duty, and Gantu reluctantly backs off.

tropes.name: Removed from the Picture
tropes.html: Inverted at the end of the movie; the first part of the credits ends with a shot of the photograph of Lilo and Nani with their deceased parents, with a cut-out of Stitch strategically placed so that it looks like he's sitting with them, symbolizing that he's now part of their ohana.

tropes.name: Removed Species Calamity
tropes.html: Defied. At the beginning of the film, Pleakley stops the Galactic Federation from destroying Earth just to kill Experiment 626 because it is considered a wildlife preserve for "endangered" mosquitos. Turns out to be Invoked, as Cobra Bubbles is revealed to have convinced the Galactic Federation of mosquitos' endangered status and the consequences for destroying them during his time as a Man in Black, keeping the Earth protected indefinitely.

tropes.name: Restrained Revenge
tropes.html: The Grand Councilwoman of the United Galactic Federation sends Jumba and Agent Pleakley on a mission to retrieve Experiment 626 in exchange for Jumba's freedom. When she tries to get a positive status report from Pleakley on Jumba's progress, she realizes that they weren't the best choices for the job, so she threatens to have Jumba and Pleakley sent to prison for failing to capture Experiment 626, who is taking refuge with Lilo and Nani. Later on, when Jumba and Pleakley decide to help Nani recover Lilo from Captain Gantu's clutches, the Grand Councilwoman claims credit for the mission, deciding not to send them to prison, but to leave them behind on Earth, joining Stitch in exile.

tropes.name: Retractable Appendages
tropes.html: Stitch's antennae, back spikes and extra arms. The scene when he first does this in the animal shelter provides the page image.

tropes.name: Revised Ending
tropes.html: The original ending featured the aliens hijacking a plane, but that was scrapped after 9/11.

tropes.name: Rewatch Bonus
tropes.html:
• Upon first viewing, when Lilo says she feeds Pudge the fish a peanut butter sandwich because he "controls the weather", viewers assume she's being eccentric as an Establishing Character Moment. However, this becomes melancholic later on as there's reason behind it: Lilo's parents died in a car accident during a rainstorm, meaning that feeding Pudge is actually a coping mechanism she developed to help process their death.
  • Not only that, but on apparent rewatching, pay close attention to the sky above Lilo after she gives Pudge his sandwich: the clouds that were gathering gradually disperse. Meaning Lilo may be right.

tropes.name: Ridiculously Cute Critter
tropes.html: When he is not being aggressive or mischievous, Stitch is absolutely adorable.

tropes.name: Right Behind Me
tropes.html:
Nani threatens Lilo after Lilo locks her out of the house just as social worker Cobra Bubbles stops by to check on her.
Nani: Oh, I'm going to stuff you into a blender, press "puree", then bake you into a pie and feed it to the social worker! And when he says "Mmm, this is great. What's your secret?", I'm going to say...(Bubbles uses his foot to hook her out of the doggie-door; she gasps) Love... and nurturing.

tropes.name: Road-Sign Reversal
tropes.html: Jumba says that Stitch's programming will draw him to large cities, where he will back up sewers, reverse street signs, and steal everybody's left shoe.

tropes.name: Roswell That Ends Well
tropes.html: Cobra Bubbles is revealed to have saved the Earth from aliens by convincing them mosquitoes were an endangered species; this occurred at Roswell... in 1973.

tropes.name: Rousseau Was Right
tropes.html: Lilo believes that everyone has some good in them even if most of their personality is bad, and her belief is put to the test with Stitch, whom Jumba had programmed to be nothing more than a destructive monster. She ends up being vindicated when Stitch overcomes his programming and becomes good by his own right, though not after going through a lot of hardship.

tropes.name: Rudeness Backfire
tropes.html: When we first see Nani, she's panicking because Lilo didn't wait for her at the hula school like she was supposed to, and a social worker is coming to their house. While she's running home, she almost gets hit by a car and angrily yells, "Watch where you're going, stupidhead!" before kicking it. The driver of that car turns out to be the social worker, Cobra Bubbles, and it leaves him with a bad first impression of her that only gets worse when he sees the untidy state of the house.

tropes.name: Rule of Three
tropes.html:
• After a failed social counseling inspection, Cobra Bubbles gives Nani three days for a second one to prove herself a competent guardian to Lilo. The third day is when everything changes
  • Soon after crash-landing on Earth, Stitch gets run over by three trucks, one after the other.
  • The fat man trying to eat his mint chocolate chip ice cream fails three times. The first time, Lilo takes a picture of him and the ice cream falls off the cone. The second time is during Stitch's rampage on the beach while Nani is applying for a lifeguard job. As people run for it, one bumps into the man and he again loses his ice cream. The third is during the climax, when the ice cream is knocked out of the man's hand by the wing of Jumba's spaceship. Yes, really.

tropes.name: Rules Lawyer
tropes.html: When the Grand Councilwoman tries to take Stitch, Lilo shows her the dog license that she bought when she adopted Stitch, meaning that the GCW would be stealing her property. Cobra Bubbles, who had worked with aliens before, mentions that "aliens are all about rules."

tropes.name: Running Gag
tropes.html: The guy whose ice cream always falls off its cone before he can eat it.

tropes.name: Running Over the Plot
tropes.html: After Experiment 626 crash-lands on Kauaʻi, he runs into a road, gets distracted by rain and a frog, and then gets run over by three tractor trailer trucks, only knocking him unconscious due to his Nigh-Invulnerability. This would lead to him being brought to the animal shelter where Lilo adopts him as "Stitch", starting the main core of the plot.

tropes.name: Safety in Muggles
tropes.html: Jumba can't open fire on Stitch because of his close company with Lilo. He enjoys reminding Stitch of it though, when he revealed the handle of his plasma weapon from inside a paper sack. This is because Cobra Bubbles convinced some aliens that humans should be protected (he claimed that mosquitoes are an endangered species, and that humans are their primary food source).

tropes.name: Say My Name
tropes.html:
• Both Nani and Bubbles shout "Lilo!" a few times after Lilo flees Bubbles's car and runs off.
  • Lilo screams Stitch's name twice in the climax. The first time is after Stitch is blasted off of Gantu's ship with the afterburners, and the second time is after he crashes the truck into the volcano and Gantu's ship comes at him again.
  • Nani screams Lilo's name again after Gantu's ship blows up.

tropes.name: Scale Model Destruction
tropes.html:
Stitch makes a scale model of San Francisco in Lilo's room... then thrashes it in a kaiju rampage. This was a way for him to tell Lilo what his true purpose is without actually saying so. She doesn't get it.
Lilo: No more caffeine for you.

tropes.name: Scary Black Man
tropes.html: Played with in the case of Cobra Bubbles. At first, he looks very imposing and acts rather uncaring. However later on, he shows himself to be a lot more than that. He does indeed want Lilo to be safe, but he doesn't want to split Lilo and Nani up because they're all they have in the world, mentioning he'll take Lilo away only because he has to. The end credits show him hanging out with them, watching movies, and having Thanksgiving dinner.

tropes.name: Scenery Porn
tropes.html: This was the first animated feature since Dumbo to use watercolor backgrounds, which was an advantage to make the island of Kauai look as luscious as possible. The only thing that was missing was the large number of moa (wild chickens) roaming around the island.

tropes.name: The Scream
tropes.html:
When Pleakley and Jumba spend their first night on Earth, and Pleakley discovers a very painful truth about the so-called wildlife preserve's so-called "endangered species":
Pleakley: Look! A mosquito has chosen me as her perch. She's so beautiful. Look, another one! And another one! Why, it's a whole flock! They like me! They're nuzzling my flesh with their noses! Now they're... they're...
(Cut to a distant shot of their campsite near the house as Pleakley screams in pain)

tropes.name: Scream Discretion Shot
tropes.html: When Pleakley gets swarmed by mosquitoes, the camera cuts away as we are treated to this.

tropes.name: Sensitive Guy and Manly Man
tropes.html: Pleakley's sensitive guy to Jumba's manly man. One has a complete refusal to destroy Earth while the other built a genetic experiment that (assuming that he hadn't been caught) would have wreaked havoc throughout the galaxy.

tropes.name: Sesquipedalian Loquaciousness
tropes.html:
• It's said that Stitch can't survive in water since "his molecular density is too great". This would mean simply that he has a higher density than water — i.e. even if he were, for example, to hold his breath, he would not be able to displace enough water to increase his buoyancy enough and he'd still be too dense to swim. In layman's terms: he sinks like a rock and can't swim.
  • Cobra Bubbles. "Allow me to illuminate to you the precarious position in which you find yourself," and "Thus far, you've been adrift in the harbor of my patience."

tropes.name: The Shadow Knows
tropes.html: When Nani walks into the kitchen complaining about Stitch, his shadow is silhouetted on the wall with his antennae, spines, and extra arms extended. She gasps and drops the phone, and the camera cuts to Stitch in his "dog" form raiding the fridge.

tropes.name: Shipped in Shackles
tropes.html: After being sentenced to exile, Stitch is secured in pod that restrains everything but his head before being loaded onto the prison transport ship. Doubles as a Tailor-Made Prison.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• When Stitch rips up a drawing of Lilo's, she exclaims, "No! That's from my blue period!"
  • Many of the background aliens have designs based on Winnie the Pooh characters. The alien who says "He's loose on deck C" appears to be modeled after Roo, the alien who calculates where Stitch will land is clearly modeled after Piglet, and "Tigger" informs the High Councilwoman that most of Earth is covered in water.
  • Mulan Wok. Also, there is a Mulan poster hanging on Nani's wall.
  • In Lilo's room, on the shelf on her easel, there's a small Dumbo doll. Doubly fitting is the fact that Dumbo was also an outcast in his film, which was also painted with watercolors like this one.
  • During the end credits, the photo around the dinner table is staged like Norman Rockwell's Freedom from Want.
  • The blonde lifeguard's red swimsuit is of the same style and cut as the iconic red swimsuits worn by the women of Baywatch.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html: The writers and animators clearly did a lot of homework to show aspects of Hawaiian culture without spelling it out for the audience. Not only that, but many aspects of the town this takes place in are based off of Hanapēpē.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Idealism vs. Cynicism
tropes.html: Heavily optimistic and in a surprisingly realistic way with Lilo and Nani's life.

tropes.name: Snark-to-Snark Combat
tropes.html:
Jumba and Stitch trade insults while brawling in Lilo's house.
Jumba: I'll put you back together again. I'll make you taller, and not so fluffy! (throws plates at Stitch, who is crawling on the ceiling)
Stitch: I like fluffy!

tropes.name: Social Services Does Not Exist
tropes.html: Averted in the most traumatizing way — the contrast of wacky alien hijinks with the reality of a teenage orphan trying and failing to support her baby sister is a main plot point.

tropes.name: Songs of Solace
tropes.html: Lilo slumps on the floor and listens to "Heartbreak Hotel" after being rejected by the other girls.

tropes.name: Source Music
tropes.html:
• The opening chant, "He Mele No Lilo", is also the song being performed by Lilo's hula class, for which she is late.
  • Stitch plays the ukulele to the solos in Elvis Presley's "(You're the) Devil in Disguise", which plays in the background.

tropes.name: Space Isolation Horror
tropes.html: Implied to be the fate of Experiment 626: he's to be taken by prison transport to a barren asteroid, and abandoned there. Perhaps, the authorities forbid capital punishment, or the condemned is too indestructible to be executed. It's still marooning on a cold, lonely rock in the void of space.

tropes.name: Space Plane
tropes.html:
• The United Galactic Federation has a fleet of them.
  • Jumba's ship counts as well, especially that its model is actually modified from a Boeing 747 model that was used for the original version of the dogfight against Gantu.

tropes.name: Spiteful Spit
tropes.html: Stitch spits on the guard keeping an eye on him. Since the cannons in the cell are locked to his genetic signature, he then realizes that he can blow up the door to his cell by spitting on it, too.

tropes.name: Split-Screen Phone Call
tropes.html:
Used for a brief moment while Lilo is on the phone with Cobra Bubbles.
Lilo: Oh good, my dog found the chainsaw.
Mr. Bubbles: Lilo! Don't hang—

tropes.name: Standard Snippet
tropes.html: Given that this movie is set in Hawaii, "Aloha ʻOe" naturally makes an appearance. However, it's not the silly instrumental steel guitar version that shows up most times this song is used as a Standard Snippet — the lyrics (about saying goodbye to someone) show up, too, in the most utterly heartbreaking fashion.

tropes.name: Stealth Hi/Bye
tropes.html: When Lilo first reveals Scrump after hula class when she wants to play dolls with the other girls, they are horrified by the doll's appearance, and Lilo doesn't notice until she's in the middle of her next line that the girls have gone.

tropes.name: Storefront Television Display
tropes.html: Stitch happens to pass an appliance store with a TV set in the front window. The set is showing an old B-movie: Earth vs. the Spider. Stitch later constructs a scale model of San Francisco in Lilo's room just so that he can go all Gojiro on it. Lilo glumly notes, "No more caffeine for you."

tropes.name: Stuff Blowing Up
tropes.html: Lilo and Nani's house, thanks to Jumba's jammed gun. And in the climax, Gantu's ship after Stitch gets Lilo out of it.

tropes.name: Suddenly Shouting
tropes.html: Pleakley does this during a call to his mother while he and Jumba are up a palm tree spying on Stitch: "Oh, can't complain, Mom. I'm camping out with a convicted criminal, and, uh, oh, I had my head chewed on BY A MONSTER!"

tropes.name: Summoned by Sobbing
tropes.html:
• Discussed when Lilo says that in her copy of The Ugly Duckling, the duckling cries out of loneliness, only for his real family to hear him and accept him the way he is.
  • After Lilo gets kidnapped by Captain Gantu, she weeps in despair before Jumba and Pleakley's ship appears to rescue her. Downplayed in that Stitch, Nani, and the aliens were already coming to save her.

tropes.name: Sundress of Innocence
tropes.html: In every one of her appearances, Lilo wears a muumuu with a flower pattern (usually either red with white palm fronds or yellow with green leaves). While a bit temperamental and prone to saying things her older sister wishes she wouldn't, Lilo is an innocent child who believes that anyone can be good. She's the main reason why Stitch pulls his Heel–Face Turn, doesn't understand why others see her as weird, and readily welcomes several aliens into her ʻohana.

tropes.name: Superior Species
tropes.html: The aliens compared to "primitive humanoid life forms", who have to begin life all over when an asteroid strikes the planet. It's justified, as from the point of view of a galactic-spanning alien empire, humans are primitive.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Happy Ending
tropes.html: Just after Stitch saves Lilo, the Grand Councilwoman arrives to take him away. Even after Stitch shows signs of being reformed, the Councilwoman points out that the law is absolute. Then Lilo points out that she bought him at the shelter, and that taking him away would be stealing. The Councilwoman then declares that Stitch will serve the rest of his sentence on Earth, under the care of Lilo and her family. As an added bonus, because of this, Lilo's family is under intergalactic protection. This means that she can't be taken away by child services, which she was initially facing.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html:
The main reason why this film is a comedy-drama instead of a straight comedy.
  • When Lilo's home gets destroyed by a bunch of aliens, it's played for laughs. When Nani and social worker Cobra Bubbles come back (just after Nani was able to convince him not to separate her from Lilo)... it leads to the social worker deciding to take the little girl away, much to Nani and Lilo's despair.
  • By extension, the entire film's slapstick is typical of the comedy genre, but it's significantly less funny from the perspective of Nani, who ends up suffering real consequences for it (losing her job, several other potential positions, her house, and nearly her sister) because of it, and Cobra Bubbles, who only sees the aftermath of what appears to be Nani's irresponsible parenting.
  • Soon after his crash-landing, Stitch attempts to take down a truck driving right at him... and gets run over.

tropes.name: Tailor-Made Prison
tropes.html: Stitch is taken to a cell where two laser cannons (locked to his genetic signature) are aimed at him that will cause him physical harm if he decides to make a break for it instead of being sent to a desert asteroid as his captives have planned, in addition to a rather sturdy door and a guard to keep an eye on him. He manages to break out anyway.

tropes.name: Take That!
tropes.html: The film has an undercurrent expressing a cynical view toward Hawaii becoming a tourist trap. Lilo takes pictures of white visiting tourists for a photo collection, reversing the objectifying behavior of tourists taking photos of residents of the places they're visiting, and Nani expresses a sour-grapes but understandable sentiment after losing her waitressing job that she was doing a hokey luau show for foreigners. The sunburned tourist Lilo photographs is also portrayed as a Butt-Monkey who never gets to enjoy his ice cream.

tropes.name: Tears of Defeat
tropes.html: Agent Pleakley is sent to Earth with Jumba Jookiba to capture Jumba's experiment Stitch (known to them as "626"), but they are either cautious because of the presence of humans or constantly failing at every turn. After a few days have passed, the Grand Councilwoman loses patience and fires them for their "incompetence". While Pleakley bursts into tears, Jumba is ecstatic at the chance to "do it [his] way" without restrictions or stealth.

tropes.name: The Teaser
tropes.html: Jumba's trial and 626's subsequent escape.

tropes.name: Technically a Smile
tropes.html: 626 bares his teeth in the most humorously creepy way when he says "Hi!" to Lilo in an attempt to show friendliness and to get her to adopt him. Considering what happens from there, you could say that it worked.

tropes.name: Tempting Fate
tropes.html: After Nani sees a fire engine drives past after the house is blown up, she quietly says, "Oh, don't turn left." It does.

tropes.name: They Wasted a Perfectly Good Sandwich
tropes.html: Poor Ice Cream Man... his mint chocolate chip scoop keeps falling off of its cone at the most inopportune moments.

tropes.name: Third-Person Person
tropes.html: Stitch, mostly, although he actually does this only twice in the movie when he strikes a conversation with the Grand Councilwoman when she comes to arrest him, and within seconds of each instance. ("Does Stitch have to go in the ship?" and "Can Stitch say goodbye?") Still, it's in the franchise's later material where this becomes a regular habit for him.

tropes.name: Threatening Shark
tropes.html: "Oh, look, a friendly little dolphin. They helped sailors during the war... It's a shark! It's a shark and it ain't friendly! Looks like a dolphin... Tricky fish! Tricky fish!" It turns out to be an octopus.

tropes.name: Throw the Book at Them
tropes.html: When Cobra Bubbles visits Lilo and Nani's house to talk about the latter losing her job, Stitch comes up to him with a book... before suddenly growling at him and chucking the book at his face, which gets Nani in even more trouble with Cobra.

tropes.name: To Catch Heroes, Hire Villains
tropes.html: In lieu of destroying the planet to recover the escaped Experiment 626 (thanks to mosquitoes being considered an endangered species), the Grand Councilwoman decides to send 626's creator, Mad Scientist Jumba Jookiba, to recapture his creation in exchange for a pardon alongside Earth expert Pleakley. Although she eventually fires them because of their incompetence and sends Captain Gantu to do the job right.

tropes.name: Tongue-Out Insult
tropes.html: Nani was about to take Stitch back to the pound when Lilo told her that O'hana means family which means nobody gets left behind. Nani tells Lilo she hates when she uses O'hana on her. Lilo responds by sticking her tongue out at Nani who returns the favor.

tropes.name: Trademark Favorite Food
tropes.html: Mint chocolate chip ice cream seems to be this for the fat guy tourist. Shame he never gets round to actually eating it.

tropes.name: Training the Pet
tropes.html: Cobra Bubbles says he wants Stitch the alien to act more like a "model citizen", so Lilo tries to teach Stitch to be good the way Elvis Presley would've wanted, such as showing him how to dance and play the guitar. Stitch's attempts to follow her orders keep ruining Nani's efforts to get a new job.

tropes.name: Translation: "Yes"
tropes.html:
• A variant occurs near the end of the film, where Stitch is trying to convince Jumba and Pleakley to help him rescue Lilo from Captain Gantu.
    Jumba: What?! After all you put me through, you expect me to help you just like that? Just like that?!
    Stitch: Ih.
    Jumba: Fine!
    Pleakley: "Fine"? You're doing what he says?
    Jumba: He's very persuasive.
  • We later learn that "Ih" just means "yes", making it funnier.

tropes.name: Trash the Set
tropes.html: When Jumba chases Stitch into the house and tries to attack him, the house gets more and more damaged, culminating in Jumba's plugged gun blowing the house up.

tropes.name: Travel Montage
tropes.html: Stitch's journey to Earth and Hawaii, as shown on the Grand Councilwoman's computer monitor.

tropes.name: Tree Buchet
tropes.html: While Jumba and Pleakley are up a tree spying on Stitch, Jumba lets himself out of the tree at the end of the scene, catapulting Pleakley away.

tropes.name: The Trickster
tropes.html: This is what Stitch is designed to be. In the words of his creator, "back up sewers, reverse street signs and steal everyone's left shoe". He's very good at being one.

tropes.name: True Companions
tropes.html: Though Lilo and Nani are blood relatives, they form an unconventional little ʻohana with their alien house guests.

tropes.name: Tuft of Head Fur
tropes.html: Stitch has a small tuft of fur on his head.

tropes.name: Unfulfilled Purpose Misery
tropes.html: Stitch is initially an artificial alien programmed to wreck large cities. Early in the story, he ends up on an island devoid of large cities while unable to swim. The results of him going through this trope for a while before he finds a new purpose in the human family that adopted him as a dog.

tropes.name: Uninhabitable to Aliens
tropes.html: Zig-zagged; ninety percent of the time, aliens can come to Earth without suffering any ill effects (as Jumba and Pleakley are able to spend several days breathing the air and eating the food without a problem). However, deep water is extremely dangerous for Stitch, who is too heavy to swim and is in real danger of drowning if he goes in over his head. Hence why he's so distressed to learn that Kauai is completely surrounded by water.

tropes.name: The Unintelligible
tropes.html: Throughout most of the film, Stitch speaks an alien language called Tantalog.note In actuality for the film, Chris Sanders just spoke a bunch of alienistic gibberish and didn't really intend to give them actual definite meanings. He stated on TikTok that it was the writing staff of Lilo & Stitch: The Series who decided to make a semi-consistent language out of his gibberish. Though he understands and can speak English, he keeps it to himself, since he is aware that he is pretending to be a dog and the woman at the animal shelter said dogs can't talk.

tropes.name: Unishment
tropes.html: Stitch's sentence for the havoc he caused is exile on Earth. The Grand Councilwoman does this intentionally, though, to avoid separating him from his newfound family, avoid violating the law of both the Federation and Earth by stealing Stitch from his owner, and still satisfying her comrades' desire to see Stitch punished for his actions.

tropes.name: Unlucky Extra
tropes.html: The fat guy tourist. Every time he runs into Lilo, he loses his ice cream. Once it was even knocked out of his hands by a spaceship.

tropes.name: Unsuccessful Pet Adoption
tropes.html: Almost happened between Lilo and Stitch when he causes trouble the first day after being adopted. Lilo manages to convince Nani not to take him back because of what their dad told them.

tropes.name: Unusually Uninteresting Sight
tropes.html: Nobody really seems to notice or care much about Jumba and Pleakley, when their disguises do almost nothing to hide themselves. Stitch is a similar case, though most characters do react to him, with their first question usually being along the lines of "what is that?"

tropes.name: Unusual Pets for Unusual People
tropes.html: Lilo, a quirky girl with a dark streak, goes to the animal shelter and gets the weirdest looking pet there, actually an escaped alien who she thinks is a puppy. Before she does, she asks the shelter attendant for a lobster.

tropes.name: Unwitting Instigator of Doom
tropes.html: Jumba plugs his own gun with a carrot when Stitch grabs it, only for this to cause the gun to overload and blow the house up.

tropes.name: Up, Up and Away!
tropes.html: Stitch assumes the one-arm-up pose after launching himself towards Gantu's ship with an exploding tanker truck.

tropes.name: Vanilla Edition
tropes.html: Disney nowadays tends to release DVDs with much fewer bonus features than Blu-ray Discs and iTunes digital copies. This movie provides an exception, as the Blu-ray Disc (which also holds Stitch Has a Glitch) contains no bonus features at all, while the "Big Wave" 2-Disc DVD (released in 2009) and iTunes Digital HD copy boast hours of extras. The blow to Blu-ray collectors gets softened just ever so slightly by Disney including disc one of the Big Wave DVD in the Blu-ray/DVD combo pack, and a digital code in the Blu-ray/Digital HD combo pack. A 2017 re-release, however, contains only the Blu-ray with just the two films and a digital code. Eventually, in they re-released the Blu-ray 2-Movie collection again in 2022 with both the aforementioned DVDs and the digital code included, and both films now have their own separate Blu-ray Discs with bonus features, albeit only uplifting the video bonuses from past DVD releases. The 2025 Ultra HD Blu-ray, which does not have Lilo & Stitch 2 included, goes back to this, with the UHD Blu-ray only containing the film, although the package includes the 2022 Blu-ray disc.

tropes.name: Verbal Deflection
tropes.html:
When Lilo is first introduced to social worker Cobra Bubbles, she notes his intimidating appearance, and asks him, point blank, if he's ever killed anyone.
Mr. Bubbles: [deadpan] We're getting off the subject.

tropes.name: Victimized Bystander
tropes.html: There's the fat tourist with an ice cream cone, which keeps dropping anytime he runs into Lilo. In his last scene, the ice cream is knocked off by the wing of a passing spaceship.

tropes.name: Villainous Rescue
tropes.html:
Throughout the film, Pleakley has wanted to catch Stitch without harming or scaring any humans. When Jumba and Stitch's fight results in a weapon going into overload, Pleakely grabs her and runs out of the house, carrying her clear of the blast radius. To be fair, he and Jumba were never really villains: they'd been ordered to capture someone who was basically a wanted criminal. And by the end, they've fully made a Heel–Face Turn.
Lilo: (as Pleakely carries her away) We're leaving Stitch?
Pleakely: Trust me! This is not gonna end well!

tropes.name: Villains Out Shopping
tropes.html: Subverted a few times with Jumba and Pleakley while they are disguised, as they are trying to blend in and use the opportunity to recapture Stitch.

tropes.name: Villain Protagonist
tropes.html: Initially played straight with Stitch, subverted after his Character Development.

tropes.name: Walking Shirtless Scene
tropes.html: David, who only gets a shirt in a few of the photos at the end of the movie.

tropes.name: Walking Swimsuit Scene
tropes.html: Nani. Both her sporty striped bikini for surfing and the green one with matching sandals and sarong for her job at the luau.

tropes.name: Weaponized Exhaust
tropes.html: Gantu turns his exhaust inward on Stitch, who is trying to rescue Lilo from the pod in the back of the ship.

tropes.name: Well-Intentioned Extremist
tropes.html: The Grand Councilwoman briefly considers gassing Earth as noted above. Fortunately, Pleakley persuades her not to.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
• When Mr. Bubbles asks, "Lilo, didn't you buy that thing at the shelter?", this causes Lilo to remember she adopted Stitch and shows her adoption papers to the GC to convince her to let Stitch stay, because if she takes him away, she'll be guilty of theft.
  • Lilo reveals the fate of her parents to Stitch.
    Lilo: That's us before... it was rainy, and they went for a drive.
  • Right after that, Lilo reveals something about Stitch so matter-of-fact, it hits you like a train.
    Lilo: I hear you cry at night. Do you dream about them?
  • In relative terms, Stitch gives one to the Grand Councilwoman:
    GC: If it wasn't for Experiment 626, none of this—
    Stitch: Stitch.
    GC: What?
    Stitch: My name Stitch.
    GC: Stitch, then. If it wasn't for Stitch— (she realizes that he just spoke calmly and rationally to her)

tropes.name: What Measure Is a Non-Human?
tropes.html: Inverted. When Gantu finally appears on earth, he captures both Lilo and Stitch at once; as he secures their pod to the back of his ship, he refers to Lilo as a snack for Stitch. Justified, as Pleakley's informal report on Earth clearly indicated that humans were the unintelligent food source for the mosquito.

tropes.name: What the Hell, Hero?
tropes.html: After Cobra Bubbles has left with the impression that Nani is incompetent as he states his visit did not go well, Nani gives one to Lilo for not waiting for her at the porch of the Hula School which she has instructed her to do so and rightfully questions her if she wants to be taken away into foster care.

tropes.name: "Where Are They Now?" Epilogue
tropes.html: The end credits feature a collection of photos showing the new family after the events of the movie.

tropes.name: White-and-Grey Morality
tropes.html: Rather unusually for a Disney film, there are no straightforwardly evil characters. No one here is truly evil, not even self-described "evil genius" Jumba and "evil experiment" Stitch. Even Gantu is simply a law enforcement officer pursuing a dangerous criminal and trying to recapture what he views as a violent, uncontrollable monster though, bringing along a defenseless human girl with said "monster" with the notion that she'd become a "snack" for it might have been going a little too far. Cobra Bubbles is sinister, but also genuinely concerned for Lilo's well-being. The Grand Councilwoman fulfills the role of a Big Bad (in terms of sending her lieutenant Gantu to Earth to hunt down the protagonist), but in terms of personality, she's closer to a Reasonable Authority Figure. The most straightforwardly dislikable characters in the movie are Mertle and her friends, but their role is minimal and their dislike of Lilo is shown to be somewhat justified. (They only turn nasty in the sequel material.)

tropes.name: Wholesome Crossdresser
tropes.html: Agent Pleakley is trying to blend in with Hawaiian tourists. Miraculously, no one notices that the petite brunette accompanying Jumba has green skin, three fingers, three legs and one eye. Nani chalks it up to Stitch's assault on him, but Jumba reassures her, "Actually, she's just ugly."

tropes.name: Wish Upon a Shooting Star
tropes.html: Lilo mistakes Experiment 626's crash landing for a shooting star and wishes for a friend.

tropes.name: Would Hurt a Child
tropes.html:
• Gantu captures Lilo alongside Stitch and doesn't seem too fazed about it, even saying he caught Stitch "a little snack", implying he thought Stitch would eat her. We know he wouldn't, but still.
  • Jumba invades Nani's house after he and Pleakley are fired by the Grand Councilwoman:
    Jumba: (to Stitch) Hiding behind your little friend won't work any more. Didn't I tell you? We got fired this morning, new rules.

tropes.name: Wouldn't Hurt a Child
tropes.html: Zigzagged with Jumba. After Lilo and Nani adopt Stitch, Jumba aims his gun at Stitch and Lilo appears. Pleakley orders Jumba not to fire. Jumba says he wouldn't fire at Lilo. Pleakley is against it because Lilo is a part of the mosquito food chain. Stitch exploits this by using Lilo as a shield from Jumba and Pleakley, making it harder for them to recapture him. This changes once Jumba and Pleakley are fired, with Jumba eagerly telling Stitch, "Oh, hiding behind your little friend won't work anymore. We got fired, new rules." He has a change of heart when Stitch persuasively convinces Jumba to help rescue Lilo after she is kidnapped by Gantu.

tropes.name: Yank the Dog's Chain
tropes.html:
The recurring fat, bald, shirtless guy never gets a chance to eat his ice cream.
  • Just when Nani gets a job thanks to David, she sees a firetruck, which alerts her something happened at the house.
  • After David brings Lilo and Stitch to shore, after the latter reveals himself to be an alien that he and Nani found out, he did not seem bothered or disturbed by the revelation, only for the Galactic Armada to arrive and arrest Stitch.

tropes.name: You Can Talk?
tropes.html: Nani demands that Stitch talk, that she knows he can and then proceeds to be shocked and slap him with a tree branch when he actually does so.

tropes.name: You Have GOT to Be Kidding Me!
tropes.html:
• The Grand Councilwoman, accompanied with a Little "No", when she sees that a trajectory of Stitch's cruiser on a monitor will land on an island (One of the only pieces of land for actual thousands of miles) instead of crashing into the sea.
  • Stitch has a very expressive seizure that non-verbally expresses this sentiment when after riding all around the island to find a large city he sees water everywhere and Lilo muses on the fact they live on, well, an island surrounded by water with no large cities, meaning there's no way he can get off or let loose his destructive urges.
  • Jumba, after capturing Stitch, who persuades him to rescue Lilo:
    Jumba: What?! After all you put me through, you expect me to help you just like that? Just like that?
  • And Pleakley, when riding a stolen motorcycle:
    Pleakley: Oh, great! I was hoping to add theft, endangerment and insanity to my list of things I did today!

tropes.name: You No Take Candle
tropes.html:
One of the truck drivers speaks broken pidgin English when Stitch's retractable back spikes puncture their tires:
Young truck driver: What we when hit? (he checks under the truck) There it is, it stay jammed under the fender!

tropes.name: Your Mom
tropes.html: Implied; during the fight where Lilo's house is wrecked, Stitch says something which causes Jumba to reply, "Leave my mother out of this!"

tropes.name: Action Survivor
tropes.html: Lara is of the "toned body" variant. She's been practicing sports (archery especially) but she has never really faced danger (beyond illegal bike races) or killed someone before going to the island, she probably never had to wield firearms before, and she's an average fighter. She holds her own very well, all in all.

tropes.name: Action Film, Quiet Drama Scene
tropes.html: The night before they are shipwrecked, Lara and Lu Ren share a quiet night at sea talking about her father.

tropes.name: Actor IS the Title Character
tropes.html: The poster for the film states that Alicia Vikander is Lara Croft.

tropes.name: Adaptation Amalgamation
tropes.html: While the movie bases its setting and most of its plot on the 2013 game, it also borrows elements from its sequel Rise of the Tomb Raider, namely the villainous group being named Trinity and Lara's Disappeared Dad serving as her motivation. Mathias is also recast from the leader of the Solarii brotherhood to a Trinity operative to fit this. Ana Miller is also featured in the story and is revealed to be working for Trinity, just like in Rise.

tropes.name: Adaptational Early Appearance
tropes.html: While Trinity is mentioned in the first game, the group is formally introduced in Rise of the Tomb Raider.

tropes.name: Adaptation Personality Change
tropes.html: Mathias in this version is much saner than his game counterpart. The only reason he's hellbent on trying to find Himiko's body is so that he could get home to his daughters as his employer at Trinity won't send people to retrieve him until he does so. He also doesn't go mad from the years stuck on the island and create a murder cult, unlike his game counterpart.

tropes.name: Adaptational Heroism
tropes.html: Surprisingly, Himiko herself counts. While she's the main villain in the 2013 game, the film depicts her as a queen who made a heroic sacrifice, having entombed herself on Yamatai to prevent the plague within her from infecting others.

tropes.name: Adaptational Mundanity
tropes.html: In the 2013 game, Himiko is an immortal spirit whose supernatural powers include Body Surfing across hosts, creating powerful ship-wrecking storms, and commanding undead samurai and oni. In the film, she has no supernatural powers and has been dead the entire time - she instead carried a rare yet deadly disease which led to her entombing herself on Yamatai to prevent it from spreading.

tropes.name: Adaptational Wimp
tropes.html:
• Himiko is much less powerful compared to her video game counterpart: In the game, she is capable of creating powerful storms to prevent anyone from leaving the island. In this film, she's just a corpse carrying a deadly disease, and is actually harmless unless you decide to touch her. That said, Lara does encounter the same shipwrecking storm as the game and her father states that Himiko kept him from leaving the island.
  • Lara herself is arguably one. Although she goes from strength to strength throughout the film, she's somewhat more reliant on others for help; Lu Ren instigated the fight that allowed her to escape Mathias Vogel and Trinity, she tearfully tells her father she's injured and is barely able to stand when she finds him.

tropes.name: Adapted Out
tropes.html:
• Despite being based on the 2013 Tomb Raider video game, Samantha "Sam" Nishimura is not present. This includes her plotline, where Samantha is a descendant of Yamatai and thus a worthy vessel for Himiko.
  • Lu Ren is seemingly a surrogate for Jonah as well.
  • In fact, every crew member of the Endurance other than Lara are absent in the movie.
  • The Stormguard, undead samurai guardians that serve Himiko as Elite Mooks don't make an appearance in the film, nor do the oni.
  • Mathias Vogel is still the primary antagonist, but instead of leading the Solarii Brotherhood, he's now a part of Trinity.
  • The 2013 game's supernatural plot elements are entirely missing from the film, having been replaced with a completely mundane explanation for Himiko's powers instead.

tropes.name: Adventurer Archaeologist
tropes.html: Lara Croft is one, naturally. Her father is also one as well. Apparently it runs in the family.

tropes.name: Age Lift
tropes.html: Ana is considerably older than her video game counterpart who is in her 40s.

tropes.name: Alternative Foreign Theme Song
tropes.html: The Japanese version contains a theme song by the female band "E-Girls" titled "Dynamite Girl", fitting for Lara Croft's personality.

tropes.name: Amazonian Beauty
tropes.html: Lara is first seen in a sparring match at an MMA gym, showing her body to be a knot of muscle. Most of the film is showing her climbing and otherwise flexing that muscle.

tropes.name: Ancient Tomb
tropes.html: Himiko's tomb, obviously.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Biology
tropes.html:
• Pretty much everything about the Himiko virus. Even the fastest viruses (Ebola, West Nile, norovirus) take 12 hours to begin causing symptoms by contact (vs. the quicker ingestion). Even the fastest ingested viruses measure symptom formation in hours rather than seconds.
  • Plus viruses cannot survive for a long time inhabiting a corpse. All mummies of that age found with evidence of having died of disease, the discovered bacteria/viruses have been so far degraded as to be useless.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Law
tropes.html: Specifically, British firearms law. At the end of the film, Lara is shown buying her iconic dual-wielded pistols (a pair of Heckler & Koch USP Match 9 mm semi-automatics) from a pawn shop...in London. For a pawn shop in most parts of the United States this would be basically realistic, but in real life private persons in England (even fabulously wealthy aristocrats) simply cannot legally own modern handguns.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Martial Arts
tropes.html: The film features a number of characters successfully use grappling choke holds to win fights, but they never once do so while using their legs to control their opponent's lower body, which is almost always essential in preventing a trained opponent from escaping. In one scene, Lara chokes a much larger mercenary using nothing but her slight body weight to keep him in the choke, so in reality he could easily just stand up.

tropes.name: Ascended Extra
tropes.html:
• In a surprising departure from the games, Sir Richard Croft is still alive and plays a major role in the film along with Lara. He also undergoes an Adaptational Badass when it is revealed that after escaping from Mathias Vogel, he had been leaving fake trails to trick Vogel into dead ends for seven years until Lara finds him, and teams up with his daughter in exploring the tomb itself and even partakes in the final gunfight before pulling a Heroic Sacrifice to stop the plague in Himiko's body from leaving the island.
  • Trinity was only mentioned briefly in the 2013 game after collecting all GPS caches before playing a larger role in the sequel. Here, they serve as the Greater-Scope Villain.

tropes.name: Beauty Is Never Tarnished
tropes.html: Largely averted, especially compared to the Angelina Jolie films. Especially once on the island you can see characters with sweat stains on their clothes. Lara herself does get banged up a lot over the course of the movie, suffering a number of visible scars with one particular puncture had her bleeding out. She also accumulates  a layer of dirt. But most of the scratches seem superficial, with only one carefully placed slash on her cheek that is mostly faded at the end of the film, and Vikander is still lovingly filmed.

tropes.name: Behind the Black
tropes.html: How in hell did the two dozen Yamatai survivors get this close to Mathias' evac helicopter without the pilots noticing them? They did have a lot of tree cover, so the pilots not noticing them from the air is reasonable and from there it would be easy to sneak up on the helicopter while it was on the ground.

tropes.name: Bleed 'Em and Weep
tropes.html: Lara is driven to tears after killing a mook sent to track her down.

tropes.name: Body Horror
tropes.html: The effects of Himiko's plague on the human body are quite graphical and definitely not pretty. Tainted Veins are the least of your worries when it hits you.

tropes.name: Boobs-and-Butt Pose
tropes.html: The first theatrical poster features Lara standing with her back to the viewer and looking back over her shoulder. The problem is, it's clearly a rushed photoshop that makes her neck look anatomically impossible. Some people even offered a corrected version on social media.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: In both the beginning and ending of the movie, Lara leaves her father's company, opening a box inside her father's secret office beneath her family crypt and visiting the same pawn shop in preparation for her next adventure.

tropes.name: Brick Joke
tropes.html: Lara says "At least we're still alive" to Lu Ren, to which he answers "No shit" when they're prisoners of Vogel's men. At the end, it's Lu Ren who says that they made it out alive, and Lara returns him a "No shit".

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Nick Frost appears in two scenes as the Jerkass owner of the pawn shop Lara goes to.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Skill
tropes.html:
• Lara is introduced in the middle of an MMA match at a gym, during which her opponent puts her in a chokehold that she can't escape from. On the island, a mercenary ambushes her and puts her in a chokehold, but despite being exhausted and injured, her will to survive drives her to successfully fights him off.
  • Her primary source of income is a bike courier, and she gets involved in a prize race to show her athletic endurance and navigate obstacles.
  • Flashbacks show Lara practicing archery from a young age, which comes in handy when she eventually goes on the offensive against Mathias and his cronies.
  • Ren Lu is shown using a gun scaring off some thugs who try to rob Lara. It later turns out he's not a bad shot himself.

tropes.name: *Click* Hello
tropes.html: The pilots of Mathias' evac helicopter are greeted this way by the Yamatai survivors.

tropes.name: Continuity Reboot
tropes.html: It has no ties to the two Lara Croft: Tomb Raider films that starred Angelina Jolie as Lara.

tropes.name: Contrived Coincidence
tropes.html: When Lara finally assumes control of her father's company in the epilogue, she's given a long list of their subsidiaries. She leafs through the Doorstopper at random, casts a glance and, among the thousands of entries, instantly spots Padna Ltd., the company whose name she saw on some Trinity crates on Yamatai, which in turn clues her into Ana's involvement with the Greater-Scope Villain.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html: The first thing we see of Lara is her getting utterly demolished in an MMA sparring match.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: The film was specifically made grittier and more realistic than the previous Tomb Raider films.

tropes.name: Dead Man Writing
tropes.html: Lara Croft's father leaves a camcorder for her in a hidden vault. When she uses it to play a message, his image says "Unfortunately, if you're watching this tape then it means that I must be dead".

tropes.name: Death Glare
tropes.html: After Richard calls Lara "sprout," Matthias mockingly does as well. Richard glares at him as if to say, "You don't call my daughter that!

tropes.name: Determinator
tropes.html: The thug kids really wanted Lara's bag that they chased her down to get it. Only to be scared of by Ren Lu with a gun.

tropes.name: Disappeared Dad
tropes.html: Lara Croft lost her father, Richard, when she was just a girl, and he's presumed dead. Later he turns out to be alive though.

tropes.name: Disney Villain Death
tropes.html: Played with for Mathias. He has the 'dramatic long fall' part covered, but his hard landing is shown, and he was as good as dead already even before he fell due to being infected with Himiko's killer plague.

tropes.name: Does Not Like Guns
tropes.html: Zigzagged, unfortunately. In a departure from established Tomb Raider tradition, this film's Lara doesn't even touch a gun of any sort at any point in the narrative despite having plenty of opportunities to pick up some badass boomsticks from the bad guys. The only thing she ever fires is her now-iconic bow. This makes it very jarring to suddenly see her purchase her previously iconic dual pistols in the epilogue, weapons she's never even hinted to have any proficiency with (and keep in mind that going Guns Akimbo with any degree of usefulness requires one hell of a lot of skill and training).

tropes.name: Doing In the Wizard
tropes.html: The game this movie is vaguely based on has an army of zombie samurai and an undead, storm-summoning witch queen. The movie just has a mundane (though potent) disease and death traps. Nothing even vaguely supernatural takes place.

tropes.name: Durable Deathtrap
tropes.html: As you might expect, the booby traps inside Himiko's tomb are fully functional despite being centuries old.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html: Lara's first scenes in London serve to introduce her character, with her doing MMA, participating in extreme sports like an illegal bicycle chase through rush hour traffic and getting into trouble with the police for it, having an estranged relationship with her Disappeared Dad and refusing to take up the Croft heritage, preferring to make a name for herself.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Loved Ones
tropes.html: Mathias has a family he's desperate to return to, damn the consequences of whatever he has to do to do so.

tropes.name: Everyone Chasing You
tropes.html: Early in the film, Lara volunteers to be chased on a bicycle by others in a 'fox hunt' event, as she needs the money from the winnings to pay for her gym fees.

tropes.name: Freeze-Frame Bonus
tropes.html: One scene from the trailers has Lara handling a brown puzzle cube detailed with gold that looks worryingly like the Lament Configuration.

tropes.name: God Save Us from the Queen!
tropes.html: How Himiko is portrayed in legend. In truth, she cared about her subjects so much she was willinglgy sealed away to prevent her "curse" from destroying them.

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html: Lara goes for a vicious one when she realizes she's outmatched by Mathias' weight and strength. Surprisingly, he completely ignores it and continues to lay the smackdown on her.

tropes.name: Handicapped Badass
tropes.html: Mathias is able to put up a good fight against Lara even after being shot in the hip.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html:
• After being infected by Himiko's virus, Richard sets off an explosion that consumes everything in Himiko's tomb (including himself) in order to destroy the virus and bury any chance of anyone ever recovering it again.
  • Himiko decided to have herself entombed in order to protect the world from the lethal plague she carried. Too bad history omitted that particular part of her legend...
  • In the finale, Lara herself appears willing to pull one when she kicks out the ladder across the Chasm of Souls to prevent Mathias from leaving with Himiko's plague, cutting off her own escape route in the process. Thankfully, she gets out okay regardless.

tropes.name: Historical Villain Upgrade
tropes.html: In-Universe. History remembers Himiko as a murderous witch who ruled through Black Magic that racked up an enormous body count before her own generals eventually overthrew her. The truth is... a bit different.

tropes.name: Hoist by His Own Petard
tropes.html: Lara, in the final fight against Vogel, uses Himiko's infected severed finger that he had cut off against him by shoving it down his throat.

tropes.name: Hostile Weather
tropes.html: The weather around Yamatai makes travel difficult, as Yamatai is located in the Devil's Sea.

tropes.name: Hotter and Sexier
tropes.html: Like the games it was based on, inverted. Lara is wearing a tank top through most of the film and we occasionally see some fanservice angles of her body, but by and large she is wearing full-length pants rather than short shorts, the tank top does not show off her stomach and she gets realistically dirty and banged up over the course of the film.

tropes.name: Iconic Attribute Adoption Moment
tropes.html: At the end, Lara returns to the pawn shop in order to buy back the pendant she sold there earlier in the film. While there, she spots a familiar-looking pistol, and decides, "I'll take two".

tropes.name: Iconic Item
tropes.html:
• Lara's bow and arrows, as well as her ice axe. She later gets her signature pistols at the end of the film from a pawnshop.
  • Lara also has her journal, which used to belong to her father.
  • Lara has her iconic backpack with her when she travels to the island. Unfortunately, she is forced to leave it behind when escaping from Mathias.

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html:
• Richard obviously had no further need of the Himiko-related documents, as evidenced by the fact that he was able to reach the island without them. If he'd just taken a few minutes to burn those documents himself, the entire movie could have been avoided. Instead, he sends his daughter on a short and convoluted treasure hunt to the place containing information about the place where he went to and never once stops to think that she might want to find out what happened to him. Also, barring the fact that the bad guys could have easily gotten into Queen Himiko's tomb by blasting their way in, there was absolutely no reason for Richard to appear at the entrance. This results in him getting held hostage and Lara being forced to open the tomb.
  • Lara during the ladder scene. Instead of flinging her pickaxe at the crippled Vogel or just pulling the rickety ladder he's using to escape, she throws down her only weapon and lunges across the gap ahead of Vogel on said ladder, which could have easily ended in her missing the jump and falling to her death. Worse yet, during the fight, Vogel picks up that same pickaxe that she threw down and nearly kills her with it and would have succeeded had Richard not blown the tomb with the explosive charges.
  • Vogel himself during the aforementioned scene, for not immediately killing Lara then and there and instead very slowly raising the axe to kill her, which costs him as the explosion caused by Richard's Heroic Sacrifice winds up distracting him.

tropes.name: Impaled with Extreme Prejudice
tropes.html: Like in the 2013 game, Lara experiences this via snapped branch when using a WWII-era parachute to escape a fatal drop down a waterfall, although she survives. Later on, in Himiko's tomb, a mook is impaled by a metal spike after a pressure trap is triggered.

tropes.name: Imperial Stormtrooper Marksmanship Academy
tropes.html: Especially noticeable when the Chinese prisoners led by Lu Ren escape under a hail of gunfire with only a couple of casualties.

tropes.name: Instant-Death Arrow
tropes.html: Lara's arrows must be dipped in some extremely potent toxin, seeing how every mook she hits drops dead on the spot regardless of where she actually hit them. A shot to the shoulder is all it takes to fell even the largest man instantly.

tropes.name: Lighter and Softer
tropes.html: In comparison to the 2013 M-rated reboot, which this PG-13-rated movie is based upon.

tropes.name: The Man Behind the Man
tropes.html: The film ends with Ana Miller (as in Rise of the Tomb Raider) revealed as being a member of Trinity and the one providing orders to Mathias Vogel, with Trinity's front being a shell company owned by Croft Holdings.

tropes.name: Mexican Standoff
tropes.html: Mathias has Richard at gunpoint while Lara has her bow aimed at Mathias, before she decides to open the tomb.

tropes.name: Missing Mom
tropes.html: Lara's mother died long before the events of the film and was a motivator for her father's work into finding the supernatural.

tropes.name: Muscles Are Meaningless
tropes.html: Averted hard. Lara is extremely fit, but still relatively petite, and this often shows whenever she gets into a physical fight. At the beginning of the film she loses hard in an MMA sparring match against a higher weight class female opponent, and at the end when she fights Mathias, who doesn't seem like an exceptionally physical individual and who has a stab wound to the leg to boot, he still manages to have the upper hand against her for most of the fight due to his larger size.

tropes.name: Mythology Gag
tropes.html: The first trailer shows Lara acquiring her iconic silver 9x19mm Heckler & Koch USP Match pistols, which she used in multiple games and the previous movies. She doesn't use them in this film, but obtains them right before the credits roll, from the pawnshop she pawned her father's jade pendant to.

tropes.name: Multiple Identity IDs
tropes.html: While going through her father's research on Himiko, Lara discovers he has multiple passports from different countries, each with a different name, causing her to realize he was up to something possibly shady and/or dangerous.

tropes.name: The Needs of the Many
tropes.html: During the Mexican Standoff between Lara, Richard and Mathias, Richard tells Lara to let him die so that Mathias can't get access to the tomb.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html: A trailer contains a scene where Lara gets her iconic pair of guns. It's literally the last scene of the movie.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html:
• Not only does Lara defy her father's instructions to burn all of his Himiko-related documents, but she also takes them with her to Yamatai. This gives Mathias exactly what he needs to find the location of Himiko's tomb when the documents fall into his hands, something her father wanted to avoid.
  • She did it again in the finale after she accepts her inheritance and signs over control of Croft Holdings' company to Ana Miller, whom she figured out too late is a member of Trinity, and that by signing control of the company over to Ana, Trinity now has full access to whatever Richard is trying to hide from them.

tropes.name: No-Holds-Barred Beatdown
tropes.html: Lara is introduced fighting (and badly losing) an MMA match, so her story actually starts with one. Her Final Battle against Mathias then subjects her to another, far worse one that naturally doesn't conform to any rules of sportsmanship.

tropes.name: No Kill like Overkill
tropes.html: Lu Ren at one point takes out an ordinary, unarmored mook perhaps 20 meters away with a direct hit from an assault rifle's underbarrel grenade launcher instead of just, you know, shooting him full of holes.

tropes.name: Not Allowed to Grow Old
tropes.html: Occurs with Richard Croft, because of the film's use of flashbacks (Dominic West portraying the younger and older Richard); also has shades of Absurdly Youthful Mother, due to the 19 year age difference between West and Alicia Vikander.

tropes.name: Only a Flesh Wound
tropes.html: Lu Ren takes a gunshot wound to his left shoulder while helping Lara escape from the Trinity work camp. That would be a really serious injury in real life; but later in the film (likely no more than a few days in the story's timeline), he is able to run around the jungle and fire a machine gun with seemingly no ill effects from his wound.

tropes.name: Pre-Mortem One-Liner
tropes.html:
Lara delivers one to Vogel before finishing him off.
"You messed with the wrong family."

tropes.name: Rejecting the Inheritance
tropes.html: Lara refuses to sign the paper work allowing her to access her family fortune because it would require her to be tied to the day to day tasks of running her family's business interests, limiting her personal freedom and autonomy.

tropes.name: Sanity Slippage
tropes.html: Richard Croft mistakes Lara as being a hallucination, because he has seen her before during his seven-year exile, only for her to disappear eventually. This time, she doesn't.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html: The "hunters" chasing Lara through London on bikes in the prologue scatter like roaches when she gets distracted and crashes into a police cruiser of all things.

tropes.name: Sealed Evil in a Can
tropes.html: Queen Himiko was a terrifying creature with the power to spread death with just a touch. She was only defeated by her own generals who bound her and brought her to an uninhabited island and sealed her there, with traps and ciphers to prevent anyone from finding and releasing her. Zig-zagged when the truth is revealed that Himiko was the carrier of a deadly disease and was willingly sealed away to prevent its spread, making the virus the evil that was sealed instead.

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html: The film ends with Lara continuing her father's work and hunting down Trinity.

tropes.name: Shipper on Deck
tropes.html: A young man at an Indian restaurant where Lara picks up deliveries clearly wants to ask her out but loses his nerve. After she leaves, his parents mock his cowardice.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The child of an archaeologist received clues that might led them to the whereabouts of their father and the legendary treasure they spent their life searching for. When they are reunited with their father, the latter berates them for deliberately handing the clues to the Big Bad which was what the father was trying to prevent in the first place. The gauntlet of traps leading to Himiko's tomb is also very reminiscent of the Grail Trials Indy had to pass.
  • Uncharted: Drake's Fortune: The body of centuries-old mummy contains an ancient virus that is capable of infecting anyone in a matter of seconds, turning them hostile. It is this reason why the mummy was contained within an uncharted island to contain the virus. The antagonist attempts to bring back the virus in order to weaponize it.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html: Most adaptions tend to Hand Wave how Lara (a British national) came to carry two pistols (handguns are illegal in the UK). This one at least acknowledges the strict firearms laws by showing that she came by them through an illegal arms dealer.

tropes.name: Skilled, but Naive
tropes.html: About Lara, Alicia Vikander said, "She has all the fierce, tough, curious, intelligent traits, but we’ve stripped away all of her experience. She hasn’t gone on an adventure just yet."

tropes.name: Spared by the Adaptation
tropes.html: Spared by the Adaptation Richard Croft is revealed to actually be alive unlike in the video games where he is dead. However this is subverted later on when he makes a Heroic Sacrifice to seal the temple up.

tropes.name: Spring-Loaded Corpse
tropes.html: Literally. Himiko's body is rigged to invoke this as one final scare for any would-be thieves or looters. The mechanism that does it is clearly seen afterwards.

tropes.name: Technically Living Zombie
tropes.html: Anyone affected by Himiko's plague seems to die at first from the horrific effects on the body, only to rise and attack whoever's in sight some minutes later.

tropes.name: Tank-Top Tomboy
tropes.html: Just like the video games, Lara wears a tank-top throughout the film.

tropes.name: Touch of Death
tropes.html: This turns out to be Himiko's true nature, as she carries a deadly plague in her body that turns anyone she touches into a mindless berserker.

tropes.name: Typhoid Mary
tropes.html: The source of Himiko's Touch of Death, as described above, was a deadly plague she transmitted by touch but was immune to herself.

tropes.name: We Are Everywhere
tropes.html: Vogel says this verbatim to Lara on how vast Trinity is. The final scene has her finding a huge map hinting he may be right.

tropes.name: Worst Aid
tropes.html: Just like in the 2013 game, Lara treats a foreign object that pierced her abdomen by pulling it out of the wound without any immediate treatment against infection or exsanguination. She gets patched up, eventually, but she had no way of knowing that when she did it.

tropes.name: You Have GOT to Be Kidding Me!
tropes.html:
Immediately after managing to avoid going over a waterfall, Lara now has to deal with finding a way to get off the wreckage of an airplane precariously situated over a great height.
Lara: Really?!

title: The End of the F***ing World
original_title: The End of the F***ing World

tropes.name: Actually Pretty Funny
tropes.html:
• During the scene with the computer with which the programmer tries to find the remaining three tickets, he offers to share the grand prize with it, only for it to ask "What would a computer do with a lifetime supply of chocolate?" Look carefully and the man's clients actually smirk at that question.
  • Mr. Wonka laughs when Mike pretends to shoot him dead.

tropes.name: Adaptational Attractiveness
tropes.html:
• Augustus in the book is disgustingly obese. In this film, he's just a bit more chubby than usual.
  • Mr. Wonka in the book is an older man with a black goatee, and illustrators often portray him as hardly taller than the kids. In this film he's of normal height, clean-shaven with blond hair, and in his late thirties to early forties. This and the toned-down costume also counts as Adaptation Dye-Job, and has since become Lost in Imitation — most subsequent adaptations and virtually all of the parody versions have clean-shaven Wonkas.

tropes.name: Adaptational Dumbass
tropes.html: In the book, Charlie got selected as Wonka's heir by being the one kid with the sense to listen to Wonka's warnings about the dangerous technology in his factory. In this version, he also ignores Wonka's warnings about the Fizzy Lifting Drink, but still gets picked as the heir because he's the only one to return his Everlasting Gobstopper, which the kids thought they'd been offered money for by a competing confectioner.

tropes.name: Adaptational Early Appearance
tropes.html: Unlike in canon, Veruca and her parents appear before her Golden Ticket is found.

tropes.name: Adaptational Jerkass
tropes.html:
• Violet was very much a Designated Villain in the book. She's shown to be far more arrogant than she is in the book, frequently taunting an unseen friend in television broadcasts and fighting with Veruca on the tour.
  • Veruca Salt, like in the book, is an insufferable brat, but despite having a rich dad, she is willing to give the Everlasting Gobstopper to Slugworth for more money.
  • Grandpa Joe to a lesser extent; he was entirely a Nice Guy in the book but tends to be a lot more dismissive and insulting towards the other four kids and their parents here — though in fairness, nothing he says about them is especially wrong. It's more pronounced when he talks Charlie into stealing some Fizzy Lifting Drink, which nearly gets them both killed and then nearly loses Charlie the lifetime's supply of chocolate.
  • This also leads to a lowkey case for Charlie, since it means he like the other kids has a moment of disobeying Wonka's warnings, no longer being the one "pure" child without a defining Fatal Flaw. The thing that makes him exceptional however is that, unlike them, Charlie quickly accepts his mistake and hands his Gobstopper to Wonka as a sign of apology, passing his Secret Test of Character.
  • Wonka himself. In the book, he at least tries to dissuade the kids from doing the things that would lead to disaster for them, even if he didn't concern himself too much after the fact. Here, the only kid he tries to dissuade is Augustus, and even then only because he's worried about having the chocolate in his river contaminated. With Violet, Mike, and Veruca, he gives only token warnings when they start doing reckless things and takes great pleasure in their misfortune.

tropes.name: Adaptational Nationality
tropes.html:
• The character trying to trick people with a phony ticket comes from Paraguay instead of Russia.
  • Also, the four bratty kids are never given a nationality in the book. Here, Veruca is English and Augustus is German, while Mike and Violet are Americans.

tropes.name: Adaptational Nice Guy
tropes.html:
• In this film, Augustus is still a Big Eater, but he's relatively well-mannered and much more noticably polite than his literary and 2005 film counterparts.
  • Compared with the book, Mike is more excitedly obsessed with TV with no truly bad part whatsoever.

tropes.name: Adaptational Villainy
tropes.html: Slugworth is only given a brief mention in the book as one of Wonka's candymaking rivals. Here, he's portrayed as a Corrupt Corporate Executive who bribes the golden ticket finders with money and a better life in exchange for stealing an Everlasting Gobstopper from Wonka. Ultimately subverted when "Slugworth" reveals himself to be an employee of Wonka who was subjecting the kids to a Secret Test of Character.

tropes.name: Adaptation Distillation
tropes.html: The most prominent example is the Oompa Loompas' songs, which are essentially 30 second recaps of the roughly five-minute ones in the original book.

tropes.name: Adaptation Expansion
tropes.html: The entire Slugworth subplot and the misadventure with the Fizzy Lifting Drinks. In the book, Charlie gets the factory as soon as the other kids were out of the running and doesn't have to pass a final test. Additionally the search for the tickets is drawn out far more than in the book - showing various attempts by people to find the tickets. We get to see a lot of things firsthand that we only heard about in passing in the book - such as a scientist making a machine to figure out where the tickets are or a character trying to use a phony ticket.

tropes.name: Adaptation-Induced Plot Hole
tropes.html: The book explains that Wonka now has the Oompa Loompas working in his factory because he no longer trusts humans, after his rival chocolate and candymakers sent in spies dressed as workers to steal his secrets and forced him to shut down his business. While that explanation is kept in this adaptation, Wonka is shown to have at least one human employee: the Slugworth impersonator Mr. Wilkinson (who doesn't appear or have any counterpart in the book), which contradicts his main reasoning for hiring the Oompa Loompas.note Of course, one likely explanation for this is Wonka doesn't trust humans when it comes to candymaking, but they're still good for errands outside Wonka's factory

tropes.name: Adaptation Name Change
tropes.html:
• Mrs. Salt is known as Henrietta here to go with her husband being Named by the Adaptation as Henry, whereas in the book she's named Angina.
  • The "Whipple-Scrumptious Fudgemallow Delight" is called the "Scrumdiddlyumptious Bar" here.
  • The Great Glass Elevator is changed to the Great Glass Wonkavator.
  • Similarly, the rather blandly-named Television Chocolate is renamed "Wonkavision".

tropes.name: Adaptation Species Change
tropes.html:
• The nut-sorting squirrels of the novel are replaced with geese that lay golden chocolate eggs. (See Pragmatic Adaptation below.)
  • The Oompa-Loompas were African pygmies indentured to Wonka in the book, while the movie changed them to silly-looking orange-skinned, green-haired little humanoid creatures to avoid all the slavery similarities.

tropes.name: Adaptation Title Change
tropes.html: Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory is an adaptation of the novel Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.

tropes.name: Adapted Out
tropes.html: Prince Pondicherry and his palace made entirely of chocolate aren't mentioned at all, likely because it would have been too hard to dramatize that Flashback convincingly with 1970s tech.

tropes.name: A.I. Is a Crapshoot
tropes.html:
In a brief scene during the "worldwide obsession" segment, a scientist programs a computer to figure out where the last three golden tickets are, but the computer has other ideas. It refuses, saying, "That would be cheating." The scientist tries to bribe the computer with the grand prize, but the computer, being a smartass, rebuffs him, asking, "What would a computer do with a lifetime supply of chocolate?"
Scientist: (operating the computer in frustration) I am now telling the computer exactly what it can do with a lifetime supply of chocolate!

tropes.name: The Alcoholic
tropes.html: Butterscotch and Buttergin; something Mr. Salt is quick to call to Wonka's attention.

tropes.name: Alliterative List
tropes.html: According to the Oompa-Loompas, chewing gum all day long is "repulsive, revolting and wrong".

tropes.name: All or Nothing
tropes.html: Although Charlie wins Mr. Wonka's contest by default (since the other children all "drop out"), Mr. Wonka disqualifies him on a technicality, delivering the news rather bluntly and cruelly. However, he subverts it a moment later by revealing that it's one last Secret Test of Character, which Charlie passes. The other children in this film supposedly leave with nothing other than the Amusing Injuries they brought upon themselves. This is different than the book. Then again, the book didn't have that contract, nor did the 2005 movie.

tropes.name: All-Loving Hero
tropes.html: Charlie Bucket. Even with how the bratty the other four Golden Ticket Winners are, he's still concerned for them in the end of the tour thought the factory, even mentioning Veruca (the worst of them) by name, and also trying to save Augustus from drowing in the chocolate river.

tropes.name: All Psychology Is Freudian
tropes.html: The troubled man relating his dream about being told where to find a Golden Ticket.

tropes.name: Americans Are Cowboys
tropes.html: In this adaptation, Mike Teevee is from Arizona, he dresses like a cowboy, and he's obsessed with violent Westerns.

tropes.name: Amusing Injuries
tropes.html:
Amusing Injuries
  • Mike Teevee's encounter with Exploding Candy (see Eat the Bomb below).
  • Mr. Wonka assures Charlie that the brats will all be restored to "their normal, terrible old selves, but maybe a little wiser for the wear", so the wacky accidents/transformations they undergo fall under this trope in this adaptation. (In the novel and some other versions, they have "reminders" of their misbehavior after they're "cured" — Violet winds up permanently blue, for instance.)

tropes.name: And I'm the Queen of Sheba
tropes.html:
A few minutes after the discussion about Loompaland and Vermicious Knids, there's this gem:
(everyone is getting onto the Wonkatania)
Mr. Salt: Ladies first, and that means Veruca!
Grandpa Joe: If she's a lady, then I'm a Vermicious Knid!

tropes.name: And Some Other Stuff
tropes.html: The only difference between nitroglycerin and wart remover is Mr. Turkentine's secret mixture.

tropes.name: And Starring
