tropes.html: It's unclear exactly when the movie is supposed to be set, but even aside from Hansel and Gretel's unexplained steampunk armory, there's a ridiculous variance in tech levels, especially among the more "mundane" firearms. Hansel and Gretel also occasionally use a lot of more modern expressions like "stay cool" and "friggin".

tropes.name: Anti-Magic
tropes.html:
• Hansel and Gretel are immune to (directly applied) witchcraft. Being children of a Grand White Witch who had the foresight to lay protection on them has its perks. The witches are generally pretty clever about bypassing it via physical or indirect attacks though, such as when Muriel telekinetically throws logs at Hansel.
  • The magic of White Witches allows them to bypass the defenses of Black Witches and kill them with ease.

tropes.name: Apathy Killed the Cat
tropes.html: Hansel has no interest in what happened to their parents, why they were left in the woods, and why they have Anti-Magic.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Biology
tropes.html:
Hansel's "sugar sickness".
  • While a witch's candy might be cursed to cause anyone who eats it to die from "sugar sickness" if they miss an injection (of presumably insulin), you can't get insulin-dependent (Type 1) diabetes from eating too much mundane, non-enchanted sugar unless you gain a lot of weight; somewhere in the ballpark of two hundred pounds. Even if you could, a regular diabetic can go for several days without insulin and not keel over dead immediately; although they would likely become extremely ill from diabetic ketoacidosis.
  • Insulin, incidentally, was not identified until 1921. Before then, diabetes was a nightmare disease that was usually an outright death sentence.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Geography
tropes.html: The real town of Augsburg has never looked anything like the small village the movie takes place in. A prospering rich center of trade would be much closer to reality. It was so large that it would periodically be the seat of the Imperial Diet (the General Assembly of the Empire). Furthermore, Augsburg not only had its own military, but contained a key base for the Holy Roman Empire, and so was literally crammed with soldiers. The Witches attacking it before they gained immortality would have been suicidal. Also, while the movie was correct in that Augsburg was surrounded by forests, the Lech River which runs through the town is completely missing.

tropes.name: Ascended Fanboy
tropes.html: In-universe. Benjamin starts as a fan of Hansel and Gretel; he collects all their newspaper articles, has a lot of witch data, and his dream is to be a witch hunter like them. He gets his chance to help.

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html: No one feels sorry for the Sheriff.

tropes.name: Attempted Rape
tropes.html: In the extended cut, after beating Gretel up, the Sheriff and his men declare their intention to rape her and pull off her jacket before Edward arrives and kills them. For viewers who only saw the original cut, this is the reason why Gretel's jacket suddenly disappears when Edward arrives.

tropes.name: Autobots, Rock Out!
tropes.html: The action scenes feature liberal use of electric guitars (in keeping with the Anachronism Stew).

tropes.name: Automatic Crossbow
tropes.html: Gretel carries an over-and-under version of this, which uses its own recoil to cock itself. It can also rotate to shoot bolts in opposite directions.

tropes.name: Bad Moon Rising
tropes.html: The Blood Moon, which turns the skies red and serves for the ritual the witches want to complete in order to become impervious to fire.

tropes.name: Badass Boast
tropes.html:
Muriel is full of them.
[as the mercenary crosses himself at her approach] "There's no use in praying, my friend. Even your God knows better than to come here."
"I go by many names... none of which you're worthy of pronouncing..."

tropes.name: Badass in Distress
tropes.html:
• Gretel may be the film's Action Girl but she ends up in distress when the village's men, led by the sheriff corner her in the woods, and is only saved by Edward the troll. She's later captured by Muriel who wants to use her heart to complete her spell.
  • Hansel a few times too, especially when he's stabbed and left to bleed out.

tropes.name: Badass Longcoat
tropes.html: Both Hansel and Gretel have very long coats, though Gretel loses hers after the sheriff attempts to rape her.

tropes.name: Badass Normal
tropes.html: • Hansel and Gretel have no magical powers other than their immunity to witch magic despite being the children of a White Witch themselves, but are very skilled at dispatching witches using conventional weapons and plenty of cunning. The latter makes them uniquely qualified to fight the the witches as the witches can't control or curse them. Gretel actually does have magic, she just didn't know about it and therefore never used it. She does pick up Muriel's wand at the end of the film, possibly hinting that she will begin practicing.

tropes.name: Bayonet Ya
tropes.html: Hansel's shotgun has a retractable bayonet.<!--* BeastAndBeauty: Some vibes this way between Gretel and Edward.-->

tropes.name: Beauty Equals Goodness
tropes.html: Played with. Hansel rightly points out that an evil witch cannot really hide their true, hideous nature as evidence that Mina isn't a witch. But Grand Black Witches can briefly hide themselves. Once she starts using magic, however, she takes on her evil form. White witches, however, are both altruistic and beautiful.

tropes.name: Beauty Is Never Tarnished
tropes.html: Played with; Gretel is just as likely to get scrapes, cuts and bruises as Hansel is, and spends at least as much time grunged up as he does. Similarly, when they are injured, neither simply wipes the blood away and is perfectly fine, showing wounds lasting across the few days over which the majority of the movie takes place. In the final scene set some prolonged period later, however, only Hansel has noticeable scars, and they only add to his rugged handsomeness.

tropes.name: Being Good Sucks
tropes.html: Feel sorry for the White Witches, given that they are not allowed to hurt humans even when they're being burned to death. While they can use their magic to fight Black Witches, they're much better with non-offensive spells.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: Muriel the Grand Black Witch, who seeks to sacrifice a bunch of children to make all evil witches immune to fire.<!--* BigDamnHeroes: Hansel and Gretel do this for a living. And [[spoiler:Edward the troll]] does it twice.--><!--* BloodFromTheMouth: Multiple times.-->

tropes.name: Blood Magic
tropes.html: What Muriel had in mind for the twelve missing children and Gretel. It would create a spell to give all the witches immunity to fire permanently.

tropes.name: Blood-Splattered Innocents
tropes.html:
• The patrons of the tavern when that unfortunate tracker explodes into Ludicrous Gibs. Hansel knows what's coming, and moves Benjamin in front of him.
  • Hansel ends up spraying several small children in the face with blood and brains when he executes a witch less than four feet from them.

tropes.name: Bodyguard Betrayal
tropes.html: Edward ultimately decides to side with the twins against Muriel.

tropes.name: Bond One-Liner
tropes.html: In the beginning, the witch complained that the fire wasn't hot enough. After she pushed the Gingerbread House witch into the oven, Gretel yelled, "Is it hot enough for you now, bitch!?"

tropes.name: Braids of Action
tropes.html: Certified Action Girl Gretel's hair is almost always braided.

tropes.name: Brother–Sister Team
tropes.html:
Hansel and Gretel, though minus the usual bickering. At least largely minus it. Gretel is forced to swat her brother upside the head at least once when he's being annoying.
Gretel: I fucking hate you.
Hans: You look like shit.
Gretel: So do you.

tropes.name: Bullet Time
tropes.html: During the epilogue, Gretel is seen shooting automatic weapons at a witch, who dodges the bullets in slow motion.

tropes.name: Burn the Witch!
tropes.html: Several witches, including Hansel and Gretel's mother are burned at the stake. Muriel's ultimate plan is to permanently make all witches immune to fire.

tropes.name: Chain Pain
tropes.html: Gretel wraps a chain around her fist at one point and near the end she tears a witch in half with a spiked chain. Hansel strangles Muriel with one.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html: Chekhov's Gun. Ben is handed a very fancy, fold up rifle (with incredibly complex ammo) and told to "wait here and shoot anything that moves". Later...

tropes.name: *Click* Hello
tropes.html:
Gretel gives one to the Sheriff when stopping him from burning a suspected witch to death. The Sheriff also has an excellent Oh, Crap! expression right at this moment.
Gretel: Let the girl go, or I'll blow your Sheriff's brains all over these fucking hillbillies.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: Director Tommy Wirkola appears as one of Berringer's deputies.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html: Any fight with Muriel up until the end results in everyone getting stomped. Also, the Sheriff and his cronies versus Edward when he rescues Gretel. Including actual stomping.

tropes.name: Daddy Had a Good Reason for Abandoning You
tropes.html: It's pretty fair to say that leaving your children in the woods to save their lives (and with full intent of coming back for them once the danger has passed but getting killed before you can) is an understandable reason for abandoning them.

tropes.name: Damsel in Distress
tropes.html:
• Mina when she was about to be executed by the misguided townspeople.
  • Gretel is briefly captured by the Sheriff's men and then by the witches.

tropes.name: Dark Action Girl
tropes.html: Witches are female, so all the dark witches qualify.<!--* TheDarkArts: They make the black witches hideous.-->

tropes.name: Death of a Child
tropes.html: Early in the movie, a boy was killed by the witches and his remains were used to create a prototype version of the potion.

tropes.name: Disease by Any Other Name
tropes.html: Hansel is described as having "sugar sickness" from his time imprisoned in the witch's gingerbread house. To the audience it is obvious he is talking about insulin-dependent diabetes (commonly known as Type 1).

tropes.name: Distressed Dude
tropes.html: Hansel as a child. He's also nearly killed by Muriel in the climax until Gretel rescues him.

tropes.name: The Dreaded
tropes.html: The reason Muriel just didn't outright assault Hansel and Gretel's home and forcefully take Gretel then and there was that she was afraid of their mother, Adrianna, the Grand White Witch. She took advantage of the fact that Adrianna would not harm humans, spreading rumors of her being a witch to the villagers so they would get Adrianna out of the way and leave Gretel vulnerable.

tropes.name: Evil Gloating
tropes.html:
• Muriel. So, so much. Hansel lampshades it, saying "you talk too much", before attacking her.
  • Also the Sheriff when he and his men have captured Gretel.

tropes.name: Evil Makes You Monstrous
tropes.html: With the exception of Grand Witches, who can change their appearance at will, you can tell when a witch has been doing evil witchy things because it causes them to mutate into an grotesque demon thing.

tropes.name: Evil Redhead
tropes.html: One of Muriel's Co-Dragons has red hair. The credits refer to her as the "Red Haired Witch".

tropes.name: Exact Time to Failure
tropes.html: A biological example. When Hansel's alarm watch goes off, he needs his insulin within thirty seconds or so or he falls over.

tropes.name: Eye Scream
tropes.html: Hansel stabs a witch in the eye at one point.

tropes.name: Face on a Milk Carton
tropes.html: But because this is olden times, the drawings of the missing children are tied around milk bottles.

tropes.name: Fantastic Racism
tropes.html: Most people, especially Hansel, view all witches as evil crones (which a lot of them are). Good ones who go by the moniker of White Witches do exist, one of which he saves from being burned and tortured, the other of which was his own mother.

tropes.name: Five Rounds Rapid
tropes.html: The Sheriff's men fire a lot at the witches, not that it does them any good.

tropes.name: Flash Step
tropes.html: Muriel does this at one point, talking to Hansel and Gretel and then suddenly showing up behind them.

tropes.name: Flying Broomstick
tropes.html: Averted as the witches fly long crooked branches. Ben still refers to one of them as a "broom" at one point, though.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: Gretel wonders why Edward saved her, given that trolls serve witches. It turns out that Gretel herself is the daughter of a Great White Witch.

tropes.name: Forgotten Fallen Friend
tropes.html: Poor Jackson never gets so much as a mention after his black-magic forced suicide, despite risking his life helping Hansel and Gretel capture a witch.

tropes.name: Fractured Fairytale
tropes.html: With the original Hansel & Gretel as a prologue, it evolves into Action Horror where the two hunt various wicked witches with different powers.

tropes.name: Game Face
tropes.html: Inverted. Grand Witches can change out of their monstrous face and look like a regular (and beautiful) woman. Crosses back to straight since Muriel spends most of the movie looking pretty and dropping the disguise to affect a straight Game Face.

tropes.name: Gatling Good
tropes.html: A White Witch-blessed Gatling gun, to be precise.

tropes.name: Gratuitous German
tropes.html: Completely averted, which is odd considering the move takes place in Germany. Doubly so when some of the actors are German, but speak with American accents. The Translation Convention is in effect.

tropes.name: Gender Equals Breed
tropes.html: Presumably the reason why Gretel and their mother were witches, but Hansel and their father were human.

tropes.name: Giant Foot of Stomping
tropes.html: How Edward ends the Sheriff.

tropes.name: Give Geeks a Chance
tropes.html: Completely averted. Despite saving her life and getting steadily more awesome throughout the film, Ben's geeky devotion shows no signs of winning Gretel over — although she doesn't particularly show interest in anyone else either.

tropes.name: Glory Hound
tropes.html: The Sheriff angrily works against Hansel and Gretel because he wants to get sole credit for stopping the witches.

tropes.name: Godiva Hair
tropes.html: Mina, when she and Hansel go Skinny Dipping in the healing pond.

tropes.name: Going Commando
tropes.html: Mina wasn't wearing any underwear under her dress.

tropes.name: Good Witch Versus Bad Witch
tropes.html: Muriel and her coven are the evil witches, but it turns out Mina is a good witch and Gretel herself is one. The straightest case in the film is when Mina attempts to fight Muriel with her wand. Ultimately she fails because white witches are more proficient at spells for healing and protection.

tropes.name: Gorn
tropes.html: The film is quite over the top with its bloodshed, decapitations and exploding body parts.

tropes.name: Half-Human Hybrid
tropes.html: Hansel and Gretel's mother turns out to have in fact been a (good) witch, which here is treated as a separate species. Their father was a normal human.

tropes.name: Handicapped Badass
tropes.html: As a result of eating so much of the gingerbread witch's candy as a child, Hansel has improbably become diabetic and needs to inject himself with medicine every couple of hours or he will die.

tropes.name: Hanging Around
tropes.html: A woodcut in the opening credits depicts witches being hanged. Also, Hansel and Gretel’s father, having left his children in the woods for their protection, is revealed to have shortly afterwards been lynched by the townspeople, who also burned Hansel and Gretel’s mother.

tropes.name: Happy Fun Ball
tropes.html: The gingerbread house to Hansel and Gretel at first. The house actually does look pretty sinister and strange.

tropes.name: Harmful to Minors
tropes.html:
• Hansel and Gretel were exposed to the evil of the gingerbread witch and it caused them to become witch hunters.
  • The children kidnapped by Muriel and the rest of the witches seem quite traumatized.
  • Also the boy who the Red Haired Witch forces to shoot his own mother. He practically breaks down.

tropes.name: Healing Hands
tropes.html: An ability of Mina's. Likely Adrianna had it too. And Gretel if she starts practicing the craft.

tropes.name: Hell-Bent for Leather
tropes.html: Both of the siblings wear a lot of black leather. See the page picture.

tropes.name: Holy Hand Grenade
tropes.html: A spell imbues water with the ability to make anything it blesses bypass dark witch magic shields. Cue Hansel unveiling a cart full of weapons, including literal grenades.

tropes.name: Horns of Villainy
tropes.html: One of Muriel's Co-Dragons, the aptly-named Horned Witch, has black spikes in place of hair.

tropes.name: Hot Witch
tropes.html: Only Grand Black Witches are capable of temporarily assuming this. White witches, however, can look perfectly human. Mina is attractive and so was the siblings' mother Adrianna. Gretel herself is stunning.

tropes.name: Human Shield
tropes.html: The Horned Witch grabs another witch for this when Mina is mowing down the witches with the Gatling gun.

tropes.name: Humble Brag
tropes.html: Hansel asks Ben if he has ever shot a gun, Ben kind of quietly remarks that he won a shooting contest at the county fair... three times. Hansel just smiles and helps him up onto his horse.

tropes.name: I Have Many Names
tropes.html: Muriel says the she has many names, but doesn't say what any of them are.

tropes.name: I'm a Humanitarian
tropes.html: The witches.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html: The Sheriff runs around accusing multiple innocent women of being witches. Turns out he didn't realize it, but he was right every time. They were just benevolent White Witches instead of evil Black Witches, and thus he unknowingly aids the Big Bad.

tropes.name: It's All About Me
tropes.html: Sheriff Berringer has this kind of attitude. He sends several men to be horribly killed just to show up Hansel and Gretel.

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: Again the Sheriff and his cronies. To some degree the town people gawking and cheering when the Sheriff was employing water torture on poor Mina.

tropes.name: Just Between You and Me
tropes.html: Muriel narrates her entire plot to Hansel and Gretel during her Evil Gloating rant, while also describing how their parents died.

tropes.name: Kill It with Fire
tropes.html: Fire is the greatest weakness for the witches. In fact, the Big Bad's main goal is to eat the heart of the Grand White Witch to make themselves immune to fire.

tropes.name: Knight Templar
tropes.html:
• The Sheriff and his cronies want to protect the town from witches and thieves, but end up causing as much damage as the witches themselves, and eventually beat Gretel severely, before Edward stomps in to save the day.
  • In the uncut version, Berringer murders the Mayor in front of the entire town, and he and his gang planned to do a lot worse than just beat Gretel up before getting fatally trolled.

tropes.name: Lampshade Hanging
tropes.html: In this case, the nature of the film itself. When the opening scene after the titles involves having hand drawn pictures of the missing children pasted on milk bottles sold in the Ausburg market, you know the film is not going to be taking itself seriously.

tropes.name: Large Ham
tropes.html: Goodness, the original witch who tried to eat Hansel and Gretel. "THIS OVEN'S NOT HOT ENOUGH! MORE WOOD!"

tropes.name: Let's Get Dangerous!
tropes.html: Mina with the Gatling gun. Benjamin when he shoots down Muriel.

tropes.name: Lightning Bruiser
tropes.html: The evil witches are inhumanly fast and strong.

tropes.name: Ludicrous Gibs
tropes.html: Everywhere, but one of the trackers exploding after being forced to eat worms takes the cake.

tropes.name: Made of Iron
tropes.html: The amount of punishment Hansel and Gretel take throughout the film is incredible. Also the witches. Possibly justified as the witches aren't really human and both Hansel and Gretel are the children of a Grand White Witch. Who knows, though Hansel can't use magic he probably got the durability of a witch. Everyone else takes a lot longer to recover from any kind of damage.

tropes.name: Mage Killer
tropes.html: The twins' Anti-Magic let them take this up as a profession.

tropes.name: Magical Defibrillator
tropes.html: Gretel defibrillates Edward using a homemade, steampunk taser.

tropes.name: The Magic Versus Technology War
tropes.html: In this setting, witches have the magic and the villagers have the tech in the form of rifles and pistols being common. Magic has the huge upper hand against technology, since witches have magical shields which deflect bullets, to the point that swinging a shovel at a witch is far more effective than using a standard gun on her. Even the more advanced tech used by Hansel and Gretel doesn't do that much except to help lead a witch to a place where the siblings can beat on her in melee. It's only when their guns are enchanted that they become a real threat to the witches (and even there Muriel soaks four shots without any ill-effects later).

tropes.name: Magic Wand
tropes.html: Used copiously by witches. Both Black Witches and White Witches. The ones of the evil witches tend to look sinister. Mina's is rather lovely and nature-inspired.

tropes.name: Man Bites Man
tropes.html: Gretel bites the Sheriff's nose.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: Mina means "protection". She blesses the weapons that the hero team use on the witch sabbath. Benjamin means "son of the right hand". Edward means "guard". Gretel is a German version of Margaret which is associated with pearls and the color white. Hansel is the odd one out, as his name is a German diminutive of John, although John or Hans is one of the standard "hero" names in fairy tales.

tropes.name: A Minor Kidroduction
tropes.html: The film naturally couldn't leave out the incident in their childhoods that prompted them to become witch hunters.

tropes.name: Monster/Slayer Romance
tropes.html: Hansel and Gretel have vowed to hunt down all of witchkind to avenge the death of their parents, but Hansel later falls in love with Mina, who's a White Witch. As it turns out, so are the two leads—their mother was a White Witch as well. Mina is eventually murdered in the climax by Muriel, the Grand Black Witch, for "betraying her kind".

tropes.name: More Dakka
tropes.html:
• Besides the automatic crossbow and Gatling gun seen in the trailers and commercials, Gretel uses a pair of triple-barreled Gatling pistols in the end credits.
  • But the scene that best demonstrates the twins' love of this trope is when Mina offers to enchant some weapons with anti-witch spells, and Hansel responds by producing a large cart full of heavy weaponry.

tropes.name: Mr. Fanservice
tropes.html: Handsome, muscular Hansel is shirtless by the pool.

tropes.name: Ms. Fanservice
tropes.html: Gretel spends the entire movie in a very form-hugging corset and tight leather pants.

tropes.name: Mundane Utility
tropes.html: Muriel twice uses her black magic wand just as a convenient way to light a fire.

tropes.name: Murder by Cremation
tropes.html: How Hansel and Gretel killed the witch they encountered as kids.

tropes.name: No-Harm Requirement
tropes.html: While the White Witches are perfectly permitted to use magic against the evil Black Witches, they not allowed to hurt humans even when they're being burned to death. Made all the more problematic by the fact that most humans in that world despise all witches.

tropes.name: Not Bad
tropes.html: After Muriel sarcastically asks Mina if she's going to hit her with a love spell, she blasts a bolt of energy at her, which hits a tree next to her. Muriel says this.

tropes.name: Of Corsets Sexy
tropes.html: Gretel wears one that allows for freedom of movement. Also Muriel clearly wears one, but she is sexy only in human form.

tropes.name: Off with His Head!
tropes.html: Another way of killing witches. Favored by Hansel and Gretel. Muriel suffers this.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: The Sheriff and his cronies all have this expression when Edward approaches and squishes each of their heads like grapes.

tropes.name: Ooh, Me Accent's Slipping
tropes.html:
• Famke Janssen seems to go from a British to Dutch to American accent throughout the film.
  • Gemma Arterton's American accent disappears when she shouts "HANSEL!"

tropes.name: One-Gender Race
tropes.html: Apparently there are no male witches. From the children of the Grand White Witch Adrianna, only Gretel is referred as a witch.

tropes.name: "Open!" Says Me
tropes.html: "Edward, wanna knock?"

tropes.name: Painted-On Pants
tropes.html: Gretel's leather pants are a bit snug, don't you think?

tropes.name: Parental Abandonment
tropes.html: In the beginning of the film, Hansel and Gretel's father leaves them in the woods. However, it is later revealed that both their parents needed to in order to save them from a mob of villagers, who most likely would have killed them for being children of a witch (though the good kind of witch).

tropes.name: Phrase Catcher
tropes.html: The candy house in the finale elicits the exact same reaction from the siblings, word for word.

tropes.name: Pride
tropes.html: According to Muriel, the reason why Adrianna chose not to run for it when the mob came for her.

tropes.name: Protagonist-Centered Morality
tropes.html: Zig zagged as the story initially seems to be playing the trope straight, with Hansel and Gretel's behavior being justifiably better because of their more weathered judgement. However, even this early, the habits of the townspeople and the duo don't differ much. Hansel wanted them to burn Mina (and ALL witches for that matter) and it's implied that Gretel would've too had she had a little more proof. Once the revelation that the townspeople were RIGHT (in a sense) is thrown in the pair's faces, they are forced to reconsider their standards. It's unclear whether the townspeople are aware that they too may have faulty witch detection guidelines and are changing theirs as a result.

tropes.name: Psychic-Assisted Suicide
tropes.html: Muriel forces a man to shoot himself in the head.

tropes.name: Punch-Clock Villain
tropes.html: Edward the troll, who only works for Muriel's coven because "trolls serve witches." Given the chance, he gladly betrays them to serve Gretel.

tropes.name: Raven Hair, Ivory Skin
tropes.html: Muriel's human form.

tropes.name: Rasputinian Death
tropes.html: Muriel's death is very drawn-out and gruesome, including being decapitated with a shovel.

tropes.name: Reckless Gun Usage
tropes.html:
• All over the place, but Hansel especially, since he's fond of slinging his shotgun over his shoulder for no other reason than that it looks cool. In one shot at the end of the film, it looks like it's pointing right at Benjamin's face.
  • Happens several times in the movie, the first time at the "burn the witch" scene with Sheriff Berringer. Hansel slings his BFG over his shoulder and casually flags one of the Sheriff's mooks. Of course, that might not have been accidental.

tropes.name: Rescue Romance
tropes.html: Gretel being saved by Edward.

tropes.name: The Reveal
tropes.html: Muriel reveals to Hansel and Gretel that their mother, Adrianna, was a benevolent white witch and that the reason why they are immune to black magic is due to being blessed by their mother with a spell of protection as children. Muriel needed the heart of a white witch as the final ingredient in the feast of the Blood Moon ritual, in order to make her and the rest of the black witches immune to fire. Adrianna was far too strong in the craft for them to overpower, so Muriel intended to have Gretel's heart instead. Muriel then spread rumours of Adrianna being a witch, causing the villagers to storm their home and burn her alive (not to mention hanging their father when he ran in to try and save her). However, their father was able to lead them into the forest and leave them there to protect them from the villagers.

tropes.name: Razor Floss
tropes.html: Hansel makes a web of blessed wires that slice through several fast-flying witches. In the extended cut, one surviving witch managed to let out a smirk before she falls apart.

tropes.name: Recursive Ammo
tropes.html: The round Ben fires at Muriel unravels in mid-air spraying tiny pellets making a great anti-aircraft (or should that be witchcraft?) weapon.

tropes.name: Reckless Sidekick
tropes.html: Averted quite strongly by the sidekick and the heroes. When fanboy Benjamin gushingly introduces himself, Gretel is actually fairly polite to him and somewhat appreciative of his hero-worship, and actually a bit impressed about all the research he did on witches and them. Hansel is more irritated, and both are a little creeped out. When Ben gets his chance to gain a sidekick role, he actually does what he was told — to hide and stand guard for a few hours, leading to a successful ambush.

tropes.name: Refuge in Audacity
tropes.html: The entire concept is Hansel and Gretel hunting and killing witches. No wonder it doesn't take itself seriously.

tropes.name: Rescue Romance
tropes.html: Between Mina and Hansel after she's saved from an accusation of witchcraft.

tropes.name: Role Called
tropes.html: Hansel and Gretel: Witch Hunters.

tropes.name: Rule of Cool
tropes.html: All over the place.

tropes.name: Say My Name
tropes.html: Gretel's scream of "HANSEL!" after she thinks he's been killed and/or seriously injured by Muriel.

tropes.name: Screw the Rules, I'm Beautiful!
tropes.html: Muriel attempts to invoke this by turning back into her beautiful form in the hopes that Hansel will feel bad about killing her. It doesn't work.

tropes.name: Schizo Tech
tropes.html: It's not really clear when this movie is supposed to be set, but some of the technology is rather advanced for the medieval period.

tropes.name: Seen It All
tropes.html: There's not much that happens in the movie which fazes the siblings, up to and including a man exploding in the middle of talking to them. Realizing that there are White Witches and that they were born from one itself, though... Didn't See That Coming.

tropes.name: Sex Signals Death
tropes.html: The white witch Mina and Hansel make love after she heals his wounds. During the final battle, the evil witch Muriel kills Mina.

tropes.name: Shape Shifter Guilt Trip
tropes.html: When Hansel is beating up the evil witch Muriel, she takes on her beautiful form (Famke Janssen) and begs for mercy. Hansel says, "Nice try," and continues the attack.

tropes.name: Shirtless Scene
tropes.html: Hansel has one when he takes off his clothes to go swimming (see Mr. Fanservice).

tropes.name: Ship Tease
tropes.html: Gretel and Edward.

tropes.name: Shoot the Hostage
tropes.html: Ben can't catch a break, can he?

tropes.name: Shotguns Are Just Better
tropes.html:
• Also Jackson.
    Gretel: Are you a good shot?
    Jackson: No. [Gretel gives him a look] That's why I use a shotgun.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• Hansel and Gretel's mother resembles Ichabod Crane's: slightly Eerie Pale-Skinned Brunette with long hair and a blue dress. Both were (or implied to be) white witches who loved their children but got killed by witch hunters.
  • Benjamin recalls the time the siblings prevented some witches from opening a hellhole under a town hall. He prepares some breakfast for Gretel that is not too cold and not too hot.
  • One of the witches at the sabbath has a giant, beard-like tumor similar to The Great Goblin. Another has a hairstyle like Yo-Landi Vi$$ar. A third is dressed exactly like the Queen of Hearts in Tim Burton's Alice.
  • The scenes with the witches flying their broomsticks in the forest and running into trees are very reminiscent of the speeder bike chase in Return of the Jedi.
  • Witches working spells with twelve children on the blood moon?

tropes.name: Shovel Strike
tropes.html: Muriel uses a shovel in her final fight. The twins eventually decapitate her with it.

tropes.name: Solitary Sorceress
tropes.html: All witches, good and bad, seem to live this way. The bad witches' isolation seems to be justified in this universe by the fact that dark witches are inherently corrupt and evil, and they start to visibly decay, which makes them too obvious to stay around people.

tropes.name: Soundtrack Dissonance
tropes.html: Atli Örvarsson's music is less fairytale, more hard rock.

tropes.name: Spellbook
tropes.html: Being a movie with witches in it there are a few.

tropes.name: Spoof Aesop
tropes.html:
Hansel delivers one to cap off the film's prologue:
Hansel: We learned a couple of things while we were trapped in that house. One, never walk in to a house made of candy. And two, if you're gonna kill a witch, set her ass on fire.

tropes.name: Squishy Wizard
tropes.html: Played straight with white witches except Gretel, but completely averted with the standard witch.

tropes.name: Stalker Shrine
tropes.html: Ben made one of the siblings, complete with a painting of Gretel. Gretel is creeped out.

tropes.name: Stealth Pun
tropes.html:
• One witch at the sabbath is dressed like a stereotypical Witch Doctor.
  • Another is half the witch she used to be.
  • The desert-dwelling witch in the epilogue is a sand-witch.

tropes.name: Stupid Good
tropes.html: Adrianna, a Grand White Witch, basically allows the townsfolk to kill her. This is a being so powerful that an entire covenant of evil witches cannot hope to take her by force. It's one thing never using your magic to harm humans on principle, but it's another thing entirely to surrender to being burned at the stake. There's no indication her magical prowess couldn't have allowed an escape without hurting anyone. Instead she's brutally murdered, her husband is hanged soon after and her children are left orphans at the mercy of witches. This plays completely into Muriel's hands.

tropes.name: Superpowerful Genetics
tropes.html: The daughter of a white witch is automatically a white witch herself, whether she uses magic or not. Additionally, it seems that power is inherited as well; Gretel doesn't practice witchcraft (as of yet) and didn't even know she was a witch until halfway through the film, but simply being the daughter of a Grand White Witch — the most powerful type of witch there is — is enough to qualify her as one, as well.

tropes.name: Super-Strength
tropes.html: The witches and Edward the troll.

tropes.name: Thanks for the Mammary
tropes.html: Ben cleans up an unconscious Gretel after a battle and surreptitiously wipes her breast. Gretel wakes up and is not amused.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html: A group of hunters hired by the sheriff are at first reluctant to go to the woods at night in an attempt to save the children, but go anyway after they are offered more money.

tropes.name: Too Good for This Sinful Earth
tropes.html: White Witches really get hit with this trope. Adrianna and Mina both end up dying. The surviving White Witch is more of an Anti-Hero.

tropes.name: Toplessness from the Back
tropes.html: Mina is shown entirely nude from the back she gets out of her dress by the pool.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Lie
tropes.html:
• The trailer makes Edward the troll appear as a bigger threat. The scene in the trailer where he's stomping through the trees is when he's coming to Gretel's rescue.
  • Hansel's line in the trailer ("Some people will say that not all witches are evil, that their powers could be used for good. I say burn them all!") is a heavily edited version of his closing narration (paraphrased) "We know there are good witches. To the rest we say: burn them all!".

tropes.name: True Blue Femininity
tropes.html: Adrianna in flashbacks. A lovely and somewhat queenly blue dress is what she is wearing when the mob comes for her.

tropes.name: Truer to the Text
tropes.html: Played with. The opening sequence with Hansel and Gretel as children is one of the rare examples of a fairytale adaptation that doesn't spare the horror and brutality of the original. The rest of the film, on the other hand...

tropes.name: Two-Person Pool Party
tropes.html: Mina and Hansel get amorous while bathing in a pond.

tropes.name: Unnecessary Combat Roll
tropes.html: Deconstructed. Hansel pulls this off at the climax. Then promptly gets hit by the bad guy right after completing it for his effort.

tropes.name: Unrated Edition
tropes.html:
Extends scenes and includes lines like:
Witch: Why don't you two go fuck yourselves? No, no, better - fuck each other!

tropes.name: Unstoppable Rage
tropes.html: When Muriel kills Mina, Hansel's subsequent assault is best described as this, culminating in him choking her with a chain and punching her body repeatedly while screaming in fury.

tropes.name: Use Your Head
tropes.html: Gretel headbutts the Sheriff when he won't get out of her face. This resulted in him being knocked off his feet with a broken nose. Towards the end of the movie, Gretel does it again, this time against Muriel.

tropes.name: Vengeance Feels Empty
tropes.html: Subverted. At the end, Hansel narrates how even though revenge won't change the past or bring their parents back, it still feels pretty damn good.

tropes.name: Villain Ball
tropes.html: The Sheriff approaches being an Anti-Villain through the first half of the movie... he's going about saving the children all wrong, with his biggest sin being not trusting Hansel and Gretel, but he clearly does want to save the town and the children. Then he goes completely off the rails after the witch attack, committing cold-blooded murder and having a long rant about breaking women like horses.

tropes.name: Villains Want Mercy
tropes.html: Muriel attempts to beg Hansel for her life when he is in the middle of unleashing an Unstoppable Rage Roaring Rampage of Revenge on her for killing his Love Interest Mina. Needless to say, it doesn't work.

tropes.name: Vomit Indiscretion Shot
tropes.html:
Both played with and played straight:
  • One of the mercenaries comes into the tavern and looks like he's about to vomit. Then he explodes.
  • Played straight with Benjamin when he sees the aftermath of the final fight scene.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html: "TROLLS. SERVE. WITCHES." Not that Gretel flickers an eyelid. More like her eyes slightly widen. She's a rather stoic lady.

tropes.name: Where It All Began
tropes.html: The location of the final battle against Muriel? The candy house in the prologue. Both twins lampshade this.

tropes.name: White Magic
tropes.html: White witches seem to primarily do healing and love spells, though remaining capable of attacking the evil black witches if necessary.

tropes.name: Wicked Witch
tropes.html: Wicked Witches are the main villains of the movie - easily identified as evil because their forms are monstrous. They can fly on brooms and of course target children.<!--* TheWitchHunter: Hansel and Gretel's stock in trade. They're far more heroic than your typical witch hunters.-->

tropes.name: Would Hit a Girl
tropes.html:
• The sheriff and his cronies beat up Gretel multiple times, with the sheriff trying to get revenge for her headbutting him earlier.
  • Hansel regarding pretty much every witch in existence, since they're monsters who were trying to kill him or innocent children.

tropes.name: Wounded Gazelle Gambit
tropes.html:
• Hansel uses a child-sized scarecrow and a music box playing the voice of a lost boy calling for help as bait to lure in witches.
  • Once Hansel hangs Muriel and proceeds to beat her up, she changes to her human form and begs for mercy. Hansel doesn't buy it.

tropes.name: You Are What You Hate
tropes.html: Muriel reveals to Gretel that she's a Grand White Witch, which she inherited from her mother, who was also a witch herself.

tropes.name: You Have GOT to Be Kidding Me!
tropes.html: Hansel and Gretel near the end ("You gotta be fucking kidding me"), when they come across the Gingerbread House from when they were kids.

tropes.name: Your Head A-Splode
tropes.html: In the final battle, more than one witch receives buckshot in their faces from Hansel's shotgun, which effectively turns their craniums into mush. Including the one witch he blasted up close.

tropes.name: You Talk Too Much!
tropes.html: Mina says it to Hansel as they're bathing together when he keeps jabbering. Hansel later says it to Muriel after a large dose of exposition.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html: This isn't the first time Steven Bauer was a drug dealer.

tropes.name: Agony of the Feet
tropes.html: Ruiz gets shot in the foot by Montel while hiding in a kids' ball pit.

tropes.name: Answer Cut
tropes.html: When Javier meets with the DEA agents, they want to take him to a safe house, but he balks at this. They ask him where he would rather go and where he'd feel safe. Cut to a public swimming pool where Javier and the two agents are both standing in the pool, wearing swimming trunks.

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html: A minor one from Ruiz, due to his use of the present tense. During his interrogation he snarkily compares Montel and Ray to Japanese Army holdouts on Pacific islands "who think World War II's still going on". The last verified holdout was repatriated about a quarter-century prior to the film's release.

tropes.name: As Himself
tropes.html: Senators Harry Reid (D-NV), Barbara Boxer (D-CA), Chuck Grassley (R-IA), and Orrin Hatch (R-UT), and Governon Bill Weld all make minor appearances in the movie. Some of the officials Wakefield meets at the border were also real law enforcement officials.

tropes.name: Assassination Attempt
tropes.html: Frankie Flowers attempts to kill Ruiz at Helena's orders, but is killed himself by a Tijuana Cartel hitman over informing on them, being shot by him and the DEA agents on the scene. However, a DEA agent is still killed by his car bomb afterward.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html:
Each storyline ends with some combination of hope and tragedy:
  • For the Mexico storyline, Manolo is killed, and while General Salazar is busted, the Obregon brothers are still in business. However, Javier is able to get his baseball field built so maybe the next generation of children will have a chance to avoid the drug trade.
  • For the Cincinnati storyline, Robert ends up walking away from his job when he realizes he's been neglecting his daughter Caroline while she descended into addiction (see the quote at the top of the page). He ends up reconciling with Caroline (along with his wife Barbara), and it seems Caroline has a better chance of staying clean than she did before.
  • For the San Diego storyline, the DEA is unable to prosecute Carlos, so he goes free, Arnie is likely dead after Carlos finds out his treachery, and Ray, Montel's partner, is dead. However, Montel is able to plant a bug in Carlos and Helena's house so the DEA can continue to keep watch on him.

tropes.name: Bury Your Gays
tropes.html: The assassin approaching Del Toro's character in a gay bar leads to his Jack Bauer Interrogation Technique. He eventually gets killed by the cartel during a failed hit for ratting out their members after torture. This was also the sole gay character in the film.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html: The last scene is a call back to Javier's comment about wanting somewhere safe for kids to play baseball at night.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Salma Hayek has one brief scene as a drug lord's wife.

tropes.name: The Cartel
tropes.html: The film deals with two real ones, the Mexican Tijuana and Juarez cartels. Many different characters are working for, against or affected by them, while both also fight each other.

tropes.name: The Cobbler's Children Have No Shoes
tropes.html: Wakefield is tasked with fighting the US war on drugs, even as his own daughter spirals into addiction. He eventually acknowledges this, saying he can't make war on his own family, and it appears he will resign.

tropes.name: Color Wash
tropes.html: Different color palettes are used for different storylines. Those taking place in Mexico are shaded yellow-brown, while the Wakefield storyline primarily in Cincinnati is cool blue. The Ayala/DEA storyline has normal coloration.

tropes.name: Colour-Coded for Your Convenience
tropes.html: Each of the three interlinking stories has its own location-based color cast.

tropes.name: Culture Clash
tropes.html: The Mexican law enforcement are shown to have a decidedly more brutal approach to the war on drugs than the Americans. Wakefield is visibly shocked when after he asks how they approach drug treatment, Salazar dismissively replies: "Addicts treat themselves. They OD and there's one less to deal with."note Of course, Salazar is also in the Juarez Cartel himself, unbeknownst to Wakefield. It's also said law enforcement in Mexico is really a more "entrepreneurial" profession (i.e. the police take bribes, as the film portrays-even the good ones).

tropes.name: The Dead Have Names
tropes.html: Montel tells Helena the name of his dead partner during their final confrontation.

tropes.name: Dead Sidekick
tropes.html: Both Mexican cop Javier Rodriguez and DEA agent Gordon have to deal with a close friend and colleague being murdered.

tropes.name: Descent into Addiction
tropes.html: The primary plotline in the Wakefield story centers on Wakefield's daughter Caroline, who develops an addiction to cocaine after being introduced to it by her boyfriend. Her parents put her in rehab, but she escapes and resorts to theft and prostitution to fund her habit. At the end of the film she's back in rehab and seems more committed to recovering.

tropes.name: Dig Your Own Grave
tropes.html: Both (comparatively) honest Mexican cops are made to do this.

tropes.name: Dirty Cop
tropes.html: More than one, including a general, who is largely based on José de Jesús Gutiérrez Rebollo, a former division general in the Mexican army who was head of anti-drug interdiction in Mexico, making him ideally poised to aid traffickers. Like the film character, he was in bed with the Juarez Cartel, letting them operate unimpeded in return for hefty bribes.

tropes.name: Drugs Are Bad
tropes.html: Caroline, Wakefield's daughter, ends up appearing to prostitute herself to get drugs.

tropes.name: Enemy Mine
tropes.html: Helena's son is threatened by a representative of the cartels, to whom Carlos supposedly owes money. This prompts her to go to Montel and Ray, even though they have arrested her husband and are monitoring her in case she's also involved in the drug trade, and ask them to intervene if they see anything suspicious going on.

tropes.name: Enlightened Self-Interest
tropes.html: Manolo does attempt to expose the general, but does so for a reward.

tropes.name: External Combustion
tropes.html: Ray is killed by a car bomb.

tropes.name: Face Death with Dignity
tropes.html: Downplayed but present with Manolo, especially given his apology to Javier for Getting them into this.

tropes.name: Four Lines, All Waiting
tropes.html: Three storylines play out.

tropes.name: Functional Addict
tropes.html:
• Seth, Caroline's boyfriend, appears to be this. Or maybe he's simply a recreational user who's avoided getting hooked.
  • Manolo, del Toro's character's partner, is subtly implied to be this.
  • Wakefield himself is accused of alcoholism by his wife.

tropes.name: Gayngster
tropes.html: The assassin, Frankie Flowers. But he's definitely better off than his girlfriend.

tropes.name: Good Cop/Bad Cop
tropes.html: At first the assassin is violently tortured, and then is "rescued" from his captors by the corrupt general, the torturer's boss. He is given a sumptuous meal and a bottle of wine, finally releasing the desired information after being told "In Vino Veritas".

tropes.name: The Guards Must Be Crazy
tropes.html: None of the agents protecting Ruiz are suspicious at all when someone comes to his door saying they are the mafia.

tropes.name: Guile Hero
tropes.html: Javier sells information to the DEA about Salazar working in conjunction with the cartel. His partner, Manolo, tries to do the exact same thing but is more careless about it and gets both himself and Javier dragged out into the desert by Salazar's own men to be killed; however only Manolo is killed and Javier is allowed into Salazar's trusted - and therefore corrupt - elite. But since Salazar is already finished, thanks to US backing via the DEA, Javier gets to take the credit for the bust and enjoy seeing his baseball park for the children be built.

tropes.name: Hoist by Their Own Petard
tropes.html: Arnie steals the money that Carlos had left for his wife and tries to use this improvishment to seduce her. If he had just given Helena the money then she would have had the protection she needed and probably wouldn't have gone to such lengths to break him out of jail, with Carlos seeking revenge against Arnie for his betrayal immediately afterwards.

tropes.name: Hyperlink Story
tropes.html: Three interlocking stories.<!--* InherentInTheSystem: The war on drugs.-->

tropes.name: The Informant
tropes.html:
• Frankie Flowers, who's a Tijuana Cartel hitman, gets captured and tortured then wheedled into giving up information to their rivals, the Juarez Cartel. Many Tijuana Cartel members are arrested due to this after they tip the police off. He's later killed for it by his cartel.
  • Javier becomes a DEA informant, giving up information on the Juarez Cartel after he gets associated with them. General Salazar, who's a top member, is arrested due to this.

tropes.name: Jack Bauer Interrogation Technique
tropes.html: The Tijuana Cartel hitman Frankie Flowers is extensively tortured after he's captured by Juarez Cartel people for information on his employers.

tropes.name: Jerkass Has a Point
tropes.html: At one point Wakefield gives a casually insensitive remark about Seth bringing her to a crime ridden part of the intercity. Seth immediately responds that the psychological impact of white people coming to black neighborhoods asking for drugs is severe as the Drug trade is inherently a quick money business. He argues that if the situation were reversed, most white kids would go into the drug trade.

tropes.name: Karma Houdini
tropes.html:
• Carlos Ayala gets away with everything, the key witness against him having been assassinated on the day he was to give testimony. But Montel hasn't given up trying to get him by planting a bug under Ayala's desk. Not to mention, the DA and local law-enforcement are watching him, since his legitimate businesses are stated to be nothing more than money laundering facilities.
  • Seth suffers no consequences from getting his girlfriend hooked on crack. However, he will have to answer for why the Drug Czar pulled him out of class.

tropes.name: Knight in Sour Armour
tropes.html:
Montel to a tee.
"The worst part about you, Monty, is that you realize the futility of what you're doing and you do it anyway."

tropes.name: Mama Bear
tropes.html: Helena. As ruthlessly as she goes about it, it's obvious that the main reason she's trying to get her husband out of jail is so that he can protect her and their son — the scene where he's threatened is the moment she realizes how dire the situation is.

tropes.name: Married to the Job
tropes.html: Wakefield. It amplifies the problems with Caroline's drug addiction, which he realizes at the end when he steps down from his new czar job to support her.

tropes.name: Meal Ticket
tropes.html: When a desperate Helena goes to visit her husband's lawyer Arnie, he hints that he could make her money problems go away if she married him. Given the expression on her face and her earlier conversation with her husband (wherein she vowed to never be poor, no matter what it took), she's at least considering it, no matter her personal squick factor.

tropes.name: Mob War
tropes.html: The Juarez and Tijuana Cartels are fighting each other throughout the film, while their rivalry has gone long into the past too. It extends to giving the police tips on each other so they're personnel are arrested, along with assassinating people.

tropes.name: Moral Guardians
tropes.html: Wakefield's job is to be this, regarding drugs, for an entire country. Meanwhile, however, his own house is not quite in order.

tropes.name: Noodle Implements
tropes.html: A variation of the Ginger Beer Trick variety of this trope is used with a Coke bottle.

tropes.name: "Not So Different" Remark
tropes.html: Wakefield's wife points out that, for all his anti-drug invective, he still drinks enough that he could not unjustifiably be called an alcoholic.

tropes.name: Open-Minded Parent
tropes.html: Wakefield's wife, Barbara, admits to knowing about Caroline's drug use and thought it would be beneficial to allow her to experiment. This backfires badly when it becomes apparent that Caroline winds up addicted.

tropes.name: Pay Evil unto Evil
tropes.html: Ayala has given his slimy lawyer Arnie several million dollars to give to Helena in the event that he (Ayala) is arrested. Ayala's arrested but Arnie makes no mention of the money to Helena, even going so far as to tell her he's tapped out when she asks for money. He then hints that he could solve all her financial problems by marrying her if Ayala is sent away for good. After Ayala is freed and two men with guns show up in Arnie's office, it's not hard to imagine what happens.

tropes.name: Police Are Useless
tropes.html: None of the agents protecting Ruiz are suspicious at all when someone comes to his door saying they are the mafia.

tropes.name: Precision F-Strike
tropes.html: Despite all the profanity in the other two storylines, Wakefield's is largely free of it, making it all the more shocking when Caroline is emboldened from being high to shout "Fuck you!" as he searches her bathroom for drugs. He's so stunned that he can only say it right back.

tropes.name: Pregnant Badass
tropes.html: Helena becomes this once she adapts to her situation and realizes what's at stake.

tropes.name: Professional Killer
tropes.html: Frankie Flowers is a hitman of the Tijuana Cartel, who prefers to use bombs. He is himself killed by another Cartel hitman for informing on them to their rivals, the Juarez Cartel. Another hitman murders Eduardo Ruiz, the main witness in the trial of Carl Ayala, a drug dealer in the US for them.

tropes.name: The Queenpin
tropes.html: Helena Ayala goes from a pampered socialite who's genuinely clueless about the true nature of her husband's business — he's a drug lord — to the epitome of this — she takes over his organization while he's in prison, and has the chief witness against him killed to ensure his freedom.

tropes.name: Reality Is Unrealistic
tropes.html: When a critic commented that it seemed unrealistic that the Caroline's high school record was almost perfect when she was taking drugs, screenwriter Stephen Gaghan pointed out that the high school record in the movie was his and that he had been abusing drugs at the time.

tropes.name: Reasonable Authority Figure
tropes.html: Wakefield's processor on the anti-drugs task force, General Landry. He's done a lot of good work, but is open about believing that his actions have had no lasting impact. He's willing to give some advice to his successor, while offering himself up as a Scapegoat in the event that's necessary.

tropes.name: The Remake
tropes.html: Originally a British miniseries, revolving around heroin from Pakistan rather than cocaine from Mexico. The movie itself was eventually remade by the USA Network as a three part miniseries.

tropes.name: Reports of My Death Were Greatly Exaggerated
tropes.html: Early on a major drug player who is dismissed as dead. It turns out he just got plastic surgery.

tropes.name: Ripped from the Headlines
tropes.html: The drug lord who is thought to have died in a surgery but turns out to be alive is based on the drug lord Amado Carrillo Fuentes, "The Lord of the Skies", who died in 1997 while undergoing a cosmetic surgery.

tropes.name: Sarcastic Confession
tropes.html: When the assassin masquerading as room service arrives at the informant's hotel room, he announces himself as "Mafia!"

tropes.name: Smuggling with Dolls
tropes.html: This trope gets taken this to the logical extreme when Helena, left running the empire after Carlos is arrested, hits on a clever way of smuggling cocaine across the border: make dolls out of odorless cocaine.

tropes.name: Those Two Guys
tropes.html: Montel and Ray. Leads to Mood Whiplash when Ray is blown up by Frankie Flowers' car bomb.

tropes.name: Throwing Out the Script
tropes.html: Wakefield interrupts himself in the middle of a carefully prepared, approved speech to make an emotional (though vague) reference to his drug-addicted daughter.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Badass
tropes.html: Formerly sheltered housewife Helena takes to drug-running quite well.

tropes.name: Tropaholics Anonymous
tropes.html: Caroline goes to this two different times. The second time, she is more sincere.

tropes.name: Undercover Cop Reveal
tropes.html: Almost. Monty, Ray, and a female agent are monitoring Helena and her son incognito when she's at the beach. One of her husband's unpaid business associates walks up, grabs the child, and threatens Helena. The three quickly agree that if the man runs off with or attempts to harm the child, they'll all break cover and rescue him. Fortunately, it doesn't come to that.

tropes.name: Van in Black
tropes.html: Played with. Helena, wife to a drug dealer who is in custody and under investigation, brings lemonade to the cops keeping an eye on her house.

tropes.name: Warm Place, Warm Lighting
tropes.html: Much of it is set in Mexico, and it is suitably golden-tinted. In contrast, scenes with the Ohio native protagonist are washed with blue.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html: When Caroline is arrested, Robert and Barbara disagree about how to handle it all. Barbara argues just a little too hard that they should be understanding and not punish Caroline too harshly. Robert gives her a look and asks, "How long have you known about this?"

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html: After Caroline's first scene just shows her taking drugs at a party with no indication of how she's connected to any of the other plotlines, Wakefield picks up his family at the Washington airport and she's revealed to be his daughter.

tropes.name: What You Are in the Dark
tropes.html: Helena did not know that her husband was a drug dealer and was horrified. But when push comes to shove she chooses to embrace her husband's choices as she refuses to let her children grow up with poverty. She ends up revealing that she is just as bloodthirsty and cold as most in the drug trade.

tropes.name: 2D Visuals, 3D Effects
tropes.html: A few famous people Kenny passes by as he falls into Hell (among them Adolf Hitler, George Burns and Mahatma Gandhi) are rendered as this. Although they're not people so much as demons.

tropes.name: Abandoned Warehouse
tropes.html: The kids have their meeting in Carl's Warehouse, a desserted and disheveled area, in order for the La Résistance to plan in secret.

tropes.name: Academia Elitism
tropes.html: While attending Mr. Mackey's anti-swearing rehabilitation, Gregory protests that he doesn't belong with the other schoolchildren, as he attended Yardale and had a 4.0 GPA. Cartman just says, "You're a fucking faggot, dude."

tropes.name: The Ace
tropes.html:
• Gregory, due to his political competence and good grades; the former being the very reason he leads La Résistance.
  • Brian Boitano, at least according to Stan's song, is described as a highly talented and incredibly competent individual that the boys look to for advice. He also has Superpower Lottery at his disposal.

tropes.name: Actually Quite Catchy
tropes.html: During Cartman's song "Kyle's Mom is a Bitch", Stan starts dancing along with the other students (except Kyle), despite him being Kyle's best friend and generally disliking Cartman.

tropes.name: Adam Westing
tropes.html: George Clooney has a cameo as a doctor who attempts to save Kenny's life. It goes without saying that Kenny dies, but the kicker is that the doctors replaced his heart with a baked potato.

tropes.name: Adults Are Useless
tropes.html: One of the movie's major themes is the adults are useless and also deals with bad parenting. The opening song even includes the line "Off to the movies we shall go/where we learn everything that we know/'cause the movies teach us what our parents don't have time to say", the last line indicating that vulgar cartoons like Terrence & Phillip are satire and an exact example of why children shouldn't turn to TV characters as role models in the absence of their parents. When the boys got in trouble at the school, the parents decided to declare war on Canada instead of dealing with the boys' behavior and teaching them when and when not to swear.

tropes.name: Affectionate Parody
tropes.html:
Trey and Matt are pretty big musical theatre fans (later having penned The Book of Mormon), and it shows; this is basically a South Park-ified entry in the Disney Renaissance (with some elements of stage musicals like Les Misérables for good measure). This is even mentioned directly in the script.
Very happy, Disneyesque MUSIC swirls in.
It is a scene reminiscent of, if not directly ripped off from, the opening number of Beauty and the Beast.

tropes.name: Afterlife Welcome
tropes.html: Kenny receives his halo and wings from other angels at the very end.

tropes.name: Anachronism Stew
tropes.html: Played for Laughs in "What Would Brian Boitano Do?", in which the eponymous skater beats up Kublai Khan while building the Pyramids of Giza.

tropes.name: Anatomy Anomaly
tropes.html: Ze Mole is the only kid to have ears.

tropes.name: And There Was Much Rejoicing
tropes.html: "It's been six weeks since Saddam Hussein was killed by a pack of wild boars, and the world is still glad to be rid of him."

tropes.name: Angry Mob Song
tropes.html: "Blame Canada" and "La Résistance". The former sung from the perspective of the Mothers Against Canada who are looking for a target to blame for exposing their children to foul language; the latter from the kids protesting their parents' war against Canada and ultimately the execution of Terrence and Phillip.

tropes.name: Animated Musical
tropes.html: Thirteen original songs are performed by cartoon characters.

tropes.name: Animated World Hypotheses
tropes.html: An ambiguous case. The Terrance and Phillip movie, as well as the TV show it was based on, is referred to as a cartoon, but the real Terrance and Phillip look exactly like the supposedly animated characters they're playing.

tropes.name: Animation Bump
tropes.html: Appropriately enough, compared to Seasons 1 and 2. Subverted, however, from Season 3 onward, as the animation team took all the data and techniques used in the film and cranked them up.

tropes.name: Animesque
tropes.html: The film naturally spoofs anime with the Dragon Ball Z-esque battle between Cartman and Saddam near the end, complete with motion lines and odd camera angles.

tropes.name: Anti-Villain
tropes.html: For being the Prince of Darkness, Satan's actually a big softy and is by far the most sympathetic villain in the Big Bad Ensemble.

tropes.name: Any Last Words?
tropes.html:
As Terrance and Phillip are about to be executed, Sheila asks them if they have any last words:
Phillip: How's aboot 'Get me the fuck out of this chair!'?

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html: "What about Ike, huh, Mom? Did you forget that your own adopted son is Canadian!?" This makes Sheila think, but ultimately she ends up shooting Terrence and Phillip because Ike wasn't brought onto the battlefield to be used as a pawn.

tropes.name: Arson, Murder, and Jaywalking
tropes.html: Cartman's cluster swear line at the end: "Fuck, shit, cock, ass, titties, boner, bitch, muff, pussy, cunt, butthole, Barbra Streisand!!"

tropes.name: Artistic License – Economics
tropes.html: Played for Laughs. During the UN meeting, we learn that Terrance and Phillip and related merchandise is responsible for almost half of Canada’s economy. Just to get a sense of how ridiculous that is, in Real Life, Canada’s single largest industry (real estate, including selling/managing/renting/leasing) makes up about 13% of Canada’s GDP.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Law
tropes.html: Sheila says that Terrance and Phillip are under citizens' arrest and produces a court order allowing it. However, court orders give government approval for such a thing, technically not making it a citizens' arrest.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Linguistics
tropes.html: "Bich" is not Latin for "generosity". (It's Luxembourgish for "beech tree", but that wouldn't make as snappy a lyric.)

tropes.name: As Long as There Is One Man
tropes.html: Parodied with "La Résistance", as the song gradually turns into Go, Ye Heroes, Go and Die, and Stan, Kyle and Cartman find it increasingly uninspiring.

tropes.name: Audience Participation Song
tropes.html: The film version of "Kyle's Mom is a Bitch": "Come on, you all know the words!" Granted, Cartman's addressing the other kids in the playground, but it's pretty obvious that he's also addressing the viewers to get up for some toe-tapping sweary fun.

tropes.name: Aw, Look! They Really Do Love Each Other
tropes.html: At the beginning, Kyle kicks Ike through a window and complains to his mother that he's adopted. Later on, it's shown that Kyle does care about Ike when the American government begins rounding up Canadian-born citizens. Kyle hides Ike in his attic so he won't be taken away and promises him that things will get better. While Kyle protects Terrance and Phillip, he asks his mother about Ike whom she adopted from Canada.

tropes.name: Award-Bait Song
tropes.html:
• "Up There", Satan's big showstopper. A specific parody of the "I Want" Song as seen in Disney Renaissance movies.
  • Parodied with "Eyes of a Child" by Michael McDonald of The Doobie Brothers.
  • This is averted by the song that actually got award nominations, "Blame Canada".

tropes.name: Backstabbing the Alpha Bitch
tropes.html: The other mothers leave Sheila on her own to go find their children, who are stuck in the middle of the battlefield.

tropes.name: Bad Guys Do the Dirty Work
tropes.html: Satan kills Saddam Hussein and pulls his demons back to Hell, though it's more of a Dog Bites Back moment for Satan.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html: Winona Ryder's ping pong ball trick. She just sits down and smacks them with a ping pong paddle, though the POV shot clearly suggests at first that she's propelling them from her vagina.

tropes.name: Barred from the Afterlife
tropes.html: After he dies, Kenny is rejected entry into heaven and falls into hell. At the end, after convincing Satan to stand up to Saddam and undoing all the damage caused by the war between America and Canada, he's allowed into heaven.

tropes.name: Barrier Maiden
tropes.html: Terrance and Phillip are the only two people preventing the apocalypse from being brought about.

tropes.name: Because You Were Nice to Me
tropes.html: At the end, after Satan finally has enough of Saddam's abuse, he agrees to pull back his minions, return to Hell, and restore everything to normal simply because Kenny asked him to and the boy was the only one to show him sympathy during his more depressed episodes.

tropes.name: Behind the Black
tropes.html: The Canadian artillery platforms come over the hill, and the camera pans back to reveal many more were already over the hill. The camera then moves over to the American general who expresses surprise, whose reaction is like he didn't see the entire Canadian artillery platoon until the camera panned out to show them all.

tropes.name: Benevolent Genie
tropes.html: Satan of all people is this! When he offers to grant Kenny any wish he wants and Kenny wishes for everything to go back to normal, he goes through with it. All the people who died come back to life and Satan calls off his invasion and returns his minions to Hell. Satan doesn't abuse Exact Words, claim Kenny's soul as payment, or do anything that a Deal with the Devil usually entails.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html: Sheila Broflovski has always had issues with people swearing around her, but this movie takes things up to eleven when she starts a war with Canada because she can't stand how Terrance and Phillip's movie "Asses of Fire" turned the mouths of South Park's kids even filthier than normal and seeks to kill Terrance and Phillip themselves due to her utter hatred of them for this.

tropes.name: Bestiality Is Depraved
tropes.html:
Played for laughs twice.
  • The first time is this conversation between Terrance and Phillip in "Asses of Fire".
    Terrance: You're such a pig-fucker, Phillip!
    Phillip: Terrance, why would you call me a pig-fucker?
    Terrance: Well, let's see. First of all, you fuck pigs.
    Phillip: [Beat] ...oh yeah!
  • Later on, Dr. Vosknocker tests the V-Chip using flash cards with words and pictures. The first obscenity he has Cartman say is "horsefucker", and the graphic depicts a man having sex with a horse.

tropes.name: Beyond the Impossible
tropes.html: When Kenny goes to Hell, there's a sign that says Hell has 900 billion people (and counting) in it. Not that many people have even existed. Maybe they were counting animals and/or aliens? Even ignoring this, the show said that Mormonism was the right religion. Mormons actually believe that only the truly wicked go to Hell and not because they weren't Mormon. Even if that wasn't the case, "All About the Mormons" called Mormonism dumb over and over and said it was a Scam Religion. Hell having that many people is absolutely incomprehensible from any perspective.

tropes.name: Big Bad Ensemble
tropes.html: Sheila Broflovski, Satan and Saddam Hussein. Sheila is responsible for creating M.A.C. and starting a war between America and Canada, while Satan and Saddam Hussein form a Big Bad Duumvirate and plot to manipulate the war to come Back from the Dead and Take Over the World.

tropes.name: Big Damn Movie
tropes.html: What the title says. Notably, it premiered not long after the series premiered on Comedy Central, though. But it still breaks a new record for an apocalyptic musical adaptation of a crude Subverted Kids' Show that nobody at the time predicted would last more than one season.

tropes.name: Big "SHUT UP!"
tropes.html:
Kyle gives one to Cartman when Cartman starts to sing "Kyle's Mom's A Bitch".
Kyle: SHUT YOUR FUCKING MOUTH, CARTMAN!

tropes.name: Big Ol' Eyebrows
tropes.html: Cartman noticeably gains very thick eyebrows in his Super Saiyan form in the climax.

tropes.name: Big "NO!"
tropes.html:
• The singer of "Hell Isn’t Good" once the Mood Whiplash kicks in.
  • Stan when the electric chairs holding Terrance and Phillip are turned on by Mr. Garrison.
  • Sheila shouts this when Kyle is able to stop the Canadian/American war... ...then shoots Terrance and Phillip.

tropes.name: Big "WHAT?!"
tropes.html:
• Kenny, when he is shown Heaven (which, due to him being a pervert, is full of naked girls)... only to have the carpet yanked out from under him when he tries to enter, and is subsequently banished to hell since he refused to go to church and went to the movies instead.
  • Terrance, after hearing Sheila Broflovski give her justification of why the US is at war with Canada to the troops at the USO show.

tropes.name: Biting-the-Hand Humor
tropes.html: The General attempts to justify the killing of Terrance & Phillip to the kids by saying they can still watch fart jokes on Nickelodeon, who is under the same parent company as Comedy Central.

tropes.name: Black Dude Dies First
tropes.html:
The army attempts to send in all the Black soldiers first as "Operation: Human Shield" and the white soldiers getting behind them as "Operation: Get Behind The Darkies", even after Chef reminds the general of the Emancipation Proclamation (the freedom of slaves). Chef defies this trope when he tells all the Black soldiers to jump out of the way at the right time.
General: Yes, soldier?
Chef: Have you ever heard of the Emancipation Proclamation?
General: I don't listen to hip-hop.

tropes.name: Blackface
tropes.html: Cartman briefly appears wearing blackface during his performance of "Kyle's Mom is a Bitch."

tropes.name: Blatant Lies
tropes.html:
In his Villain Song, Saddam says that he can change. He never says that he will change, though. Big difference.
  • When he shouts out "Just watch, I'm changing!", all he actually does is breakdance.
  • Also, every time Saddam tells Satan, "I love you," when he really wants to be resurrected and take over the world.

tropes.name: Blood from the Mouth
tropes.html: After Ze Mole is severely mauled by guard dogs, shortly before he dies from his wounds he coughs up blood.

tropes.name: Book Burning
tropes.html: The parents of South Park hold a massive bonfire of Canadian media to protest how Canada produced the filthy comics Terrance & Philip. Later, it escalates into rounding up Canadians and sending them to "happy camps", and eventually results in the US invading Canada and starting World War III.

tropes.name: Bookends
tropes.html: The film begins and ends with the song "Mountain Town" sung by the main characters.

tropes.name: Bribing the Homeless
tropes.html: The boys pay a homeless man (entitled "Mr. Homeless Guy") ten dollars to help them sneak into the Canadian R-rated movie Asses of Fire.

tropes.name: Bring My Brown Pants
tropes.html: Kyle pees his pants when Terrance and Phillip are being electrocuted.

tropes.name: Bullying a Dragon
tropes.html: Saddam's constant verbal abuse towards Satan eventually becomes his own un-doing once Saddam calls Satan a "weak, stupid cum bucket".

tropes.name: Butt-Monkey
tropes.html: Cartman; he gets a V-chip implanted and shocks him anytime he swears (after cussing the most out of the boys and singing a insulting song of Kyle's mom, Shelia), until the end where he uses the electric powers to stop Saddam Hussein.

tropes.name: The Cake Is a Lie
tropes.html: Sorry if you came to La Résistance hoping for punch and pie.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html:
• Many quotes and events occurred previously in the Jesus vs. Santa short.
    • The "Don't call me fat, you butt-fucking son of a bitch!" quote by Cartman was previously said by him in the short.
    • Terrance and Phillip weren't the first characters in the series to use the insult "pigfucker"; Cartman used it in the short.
    • Due to the conflict of whether to help Jesus or Santa, Stan asks "what would Brian Boitano do?", and luckily for the boys, he actually appears (unlike in the movie, where Brian Dennehy appears after mishearing his name).
  • This is the third time Kyle has played "kick the baby" with Ike, the first was in "Cartman Gets an Anal Probe" and the second was in "Ike's Wee Wee".
  • Cartman previously sang his "Kyle's Mom's a Bitch" song in "Mr Hankey the Christmas Poo".

tropes.name: Calling the Old Man Out
tropes.html: Kyle does this to Sheila near the end. She wasn't pleased.

tropes.name: Camp Gay
tropes.html: Big Gay Al. It goes even further with his big musical number, "I'm Super", where he flaunts his flamboyant homosexuality to show that he's indeed gay beyond the sense of just being extremely happy.

tropes.name: Canadian Equals Hockey Fan
tropes.html: During "Blame Canada", the Mothers Against Canada criticize Canada for "all their hockey hullabaloo".

tropes.name: Captivity Harmonica
tropes.html: Ike's reaction to being forced to hide in the attic.

tropes.name: Car Cushion
tropes.html: Conan O'Brien, after his My God, What Have I Done? moment, jumps out of the window and lands on a car. All the car's owner does is turn the alarm off.

tropes.name: Celebrities Hang Out in Heaven
tropes.html: Inverted. When Kenny's falling to Hell , he sees Adolf Hitler, Mahatma Gandhi and George Burns.

tropes.name: Celebrity Casualty
tropes.html:
• The film is set roughly in its release year of 1999 where "It's been six weeks since Saddam Hussein was killed by a pack of wild boars, and the world is still glad to be rid of him." The real Saddam Hussein would be hanged in 2006.
  • Conan O'Brien kills himself out of guilt for being complicit in Terrance and Phillip's arrest.note Amusingly, this scene is what was shown to the real Conan O'Brien on his show when Trey Parker and Matt Stone were guests. Conan jokingly remarked that they got his voice wrong.
  • Bill Gates is shot to death for not having Windows 98 running without glitches.
  • "All the Baldwins are dead?"

tropes.name: Celebrity Power
tropes.html:
• Brian Boitano, as represented by "What Would Brian Boitano Do?" Apparently in possession of fire breath, and a Time Machine, among other strange powers.
  • "Barbra Streisand" is a swear word profane enough to trigger the V-Chip.

tropes.name: Censored Title
tropes.html: On the back cover of the soundtrack album, "Uncle Fucka" is censored as "Uncle F**ka".

tropes.name: Chainsaw Good
tropes.html: The Canadians use chainsaws as melee weapons.

tropes.name: Character as Himself
tropes.html: The film credits Saddam Hussein as himself, though the voice was actually done by Matt Stone.

tropes.name: Cheated Death, Died Anyway
tropes.html: When the Canadian army bombs the Baldwin family manor, Billy Baldwin miraculously survives. He comes dancing out the wreckage taunting the planes, "Ha ha, you missed me!" Then one more plane flies over and drops a bomb that scores a direct hit.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html: Cartman's V-chip. It later malfunctions and can be used as a weapon.

tropes.name: Chekhov's News
tropes.html:
The news reporter's line during "Mountain Town":
"It's been six weeks since Saddam Hussein was killed by a pack of wild boars, and the world is still glad to be rid of him."

tropes.name: Children's Covert Coterie
tropes.html: The kids create a secret group aptly named La Résistance dedicated to save Terrence & Philip from being executed.

tropes.name: Choose Your Own Reward
tropes.html: At the end of the film, Satan finally grows a spine and stands up to Saddam Hussein, his abusive boyfriend, by killing him. The Prince of Darkness credits Kenny (who'd died and been sent to Hell earlier) for giving him the courage to defeat Hussein and offers him "any wish he wants" as a reward. Kenny's choice: for Satan to hit a cosmic Reset Button and restore Earth to how it was before the American-Canadian War began, even though that means he'll be sent back to Hell. Satan agrees and triggers a World-Healing Wave that brings all the dead back to life—and in a case of Sweet and Sour Grapes, Kenny gets to ascend to Heaven because his wish was truly selfless.

tropes.name: Cluster F-Bomb
tropes.html: When Cartman's V-chip malfunctions near the climax, his newly-gained electrical powers are fueled by this trope. "Uncle Fucka" also qualifies. On a meta level, the entire film qualifies.

tropes.name: The Comedy Drop
tropes.html: During the "Blame Canada" number, a couple drops their infant while rushing off to join Mothers Against Canada, a not-so-subtle metaphor for the fact that the group isn't really about protecting kids so much as it is an invitation to avoid parental responsibility.

tropes.name: Comically Inept Healing
