On a quest that consistently involves events from Greek Mythology, Annabeth (who is supposed to be the goddess of wisdom's daughter) enters the Lotus Casino and eats the Lotus blossoms inside, after she is saved she figures out that they are the lotus eaters from the Odyssey.

tropes.name: Informed Ability
tropes.html: We are told that Annabeth is a wise combat schemer, probably a combat pragmatist, but in the movie she offers no actual aid to the heroes and just kind of acts like a tag-along child with specks of damsel in distress. All the combat and ideas on how to solve problems are given by Percy the only exception being the idea to keep Medusa's head for later.

tropes.name: Informed Flaw
tropes.html: Percy brings up his dyslexia and ADHD as though they're major and recurring problems in his daily life, but we don't see any signs of them hindering him onscreen.

tropes.name: Large Ham
tropes.html: Hades.

tropes.name: MacGuffin
tropes.html: The three pearls the trio needs to get from the Underworld.

tropes.name: Mook Chivalry
tropes.html: Annabeth's team members in Capture The Flag attack an enhanced Percy Jackson one by one. Percy, unsurprisingly, just curbstomps each of them.

tropes.name: Mushroom Samba
tropes.html: The effect of the lotus blossoms, apparently.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html: Percy slicing off the Hydra's heads, not knowing that it would come back with ten instead of five.

tropes.name: Product Placement
tropes.html:
Apple products. Also, when Percy, Annabeth, and Grover go to see Luke on how to get into the Underworld, he's playing Modern Warfare 2, more specifically the "Favela" map on the OpFor side.
  • In the sequel, UPS is revealed as being secretly run by Hermes.

tropes.name: The Queen's Latin
tropes.html: The gods all have British accents in the movie.

tropes.name: Race Lift
tropes.html: This was done to Grover, Hephaestus, and Persephone.

tropes.name: Rock Me, Asmodeus!
tropes.html: Invoked. Hades has the appearance and mannerisms of a Heavy Metal star.

tropes.name: Red Herring
tropes.html: Hades is not the main villain. Although he is an asshole.

tropes.name: Running Gag
tropes.html: Grover getting flirted with by hot girls, from the camp to Persephone in the Underworld counts.

tropes.name: Shirtless Scene
tropes.html: Remember those two scenes with Percy swimming, which was the first thing shown in the adverts of this film? It wasn't in the book.

tropes.name: Shmuck Bait
tropes.html: "Do not open this fridge! Ever!"

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• While passing the river of lost dreams thing in Hades, one can see a little sled floating by.
  • It's mentioned that Medusa's eyes need to be opened to activate her power from her decapitated head. Instead we see them open automatically, just like in Clash of the Titans.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Adaptation Modification
tropes.html: The film is a Type 2 (Recognizable Adaptation). It keeps some things from the books intact, but also changes a lot of stuff around.

tropes.name: Soft Glass
tropes.html: Averted. Grover yells in pain and warns Percy and Sally of broken glass after he crawls through a broken windshield.

tropes.name: Standard Female Grab Area
tropes.html: A justified example. Annabeth is subdued by a terrified woman grabbing onto her wrist - because the woman gets turned to stone by Medusa.

tropes.name: Talking the Monster to Death
tropes.html: Inverted by Medusa, who manages to get a random woman to open her eyes and be turned to stone simply by talking to her.

tropes.name: Title Drop
tropes.html: Count the number of times they say some variation of "Lightning Thief" in this movie.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Lie
tropes.html: The teaser trailer showed a more book-accurate scene of Percy accessing Olympus by speaking to the Empire State Building's doorman and then taking the elevator up from the lobby. In the film proper, Olympus is only shown to be accessible via a secret elevator on the observation deck.

tropes.name: Vehicle Vanish
tropes.html: At the beginning, Percy briefly glimpses his father watching him while on a school field trip, only for Poseidon to vanish when a vehicle passes between them.

tropes.name: Waist-Deep Ocean
tropes.html: In the film's opening, Poseidon rises straight up out of the ocean as a giant humanoid and walks to shore before assuming a human-sized form.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: What exactly was the reaction of the mortal world to discovering that a life-sized stone statue of the Hydra had turned up in the Nashville Parthenon overnight? One has to wonder, and can only wonder, since the movie doesn't follow up on this once the trio leave. The Mist, which would normally be the explanation for this in the books, isn't acknowledged until the second film and doesn't work as potently as it's supposed to in that film.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html:
• Hermes (Nathan Fillion) gives Percy powerful winds in a thermos from a Hercules-themed TV show that he describes as being "[the] best tv show ever (So of course...canceled)." A good number of people may say the same regarding a show that Fillion became well known for. He also tells Percy and Annabeth, "It's cute how you finish each other's sentences."
  • This is not the first time Anthony Head has played the mentor to a chosen one.

tropes.name: Adaptational Attractiveness
tropes.html:
• In the books, Clarisse is described as having the height of a basketball and the "broad, lean, and muscular body of a size XXXL rugby player", also making her the most physically adept female fighter at Camp Half-Blood. She's also said to have large, strong hands and small beady-looking pig eyes. In the film, she's played by Leven Rambin, and clearly is much more traditionally beautiful.
  • Tyson himself isn't too hard on the eyes when shown with two eyes.

tropes.name: Adaptation Explanation Extrication
tropes.html: After the manticore is killed, it crumbles into dust. No explanation is given in the film for this; however, the books make a point that monsters become dust/sand after being killed. Additionally, they aren't truly killed so much as their souls are sent to Tartarus, where they can be reincarnated later on. Also, in the books, Anaklusmos (Percy's sword) is enchanted to always reappear in Percy's pocket, which Luke might not know about. Though frankly, neither would someone watching the film.

tropes.name: Adaptation Personality Change
tropes.html: Clarisse. In the books, she acts all tough-as-nails and bitter to anyone who isn't a child of Ares, and is the stereotypical schoolyard bully of Camp Half-Blood as a result (prior to her Character Development). This is due to the fact that she was under pressure from her father Ares to outshine her brothers and was threatened a beating if she fails. However, she also cares deeply for the Camp and would put her own life at risk for the sake of the Camp's wellbeing. Here, she is both an athletic tomboy and semi-Genki Girl, and has the gift of going on many quests while Percy is the "one-quest wonder", while both any of her care for the Camp's wellbeing and her being pressured by her father are Adapted Out.

tropes.name: Adapted Out
tropes.html:
Oreius and Agrius, Tantalus, Hylla, Reyna, Circe, the Party Ponies, the Laistrygonian Giants (though one does appear on Luke's boat), and Scylla (who was only mentioned offhandedly by Clarisse).
  • On a related note, Annabeth's conflicted feelings for Luke are left out; whereas a major conflict between her and Percy in the books was whether or not Luke had become completely evil, Annabeth in the film is clearly on Percy's side.

tropes.name: Adaptational Backstory Change
tropes.html: In the books, Percy’s sword, Riptide, was said to have been used by Hercules before him; it originated in the form of a hairclip that was owned by Zoë Nightshade, a former Hesperide who aided Hercules in one of his labors. The film changes its backstory to that of a weapon used by Poseidon himself during the Titanomachy.

tropes.name: Adaptational Superpower Change
tropes.html: Regarding Percy's nautical intuition. In the book, it simply manifests through him automatically knowing the answers to things or being able to recount his position instantaneously. In the movie he's able to visualize this information as lines, marks, and numbers on the surface of the water, like one would view latitude and longitude on a map.

tropes.name: Adaptational Villainy
tropes.html: Silena Beauregard is shown to be working with Luke. Which is one hell of a played with trope, considering that in the books she was revealed as the mole in the fifth book, with it being established that she was passing information to him as soon as Sea of Monsters, when Luke had Percy's coordinates right as he left camp.

tropes.name: Adaptational Wimp
tropes.html:
• The Princess Andromeda, Luke's cruise ship from the books, is here portrayed as a yacht. Not quite as impressive, really. The Princess title is even dropped from the name.
  • Kronos's true form in the books is said to be so powerful that its mere presence alone is enough to incinerate cities and non-deity beings, such as half-bloods (even those with the Curse of Achilles). Here, Kronos takes on his true form and none of its detrimental effects occur. He also gets easily killed again by Riptide (which wasn't even the "cursed blade" that's mentioned in the books' version of the Great Prophecy).
  • The Golden Fleece's powers are put into question given the abandoned theme park it is in is completely barren and devoid of life, whereas in the book, the Fleece would instantly bring natural life to wherever it is placed. Not that the film's Fleece wasn't capable of reviving Kronos, Annabeth, and Thalia's tree (and the girl herself). Also, this is how it looks in the film: a thin fabric sheet with gold stitching of an abstract ram. Not as impressive as the hide of a ram in solid gold.

tropes.name: Age Lift
tropes.html: Not to any of the characters (as the first film had already taken care of that), but to the age of the fated hero in the Great Prophecy, which is changed from 16 years of age to 20 years of age.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Ending
tropes.html: Kronos, the Big Bad of the Percy Jackson pentology, is resuscitated by the Golden Fleece, and is then effortlessly defeated by Percy. The Great Prophecy is supposedly fulfilled. You'd think that's the end of the film series, right? Well, okay, it is, but not because the filmmakers wanted it to be. The movie also ends with Chiron implying future events for future films note If his line, "A lot can happen between now and your 20th birthday" is anything to go by, Thalia's resuscitation (courtesy of the Golden Fleece) as per the book, and Percy believing that Thalia is the fated hero in the Great Prophecy.

tropes.name: Amusement Park of Doom
tropes.html: "Circeland," which is built on Polyphemus's island. The Cyclop's lair is in one of the rides.

tropes.name: Arson, Murder, and Jaywalking
tropes.html: To find Kronos's tomb, Luke had to crawl through the depths of Tartarus...and then Cleveland.

tropes.name: Art Shift
tropes.html: When the Oracle tells Percy the story of the Titanomachy, animation that resembles stained-glass windows is used.

tropes.name: Attack of the 50-Foot Whatever
tropes.html: In a huge departure from the books, Luke manages to resurrect Kronos with the Golden Fleece. Kronos then arises from his tomb, as a demonic giant, complete with horns and fiery eyes.

tropes.name: Back from the Dead
tropes.html: Thalia, like in the books. Annabeth and Tyson as well.

tropes.name: Bland-Name Product
tropes.html: "Demigoogle," which appears to be a demigod search engine of sorts. As in, one can track a demigod's location by searching for them on it.

tropes.name: Body Horror
tropes.html: Thalia turning into a tree; the trunk GROWS out of her stomach. In present day, the tree roots still vaguely retain her features.

tropes.name: Canon Foreigner
tropes.html: Ichneutae, the Red Shirt satyr that accompanies Clarisse in her quest for the Golden Fleece.

tropes.name: Chickification
tropes.html: Annabeth goes from a skilled, badass warrior (in the novels, not the first film) to a racist who is little more than dead weight.

tropes.name: Clothing Damage
tropes.html: When Annabeth is stabbed by the Manticore, her jacket, shirt and top are naturally ruined. Later she is seen dressed in bloodied shirt with hole, while her jacket is discarded.

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html: Mr. D takes over Tantalus' role as being the person to assign Clarisse to go after the Fleece since Tantalus is Adapted Out.

tropes.name: Convection, Schmonvection
tropes.html: Kronos had swallowed both Luke and Grover whole yet they came out unscathed after his defeat.

tropes.name: Cool Boat
tropes.html: The Andromeda may be a far cry from the cruise ship she was in the books, but she's a pretty yacht, nonetheless.

tropes.name: Decomposite Character
tropes.html: An example of this and Retcon: Annabeth in the first movie appeared to be a Composite Character of Annabeth (the book version, anyway) and Clarisse, who was nowhere in the film. In Sea of Monsters, Clarisse is shown to be attending Camp Half-Blood.

tropes.name: Depending on the Writer
tropes.html:
• Whether or not Tyson is subject to Adaptational Intelligence, such as when Tyson knows certain things like Polyphemus having the Golden Fleece and Circeland being built on top of Polyphemus's island, but also saying/doing dumb stuff like mistaking the United States Capitol for Olympus and dropping the Thermos of Winds into the ocean.
  • One notable case is how the Mist works in this film. Annabeth applies the Mist (which is depicted as a spray-on bottle that is "crazy hard to come by" needed to be reapplied every once in a while) on Tyson, but later on in the café scene, we see a character named Hekatonkheires, who appears as a normal person in the eyes of café patrons, showing the Mist working as it should in the books.

tropes.name: Disney Death
tropes.html: FIVE of them in The Sea of Monsters. Tyson, as he Sherlock-falls from the cliff and comes back alive; Grover and Luke, who were eaten alive by Kronos and reappeared unharmed after he's defeated; Annabeth near the climax, revived within a minute by the Golden Fleece; and Thalia in the epilogue.

tropes.name: Early-Bird Cameo
tropes.html:
• Ethan Nakamura and Silena Beauregard are on the Princess Andromeda with Luke.
  • Kronos appears in the final battle.
  • Dr. Thorn, a manticore, first appears in the third book. Here, while it's not made clear if it is Dr. Thorn, a manticore appears in this film as a member of Luke's army.

tropes.name: Eldritch Abomination
tropes.html: Kronos: A horned giant whose fragmented body separates and rejoins in pieces as he moves. Also possesses some Volcanic Veins.

tropes.name: Fantastic Racism
tropes.html: Against Tyson, just like in the books, but it's toned down here in comparison.

tropes.name: The Film of the Book
tropes.html: Like the previous movie, it is based on the book of the same name, as mentioned.

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html: So many characters love it. Luke trying to imprison the son of Poseidon on a boat, Luke not searching Percy for his sword disguised as a pen when he ties him up, Percy and his brother hugging instead of stopping the Golden Fleece from resurrecting Kronos, the group crying over Annabeth's body even though they've just gotten the fleece that can heal anyone or anything. Every bad guy saying that Percy can't stop them because he's destined to destroy Mount Olympus even though the prophecy explicitly states he will have the chance to save it. The plot wouldn't move at all if the goddess of wisdom had been a bit more generous with her gift. However, in the books, Anaklusmos is enchanted to always reappear in Percy's pocket, which Luke might not know about. Though frankly, neither would someone watching the film...

tropes.name: In the Back
tropes.html: After Percy defeats Kronos, Annabeth is mortally stabbed in the back by the Manticore’s stinger. She fortunately does get revived with the Golden Fleece, however.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo Cut
tropes.html:
Mr. D shoots down Annabeth's and Grover's plan, but says he has said idea one cut later.
Mr. D: [regarding the idea on getting the Golden Fleece] It's a terrible idea.
(Cut to him speaking to the campers)
Mr. D: I've had a grand idea!

tropes.name: Jesus Was Way Cool
tropes.html: Mr. D thinks so, at least; he's apparently a fan of the wine miracle from the wedding. Especially since we just saw Zeus transform Mr. D's wine into water. Interesting, when you consider how the two are usually compared to each other in Real Life. It's also about the most insulting thing he can say to Zeus, who is obviously listening to him at all times.

tropes.name: Lamprey Mouth
tropes.html: Charybdis has a truly gigantic one.

tropes.name: The Load
tropes.html:
• Tyson. The guy is so annoyingly clumsy and incompetent it's a miracle he hasn't killed himself yet. At least Book!Tyson has shown some competence here and there.
  • To a minor extent, Annabeth, thanks to some chickification and her thunder now taken over by Clarisse.

tropes.name: Mythology Gag
tropes.html: Some of the quests Percy mentions Clarisse completing — fighting a bronze dragon, recovering Ares' stolen chariot, etc. — were taken from some of the short stories in the original series. Ironically, whereas Percy played a pretty big role in those stories, the film states that Clarisse was the one to complete those, with Percy being mostly ineffectual.

tropes.name: Our Minotaurs Are Different
tropes.html: The mechanical, fire-breathing Colchis Bull tears up a lot of Camp Half-Blood.

tropes.name: Our Zombies Are Different
tropes.html: They prefer the term "Undead Confederate Soldiers whose lives have been given in tribute to Ares." But "zombie" works just as fine, but judging by one group that stopped what they were doing at that name, it's subjective.

tropes.name: Pragmatic Adaptation
tropes.html: Due to the Age Lift the characters got since the first film, the Great Prophecy sets the age of the prophesied demigod from sixteen to twenty.

tropes.name: Rage Helm
tropes.html: Kronos' face appears to have been designed with this in mind.

tropes.name: Remember the New Guy?
tropes.html: After Clarisse was Adapted Out of the first film, and Mr. D was reduced to a cameo in the Hall of the Gods in the first film, they suddenly appear in the sequel, with everyone acting like they were always there.

tropes.name: Sadly Mythtaken
tropes.html:
The film took both a chainsaw and Gorilla Glue to the original story of how Kronos was first defeated and rebuilt it into something different:
  • The reason why Kronos ate his children to begin with was omitted: Kronos was foretold a prophecy where his children will become the new monarchs of the Earth. Out of paranoia, he ate his children the very moment they were born to prevent this from happening.
  • Only Zeus was able to evade being swallowed, courtesy of his mother, Rhea. Poseidon and Hades were among the swallowed and thus could not have escaped as well. Later, Zeus tricks Kronos into vomiting up Zeus's other siblings by giving him an emetic made of mustard and wine.
  • Zeus, Hades, and Poseidon were not the only ones who fought against Kronos; the other siblings included Hera, Demeter, and Hestia (all of whom were also freed from Kronos). The Hekatonkheires and the Cyclopes were also the Olympians' allies after Zeus freed them. They all teamed up and waged war on the Titans, inciting the Titanomachy which eventually ended in the Olympians' favor and the deposition and eternal imprisonment of Kronos, and Zeus becoming the new king of the gods.
  • Poseidon and Hades did not use swords to defeat Kronos, the Cyclopes gave them their respective iconic items: For Zeus, his thunder and lightning, for Poseidon, his trident, and for Hades, his Helm of Darkness.

tropes.name: Say My Name
tropes.html: Grover yells Annabeth’s name after the Manticore mortally stabs her.

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html: Luke survives (but is at the moment captured by Polyphemus), and Thalia is alive once more. Percy Jackson then hypothesizes that she is the foretold half-blood that the Oracle spoke of.

tropes.name: Shark Fin of Doom
tropes.html: Charybdis' teeth are mistaken for this at first.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: Tyson's get-up (both in shades and under Mist's effects) is close to resembling Encino Man.

tropes.name: Snake Talk
tropes.html: Averted. Hermes' staff includes two snakes adorned on it that can talk, but they speak normally, without the typical hissing. Hermes actually admonishes them for this, saying that they should speak Snake Talk just to please any guests he brings around.

tropes.name: Taken for Granite
tropes.html: After the manticore stabs Annabeth with its stinger, Clarisse retaliates by cutting it off while Grover helps fight it, which results in the manticore to be petrified into stone while having an emaciated form before crumbling into dust.

tropes.name: This Explains So Much
tropes.html:
Polyphemus concludes with this when Grover rips off his Cyclops maiden disguise.
Polyphemus: Wait, you're a dude? Well, that explains a lot.

tropes.name: Titanomachy, Round Two
tropes.html: The film follow loosely the plot of the first two books, with numerous departures. One of them being an early confrontation with Kronos, who appears in this adaptation as a large monstrous being made from fire and lava (and revived earlier than in the books).

tropes.name: Title Drop
tropes.html: Count the number of times they say some variation of "Sea of Monsters" in this movie.

tropes.name: Truer to the Text
tropes.html: The sequel is more faithful to the books, returning Annabeth's hair color back to blonde, introducing Dionysus as the dispassionate camp leader, Camp Half-Blood's backstory of being protected by Thalia Grace, the Oracle of Delphi being a mummified corpse in an attic, and finally bringing in the book's Myth Arc about the prophecy of a child of the Big Three and Kronos's return. Though, things end up muddled due to the deviating nature of the first film, as well as the major story condensation.

tropes.name: Uncertain Doom
tropes.html: Nothing is made known of Luke after being spotted by Polyphemus. Adding to this ambiguity is the fact that the end of the film sets up another sequel, which would never be made.

tropes.name: Ungrateful Bastard
tropes.html: How does Kronos thank Luke for resurrecting him? By swallowing Luke whole.

tropes.name: Womb Level
tropes.html: Non-video game example. Inside Charybdis.

title: Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle
original_title: Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle

tropes.name: Actually Pretty Funny
tropes.html: Sister Barnes notes that she thought some of the songs in that musical from the South Park guys were pretty funny, whereas Sister Paxton was less fond of it.

tropes.name: Ambiguous Situation
tropes.html:
• How many of Mr. Reed's mistaken facts and erroneous statements are due to him just being wrong and not as smart as he thinks he is and how many are deliberate misstatements used to prop up spurious arguments or to try to play mind games with Sister Paxton and Sister Barnes? He doesn't seem to take it well when the sisters contradict him, though he does seem to intentionally mispronounce "Moroni" just to give the girls a chance to correct him.
  • The ending: Did Sister Barnes come back from the dead to kill Reed, or was she merely misidentified as dead earlier? For that matter, did Paxton manage to escape the house, or was she merely imagining it as she died? Was the butterfly she saw landing on her hand that seemed to vanish a miracle, a message from Sister Barnes, or a hallucination?

tropes.name: Artistic License – Chemistry
tropes.html:
• Saftey matches are "safe" due to the lack of red phosphorus on their heads, making it very hard to strike them without the phosphorous strip on the box. As opposed to "strike anywhere matches", you would need a coarse but relatively flat surface in order to generate enough heat from friction to light a safety match that way. Using a rough, soaking wet rock would not work in reality.
  • Scented candles actually smell very noticeably different than the original scents they are designed to mimic. Paxton and Barnes would have been able to detect immediately that no blueberry pie was being baked.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Religion
tropes.html:
• While laying out his thesis on religion to the protagonists Mr. Reed makes a series of claims to back up his argument that have very little basis on real world facts, such as: the small shrine devoted to pre-Christian deities that he claims have their birthdays on December 25 as proof that the story of Jesus is wrong, despite many of the deities he lists having their birthdays in dispute, assuming they born at all (Mithras sprang from a rock); citing Horus as having twelve disciples, which has no basis in actual mythology but is popular pop mythology; and perpetuating the common saying that Judaism is the oldest monotheistic faith during his monopoly analogy, ignoring Zoroastrianism outright. Considering Sister Barnes points out that he's focusing on trivial surface aspects and ignoring differences ("One of them has a frickin' bird head!"), this may be deliberate.
  • Despite being experienced Mormon missionaries, Sisters Barnes and Paxton approach their conversation with Mr. Reed much like a casual conversation. They let moments of awkward silence stretch out and react with stunned shock when Mr. Reed raises the issue of polygamy. In real life, Mormon missionaries train extensively to make these conversations productive and have practiced answers for questions about polygamy and other controversial aspects of the church. As Mr. Reed himself points out in the film, they're effectively salesmen. This can be partly explained by both Sisters being new to it and Reed not exactly being a typical interview subject.

tropes.name: Bathos
tropes.html: Reed's argument about religion is done using an extensive Monopoly analogy, something that manages to be both outlandishly funny and terrifying.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html: When Mr. Reed during one of his earlier theology debates uses Sister Barnes father's tragic death from Lou Gehrig's disease as his argument, she can't even hide her rage at him for bringing that up.

tropes.name: Bigger on the Inside
tropes.html: Mr. Reed's house appears to be fairly normal and modest. Once inside, it almost becomes a mundane case of Alien Geometries - Reed tells the missionaries that they saw the back of the house and they know it's a clear walk, but underground it's huge with multiple staircases and an entire secret wing of the house for Reed's prophets/wives.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: Sister Barnes is able to kill Mr. Reed before dying herself and Sister Paxton escapes.

tropes.name: Butterfly of Death and Rebirth
tropes.html: While discussing what happens after death, Paxton says she wants to be reincarnated as a butterfly and land on the fingers of her loved ones to let them know her soul continued on. In the film’s final moments, a butterfly lands on her own fingers, only to disappear, leaving it ambiguous whether it was a hallucination or a sign from Barnes.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html: After sneaking a knife down into the basement, Barnes gives it to Paxton and says she'll distract Reed to give her an opening to stab him, at the signal of "magic underwear". Before they can enact this plan, Reed slits Barnes' throat. Later on, Reed monologues that Mormonism, and by extension religion, controls everything Paxton can do, from who she speaks to right down to making her wear magic underwear. Paxton immediately stabs Reed in the throat.

tropes.name: Celebrity Paradox
tropes.html: Paxton references Spider-Man early on in the film. Topher Grace, who plays Elder Kennedy, was in Spider-Man 3.

tropes.name: Cell Phones Are Useless
tropes.html: One of the first signs that something is direly wrong in Mr. Reed's house is when he reveals casually to Barnes and Paxton that there is steel in the walls, preventing phone signal. He saw through Paxton's Phoney Call immediately.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• When the girls enter Reed's house, he asks them if they're okay with the metal in the walls. It's a line that's not given much attention until he brings it up again: the metal interferes with phone signals and he could tell that Paxton wasn't actually making a call to their ward.
  • The knife that Sister Barnes steals from Mr. Reed's living room. She gives it to Sister Paxton with instructions to stab him, but Sister Paxton doesn't manage to attack him before Mr. Reed kills her. However, it then finally comes back when Sister Paxton uses it to stab Mr. Reed.
  • When they try to escape in the basement, Sister Paxton and Sister Barnes break off a wooden board with nails attached to it and the camera even lingers on it in the background. This is ultimately used by Sister Barnes in the climax to kill Reed.

tropes.name: Clean-Cut Naïve Mormon
tropes.html: The two protagonists are this. Sister Paxton is a sweet, blonde, and timid young woman, serving as a Mormon missionary. She is the the light feminine to her companion Sister Barnes' dark and is contrasted by lacking what Barnes has, which is her dark hair, sharper wit, and her bleaker life experience (her father died of a slow-moving degenerative disease). They both discuss having sex with boys while in private though, and Sister Barnes turns out to have a secret contraceptive implant later, going against the church's rules. Paxton appears to merely talk about these things, but both are less naive than they first might appear.

tropes.name: Control Freak
tropes.html: Reed, definitely. It turns out that he believes control is the "one true religion" and that there's little difference between him keeping women in cages and brainwashing them into compliance with his mind games and any of the prophets of the established religions.

tropes.name: Creepy Dollhouse
tropes.html: Mr. Reed has a big dollhouse version of his own house. He's shown whittling wooden doll miniature versions of Barnes and Paxton as they're imprisoned in his basement.

tropes.name: Crucial Cross
tropes.html: The wooden board Sister Barnes and Sister Paxton find has three nails. Like the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.

tropes.name: Deconstruction
tropes.html: Of religion and the idea of control.

tropes.name: Dead Hat Shot
tropes.html: After Reed is killed, the camera lingers on his eyeglasses for a few seconds.

tropes.name: Decoy Protagonist
tropes.html: While Sisters Barnes and Paxton work together throughout, Barnes is initially given slightly more focus. She is played by the better-known actress, has a more detailed backstory, is more proactive, and her worldliness and doubts about religion make her better at intellectually opposing Reed. However, Barnes is killed in the second act, and Paxton becomes the sole protagonist for the rest of the film.

tropes.name: Defiant to the End
tropes.html: Bleeding and with no reasonable expectation of survival Paxton responds to Reed's suggestion that she pray with an explanation of an experiment that seemingly proved that prayer makes no difference, before declaring that nonetheless it's nice to pray for others even if it doesn't produce results, and starting to pray.

tropes.name: Didn't Think This Through
tropes.html:
Part of Reed's manipulations is to induce this in his victims. There are two particularly plot-relevant ones:
  • Barnes becomes so focused on repudiating Reed's attack on her faith and Paxton is so focused on simply getting out that they walk into the obviously sinister basement on the off-chance that the obviously threatening man is telling the truth about it leading out, rather than insisting on going back into the front room to wait for the elder who they fully expect will come looking for them when they don't report back on time. Reed may well have had a contingency plan for using coercion if manipulation failed, but the fact that it doesn't occur to either of them shows how effective his manipulations are.
  • They are so rattled that they don't take an obvious chance to simply physically attack him together when he comes down into the basement. Despite earlier planning to do exactly that once they know they're trapped, when the opportunity actually presents itself they're too shaken to realise that their attempt to start a fire wouldn't help them at this point even if they were successful, and it's so hard for them to work themselves up to use violence that Reed is able to strike first.

tropes.name: Enter Stage Window
tropes.html: Barnes proposes an inversion twice, attempting to exit through a window: In the first instance, Paxton notes that the window is too small to fit through, while in the second, she points out that the window is covered by a cage.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html: The opening scene features Sisters Barnes and Paxton chatting about penises and pornography. They are careful with their language, and clearly slightly nervous about the topic, but they are not prudish or judgmental in a fire-and-brimstone way, showing that despite the reputation Mormons have they are just ordinary, cheerful and thoughtful young women. Their manners of speaking, with Paxton's chipper chattering contrasted with Barnes' terseness, also establish each one's place in the Red Oni, Blue Oni dichotomy.

tropes.name: Evil Brit
tropes.html: It's never pointed out but Hugh Grant plays Mr. Reed with his natural English accent meaning he is a British expat living in America who kidnaps women, cages them and starves them.

tropes.name: Extremely Short Time Span
tropes.html: At most, the movie covers from the afternoon of one day to the afternoon of another, but it may be as little as one evening to the following morning.

tropes.name: Failed a Spot Check
tropes.html: As convincing as his theory on religion might seem, Barnes points out that there's several glaring holes in Reed's argument: for example, he mentions that Judaism is only practiced by a very small fraction of the world population despite being the original Abrahamic religion since they don't seek to convert anyone, which fails to account for the Holocaust and the religious persecution that Jews have faced throughout history.

tropes.name: Faux Affably Evil
tropes.html: Reed spends much of the film seeming to be truly Affably Evil and Ambiguously Evil, but in the end, he reveals that everything he's done throughout the film has been to manipulate Sister Paxton into doing exactly what he wants her to do because of his belief that the one true god is "control".

tropes.name: Final Girl
tropes.html: Barnes and Reed both die, leaving Paxton as the only survivor.

tropes.name: Fingore
tropes.html: Reed chops off one of his caged prophets' finger with pruning shears while clipping her fingernails, just to prove his point about control to Paxton.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
A number of examples:
  • Reed, fitting with his delight in showing his intellectual superiority, deliberately sprinkles these through the initial conversation, or draws their attention to things they could have noticed earlier (him greeting them with a watering can in hand despite it pouring with rain and him not having any obvious indoor plants, his mentioning that there's metal in the walls shortly after they come inside, quickly revealing that he's highly knowledgeable about Mormonism, the scented candle, that they could see that his house is small so they could easily leave through the back, but is also on a hill so it follows that they would need to go down before going out).
  • In the opening scene, Paxton establishes herself as the missionary with no doubts about her Mormon faith. However, inside Reed's house, she wistfully states that she hopes to reincarnate as a butterfly even though animal reincarnation is obviously nowhere in Mormon theology, establishing that there is more to her than blind faith.
  • Some things Reed claims earlier appear to be either lies or manipulative Exact Words, for example his wife baking a blueberry pie appears to be a lie but turns out to be partially true, and that the front door can't be opened because its deadbolts are on a timer (without mentioning that he can reset it at will) leading the audience to suspect that he might be manipulatively honest rather than a liar. Him directly telling Elder Kennedy that he is the first person to come to his door today is categorically untrue, thus hinting that everything he says may be lies.
  • Reed falsely attributing, “With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility,” as coming from Voltaire is the first sign that he's not as smart or intellectual as he thinks. Assuming it’s not part of the manipulation of course…
  • Reed notices Sister Barnes scratching her elbow, and the camera zooms in to follow his gaze to the inside of her bicep. Later, he cuts into this part of her arm with a box cutter after she (seemingly) dies, and extracts a metal device. He tries to insist it is a microchip, but Sister Paxton correctly identifies it as a contraceptive implant.

tropes.name: Genre Shift
tropes.html: The film appears to be, and is presented by the trailers as, a theological discussion-heavy variant of the standard "young women get trapped in a house with a game-playing psychopath" story. By the end of the film it's still exactly that, despite it being teased that either the resurrection miracle is real and there is true supernatural power at work, or that it might be about to be revealed that simulation hypothesis is actually true.

tropes.name: A God Am I
tropes.html: Implicit. Reed says that, with control being the one true religion, all of the women in his basement are there by choice. With him as the authority figure, that would make him their god. He certainly takes great pleasure in the power he holds over them.

tropes.name: Hair-Contrast Duo
tropes.html: Barnes is an experienced and talented missionary with a sad backstory and dark hair. Paxton is a youthful Motor Mouth with lighter hair.

tropes.name: Hidden Depths
tropes.html: Paxton is chipper, outgoing, and somewhat naive, especially compared to the more experienced and worldly Barnes. While she admits she isn't as smart as Barnes is, she's still able to figure out that Reed orchestrated the Prophet's resurrection and realizes the point he wants to make based on nothing but simple intuition.

tropes.name: Holier than Thou
tropes.html: Played straight with Mr. Reed, who believes he's morally and intellectually superior to the two missionaries and that he's found the one true religion. Subverted with Sister Barnes and Sister Paxton, who, despite being pious missionaries looking to convert others to Mormonism, are shown to be a lot more open-minded and nuanced with their faith.

tropes.name: Hollywood Atheist
tropes.html: Memorably Zig-Zagged by Mr. Reed. He's a smug egomaniac who doesn't believe in any real faith, but he makes cogent arguments and does believe in "the one true religion". It's eventually revealed to be control, as he feels the only purpose of religion is to dominate people. He's also portrayed as a self-righteous, hectoring fundamentalist intolerant of other beliefs, as opposed to the main characters, who are Mormon missionaries but respectful and open-minded. It's even implied that Paxton doesn't completely believe in God by the end, and is certainly at minimum agnostic, but still prays and spreads it out of a desire to be kind to others anyway, while the coarser, bolder Barnes is clearly more resolute in her beliefs being true.

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html: A tragic case, Paxton and Barnes should have insisted on seeing Reeds “Wife” instead of taking Reeds word for it before ever stepping foot in his house. Had they done this, he would never have been able to produce his non-existent wife and that would have been enough evidence to tell them that he was not safe. It’s always better to "Be weird. Be rude. Stay alive." as Crime Junkie puts it than to ignore warning signs and put yourself in danger.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html:
• During the climax, Mr. Reed gloats that he knew everything Sister Paxton was going to do that night... seconds before she stabs him with his own knife.
  • Mr. Reed orchestrates a resurrection trick in one of his mind games. He meets his end at the hands of the resurrected Barnes.

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: The girls that Sister Barnes and Paxton encounter early in the movie, they hold up a car by filming themselves dancing in the middle of the road and immediately afterwards approuch the pair asking for a photo with them, only to pull Paxton’s skirt down to publicly humiliate her.

tropes.name: Know-Nothing Know-It-All
tropes.html: Downplayed with Mr. Reed, who’s clearly far more knowledgeable than the average person, but is demonstrated several times to be not as smart as he thinks. Mr. Reed prides himself on having researched all religions and toying with his victims by poking holes in their beliefs. However, he falsely attributes, “With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility,” to Voltaire, and, as Barnes notes, his argument that there are more Christians than Jews because of better marketing relies on ignoring complicating factors like The Holocaust or the various other periods of persecution and slaughter that reduce Jewish numbers.

tropes.name: Light Feminine and Dark Feminine
tropes.html: Barnes has dark hair, dark eyes, wears dark clothing and has an unusually deep voice. Paxton has light-brown hair with light eyes, wears pink and has a far more traditionally feminine voice.

tropes.name: Literal Metaphor
tropes.html: The Sisters don't talk about Taco Bell, instead calling it "Taco Hell". It has nothing to do with how bad the food is. Barnes got food poisoning there and was clinically dead as doctors operated on her kidneys. In essence, it does involve actual hell.

tropes.name: Made of Iron
tropes.html:
All three main characters to a certain extent.
  • A sliced throat, bleeding out for 20 minutes, and a mutilated arm doesn't stop Sister Barnes killing Mr. Reed.
  • Mr. Reed is able to climb a long ladder, and stab Sister Paxton, with a letter opener going completely through his throat.
  • Sister Paxton, after being stabbed in the abdomen, is able to drag herself up a long staircase, and then physically climb up and crawl through an air duct, and stumble out into dawn snow.

tropes.name: Maybe Magic, Maybe Mundane
tropes.html:
• Reed might have discovered the "one true religion", and what reality and the afterlife really is. He could also be an ordinary serial killer playing mind games with his victims for fun, with the latter looking much more likely.
  • From the climax of the film Sister Barnes' coming back from death/near-death just long enough to kill Reed and save Paxton could be a miracle or just remarkable resilience. The last shot of Paxton seeing a butterfly on her hand, then the camera revealing there isn't one could either mean that Barnes has come back to say goodbye in the form that Paxton spoke about earlier, or could just be an ordinary hallucination brought about by shock and blood loss.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: 'Mr. Reed' sounds an awful lot like 'mystery'. There's also the fact that (as Paxton notes in a pun) "Reed" sounds like "read", which he clearly does a lot of.

tropes.name: Minimalist Cast
tropes.html: Barnes, Paxton, and Reed are largely the only three characters onscreen, with Elder Kennedy and the Prophet having minor roles. Everyone else is relegated to extremely brief bit parts.

tropes.name: The Missionary
tropes.html: The two girls identify themselves as members of the Church of Jesus Christ when they approach the home of Mr. Reed, looking to convert him.

tropes.name: Monster Misogyny
tropes.html: A dramatic undercurrent rather than an exploitative or flippant one. All of Reed's victims are women, who he tortures, keeps in cages, treats like servants, and he seems on some level to be trying to "convert" Paxton, while killing the bolder Barnes. He interacts amicably with the only other male character seen in the film, though obviously pushing him away, and there's clearly a gendered aspect to his philosophy of control as the most truest religion in the world.

tropes.name: Mundane Solution
tropes.html: The Reveal about whether or not "the prophet" came Back from the Dead. She didn't. Mr. Reed killed the first prophet, then switched her dead body out with another prophet, who looked very similar to her in order to fool Barnes and Paxton.

tropes.name: Nice Girl
tropes.html: Sister Paxton is sweet, bubbly and very kind-hearted. Actually becomes a Defiant to the End moment when she thinks she's about to die, but decides to pray for both herself and Reed because it's "nice" to pray for others, even for him, even though she just quoted the study that indicated prayer didn't actually accomplish anything.

tropes.name: No Full Name Given
tropes.html: For any of the named characters, all of whom are on a Last-Name Basis. There's Sisters Paxton and Barnes, Elder Kennedy, and Mr. Reed.

tropes.name: No Name Given
tropes.html: The "prophets" imprisoned in Mr. Reed's basement don't seem to have names anymore.

tropes.name: Not the First Victim
tropes.html: Either played with or subverted. Mr. Reed locks Sisters Barnes and Paxton in his basement after terrorizing them, ultimately killing Sister Barnes. When they discover the "prophet" also imprisoned in the basement, they naturally assume Reed has done this before. However, when Reed finds them, he reveals that not only does he have multiple women locked in an attic annex to his house, but they're also there willingly. This is ambiguous because he owns up to starving them "to sharpen their psychic senses" and none of them look mentally or physically well despite his reassurances, suggesting that some or all of them may have been imprisoned there.

tropes.name: Nothing Is Scarier
tropes.html: A surprising amount of this movie is just Hugh Grant debating theology with two young Mormon women. And it's terrifying.

tropes.name: Not Too Dead to Save the Day
tropes.html: Either this or Not Quite Dead, but Sister Barnes manages to come back from looking very dead via a Slashed Throat to miraculously save Sister Paxton's life.

tropes.name: Offscreen Villain Dark Matter
tropes.html: As the movie progresses it becomes apparent that Mr. Reed must have access to some substantial source of funds, as it is never explained how he is able to finance the construction and maintenance of such a massive and labyrinthine house, filled with artwork.

tropes.name: Pants-Pulling Prank
tropes.html: A group of teenagers, pretending to want a photo with Sister Barnes and Sister Paxton, asks the missionaries if they really wear "magic underwear". They pull down Sister Paxton's skirt, exposing her temple garments and humiliating her. This pays off later when Sister Barnes chooses "magic underwear" as a secret code phrase to cue Sister Paxton to stab Mr. Reed.

tropes.name: Perfect Poison
tropes.html: The "prophet" eats a literal handful of blueberry pie and drops dead less than five minutes later. Mr. Reed claims the pie contained a mixture of wolfsbane and belladonna.

tropes.name: Pop-Cultural Osmosis
tropes.html: Paxton recognizes "with great power comes great responsibility" as coming from Spider-Man, though Reed corrects her (wrongly) by attributing it to Voltaire. It's a seemingly throwaway line that sets up his later thesis: every single world religion is an iteration of each other, diluted into different forms throughout human history, and thus there is no true religion.

tropes.name: Pop-Cultural Osmosis Failure
tropes.html: Mr. Reed is frustrated that the missionaries don't get any of his references to 1990s pop culture, including Radiohead's "Creep" and Jar-Jar Binks of The Phantom Menace.

tropes.name: Red Herring
tropes.html: A number (the film runs on mind games) but the most relevant one is when Reed appears to express a belief in the simulation hypothesis after murdering Barnes, seemingly leading up to a reveal that he honestly thinks he has just killed an NPC rather than murdered a real person due to the way flames behaved around them (or possibly even the film revealing that he's right in a shocking Genre Shift). Nothing comes of it, and it's almost certainly just another mind game. Sister Paxton guesses that he pivoted to extorting theory after the "prophet" went off script and ended her scripted description of the afterlife with "this isn't real", and Reed is improvising this explanation on the spot to cover this.

tropes.name: Red Oni, Blue Oni
tropes.html: Though it becomes a small Hourglass Plot throughout the story, Sister Paxton starts off as the "red oni" (chipper, chatty, and optimistic) to Sister Barnes's withdrawn, quieter blue oni. Barnes transforms more into the red oni as she becomes more challenging of Reed and makes a plan to kill him, while it takes Sister Paxton a much longer time to get there as she becomes sadder and more withdrawn through captivity.

tropes.name: Repurposed Pop Song
tropes.html: The trailer includes the song “The Air That I Breathe” by the Hollies. It's plot-relevant in the film proper, with Mr. Reed using the lawsuit against Radiohead for "Creep" being plagiarized from it as part of his metaphor about religious iteration.

tropes.name: Riddle for the Ages
tropes.html: By the end of the film, we still know virtually nothing about the various captive "prophets"/wives are; who they are (or used to be), how he captured them, how long they've been there, how he's evaded detection etc.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
• Befitting the premise, The Book of Mormon is referenced as "that South Park musical." Paxton doesn't like that it makes fun of them, while Barnes has listened to some of the songs and thinks they're funny.
  • Reed uses various editions of Monopoly as a metaphor to demonstrate his theory about iterations in religion (with the Bob Ross edition of the game used to describe Mormonism), and later references The Phantom Menace when speaking about how nearly all religions have similar stories passed down to them. While both of the girls know what Monopoly is, Reed is rather dismayed to learn that neither of them understand his Jar Jar Binks impression.
  • Paxton (correctly) attributes "With great power comes great responsibility" to Spider-Man (while Reed incorrectly attributes it to Voltaire) and she later comments "The only way out is through", attributing it to Swamp Thing while Reed attributes the line to Robert Frost ("A Servant To Servants"). Both are correct, but neither is the original.

tropes.name: Shown Their Work
tropes.html: The "Taco Hell" incident, a mass food poisoning from contaminated onions, is based on a real incident on the east coast from 2006, and as Barnes is originally from Philadelphia, they may be one and the same.

tropes.name: Slashed Throat
tropes.html: Reed kills Sister Barnes this way, claiming she will come back to life. She doesn’t… maybe.

tropes.name: Smarter Than You Look
tropes.html: While the more naïve, sheltered, and scared Paxton spends most of the film just following Barnes along in attempting to outwit Reed, she proves to be more observant and clever than she initially seems. She picked up on enough things to figure out how Reed’s tricks operate and deduces his motivations. Even her views on faith are more complex than Reed assumed: She reveals she read a study that proves praying doesn’t actually save lives, but she does so anyway because she sees value in expressing care for other people.

tropes.name: Smug Snake
tropes.html: Reed is erudite, intelligent and educated but he's nowhere as smart or as well-educated as he thinks he is, making careless errors with quotes and even bungling basic historical facts. Once someone knows about the subjects he discusses, they're quick to poke holes in his logic and he grows increasingly frustrated as his gaslighting techniques fail. Ultimately, he's little better than a petty sadist with a surface level knowledge but little else.

tropes.name: Snow Means Death
tropes.html: It's bright and sunny outside as the Sisters approach Mr. Reed's house. However, once they start talking with him, it begins snowing heavily, with regular scenes showing the storm while they're are imprisoned inside, especially when someone else is approaching the house.

tropes.name: Suspiciously Similar Song
tropes.html: Discussed In-Universe by Mr. Reed where he said that "Creep" by Radiohead was proven in court to be a rip-off of "The Air that I Breathe" by The Hollies.

tropes.name: Taking You with Me
tropes.html: Subverted and played straight. Mr. Reed who is already mortally wounded, attempts to pull this on Sister Paxton who is wounded herself from him. However Sister Barnes manages to save Paxton by killing Reed by whacking him in the face with the plank board covered in nails. Barnes herself then immediately succumbs to her own wounds Reed inflicted on her earlier.

tropes.name: Villain Ball
tropes.html: If Reed had simply wanted to invite the girls in to make them listen to his speech and theory about religion to try to shake the girls faith before unlocking the front door and letting them go, that's one thing even it would still be wrong because he made them feel unsafe, violated their autonomy and used the situation to push his views onto them, but it’s clear by the end that regardless of his theological arguments, ultimately he simply wanted to hold power over others and get to kill, torture and hold people captive for his own depraved amusement.

tropes.name: Villain Has a Point
tropes.html: Zig-zagged in regards to Reed about religion. While he's not wrong about various religions being adapted from one another, or religion's role in various atrocities across history, he's also nowhere near as well-read and knowledgeable as he thinks he is, generalising and misattributing various facts.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html: Sister Barnes announces that she knows how Mr. Reed performed his supposed "miracle."

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html: Though it's revealed on the poster and in the trailer. Sister Barnes turns the candle around and reveals it's "blueberry pie" scented, thus revealing that Mr. Reed was lying at a minimum about his wife baking it. It turns out he's lying about his wife, period.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: The film spends a significant amount of time cutting to Elder Kennedy's search for the missing girls only to drop him after he gets fooled by Reed. While one could argue that his role in the story is effectively over at that point, we never find out what becomes of him - especially notable as he's played by such a recognisable actor.

tropes.name: Wicked Pretentious
tropes.html: Mr. Reed presents himself as being very sophisticated and well-read, and to his credit he does clearly read a great deal, but over time it becomes obvious that not only does his understanding of classical and religious works have a surface-level understanding at best, but his personal tastes seem to skew towards more conventionally popular stories from the 20th century. And that's not even getting into the fact that he's a serial kidnapper.

tropes.name: A Boy and His X
tropes.html: In this case, a man and his giant albino gorilla. The emotional core of the movie is the strong friendship between Davis and George.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html: Possibly in the case of Agent Russel, played by Jeffrey Dean Morgan. When he enters the scene, he is whistling, much he does as Negan in The Walking Dead. Near the end of the scene, he also says "he is deeply sorry", which he also said during his first appearance in the same show. He also swears frequently, something Negan is well known for doing.

tropes.name: Adaptational Badass
tropes.html:
• In the original game, the military could defeat the monsters, albeit with a lot of shots usually from jets and giant robots, with the infantry and lighter vehicles being little more than an extra thing to smash. In this movie, nothing the military does can do the monsters lasting damage thanks to their durability combined with regeneration.
  • Lizzie is the most dangerous and biggest of the three monsters while they were all roughly equal in strength in the games. In addition, Lizzie's health could be damaged by bombs in the games, as in the movie nothing Davis throws at Lizzie works to take her down.

tropes.name: Adaptational Heroism
tropes.html: George. In the games he was perfectly willing to destroy cities and eat civilians just for fun, here, however, his aggression and destructive nature is simply a result of his mutation that he can’t control, and when he returns to normal he fights against the other monsters to save the city.

tropes.name: Adaptational Nonsapience
tropes.html:
Besides being changed to standard mutated animals, the monsters have been changed to look less anthropomorphic:
  • George is fully bipedal in the games, but here he knuckle-walks like a regular gorilla.
  • Ralph is a giant werewolf in the games, so naturally he stomps around on his hind legs like a human. Since he's a mutated wolf in this film, he's on all fours.
  • Lizzie is quadrupedal as a regular crocodile, while in the games, she walked on hind legs. This change might have been made to ensure Lizzie doesn't parody Godzilla as much as the games did.

tropes.name: Adaptational Superpower Change
tropes.html: Ralph in this film has patagium that helps him glide like a flying squirrel and grow launchable quills, which he couldn't do in the games.

tropes.name: Adaptational Villainy
tropes.html: The woman in the red dress in the game is just a helpless victim. Claire Wyden, her counterpart in the film is the Big Bad.

tropes.name: Adaptation Dye-Job
tropes.html: George has gone from being a brown gorilla to an albino one, partly to differentiate him from King Kong (who just had his own film come out the year before) and partly so that any wounds he receives will be more visible, emphasizing his relative vulnerability and making us worry that he might not survive the movie. Curiously enough, while he has a more exotic color, the other monsters are given more realistic colors with Ralph going from blue to brown and Lizzie going from vibrant green to a duller shade of green; wounds they receive are less noticeable, therefore, making the more villainous monsters seem invulnerable.

tropes.name: Adaptation Name Change
tropes.html: The evil MegaCorp behind the three monsters is named ScumLabs in the games. Here, it’s called Energyne for obvious reasons.

tropes.name: Adaptation Species Change
tropes.html:
• Rather than being humans mutated by random mutagenic materials or by Scumlabs, George, Ralph, and Lizzie are a gorilla, wolf, and crocodile mutated by a rogue genetic experiment.
  • The film changes Lizzie from a Not Zilla to a giant crocodile.

tropes.name: Affectionate Nickname
tropes.html: How Ralph got his name: footage of him went viral and the internet promptly named him.

tropes.name: Africa Is a Country
tropes.html: Invoked by Connor, an idiot, when he wonders aloud whether Blood Diamond is set in the same region of Africa as Uganda (it isn't; Blood Diamond is set in Sierra Leone, which is practically on the other side of the continent from Uganda) but insists that it's all "Mother Africa".

tropes.name: A Lizard Named "Liz"
tropes.html: The reptilian mutant is named "Lizzie", although this is never stated onscreen. Also, it becomes rather unfitting as she isn't exactly a lizard in this version. Then again, by the end of it she isn't exactly a crocodile either...

tropes.name: Albinos Are Freaks
tropes.html: It's stressed that albino gorillas like George are extremely rare. George is also portrayed as an unusually smart and large gorilla even before he mutated.

tropes.name: Always a Bigger Fish
tropes.html: At first, everyone thought George and Ralph were bad news. Then Lizzie shows up.

tropes.name: Amplified Animal Aptitude
tropes.html: Played with. There's some discussion about how George and Ralph are overriding their instincts to work together while the pair are on their way to Chicago. George, even before the pathogen, seemed to be the most intelligent of the San Diego gorillas.

tropes.name: Animal Nemesis
tropes.html: Though it should be noted that Okoye likes animals and is trying to save at least George from the military.

tropes.name: Ape Sign Language
tropes.html: George is an albino Gentle Gorilla who communicates with his handler Davis Okoye using ASL. When George is affected by a drug that turns him into a gigantic rampaging Killer Gorilla, he stops signing as a sign of him becoming a mindless brute; after receiving a cure, his intelligence returns and he starts signing again.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Animal Care
tropes.html:
• Claire keeping a lone pet rat is either this or Bad People Abuse Animals, as rats are hypersocial and need companions of their own kind.
  • Looking a gorilla in the eye is actually a really bad idea. Even if they know you, they see that as a challenge. Likewise, they don't smile, so much as they show teeth. Obviously that happens here because of the Serkis Folk aspect of the film, but still.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Biology
tropes.html:
• Mutagen or not, the three creatures couldn't simply have gotten so big unless they consumed a lot of additional mass (this is only slightly mentioned, as Ralph cannibalizes his fellow wolves and a whole squad of hunters, Lizzie attacks a few boats, and George is shown crying in hunger). Also, while their size is a little more plausible than skyscraper-high kaiju, they are still way too big to support their weight while retaining their original build (they'd have to have much thicker limbs and stockier bodies.)
  • George and Lizzie indeed do have much thicker, more pillar-like limbs to be more able to support their weight, as well as George being quadrupedal to support his weight. Ralph on the other hand, has the skinny build and agility of a normal-sized wolf, even though he is now a hundred times bigger and should display the same lumbering weight that George and Lizzie do.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Geography
tropes.html: Lizzie originated from the Everglades in Florida. Since there are no bodies of water connecting the Everglades to Chicago, Illinois and Lizzie went undetected by humans until her arrival, a fan theory arose that Lizzie burrowed underground.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Military
tropes.html: Somehow they manage to shove a MOAB into a B-2 Spirit bomber when the actual MOAB is so large it can only be dropped from a C-130 Hercules transport by shoving it out the back hatch. They also overstate it's firepower quite substantially. While the MOAB is large, it creates the equivalent of 11 tons of TNT in explosive force, that is not nearly enough to level most of the city, as described in the movie.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html: Ralph glides, despite being weighing several tons.

tropes.name: Ascended to Carnivorism
tropes.html: George, as a gorilla, was presumably herbivorous before being exposed to the mutagen. As a giant, he starts eating people, which is how he receives the antidote before the climax.

tropes.name: Ask a Stupid Question...
tropes.html: While hunting for Ralph, Burke's team encounters a bunch of fleeing deer. One mercenary asks, "What do you think scared them?" before Ralph runs up, grabs him with his jaws and slices him in half. Did he just forget immediately they were going after a giant wolf?

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html: Claire ends up becoming this, as she is swallowed whole by a pathogen-infected George... while holding the cure that restores his sanity.

tropes.name: Attack Its Weak Point
tropes.html: Lizzie's armoured hide makes her impervious to nearly anything thrown at her, however she has a distinct weakness in her gills which Okoye takes advantage of by throwing a grenade belt into one. She also has another weakness, her eyes.

tropes.name: Attack of the 50-Foot Whatever
tropes.html: Three of 'em.

tropes.name: Bad Boss
tropes.html:
Claire's Establishing Character Moment, before we even lay eyes on her, she's on the comm refusing to let the sole surviving astronaut on her company's space station (which is in the process of blowing up) evacuate unless she rescues the research material.
Claire: Let me be clear. Either you come home with my research or you don't come home at all.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch Comment
tropes.html: A variation. When Claire worriedly wonders why Kate put the antidote in the former's purse, the latter responds she's "feeding the monster to the gorilla."

tropes.name: Because You Were Nice to Me
tropes.html: Russell helps Davis and Caldwell escape the US Air Force base by giving them the keys to a Medivac chopper because Davis pulled him out of the plane saving him from an angry, rampaging George.

tropes.name: Behemoth Battle
tropes.html: Once the radio signal that brought the beasts to Chicago is shut off, Okoye convinces George to aid in the fight against the other two monsters.

tropes.name: Berserk Button
tropes.html: Due to his experience as a baby, George becomes extremely aggressive when guns are pointed his way.

tropes.name: Better with Non-Human Company
tropes.html:
Okoye is stated to like animals a lot more than people.
Okoye: Yeah, well, animals get me.

tropes.name: Beware My Stinger Tail
tropes.html: One of the mutations Lizzie receives is a spiked club on the end of her tail.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: Claire Wyden (played by Malin Åkerman) is the person behind the experiment that transforms George, Ralph, and Lizzie into monsters. After she's killed by George, Lizzie becomes the Final Boss for the climax.

tropes.name: Big Damn Heroes
tropes.html: George as he kills Lizzie by impaling her in the eye with the same rebar that she threw him into that went through his chest.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html: Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson's character, Davis Okoye, signs his name as "Rock." Also an Actor Allusion.

tropes.name: Bloodless Carnage
tropes.html: Mostly averted, though played straight when Lizzie chomps off Ralph's head and swallows it whole. There (thankfully for the shocked audience) isn't a geyser of blood spurting from Ralph's neck.

tropes.name: Canon Character All Along
tropes.html: Claire Wyden turns out to be the woman in the red dress.

tropes.name: Canon Foreigner
tropes.html: Davis Okoye and the rest of the human characters were created specifically for the film.

tropes.name: Casting Gag
tropes.html: Joe Manganiello, who has the role of Burke, the leader of the mercenaries sent to hunt Ralph (originally a werewolf-type monster in the arcade/video games), was a werewolf in the series True Blood.

tropes.name: Character Tics
tropes.html: Despite his disinterest in people or romance, Davis is very particular about unseemly behavior in front of ladies, whether they're gorillas or humans.

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html: George being albino and predominantly white gives him a similar appearance as Harry the Yeti from Rampage: Total Destruction. Similarly, Lizzie being changed to a crocodile means that her gender and name was combined with Crock, a crocodile monster from the same game.

tropes.name: Convenient Cranny
tropes.html: Lizzie spends her final moments trying to chomp down Davis, whose Grenade Launcher is out of ammunition and have fully exhausted all his weapons and can only take cover in a ledge too narrow for the monster to reach. Luckily, this is when George's Big Damn Heroes moment comes in.

tropes.name: Conveniently Empty Building
tropes.html: Downplayed; the military is only convinced that they need to evacuate Chicago once their attempt to stop George and Ralph outside town fails. Thus, while most of the buildings are empty, there are plenty of people who still need to be evacuated.

tropes.name: Corrupt Corporate Executive
tropes.html: Claire and Brett indulge in illegal genetic research, intentionally lure the giant animals to Chicago (putting countless lives in danger in the process) just for a chance to recover samples from them after the military saves them the trouble of killing the animals, set up Kate as the fall guy for their own deeds, and later take her prisoner at gunpoint (trying to kill Davis in the process) in order to ensure their research can continue.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: Brian Colin, who designed the original game, appears running from George.

tropes.name: Curb-Stomp Battle
tropes.html: Naturally any attempts by the humans to stop the monsters. Once the monsters turn on each other, Lizzie swiftly kills Ralph with little effort on her part. George fares only slightly better, considering he has to be repeatedly saved by Okoye.

tropes.name: Curse Cut Short
tropes.html: "Mess with him, mess with me, you mother*BOOM*"

tropes.name: Cut Lex Luthor a Check
tropes.html: Energyne has developed genetic editing to such a point where they can edit every single cell in a grown organism and implant them with highly complex new functions. Curing any kind of cancer, any and all chronic virus infections, any and all genetic diseases and repairing most types of organ failure would be MUCH easier with this tech than creating these kinds of composite monsters. Immortality treatments and super doping would be harder, but still easy compared to transferring complex traits between species. One really has to wonder what caused Claire and Brett to go into the monster making business, when following Kate's line of research could likely have made them the richest individuals to have ever existed. And probably immortal at that.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: The original games can best be described as campy, tongue-in-cheek parodies of kaiju movies. This film serves as a more straightforward kaiju flick that takes the idea of giant mutated animals much more seriously, although the end result is still pretty fun and goofy.

tropes.name: Dead Star Walking
tropes.html: Joe Manganiello plays a badass mercenary... who is quickly dispatched by Ralph.

tropes.name: Death by Adaptation
tropes.html: Ralph and Lizzie are both alive and well in original games, but died here.

tropes.name: Death by Looking Up
tropes.html: As George leaps at Lizzie with a rebar spear, she looks up just in time to be struck right through the eye.

tropes.name: Defiant to the End
tropes.html: The moment Burke knows he's perfectly screwed because Ralph has killed all of his men and he feels a *Drool* Hello falling on his shoulder, he tightens his grip on his assault rifle and prepares to turn around to shoot, even as he's being eaten. Ralph is much faster on the draw, or in his case bite.

tropes.name: Designated Girl Fight
tropes.html: Between Kate and Claire in the climax.

tropes.name: Destroy the Product Placement
tropes.html: George tears off a chunk of a Dave & Buster's so he can throw it at U.S. soldiers shooting at him.

tropes.name: Didn't See That Coming
tropes.html:
Throughout the majority of the movie, everyone (including the villains) thought that the only other creature affected by the pathogen alongside George was Ralph, with only the audience knowing better. As such, the appearance of Lizzie during the climax took everyone by surprise.
Okoye: Well that sucks.

tropes.name: Didn't Think This Through
tropes.html: George attempts to deliver a punch to Lizzie's face. Which is a very unwise attack move that backfires because Lizzie captures his arm with her jaws, nearly biting it off and leaving George with painful bite marks, slowing him down, allowing Lizzie to bite him on the legs as well and start flailing him around.

tropes.name: Dire Beast
tropes.html: The three monsters pretty much qualify, being bigger, nastier-looking versions of normal animals.

tropes.name: Disney Death
tropes.html: George seems to have died from his wounds after his fight with Lizzie... only to flip Davis off to show he's alive.

tropes.name: Drill Sergeant Nasty
tropes.html: Colonel Blake. He's a "shoot first, ask questions later" colonel who puts the lives of many Chicago civilians at risk by ordering firepower upon the monsters even though Chicago has not yet been evacuated, making the monsters proceed to attack and cause even more destruction.

tropes.name: Dude, Not Funny!
tropes.html: Davis takes great issue with George's twisted sense of humor, which includes pretending to be a Killer Gorilla to scare the shit out of a new employee at the Wildlife Sanctuary, repeatedly Flipping the Bird, and pretending he was killed in battle just to see Davis cry.

tropes.name: Eaten Alive
tropes.html: As expected, quite a few people are devoured by the beasts. In Claire's case, to ensure George is given the antidote that will stop his rage.

tropes.name: Escaped Animal Rampage
tropes.html: George at the zoo goes berserk due to the mutagen giving him uncontrollable rage and rapid growth, sending zoo-goers panicking and running.

tropes.name: Expy
tropes.html: Kate Caldwell could be one for Dr. Elizabeth "Betty" Veronica from the games.

tropes.name: Eye Scream
tropes.html: George stabs Lizzie in the eye.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html: Brett, whether due to cowardice or cautiousness or any other reason, absolutely refuses to let Claire “liquidate” Kate for the longest time, and only succumbed to his sister’s insistence on her plan of driving George berserk in order to crash the plane he was on (and kill Davis, Kate, and Russell in the process) when Brett became afraid that there was now a real risk of him going to jail himself.

tropes.name: Family-Unfriendly Violence
tropes.html: The film actually packs a lot of surprisingly gory moments involving humans killed by monsters, with severed body parts and even a bisected torso being shown mostly onscreen.

tropes.name: FBI Agent
tropes.html: Homeland Security Investigations, although once George goes crazy on the plane they became useless fodder unable to contain him. The actual FBI later shows up to investigate the Wydens and is led by Agent Park.

tropes.name: Final Girl
tropes.html: Subverted with the final astronaut in the Action Prologue, Dr. Kerry Adkins, who seems to be the Hero of Another Story, but it's a story that doesn't end well for her.

tropes.name: Find the Cure
tropes.html: Davis Okoye's goal is to find a cure for George's mutation, not only to end the monstrous ape's rampage but to save his friend.

tropes.name: Fire-Forged Friends
tropes.html: Davis prefers animals to people after many bad experiences with poachers. But by the end of the movie, he has begun to consider Russell and Caldwell his friends.

tropes.name: Flipping the Bird
tropes.html: George does it, and it's only his second most offensive hand gesture.

tropes.name: The Foreign Subtitle
tropes.html: In Japan it's Rampage: Kyoju Dairantou (Giant Beast Melee). It's pretty clear where they're going marketing-wise.◊ The one from Brazil, adequately, translates to Total Destruction, the last video game in the series.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html:
• We see only a glimpse of Ralph flying during Burke's hunt for him before this ability is fully revealed. At first glance, it would appear as if Ralph was simply in a weird pose as he leapt.
  • Fans of the original arcade and video game are tipped off to what will happen to Claire when she wears the red dress.

tropes.name: Fun with Acronyms
tropes.html:
• CRISPR is the gene editing tech that made Project Rampage possible. The acronym is not stated in the film.note Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
  • OGA on the other hand, as observed by Davis, stands for "Other Government Agency" as a way to avoid identifying themselves and to use and abuse their authority because no one knows to whom they answer.

tropes.name: Genre Shift
tropes.html: Though both are quite ridiculous, the film is an over the top action flick, while the games were cartoonier, with abundant slapstick and big helpings of Black Comedy.

tropes.name: Genetic Engineering Is the New Nuke
tropes.html: George, Ralph, and Lizzie are mutated into kaiju by a genetic editing mutagen created by Claire Wyden.

tropes.name: Genius Bruiser
tropes.html: Davis. He's clearly an extremely knowledgeable primatologist with a ton of practical skills

tropes.name: Gentle Gorilla
tropes.html: George prior to his mutation. He returns to this (but as a literal Gentle Giant this time) after he eats the cure to the Unstoppable Rage.

tropes.name: Giant Equals Invincible
tropes.html: Zigzagged. While the monsters do repeatedly shrug off every weapon that the humans use against them, they're not actually immune to damage from those weapons. One of the abilities they gain from the mutagen is a Healing Factor that becomes progressively stronger as they continuously grow bigger. By the time they reach kaiju size in the climax, their injuries are healing within seconds, allowing them to effectively No-Sell anything short of a MOAB (or each other).

tropes.name: Giant Flyer
tropes.html: Ralph's mutations have given him flying squirrel style skin membranes.

tropes.name: Gone Horribly Wrong
tropes.html: You know, Claire and Brett's plan to bait the monsters to the city might have worked if not for the giant croc they didn't realize was coming. The military was all prepped up to take on Ralph, and Davis is doing everything he can to help George, who's been growing at a lesser rate than Ralph, but no one is ready for Lizzie.

tropes.name: Goodness Equals Beauty
tropes.html: Not exactly beauty, but George is far less monstrous in appearance than Ralph or Lizzie. Ralph has spines and skinflap wings; Lizzie is covered in spikes and tusks and fangs; George is just bigger.

tropes.name: Green Gators
tropes.html: Lizzy, depicted as a gigantic mutated American crocodile instead of a Not Zilla, has murky green skin, as opposed to Ralph's grey fur and George's albinistic white fur and pink skin.

tropes.name: Grenade Launcher
tropes.html: Okoye takes a grenade launcher, along with a belt of grenades, from an abandoned military Humvee to use against Liz.

tropes.name: Half the Man He Used to Be
tropes.html: A mercenary on Burke's team (the first one to die) is bitten into two pieces by Ralph on-screen.

tropes.name: Harmless Villain
tropes.html: Brett Wyden is simply incompetent at anything he does, and it's pretty clear from the first scene that his sister Claire is the real brain and brawn behind all their evil schemes. He panics a lot when things don't go his way, and he doesn't have the courage to pull the trigger once he and Claire have Okoye and Kate at gunpoint, and immediately bails on his sister when the situation becomess too hot to handle. Doesn't quite save him from the Karmic Death, though.

tropes.name: Hate Sink
tropes.html: Claire Wyden can be this for being manipulative, cruel and cold-hearted. It's bad enough she sets up the monsters so the military will kill them and enable her to dissect the animals' corpses. But it's worse once you learn she fired Caldwell when the latter suspected her research to help cure her ailing brother was being exploited as a weapon.
